On the US border in Texas, Trump deportation drive galvanises midterm vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:22:54 UTC
19:22:54 KST

On the US border in Texas, Trump deportation drive galvanises midterm vote
Border issues helped propel Trump in the Rio Grande Valley in 2024; His deportation policies could bury Republicans.
Rio Grande Valley, Texas – Leaning over plates of tamales, pan dulce, and sugar skulls, community organisers and local residents in the border city of Brownsville remembered the dead.
This year’s Dia de los Muertos, or Day of the Dead, vigil honoured victims of state violence, including those killed in immigration enforcement and detention. Just days before the US midterm election on November 3, the event reverberated in a region long subject to Washington, DC’s shifting political winds.
“The atmosphere here in the Rio Grande Valley when it comes to ICE detentions and the ICE raids, there’s just the overall feeling amongst folks that there’s no real due process to this,” said Mark Anthony Vasquez, a 52-year-old community organiser.
“What is it that we can do to move together and build together to try to make it past this, and make that change that we seek?”
Down the block, at a bookstore panel on border and immigration policy, 24-year-old Juliana Garcia raised her hand to ask advice on how to find a lawyer able to navigate the aggressively shifting policies of the administration of US President Donald Trump, which has used both an increase in physical enforcement, as well as a reinterpretation of administrative policies, to fuel its mass deportation campaign.
Garcia’s aunt, a well-known member of the community in the nearby border town of Progreso, was deported just weeks ago, after being called to a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) hearing. There she learned she had missed a court date related to her immigration status.
In the stress of the moment, she signed a voluntary deportation form.
“Within 36 hours, she was deported,” Garcia told Al Jazeera, tucked between bookshelves. “People are waking up, and they’re remembering that politics, regardless of what branch you’re in, it’s going to impact you every day.”
Shifting dynamics
Views on immigration are complex in the Rio Grande Valley, a geographic and cultural region located in subtropical southeast Texas with about 1.5 million residents. That complexity has only increased in recent years as border policy and immigration enforcement have become increasingly partisan, leading, reformers say, to dramatic policy swings that prevent more sustainable solutions.
It is not difficult to find Latino – or Tejano, the local term for Texans of Latino descent – residents wary of the years preceding Trump’s return to office. After the restrictive policies of Trump’s first term, border crossings increased dramatically under US President Joe Biden, fuelled in part by the end of a COVID-era policy that made asylum seekers wait for their cases to be processed in Mexico.
Some felt the border region was left to deal with the fallout from the influx. That discontent has been credited, in part, with Trump’s success in the once-reliably Democratic region in the 2024 presidential election.
In Hidalgo County, home to the city of McAllen, Trump won 51 percent of the vote in 2024, a three-point margin over Kamala Harris. In 2020, Biden beat Trump in the county by 17 percentage points.
In neighbouring Cameron County, Trump won by about five percentage points in 2024, despite a 13-point loss in 2020.
Voter Jose Arizpe, a 40-year-old resident of Brownsville, assessed the two years since Trump took office as a “positive change”, with fewer asylum seekers waiting in the US for their cases to be processed.
Upon taking office, Trump declared a state of emergency at the border, staunching asylum claims in what rights groups say runs counter to US law. The US Supreme Court has since ruled that US border agents can physically block asylum seekers from reaching US soil to claim asylum.
“A lot of people claim that they support illegals and want to let them in,” said Arizpe, a regular Republican voter, “but then, I say ‘well let them in your house’. And they don’t want to do it, right?”
On border policy, “at first, I supported Trump,” said Martin Torres, a 55-year-old who cast his ballot for Democrats at a public library in Brownsville as part of the state’s early voting.
But domestic enforcement, and its impact on the local workforce, soured his views.
“Now he changes everything,” he said.
A report from the Caminos Institute has estimated the region has lost $180.6m in economic activity due to the Trump administration’s immigration policies, including in construction and restaurants.
Other voters saw Trump’s approach as fuelling bigotry. Last year, the US Supreme Court lifted a lower-court order barring immigration officials from considering “apparent race or ethnicity”, as well as language spoken, when on patrol. Rights groups say the decision effectively allows racial profiling.
In Texas, a state law also lets local officials stop individuals they suspect entered the country illegally.
“I just see a lot of discrimination going on,” said George Castorena, a 46-year-old department of education worker, who said he was voting for change.
To be sure, midterm elections can only offer incremental change on an issue as entrenched as immigration enforcement and border policy.
Democratic control of the House of Representatives would at best serve as a bulwark against the Trump administration legislating more immigration enforcement funding and policy, while opening the door to investigations into the administration’s approach.
Control of the Senate, which could be determined by the contest between Texas Republican Ken Paxton and Democratic challenger James Talarico, could further increase the party’s leverage.
A change in the governor’s office, meanwhile, could end Texas Governor Greg Abbott’s myriad uses of state agencies to support federal immigration enforcement. But Democrat Gina Hinojosa, if she were to pull off an upset, would be largely constrained by a likely Republican-dominated state legislature and a mountain of pre-existing law.
A galvanising moment?
Although a more lasting transformation remains far off, evidence suggests the local dismay runs deep.
A poll conducted by the American Civil Liberties Union of Texas found that only 34 percent of respondents from the area felt that immigration enforcement by both local and state officials had made their communities safer. Fifty-three percent said it made their lives harder without improving safety.
Meanwhile, 64 percent felt ICE tactics have gone too far. The numbers broadly align with polls showing Democratic challenger Bobby Pulido leading Republican incumbent Monica De La Cruz and Democratic incumbent Vicente Gonzalez leading Republican challenger Eric Flores in two Rio Grande Valley congressional districts.
Republicans, eyeing Trump’s success in 2024, viewed the races as strong prospects early in the election season.
“What this survey conveys is: people along the border in the Rio Grande Valley are not in alignment with what they probably voted for back in 2024,” Osvaldo Grimaldo, a policy strategist at ACLU of Texas, told Al Jazeera.
Even prominent community figures who support Trump’s policies acknowledge a broader change in sentiment.
Eli Lara, the lead pastor at the non-denominational New Life Family Church in McAllen, Texas, said locals have been dismayed by the wide scope with which the administration has targeted undocumented individuals.
“The immigration issue is bigger because [the community] is seeing people being taken,” he told Al Jazeera. “I don’t like the separation of families, but here’s the thing: there are consequences for choices.”
That view held even for a congregant who had recently been deported in connection with a past drug possession conviction.
“He’s been faithful [to the church] for two, three years, but they picked him up,” Lara said. “Why? Because he had a bad criminal record in the past. God forgives, but the government doesn’t.”
Voter Garcia, who volunteers with the Hidalgo County Young Democrats, was among those who believed the current situation could galvanise the Rio Grande Valley.
She pointed to several instances that have recently shaken the region, including the assault of a 17-year-old by immigration agents in the town of Alamo in the Rio Grande Valley, and the fatal ICE shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in July 2026 in the Texas city of Houston.
“I’ve had a lot of people tell me, ‘Why do I care about politics? Politics doesn’t affect me,'” she said. “And with all of these ICE raids, they realise politics does affect them, and it sucks that it took a lot of trauma to really bring that to people.”

North Korea’s Reaper copy Saetbyol-9 fires a new cruise missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:21:37 UTC
19:21:37 KST

- North Korea released the first images of its Reaper-like Saetbyol-9 drone firing an air-launched tactical cruise missile during an Oct. 29 demonstration.
- The drone carried Korean People’s Army Ground Force markings, and KCNA claimed drone-fired missiles hit an island target with 100% accuracy.
North Korea has released new images of its Saetbyol-9 attack drone, a near copy of the U.S. MQ-9 Reaper, firing an air-launched tactical cruise missile during a live-fire demonstration Kim Jong Un watched, state news agency KCNA showed on Oct. 30.
A KCNA photo taken from the drone’s own wing shows a black cruise missile with a pointed nose and a yellow band mounted under the wing, while a second cruise missile streaks away below the clouds after launch. The drone carries the markings of the Korean People’s Army Ground Force, the North’s army, and the serial number 2101003 on its nose, which suggests the aircraft is assigned to ground units for reconnaissance and strike missions rather than only to the air force. KCNA said missiles fired from drones and ground-launched cruise missiles hit an island target with 100% accuracy, a claim that cannot be independently checked.
South Korean analysts at the Korea Defense and Security Forum said the weapon is a tactical air-to-ground cruise missile with a seeker in the nose to guide it onto its target, Financial News reported, and called it the first time North Korea has shown a Saetbyol-9 launching such a missile. North Korea has not given the missile a name or released its range, warhead size or guidance method.
The launch was part of a firepower demonstration that followed North Korea’s “Unmanned Aeronautical Technology Development-2026” exhibition, where Kim called for the country to seize “absolute superiority” in drone technology. The drill also involved tactical suicide drones, ground-launched cruise missiles and a battalion of 600 mm multiple rocket launchers, and South Korea’s military detected around 10 short-range ballistic missiles fired from the Wonsan area the same day.
The Saetbyol-9, or “Morning Star-9,” is propeller-driven and closely mirrors the shape of the MQ-9 Reaper, with a wingspan of roughly 20 m (66 feet), the same as the American drone. It first appeared in July 2023 alongside the larger Saetbyol-4, a long-range reconnaissance drone modeled on the U.S. RQ-4 Global Hawk, which North Korea also put on display at this week’s exhibition. A brief North Korean video from 2023 appeared to show the Saetbyol-9 firing a pair of missiles that resembled the U.S. Hellfire, and a U.S. Army general said in 2024 that North Korea was arming its drones with reverse-engineered copies of the Hellfire.
The new photos show a different, larger-looking store under the wing. A cruise missile flies on wings and an engine for most of its flight, which typically gives it longer range than a rocket-powered missile like the Hellfire and lets a drone fire from farther away from enemy air defenses. Without official data, it is not possible to say how far the North Korean missile can fly.
South Korean officials have questioned how much combat value the Saetbyol-9 adds. In March, the South Korean military said the drone barely imitates the Reaper’s appearance without matching its capabilities, while noting it had spotted new aircraft in the same category with a modified shape and paint scheme. In September, state media showed Kim touring production lines with airframes matching the Saetbyol-4 and Saetbyol-9, the clearest sign yet that North Korea intends to build both in numbers.

Economy minister warns France could ‘hit the wall’ as new figures show GDP contraction
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:19:54 UTC
19:19:54 KST

France's Economy, Finances and Industry Minister Roland Lescure leaves after attending the weekly cabinet meeting in Paris on Oct. 28, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — France’s economy shrunk by 0.1% in the third quarter of 2026, according to fresh estimates from national statistics agency Insee, pushing the country closer to recession and further complicating the government’s efforts to stave off a debt-driven financial crisis.
Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure said Friday that this summer’s extreme heat and spiking energy prices were responsible for the negative growth.
In an interview with Franceinfo, he said the new figures give added urgency for lawmakers to pass the 2027 budget proposed by the government, which aims to bring the deficit down to 5% of gross domestic product next year with €43 billion in savings.
Advertisement
“If we don’t have the budget adjustment we put in the budget, we will hit the wall,” Lescure said.
But France’s fragmented parliament failed to pass budgets before the new year in both 2024 and 2025, and the spring 2027 presidential election may further complicate efforts to seek compromise this time around. That could force Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu to push through the budget using a constitutional backdoor that bypasses a parliamentary vote, but it would expose the minority government to potential motions of no confidence.
Lescure insisted that adopting a budget for next year was key to “reassure markets” and relaunch growth in the last quarter of the year. The French economy contracted by 0.1% in the first quarter of 2026 and recorded no growth in the three months that followed.
That anemic growth will likely complicate the government’s pledge to bring the deficit down to 5.4% of GDP this year, as the target was based on the assumption the economy would grow by 0.5% in 2026.
“The French economy is at a standstill,” Lescure said. “It has to restart.”

Russia’s flagship independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta announced Friday it was closing, saying it had been “killed” by state pressure after years of repression targeting its journalists whose reporting was critical of the Kremlin and its Ukraine war.
The closure of Novaya Gazeta – one of the last outlets to openly criticise Russia’s offensive – marks a new low in Moscow’s campaign against dissenting voices that gained speed after the Kremlin sent troops into its neighbour in 2022.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Since then, the newspaper, long considered a bastion of independent journalism, has seen its media license revoked, journalists and editors questioned, detained, and their homes searched.
It was also branded a “foreign agent” -- a label reminiscent of Soviet-era repression used to stifle dissent.
“Novaya Gazeta has been killed. Novaya Gazeta is ending its existence,” editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov said in a statement published on YouTube on Friday morning.
In the emotional video, Sokolov said that “the Russian authorities -- the Russian special services -- have forced the editorial team to end its work.”
Founded in 1993 after the collapse of the Soviet Union, Novaya Gazeta was one of Russia’s most reputable and renowned organisations reporting and documenting human rights abuses.
Mikhail Gorbachev, the last leader of the Soviet Union, donated some of his Nobel Peace Prize money to help set up the paper.

-‘Finished off’ -
Several of its reporters have been murdered in killings widely seen as retribution for their work.
They include Anna Politkovskaya, who spent years investigating allegations of abuses by Russia’s military during its campaigns in Chechnya.
She was found dead in her apartment block on President Vladimir Putin’s birthday in October 2006.
Founder and former editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov, jointly won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021 for his efforts to safeguard freedom of expression at the helm of the paper.
He had to formally step down from the post two years later after being declared a “foreign agent”.
“For nearly five years of war, we managed to operate while completely surrounded by intelligence services. But now, that’s it. We’ve ended up in a kill zone,” Sokolov said on Friday.
“This isn’t just our own private story -- it’s the story of a country and a society that are being finished off in exactly the same way.”
The paper, which used to be published several times a week, cut down production inside the country after the war began, but its online version was still available despite court orders.
In recent months, the Russian authorities searched the home of Sokolov and earlier this year arrested one of its journalists, Oleg Roldugin.
Charged with “unlawful access to computerised information”, he pleaded not guilty, according to state media, and is under house arrest pending trial.
International media rights groups have slammed Russia’s years of targeting Novaya Gazeta, with Reporters Without Borders calling on Moscow to “put an end to the judicial harassment” of its journalists.
“Human rights and freedoms have been abolished, and their defence has been equated with a crime,” Sokolov said in the video statement, adding: “Beliefs have become state treason.”
“The murder of Novaya Gazeta is yet another piece of evidence. All these years we wrote precisely about this, for as long as we could. Thank you to everyone who listened to us. And the final issue will come out.”

Trump not planning to back Bolsonaro's claim to be Brazil's leader, sources say

Trump not planning to back Bolsonaro's claim to be Brazil's leader, sources say
WASHINGTON, Oct 30 - The Trump administration does not plan to back Flavio Bolsonaro's claim to be Brazil's rightful leader, despite helping the defeated candidate reach the US after years of supporting him and his father, a US official and another person familiar with the matter said on Thursday.
President Donald Trump has said Brazil's election on Sunday looked "rigged" but has pointed out that he offered no endorsement in the hotly contested race. Trump has also said he gets along well with incumbent leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the 81-year-old former union leader who beat the odds to clinch reelection by 3.5 percentage points.
The US official and the person familiar with the matter, who both spoke on the condition of anonymity, said Trump has no current plans to support Bolsonaro's political ambitions even as the administration allowed him into the country, though they said the president could change his mind.
The Trump administration's posture suggests the president may be reluctant to cause a fresh crisis in relations with Brazil, which have gone through ups and downs in recent months.
LAST-SECOND DEPARTURE AFTER COURT RULING ON PASSPORT
A third US official, also speaking on the condition of anonymity, said Bolsonaro's political capital had fallen now that he is in self-exile. Many conservatives in Brazil who had expected him to lead the opposition in the coming years have criticized his flight.
The White House referred a request for comment to the State Department, which did not reply. The Brazilian government and a representative for Bolsonaro did not respond to requests for comment.
Flavio's father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is imprisoned in Brazil for attempting a self-coup to stay in power after losing his reelection bid in 2022.
Some Brazilian officials, also speaking on the condition of anonymity, told Reuters that Bolsonaro's departure helps Lula by weakening the conservative opposition in Brazil's Congress.
Bolsonaro's flight was a last-second decision that came after a Brazilian Supreme Court justice ordered him to turn in his passport, granting a request by federal police who are investigating him over two alleged money-laundering schemes, US officials and others familiar with the matter said.
The police request came in just minutes after the election was called for Lula, according to Brazilian media reports, a timeline that some conservatives have pointed to as evidence of political motivation.
Supporters of Lula's government point out that, days before the election, Flavio's brother, Eduardo, suggested publicly that Flavio should leave Brazil if he lost. Eduardo, a former congressman who himself lives in the US, was convicted in Brazil in June of courting interference from the Trump administration in his father's trial.
Argentine authorities said that Flavio Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters crossed a bridge into northern Argentina at 10:50 p.m. on Tuesday before boarding a chartered aircraft at 11:30 p.m. Bolsonaro and his family then flew to Miami via Ecuador.
It is unclear how Bolsonaro traveled from his home in Brasilia to the bridge crossing 750 miles (1,300 km) away or exited Brazil without the knowledge of Brazilian customs officials. But during that journey, Bolsonaro contacted multiple US officials regarding his departure, according to one of the US officials.
Jason Miller, a Trump adviser who is close to the Bolsonaro family, helped arrange the flight from Argentina, the person familiar with the matter said. During Bolsonaro's journey, Secretary of State Marco Rubio recommended to Trump that Bolsonaro be admitted, a recommendation the president signed off on, according to the US official.
During Bolsonaro's two-leg flight, State Department officials scrambled to determine the best legal route for admitting him and his family, discussing the matter with Department of Homeland Security personnel, the official said. Ultimately, US authorities granted them humanitarian parole at the border, a temporary status given to individuals when urgent humanitarian concerns or a significant public interest are at play, the official added.
In an open letter posted on X on Wednesday, Bolsonaro declared himself "the elected president." He then deleted that version and updated it with another letter in which he said he was Brazil's rightful "leader."
BRAZILIAN POLITICS WORTHY OF A TELENOVELA
The Bolsonaro departure was the latest chapter in a tumultuous period in Brazilian politics and in US-Brazil relations.
Bolsonaro's father was president from 2019 to 2023, then lost reelection to Lula and was jailed last year for his self-coup attempt. Lula himself spent 17 months in jail in 2018 and 2019 on corruption charges that were later annulled.
The US last year slapped sanctions on the judge overseeing the trial of the elder Bolsonaro and other Brazilian officials. Washington lifted the sanctions after Trump and Lula had a notably cordial interaction at the UN General Assembly.
During the campaign, Brazil objected to what it called attempts by some US officials to boost the Bolsonaro campaign, and the government has refused to seat the incoming US ambassador to Brazil, a close Rubio ally, in part due to those objections.
Reuters reported last week that two conservative State Department officials successfully pushed for the Brazil sanctions as well as terrorist designations of two Brazilian organized crime groups, measures aimed at tilting the election in Bolsonaro's favor.
Still, even as Trump has attacked the way Brazil conducted the election, he has refrained from criticizing Lula.
"I like Lula, I get along with him very well," Trump told reporters on Monday. "I just think it had a very bad look, the election." REUTERS

The family thought he was a priest. Mexico’s Catholic Church says he was an impostor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:16:49 UTC
19:16:49 KST

The family thought he was a priest. Mexico’s Catholic Church says he was an impostor
MEXICO CITY, Oct 30 -
• For the photo essay click here:
When Rev. Jesús Romero arrived at the funeral of Dahina Loaiza in Mexico City in December 2024, her sister Roberta Loaiza sensed something was off.
Wearing a cardinal’s cap and Ferragamo shoes, Romero skipped over the Catholic liturgy and granted general absolution to dozens of mourners, a rite the Church reserves for exceptional circumstances such as imminent danger of death.
“He said he held a really high-ranking position as a priest and had the power to absolve everyone,” Loaiza told Reuters.
Elena D'Acosta, a devout Catholic and family friend who had assisted Romero during the ceremony, was so alarmed that she contacted the Archdiocese of Mexico City.
Three months later, Bishop Salvador González issued a press release warning that Romero was impersonating a priest and that no diocese in Mexico had any record of him.
The discovery was painful for the Loaizas, who had paid Gayosso, one of Mexico’s biggest funeral providers, for Romero to conduct the service.
“They took advantage of us when we were in an incredibly vulnerable moment,” Loaiza said.
Romero could not be reached for comment.
Gustavo Torres, the commercial manager for Gayosso, said the company has no formal system for verifying clergy and was unaware of the allegations until approached by Reuters. The company apologized, and Torres said it would investigate.
WHY IMPOSTORS ARE THRIVING
Mexico is grappling with a growing number of unauthorized clergy, offering funeral Masses, baptisms, First Communions, weddings and patron-saint celebrations, according to Reuters interviews with officials in nine of the country’s archdioceses.
The damage goes beyond money: the Catholic Church does not recognize sacraments by what it calls “fake priests,” so families may have to repeat them.
With more than 120 million Catholics, according to Vatican data, Mexico has the world’s second-largest Catholic population after Brazil. Faith permeates daily life and national identity.
Dioceses elsewhere in Latin America are also warning about impostors performing religious services or soliciting donations, ahead of Pope Leo's visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru next month.
Church authorities say there have long been isolated cases of people posing as priests. But seven Mexican dioceses said the frauds have spread since the COVID-19 pandemic as families scrambled to find priests to pray for sick relatives and conduct funeral rites.
“A lot of impostors started to appear,” said María Magdalena de Ibarrola, the chancellor, or record-keeper, of the Archdiocese of Mexico, the country’s largest. She estimates hundreds of fake priests are operating in Mexico.
Researchers and church officials blame a shortage of priests and a widening gap between cultural Catholicism and the institutional church.
Mexico has 17,331 priests, according to Vatican data, or one for nearly 7,000 Catholics. That’s more than three times as many Catholics per priest as in Europe, which has one for every 1,882.
“Celibacy and related commitments simply no longer carry the prestige they once did,” said Elio Masferrer, a religion expert at Mexico’s National School of Anthropology and History.
Many younger Catholics treat weddings and baptisms mainly as family traditions.
“They want a Catholic ceremony if possible, but they’re often disconnected from what that actually entails, including the requirement that a liturgical act should be officiated by an ordained minister,” said Rev. Guillermo Gutiérrez, director of the Center for Family, Bioethics and Society Studies at the Pontifical University of Mexico.
Social media has moved into that gap. Facebook Marketplace is full of ads for "express religious services" that rarely mention the Church does not recognize the providers. Religious certificates sell for $30 to $100.
Reuters contacted five sellers on Facebook Marketplace in Mexico. All offered “original” certificates for baptisms, First Communions and Confirmations that they said came from parishes.
Three of the parishes said they don’t provide documents through Facebook Marketplace. A fourth parish doesn’t exist. The fifth seller claimed to be linked to a parish but wouldn’t identify it.
When contacted by Reuters, Meta said the listings violated its policies, which prohibit the buying, selling or trading of real or fake documents. The company said it had removed the five listings and disabled the Facebook group identified by Reuters for breaching its rules.
Meta did not respond to questions about whether it was taking any broader measures.
‘I'M A REBEL PRIEST’
De Ibarrola, the chancellor, said fake priests tend to fall into three buckets: suspended or excommunicated clergy; seminary dropouts or others familiar with Catholic rituals; and those with little or no religious training who simply claim to be priests.
For parishioners, the line between the Catholic Church, impostor riests and breakaway churches can be hard to see.
José Tomás Sierra, known as Father Chema, said he started his studies at the Catholic seminary in Toluca at 14, left due to personal reasons, and then returned years later. The seminary said its records show Sierra attended for one year and did not return.
Calling the seminary a "bad experience," Sierra said he pursued the priesthood on his own, building a church, the Parish of Mercy, on Toluca’s outskirts in 2009 and growing a congregation.
Jonás Jaime Pedraza, chancellor of the Archdiocese of Toluca, said church records show Sierra sought to join the Order of Mercy in 2010. A year later, Pedraza said, the archdiocese began receiving reports about a priest celebrating Mass in the town of San Buenaventura and alerted local parishioners that Sierra was not affiliated with the Catholic Church.
In 2019, Sierra said he became a priest in the Brazilian Catholic Apostolic Church, which does not recognize the pope’s authority and allows clergy to marry.
With a neatly trimmed beard, tattooed eyebrows and a penchant for profanity, Sierra cuts an unconventional figure for a priest.
“I’m a rebel priest, I’m very rebellious. I like breaking rules,” he said.
Sierra’s church in Toluca is where Paloma Peña’s daughter received her First Communion in August 2025.
Peña, a mother of two, had heard from a neighbor about a religious instructor, Gabriela Carrasco, who could prepare children for communion in six months.
The Archdiocese of Toluca typically requires three years.
Carrasco told families to pay $200 for the course and for a priest to administer the sacraments.
She did not answer questions about the ceremony.
When the day for the First Communion arrived, the priest introduced himself as a monsignor and gave sacraments to around 40 children, Peña said.
The certificate had the wrong date. But Peña said she did not learn of the extent of the fraud until May when a priest from Mexico City, Rev. Manuel Sánchez Padilla, said his parish had been listed on the document without his knowledge. The certificate also bore the signature of a priest who had died in 2020, according to documents reviewed by Reuters.
Sierra acknowledged the deception but denied involvement. He said he had lent his church to a colleague from the Brazilian Apostolic Church and blamed the religious instructor.
For Sánchez, the case was part of a wider pattern. Since he took over his parish in 2025, he said he has uncovered a string of fake certificates issued in the name of priests who previously served there.
His parish now uses embossed seals and has digitized records back to the 1980s.
Even so, in July he received a forged marriage certificate with a signature from a priest whose name closely resembled his own — Father Manuel Sánchez Tapia — and from his own parish.
For Sánchez, the deceptions arise from treating faith as a formality. "It’s really about seeking to live out one’s faith," he said. "Which is quite a challenge, isn't it?" REUTERS

G20 Diplomats Meet In Atlanta Amid Divisions Over Russia, Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:16:00 UTC
19:16:00 KST

ATLANTA, Georgia -- Foreign ministers from the Group of 20 leading economies are gathering in Atlanta on October 30-31 for talks expected to highlight continuing divisions among Western governments over Russia's war in Ukraine, as the United States seeks to steer the forum toward economic growth, energy security, and trade.
The Atlanta meeting, chaired by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, comes ahead of a G20 leaders' summit scheduled for December in Miami, which US President Donald Trump will host. Russian President Vladimir Putin has been invited, although it remains unclear whether he will attend.
The presence of Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov in Atlanta has revived a debate among Western governments over whether engaging with Russian officials at international gatherings risks signaling a return to business as usual while Moscow's war on Ukraine continues.
RFE/RL has learned that there will be no traditional family photograph ahead of the summit this year. While the reason for the change remains unclear, some Western diplomats are said to have been unwilling to appear alongside Lavrov in an official group photograph.
Western diplomats told reporters that organizers were considering holding two group photographs, one including Lavrov and another without him.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said he would not avoid a group photograph with all participants, as dialogue was part of his job. But he stressed that there could be “no normalcy” with Moscow as long as the war continues.
“For the first several years after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the United States and its European allies were united in refusing to return to ‘business as usual’ with Moscow, including by avoiding legitimizing it through normal diplomatic engagement,” Nicholas Lokker, an adjunct fellow with the Transatlantic Security Program at the Washington, D.C.-based Center for a New American Security, told RFE/RL.
“That consensus has since broken down,” he added.
Tensions over engagement with Russia have surfaced at previous G20 summits.
At an August finance meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, European delegates made their displeasure known after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent held a bilateral meeting with Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov.
European representatives insisted that Siluanov be excluded from the meeting's “family photo,” Lokker said.
Ukraine's absence from the Atlanta gathering adds another point of friction. Washington limited invitations to formal G20 members, leaving Ukraine and South Africa off the guest list.
Moscow, for its part, has complained about the arrangements. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said visas for the delegation had been resolved only at the last minute, suggesting that “not everyone in Washington is happy” about Lavrov's participation.
Lavrov has said he intends to use the meeting to advocate reform of global economic institutions and a more multipolar world order.
Washington's 'Back To Basics' Agenda
The State Department says the United States wants to bring the G20 “back to basics,” with an agenda focused on economic growth, deregulation, innovation, energy, and trade.
Other priorities include strengthening supply chains, protecting freedom of navigation, and improving access to critical minerals, food, and fertilizer. Washington is also supporting Poland's bid to become a full member of the G20.
The agenda reflects the Trump administration's emphasis on economic competitiveness and energy security, and its desire to make the forum a venue for practical cooperation on issues affecting global markets.
James Lamond, a senior fellow with the Democratic Resilience Program at the Washington, D.C.-based Center for European Policy Analysis, said the focus on innovation, energy security, supply chains, and critical minerals was welcome.
But he told RFE/RL that discussions would likely be dominated by the wars in Ukraine and Iran, making it difficult for ministers to concentrate on the G20's economic priorities.
Lamond said Lavrov's presence would make a substantive discussion of Ukraine difficult, particularly because Kyiv is not represented at the meeting.
“Anything of substance cannot be negotiated without Ukraine being represented,” he said.
He also pointed to growing European concerns about Russian hybrid warfare, citing an armed drone incident at Leipzig airport, sabotage at factories, damage to undersea cables, increased cyber intrusions, and false-flag hate crimes. Russia has denied involvement in such activities.
Those concerns, he said, underscore the need for governments to address security threats that extend beyond conventional military conflict, such as cybersecurity.
Energy security, another major US priority, will be difficult to address without considering the conflict involving Iran and the wider Middle East, he said.
US officials have told several countries in the region and other allies to prepare for the possibility of renewed US military strikes against Iran following the November 3 midterm elections, as well as potential Iranian retaliation.
The prospect of further escalation adds uncertainty to discussions about energy supplies and the security of key shipping routes, even if the conflict is not formally at the center of the Atlanta agenda.

It Sure Looks Like the Department of Education Is Promoting a Right-Wing ‘Harry Potter’ Meme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

At first glance, the Department of Education’s October 27 X post seems like generic Harry Potter-esque slop.
It shows a trio of students walking toward a sprawling Hogwarts-like castle while a young girl with long, flowing white-blonde hair watches them from the foreground, accompanied with the text “There’s Magic in Learning!” and “Make Education Great Again.”
But for a hyper-online, highly radicalized subset of the internet, the state was not just communicating a vague policy stance—it appeared to be adopting the deeply-coded visual language of the “Malfoid.”
The reaction online was immediate. On X, Bulwark reporter Will Sommer quickly diagnosed the situation, posting that the Department of Education was “embracing the ‘malfoid’ meme, a right-wing fan fiction idea about a female Draco Malfoy who Harry Potter could fall in love with.” Others responded with Malfoid art and AI-generated clips, including some featuring President Donald Trump.
The Malfoid concept did not come from conservative think tanks but began in creatively chaotic fan fiction websites like Archive of Our Own (AO3). Gender-bending characters—taking a canonically male character and rewriting them as female or vice versa—is a time-honored tradition in fandoms. However, in these specific stories, the gender-flipped female Malfoy character is not just a narrative experiment for someone’s crackship. She is a potent avatar for toxic elitism, with a ruthless obsession with “blood purity.”
The term Malfoid is a portmanteau combining “Malfoy”—the last name of Harry Potter’s school nemesis Draco—with “foid,” which is short for “femoid” or “female humanoid”—a highly offensive incel term used to describe women.
In the original books, Malfoy is prejudiced against wizards whose heritage is mixed with muggles (non-wizards), but it’s framed as a moral failing to be overcome or punished. In Malfoid fan fiction, however, the character's bigotry is romanticized, transforming her into a right-wing aesthetic vehicle actively propagated by far-right meme channels and Telegram groups. Potter is no longer a traditional hero, but a stand-in for disaffected young men who fantasize about a relationship with a beautiful, cruel silvery-blonde girl.
A quick search of platforms like Reddit and Tumblr for the term brings up a wide range of art, AI-generated and drawn in heavily stylized anime aesthetics, featuring a busty wide-eyed blonde demeaning a blushing and devoted Potter.
The character is also depicted as explicitly anti-queer and anti-trans, as the word “foid” becomes a way for the far right to claim that this gender swapping is correcting an error.
For young, radicalized internet users, the Malfoid provides a ready-made, pop-culture-literate mascot for ethno-nationalism. She is the ultimate “guy’s girl” updated for the digital age, injected with a dark, pop culture edge that makes her more appealing to a terminally online demographic than traditional political propaganda. It’s an effective way to package white supremacy and conservative purity ideals into a highly shareable, visually appealing internet aesthetic.
Prominent right-wingers using fantasy and fiction to promote their ideals is not a new phenomenon. For years, J.R.R. Tolkien’s The Lord of the Rings has been relentlessly co-opted by several prominent figures on the political right, including Peter Thiel and Elon Musk. Similarly, the Trump administration has normalized communicating to the public via memes. Trump’s own feed on Truth Social is a constant stream of AI-generated meme imagery, and various government departments, such as DHS, have previously utilized memes and Tolkien's work to make light of deeply serious issues like ICE raids. Since dropping the Malfoid meme, the Department of Education has continued its “There is Magic in Learning” X posts with images referencing The Lord of the Rings and Avatar: The Last Airbender.
Leslie Hahner, a communications professor at Baylor University, says the “collapse of boundaries between internet subcultures and mainstream institutions” is a defining feature of modern politics. “Symbols that once circulated in niche online communities now regularly appear in political campaigns, government communications, and major media coverage,” she says, noting that while memes might have a bigger reach, this strategy becomes dangerous when adopting toxic internet culture.
She says the use of “incel imagery” raises uncomfortable questions. “Is the agency unaware of the symbol’s cultural baggage, or does it believe these associations are useful for attracting engagement from relevant audiences? Either possibility is significant,” Hahner tells WIRED. “If officials are unaware of the connotation, it suggests a lack of cultural literacy or an inability to safeguard learners from toxic symbols. If they are aware, it raises questions about why a federal institution would choose to amplify imagery tied to dehumanizing online discourse.”
In response to WIRED’s request for comment, the Department of Education quoted Albus Dumbledore in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: “Of course it’s happening inside your head, Harry. Why should that mean it’s not real?”
By utilizing the visual markers of the Malfoid, the institution signals continuing cultural alignment to a radicalized, terminally online base without ever triggering the alarm bells of traditional media oversight. It is an algorithmic wink, assuring the most extreme corners of their constituency that the institution shares their foundational worldview.
We are witnessing the end of traditional political persuasion. Policy papers, detailed legislative agendas, and traditional campaign speeches simply do not enthuse the youth anymore; aesthetic identity does. Modern political operatives understand that young voters have been trained on platforms like TikTok and Wattpad to consume information through hyper-specific tropes rather than cohesive, logical ideologies.
The internet is no longer a reflection of our political reality. Our political reality is simply executing the tropes of the internet, and the state is perfectly happy to play along.

One-in-ten respondents meanwhile said they somewhat disagreed with the decision, while just four percent fully disagreed.
A total of 1,000 people took part in the survey, which was carried out by Taloustutkimus. The margin of error is three percentage points in either direction.

WASHINGTON, Oct 30 - Donald Trump's administration is intensifying legal action against US states with just days to go until a midterm election that will decide the balance of power in Washington during his final two years in office.
In Alaska, the Justice Department filed an amended lawsuit on Thursday seeking to block the certification of results in the event of a narrow Republican loss in a hugely consequential Senate race, citing a New York Times report that Democratic operatives recruited a spoiler candidate to siphon votes from the Republican incumbent.
In California, meanwhile, the DOJ is escalating its pressure campaign against state election officials, issuing subpoenas as part of a criminal probe into alleged voting by non-citizens, according to copies of documents seen by Reuters.
The moves, taken together, represent an extraordinary federal intervention in state elections, which are administered locally under the US constitution. As November 3 nears, election officials around the country have told Reuters they are bracing for further legal challenges from Washington.
The dispute in Alaska, home to one of about 10 highly competitive Senate races, could leave control of the chamber unclear for weeks. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win back the majority from Republicans.
If Democrats take one or both chambers of Congress, they could launch probes into Trump's administration and increase pressure on the president to end the war in Iran.
TRUMP SCALES BACK TRAVEL
On Friday, Trump will campaign in Florida, hoping to galvanize his supporters in a state he won handily in 2024 but where early voting has tilted toward Democrats.
It will be his latest stop in a state Republicans usually expect to win, following campaign events earlier this week in Mississippi and South Carolina.
The president canceled planned weekend rallies in Kansas and Iowa and will instead participate in some 20 virtual campaign appearances before Tuesday, according to the Republican National Committee.
Former Vice President Kamala Harris, who Trump defeated in the 2024 election, will rally for Democrats in Atlanta on Friday.
"The last year and a half, it's been difficult," she told the crowd on Thursday at an event in Macon, Georgia. "Now we're in the phase where we can do a whole lot."
More than 44 million Americans had already voted as of Thursday evening, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, less that two million shy of the total from the 2022 midterms.
At a polling center on Thursday in Columbus, Ohio, home to highly competitive Senate and governor's races, election official Antone White said turnout was about twice as high as 2022.
Among those waiting to cast their ballot was Sadirah Simmons, a senior citizen living on a fixed income. "The economy is not getting any better," she said. "You have to go out and vote if you want change."
ALASKA SENATE DISPUTE
In its revised lawsuit in Alaska on Thursday, the Justice Department wrote that operatives for Democratic candidate Mary Peltola orchestrated a "sham campaign for the purpose of misleading Alaskan voters."
The New York Times reported Wednesday that the operatives recruited a candidate with the same name as incumbent Dan Sullivan.
Republican Governor Mike Dunleavy called for a state investigation and said in an interview with News Nation that any finding of illegality "may in fact impact whether someone is seated in the US Senate."
Alaska election officials called the amended lawsuit "meritless" in a court filing on Thursday night, saying it has "cast a cloud over Alaska’s election that is contrary to the public interest."
Peltola's campaign did not immediately respond to the amended complaint but has previously said it had "no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.”
The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has denied involvement and accused Republicans of propping up candidates of their own in other races.
Daniel J. Sullivan has previously denied that his aim was to cause confusion or divert votes from Dan S. Sullivan.
“This guy's existence is gonna hurt Mary Peltola so much more than it helps her," said Alaska-based elections and campaign attorney Scott Kendall. But with so few undecided voters left, he added, the revelations were unlikely to impact the outcome of the race.
Julie Wyatt, a 62-year-old logistics manager who lives in the capital of Juneau, said such trickery was nothing new in Alaskan politics, and she still planned to vote for Peltola.
"If the Republicans are this desperate, Mary has them on the ropes,” she wrote in an email.
CALIFORNIA SUBPOENAS
In California, meanwhile, the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder's office received grand jury subpoenas last week as part of a DOJ probe into alleged non-citizen voting, according to copies of the documents seen by Reuters on Thursday.
"At every step, the US Department of Justice has taken a confrontational, adversarial approach," Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan said in a statement on Thursday. "Election officials are acting in accordance with state and federal law."
A Justice Department spokesperson declined to comment on the subpoenas but said that California and the federal government "agree that non-citizen voting is properly addressed through criminal law." REUTERS

North Korea shows kamikaze drone blowing up a mock U.S. Abrams tank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:11:15 UTC
19:11:15 KST

- North Korean photos show a loitering munition destroying a mock U.S. Army M1 Abrams tank during an Oct. 29 demonstration watched by Kim Jong Un.
- The drone’s tandem cross-shaped wings and rear propeller closely resemble the Hero-400 made by Israel’s UVision.
North Korea has released images of a loitering munition diving onto and destroying a mock-up of a U.S. Army M1 Abrams tank, part of a firepower demonstration Kim Jong Un watched on Oct. 29, and the drone in the photos closely resembles the Hero-400 built by Israeli company UVision.
The photos, published by state news agency KCNA on Oct. 30, show a slender drone with two sets of cross-shaped wings, one near the nose and one near the tail, descending at a steep angle toward a sand-colored tank target built to look like an Abrams, with its distinctive angular turret and gun.
A second frame shows a large fireball where the target stood. KCNA did not name the drone, give its range or warhead size, or say how many were used.
The demonstration followed North Korea’s “Unmanned Aeronautical Technology Development-2026” exhibition, where Kim called for the country to seize “absolute superiority” in drone technology, Reuters reported, citing KCNA. Tactical suicide drones, tactical cruise missiles, multipurpose drones and a battalion of 600 mm multiple rocket launchers took part. Other targets in the drill were built to resemble South Korean Army guard posts along the Demilitarized Zone and K9 self-propelled howitzers, the open-source account Korea Defense Blog noted in a post.
Exhibition photos show Kim leaning in to inspect a row of the same type of drone, mounted on stands with serial numbers on their fuselages, which suggests the system has moved beyond a single prototype.
The layout matches UVision’s Hero family: a long tube-shaped body, tandem cruciform wings and a propeller at the rear, a design that lets the munition fold into a launch canister and loiter before diving onto a target. The Hero-400EC, the larger long-range version, weighs about 40 kg (88 pounds) at takeoff, carries a 10 kg (22-pound) warhead and can stay airborne for up to two hours, according to the company. Photos alone cannot show whether North Korea’s drone matches that size or performance, or how it is guided onto its target.
North Korea has shown similar designs before. When Kim toured drone factories in September, state media photos revealed a one-way attack drone resembling Israeli loitering munitions on an assembly line, alongside airframes matching the Saetbyol-4 and Saetbyol-9 reconnaissance and strike drones, which copy the look of the U.S. RQ-4 Global Hawk and MQ-9 Reaper.
The choice of target stands out because the design North Korea appears to have copied is in American service. The U.S. Marine Corps has used the Hero-400, and in 2025 the U.S. Army awarded UVision’s U.S. partner Mistral a $982 million contract for loitering munitions. U.S. Army armored units rotating through South Korea operate the M1 Abrams.
Loitering munitions attack from above, where tank armor is thinnest, and both Russia and Ukraine have used them in large numbers against armored vehicles. South Korea’s military said North Korea fired around 10 projectiles on Oct. 29, including short-range ballistic missiles, from the Wonsan area during the same demonstration.

Agricultural drones make first flights in Estonia as rules start to ease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:11:00 UTC
19:11:00 KST

Agricultural drones make first flights in Estonia as rules start to ease
Agricultural drones capable of crop-spraying and seeding are making their first flights in Estonia, though strict safety rules still limit wider use.
Simpler survey drones have been in use by Estonian farmers for several years already, to gather field data. From this week, the law permits the aerial spraying of plant protection products, though under strict conditions.
Farmers have been trained at a Rural Knowledge Center (METK) open day at the Nurmsi drone center in Järva County on Thursday, learning to use drones for field monitoring as well as for sowing and weed control.
"Weed infestation, sowing errors, drainage system failures — a great deal of different information. Together with the Rural Knowledge Center, we are currently learning spectral analysis, how to analyze the light reflected from plants by spectral bands," said Madis Pruus, agronomist at Järva County-based agricultural concern Väätsa Agro.
That analysis reveals the health of a given crop. Väätsa Agro has been using simpler and lower-cost drones for six years now, to gather information from fields. This helps in making production decisions.
METK estimates that drones are still not a regularly used tool in day-to-day Estonian agriculture, even as they can perform about a dozen different tasks.
"A drone allows precision farming techniques, variable-rate work cards or spot treatments only," said Ainar Härm, drone technology engineer at METK. For example, if there is a patch of thistles in the middle of a field, only that patch can be treated. "We don't have to go and treat the whole field," he added.
Drones have other advantages too, for instance being lightweight or, since they are airborne, not leaving much of a footprint at all, unlike heavy agricultural plant.
"Since an agricultural drone is light and doesn't flatten down the field, you can work field edges in spring when the fields are soft. You can fertilize and spread seeds," said Anti Konsap, senior engineer at METK.
The main obstacle so far to wider use has been strict restrictions on drone flying, though the situation is gradually improving, experts say.
"From yesterday the law permits the use of plant protection products for aerial spraying, but according to special conditions. It is very important to remember that the product itself must also be approved for aerial use. To my knowledge that list is still extremely short," said Taavi Võsa, researcher in agro-technology at METK.
Farmers who attended the open day said that although drones may turn into an efficient aid, they will fully replace neither the tractor nor the farmer at any time soon.

Ukrainian forces ‘hunt down’ and kill Russian nuclear plant worker
A Ukrainian drone strike has killed a worker while he was traveling to the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant, the Russian facility’s management reported on Friday morning.
The statement described Thursday’s attack as “barbarism” and part of a “hunt” targeting plant personnel.
“Strikes such as this one not only affect particular people. They are designed to intimidate plant workers, seed panic and tensions among those who ensure the atomic site operates safely every day,” it said.
Russia’s nuclear energy agency Rosatom mourned the death of the worker, who was employed as a welder and was traveling to work on an e-scooter when he was targeted.
The incident was first reported on Thursday by Maksim Pukhov, the mayor of the city of Energodar, near which the Zaporozhye NPP is located. He identified the victim as a man in his early 40s but did not mention his connection to the plant.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) condemned the incident, saying any attack on the facility is “completely unacceptable” and urging “maximum military restraint” around the Zaporozhye plant.
Moscow has repeatedly criticized the UN nuclear watchdog for failing to explicitly blame Ukraine for attacks on Europe’s largest nuclear power plant, including strikes targeting its personnel.
Rosatom head Aleksey Likhachev told an IAEA conference in September that 20 people, including nine plant employees, had been killed since Ukrainian forces intensified drone and artillery strikes against the facility in late April.
Among the victims were chief engineer Aleksandr Yakovlev and driver Dmitry Filippov, who were killed in July when a drone struck a car carrying the senior employee.
Russian management took control of the Zaporozhye NPP in 2022. Residents of Zaporozhye Region voted to join Russia in a referendum later that year, which Kiev rejected as a “sham” vote. The IAEA established a permanent on-site observer mission at the plant in September 2022.

The discussions were described as cordial rather than confrontational. It remains unclear whether Washington delivered similar messages to other European governments.
One US official declined to comment on the allegations, telling Reuters: “Private conversations among allies are just that, so we will not comment on these allegations.”
Among the statements that reportedly concerned US officials were remarks by European leaders suggesting that Russia was increasingly cornered and resorting to desperate measures as its invasion of Ukraine slowed.
Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, who is involved in a review of US troop levels in Europe, was among those delivering the message, Reuters’ sources said.

Russian Foreign Minister Arrives in US for G20 Amid Outcry

“We are helping you. The Americans are there,” one European official said, describing the Pentagon’s recent messaging. “Just don’t be loud. Don’t make noise.”

Meanwhile, Putin said Moscow was “ready” for a war with Europe but did not want such a conflict, warning that any escalation would leave no winners.
Speaking after the Russia-Africa summit on Oct. 29, he also dismissed the prospect of inflicting a strategic defeat on Russia by 2030 as “hardly possible.”

He also defended Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre for holding a phone call with him on Oct. 27, saying the two leaders were right to seek dialogue despite criticism from other European officials.

The Kremlin has maintained that a lasting peace in Ukraine would require Russia’s interests to be taken into account. On Thursday, it also ruled out European participation in the next round of Ukraine-US negotiations scheduled for November in Abu Dhabi.

Authorities in Greece and Turkey have released severe rainfall and flooding warnings, as a further 100-150mm (nearly 4-6in) of rain is expected this week in central Greece and western parts of Turkey, with locally higher totals possible.
Travelling eastwards towards south Asia, strong winds and heavy rainfall have swept across the Indian regions of Odisha and Andhra Pradesh as Cyclone Arnab made landfall. With wind gusts in excess of 85mph (140km/h) and rainfall totals in some regions exceeding 200mm, the severe storm has prompted mass evacuations of more than 180,000 people, as well as widespread disruption to energy and transport infrastructure. The cyclone will weaken as it continues to traverse northwards over the coming days, though will continue to deliver heavy rain to parts of northern and central India as it does so.
Heading towards the western Pacific Ocean, Typhoon In-fa was upgraded on Wednesday to super typhoon status, with exceptionally strong sustained wind speeds of 150mph (240km/h), with winds gusting over 185mph (296km/h). Travelling north-westwards, it is expected to avoid Guam, which was hammered by Typhoon Champi earlier this month. However, In-fa is expected to affect the Mariana Islands, which have already been battered by four super typhoons this year alone.
Meanwhile, across the Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Vance has been affecting parts of western Mexico. Though it has recently weakened to a tropical depression, Vance brought heavy rain and dangerous coastal conditions, with the regions of Sinaloa, Durango and Nayarit recording 50-100mm of rain, with some areas locally exceeding 150mm. The high rainfall totals are expected to cause disruption due to flooding and landslides, with the storm swell resulting in dangerous surf and rip current conditions off the coast.

Democrats have long known heartbreak in Texas. Could this finally be their year?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:06:43 UTC
19:06:43 KST

Democrats have long known heartbreak in Texas. Could this finally be their year?
FORT WORTH, Texas, Oct 30 - Texas has been the Democratic Party’s great, unrealized hope for three decades: a vast and fast-changing state that often seems within reach, only to slip away.
On the eve of a midterm election that could decide control of the US Senate, Democrats are dreaming again about breaking the Republican stranglehold on the Lone Star State, even as they brace for heartbreak.
Most polls show Democrat James Talarico, a 37-year-old state representative, seminarian and former schoolteacher, narrowly ahead of Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton. In the governor's race, Democratic state Representative Gina Hinojosa is trailing three-term Republican Governor Greg Abbott by just a few points.
No Democrat has won statewide office in Texas since 1994, the longest drought in the nation. Ending it would reverberate far beyond this state of 31 million people, redrawing America’s political map ahead of a wide-open contest for the presidency in 2028.
“This is the most competitive election between the parties that we have seen here since the early stages of Republican hegemony,” said James Henson, director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin (UT). “If Talarico or Hinojosa win, it’s a political earthquake.”
For the first time since 1972, Democrats are contesting every state and federal race, testament to a party that says it is investing in its future rather than just individual candidates.
Interviews with more than 40 voters, activists and organizers on both sides of the partisan divide revealed three potential cracks in the Republican coalition -- Latinos jolted by President Donald Trump’s immigration raids; conservative women uneasy about Paxton’s alleged marital infidelity and, to a lesser degree, Republican men squeezed by rising prices and the war with Iran.
Tyson Jex, 33, a suburban father of three, has always voted a straight Republican ticket. This year he’s undecided.
“We have conservative people in power, but it doesn’t seem like anything changes,” he said.
TWO PLAYBOOKS
Many Texas Republicans remain confident in their chances on November 3, believing the political fundamentals are still in their favor.
About 49% of Texas voters identify with or lean toward the Republican Party, compared with 40% for Democrats, according to UT polling.
Then there's the money: Republicans have spent over $300 million on ads supporting Paxton, dwarfing the $102 million spent for Talarico, according to FEC data.
Dave Carney, Abbott’s chief strategist and a veteran of Republican campaigns in Texas, added that the party’s ground game is peaking late by design. “We’re going to win, absolutely," he said, referring to both Republican candidates.
For their part, Talarico and Hinojosa have focused relentlessly on the cost of living and the outsize political influence of billionaires like Elon Musk, who poured nearly $160 million into Texas to buoy Paxton.
“We have an affordability crisis because we have a corruption crisis,” Talarico said at a rally in the city of Temple last week to thunderous applause.
Republicans, meanwhile, have leaned into culture-war issues. In ads, Paxton has hammered Talarico over his support for transgender rights and branded him a heretic for his progressive Christianity.
Rallying for Paxton last week at a brewery in the small town of Sanger, just north of Dallas, speakers riled up a raucous crowd by painting Talarico as a radical leftist and describing the election stakes as existential.
“If we lose one race this cycle, Texas will be a battleground state for the rest of our natural lives,” warned state Representative Andy Hopper.
Neither the Paxton nor the Talarico campaign made its candidates available for an interview.
LATINO BACKLASH
Tarrant County, home to the city of Fort Worth, is the most conservative of Texas’ big urban counties and is seen as a bellwether. In the 2020 presidential race, Joe Biden was the first Democrat to carry it since Lyndon Johnson in 1964, winning by less than 2,000 votes; Trump easily won it back in 2024.
The challenges facing Republicans among Latinos and women voters come into focus here.
Latinos helped deliver Texas to Trump in 2024, giving him 55% of their votes in a dramatic swing away from Democrats, according to exit polling.
Now, their enthusiasm is surging in the opposite direction. Among likely Latino voters, Talarico leads 54% to 41% and Hinojosa 56% to 42%, UT polling shows.
About 1.56 million Latinos had cast ballots as of Wednesday, nearly double the number who had voted at the same point in 2022's midterms, according to TargetSmart, a data firm that works mainly with Democrats.
Latinos make up roughly 28% of early voters, up from 20% at the same time four years ago, the data shows, while white, rural turnout is lagging significantly behind 2022 levels.
“Higher Latino turnout is almost certainly going to be good for the Democratic candidates,” said Tom Bonier, a senior adviser at the firm.
While Hispanics account for nearly a third of Texas’ eligible voters, their 2024 turnout trailed that of non-Latino whites by more than 20 points, according to the Census Bureau.
This year feels different for people like Rick Arredondo, a 52-year-old welder in Fort Worth’s heavily Latino northside. He rolled up to a polling station on his bike last week, eager to vote for the first time in his life.
He said he would cast his ballot for Democrats after immigration agents detained and deported his neighbor.
“Anybody that’s my skin color is fair game,” said Arredondo, a US-born citizen who now carries his passport for fear of being swept up in a raid. “Politics finally reached me in my little corner of the world.”
Down the street, Vanessa Dalay, 23, said she had skipped past elections but wouldn’t make the same mistake again.
“The deportations have radicalized me,” she said.
For Carlos Ronquillo, a 35-year-old house painter who voted for Trump in 2024, his anger over the raids has been compounded by economic struggle.
“I’ve got a diesel truck and I’m spending over $200 to fill it up,” Ronquillo said while getting a tire fixed at a Fort Worth shop. “That’s bad enough. But then you have ICE taking everybody, not just the criminals they said they would.”
Chuck Rocha, a Democratic strategist advising the Talarico and Hinojosa campaigns, said that in focus groups that many Latinos still back closing the border and deporting lawbreakers.
“But none of us signed up for (ICE) to be in our community, picking up our cousins and our aunts and uncles,” he said.
TROUBLE AT HOME
Republican organizers say a different issue is troubling women voters, one particular to Paxton, who beat incumbent John Cornyn in the party primary with Trump’s backing.
Paxton’s wife, state Senator Angela Paxton, filed for divorce last year on “biblical grounds,” accusing him of adultery. Paxton has declined to discuss the matter publicly.
Jill Tate is president of the Texas Federation of Republican Women, a grassroots group with more than 10,000 members in 160 clubs. She estimates about 40% of the conservative women her members are talking to have doubts about Paxton because of his marital problems.
“I’ve never seen us have to work quite so hard to win in my 30 years,” Tate said while canvassing in Allen, a deeply conservative suburb of Dallas.
Lauren Stewart, a 25-year-old Republican in Temple, said her religious upbringing made it hard to overcome her reservations about Paxton.
“I might skip voting in that race,” Stewart said. "I’ve heard that from a lot of my friends, too.”
Among likely Republican voters, 71% of men view Paxton favorably, compared with just 59% of Republican women, UT polling shows.
That might not matter in a typical year. But with polls showing Democrats more energized, it could be crucial.
“This is an election where small increments of voters matter,” Henson said. REUTERS

Toxic online subcultures fuelling Asia’s school attacks
Security experts urge vigilance as teenagers across Southeast Asia turn to radical online networks that celebrate notorious mass murderers

Recent school attacks across Malaysia have shone a light on a troubling trend of teenagers joining an online subculture that glamorises real-life killers, according to a prominent security analyst.
Three violent incidents in Malaysian schools – in Kuching on October 21, Banting in July and Bandar Utama in October last year – could be linked to the True Crime Community (TCC), said Munira Mustaffa, founder of Kuala Lumpur-based security consulting firm Chasseur Group.
In the Kuching case, the suspect live-streamed an axe attack on a teacher, while a female student who stabbed her schoolmate in Banting flashed an “OK” hand gesture in a TikTok video posted before the assault.
The TCC subculture typically glorifies serial killers and mass murderers – such as the 1999 Columbine High School massacre in the United States – while instilling a narrative among members that the world is cruel towards them. Adam Lanza, who murdered 26 people at Sandy Hook Elementary School in 2012, had reportedly taken part in similar online communities before the killings.

Seven governor races to watch as voters weigh Trump, economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30

Seven governor races to watch as voters weigh Trump, economy
NEW YORK, Oct 30 - Three dozen governors' races will be decided in the November 3 elections, with President Donald Trump's unpopularity and the cost of living at the top of voters' minds, alongside local concerns ranging from water rights and data centers to cancer rates.
Some races have turned ugly, including an Ohio contest between Republican Vivek Ramaswamy and Democrat Amy Acton that features the Democrat's estranged mother in an attack ad. Others could be history-making, such as Georgia Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms' bid to become the country's first Black woman elected governor.
Democrats now hold 24 governorships and Republicans 26. If Democrats can manage a net gain of at least two seats they will lead a majority of states for the first time since 2010.
Here are seven key governor races to watch:
ARIZONA
Water has become a key campaign issue in drought-hit Arizona, where Democratic Governor Katie Hobbs is seeking reelection against Republican US Representative Andy Biggs. Other top issues are cost of living and immigration, with Hobbs seeking to position herself as tougher on border security than many national Democrats.
Biggs is a former head of the right-wing US House Freedom Caucus, which has pushed for deep cuts in federal spending.
Abortion rights have featured prominently in the race, with Hobbs a supporter while Biggs has a long record as an opponent. Arizona voters approved a constitutional amendment protecting abortion rights in 2024.
MICHIGAN
Michigan's race is one of the most competitive gubernatorial contests, pitting Democrat Jocelyn Benson, the state's top election official, against Republican US Representative John James. The candidates are battling to succeed term-limited Democratic Governor Gretchen Whitmer, making it one of 19 open-seat races this cycle.
Michigan is a closely divided swing state that Trump won in 2016 and 2024, while Democrat Joe Biden carried it in 2020. Neither party has elected back-to-back governors in the state since the 1960s.
GEORGIA
Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire healthcare executive, is running against Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor, to succeed Republican Governor Brian Kemp. A Bottoms win would make her the first Black woman elected governor in the US and the first Democrat elected governor of Georgia in more than a quarter century.
Because Georgia will likely be a key presidential battleground in 2028, both parties view the gubernatorial race as an early test of voter sentiment.
Jackson, who has spent more than $100 million of his own money on the race, has generally aligned himself with Trump's agenda, while Bottoms has sought to mobilize the diverse Democratic coalition that helped Biden win the state in 2020.
Bottoms rose to national prominence in 2020 as she guided Georgia's largest city through protests, civil unrest and the COVID pandemic. Her base is in the Atlanta metro area, whose rapid growth has reshaped Georgia politics.
OHIO
The race between Republican entrepreneur Ramaswamy and Democrat Acton, a physician, drew national attention over an explosive attack ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother. In a video run by the Ramaswamy campaign, Donna Arthur disputes Acton's account of a childhood marked by homelessness and sexual abuse and urges Ohioans not to vote for her.
Acton, a former director of the Ohio Department of Health who led the state’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic, has said she was sexually abused by her stepfather. The stepfather, who died in 2004, fled the state after he was charged with raping his stepdaughter and never stood trial.
The state's reputation as a perennial swing state faded after 2016 when Trump won it with strong support from working-class voters, who helped to turn it into a reliably Republican state. The race is being watched as a test of whether Democrats can turn economic dissatisfaction into votes. Democrats have won just one of the state’s last nine gubernatorial elections.
IOWA
Iowa is holding its first open governor's race since 2006, after Republican Governor Kim Reynolds said she would not seek reelection. State Auditor Rob Sand, the only Iowa Democrat currently holding statewide elected office, faces Republican businessman Zach Lahn.
The state's incidence of cancer, at the second-highest rate in the country behind Kentucky, has emerged as a major campaign topic alongside kitchen-table issues such as the cost of living. Interest has been fueled by worries that exposure to nitrates, pesticides and other environmental contaminants may be contributing to the high cancer rate.
The race has also focused on education and government accountability. Sand has campaigned as an independent watchdog critical of Republican fiscal management and the state's private-school voucher program.
Lahn has embraced lower taxes, school choice and a more conservative approach to social issues.
NEVADA
In a contest centered on affordability, Republican Governor Joe Lombardo is in a neck-and-neck race with Democratic challenger Aaron Ford, the state’s attorney general.
Nevada residents have voiced concerns over tariffs, a tourism slowdown and high gas prices, giving Ford an opening to defeat Lombardo despite the incumbent's 2-1 fundraising advantage.
Data centers have also emerged as a central campaign issue. Ford has proposed a halt to new data-center tax abatements and wants to require that developers shield residents from higher energy costs. He has also called for strong regulations to protect jobs from AI.
Lombardo, while imposing new restrictions on some of the tax incentives that lured the industry to the state, has generally championed data centers as an economic driver.
WISCONSIN
A central question in Wisconsin’s gubernatorial race is whether voters, who backed Trump in 2024 and Biden in 2020, want a governor aligned with the Republican president. Republican Tom Tiffany, a three-term US Representative endorsed by Trump, has played down that connection. His Democratic opponent, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, has sought to link Tiffany to Trump's agenda.
In Congress, Tiffany has supported conservative causes such as gun rights and lower taxes, and co-sponsored federal legislation that would have banned most abortions after about six weeks of pregnancy. Crowley supports abortion rights and has framed reproductive rights as a key campaign issue. Wisconsin bans abortion after 20 weeks and requires a 24-hour waiting period as well as parental consent for minors. REUTERS

Seven Rotterdam police officers to face trial over arrest death

Seven Rotterdam police officers to face trial over arrest death
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Seven police officers will go on trial in January next year over the death of a 32-year-old man who was held in a “prone position” on the ground for a long time after being tasered during an arrest in Rotterdam in 2023, the public prosecution department (OM) said on Thursday.
Two officers chased the man on June 9 that year, first in a police van and then on foot, after reports that he had crashed his bicycle into a car and then cycled on.
When he ignored their instructions, one officer used a taser, but it did not incapacitate him or stop him from further resisting. More officers arrived and several of them pinned him down. Soon after he became unwell and was given CPR but died in hospital.
In February 2024 the OM said it would prosecute eight officers after an investigation by the Rijksrecherche, which investigates the police. A pathologist concluded the man’s death could have been caused by the way he was restrained.
The officers are accused of breaching the rules on the use of force with fatal consequences, which has been a criminal offence in its own right since July 2022.
The OM said on Thursday it had dropped a case against an eighth officer, as he was still in training and was following instructions.
The case will be heard on January 19 and from February 15 to 18 by the Blauwe Kamer, a special court in Utrecht that handles cases against police officers. The court will rule on all seven cases at the same time.
In September another Rotterdam man, Alfredo Goeloe (51), died during an arrest after collapsing while officers held him on the ground. That incident led to protests in the city. The Rijksrecherche is investigating his death as well.
