Oleshky evacuation begins but volunteer claims Russia already moved people outside of agreed terms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:40:07 UTC
18:40:07 KST

Oleshky evacuation begins but volunteer claims Russia already moved people outside of agreed terms
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Twenty-five buses with a capacity of 750 passengers, along with ambulances for people with limited mobility, have been prepared to evacuate residents from Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast, Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 29.
Lubinets's statement comes amid claims that Russia had begun evacuating residents before the agreed date.
"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to leave safely. At the same time, those who have decided to stay can stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian support," Lubinets said.
Lubinets and Russia's Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova held a joint press briefing in Armiansk, Russian-occupied Crimea, ahead of the evacuation from Oleshky.
Lubinets said the Ukrainian and Russian delegations were accompanied by media representatives "from three countries." However, photos published by Ukraine's Ombudsman's Office show predominantly Russian media outlets.
As of nearly 11:30 a.m. Kyiv time, the Ukrainian delegation had safely reached Oleshky, and the ceasefire had been in effect for 80 hours and was still holding, Lubinets said.
Lubinets added that he was speaking with local residents to hear about their needs and understand what kind of assistance they required most.
David Arakhamia, head of President Volodymyr Zelensky's parliamentary faction, said around noon local time that humanitarian aid had been delivered to Oleshky and that "technical support" was being provided to those wishing to evacuate.
Five hundred twenty-seven residents of Russian-occupied Oleshky plan to travel to Ukrainian-controlled territory, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said in response to questions from lawmakers during a public government Q&A session on Oct. 30.
Koretskyi later wrote on Telegram that he had shared the figure "by mistake" and that "no exact numbers" were available at the time.
Koretskyi also said during the Q&A session that preliminary medical examinations of residents preparing to leave were expected to be completed by 2 p.m. local time on Oct. 30. Residents of Oleshky will then travel to Belarus before crossing into Ukraine, the prime minister added.
Demining of designated routes has been completed, and a humanitarian convoy is ready to depart, Lubinets announced on Oct. 29. Meanwhile, Kherson regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin reported that one person was injured by the explosion of a Russian mine on the same day.
Residents wishing to leave the city will be able to do so until 2:00 p.m. local time, with security measures arranged for their evacuation. Humanitarian aid distribution is scheduled to begin after 2:30 p.m., according to the ombudsman.
According to a local Telegram group, residents of Oleshky are waiting for the convoy amid heavy rainfall, while the buses had not yet arrived. Residents know where to register, are being asked where they want to go, and are being given tickets.
Russian state news agency TASS, citing Lantratova, also reported that buses had been prepared for Oleshky residents, including ambulances and a special bus for people traveling with pets.
Kseniia Arkhipova, an evacuation volunteer from Oleshky who is now based in Ukrainian-controlled territory, said that Russia had violated the terms of the agreement by starting the evacuation early.
Footage broadcast by TASS also appears to show civilians being moved with only Russian forces present and before the agreed-upon date of departure, Oct. 30. TASS also showed interviews with people it claimed were evacuated from Oleshky on Oct. 29.
The Russian-installed head of occupied Kherson Oblast, Volodymyr Saldo, claimed on Oct. 27 that residents will have a choice — either to stay in Russia or to travel to Ukrainian-controlled territory "to reunite with their families."
But a source familiar with the events unfolding on the ground, speaking to the Kyiv Independent on condition of anonymity, said on Oct. 29 that Russia was already taking steps to ensure as few people as possible left for Ukraine.
They said that patients at the city's only functioning hospital were being registered and told they faced filtration if they left, Russian forces had refused to go house-to-house to inform sick and immobile people that the evacuation was happening, and those living in outlying villages had been told they could be shot if they approached the assembly point.
Some residents expressed fears in local Telegram chats that they could be taken to "concentration camps."
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha previously warned that Russia is preparing to stage "dozens" of videos, and President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 25 that Russia will likely "do everything it can to clear the roads in such a way that these people head toward Russia and remain there."
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion. Located across the Dnipro River from Kherson, the city has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces, which have prevented humanitarian aid from reaching residents.
Residents have faced severe shortages of food, water, and electricity. Mined roads and constant drone attacks have made safe evacuation virtually impossible, and civilians trying to flee on the only roads in and out of the city have frequently been targeted by drones.
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 29 accused Ukraine of "creating a humanitarian catastrophe" in Oleshky, despite the fact that Russian forces have been in control of the city since 2022.

At least 16 civilians killed in drone attack on displacement camp in Ethiopia

Andrew Wasike 
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
At least 16 civilians were killed and 22 others injured Thursday when a drone strike hit a camp for people displaced by conflict in Ethiopia's northern Amhara region, local media and conflict monitors reported.
The attack targeted the Hayiq Jari 2 Turk camp near the town of Hayiq, approximately 430 kilometers (267 miles) northeast of the capital Addis Ababa, killing three pregnant women, an 8-year-old girl and students among others, according to residents.
"The drone struck the camp five times, at least, at intervals of 15 minutes, while IDPs were inside their shelters. We never expected a drone to attack the camp," a witness told Ethiopian news outlet Addis Standard.
Conflict tracker Frontlines Ethiopia also documented the Oct. 29 attack, while other local accounts reported both drone and artillery fire in the area.
Residents said more than 20 shelters caught fire, forcing families to flee and separating children from their relatives.
The wounded were taken to Hayiq Hospital, with those in serious condition transferred to Dessie Hospital for specialized treatment.
The camp houses more than 1,800 internally displaced people, many of whom fled violence in the Oromia region, including the Wollega area.
The attack has further strained humanitarian conditions for families already facing shortages of food, medicine and shelter following reductions in aid.
Amhara has experienced prolonged fighting between federal security forces and Fano militias since 2023, with military operations, including drone strikes, affecting civilian communities.
The violence comes amid broader instability in Ethiopia, including renewed fighting in the northern Tigray region and escalating tensions with neighboring Eritrea.

European air traffic expected to shrink by 110,000 flights amid Middle East tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:38:06 UTC
18:38:06 KST

Gokhan Yildiz and Emir Yildirim
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
The ongoing conflicts in the Middle East are expected to slow European air traffic growth, leading to a loss of around 110,000 flights in 2026, according to forecasts from aviation agency Eurocontrol.
The European aviation sector performed below growth expectations despite strong passenger demand in the summer.
The number of flights in the European Civil Aviation Conference (ECAC) region is expected to grow by 1.7% this year to 11.2 million, below the previously projected 2.7% growth, marking a 1-percentage-point downward revision.
Developments in the region that prompted changes in flight routes and sent jet fuel prices soaring affected the growth outlook for European aviation, but Eurocontrol expects growth to regain momentum next year, with a projected 3.2% increase to 11.6 million flights in 2027.
The downward revision to this year's growth forecast fueled expectations that the number of flights next year may also fall short of estimates.
Eurocontrol assumes the situation in the Middle East will stabilize by the end of the first quarter of 2027, but a more pessimistic scenario forecasts tensions persisting until the end of the first quarter of 2028, with high fuel costs and weak economic growth limiting air travel demand.
The recovery in air traffic is expected to become more pronounced next year, but the organization noted that the recovery could be stronger in Türkiye and some Eastern Mediterranean countries.
The number of flights across Europe is expected to rise by an average of 2.1% per year from 2026 to 2032, while the total number of flights in the region is estimated to reach around 12.8 million by 2032, according to Eurocontrol.
While the organization expects the medium-term growth outlook to remain largely the same, the number of flights may fall slightly short of previous expectations due to geopolitical developments.
Eurocontrol's network management report recorded an average of 35,679 flights per day in European airspace last month, up 2.5% month-on-month.
The busiest day was Sept. 4, when 37,548 flights were recorded in European airspace. Total delays due to air traffic flow management reached a little over 2.4 million minutes, according to the report.
Capacity constraints, adverse weather and air traffic management issues affected operational performance despite the rise in air traffic.
Geopolitical developments, airspace restrictions, energy prices and air travel demand will determine trends in the coming period, the organization said.

British firms test AUKUS underwater tech off San Diego
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:36:54 GMT
18:36:54 KST

Two British companies funded by UK Defence Innovation have taken underwater communications and autonomy software to Maritime Big Play, the trilateral exercise held off San Diego last week, where innovators from Britain, the United States and Australia put emerging AUKUS technologies into the water together, according to UK Defence Innovation.
SEA Ltd of Frome in Somerset and Decision Analysis Services of Basingstoke both received their funding through the AUKUS Maritime Innovation Challenge, the competition run to find undersea communications and autonomy capabilities across the three nations, and both demonstrated technologies aimed at what happens beneath the surface.
SEA demonstrated its Acoustic Deployment Environment Planning Tool, which uses high-resolution environmental data and acoustic modelling to predict and optimise how underwater communications will perform in a given patch of ocean. The toolset builds on systems that have supported the Royal Navy for more than two decades and was developed further with UKDI support ahead of the exercise.
Marcus Donnelly, environmental data science technical lead at SEA, said: “Underwater communications are critical to modern maritime operations, particularly as navies make greater use of autonomous and uncrewed systems. Building on SEA’s decades of acoustic modelling expertise, our Acoustic Deployment Environment Planning Tool software combines high-resolution environmental data with sophisticated acoustic modelling techniques to help operators predict and optimise communications performance in complex underwater environments, supporting situational awareness, command and control, and more effective operations.
“Demonstrating the capability in an operational environment off San Diego will allow us to further test, refine and evolve the technology alongside other advanced maritime capabilities. The toolset has its roots in proven anti-submarine warfare modelling capabilities, including systems that have supported the Royal Navy for more than 20 years, and we see significant long-term potential as reliable underwater communications become increasingly important to future AUKUS and other maritime operations.”
Decision Analysis Services demonstrated the Autonomous Fleet Task Assignment Framework, software written to let a group of uncrewed underwater vehicles divide work between themselves when the link back to a command node is degraded or gone.
Anthony Dunn, lead consultant at Decision Analysis Services, said: “Our Autonomous Fleet Task Assignment Framework (AF-TAF) enables Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) to collaborate with less reliance on C2 orchestration, improving responsiveness and reliability in communications degraded or denied environments. Using distributed decision-making, AUVs dynamically allocate tasks to one another, adapt to changing conditions, and maintain mission effectiveness. Together with an accompanying simulation, AF-TAF supports defence planners in optimising fleet structures and operational scenarios, supporting a more resilient, agile, and capable maritime force for future UK and allied operations.”
Both problems come from the same physical fact, because radio does not travel through seawater. Indeed, submarines and uncrewed underwater vehicles communicate acoustically, at data rates measured in bits where a radio link would carry megabits, over ranges that change with temperature, salinity, depth and the shape of the seabed. A sonar operator who knows how sound will bend that day knows where a message will get through and where it will not, and a fleet of autonomous vehicles that can carry on working while nobody is talking to them removes the dependency altogether.
Both capabilities point at the same future, in which a handful of crewed platforms direct large numbers of uncrewed ones. The Strategic Defence Review’s hybrid navy rests on that arrangement, and the Defence Committee reported this month that the department has accepted a serious anti-submarine warfare gap. Autonomous underwater systems are meant to help close it.
AUKUS Pillar Two covers the advanced capabilities strand of the partnership, separate from the nuclear-powered submarine programme, and undersea warfare has been one of its more productive areas because all three navies face the same problem in the same water.
Sir Stephen Lovegrove, the Prime Minister’s Special Representative on AUKUS, attended the exercise. SEA and Decision Analysis Services will now use what they learned off San Diego to refine their systems.

Tech firms were again on the back foot on Friday after another round of disappointing earnings from Wall Street titans, fanned already by deep concerns about the AI investment boom.
AI-linked tech firms suffered steep losses after Amazon's quarterly report fell short of analysts' expectations for profit and revenue, while Intel's earnings forecast missed estimates owing to weak demand for PC processors and supply chain problems.
The announcements came a day after Google parent Alphabet reported weaker revenue growth from its advertising and search businesses, while saying it would ramp up capital expenditure.
Alphabet plunged more than 12%, while Amazon tanked more than 7% in after-hours trading, having lost more than 4% before the close. Intel dropped 23%. The Nasdaq finished down more than 1%.
The selling continued in Asia, where South Korean chipmaker SK hynix dived more than 7% and rival Samsung lost 3%, well off their morning lows.
Japanese semiconductor firm Kioxia shed more than 7%, while Advantest and SoftBank skidded nearly 6%.
TSMC in Taiwan lost 1.9%.
"This earnings season has been tough on AI players, with most getting punished against a backdrop of AI bubble and inflation fears," said Anna Wu of Floodlines Research.
"The concern isn't that AI demand has already slowed. It's that higher funding costs and credit risk could eventually force hyperscalers to slow their build-out."
The sell-off hit most broader markets in the region, with Seoul diving more than 3%, while Tokyo and Taipei shed more than 2%.
There were also losses in Shanghai, Singapore, Bangkok, Jakarta and Manila, although Hong Kong, Sydney, Mumbai and Wellington rose.
Paris stocks were flat as data showed that the French economy had contracted in the third quarter, compounding concerns about public finances and growing political tensions.
London rose, while Frankfurt fell.
Friday's retreat was a far cry from the optimism seen earlier in the week, when SK hynix said operating profit had soared 632% and AI giant Anthropic reported a first-half revenue surge of about 1,300% in its IPO filing.
Iran fears lift oil
The results have been unable to soothe investor worries about the eye-watering amounts firms are pumping into AI and when that will see a profit, while surging borrowing costs are fuelling fears over company finances.
Focus is now turning to Tuesday's US midterm elections and the impact they could have on the final two years of Donald Trump's presidency, with some speculating that he could ramp up his war on Iran, which could send oil spiking again.
"There's been a lot of talk that once these are out of the way, the US could go all shock and awe on Iran? I'm not sure how the midterms would affect that if he loses control of both Houses," said Michael Hewson, of MCH Market Insights.
"Does the outcome matter for the markets, probably not, although a crude oil price which moves above $120 a barrel could well be another story. This remains a much bigger risk for markets than anything the US midterms might bring about."
Fears of a ramping up in US-Iran hostilities were stoked by a report in the Wall Street Journal saying Trump's top Middle East commander had briefed him on military options for Tehran.
Both main contracts climbed more than 1%, with Brent heading towards $120 a barrel for the first time since April.
Bitcoin, meanwhile, tumbled around 5% to a one-month low of around $76,400 after crypto platform Binance said it had fallen victim to a major hack that had impacted more than $6 billion in funds.
The world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes posted a series of sometimes contradictory messages on X, insisting that "user funds are completely safe" but also saying it would "cover all losses".
It said later on its X account for Latin America that "the total estimated impact is around $6.3 billion".
"We have worked with blockchain partners to freeze the affected assets, with ~$3 billion frozen on-chain so far," it added.
That would be four times the amount impacted in the biggest-ever cyberattack of its kind to date, which saw $1.5 billion (€1.34bn) taken in February 2025 from the Bybit platform.
On currency markets, the yen strengthened against the dollar after the Bank of Japan held steady on interest rates and said inflation had topped its 2% target.

EU lacks basis for talks with US, Russia on Ukraine — source in Brussels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:35:53 UTC
18:35:53 KST

BRUSSELS, October 30. /TASS/. The European Union lacks a common negotiating position that would enable it to engage in talks with the United States and Russia on Ukraine. According to a diplomatic source in Brussels who spoke to TASS, the European Commission’s objective in discussions among EU member states on possible negotiations with Moscow is not to secure a specific outcome, but rather to retain control over the process and prevent divisions from emerging within the bloc.
"The European Commission’s actions in the internal EU debate on potential negotiations with Russia are not aimed at finding a solution to end the conflict in Ukraine. They are directed solely at maintaining control over any attempts at negotiation, in order to prevent any fractures in EU unity regarding the confrontation with Russia and support for Ukraine," the source said.
The source stressed that meaningful negotiations require "a clearly defined negotiating position, including an understanding of possible compromises and the desired outcome."
No Basis for Negotiations
"Any negotiating position adopted by the European Commission on behalf of EU member states must first be agreed upon by the member states within the Council of the EU. Only then can the Commission be granted a clear mandate to conduct the talks. None of these conditions has been met," the source noted.
According to the source, EU member states have failed to formulate a common position identifying the compromises Europe might be prepared to consider in discussions with Washington and Moscow aimed at resolving the conflict in Ukraine.
Instead, the debate within the bloc has focused on who might represent Europe in potential negotiations - a discussion that ultimately led nowhere.
"Brussels is now left with a 20-point document drafted by EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, which merely reiterates demands put forward in 2022, without taking current realities into account," the source told TASS.
The document calls for Ukraine’s membership in the EU and NATO, the preservation of its territorial integrity, and the strengthening of its armed forces. However, it makes no mention of what concessions the European Union might be willing to offer to help bring the conflict to an end.
"In short, the European Commission has no substantive basis for negotiations with Russia. Nevertheless, it insists that even technical contacts with Moscow concerning Ukraine must be coordinated by the head of Ursula von der Leyen’s cabinet. In other words, the objective is not to reach an agreement, but to keep the entire discussion surrounding contacts with Russia under its control," the source explained.
Political Masochists
Earlier, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov described EU leaders as "political masochists" for continuing to support Kiev despite the worsening situation in their own countries.
He stressed that European leaders were trying to convince their populations that they must sacrifice "everything - wages, jobs, the scope of healthcare services and, essentially, social benefits" to enable Ukraine to defeat Russia.
Lavrov also recalled recent remarks by German Chancellor candidate Friedrich Merz, who stated: "The main thing for us is not Germany, not the European Union, not NATO, not the US, and not China - the main thing is to defeat Russia."

You can pry Halloween from my cold, witchy fingers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:35:52 UTC
18:35:52 KST

You can pry Halloween from my cold, witchy fingers
Molly Quell
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
You can pry the pumpkins from the cold, dead hands of our regular columnist Molly Quell, who is going to celebrate Halloween despite some Dutch naysayers.
I am throwing a Halloween party. I like Halloween. It has cooler vibes than other second tier holidays (Valentine’s Day, Easter) and less stress than the major ones (Christmas, and for Americans/Canadians, Thanksgiving.)
I have gotten some pushback, however, from some of the Dutchies in my life, who are balking at the “Americanisation” of it all.
“What about Sint Maarten?” a Dutch friend asked me, half joking. The traditional Dutch holiday is celebrated on November 11, named after a Roman soldier who converted to Christianity. Children carry paper lanterns and go house to house, singing, in exchange for sweets.
“You are welcome to celebrate it,” I said. “I don’t.”
“I don’t celebrate Halloween,” she retorted.
“I’ll put you down as a ‘no’ then,” I said.
If my friend does celebrate Sint Maarten, she’s in the minority even in the Netherlands. By some estimates, only 30% of kids are out slinging their lanterns (or in some places, hollowed out turnips) for sweet rewards.
In Utrecht the holiday is celebrated widely, as Sint Maarten is the city’s patron saint. Further afield, however, there’s barely a single flame out on a chilly November evening.
Halloween, on the other hand, is everywhere. Hema has pumpkin candles and Takkie in a witch’s hat. There’s trick-or-treating for kids in community centres, spooky canal tours in Amsterdam, horror movies at every Pathé across the country.
That’s significantly better than a hollowed out turnip.
I admit, the broader point my friend was making is correct. American culture is becoming increasingly dominant and, as many become disillusioned with the United States under the current administration, there will be more and more backlash to things seen as symbols of the country.
There are a lot of American things the Netherlands shouldn’t import. I am on record saying we should ban American influencers from moving here. I am also opposed to importing prudish attitudes towards sex.
Takkie in his little witch’s hat is adorable and I am choosing to defend his (and my) right to celebrate Halloween.
I’ve always been a little surprised that Dutch people don’t embrace Halloween more. They love to dress up in absurd costumes for every other holiday. Have you seen Brabant during Carnival?
Plus, there aren’t really any holidays in autumn. In fact, earlier this year I argued that rather than making Liberation Day (May) a public holiday, as prime minister Rob Jetten suggested, we do Prinsjesdag (September) instead.
Half the country shuts down anyway for the annual announcement of the budget (in 2026, this was even more true, as the train lines were sabotaged) and there’s even a bit of a costume element with the hats.
We need something to celebrate in the fall to take our minds off the impending darkness of winter and Halloween is already right there. It already has built-in rituals, themed food (I will die on this hill defending candy corn) and no obligation to spend time with family.
While the pumpkin spice lattes and the knife-wielding maniacs on film may be an American export, Halloween doesn’t originate in the United States. Historians think it started as a Celtic pagan festival and was taken across the pond by Irish and Scottish immigrants.
And what is a bigger rebuff to the current American administration than celebrating immigration?

30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
The French economy unexpectedly contracted 0.1% in the third quarter of 2026, falling well short of market expectations for 0.3% growth, preliminary official data showed on Friday.
The slight decline followed a flat reading in the second quarter, according to the National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies.
A sharp deterioration in foreign trade weighed heavily on the economy, deducting 0.6 percentage points from gross domestic product growth after contributing 0.6 percentage points in the previous quarter.
Exports fell 1.7% during the July-September period, driven down by a 9.1% drop in transport equipment shipments, particularly aeronautics, alongside a 7% slump in agricultural exports.
Imports remained virtually flat, edging up 0.1% after expanding 0.9% in the second quarter.
Total production of goods and services slipped 0.1% during the quarter as manufacturing output fell 1.4%, affected by weak car manufacturing, poor summer harvests and reduced power station availability amid heat waves.
Construction output decreased 0.4%, while market services output rose 0.3%, supported by a 1% expansion in information and communication services.
Final domestic demand excluding inventories contributed 0.1 percentage points to growth, matching its performance in the second quarter.
Household consumption growth accelerated to 0.4% from 0.2% in the previous quarter, bolstered by electric vehicle purchases, rebounding electricity spending and recreational services.
Public administration consumption rose 0.3%, continuing its upward trend after a 0.4% increase in the second quarter.
In contrast, total investment, measured as gross fixed capital formation, fell 0.6% in the third quarter following a 0.5% contraction in the preceding three months.
Investment in manufactured goods dropped 1.9% on declines in transport equipment, while construction investment decreased 0.5%.
Changes in inventories provided a positive contribution of 0.4 percentage points to gross domestic product growth, largely driven by aerospace products after a sharp drawdown in the second quarter.

German import prices surge 10.4% in September on Middle East energy shock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:32:32 UTC
18:32:32 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
German import prices surged 10.4% year-on-year in September, marking the steepest annual increase since November 2022 as the war in the Middle East drove up energy costs, official data showed on Friday.
Import prices rose 2.1% from the previous month, accelerating from an 8.3% annual increase in August and 6.8% in July, according to the Federal Statistical Office.
The escalation of the Iran war had the largest impact on energy import prices, which surged 61.8% compared to September 2025 and 14.5% compared to August.
Considerable annual increases were recorded across all energy imports, led by electricity at 96.2%, mineral oil products at 81.3%, crude oil at 59.3%, natural gas at 53.9% and hard coal at 25.1%.
Within mineral oil products, prices doubled for lubricating oils, aviation turbine fuel, diesel and heating oil compared to the previous year.
Excluding energy, import prices rose 5.5% year-on-year in September and 0.5% month-on-month.
Intermediate goods import prices climbed 11.1% on an annual basis, driven by a 26.8% jump in non-ferrous metals, with copper up 37.9%, aluminum up 23.4% and precious metals up 22.1%.
Imported capital goods were 4.5% more expensive than a year earlier, while consumer goods edged up 0.2%.
In contrast, imported agricultural products fell 0.9% year-on-year, led by drops in live pigs by 34.9%, raw cocoa by 21.2% and green coffee by 15.2%.
Export prices rose 5.3% year-on-year in September, recording the largest annual increase since February 2023, while edging up 0.6% from August.
The effects of the Iran war were also clearly visible in export prices, with energy exports jumping 58.3% year-on-year and 9.2% month-on-month.
Export prices for mineral oil products rose 74.1% annually, aviation turbine fuel jumped 114.3% and natural gas rose 31.7%.
Intermediate goods exports, which account for a major share of total shipments alongside capital goods, increased 7.2% year-on-year.
Agricultural export prices rose 6.7% compared to September 2025 and climbed 2.8% from the previous month.

Most Ukrainians optimistic about future, unity - KIIS poll
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:30:43 EET
18:30:43 KST

Most Ukrainians (61%) believe that in 10 years Ukraine will be a prosperous country within the European Union, while 27% share the pessimistic view that in 10 years Ukraine will be a destroyed country with a significant outflow of population, according to a study conducted on October 8-16 by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS).
"Over the past year (since December 2025), the level of optimism fluctuates somewhat, but relatively insignificantly. In particular, we do not see significant changes over the past few weeks and months... The current survey was conducted against the backdrop of intensified terror and the 'diesel deal' and further pressure on Ukraine. That is, despite these factors, the level of optimism remains (at least for now) at the same level," KIIS said.
Most Ukrainians (59%) also believe that Ukrainians are overcoming contradictions and moving toward a cohesive nation. At the same time, a third of the population (34% now) believe that internal contradictions are deepening and Ukrainians are heading for a split.
More of the younger respondents see a movement toward a split: it is 24% among respondents aged 60 and older and rises to 41% among those aged 18-29, the study says. There are no significant differences between age groups in views of the future.
KIIS also compared respondents' views of the future, unity and the war, and found that those who share pessimistic views of Ukraine's future and unity also have more pessimistic views on issues of war and peace. In particular, significantly more of them insist that the Ukrainian authorities should have been more accommodating in negotiations and are ready to approve the withdrawal of Ukrainian troops from Donetsk region.
"Given all the circumstances, including a war that has lasted almost five years and it is unknown when it will end, intensified Russian terror, pressure from some strategic partners, domestic political upheavals and so on, the current level of optimism is high and shows the resilience of Ukrainians. At the same time, optimism or pessimism about the future and the perception of unity remain important components of information security now. As the survey results show, those who succumb to pessimistic narratives are far more ready to end the war on any terms, in fact capitulation. Clearly our Russian enemy understands this and therefore tries to use any pretext to impose and spread despair in society," KIIS Executive Director Anton Hrushetsky said in comments on the study results.
According to him, supporting and, where possible, strengthening healthy optimism about Ukraine's future and the unity of society is now important for preserving the population's moral and psychological resilience and the Ukrainian nation's higher defense capability.
"Responsibility for this lies on all actors, the authorities, the opposition, civil society with the media, and ordinary citizens," Hrushetsky said.
The survey was conducted by telephone interviews (CATI) on a random sample of mobile phone numbers in all government-controlled regions of Ukraine among 1,031 adult respondents. Under ordinary circumstances, the formal statistical error of such a sample (with a probability of 0.95 and a design effect of 1.3) would not exceed 4% for indicators close to 50% and 1.7% for indicators close to 5%. Under wartime conditions, a certain systematic deviation is added to the formal error.

Swiss housing shortage stops many setting up home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:29:28 UTC
18:29:28 KST

Swiss housing shortage stops many setting up home
Due to a lack of affordable housing, tens of thousands of people in Switzerland have put off setting up home independently.
This is a conservative estimate, as the property consultancy Wüest Partner explained in a study published on Thursday. If the housing market were less tight, as many as 40,000 to 50,000 additional households could be created.
Young adults are particularly affected. They are staying with their parents for longer or sharing a flat with others. In some cases, separated couples are also unable to afford a second home.
More
Buy or rent? Find out where you can afford to live in Switzerland
The housing shortage is also leading to a shift in demand towards more affordable regions. As a result, the canton of Zurich is now losing a net total of around 3,500 residents a year to other cantons, particularly Aargau, Thurgau and Schaffhausen. Before the pandemic, Zurich had been gaining around 1,850 people a year from other cantons.
This trend is particularly evident among young adults. The annual net inflow of 15- to 34-year-olds from other cantons to Zurich has halved to around 2,750 people compared with the pre-pandemic period. At the same time, the proportion of young adults living alone has been falling since 2022, particularly in Zurich, Schwyz and Zug.
+ Zurich: Welcome to the world capital of housing shortages!
More new-builds offer little relief
Despite the upturn in construction activity, there is no sign of the situation easing for the time being. Wüest Partner forecasts a net increase of around 45,000 flats by 2026, rising to around 50,000 by 2027.
This means more flats are being built than the approximately 40,000 new households formed annually in recent years But the additional supply is also likely to enable people who have so far postponed setting up a household to do so, thereby triggering new demand.
Consequently, pressure on rents remains high. In the third quarter of 2026, advertised rents across Switzerland were 1.9% higher than the previous year’s level. This was despite the number of rental flats advertised reaching its highest level since early 2024.
The city of Zurich is an exception, where asking rents fell by 1.7%. According to Wüest Partner, this could indicate that a price threshold has been reached which is now barely affordable for many households.
For 2027, property experts anticipate a further rise in asking rents across Switzerland of 0.9%. Rents for existing tenancies, however, are likely to remain stable.
Prices for owner-occupied property are also continuing to rise. In the third quarter, flats cost 5% more than a year earlier, whilst detached houses rose in price by 3.2%. For 2027, Wüest Partner expects further price rises of 3.5% and 3.1% respectively.

Russia's legal siege over assets continues, costing Euroclear hundreds of millions of euros in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:29:15 UTC
18:29:15 KST

Russia's legal siege over assets continues, costing Euroclear hundreds of millions of euros in 2026
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Russian sanctions and countermeasures against the Belgian company Euroclear, which holds over 200 billion euros ($224 billion) in Moscow's immobilized assets, continue to cost the company hundreds of millions of euros, according to an Oct. 30 earnings report.
The EU voted to immobilize all Russian government assets within the bloc promptly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The bloc agreed in December 2025 that the immobilization would remain in place indefinitely.
Belgium, and Euroclear specifically, holds by far the largest share of the Russian government's overseas assets, 204 billion euros ($228 billion), according to Euroclear's latest report.
Even as Euroclear "delivers record business income," the responsibility for upholding EU sanctions against Russia comes with a high financial cost.
"Russia sanctions and countermeasures resulted in a loss of business income of 27 million euros ($30 million) and in direct costs of 233 million euros ($261 million), of which 162 million euros ($181 million) is attributed to provisions for claims in Russian courts," reads the Euroclear report for 2026.
Euroclear is facing "multiple proceedings in Russian courts," including a case launched by the Russian Central Bank that seeks to challenge the immobilization of its assets.
"Euroclear strongly contests the Central Bank of Russia's claim, which is without merit," the company said.
Those costs can be covered by the interest generated from Euroclear's investment in the assets, and the EU has made clear in multiple sanctions packages that it will support companies being adversely affected for upholding the bloc's sanctions regime.
And so far in 2026, Euroclear notes that the assets have generated 3.6 billion euros ($4 billion).
The bulk of the interest earnings is, however, turned into a so-called windfall contribution, which Euroclear transfers to the European Union for the purpose of supporting Ukraine.
Euroclear has so far made five windfall payments since the first payment in July 2024. The total of that assistance stands at 8 billion euros ($9 billion), of which the most recent payment of 1.4 billion euros ($1.6 billion) was made in August 2026.
The Russian assets held by Euroclear are continually being eyed by Ukraine as a potential quick win to bankroll its defense.
Most recently, Deputy Prime Minister for European Integration Vsevolod Chentsov and former Prime Minister Arseniy Yatsenyuk repeated the idea of transferring the assets to a European custodian, where they could be used to provide immediate financial support, during an event in Brussels on Oct. 28.
The idea was, however, dead on arrival because moving Russia's assets from where they are currently held already introduces legal and business risks for Euroclear, which plays a significant role in the global financial system.
Now, the European Commission is compiling options to maintain financial support for Ukraine. Senior EU officials told the Kyiv Independent that potential use of the assets would be included, but "at the bottom," as the least desired option.

this 1950s modular house by jean and claude prouvé has moved across france
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:25:44 UTC
18:25:44 KST

this 1950s modular house by jean and claude prouvé has moved across france
the prefabricated residence was dismantled and restored before finding a new life as a holiday rental in a grove of olive trees.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
maison prouvé 58 finds a new home near saint-paul-de-vence
Maison Prouvé 58, a prefabricated house developed by Jean Prouvé and his son Claude in 1958, has been reconstructed near Saint-Paul-de-Vence in southern France after being saved from demolition in Alsace. The low, L-shaped residence now stands among pine and olive trees, overlooking the Mediterranean landscape. Recently reopened through Les Maisons CAB, the house is available for overnight stays (see here).
The building originally stood in Epfig, a village in northeastern France, where it was commissioned by local notary Édouard Degott. It remained there for more than sixty years, undergoing several alterations along the way. When the municipality acquired the property for redevelopment, plans for a new residential care facility threatened the house with demolition.
Belgian art collector Hubert Bonnet acquired the structure in 2021 and arranged for its dismantling the following year. Its components were transported to Nancy for restoration before being reassembled in Provence, where its aluminum facade and long stretches of glazing now face an entirely different landscape.
jean and claude prouvé’s experiments in prefabricated housing
The original commission began with Jean Prouvé, whose experiments with industrialized construction had already produced a series of lightweight, demountable buildings. Working in Paris at the time, he entrusted the project to Claude, who developed the architectural plans and oversaw construction. The house was completed in 1959, despite the 1958 date retained in its present-day name.
Archival research from the École Nationale Supérieure d’Architecture de Nancy reveals an eventful construction process. Delayed deliveries of facade panels and glazing slowed work on site, and Claude eventually helped assemble the window frames himself. The difficulties offer a glimpse into the practical challenges of building with factory-made components at the time.
The house uses many of the construction principles developed by Jean Prouvé. Prefabricated sandwich panels contain an insulating core beneath ribbed aluminum surfaces, while broad expanses of glazing sit behind slender metal columns along the garden-facing facade. Laminated wood elements support the roof, which is finished in folded aluminum.
a compact interior furnished with modernist design
Inside Maison Prouvé 58, a central corridor separates the private rooms from the shared living spaces. Two bedrooms and a playroom occupy the western side, arranged around a bathroom, while the kitchen and living areas gather around a fireplace to the east. The house spans approximately 115 square meters, with generous windows connecting its compact interior to the surrounding garden.
Wood introduces warmth against the metal construction, and the open connections between rooms give the modest plan a sense of space. The broad glazing also brings daylight deep into the house, where the slender structural elements leave much of the surrounding landscape visible.
The interiors are furnished with works by Jean Prouvé and Charlotte Perriand, alongside pieces by Pierre Jeanneret and Le Corbusier. A Prouvé desk and daybed share the rooms with Perriand’s Nuage shelving, extending the architectural story into the furnishings themselves. These objects belong to Bonnet’s wider collection of 20th-century design, though here they return to their intended purpose as furniture within a home.
a second life for modernist architecture in southern france
Maison Prouvé 58 now forms part of a nearly 4,000-square-meter estate alongside Le Clos du Père François, a traditional Provençal farmhouse dating to around 1850. The older residence has also been restored, with interiors furnished primarily by Jean-Michel Wilmotte and contemporary artworks throughout. Its stone construction provides a striking contrast to the thin industrial envelope of its modernist neighbor.
Outside, landscaped gardens connect the two buildings, with a swimming pool set against the surrounding greenery. A large wall painting by Swiss artist Claudia Comte introduces another contemporary element to the property, which forms part of Bonnet’s wider collection of art-filled residences.
Fondation CAB inaugurated the two properties in October 2026, opening them for stays through Les Maisons CAB. Maison Prouvé 58 accommodates four guests across two bedrooms and is rented together with the adjoining farmhouse. More than six decades after its first assembly in Alsace, the house has been taken apart and built again, giving a new purpose to a structure originally designed around the possibilities of prefabrication.
project info:
name: Maison Prouvé 58, formerly Maison Degott
design: Claude Prouvé, working with Jean Prouvé’s construction system
original completion: 1959
original location: Epfig, Alsace, France
current location: Saint-Paul-de-Vence, France
area: 115 square meters
reopening: October 2026
owner / collection: Hubert Bonnet, Fondation CAB
hospitality operator: Les Maisons CAB

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has signed decrees imposing sanctions on 10 companies and 19 Russian citizens involved in creating Russia's 'Rassvet' satellite communications system, and on 39 vessels of the Russian shadow fleet.
Decrees No. 1072/2026 and No. 1073/2026 have been published on the president's website.
According to the president's press service, Russia plans to use Rassvet to command troops and to guide and control strike drones, including Shaheds, and missiles in Ukraine online.

Sanctions were also imposed on five companies that supply foreign industrial equipment, electronic components and optical systems to Russia, develop industrial computers and space technology, and manufacture high-precision parts. In particular, products of 5S Group were used in Bureau 1440's developments.
A separate sanctions package covers 39 sea vessels flying the flags of Russia, Barbados, Liberia, the Marshall Islands, Panama, Hong Kong and other countries. They provide for exports of Russian oil, oil products and gas condensate to China, India, Egypt, Turkey and other states.
The vessel Vasily Dinkov alone made 15 operations in the first half of 2026 carrying about 726,000 tonnes of Russian crude oil.
Ukraine will pass information about the vessels to partners for synchronizing sanctions in other jurisdictions. Some of them are already under restrictions by the EU, the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Switzerland and Australia.

Halloween in Portugal: from Pão por Deus to Goat and Canhoto, how Portugal celebrates Witches' Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:22:55 UTC
18:22:55 KST

Carved pumpkins, sinister masks and children knocking on doors. Besides Halloween, "Pão por Deus" survives: in Portugal these are two ways to mark the year's scariest time.
Fake spider webs, witches' hats flying over ceilings, skeletons waving or glowing pumpkins smiling at us. This is the scene we now find in shops, schools and shopping centres. It means we are getting close to one of the scariest nights of the year: "Halloween".
Although it is not a tradition of Portuguese origin, it is no surprise that on the night of 31 October a group of children in scary costumes knock on our door for the traditional "doçura ou travessura" - "trick or treat" in the English version.
And although it is increasingly popular, Halloween is not the only event that marks this time of year. In Portugal there is another tradition which, despite the differences, has something in common with this imported celebration: children also go out into the streets and walk from door to door asking for offerings: it is "Pão por Deus".
This tradition is reserved for the morning of 1 November, All Saints' Day in Portugal - a public holiday when those who have passed away are remembered - and it is still kept alive in some places.
Although its origin is not agreed upon, it is believed that "Pão por Deus" emerged in the 15th century in a pagan context and is linked to ancient customs of sharing food in memory of the dead.
The tradition took on another dimension because of the 1755 earthquake, which struck Lisbon precisely on 1 November and left thousands of people in misery. According to this version, a year after the tragedy the poorest began the custom of going from door to door asking for bread to stave off hunger.
Nowadays it is mainly children who keep this practice alive, always with their cloth bags, often decorated by themselves or even handed out by local councils in some areas. The offerings also tend to be different: besides the traditional bread, cakes or dried fruit, people now give sweets or even money.
The tradition also involves reciting verses and songs, and there is no shortage of different quatrains: "Pão por Deus, Fiel de Deus, little cake in the bag, you walk with God"; or "Pão por Deus, for the love of God, put it here in the little bag, let everything be for the love of God". In some regions people also sang: "Little cakes and little cakes for me and for you, to give to the departed who are dead and buried".
The celebration takes different forms from region to region. In Estremadura it is known as "Dia do Bolinho", when the practice consists of giving traditional cakes of the season.
In the Azores one of the traditions linked to this time of year is caspiadas, cakes shaped like skulls in honour of the dead, which still survive in some places.
In Beira Baixa the tradition is more closely linked to godparents, who give a cake, the Santoro, to their godchildren.
The Portuguese tradition tends to be peaceful. Unlike what happens with the traditional "trick or treat", there is no such obvious link between refusing to give something and possible pranks. In Pão por Deus the spirit of sharing prevails, along with the desire to keep alive a tradition that is passed down from generation to generation.
Other traditional celebrations on "Halloween" night
There is a Portuguese celebration that comes close to the Celtic roots that gave rise to Halloween and is held in the north of the country, in a village in the district of Bragança, Cidões. It is called the "Festa da Cabra e do Canhoto" and is organised by the Associação Raízes Aldeia Cidões (source in Portuguese). (source in Portuguese)
As in the Celtic festival of "Samhain", which gave rise to Halloween, the tradition dictates that a large bonfire should be lit.
The "canhoto" that gives the festival its name is a large burning log and represents evil and hidden forces. The tradition also says that the canhoto and the firewood have to be stolen and will only burn if this condition is met.
Goat is cooked in large pots over the bonfire and roasted chestnuts are eaten.
It is around the bonfire that the ancestral tradition of Celtic origin is revived. The Celts, including the tribe of the Zoelas, lived in the Bragança and Vinhais region and at this time of year celebrated the farewell to the "bright season" to make way for the "dark season". It was believed that in this transition the world of the living and the world of the dead met.
The festivities are completed with Celtic-style performances such as dances, fire-breathers, pipers, drums and the arrival of the Careto, a figure from Trás-os-Montes, on an ox-drawn cart.
Further north, in the village of Vilar de Perdizes, in the municipality of Montalegre, the "Noite dos Fachos" is celebrated, a tradition full of mysticism. The participants, usually younger people, tend to "steal straw" and climb to the top of the mountains of the Serra do Larouco with the fachos (lit torches), shouting to scare away spirits, demons or witches.
The mountain range, at more than 1,500 metres above sea level, inherited the name of a Celtic deity, "Larouco", which helps to explain the link with these supernatural rituals.
Halloween, which only arrived in Portugal in the 1990s, was already well established in Vilar de Perdizes, which marks the Day of the Witches under the banner of the "Aldeia Assombrada" (source in Portuguese).
The true representation of globalisation
The Halloween tradition as we know it today is already a version shaped by many influences and customs. Its roots go back in part to the Celtic festival of "Samhain", held at the end of October and associated with the end of the harvests and the arrival of winter.
During this celebration it was believed that the world of the dead and the world of the living were closer together. The Celts thought that the spirits of the dead could return to the world of the living and, over time, customs emerged associated with this belief, such as lighting bonfires and wearing disguises.
From the 7th and 8th centuries onwards, with the spread of Christianity and the celebration of All Saints' Day on 1 November, pagan and Christian traditions began to influence each other, helping to shape the celebrations that we now associate with Halloween.
The term "Halloween" comes from the English expression "All Hallows' Eve", which means the eve of All Saints' Day.
However, it was also with Irish immigration to the United States between 1845 and 1849, during the devastating Great Famine in Ireland, that the tradition began to take new forms and to move closer to what we know today. In the United States costumes, illuminated pumpkins and other practices that we associate with this night became increasingly popular.
The city of Anoka in Minnesota calls itself the "Halloween Capital of the World" and is known for having organised in 1920 one of the first large-scale community celebrations dedicated to this date.
It was in this city that a parade was organised which helped to consolidate a tradition of public Halloween celebrations. Today its best-known symbols include pumpkins, witches, skeletons and other frightening costumes.
Other Halloween celebrations in Europe
In many European countries Halloween is celebrated in a way very similar to the North American tradition, but in some places there are very distinctive ways of marking the Night of the Witches. Here are some examples.
Transylvania, Romania
The region of Transylvania in Romania is now associated with the celebration of Halloween, largely thanks to the vampire imagery created by the Irish writer Bram Stoker in his 1897 novel "Dracula".
Bran Castle (source in Portuguese)is marketed as "Dracula's Castle" and has provided the perfect backdrop for Halloween celebrations, themed events and horror-inspired parties. Visitors are taken on a tour through a gloomy atmosphere, very much in the Halloween style.
Bruges, Belgium
From romantic streets to a dark setting, Bruges is transformed at Halloween.
From a storytelling session about the tale of the water ghost that is said to haunt the Lake of Love, to a night-time walk through the city's darkest legends, myths and stories, anything is possible on the night of 31 October.
The "Historium", an interactive and immersive tourist attraction located on the Markt (Market Square), also gets into the spirit with a spooky decoration of pumpkins, spider webs and bats, in the style of a haunted house. There is also a virtual reality experience dedicated to Halloween and a Museum of Torture for those brave enough.
Edinburgh, Scotland
In Edinburgh Halloween is taken very seriously with the Samhuinn Fire Festival (source in Portuguese), which is nothing more than a modern re-creation of the ancient Celtic traditions of the Scottish capital, with colourful costumes, fire performances and a lively procession through the cobbled streets.
This festival also exists in Sintra, Portugal, where it is held at Quinta da Ribafria.
Derry, Northern Ireland
In the city of Derry in Northern Ireland the roots of Halloween are also revived with the Derry Halloween festival.
Presented as one of the biggest Halloween festivals in Europe, the event features light shows, acrobatic banshees and circus performers inspired by Celtic traditions.
Visitors can also pick out pumpkins or take part in craft workshops before live music and performances take over after dark

Spanish train was travelling at 160kmh when it smashed into second one, report finds
- The Spanish train crash near Urda killed at least 69 people and left 64 missing. It is Spain’s deadliest rail accident since 2013.
- A preliminary report says the Renfe train was travelling at 160kmh to 200kmh. The crash followed signalling failure and control centre errors, with protocol ignored.
- The disaster has reopened safety concerns on Spain’s high-speed rail network. Investigators will use the black box to confirm the exact speed and cause.
AI generated
MADRID – The Spanish train that smashed into a second stationary one, killing at least 69 people on Oct 28, was travelling at a speed of at least 160kmh, according to a preliminary report about the accident.
The Civil Guard said it has received reports of 64 people missing in what is already Spain’s deadliest train accident since 2013.
The authorities have carried out 49 autopsies so far and identified five people, three women and two men, Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, said on state television network TVE.
“Testing is proceeding slowly, although families will be contacted throughout the day so that they can come and collect their results,” Padilla said on Oct 30.
It is unclear how many of the missing were among the bodies still to be identified.
The crash, which happened near the town of Urda in central Spain, followed another fatal accident in January involving the same rail companies on the same line. It has reopened a debate about safety and maintenance on Spain’s high-speed rail network, the most extensive in Europe.
The collision occurred after several trains were automatically stopped due to the failure of the automatic signalling system, after which the central control centre in Madrid took over.
A train operated by state-owned Renfe was authorised to proceed, even though there was a stationary Iryo-operated train ahead, according to Transport Minister Oscar Puente.
Audio of communications between the control centre and the train drivers obtained by El Pais showed how a controller authorised the Renfe train to continue on its journey at a normal speed, which Puente said disregarded a protocol to travel at no more than 40kmh in such circumstances.
The audio also showed the controller authorised the Renfe train, carrying 379 passengers and seven crew, to renew its journey when it should have been the Iryo train in front, which carried 147 passengers and five crew, to proceed first, according to protocol.
Sequence of malfunctions
“The sequence of malfunctions, instructions, and actions eventually led to the collision, in the absence of the necessary mitigating barriers,” according to the preliminary report by the Independent Authority for the Technical Investigation of Accidents and Incidents (AITAT).
It estimated that the Renfe train was travelling at a speed of between 160kmh and 200kmh when the collision occurred.
AITAT said it would not be able to confirm the exact speed of the train until it extracted information from the train’s black box.
“The scene was devastating. You saw carriages completely burnt out, as if they’d exploded. What you see coming out were people in a very bad way, and others who start pulling out the bodies of the deceased and placing them right there next to where we were,” Sebastian Herrero, who was travelling near the front of the Iryo train, said. Asylum applications drop 13% under EU migration pact
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:17:07 UTC
18:17:07 KST

Asylum applications drop 13% under EU migration pact
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The number of first-time asylum applications in the Netherlands fell by 13% in the third quarter of 2026, compared with the same period last year, according to figures from national statistics bureau CBS and immigration service IND.
The downward trend follows the implementation of the new European Union Migration Pact, which came into effect in June this year, with tighter guidelines, the abolition of permanent asylum residence permits and stricter criteria for family reunification.
Several of those changes echo measures pushed by former asylum minister Marjolein Faber (PVV), who promised the “strictest asylum policy ever” and wanted to make the Netherlands “as unattractive as possible to asylum seekers”. Her emergency asylum law was rejected by the Senate in April.
In the third quarter of 2026, some 5,900 people filed an asylum application for the first time, 850 fewer than a year earlier. Asylum applications from Eritreans and Syrians halved, while 1,500 fewer family reunification applicants came to the country than a year ago.
Eritreans submitted the most asylum claims, followed closely by Syrians. According to CBS, the number of Ukrainian applications increased from 15 to 140, while the number of applications from people from Ethiopia decreased from 290 to 75.

Russia’s Defense Ministry proposes delaying December military pay until January
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:15:59 UTC
18:15:59 KST

Russia’s Defense Ministry has drafted an order that would postpone service members’ December pay to January for the first time in at least 18 years, the independent Russian news outlet Verstka reported.
Under current rules, service members are paid for the previous month between the 10th and 20th of each month, and for December, by December 25. The Defense Ministry wants to push the December payments back to January 11–21 of the following year.
If adopted, the changes could take effect as early as this year.
Service members of the Joint Group of Forces fighting in Ukraine would be exempt, continuing to be paid under the old schedule before the New Year. Contract soldiers would also be treated differently: in December, they are supposed to receive a bonus along with their pay.
Russian service members have received their December pay before the end of the calendar year since at least 2008, according to official records Verstka reviewed. The outlet said the practice was likely also observed during the Soviet era.
Authorities in Stavropol Krai decided to postpone until 2027 the payments to the families of those killed and wounded in the war, it was reported the day before. The payments are normally supposed to arrive within five business days of a claim’s approval, but authorities can delay payment if the regional Labor Ministry’s account lacks funds.
Regions have also been cutting payments to the families of the deceased one after another in recent months. In the Ulyanovsk region, the payments were cut by a factor of 20, while in the Saratov region, they were cut by a factor of 10.

Unknown Russian USV Attacks Container Ship That Sinks in Bulgarian Waters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:15:53 UTC
18:15:53 KST

An unknown Russian naval drone was recorded attacking the CONTSHIP JET container ship in the Black Sea, which later sank off the Bulgarian coast.
Bulgarian outlet Maritime.bg published the video, while Reuters reported the preliminary identification of the vessel.
The footage, filmed from aboard the vessel, shows a USV approaching at high speed, moving alongside the container ship’s starboard side before turning towards its hull.
According to analysts at Ambrey Analytics, the vehicle is approximately 5–6 metres long and has a matte black hull. Its manoeuvring pattern may indicate that it is remotely controlled.
Experts believe the naval drone may be a modified version of the Russian Murena-300S vehicle or its derivative.
The Murena-300S is designed for reconnaissance, patrol and mine-laying missions. It can also be used as a kamikaze boat or an FPV drone carrier. Its stated operational range is up to 500 km.
The attack on the CONTSHIP JET took place on October 28 in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone, near Cape Kaliakra. The Liberian-flagged vessel was sailing from Haifa, Israel, to Constanța, Romania, when it was attacked by three naval drones.
The container ship sustained significant hull damage in the attack and sank off the Bulgarian coast. There were 18 crew members on board: 14 Filipino nationals and four Ukrainians. All crew members were rescued and taken to the port of Varna.
The vessel was carrying 421 containers, including those containing lithium-ion batteries, acids and industrial components.
According to Commander of the Bulgarian Navy, Kiril Mihaylov, the military received a warning about the threat of naval drones from a French patrol aircraft but was unable to prevent the attack.
In total, at least six civilian vessels were attacked by USVs off the Bulgarian coast in October.
Militarnyi previously reported on the specifications of Russian drones disclosed by the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine, including the Skanda reconnaissance USV, the Murena-300S and other strike platforms.

Fire Point is scaling up production of Flamingo missiles and FP-1 and FP-2 attack drones, Stielerman says
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:13:38 EET
18:13:38 KST

Fire Point is scaling up production of Flamingo missiles and FP-1 and FP-2 attack drones, Stielerman says
Kyiv • UNN
Fire Point is increasing production of FP-5 Flamingo missiles and FP-1 and FP-2 drones. The company is also developing FP-7 and FP-9 ballistic missiles.
Ukrainian weapons manufacturer Fire Point is scaling up production of the FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles and FP-1 and FP-2 attack UAVs. In addition, the company is working on the production of the FP-7 and FP-9 ballistic missiles. This was reported by Fire Point co-founder and chief designer Denys Shtilerman, UNN writes.
Context
Earlier, a scandal erupted on social media over a wave of manipulations, prompted by a fragment of an old interview with Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh that had been taken out of context and circulated in edited form. The video clip was edited in such a way as to suggest that Terekh had said the company had stopped producing FP-5 "Flamingo" cruise missiles. Fire Point CEO denied this information. In fact, the issue was not abandoning the "Flamingo," but rather the absence of plans to create additional cruise missile models.
Details
Denys Shtilerman emphasized that, on the contrary, the company is working to scale up production of the Flamingo, FP-1, and FP-2.
We continue to manufacture them (the "Flamingo" missiles — Ed.). Moreover, I guarantee that we are constantly scaling up production of both FP-5 cruise missiles and FP-1 and FP-2 drones, and are actively working on the production of FP-7 and FP-9 ballistic missiles
Shtilerman called the wave of manipulation about the cessation of missile production another attack on the company.
For me, it was hugely disappointing to see how some people eagerly spread a distorted statement from Iryna's interview without even checking the original source. In doing so, they help spread Russian narratives. The fact that the enemy is devoting so much effort to information warfare is yet another confirmation of our strength
Shtilerman noted that Ukraine is now stronger than ever in its history and is fighting against the entire "axis of evil."
Our army and our weapons are the best in the world. Direct proof of this is the incredible achievements on the battlefield and the fact that Ukraine initiated and is leading the project to create the pan-European "Freyja" ballistic shield. We need not to devour one another, but to unite in the fight against Russia, which is waging a genocidal war against Ukraine every day, and direct our forces toward victory. Let us all focus on this
To remind you
Freyja is a Ukrainian-initiated project for a joint European antiballistic system, the first track of the Antiballistic Coalition, which includes 10 countries and more than a dozen leading European defense companies. The system is intended to intercept Russian ballistic missiles.
The project is built around the Ukrainian FP-7.x interceptor missile developed by Fire Point, while the other components are supplied by European manufacturers. As reported by UNN, Fire Point Chief Executive and Technical Officer Iryna Terekh said that development had reached the stage of technical integration of the entire ecosystem — radars, a launcher, a data transmission channel, and a command center — while tests are conducted up to twice a week.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported that Ukraine had completed its part of the work on the Freyja antiballistic project, while partner countries continue working on their part in order to proceed to testing the first system as soon as possible.

More than charity: the couple giving Israel's most vulnerable children a second chance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:11:40 UTC
18:11:40 KST

Some partnerships begin with a donation and, over the years, become part of an organization's story. That has been the case for Jane and Larry Sherman and Orr Shalom, an Israeli organization that provides homes, stability and support for children, teenagers and young adults at risk, offering them the opportunity for a different future.
For more than 25 years, the Shermans have supported Orr Shalom out of a belief that every child deserves to grow up in a safe, loving and supportive environment. That commitment has guided their involvement with the organization through decades of philanthropy and changing needs.
While many charitable contributions focus on individual projects or limited periods, the Shermans' partnership has continued for more than two decades, growing alongside Orr Shalom and adapting to the needs of the children and young adults it serves.
A journey that began with a home
The couple's relationship with Orr Shalom began with the need to find a home for five Ethiopian children who had nowhere to go. The Shermans helped the organization establish a group home where the children could find stability, warmth and a sense of belonging.
Jane has described the connection as deeply personal, saying the couple came to regard the five children as members of their family. She credited their subsequent success to "the love and caring and stability they received" at the Orr Shalom group home where they grew up.
What began with those five children eventually expanded into support for Orr Shalom's Graduate Program, which helps young adults transition from out-of-home care to independent living.
For young people who grow up in residential care, turning 18 can bring significant challenges. Many leave the system without a stable support network or someone to help them navigate the practical demands of adulthood, from paying rent and pursuing an education to making their first independent financial and personal decisions.
Orr Shalom's Graduate Program was established to help bridge that gap. The Shermans' support for the initiative reflects their belief that responsibility for a child's well-being does not end on their 18th birthday.
A home named in their honor
Last week, Orr Shalom held a ceremony in Mevaseret Zion to honor Jane and Larry Sherman by renaming its family group home after them. The home, now known as Beit Sherman, recognizes their more than 25 years of involvement with the organization.
"Naming the family group home in Mevaseret Zion after Jane and Larry Sherman expresses our appreciation for more than 25 years of partnership," said Yair Medalion, CEO of Orr Shalom. "Jane has accompanied Orr Shalom's work from the founding of a home for children, through the development of the Graduate Program, and on to her support of foster care as a nurturing response. Their continued contribution affects the lives of many children and young people."
Beit Sherman continues to provide children with a warm, home-like environment. For those who grow up there in the coming years, the name will serve as a lasting reminder of the couple's commitment to helping children build more secure futures.
Changing needs in the wake of October 7
Ahead of the ceremony, Jane spoke with Naomi Segal on a Kan English podcast about her philanthropic work and the couple's longstanding involvement with Orr Shalom. The episode described her as a longtime leader in Jewish philanthropy whose connection to the organization, together with Larry, spans decades and remains deeply personal.
Their conversation also addressed the changing needs of Israeli society, particularly following the October 7 attacks and the ensuing war. Children and young adults already facing difficult circumstances have been especially vulnerable to the effects of the conflict, increasing the need for stable homes and reliable support systems.
Jane emphasized that children and young adults who were already considered at risk before October 7 have become even more vulnerable since the war began. Her comments highlighted the importance of adapting existing programs to meet new challenges while maintaining the support networks established over the years.
For a donor who has worked alongside an organization for decades, that continuity also provides an understanding of how children's needs evolve and why sustained support remains essential during periods of crisis.
The value of a long-term partnership
The story of Jane and Larry Sherman illustrates how philanthropy can extend beyond a single donation or project. A long-term partnership allows an organization to plan ahead, develop new programs and respond to changing circumstances, particularly during periods of crisis. It also reflects the trust that develops over time between donors and the organizations they support.
For Orr Shalom, the Shermans' involvement has helped establish a home for children, expand support for young adults leaving care and sustain the organization's work across generations.
Behind every home and every program are children and young people who need stability, care and someone willing to invest in their future. For more than 25 years, Jane and Larry Sherman have been part of that effort.

Philippines' Bangsamoro elects chief minister, ending over 7 years of interim rule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:11:23 UTC
18:11:23 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
Lawmakers in the southern Philippines' Bangsamoro autonomous region elected Abdulraof "Sammy Gambar" A. Macacua as chief minister Friday, marking the transition from more than seven years of interim administration to an elected government, regional authorities said.
Macacua secured 51 votes against 27 for Murad Ebrahim during the first plenary session of the 80-member Bangsamoro Parliament in Cotabato City, the regional capital, according to an official statement.
One lawmaker was absent, while another abstained.
The assembly also elected lawyer Amer Zaakaria "Mikee" A. Rakim as speaker with 51 votes.
Both officials were sworn into office after the vote.
Earlier Friday, 79 of the 80 lawmakers took their oaths following the region's first parliamentary elections on Sept. 14.
The vote marked a milestone in a decades-long peace process that led to the establishment of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) in 2019.
The region had been governed by an interim administration initially led by Ebrahim, chairman of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF).
Macacua, a former chief of staff of the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces, succeeded Ebrahim in March 2025 after being appointed chief minister by Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
The elections followed the 2014 Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro, which paved the way for the creation of the Muslim-majority autonomous region and the transition from armed conflict to parliamentary governance.
The new parliament comprises 40 regional party representatives, 32 district representatives and eight sectoral representatives.
Macacua's Bangsamoro Federalist Party secured 16 seats in the elections, followed by Ebrahim's United Bangsamoro Justice Party (UBJP) with 15.

Türkiye's economic confidence index falls 3.9% in October
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:09:37 UTC
18:09:37 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
Türkiye's economic confidence index fell 3.9% month-on-month to 97.3 in October, official data showed on Friday.
The drop pushed the index below the 100-point threshold, down from 101.3 in September, according to the Turkish Statistical Institute.
A reading above 100 indicates an optimistic economic outlook, while a reading below 100 reflects pessimism.
The decline was driven primarily by a sharp drop in consumer confidence, which sank 7.7% from the previous month to 84.8 in October.
Confidence in the real sector, representing the manufacturing industry, decreased 1.4% month-on-month to 101.1.
The services confidence index fell 2.4% from September to 109.2.
In contrast, the retail trade confidence index rose 1.1% on a monthly basis to reach 112.5.
The construction sector confidence index edged up 0.4% month-on-month to 83.3.
