Türkiye's tourism revenue rises 5% to $25.5B in Q3
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:09:20 UTC
18:09:20 KST

Gokhan Ergocun
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
Türkiye's tourism revenue rose 5% year-on-year to $25.53 billion in the third quarter of 2026, official data showed on Friday.
Revenue generated directly from visitors amounted to $25.29 billion, while transit passenger income contributed $231.96 million, according to the Turkish Statistical Institute.
Turkish citizens residing abroad accounted for 14% of total tourism revenue during the July-September period.
Individual expenditures made up $17.11 billion of the quarterly total, while package tour spending stood at $8.18 billion.
The number of departing visitors slipped 1.6% year-on-year to 23.26 million in the third quarter.
Turkish citizens living abroad represented 13.6% of all visitors, totaling 3.16 million people.
Visitors staying overnight spent an average of $107 per night, while the average spending for expatriate Turkish citizens was $68 per night.
Package tours accounted for 32.3% of total expenditures, followed by food and beverages at 20.5% and accommodation at 12.5%.
Health-related expenditures jumped 23.6% compared to the third quarter of 2025, accommodation spending rose 19% and domestic transportation expenses climbed 12.1%.
Travel, entertainment, sports and cultural activities were the primary reasons for visiting Türkiye, cited by 74.5% of visitors, followed by visiting relatives and friends at 16.9% and shopping at 3.7%.
Among expatriate Turkish citizens, visiting relatives and friends was the leading motivation, accounting for 63.9% of visits.
Tourism expenditure, consisting of spending by Turkish residents traveling abroad, surged 22.6% year-on-year to $3.04 billion in the third quarter.
Individual spending abroad totaled $2.57 billion, while package tour expenses accounted for $467.64 million.
The number of Turkish residents traveling abroad increased 24.2% year-on-year to 4.2 million, with an average expenditure of $723 per person.

Adel Abdel Rahim and Lina Altawell
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
A drone attack on an electricity substation in the northern Sudanese city of Shendi early Friday caused a citywide blackout, eyewitnesses told Anadolu.
Witnesses reported hearing explosions and seeing smoke rising from the facility in River Nile state.
Videos circulated by activists on social media also appeared to show a fire at the site.
There was no immediate comment from Sudanese authorities on the incident or the extent of the damage.
The strike followed drone attacks Thursday on the Umm Dabakir thermal power station in White Nile state and the Kadugli power station in South Kordofan state.
On Wednesday, drones targeted the Al-Managil power station and other sites in central Gezira state, cutting electricity to the city.
A day earlier, Sudan's Energy and Petroleum Ministry reported widespread outages across several states, including Khartoum and River Nile, after a drone strike knocked a power station out of service. The ministry blamed the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
On Monday, Sudan Electricity Holding Company accused the RSF of targeting five electricity substations in Sennar, Gedaref and Gezira states.
Sudanese authorities and rights groups have repeatedly accused the group of attacking civilian infrastructure. The RSF generally does not respond to such allegations and maintains that it works to "protect civilians."
The Sudanese army and the RSF have been fighting since April 2023 in a conflict stemming from disagreements over the integration of the country's military forces.
The war has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, amid a worsening humanitarian and hunger crisis.

UK house prices grow at slowest pace in two years as mortgage rates rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:05:48 UTC
18:05:48 KST

UK house prices grew by an annual rate of just 0.5% in October, the slowest pace in more than two years, as higher mortgage rates put off potential buyers.
The average price for a property in the UK stood at £273,566 in October, flat on the previous month and down from 0.8% in the year to September, according to the lender Nationwide.
The slowdown in the market comes as buyers face higher borrowing costs. This month the average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage hit the 6% barrier for the first time in three years.
The average stood at 5.99% on Thursday, according to the financial information provider Moneyfacts, while the average two-year rate was not far behind at 5.97%.
There has been no change in the Bank of England base rate since last December but volatility in the bond market has driven up the swap rates that influence the pricing of fixed-rate mortgages.
While the Bank of England has kept its key interest rate on hold at 3.75%, expectations are growing that next week the monetary policy committee will vote to increase the rate for the first time in three years to 4%.
Robert Gardner, the chief economist at Nationwide, said the Middle East conflict had fed concerns around inflation, driving up expectations of higher interest rates.
Property prices are likely to fall further, he said. “Surveyors report that new buyer inquiries remain weak.
“Consumer sentiment dipped noticeably in October, with households becoming less confident about the outlook for the general economy as well as their own financial situation in the year ahead.”
Tom Bill, the head of UK residential research at Knight Frank, added that the impact of rising mortgage costs “eclipses any support measure announced in this week’s budget”.
This week the chancellor, John Healey, confirmed the government’s new £4.7bn Your First Home scheme, which is designed to give a helping hand to first-time buyers who do not have access to the “bank of mum and dad”.
Bill added: “The absence of major shocks from the chancellor may produce a modest relief bounce in coming months. However, asking prices will need to reflect the much tougher financial landscape that buyers face.”
Rob Wood, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Pantheon Macroeconomics, said the government’s new scheme could provide a “modest boost” to the market but that prices were likely to remain subdued next year.

Russian independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta to close
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:05:21 UTC
18:05:21 KST

The Russian independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta has announced it is closing, citing pressure from authorities who recently searched the home of its senior editor and earlier this year detained one of its journalists.
“Novaya Gazeta is ceasing to exist,” the editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, said in a video statement published on YouTube on Friday. “The Russian authorities – the Russian special services – have forced the editorial team to end its work.”
Russia has introduced near-Soviet levels of censorship since sending troops to Ukraine, pushing the vast majority of independent journalists into exile. Novaya Gazeta, a bastion of independent journalism in Russia, is classed by Moscow as a “foreign agent”, a label used to stifle dissent.
Sokolov said: “Novaya Gazeta has been killed … On November 9 we will turn off the lights in our home, where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down the servers and leave.”
This month Sokolov was taken in for questioning and Russian authorities searched his home over a criminal case involving one of his colleagues, Oleg Roldugin, who was arrested in April.
Roldugin was detained and charged with “unlawful access to computerised information”, without any details being given. He pleaded not guilty, according to the state RIA news agency.
Roldugin is awaiting trial while under house arrest that has been extended until 10 November, according to Novaya Gazeta.
Russia has intensified its crackdown on independent news outlets since its offensive on Ukraine in February 2022. Novaya Gazeta cut down production inside Russia after the offensive began. Authorities revoked its media licence the same year.
The paper’s then editor-in-chief, Dmitry Muratov, jointly won the Nobel peace prize in 2021 for his “efforts to safeguard freedom of expression” at the helm of the paper.

Russian attacks across Ukraine kill 27, injure 127 over past day as 'horrific attack' strikes Dnipro train station
At least 27 people were killed and 127 injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, with a daytime drone strike on Dnipro's train station accounting for the highest number of casualties, local authorities said.
A Russian attack struck a platform at Dnipro railway station on the morning of Oct. 29, killing at least 15 people and injuring at least 14 others, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.
A passenger train was preparing to depart for Zaporizhzhia when the station was struck by a Russian jet-powered drone, Ukrainian Railways wrote on social media. According to Ukraine's Air Force, Dnipro was targeted by four Russian jet-powered drones at around 11 a.m., three of which were shot down by Ukrainian air defenses before reaching their targets.
"A horrific Russian attack on Dnipro train station," President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on social media in response to the attack. "The Russians used a drone to attack a platform where a regular commuter train and a regular passenger train were standing."
International leaders reacted throughout the day, condemning the attacks against the backdrop of reported progress in peace negotiations.
Later in the day, Dnipro Mayor Borys Filatov reported that a Russian drone struck the dormitory of a vocational school in Dnipro, setting the entire fifth floor on fire. There were no injuries, Filatov said, as the students had managed to reach the shelter before the strike.
Throughout the day, Russian attacks across Dnipropetrovsk Oblast injured four more people, including a 15-year-old girl, Hanzha said in an evening statement on Oct.29.
Following the Russian attacks overnight, about 350,000 people in the oblast were left without electricity, Hanzha said in the early morning.
Beyond strikes on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Russia launched ballistic missiles, four guided aerial missiles, and 113 Shahed-type drones, including 83 jet-powered drones, against Ukraine overnight on Oct. 30, according to Ukraine's Air Force.
The main targets of the attack were in Kyiv, Poltava, and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts, according to the Air Force.
Ukrainian air defenses intercepted or suppressed three of the guided missiles and 96 Russian Shahed-type drones, including 71 jet-powered drones, across 17 locations, the Air Force said.
The Air Force did not specify how many Russian ballistic missiles were launched or how many were intercepted.
In Chernihiv Oblast, Russian forces struck central Chernihiv in northern Ukraine around noon on Oct. 29 with Banderol cruise missiles, killing two 15-year-old girls, regional governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
The attack injured 25 other people, including four children, Chaus said. The youngest child is 10 months old, while the others include a 10-year-old girl and boys aged 16 and 17, he added. Eight people remain hospitalized.
Oct. 30 has been declared a day of mourning in Chernihiv.
In the city of Kremenchuk in Poltava Oblast, at least three people were killed and 32 injured, including six children, after Russian drones struck an apartment building in a residential area, regional governor Vitalii Diakivnych said.
Oct. 30 has been declared a day of mourning in Poltava Oblast.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Russian attacks killed two people and injured 23 others, including a child, over the past day, the local authorities said.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks over the past day injured five people, regional governor Vadym Filashkin said.
Russian attacks over the past day killed four people and injured 21 others in Kharkiv Oblast, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
Four people were killed and 12 others injured in a Russian attack on the city of Izium, while six people were injured in Lozova. Three more people were injured in separate attacks in the city of Kharkiv, the village of Shevchenkove, and the village of Zatyshshia.
Russian forces attacked the oblast using FPV drones, other types of drones, glide bombs, and missiles, Syniehubov added.
In southern Kherson Oblast, a localized ceasefire aimed at allowing the evacuation of people from Russian-occupied Oleshky remains in effect. Regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin reported that one person was injured by the explosion of a Russian mine. No shelling or strikes targeting civilian or critical infrastructure were recorded over the past day, he said.
In Kyiv, Russian ballistic missile and drone attacks overnight killed one person and injured another, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration. In the Dniprovskyi District, a residential building was damaged in the attack, while a fire broke out at a non-residential building in the Darnytskyi District.
In Sumy Oblast, Russian attacks over the past day injured one person, according to the regional military administration. Russian forces attacked nine communities in the oblast using artillery, mortars, FPV drones, other drones, and glide bombs.

Hsiao calls for trusted drone supply chain at Taiwan forum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:02:49 UTC
18:02:49 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) called for a China-free drone supply chain and closer international cooperation at the 2026 Taiwan Drone Forum on Friday, CNA reported.
Hsiao said that although Taiwan entered the drone industry relatively recently, it has strengths in semiconductors, precision engineering, and advanced manufacturing. She added that Taiwan’s drone exports in the first half of 2026 exceeded those for all of 2025.
Hsiao said President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) aims to strengthen Taiwan’s self-defense and deterrence through drone development. The government’s approach combines security needs with civilian innovation and international cooperation, she said.
Hsiao also praised the Global UAV Academy for connecting the public and private sectors and promoting international cooperation. She outlined three priorities for strengthening Taiwan’s position in the drone supply chain for democracies: trusted components, AI and software innovation, and international partnerships.
On supply chains, Hsiao said authoritarian regimes exploit backdoors and other countries’ dependence on their products. She said democracies need reliable alternatives and that Taiwan aims to ensure components such as microprocessors and flight controllers meet cybersecurity and operational standards.
On technology, Hsiao said AI and software innovation are crucial to drone development. Taiwan is integrating AI into autonomous platforms to enable real-time decisions and navigation when GPS is unavailable, she said.
On international cooperation, Hsiao said Taiwan should work with other countries on research and development, technology transfer, production, and procurement. She said its development and mass-production capabilities could help meet global demand.
Hsiao cited the foreign ministry’s donation of four maritime patrol and rescue drones to Palau, along with training, as an example of drone diplomacy, per CNA. Taiwan can also strengthen cooperation by sharing its expertise in civilian applications, she said.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Council of Indigenous Peoples Minister Ljaucu Zingrur (曾智勇) apologized Friday for comments he made at a campaign event for Taitung County Councilor Lavuras (何長成) on Saturday, saying he had failed to consider his official capacity when making the remarks.
While voicing support for Taiwu Township Mayor Pan Ming-fu’s (潘明福) reelection bid in Pingtung County, Zingrur said he had promised to approve NT$25 million (US$766,300) in funding before reviewing the documents, per China Times. He added that because he knew Pan but not his opponent, he would not be able to approve subsidies if Pan lost the election.
Zingrur later apologized, saying his lighthearted remarks about government operations failed to take his position as a government official into consideration, per CNA. He stressed that Pan had submitted the relevant documents and that the infrastructure project was subject to all required oversight.
Zingrur emphasized that, as council minister, his duty was to serve all Indigenous peoples, regardless of their political affiliations.
KMT candidate for Taiwu Township mayor Ljavuras Paljasasav (曾大衛) said that while he respected Zingrur’s personal relationship with Pan, the minister should not have suggested the distribution of state resources could depend on political affiliation.
KMT Legislative Caucus Secretary-General Hsu Yu-chen (許宇甄) accused Zingrur of violating laws governing political neutrality among government officials, per Tai Sounds. She also called on the council to disclose information about the subsidy projects Zingrur mentioned at Saturday’s event.
DPP Legislator Saidhai Tahovecahe (伍麗華) acknowledged that Zingrur had misspoken. However, she said statistics showed no disparities in central government subsidies to Indigenous municipalities, noting that KMT-governed townships received slightly more funding than those governed by the DPP.

21.47% of students earn top grade in Taiwan English listening test
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:02:28 UTC
18:02:28 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A total of 21.47% of students who took Taiwan’s first Test of English Listening Comprehension (TELC) for the 2027 academic year earned the top grade, down from 22.59% in the same session last year, according to statistics released Friday by the College Entrance Examination Center.
A total of 90,914 students registered for the test, which was administered across 33 examination districts and 2,647 testing rooms. The overall absentee rate was 3.6%, up 0.26 percentage points from 3.34% in the first test session last academic year.
TELC grades are divided into four levels: A (almost full comprehension), B (general comprehension), C (partial comprehension), and F (minimal comprehension). Of the 87,644 students who sat for the exam, 21.47% earned an A, 37.15% a B, 36.12% a C, and 5.26% an F.
The test consists of 40 items across five sections: picture description, question-response, conversations, short talks, and long-passage listening.
Students performed best in the conversations section, with a correct-answer rate of 73.29%, followed by picture description at 67.37% and question-response at 65.17%. Short talks and long-passage listening had the lowest correct-answer rates, at 61.16% and 60.57%, respectively.
Among students earning an A, correct-answer rates exceeded 90% in four of the five sections, with conversations producing the highest rate at 96.88%. Their correct-answer rate for long-passage listening was slightly lower, at 89.77%.
For students earning a B, correct-answer rates ranged from 69.26% for long-passage listening to 85.16% for conversations. Students earning a C performed best in conversations, at 54.26%, while those receiving an F had their lowest correct-answer rate in long-passage listening, at 19.85%.
Compared with the average results of the first test sessions over the previous four academic years, this year’s distribution showed a slightly higher proportion of C grades, at 36.12%, up 1.13 percentage points. The proportions of A, B, and F grades were slightly lower, by 0.21, 0.6, and 0.32 percentage points, respectively.
Overall, the results showed little difference between male and female students. Boys accounted for 48.36% of test takers and girls 51.64%. Boys had higher proportions of both A and F grades, while girls had higher proportions of B and C grades.
The center reported 350 examination violations, down 99 from 449 during the same testing session last academic year. The most common violation involved students failing to present an original, valid identification document, accounting for 321 cases, compared with 412 a year earlier.

Five Chinese golfers advance at Asia-Pacific Amateur Championship
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:02:28 CST
18:02:28 KST

AUCKLAND, New Zealand, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Defending champion Fifa Laopakdee of Thailand maintained his lead after the second round of the 2026 Asia-Pacific Amateur Championship at Te Arai Links in New Zealand on Friday, carding a one-over 72 to reach seven under par for a 36-hole total of 135, two strokes clear of the field.
Five of the seven Chinese golfers competing in the tournament made the cut, with Wu Qiyou leading the Chinese contingent in a tie for sixth.
The 72-hole stroke-play tournament features a cut after 36 holes, with the top 60 players and ties advancing to the final two rounds. After Friday's second round, the cut fell at 155, or 13 over par, with 62 players qualifying for the next round.
Laopakdee, who secured Thailand's first AAC title last year, started his second round from the 10th tee on Friday morning. He was two under par through his first nine holes, but faced tougher conditions as the wind picked up after the turn. He eventually signed for a one-over-par 72.
"As you can see it's a little windy," said Laopakdee, 21. "Overall, it was a grind out there for me. Had a great front nine, shot two under par, then back nine, just didn't make any putts. Got two 3-putts and then coming down the stretch had a great chance of birdies but I just missed all of them. But if you ask me all week, I would take seven under for the first two rounds, and I think I'm in good position for the weekend."
Wu sits in a tie for sixth after two rounds, six strokes behind Laopakdee. He carded six birdies and seven bogeys on Friday to finish one over par for the round.
"There's been a lot of mistakes, and that's something I can work on over the next two rounds. In these windy conditions, the wind has a big impact on the putting line. It's important to get used to the tougher conditions and try to avoid taking more than two putts on each green," Wu said.
Chinese golfers Li Zhi, Zhou Ziqin, Hou Zenghao and Wang Yixiang also made the cut, while Cui Jingguo and Liu Yiming missed out on the final two rounds.
The 17th edition of the championship runs from October 29 to November 1 on Te Arai Links' South Course, with 120 players from 39 countries and regions competing in the 72-hole stroke-play event.
The winner will earn invitations to the 2027 Masters Tournament, the 155th Open Championship and the 132nd Amateur Championship. ■

France's GDP contracts 0.1 pct in Q3
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
17:02:14 CST
18:02:14 KST

PARIS, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- France's gross domestic product (GDP) contracted 0.1 percent in the third quarter of 2026, according to preliminary data released Friday.
The decline came despite continued growth in final domestic demand excluding inventories. Household consumption accelerated, rising by 0.4 percent after a 0.2-percent increase in the second quarter, while government consumption grew by 0.3 percent, following a 0.4-percent increase.
Overall, final domestic demand excluding inventories contributed 0.1 percentage points to GDP growth, unchanged from the previous quarter, according to figures published by the French National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (INSEE).
The contribution of foreign trade to GDP growth turned negative in the third quarter, subtracting 0.6 percentage points from growth, compared with a positive contribution of 0.6 percentage points in the previous quarter. Exports fell by 1.7 percent, reversing a 2.8-percent increase in the second quarter, while imports remained almost unchanged, rising by 0.1 percent after a 0.9-percent increase.
INSEE added that France's consumer price index is expected to surge by 3.4 percent year on year in October, up from 3.1 percent in September.
Inflation is expected to accelerate mainly due to energy prices, which are set to rise for the fourth consecutive month, particularly because of higher gas and petroleum product prices.
"Growth has been absent for three consecutive quarters," the country's Economy and Finance Minister Roland Lescure said Friday in an interview with local broadcaster Franceinfo. "If we do not achieve the fiscal consolidation set out in the budget, we will hit a wall." ■

Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan sign 14 cooperation documents at interregional forum
Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan have signed 14 documents on interregional, interagency and business cooperation during the II Kazakhstan-Kyrgyzstan Interregional Cooperation Forum in Bishkek, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The forum, titled “The Role of Regions in Developing Strategic Partnership,” is co-chaired by Kazakh Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and Chairman of the Kyrgyz Cabinet of Ministers and Head of the Presidential Administration Adylbek Kasymaliev.
The following documents were signed in the field of interregional cooperation:
- A Memorandum of Cooperation between the administration of East Kazakhstan region and the Office of the Presidential Plenipotentiary Representative in Kyrgyzstan’s Issyk-Kul region.
- An Agreement on establishing twin-city relations and developing cooperation between the Shchuchinsk-Burabay resort area in Kazakhstan’s Akmola region and the Issyk-Kul Lake resort area in Kyrgyzstan’s Issyk-Kul region.
- A Memorandum of Understanding between Almaty region and the Office of the Presidential Plenipotentiary Representative in Kyrgyzstan’s Jalal-Abad region.
- A Memorandum of Understanding between Kyzylorda region and the Office of the Presidential Plenipotentiary Representative in Kyrgyzstan’s Jalal-Abad region.
- A Memorandum of Understanding between Karaganda region and the Office of the Presidential Plenipotentiary Representative in Kyrgyzstan’s Jalal-Abad region.
- A Memorandum of Cooperation between the adinistration of Zhetysu region and the Office of the Presidential Plenipotentiary Representative in Kyrgyzstan’s Naryn region.
- An action plan for 2026–2030 to implement the Agreement on establishing twin-city relations between the administration of Almaty and Bishkek Mayor’s Office, signed on December 12, 1997.
- A Memorandum on establishing twin-city relations between Turkistan and the city of Manas in Kyrgyzstan’s Jalal-Abad region.
In the healthcare sector, the following agreement was signed:
- An Agreement between the ministries of healthcare of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan on cooperation in cross-country procurement of medicines and medical devices.
The following documents were signed in the field of business cooperation:
- A contract between Kazakhstan’s Dobrye Traditsii and Kyrgyzstan’s Prod Impex LLC for the supply of canned products.
- A distribution agreement between Kazakhstan’s Dobrye Traditsii LLP and Kyrgyzstan’s Alaiku Organics LLC for the supply of traditional beverages.
- A distribution agreement between Kazakhstan’s Satu Company LLP and Kyrgyzstan’s Alaiku Organics LLC for the supply of traditional beverages.
- A cooperation agreement between Kazakhstan’s Astana Motors and Kyrgyzstan’s Trust Technologies LLC (IVOX Group) to promote Kazakh-made commercial and special-purpose vehicles on the Kyrgyz market.
- A Memorandum of Cooperation between Kazakhstan’s GT OilService and Kyrgyzstan’s Tan Auto LLC to promote FerTurino motor oil on the Kyrgyz market.
Earlier, it was reported that Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov arrived in Bishkek on an official visit.
The II Kazakhstan-Kyrgyzstan Interregional Cooperation Forum has kicked off at the Ala-Archa State Residence in Bishkek today.
Addressing the forum, Bektenov said that Kazakhstan’s trade turnover with Kyrgyzstan reached $2.3 billion in 2025, up 33% year-on-year.

The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) confirmed the alert upgrade, warning of increased volcanic activity and the potential for further eruptions.
According to PHIVOLCS, the eruption produced a dense ash plume that rapidly rose approximately 3,000 meters above the volcano's summit crater. Moderate winds carried the plume west-southwest, with ashfall expected in the communities of Daraga, Guinobatan and neighboring municipalities in Albay province.
The agency explained that Alert Level 3 indicates a significant increase in volcanic activity, including sustained volcanic earthquakes and powerful emissions of steam and ash.
PHIVOLCS warned that Mayon has entered a new phase of magmatic eruption, increasing the likelihood of lava flows in the coming days and weeks.
Authorities also cautioned residents about potential volcanic hazards, including lava flows, rockfalls and other dangerous phenomena associated with increased volcanic activity.
Mayon volcano, also known as Mount Mayon, is an active stratovolcano located in Albay province in the Bicol region of the Philippines, on the southeastern part of Luzon Island. It is among the country's most closely monitored active volcanoes due to its history of eruptions and potential risks to nearby communities.

WHO names candidates for director-general
Seven candidates will compete to become the World Health Organization’s next director-general. Member states submitted their nominations ahead of the May 2027 election, Qazinform News Agency reports.
WHO announced the candidates on October 29. Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Belgium, Spain, Indonesia, China and Botswana each proposed a nominee.
Hanan Mohammed Al-Kuwari, nominated by Qatar, served as public health minister from 2016 to 2024. She also led Hamad Medical Corporation from 2007 to 2024. She now advises Qatar’s prime minister on public health affairs. Al-Kuwari chaired WHO’s Executive Board in 2023-2024.
Hanan Balkhy, Saudi Arabia’s nominee, became WHO’s regional director for the Eastern Mediterranean in February 2024. Previously, she served as WHO’s assistant director-general for antimicrobial resistance from 2019 to 2024. A physician specializing in pediatric infectious diseases, she also led infection prevention programs in Saudi Arabia.
Hans Henri P. Kluge, nominated by Belgium, has led WHO's Regional Office for Europe since 2020. Previously, he headed its Division of Health Systems and Public Health from 2009 to 2020. His earlier work included tuberculosis programs with WHO and Doctors Without Borders. He also helped establish WHO’s primary health care center in Almaty.
María P. Neira, Spain’s nominee, has led WHO’s work on environmental health and climate change. She previously served as Spain’s vice minister of health and headed its food safety agency. Neira began her humanitarian work with Doctors Without Borders in Central American refugee camps. Her medical background includes endocrinology and public health.
Budi Gunadi Sadikin, nominated by Indonesia, has served as health minister since December 2020. He led the country’s COVID-19 response and national vaccination program. Previously, he served as vice minister of state-owned enterprises and chief executive of Bank Mandiri. His career spans banking, industry and government.
Li Song, China’s nominee, has served as a secretary of the All-China Women’s Federation secretariat since September 2023. She previously headed the National Health Commission’s Department of Women and Children Health. Her work has focused on maternal and child health, alongside women’s rights and development. She holds a doctorate in medicine from Peking University’s School of Public Health.
Gevorg Tamamyan, nominated by Botswana, is an Armenian specialist in pediatric cancer and blood disorders. He heads the Pediatric Cancer and Blood Disorders Center of Armenia. He also leads Yerevan State Medical University’s Department of Pediatric Oncology and Hematology. Since 2024, he has served as president of the International Society of Pediatric Oncology’s Asian branch.
The candidates will meet member state representatives in Geneva on November 18-19. WHO will broadcast the forum in its six official languages.
In early 2027, the Executive Board will shortlist five candidates and interview them. It will then nominate up to three for consideration by the World Health Assembly.
A second candidates’ forum will take place on March 15, 2027.
The World Health Assembly will appoint the new director-general in May 2027. The successful candidate will take office on August 16, 2027.

The seasonally adjusted index of industrial production, which excludes the agriculture, livestock and fishery sectors, grew 3.0 percent in September from a month earlier, the fastest monthly increase in more than 15 years, since March 2011, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics.
Industrial output turned around from a contraction of 1.2 percent in August, driven by a booming semiconductor sector, the end of labor strikes at automakers and the positive impact of new vehicle launches.
The retail sales index, a key gauge of consumer spending, rose 3.6 percent last month, posting the largest increase in three years and seven months, since February 2023.
Sales of durable goods, such as passenger cars, advanced 4.4 percent, while sales of non-durable goods, including food and beverages, rose 4.2 percent.
Facility investment also rebounded, expanding 5.3 percent in September from the previous month after plunging 9.7 percent in August. ■

The Best Leaf Blower We’ve Tested Is Ready for Halloween
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:01:00 UTC
18:01:00 KST

Where I live, it's officially leaf season, and they are everywhere. Driveways, sidewalks, and even blowing into my garage, where they stick to people's feet as they come inside. Luckily, we have exhaustively tested all the major battery-powered leaf blowers on both fabric leaves and concrete blocks, and one model blew away the competition: the Ego Power+ 880 CFM, which delivered gaslike power while somehow also being the quietest. It even knocked over a 5-pound brick paver without having to engage turbo mode—the only one we tested that was able to do so.
Luckily, it's on sale at Lowe's this week, along with an extra backup battery so you never have to worry about running out of juice. It serves a practical purpose, to be sure, but there's also a less practical purpose that WIRED contributing reviewer and leaf blower expert Sal Vaglica is happy to demonstrate.
Watch Sal show you how to turn the Ego leaf blower into a DIY toilet paper cannon—just in time for Halloween. (Sale ends November 4.) —Kat Merck
How to Build a Toilet Paper Cannon
With a few hardware-store parts—some you may already have at home—you can turn a battery-powered leaf blower into a toilet paper cannon that unrolls a single- or double-ply roll in seconds. Once assembled, you can use it to decorate a house or children. A blower’s airflow, usually measured in cubic feet per minute (cfm) and miles per hour (mph), helps power the effect. The fast-moving air creates a lower-pressure stream, while the still air around the roll pushes it toward that stream. As air follows the roll’s curve, it helps lift the roll, and friction carries the paper along. Bernoulli’s principle is part of the trick, along with curved-surface lift and the airflow pulling the paper forward.
To figure out where to position the toilet paper relative to the blower, I spoke with Saffron Wyse, associate principal at the international engineering firm Thornton Tomasetti, where she specializes in fluid dynamics. “Positioning the roll underneath the nozzle is slightly better because then you’re pulling the paper upward into the airstream, and you want it to go upward because that stream is going to do the bulk of the work for you,” she says.
All leaf blowers come with a tapered round tube, but some, including the Ego I used, also have a wide, flat attachment. The tapered round tube is the most stable solution, says Wyse, because it gives you a tall, wide airstream. But I’m building this for speed, which favors the flat attachment. "Having a thin nozzle arrangement that’s trying to flatten the airstream probably gives you more force, more velocity, so it’s likely to go further,” says Wyse. You could replicate such an attachment with duct tape and cardboard if your leaf blower didn’t come with one.
How to Build a Toilet Paper Cannon, step-by-step:
Start with a mini paint roller made for standard nap rollers. Avoid models designed for foam rollers, because they are too narrow. Slide a toilet paper roll onto the cage. If it fits loosely, wrap the cage first in painter’s tape, then in duct tape, adding layers until the roll grips securely. The painter’s tape ensures you’ll be able to use the roller for painting later on.
With the TP on the roller, position it beneath the leaf blower’s nozzle, about 3 to 4 inches from the tip and centered in the airstream. Use 12-inch strips of duct tape to secure the roller handle to the blower first, measure again, then add more tape to secure it. To help protect the nozzle from adhesive residue, apply painter’s tape to it before adding the duct tape.
Pull the first few sheets free from the roll, squeeze the trigger, and let the paper fly. —Sal Vaglica

Houthis sending Taiz ‘back to the stone age’, governor of besieged Yemen city says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:00:50 UTC
18:00:50 KST

The Houthis are trying to send the city of Taiz back to the stone age, the city’s governor said in a briefing designed to urge the international community to do more to lift the month-long siege.
Nabil Shamsan said massacres were taking place in Yemen’s third city, that oxygen and water supplies were running out and that rubbish was piling up in the streets due to landfill sites being either full or inaccessible.
The city’s daily minimum water needs are estimated at about 35,000 cubic metres, he said, but no more than 1,000 cubic metres was being allowed to reach it each day and that water shipments were being stopped at Houthi roadblocks surrounding the city.
With food stocks depleted and the price of wheat soaring, he said “citizens are heading back to the stone age”. Restaurants had closed due to the lack of fuel.
Shamsan said that as many as 1,800 people were in need of dialysis treatment but were unable to access supplies, that 120 health centres had been suspended and schools had closed, affecting hundreds of thousands of children.
He said 64 people had been killed, including civilians, from August to 20 October 2026 and a further 173 injured. More than 6,400 newly displaced families, each averaging seven members, had come to the city to flee the fighting.
“We are not talking about living, just surviving,” he said.
His account contradicted one given by the Houthi leader, Abdul-Malik Badr al-Din al-Houthi, who said: “The way is open for food, medicine, and humanitarian aid to enter the city and even for Saudi-backed groups to do so. Anyone who wants to verify that there is no siege on the city of Taiz can go to the city and see.”
Shamsan said that Houthis forces had a near-total grip on the roads into the city, adding the group had issued a choice to the more than 800,000 inside the city “either to leave or to die”.
He accused the Houthis of not waging a military battle but a battle to change the identity of Yemen, with captured villages being taken over by new religious leaders with education and religious curricula being changed. “This is not a military war but a war of vengeance,” he said.
People in occupied territories were being required to show loyalty to the Zaydi religion and to sign forms affirming they had joined the Houthis. “They are not starting a war but an revolution in identity,” Shamsan said, adding that scores of children from each village were being forcibly ordered without their parents’ consent to join the frontlines in Saada and elsewhere.
Vowing the people of Taiz would resist until the end, he said statements of solidarity were of no use and that what was needed was access for aid agencies, including the UN, to deliver supplies to the city.
Shamsan was reluctant to divulge details of the state of the military campaign, but said shelling of the city was becoming more frequent and that communication between the city and rural areas had broken down. Houthis now controlled the mobile networks and were sending messages to citizens to end their resistance, while eavesdropping on all conversations, he said. Mobile networks were “completely disrupted”, he said, adding that he was speaking only 2-5km from the frontlines.
Most independent agencies agree that life inside the city is rapidly deteriorating. Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “Renewed efforts by the Houthis to cut off food, water, and medicine to Taiz show their utter disregard for civilian lives.
“Throughout the 12-year-long siege of Taiz, the Houthis have bombed, starved and denied humanitarian aid to a million residents of the city with scant adherence to international law.”

‘It’s been a whirlwind’: the Essex lawyer who quit her job and became voice of Netflix’s hit show Spike
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:00:50 UTC
18:00:50 KST

Emily McGonagle was on maternity leave from her job as a lawyer, juggling the care of her new baby and her toddler son, when the daily diet of TV cartoons made her think about an unlikely career change.
Watching Peppa Pig and Paw Patrol, her older son’s favourites, “it occurred to me: who does this job?”, says the 42-year-old from Essex. “How do you get into it? Even when I was watching TV commercials, I’d think: well, how do you do that?”
McGonagle had been commuting to her demanding legal job in London from the family home in Colchester, but was ready for a more flexible work-life balance. She had always loved performing in school plays and knew she had a talent for accents – so why not look into how to become a voice actor?
A decade on, she is voicing one of the most popular Netflix TV shows in the world. McGonagle plays eight characters in an animated series called Spike about a young dragon and his friends. When the programme launched on the streaming network on 12 October it quickly became the seventh-most-watched programme globally in any genre.
“These past few weeks have been a bit of a whirlwind and very surreal,” says McGonagle. “It’s just amazing to me that one day I was watching Peppa Pig with my kids wondering how you get into it, and today I’m turning on Netflix and seeing Spike next to Peppa Pig in the top 10. It is honestly amazing. I could never in my wildest dreams have imagined that I would get to this point.”
When first looking into the industry as a young mum, she says: “I realised that with the right training and setup with professional audio equipment, I could do it from home – which was a revelation to me because I had assumed everything was done in a studio.”
With the support of her husband, Ciarán, she converted a large wardrobe into a soundproofed vocal booth and began auditioning for voiceover jobs that were offered online. She started with a few corporate training videos, before getting some commercial TV and radio adverts, even voicing a Formula One-themed go-kart ride.
But the ambition to work in children’s animation never wavered, so she looked into drama classes at her local theatre, then took some specialist courses in acting for voice animation. The roles in Spike came about when McGonagle saw the project advertised “on LinkedIn, of all places” by the Lithuanian animation company behind it. Originally screened on YouTube, its snowballing popularity among hard-pressed preschooler parents eventually attracted the attention of Netflix.
Voicing multiple different characters in the same project can be a challenge, says McGonagle (She provides the voices for 20 in the video game Game of Thrones: Kingsroad, “and that was a lot”).
How does she keep them distinctive? “I write a bio for my characters and think about what they look like, how old they are, where they might be from and give them some backstory in order to bring that character to life. And then I will adapt my voice to make it younger, make it older, or I might add an accent. It’s all about the way in which you move your body and even your mouth itself.”
The characters she voices in Spike include the main character’s mother, a girl giraffe, a boy elephant, and the canine police officer. Some speak with various English accents, some American. “Those were just the accents and characters I put forward when I auditioned,” she says. “It’s not ultimately my decision.”
“It’s a very international team and we do all communicate online but there haven’t been any in-person meetups. We have spoken on Zoom calls but nobody has ever met in person because we all have our own home studios,” she says.
McGonagle’s sons, Finn and Jack, are now 11 and nine, and far too old for preschool dragons. They must be proud of her unusual career path, though? “They’re not really that bothered by it, which is probably a good thing,” she says. When she read them bedtime stories when they were younger, “honestly, they would just tell me: ‘Ah stop, don’t do the voices’.
“Quite often I’ll be going around the house talking in different voices just to practise and they do get annoyed with it.”

I’m a gen Z voter. Content creators have far less power than politicians think | Alex Bronzini-Vender
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:00:50 UTC
18:00:50 KST

In tight races, any group that shifts a few points can be called decisive. In 2024, however, gen Z voters actually earned the spotlight.
Take Michigan, where Donald Trump won by about 1.4 points: he and Kamala Harris evenly split the youth vote, a 24-point collapse in the Democratic edge since 2020. If young voters made up just 15% of the state’s electorate, their swing toward the president would be worth roughly 3.6 points, larger than Trump’s entire margin of victory.
Ever since, both parties have scrambled to court the tastemakers who seem to have gen Z’s ear.
At her debut briefing, the former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt reserved a “new media seat” in the briefing room, inviting podcasters, influencers and content creators to apply for credentials. The NRCC, House Republicans’ campaign arm, has paid more than $120,000 to a network of conservative influencers, listing the expense simply as “media”.
Not to be outdone, the DNC has partnered with more than 500 online personalities through its “Influencer & Creative” operation – and has lately floated the idea of a creator-hosted debate during the 2028 primaries.
The same wishful theory undergirds all these efforts: both parties seem to think online creators can simply upload political opinions straight into our heads.
As a zoomer myself, I find this theory rather patronizing. More to the point, it isn’t true: there’s little evidence that online creators play much of a role in how zoomers actually vote. And if young voters decide these midterms, influencers shouldn’t get the credit.
Plenty of people watch influencers, but very few people deeply trust them.
In a survey this year by the Media Insight Project, 63% of 18-to-34-year-olds said they get news from influencers “at least sometimes”. Yet among teens and adults who actually receive news from these people, just 9% report having a great deal of confidence in what they are being told. (AI chatbots enjoy a nearly identical rate of trust, at 10%.)
Other polls have found much the same thing: when YouGov surveyed young voters across eight battleground states in September on whom they actually turn to for political advice, half named a family member and three in 10 named a friend. Just 6% named an influencer.
In another survey of young people released this spring by Circle, a civic-engagement research center at Tufts, just 9% of respondents said they got political information from social media posts by influencers and celebrities. Another 14% pointed to podcasts hosted by influencers, artists, comedians or other celebrities.
By contrast, 45% of respondents – the largest share – got their information from political, advocacy, or community organizations they follow, while nearly a third cited conversations with family and friends.
To whatever extent that internet personalities actually persuade people, their powers rest entirely on the illusion that they speak for themselves. Naturally, both parties have responded by shattering that illusion.
Campaigns and their allies increasingly pay for those voices, often at exorbitant prices. In this year’s race for California governor, Tom Steyer paid at least 17 influencers $5,000 or more apiece, while Katie Porter’s campaign paid one lifestyle creator $25,000 for what appeared to be a single post. A TikTok creator with 1.7 million followers said a Republican-affiliated group had offered her $36,000 for a video, and a company with deep Republican ties once paid a squad of gen Z creators to defend Ken Paxton, now Texas’s Republican Senate nominee, on X.
Some influencers attempt to keep these “partnerships” hidden. The New York Times found that Josh Greene, a progressive creator with nearly 800,000 followers, had not always disclosed the fact that he’d taken money from at least seven candidates and allied groups this cycle.
And when the payments do come to light – as they tend to – they risk destroying the very credibility that campaigns were trying to buy. As the Rainey Center for Public Policy found this summer, 47% of voters said they’d trust a creator less after learning a political post had been paid for by a campaign; only 11% said they’d trust them more.
Obviously, the internet matters. Zohran Mamdani, who won young men by roughly 40 points in last year’s New York mayoral race, has said many New Yorkers he met knew him only from his appearances on podcasts such as Flagrant, hosted by the comedian Andrew Schulz. (As Mamdani put it, Democrats should “stop treating young people and young men with the condescension that we often see and hear in our politics”.) And Trump’s tour of the podcasting sphere in 2024 had racked up more than 100 million YouTube views by the day after the election that year.
Still, both appearances were interviews, not simply paid content. Even if the questioning is friendly, the candidates still do most of the talking. And the podcast-interview format itself isn’t magic: Kamala Harris’s appearance on Call Her Daddy seems to have done little to move young voters.
Every older generation finds the next one inscrutable, and gen Z is an especially tough read. Older Americans can be forgiven for struggling to grasp what it means to come of age in the era of social media. (Our memes are, admittedly, really weird.)
Still, if you ignore our screen time, we’re pretty normal after all. Like swing voters twice our age, we’ve ditched the Republican party because prices remain stubbornly high. For all the money Washington is spending to decode our political decision-making, the most surprising thing about gen Z voters may be just how boringly ordinary we are.
- Alex Bronzini-Vender is a writer living in New York

2026 science Nobel Prizes: Who are the winners, and is there a gender gap problem? | Password
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:00:40 UTC
18:00:40 KST

Password is Euronews Tech Talks’ new monthly series unpacking tech and health tech news from Europe and the world. In this first episode, we discover who the scientists awarded Nobel Prizes are, and whether the award has a gender gap issue.
For science enthusiasts, October is an exciting time of year, when the brightest minds are recognised for their work with the Nobel Prizes, the Oscars of the science world.
Earlier this month, Euronews reporters Marta Iraola Iribarren and Pascale Davies were part of the team that followed the awarding of the prestigious science medals in physiology or medicine, physics and chemistry.
In the first episode of Password, our journalists discuss the winners, their discoveries, and why in 2026 only men made it into the group of science laureates.
2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to the United States scientist Karl Deisseroth and German scientists Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.
“It is a method that makes it possible to show how nerve cells shape memories and feeling behaviours in the living brain,” Iraola told Euronews Next.
This research is widely considered a step forward in understanding how the still-mysterious brain works, and could bring about new, important medical applications.
Optogenetics, for instance, is behind a gene therapy that is currently being tested in clinical trials and shows early promise of partly restoring sight in blind people.
2026 Nobel Prize in Physics
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded to the Belgian scientist Francis Halzen for his contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos.
“His work has given us a whole new way to explore the universe,” said Davies. “He turned a massive block of ice in the South Pole into a detector that can see basically almost invisible particles that reach Earth from outer space, and he called the device the IceCube,” she explained.
The IceCube Neutrino Observatory was built between 2004 and 2010, stemming from Halzen’s idea and research. The project now comprises an international team of more than 450 people from 14 countries.
Among them is Gwenhaël Wilberts De Wasseige, a professor at the Université Catholique de Louvain, in Belgium, where Halzen conducted his higher education.
Wilberts De Wasseige explained that despite being based in the United States, Halzen keeps strong ties with Belgium and especially the Belgian universities, four of which are part of the IceCube project.
“It was just a question of time, and to see him getting the prize and dedicating it to all the people that started the adventure with him, continued the adventure and all the PhD students, to all the technicians who keep making the IceCube better, that was something very special,” she told Euronews Next.
2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to French scientist Henri B. Kagan and Japanese scientist Kenso Soai for research into molecular mirror images.
“It has actually very practical applications; one for example is for pharmaceutical development,” Iraola explained.
Some molecules, such as amino acids, occur in two variants that are mirror images of each other, yet living organisms use only one of them. These researchers discovered how chemical reactions can amplify an initial excess of one mirror-image form and produce only one of the two possible forms.
Do Nobel Prizes have a gender gap issue?
Except Anne Carson, who won the Nobel Prize in Literature, and Navanetham Pillay, who won the Nobel Peace Prize, the other 2026 laureates were all men.
“In the science awards, women are underrepresented because this reflects a broader underrepresentation of them in this area of research,” said Iraola. However, she is hopeful that things will change in the future.
Since Nobel Prize awards are handed out to research projects that take decades to develop, today’s winners reflect the gender norms of the 1970s, 1980s and 1990s when science was often inaccessible to women, Iraola explained.
“However, the number of women awarded has slowly increased in recent decades, and hopefully we will keep seeing this trend,” she added.
Euronews Tech Talks is a podcast produced, written, presented and published in English.

SEPA for Ukraine: Cheaper Euro Transfers, Benefits for Business, and a New Level of Financial Integration with the EU
Ukraine

18:00:40 KST

The Verkhovna Rada has until mid-November to consider the legislative package necessary for Ukraine’s accession to the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA). This is the deadline by which Ukraine can submit its application for membership to the European Payments Council. At first glance, this appears to be a technical banking reform, but for Ukrainian businesses and millions of citizens, its implications could be quite practical: cheaper and faster transfers in euros, reduced dependence on correspondent banks, and deeper integration of the Ukrainian financial system with the European one. SEPA primarily concerns payments in euros. The hryvnia remains Ukraine’s national currency.
The main bill, No. 14327-d, was registered on April 6, 2026, and included on the agenda of the current session of the Verkhovna Rada. At the same time, parliament is expected to consider related bills No. 15501 and No. 15503, which are necessary to bring Ukrainian legislation into line with EU requirements and the criteria of the European Payments Council. As of October 29, these bills are still awaiting consideration by parliament.
SEPA is essentially a single area for cashless payments in euros. Its goal is to make fund transfers between banks in different countries as similar as possible to domestic payments—with uniform technical standards, clear rules, and a minimal number of intermediaries.
As of fall 2026, the SEPA network covers 41 countries and territories. In addition to all EU member states, it includes the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein, as well as countries that have recently joined the system, notably Moldova, Albania, Montenegro, North Macedonia, and Serbia. It is important to note that participation in SEPA does not imply either EU membership or a country’s adoption of the euro. However, it does represent a form of partial European integration.
“SEPA is often referred to as a ‘financial visa-free zone,’ and there is some logic to that. But it is more accurate to speak of Ukraine’s connection to Europe’s unified payment infrastructure. This is not a transition to the euro, nor is it the lifting of currency restrictions during martial law. It is the ability to make a transfer in euros from a Ukrainian bank to a bank in Germany, Poland, France, or another SEPA country, or to transfer funds to Ukraine much more cheaply and quickly, just like a regular domestic payment,” notes Olga Vasylevska-Smaglyuk, author of the bill and deputy chair of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Finance, Tax, and Customs Policy
Today, a significant portion of international bank transfers made by Ukrainian businesses go through the correspondent banking system. A payment may involve one or more intermediary banks, and the final fee and the time it takes for funds to be credited are not always clear to the customer in advance.
SEPA creates a more standardized model. One of the basic schemes is the SEPA Credit Transfer—a standard credit transfer in euros. Alongside it is the SEPA Instant Credit Transfer, which enables instant payments, as well as direct debit schemes.
At the same time, Ukraine has been preparing technologically for this integration for several years now. In April 2023, the NBU migrated the Electronic Payment System to the international ISO 20022 standard and switched to 24/7 operation, and since December 2024, instant credit transfers have been operating in Ukraine via the SEP. The NBU itself has referred to IBAN and ISO 20022 as the technological foundation for future integration with SEPA.
The economic impact could be significant. The Ministry of Finance has estimated Ukraine’s potential savings on international transfers following the launch of SEPA at 70–100 million euros annually. Among the expected results, the ministry also cites a reduction in bank fees, faster cross-border payments, and lower transaction costs for exporters.
These savings may be most noticeable not for companies that make a few large payments per year, but for businesses with a steady flow of transactions in euros. These are primarily IT companies, service exporters, small and medium-sized businesses, e-commerce firms, logistics companies, and enterprises that regularly settle accounts with European suppliers.
“For a small exporter, a fee of EUR 20–50 per international payment may seem small, but when there are dozens or hundreds of such payments, the costs become significant. SEPA is particularly important for economies characterized by a large number of relatively small transactions. In addition to the fee itself, businesses gain predictability: it’s easier to plan when the money will reach the counterparty and how much the payment will actually cost,” emphasizes Member of Parliament Olga Vasilevska-Smaglyuk.
For individuals, the effect can be just as noticeable. This includes money transfers between Ukrainians residing in the EU and their families in Ukraine, payments for education, services, and rent, receiving income from European clients, and other transactions permitted by foreign exchange legislation.
The experience of neighboring Moldova is instructive for Ukraine. It joined the SEPA geographical zone in March 2025, and the operational connection of Moldovan banks began on October 6 of that same year. During the first year of operation, approximately 1.2 million transactions were processed via SEPA. According to estimates by the National Bank of Moldova, the average cost of a cross-border transfer in euros fell from the range of EUR 20–150 to approximately EUR 1, and the total savings for citizens and businesses over 12 months amounted to EUR 16.4 million.
It is not possible to mechanically apply Moldova’s figures to Ukraine: the scales of the economies, banking systems, foreign trade, and the volume of international payments differ significantly. At the same time, this example shows that the impact of SEPA can be felt not only in financial sector statistics but directly in customer fees.
However, integration has another side to it. Technologically modernizing banks is not enough to join SEPA. Ukraine must bring its anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing legislation into line with European standards and FATF requirements.
That is why the legislative package largely concerns AML/CFT, the identification of ultimate beneficial owners, the transparency of financial institutions, and access by competent government agencies to the information necessary for financial investigations. The Ministry of Finance explicitly states that fulfilling these conditions is a necessary prerequisite for Ukraine’s application to join SEPA.
“SEPA is not just about low-cost transfers. The European payment system is built on a high level of trust between banks and regulators. Therefore, Ukraine essentially faces a simple choice: if we want to enjoy the benefits of the European financial infrastructure, we must comply with European rules regarding the origin of funds, beneficial ownership, financial monitoring, and anti-money laundering,” the expert explains.
At the same time, the mere adoption of these laws will not mean Ukraine’s immediate accession to SEPA.
After establishing the necessary legislative framework, the country must undergo an assessment procedure by the European Payments Council (EPC). Only after the EPC’s decision can Ukraine be included within the geographic scope of the SEPA schemes. The next stage involves the accession of specific Ukrainian banks and payment institutions to the relevant schemes and ensuring their technical readiness.
Experience from other countries shows that a certain amount of time elapses between a political decision, a country’s inclusion in SEPA, and the actual appearance of such payments in banking applications. For example, the decision to include Serbia was made in May 2025, with the earliest date for operational readiness set for May 2026.
“The biggest mistake is to expect that, after the Verkhovna Rada votes, a transfer from Berlin to Kyiv will cost one euro the very next day. The law opens the door, but what follows requires an application from Ukraine, a decision by the European Payments Council, the integration of banks, and technical implementation. This is a process, not a one-time event,” emphasizes Olga Vasilevska-Smaglyuk
SEPA does not override the currency restrictions imposed by the National Bank during martial law. The infrastructure determines how an authorized payment is technically executed, but it does not create the right to conduct a transaction that is restricted by currency legislation.
Similarly, SEPA does not automatically mean zero bank fees. Fees charged by specific banks may vary, and costs associated with the exchange rate will still apply when converting hryvnia to euros. The main change lies in standardization, a reduction in the number of intermediaries, and a potential sharp decrease in the cost of cross-border euro payments specifically.
For Ukraine, joining SEPA could become one of the most tangible elements of economic integration with the EU for citizens and businesses even before full membership. While trade integration removes barriers to the movement of goods, SEPA effectively eliminates some of the financial “friction” in the movement of money.
And that is precisely why the outcome of the reform should not be assessed solely based on the passage of laws or decisions by the European Payments Council. The true measure of success will be how many Ukrainian banks actually connect to SEPA, what the fees for customers will be, and how much faster and cheaper Ukrainian businesses will be able to receive and send euros.

====================================================================================================

The Iran War’s Impact on Oil Is Hitting Key Senate Races Hard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Now in its ninth month, the war in Iran has hit American pockets hard, and it could shift the balance in key midterm races that decide who controls Congress.
The serious damage to refineries and other facilities in the Middle East, combined with ongoing uncertainty about whether the Strait of Hormuz will remain open, have kept oil prices inflated. Americans have paid for it: The Center for American Progress estimates that the war has cost each US household at least $1,200.
Rising costs are among the reasons the war has been deeply unpopular, and Tuesday’s midterms are likely to be a referendum on how the White House has handled the impact. Democrats are trying to use that to their advantage to win races in places where the high price of diesel, home heating oil, and fertilizer are particularly top-of-mind for voters. Here’s how it’s playing out in key states across the country.
A Fight Over Diesel in Texas
High diesel prices are affecting voters in every state, but it’s a particularly acute problem in Texas, where Governor Greg Abbott issued a state of emergency over diesel prices last month. The state, which traditionally had some of the lowest diesel prices in the country, has seen prices surge more than 80 percent compared to last year. That’s roughly 10 percent above the national average, according to AAA data.
Abbott is facing a tough reelection campaign, and his opponent, Gina Hinojosa, has used the war as an attack line against Abbott. She has pressured Abbott to suspend a state gas tax on diesel. The Texas Democratic Party issued a statement following the state of the emergency declaration calling on Abbott to “demand that Donald Trump lift his absurd tariffs and halt the unnecessary war that are driving up costs for Texans.”
Fuel prices have also factored into the heated Senate race between Democrat James Talarico and Texas attorney general Ken Paxton. Talarico has also called on Paxton to support suspending the federal gas tax—a move that is supported by some high-ranking Republicans, including Trump—and accused him of “choosing to support the war driving up diesel prices.”
High Heating Costs in Maine
More than 80 percent of the 4.9 million households in the US that heat their homes with oil are located in the Northeast. It’s a particularly popular form of heating in Maine, where more than half of households in the state rely on it.
With winter approaching and prices now nearly double what they were last year, heating oil has played a big role in the contentious Senate race between incumbent Republican Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson.
State Democrats have seized on Collins’ early support of the war to attack her. (She has come out against the conflict in recent months.)
In a sign that the race is uncomfortably close, the White House released a tranche of heating oil reserves in a bid to temporarily draw down the price of the fuel.
“Families are spending a lot more to fill up a tank than they did a year ago,” says Mark Wolfe, the executive director of the National Energy Assistance Directors Association, which predicted that households in the Northeast could spend an additional $3.8 billion on heating oil this winter.
Unlike price spikes on diesel fuel, which may filter to consumers through higher prices on a number of different products, heating oil itself is a consumer good: Families pay directly for the oil to be delivered to their homes. The impact to voters’ pocketbooks, Wolfe says, is “very immediate.”
Fertilizer Prices Shake the Midwest
High diesel prices have hurt farmers, but so, too, has the cost of fertilizer.
Nitrogen-based fertilizers, like ammonia and urea, are made from natural gas by-products, and some of the world’s biggest producers are based in the Middle East. While some production has restarted, it remains well below its prewar average. Urea prices spiked earlier this year.
“If you're going to plant crops like wheat and corn, you have to apply nitrogen,” says Josh Linville, the vice president of fertilizer at financial services company StoneX.
Sulfur, which is also made from oil and gas by-products, is a crucial ingredient in other types of fertilizer. Sulfur prices have more than doubled since the start of this year, thanks to supply chain issues in the Gulf. Farmers who use sulfur-based fertilizers, Linville says, have had to make tough choices about how to manage their crops.
These stresses have put fertilizer front and center in tight races in states like Ohio, Iowa, and Illinois. VoteVets, a PAC that supports Democrats, aired an attack ad against Republican Senate nominee Ashley Hinson in Iowa earlier this month that highlights her record of voting in favor of attacks on Iran.
“Record gas prices. Record fertilizer costs. Farms going under,” the ad intones. “And Ashley Henson’s voting for all of it in Washington.”
In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown’s campaign has aired an ad in recent weeks pinning high diesel and fertilizer costs on his opponent, incumbent senator John Husted, again by bringing up his track record of voting for the war.
Whether that can peel off enough farm voters—a core Republican constituency—to swing the race to Brown remains to be seen. But the costs on farmers are mounting, and there’s little relief in sight with uncertainty looming over Iran. “That farmer’s sitting there saying, ‘I have to farm, but it’s not a matter of can I make money,’” Linville says. “It’s ‘how do I lose the least amount of money next year?’”

Rotterdam's Echo is a Tokyo-inspired listening bar inside the brutalist Groot Handelsgebouw
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Rotterdam’s Echo is a Tokyo-inspired listening bar inside the brutalist Groot Handelsgebouw
Creative director Jeﬀ Hoogendijk, DJ and producer Khalil Ryahi and architect Paul Cournet have teamed up to open a listening bar in Rotterdam, featuring a bar made from shipping crates and ombré mirrors by Sabine Marcelis.
Inspired by visits to listening bars in Tokyo, the trio envisioned Echo as a flexible space that can host different events and activities, but primarily focuses on the experience of music.
Located on the ground floor of Groot Handelsgebouw, a post-war office block opposite Rotterdam Centraal station, the bar has an interior designed by Cournet’s architecture and design studio, Cloud.
Cournet said the idea was to adapt the concept of the listening bar to the creative energy of Rotterdam.
“We wanted to make it super local,” he told Dezeen.
The main bar, which functions as both a service counter and the DJ area, exemplifies this approach.
Built by Baleart Handlers, a company that manufactures wooden shipping crates specifically for transporting artworks, it’s a reminder that Rotterdam is home to Europe’s largest seaport.
Its sides are printed with the words “handled with care”, which became Echo’s tagline.
“We thought it would be so cool make the bar an art crate because we treated everything, from music to hospitality, as if it were art,” said Cournet.
“We always wanted to do everything in the best way possible.”
The space features several works by Rotterdam-based designer Marcelis, who is Cournet’s partner.
Her signature ombré mirrors adorn the walls, reflecting shades of red and gold, while a linear resin lamp hangs above the bar.
Polish brand Tylko supplied much of the furniture, including the modular shelving that extends across the walls to create space for displaying vinyl.
Cournet previously worked with the furniture company on its Berlin showroom, a project that led to a collaboration with audio company Form Follows Frequency.
Together, they developed a colourful system of speakers and subwoofers that slot precisely into Tyklo’s shelving, which launched earlier this year.
These speakers form part of the sound system for Echo, along with two sculptural speaker towers that stand either side of the bar.
“There’s a contrast between the rawness of the exposed concrete and the more refined elements, like the sound system or Sabine’s mirrors,” said Cournet.
“When you put them together, it creates a tension that I find interesting. The concrete feels a bit softer.”
ECHO is one of several listening bars to have opened recently – with others including Bar Bardo in Milan and Upstairs at Hausu in London – but it is the first of its kind in Rotterdam.
The space shifts from a coffee shop by day to a bar by night, and includes a curated retail offering.
It can also morph to accommodate exhibitions, listening sessions of 20 to 40 people, or seated dinners for up to 40 guests.
Since opening in early September, the team has invited various local record stores to contribute to the event programme.
“Rotterdam has this really long history with music, with a lot of famous DJs and people who were pioneers in the music scene in the 1990s and 2000s,” added Cournet.
“It feels like the project has really resonated with that community.”

Ukraine imposed sanctions against those involved with &quot;Rassvet&quot; and Russia&apos;s &quot;shadow fleet&quot;

Ukraine imposed sanctions against those involved with "Rassvet" and Russia's "shadow fleet"
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine imposed sanctions against 10 companies, 19 Russians, and 39 shadow fleet vessels. The restrictions are intended, among other things, to thwart the creation of "Rassvet".
Ukraine has imposed sanctions on companies and individuals involved in the creation of Russia’s own satellite system, "Rassvet," for use in the war, as well as on shadow fleet vessels. The Office of the President reported this on October 30, UNN writes.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed decrees enacting decisions by the National Security and Defense Council of Ukraine to impose sanctions on Russian companies and individuals involved in creating the "Rassvet" satellite communications system, as well as on 39 vessels belonging to Russia’s shadow fleet
The sanctions package concerning the "Rassvet" system includes 10 companies and 19 Russians associated with them. They are involved in work on launching the "Rassvet" system, which the aggressor plans to use on the territory of Ukraine to continue its aggressive and unprovoked war, the OP stated.
Russia, as noted, seeks to have a satellite system similar to the Starlink network that would enable it to command troops and guide and control strike drones, including "Shaheds," and missiles online. Deploying this system could help Russia not only continuously control weapons in real time in Ukraine, but also create threats to other countries.
According to reports, the companies against which sanctions have been imposed include:
-  "Bureau 1440" – the developer, coordinator, and systems integrator of the "Rassvet" project; 
-  "Labs 1440," affiliated with this entity – specializes in producing solar panels for spacecraft; 
-  "FAB Rassvet" – engaged in the development, production, and support of low-Earth-orbit communications satellites and subscriber terminals; 
-  the Belarusian enterprise "Aerospace Instruments" – develops and prototypes components for aerospace systems. 
It was also stated that sanctions have been imposed on "5S Group," which supplies foreign industrial equipment to Russia and develops industrial computers under the RMatic brand. One of them was supplied to the sanctioned manufacturer of electronic warfare systems and "Orlan" drones and used in research and development work in the interests of "Bureau 1440." In addition, sanctions have been imposed on "Production Association 'Aquamash'" – which specializes in the machining of metal products and the manufacture of high-precision parts; "El-Optics" – which supplies, services, and integrates optical, telecommunications, and laser equipment, photonics, and quantum communications systems; "Elesar-Group" – which supplies Russia with foreign-made electronic components and equipment; "Small Spacecraft" – which specializes in developing space technology and ground-based satellite communications systems.
"Rassvet" is Russia’s attempt to create its own low-Earth-orbit satellite system and use it in the war against Ukraine and to create threats to the entire world. The project depends on foreign technologies, equipment, and components, so we are targeting these supply chains already at the development stage and calling on partners to synchronize sanctions," said Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the adviser and Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy.
In addition, another sanctions package against the shadow fleet has been introduced. The package includes 39 maritime vessels flying the flags of: Russia – 17, Barbados – 3, Liberia – 3, the Marshall Islands – 3, Panama – 3, Hong Kong – 2, Djibouti – 2, the Bahamas – 1, Equatorial Guinea – 1, Zimbabwe – 1, Cameroon – 1, Palau – 1, and Sierra Leone – 1.
According to reports, they facilitate the export of Russian oil, petroleum products, and gas condensate, which are the most important source of revenue for the aggressor state’s budget and are subsequently directed toward the war against Ukrainians. These vessels transport Russian energy resources to the ports of China, India, Egypt, Türkiye, and other countries. Just one of them – Vasily Dinkov – carried out 15 operations transporting approximately 726,000 tonnes of Russian crude oil in the first half of 2026 alone.
Some of the vessels are already under sanctions imposed by the European Union, the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, Switzerland, and Australia. Ukraine will provide all the information to its partners for the full synchronization of sanctions across international jurisdictions.
