Opinion:  Don’t just pass through Copenhagen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:59:30 UTC
17:59:30 KST

The author: Madison Hoang is a Vietnamese national based in Boston. From 2025–26, she studied Political Science at the University of Copenhagen.
Hotels and tourist sites are now restricting influencer photoshoots, Lauren Cochrane reported in The Guardian. But treating places as backdrops goes beyond influencers. Many of us can travel for a weekend or live somewhere for months and still treat it like a place we’re only passing through. Being a global citizen means staying in conversation across cultural difference long enough to understand people we may never fully agree with, and finding connection with them anyway.
I learned this during the year I lived in Copenhagen. When I rented my first bicycle, I walked it home for an hour, too afraid to join the cyclists who seemed to glide through every turn and knew every unwritten rule as if born with pedals strapped to their feet. The shop owner had told me, “It’s a straight line back, you’ll be fine.” I could only find the courage to wobble home in the last few minutes, my GPS strapped to the handlebars.
That was the first of many times living abroad humbled me.
I grew up between the motorbike-choked streets of Vietnam and suburban America, so I assumed I already knew how to live anywhere in the world. But Copenhagen complicated my belief that experiencing more of the world meant understanding more of it.
At first, I fell into a rowdy international friend group, and we spent our weekends hopping between countries. I loved those trips, but constant movement did not create connection. Some nights in Copenhagen felt lonelier than being alone. Even amid adventures and laughter, we were all looking at Copenhagen as if it were a backdrop, close enough to witness but not to touch.
Then I stumbled into a coffee shop in Vesterbro, where the Vietnamese-Danish owner made coconut coffee that rivaled the ones I missed from home. I kept returning, seeking solace in our conversations as two people who knew what it was like to live between cultures.
When I confessed my loneliness to the owner’s Italian-Danish friend, he offered simple advice. This is temporary. What’s wrong with partying with your international friends, traveling Europe, and leaving with beautiful memories?
Still, I could not shake the feeling that the point of living abroad was bigger than this. My friends were mostly internationals like me. But when I tried to reach out, the Danes I met were slower to open up than the Americans and Vietnamese I was used to. I blamed Danish culture for my loneliness, assuming Danes had childhood friend groups and little reason to make room for a foreigner.
Staying curious helped me understand the slowness, even if I didn’t agree with it. I can only speak for the Danes I’ve met: some took gap years, moved to remote places on a whim, or drifted through odd jobs until one resonated. The same people who took their time opening a friendship also gave themselves permission to stay young and try new things without seeing it as falling behind. What I had read as indifference was an approach to relationships, work, and life that was patient, intentional, and genuinely theirs. I still valued the more immediate openness I knew from home, so I kept reaching out first, even when it felt like too much. But I could finally see where the slowness came from, and it was not always personal.
Kwame Anthony Appiah gave language to what was happening. He argues that deep cultural differences do not make cross-cultural conversation impossible because we do not always have to agree to understand each other. To me, that describes global citizenship. It means remaining
curious in conversation until the difference becomes understandable. That understanding can allow us to connect with the people who are most different from us, without ever asking us to erase our differences.
The more I understood what frustrated me, the more curiosity I brought to the Danes I met, reaching out to the same people and places and lingering longer in conversations. The slowness gave way to invitations, evenings stretched later, and ordinary moments grew more sacred the longer we stayed inside them: sunset swims in the canals, slow bike rides over worn cobblestones, laughter echoing through empty palace squares at midnight.
I traveled less when I realized I was rushing through new places, while a deeper conversation was already unfolding in Copenhagen. At first, I counted how many countries I could visit. By the end, I counted how many weekends I had left in Copenhagen. It had stopped being a backdrop and become a conversation I wanted to remain inside.
When spring settled in, familiar faces began appearing in my own courtyard, and I realized there were people who would care if I stopped showing up. Connection came not from agreeing with them about everything or giving up who I was, but from staying in conversation long enough to be understood in return.
The café owner’s friend offered me a version of living abroad that treated its temporariness as a reason not to invest too deeply. I had arrived thinking the same. But the real obstacle wasn’t the fact that it was temporary, but the fact that I treated Copenhagen as a backdrop. It is easy to visit a place, but understanding it requires staying in conversation without losing myself. I never had to become Danish to feel connected to a city and its people.
So to the internationals arriving in or living in Copenhagen, reach out even when it feels uncertain. Stay curious a little longer than feels comfortable, and keep listening to the person in front of you despite your differences.
By my final months, I rarely glanced at my GPS for directions. The map had become familiar, and most turns had settled into muscle memory. Sometimes I took the longer way home, in no rush to be anywhere else.

How is Iran shaping new regional order?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:57:36 UTC
17:57:36 KST

The emphasis of Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, in a meeting with the Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, on managing the Strait of Hormuz and expanding bilateral relations with neighbors goes beyond stating two priorities in Iran’s foreign policy. This emphasis should be seen as a sign of the need to review the foundations of the Persian Gulf security order; an order that has been based on the US military presence for decades, but recent developments have seriously questioned its credibility and effectiveness. The main issue today is not simply how to deal with the consequences of the US and Zionist aggression against Iran, but how to transform the results of this confrontation into sustainable security arrangements that are commensurate with the new realities of the region.
The End of US Security Monopoly
The security architecture of the Persian Gulf in the past decades was based on the assumption that the US military presence, the establishment of numerous bases, and Washington’s support for regional partners would prevent the emergence of major threats.  Based on this model, the countries of the region relied on an external power to ensure their security, claiming to have superior military power and the ability to protect its allies. However, the recent aggression against Iran and Tehran’s military response revealed the limitations of this model.
 
The vulnerability of US military installations in the region is not simply an operational issue or an irreparable loss; this fact is directly related to the credibility of Washington’s deterrence. When a military power’s bases are exposed to attacks from an adversary, security can no longer be measured solely by the number of troops, the volume of weapons, or the extent of military deployment. The ability to impose costs on the adversary and prevent its goals from being achieved is also a determining part of the power equation.
By resisting and responding to aggression, Iran has shown that US military superiority does not mean unlimited authority to determine the security fate of the region. This development provides an important basis for reviewing the calculations of neighboring countries. Of course, it cannot be concluded that all these countries have moved away from previous security arrangements in the same way; But it is clear that unilateral reliance on foreign power can no longer continue without assessing its costs and risks. The future order will be formed when security is no longer the monopoly of trans-regional powers and regional countries have a real role in determining its rules.
The Strait of Hormuz; Iran’s Geography of Power and Strategic Depth
Among the components of Iran’s power, the Strait of Hormuz has a position beyond economic and commercial importance. This waterway is located at the junction of regional security with the global economy, and Iran’s geographical location provides the possibility of directly influencing the strategic calculations of major powers. The importance of this position becomes even more apparent when we realize that energy security, transportation costs, and the stability of global markets are to some extent dependent on the conditions prevailing in this passageway.
 
From this perspective, managing the Strait of Hormuz should be considered part of the grand strategy of protecting Iran’s national security. The experience of the recent confrontation has shown that a country’s defense capability is not limited to its equipment and military forces alone;  Geography can also be a determining factor in deterrence. Iran differs from many regional players in enjoying this advantage, and this component cannot be removed from its security calculations.
The strategic importance of Hormuz actually stems from the connection of three elements: Iran’s geographical location, the dependence of the global economy on a stable energy flow, and the impact of developments in this waterway on the security calculations of foreign powers. This connection means that no strategy to exert pressure on Iran can ignore its regional and international consequences.
However, effectively utilizing this advantage requires a distinction between strategic capacity, legal rights, and the way in which the waterway is managed. Protecting Iran’s rights and interests, protecting national security, and confronting external threats must be accompanied by an understanding of the economic and diplomatic consequences of decisions. Geopolitical power becomes a sustainable advantage when it can be used to serve deterrence, strengthen the country’s negotiating position, and consolidate its regional position. Hence, the management of Hormuz is not a short-term issue, but part of the long-term equation of Iran’s security and independence.
Neighbors; the Complementary Component of National Authority
Despite the crucial importance of defense power and geopolitical position, no sustainable security order can be built solely through military deterrence. The complementary component of Iran’s strategy is to build a network of strong bilateral relations with its neighbors; relations that are based not on short-term considerations and fragile agreements, but on mutual interests and long-term cooperation.
Despite their differences in political structures and foreign policy priorities, countries surrounding Iran face common issues in many areas. The security of shipping lanes, the stability of the energy market, regional trade, transportation, water resource management, and countering transboundary threats are all areas for defining common interests. Expanding cooperation in these areas can create constructive interdependence and increase the cost of confrontational policies.
From this perspective, neighborhood diplomacy should not be viewed simply as a tool for reducing occasional tensions; it should become part of Iran’s national security infrastructure. The deeper the economic, political, and security ties between Iran and neighboring countries, the less likely it is that disputes will escalate into crises, and the more room there is for managing them through dialogue.
Of course, achieving this goal requires a balanced approach. While maintaining its strategic independence and deterrence, Iran must also understand the legitimate concerns of its neighbors and, through dialogue, transparency, and practical agreements, expand the basis for mutual trust. Sustainable relations are formed when cooperation with Iran brings tangible gains to its neighbors and mutual interests replace calculations based on constant competition.
From Defensive Victory to Consolidation of Regional Order
The most important challenge facing Iran is to transform its defensive achievements and geopolitical advantages into a sustainable framework for regional security. Victory in the field does not in itself guarantee the formation of a new order; this achievement becomes sustainable when it is consolidated in the form of solid political relations, economic cooperation, regional mechanisms, and reliable security arrangements. In such a framework, managing the Strait of Hormuz and strengthening relations with its neighbors are not two separate paths. The former strengthens Iran’s capacity to protect vital interests and increase the cost of aggression, and the latter provides the opportunity to transform this power into sustainable cooperation and stability. Deterrence without diplomacy may lead to erosive competition, and diplomacy without the support of power will also be vulnerable to external pressures. The connection between the two is the basis of a realistic regional strategy.
The new Persian Gulf order will be formed when the security of the countries of the region is based not on the assumption of superiority and unlimited support of a foreign power, but on mutual recognition of interests, respect for national sovereignty, and shared responsibility. Iran, relying on its defense capabilities, the strategic location of the Strait of Hormuz, and the development of constructive relations with its neighbors, has the capacity to play a pivotal role in this process. The emphasis on these two components ultimately reflects a fundamental principle: sustainable security of the region must be built by the countries of the region and with their active participation, rather than its fate being left to the decisions and competitions of extra-regional powers.

The first humanitarian operation in years in Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky offers a fragile glimmer of hope for civilians trapped by war, but raises grave concerns over Moscow's true intentions and the fate of those seeking evacuation to Ukrainian-controlled territory.

Asked by Euronews whether the localised ceasefire could become a first step towards a wider agreement, Yatsenyuk gave an unequivocal response.
"My answer would be very short. No."
Pressed on whether Russia would agree to a ceasefire, he added: "No way."
His remarks come as Ukraine and Russia prepare to deliver humanitarian assistance and evacuate civilians from Oleshky, a town in southern Ukraine's Kherson region that has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion.
The operation follows a six-day localised ceasefire brokered with the involvement of US First Lady Melania Trump. Ukrainian and Russian officials confirmed on Thursday that demining of evacuation routes had been completed and a humanitarian convoy was ready to depart.
Evacuations were scheduled to take place until 2 pm local time (1 pm CEST) on Friday, with aid distribution planned afterwards.
But serious questions remain over the fate of civilians wishing to leave, particularly those seeking to return to Ukrainian-controlled territory through a route involving occupied Crimea, Russia and Belarus.
Yatsenyuk accused Moscow of treating the remaining residents as hostages and using their plight to stage a propaganda operation portraying Russian forces as rescuers.
"And in this way, they try actually to buy some kind of positive attitude from the White House. That's my take," he said.
"There is no way to trust Russians, period," Yatsenyuk added, warning that the humanitarian mission could be exploited for propaganda purposes.
He argued that Washington had a particular responsibility to ensure civilians received humanitarian assistance and were free to decide whether to return to Ukrainian-controlled territory.
The former prime minister also addressed the presence of American journalists covering the operation, urging them to report independently rather than amplify Moscow's narrative.
"We kindly ask you folks to be journalists and to tell the truth, but not to parrot Russian propaganda," he said.
'Putin is ready to end the war on his terms'
Yatsenyuk's scepticism extends to the latest US-led diplomatic efforts to bring Kyiv and Moscow back to the negotiating table, with further technical-level talks being discussed for November, potentially in Abu Dhabi.
He dismissed Russia's willingness to resume negotiations as an attempt to create the appearance of progress without making meaningful concessions.
"Putin is ready to end the war on his terms," he said, arguing that the Russian president would accept only an agreement amounting to Ukraine's capitulation.
Yatsenyuk accused Moscow of using negotiations to buy time, circumvent sanctions and deepen divisions between Washington and its European allies.
He argued that Putin's ultimate objective remained unchanged: bringing the whole of Ukraine under Russian control.
Despite his pessimism about the prospects for a breakthrough, Yatsenyuk insisted that Washington and Kyiv should continue pressing Moscow to accept an unconditional ceasefire.
Europe must be 'at the table', not 'on the menu'
The former prime minister also warned against excluding European countries from negotiations over Ukraine's future, accusing Moscow of deliberately seeking to marginalise the European Union.

The US-Israeli war against Iran is increasing already high public debt and pushing up interest rates, with creditors questioning whether the US can sustain its outstanding debt of $40 trillion.

France has imposed new restrictions on Israeli defense companies ahead of the Euronaval maritime defense exhibition, scheduled to open near Paris on Tuesday, November 3, Defense & Tech learned on Friday.
As preparations continue for Euronaval, the world's largest naval defense exhibition, the French government has informed organizers that it is once again imposing a "clearly defined and highly restrictive framework" on nongovernmental Israeli exhibitors participating in the event, which will be held in Villepinte, near Paris.
The Israeli companies will be restricted from fully displaying “offensive weapons.”
Officials at the Defense Ministry described the measures as part of a systematic policy aimed at excluding Israeli defense technology from the international stage under the guise of political considerations.
Elbit to present underwater drones at Euronaval
Elbit announced on Thursday that it will present its Unmanned Underwater Vehicle (UUV) capabilities at Euronaval for the first time, marking the expansion of the company’s autonomous maritime offering into the underwater domain.
These new capabilities were added to Elbit Systems’ portfolio following the acquisition last week of International Submarine Engineering Ltd. (ISE), a provider of autonomous underwater systems that has delivered more than 250 underwater vehicles to customers in over 20 countries worldwide.
The new UUV solutions will be showcased alongside the company’s Seagull family of Unmanned Surface Vessels (USVs) and additional maritime solutions from Elbit Systems’ naval portfolio.
France's history of restrictions on Israeli defense exhibitors
The move marks a continuation of a policy France has pursued for two consecutive years. In October 2024, Israeli companies were initially barred from participating in Euronaval, a decision that was ultimately overturned by a commercial court in Paris.
The same pattern has emerged at other defense exhibitions. At the Eurosatory exhibition in June, France prohibited official Israeli government representation and the establishment of an Israeli national pavilion. Israeli companies were allowed to display only products intended for air defense or protection against ballistic missiles, while displays of offensive weapons were entirely prohibited.
In practice, exhibition organizers went even further, erecting wooden panels to block access to the booths of several Israeli companies, including Smart Shooter, Controp, Aeronautics, and Marom. Some of the booths remained blocked throughout the exhibition.
The policy was most visible at the Paris Air Show in Le Bourget in June 2025, when organizers erected black walls overnight around the booths of Israel Aerospace Industries, Rafael, and Elbit Systems shortly before the exhibition opened.
Ahead of the next Paris Air Show in 2027, Israeli companies have been told they will not receive significant exhibition space, with organizers citing limited availability.

Israeli Arabs, Palestinians view path to coalition through political clout - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:55:52 UTC
17:55:52 KST

Israel’s October 27 parliamentary elections have left Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu facing a struggle to remain in office, with neither his bloc nor the opposition securing the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset. A record showing by Arab parties has placed their lawmakers at the center of the battle over who governs next.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
With the vote count completed Thursday, preliminary results gave Netanyahu’s bloc 53 seats, down from 68 in the outgoing Knesset, while the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot held 48. The Joint List won 11 seats and Ra’am eight, giving the two Arab-led parties a combined 19 seats, nearly double their previous representation. Official certification is expected November 4.
Together, the opposition and Arab parties would command 67 seats, enough to replace Netanyahu if they could agree on a governing arrangement. But the arithmetic masks deep political divisions. Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Liberman have previously rejected reliance on Arab parties, while Democrats leader Yair Golan has urged cooperation to remove Netanyahu.
For Palestinian citizens of Israel, the results reflect political mobilization fueled by frustration over domestic policies, organized crime and successive wars. For Palestinians in the West Bank, the possibility of change is being viewed more cautiously.
Nidal Foqaha, a Palestinian political analyst based in Ramallah, told The Media Line that the Arab parties’ success reflected growing insecurity among their voters.
“This achievement is also attributed to the situation in which Arabs in Israel feel that they are threatened, given the last four years of the policies of the government of Israel, and specifically the policies of ministers like [Itamar] Ben-Gvir,” he said.
Foqaha pointed to crime, budget allocations and political rights among the concerns driving Arab voters, alongside developments affecting Palestinians in the West Bank.
Reem Hazzan, a member of the political bureau of the Communist Party of Israel and Hadash, which is part of the Joint List, said the election exceeded expectations.
“It was a great joy that this happened because it means that the people went out and voted and protected themselves, and showed that if they want power, they also know how to get it,” she told The Media Line.
Hazzan linked the turnout to anger over the war in Gaza, conditions in the West Bank, organized crime within Arab communities and the policies of Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition. She said voters increasingly regarded those issues as interconnected and believed that removing Netanyahu and his allies could bring tangible improvements.
But the Arab parties’ gains have also prompted accusations of election fraud and foreign interference from Netanyahu’s Likud party.
Likud has alleged bribery, intimidation and other irregularities in Arab communities, citing suspected cash payments linked to Ra’am ballots. It has also accused Qatar of financing efforts to influence the election, an allegation Doha denies.
CEC directs Shin Bet to investigate suspicions of foreign election interference
In a letter dated Wednesday and made public Thursday, Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg directed the Shin Bet security agency to investigate suspicions of foreign interference and election bribery, stressing that the allegations had not been verified. Separately, police arrested seven suspects in southern Israel in connection with alleged vote-buying.
Neither investigation has established widespread electoral fraud. Acting Central Elections Committee Director General Dean Livne said there was no basis for claims of systematic violations of election integrity. The Shin Bet said its inquiry originated from intelligence collected independently of political parties and did not implicate Arab voters as a community. Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas denied his party’s involvement in wrongdoing and welcomed an investigation.
Hazzan rejected Likud’s allegations as an attempt to undermine Arab political representation.
“If there are any allegations of someone moving money from Qatar, they should look into Netanyahu,” she said, apparently referring to a separate investigation into allegations involving Netanyahu aides and work performed for Qatar.
Hazzan also alleged that Netanyahu and the Shin Bet had been preparing to challenge the election results before voting began.
“We actually see it as just a continuation of delegitimizing, of undermining the people’s will of how they voted,” she said.
That allegation has not been independently established. Although Israeli media reported before the election that Likud was preparing complaints about voting irregularities in Arab communities, the Shin Bet said its investigation originated independently and that no political actor had access to its intelligence before the election concluded.
Likud rejected Eisenkot’s accusation that Netanyahu was attempting to delegitimize the results. In a statement published Thursday on its Telegram channel, the party accused Eisenkot of conducting “an influence operation to whitewash and legitimize election bribery” on behalf of prospective Arab-party partners. It also alleged that a government supported by those parties would depend on votes bought with foreign money. Those claims remain unproven.
Despite the dispute, the Joint List remains willing to support an alternative government, even without formally joining the coalition.
“We have already expressed our position, and we said that we are very much willing to support, to vote in favor of an alternative government in order to get rid of Netanyahu,” Hazzan said.
Arab participation in government is not without precedent. Ra’am joined the Bennett-Lapid coalition in 2021, becoming the first independent Arab party to do so. This time, however, opposition leaders remain divided over accepting Arab parliamentary support.
Eisenkot’s Yashar party won 21 seats, Bennett’s B’Yachad party 12, the Democrats eight and Liberman’s Yisrael Beyteinu seven. Without Liberman, a theoretical 67-seat anti-Netanyahu majority would fall to 60.
That would not necessarily prevent a new government from taking office. Under Israeli law, the initial confidence vote requires a majority of votes cast, not necessarily 61 affirmative votes. Bennett’s government, for example, was approved in 2021 by 60 votes to 59, with one abstention.
Even so, a minority government would need sufficient cooperation to survive subsequent parliamentary votes.
“They need to be courageous. We are not mistaken about who Liberman, Bennett and Eisenkot are. They are right-wing. They are not left-wing,” Hazzan said.
She argued that opposition leaders must decide whether their commitment to removing Netanyahu outweighs their reluctance to accept support from the Joint List and Ra’am.
Foqaha expressed similar doubts, suggesting that the main obstacle was not necessarily disagreement over Palestinian statehood but the unwillingness of opposition leaders to work with Arab lawmakers.
Without such cooperation, a national unity government involving Likud and some of Netanyahu’s rivals could become an alternative. That might allow Netanyahu to remain in office, potentially under a rotation agreement, while giving opposition parties influence over security policy and ministerial appointments.
But Eisenkot and other opposition leaders campaigned against Netanyahu, and joining his government could alienate their supporters. Any agreement would also have to address whether Netanyahu’s current partners, including National Security Minister Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, would remain in government.
If negotiations fail, Israelis could face another election.
Once the official results are published, President Isaac Herzog will consult representatives of the parliamentary factions and assign a Knesset member the task of forming a government. The first candidate will have 28 days, with a possible extension of up to 14 days.
If that effort fails, additional candidates may receive opportunities to form a government. Should the process be exhausted without success, another election would follow. Netanyahu would remain prime minister at the head of the outgoing government until a successor took office.
Another election could give Netanyahu an opportunity to recover lost support. It could also prove costly for an opposition that cannot be certain Eisenkot’s electoral appeal or the unusually high Arab turnout would be repeated.
Foqaha cautioned against assuming that Netanyahu would emerge stronger from another vote.
“What he couldn’t achieve a couple of days ago, he won’t be able to achieve in three or four months from now,” he said.
Nevertheless, Foqaha said Palestinians in Ramallah remained realistic about Netanyahu’s political durability, particularly because Likud retained its position as the largest party in the Knesset.
“People here in Ramallah are also very realistic. We know that, with the current situation, there is not really any signal telling us that Netanyahu will be out forever,” he said.
“He is still the main player.”
For Palestinians in the West Bank, Foqaha said, a change in government would not necessarily bring an immediate breakthrough on statehood. Nevertheless, the departure of some of Netanyahu’s more hard-line ministers could create opportunities for practical improvements.
“We believe that any Israeli government which does not include ministers like Ben-Gvir, Smotrich and [Settlement and National Missions Minister] Orit Strock, and those very radical guys, can at least start with small, doable things,” he said.
He identified financial conditions, security and protection from settler attacks as areas where a new government could make a difference.
Hazzan also pointed to the treatment of Palestinian prisoners as a reason Arab voters wanted a change in government.
“If we can get Ben-Gvir out of the government, it means more bread for the prisoners. It means less torture in prison, and people really thought about it,” she said.
The election has thus produced a political paradox: Arab parties have secured unprecedented parliamentary representation, and their support could determine whether Netanyahu remains in power, yet the opposition remains divided over accepting that support.
For Arab voters, the test is whether their electoral strength can translate into meaningful political influence. For Palestinians watching from Ramallah, it is whether the next Israeli government brings any improvement to their daily lives.

Ukraine's Defense Forces hit the Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery in Russia's Samara Oblast with FP-1 drones early on 30 October, Ukrainian drone maker Fire Point said, adding that one of the units hit hydrotreats diesel fuel. The strike came hours after WSJ reported that Ukraine had paused strikes on Russian refineries under pressure from US President Donald Trump until after the US midterm elections on 3 November.
Russia is pounding Ukraine's power grid and cities ahead of winter, with a mounting civilian toll, including 14 people killed on a Dnipro railway platform on 29 October. Ukraine's long-range drone strikes on Russian refineries, one of its most effective operations against Moscow, target the oil money that pays for that war. Trump has pressed Kyiv for weeks to stop them, blaming them for high global fuel prices, and Ukraine went quiet without saying so and without getting what it asked for in return, WSJ reported. The Samara strike is the first on Russian oil since then. Kyiv has not said whether the pause is over.
Fires spread across a refinery that makes jet fuel for Russia's military
Residents of Novokuibyshevsk reported drones, explosions, and a fire before dawn. Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ posted the first photos on Telegram at 05:24 Kyiv time, and Russian Telegram channel Astra geolocated the fire to the refinery, citing its open-source analysis of residents' photos.
By morning, Exilenova+ counted at least 11 separate fires at the refinery. Samara Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said air defense and mobile fire groups were repelling an attack, Astra reported. The region had declared a drone alert and closed its airport.
Fire Point said its FP-1 drones scored numerous hits on the refinery grounds, and that one of the units hit hydrotreats diesel fuel. The footage published so far shows several smoke columns over the plant but does not show which units burned. The Rosneft-owned refinery has a design capacity of 8.8 million tons of oil a year and is one of the main producers of jet fuel, according to its website. Astra says it supplies jet fuel to Russia's military. The plant lies about 910 km from the front line. Ukraine's General Staff has not commented.
Ukrainian drones have hit the plant before. Ukraine's military said its forces hit it in August and caused a fire.
It is the first fire at a Russian refinery since 15 October, when Ryazan's governor reported one at the city's refinery. It is also the first reported strike on Russia's oil industry since 20 October, when Ukrainian drones hit a Druzhba pipeline pumping station in Tambov Oblast. WSJ called that strike the last before the pause.
All three Rosneft Samara refineries now offline or reduced as drones halt Kuibyshevsky operations yesterday
WSJ claims: Ukraine paused refinery strikes until after the US midterms
Ukraine's military paused its strikes on Russian refineries after weeks of pressure from Trump shook Kyiv's confidence in US support, people with knowledge of the operations told WSJ. The unofficial pause began early last week and is expected to last until after the midterms, and possibly deeper into November. Units carrying out long-range strikes were told in mid-October that the refinery campaign was effectively on hold once missions already under way were completed, two military officials said. Hours after the report, the Novokuibyshevsk strike called that account into question.
Ukraine's government has not announced a pause. Zelenskyy told reporters in Kyiv on 27 October that “our guys tried to be a little more careful during these days. But they do not have an order” not to hit refineries, according to WSJ. He said drone units were hitting other kinds of targets in Russia.
Trump's envoy Jared Kushner repeated the demand to stop the strikes at a meeting with Zelenskyy in Oslo on 20 October, two US officials told WSJ. One of them called the conversation “very tough.” Kushner, who joined remotely, said he and envoy Steve Witkoff were spending a lot of time, energy, and jet fuel on mediating with Moscow, and that a 30-day pause on refineries would be a way for Ukraine to show gratitude, the official said.
Energy truce with strings attached: Kyiv reportedly told to spare Russian refineries or lose US intelligence and arms
Zelenskyy had asked for something in return, WSJ reported: a mutual energy ceasefire with Russia, Patriot missiles for Ukraine's grid, or permission to use Starlink inside Russia so drones could destroy Russian missile launchers. None of those ideas got far. Some of Kyiv's European backers also nudged Zelenskyy to pause until after the midterms, a senior European official said.
The pause showed in Russia's oil industry. Russian refinery utilization at the end of October was 25% higher than at the start of the month as drone attacks subsided, Reuters reported, according to The Moscow Times.
Russia claims over 1,000 drones for a second night as Moscow's airports close again
Russia's Defense Ministry said it downed 1,043 Ukrainian drones overnight over 19 regions, including Samara Oblast, the Moscow region, and Tatarstan. The night before, it claimed 1,214.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin stated that 862 drones flew toward the Moscow region between 20:30 on 29 October and 07:30 on 30 October, that most were downed on the far approaches, and that 170 were downed on approach to the capital. Russia's aviation agency restricted flights at all four Moscow airports, Astra reported. A day earlier, more than 460 flights were delayed or canceled at Moscow and St. Petersburg airports, Astra counted.
In Starodub, in Russia's Bryansk Oblast, about 35 km from the Ukrainian border, a building of the Konservsushprod plant, which makes canned food for the Russian army, appeared to be on fire in readers' photos and videos, Astra reported, saying the plant was presumably attacked and that its open-source analyst had not verified the footage. The Atesh partisan movement reported a blast in Aleksandrovka in Rostov Oblast, and air defense fire and an explosion in Orel.

Which vaccinations should you have this autumn and which are recommended in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:30:13 UTC
19:30:13 KST

In Germany new recommendations for coronavirus vaccinations now apply. Even last year far fewer people had themselves vaccinated against flu.
In the United Kingdom, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, 56, deliberately had his flu jab in front of the cameras. And in New York, the 35-year-old mayor Zohran Mamdani was already seen at the beginning of October laughing with a badge reading "I got my flu shot".
However, the flu jab hype is not felt in Germany, where fewer and fewer Germans are getting vaccinated.
As the German medical magazine Ärzteblatt reports, the share of people aged 60 and over who were vaccinated against flu in 2025 was 34%. According to the German federal government agency Koch Institute (RKI), this is the lowest level in 17 years.
Vaccination is recommended for people aged 60 and over; for everyone with chronic illnesses; for residents of care homes; for medical staff; for pregnant women; and for people who have contact with certain animals such as pigs or poultry, based on RKI recommendations.
Older people in particular should get vaccinated against flu before winter. In addition to the flu shot, immunisation against pneumococci is recommended for older people in Germany, as well as against herpes zoster, or shingles. Vaccination against the respiratory disease RSV should be discussed with a doctor as well.
Is another coronavirus vaccination needed?
Coronavirus vaccination is recommended for those over 75 or who belong to a risk group, such as patients with weakened immune systems or medical staff. Pregnant women with health risks should also be immunised.
Because of the reduced recommendation, however, not all patients with statutory health insurance now have the coronavirus vaccination fully reimbursed.
According to the RKI, as early as 2025, only 16% of people over 60 in Germany were still getting vaccinated against COVID-19.
Measles vaccination is compulsory for children in Germany
There is a special vaccination schedule (source in German) for babies and young children. Among other things, it provides for immunisation against the respiratory virus RSV, tetanus, diphtheria, whooping cough, polio, hepatitis B, meningitis, measles, rubella and mumps.
In the United States, there have recently been waves of severe measles cases because of a lack of vaccination protection.
In Germany, the Measles Protection Act requires proof of vaccination or immunity for children before they start nursery or school and for people born after 1970 who work in childcare or healthcare facilities.
Vaccinations are good for health
Several studies indicate that vaccinations can have positive effects beyond the protection provided by immunisation against a specific disease. Research is being carried out into how far the flu jab protects against cardiovascular complications and which vaccinations can help prevent dementia.
The Deutsches Ärzteblatt reports evidence of so-called heterologous or non-specific effects, in which a vaccination influences the immune system in such a way that the immune response to other pathogens or diseases also changes.

New customs processing fee takes effect – what parcel recipients need to know

From 1 November 2026, a new EU-mandated processing fee of two euros will apply to private individuals' online purchases imported into the European Union (EU) from non-EU countries. International technology and logistics group Omniva explains what these changes will mean for Latvian residents shopping on foreign online stores and platforms.
"It is important to understand that the two-euro fee will not apply to each parcel as a whole, but to each separate goods category listed in the customs declaration. For example, if you order three pairs of trousers, the fee will be two euros. However, if you purchase trousers, a lawnmower and a soup ladle in a single order, the fee will be six euros because these items belong to three different product categories," explained Jānis Andžāns, Head of Communications at Omniva.
The fee will apply to goods imported from countries outside the EU, including China, the United States and the United Kingdom.
It will apply regardless of the value of the goods, including purchases exceeding 150 euros.

As part of the celebrations marking the 70th anniversary of Italy’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations (1956–2026), Italy has donated a new set of uniforms to the UN Office in Geneva for the guides at the Palais des Nations, the historic, recently restored complex of rationalist architecture that houses the work of UN delegates. Every year—as explained in a statement from the Mission—thousands of visitors from all over the world are welcomed to the Palais to learn about the work of the United Nations, discover its prestigious negotiation rooms, and explore from the inside the value and importance of multilateralism. For many, their first point of contact is with a tour guide at the UN complex in Geneva: hence the significance of the uniforms in projecting the Organization’s identity. Thanks to the efforts of the Pistoletto Cittadellarte Foundation, the new uniforms are the result of a collaborative effort involving Italian designers from the Fashion B.E.S.T. network, who are committed to circular production. The uniforms, made from eco-sustainable fabrics, are specifically inspired by the principles of social responsibility promoted by artist Michelangelo Pistoletto and his concept of the “Third Paradise”—a balance between nature, society, and innovation, the statement explains. For the guides, the uniforms thus serve as a reminder of the United Nations’ commitment to collaboration, inclusion, and sustainability. As noted by Permanent Representative Luigi Maria Vignali, by combining Italian creativity with responsible production, the uniforms reflect the very values that underpin the UN’s mission, as well as Italy’s ongoing support for the Sustainable Development Goals. After all, fashion can serve as a universal language of unity, dialogue, and respect for the planet, the statement emphasizes, while also thanking the various companies involved in the initiative.

Philippines raises Mayon volcano alert to level 3 after explosive eruption
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:53:27 UTC
17:53:27 KST

One of the Philippines' most active volcanoes fired a dark column of ash thousands of metres into the sky on Friday in a "moderately explosive eruption" that lasted nearly six minutes, the state seismology office said.
There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage in towns and cities surrounding Mount Mayon, but the country's volcano institute raised the alert level from 2 to 3 on its 0-5 scale and called for evacuations within six kilometres of the crater.
The 3,000-metre ash column gradually drifted southwest onto nearby population centres, the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology said in a bulletin.
"Mayon is in a new phase of magmatic eruption, with increased chances of lava flows and hazardous PDCs (pyroclastic density currents)... affecting the upper to middle slopes of the volcano in the immediate days to weeks," it said.
It urged local officials to evacuate areas near the crater "due to the danger of PDCs, lava flows, rockfalls and other volcanic hazards", with planes also advised to avoid flying close to the mountain.
The 2,462-metre Mayon, rising in a near-perfect cone about 330 kilometres southeast of Manila, is one of three Philippine volcanoes that have shown elevated levels of activity this year, though no major eruptions occurred.
In June 2023, more than 12,000 people living on its lower slopes were moved to evacuation centres to protect them from ash and toxic gases spewing from its crater.
Earthquakes and volcanic activity are common in the Philippines due to its position on the Pacific "Ring of Fire", where tectonic plates collide.
The country's most powerful eruption in recent decades was Mount Pinatubo in 1991, which killed more than 800 people and produced an ash cloud that travelled thousands of kilometres.

What happens to the brain when you eat peanuts daily? New study reveals striking results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:53:25 UTC
17:53:25 KST

Does eating peanuts every day help to maintain memory as we get older?
A recent scientific study indicates that eating peanuts daily may help improve the brain's response to insulin in areas linked to memory in older adults.
The study was published in the journal "Food & Function", and was carried out by researchers from the medical centre at Maastricht University in the Netherlands, with the aim of examining the effect of regular peanut consumption on the brain's response to insulin with advancing age.
The experiment involved 31 healthy people aged between 60 and 75 years.
The participants ate 60 grams of roasted peanuts with their skins and without salt every day for 16 weeks, then the researchers compared the results with another period during which they did not eat peanuts.
Improved brain response to insulin
The results showed an improvement in the response of areas in the right hemisphere of the brain to insulin, including parts of the hippocampus, the parahippocampal gyrus, the lingual gyrus and the posterior cingulate gyrus, which are areas involved in memory processes and other cognitive functions.
To measure this response, the researchers gave the participants insulin through the nose, then used magnetic resonance imaging based on arterial blood labelling to measure changes in blood flow to brain regions.
Insulin plays a role in a number of brain processes linked to learning, memory and communication between nerve cells.
The brain's response to this hormone may become less effective with advancing age, a change that is associated with age related cognitive decline.
However, the researchers did not demonstrate that eating peanuts prevents cognitive decline or stops dementia from developing, but they observed changes in the response of specific brain regions to insulin.
These findings build on previous research by the same team on the same dietary intervention, published in the journal Clinical Nutrition in 2025, where the results showed a 3.6% increase in total blood flow to the brain, along with a 5.8% improvement in verbal memory after the 16 week intervention period.
The researchers believe that the nutritional composition of peanuts may explain some of these effects, as they contain unsaturated fats, fibre, vitamins, minerals and biologically active plant compounds, as well as plant protein.
Peanuts are also a source of the amino acid L-arginine, which the body uses to produce nitric oxide, a compound that helps regulate blood vessel functions and may in turn be linked to learning and memory processes.
Is eating peanuts enough to protect memory?
These findings still need further research to determine to what extent the recorded changes in the brain's response to insulin are reflected in memory and mental performance.
The experiment was limited to 31 people, and the indicators observed by the researchers are not enough to state with certainty that peanuts provide protection from Alzheimer's or other dementia disorders.
Conducting studies on larger numbers of participants and following them for longer periods would help to clarify this relationship and determine whether the potential benefits continue over time.

Latvia to chair UN Security Council for first time, with Ukraine among its priorities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:52:00 UTC

Latvia to chair UN Security Council for first time, with Ukraine among its priorities
That is according to The Baltic Times, Ukrinform reports.
Latvia's Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Sanita Pavluta-Deslandes, said that the presidency of the UN Security Council is a time when the presiding country's role in the UN Security Council is most visible.
She believes that Latvia's contribution to the work of the UN Security Council has been "consistent and purposeful at all times," but Latvia will be able to use the presidency both to defend Latvia's interests and values and to promote the country's visibility, as well as to demonstrate a responsible stance.
The UN Security Council's agenda consists mainly, or 90 percent, of cyclical, mandatory, and regular meetings; however, the presiding country may include one or two so-called ad hoc meetings on the agenda to highlight a topic of particular importance to it.
Pavluta-Deslandes added that Latvia would devote these meetings to its national priorities at the UN Security Council.
She said that through its participation in the UN Security Council, Latvia has gained an even better understanding and awareness that it must defend its independence and freedom every single day.
She noted that this is the main goal of Latvia's membership in the UN Security Council: strengthening its own security, including by supporting Ukraine.
"We are making every effort to keep Russia's war in Ukraine high on the UN Security Council's agenda, to prevent the normalization of Russia's aggression against Ukraine, to counter Russian propaganda and lies, and to explain Russia's imperialist goals and their global consequences to the international community," Pavluta-Deslandes said.
This year, the UN Security Council has held 16 official meetings on Ukraine. Almost all of them were convened by Latvia together with its European allies at Ukraine's request.
Last year, UN member states voted to elect Latvia to the UN Security Council for the 2026-2027 term.

Bitcoin fell amid a $6.3 billion hack of Binance, with the attack attributed to North Korean hackers
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:51:41 EET
17:51:41 KST

Bitcoin fell amid a $6.3 billion hack of Binance, with the attack attributed to North Korean hackers
Kyiv • UNN
TRM Labs linked the attack on Binance to the North Korean group TraderTraitor. The exchange froze $3 billion and suspended withdrawals. Bitcoin fell amid news of the attack on Binance.
North Korean hackers were behind the $6.3 billion attack on the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, according to the U.S. blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs. UNN reports this with reference to Reuters.
Details
"The attacker withdrew approximately $6.36 billion from Binance wallets across ten blockchains, most of it in approximately 20 minutes," TRM Labs said in a blog post on its website.
"TRM attributes the attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea's elite hacking unit, based on reliable intelligence both on and off the network. We make this conclusion with a high degree of confidence," TRM Labs stated.
According to Bloomberg, on Friday, October 30, Binance Holdings reported that funds totaling $6.3 billion had been affected, of which $3 billion in cryptocurrency had been frozen, and the company suspended all withdrawal operations while it cooperated with law enforcement and completed a security system upgrade. Withdrawals are expected to resume by Sunday, co-founder Yi He said in a post on X.
The company will cover all losses and "users' funds are safe," the statement said.
The hack dealt a blow to a developing industry seeking to expand into traditional finance. Before this, the largest publicly known cryptocurrency hack occurred at the Bybit exchange in February 2025, when attackers stole tokens worth nearly $1.5 billion.
Previously known episodes of theft and fraud among crypto giants such as FTX and Mt. Gox paved the way for prolonged bear markets that the industry had sought to heal from as part of the new era of cryptocurrency regulation promised by U.S. President Donald Trump.
The largest token, Bitcoin, fell amid news of the attack on Binance, dropping below $77,000 for the first time in more than a month. Later during the Asian trading day, it partially recovered its losses, trading at around $78,400 at 2:45 p.m. Singapore time.

Most Russian missiles fired at Ukraine ‘contain Swiss parts’
Almost all Russian drones and missiles fired at Ukraine contain electronic components from Swiss companies, according to the Ukrainian intelligence service.
Ukraine says it has identified parts made by 11 Swiss companies that play a crucial role in missiles, such as microcontrollers, navigational data processors, voltage converters, sensors and memory chips.
The Ukrainian military intelligence service HUR regularly publishes an inventory of electronic components found in the wreckage of Russian weapons. Swiss components have also reportedly been found in North Korean ballistic missiles fired at Ukraine.
More
Switzerland leads Europe in technology found in Russia’s weapons
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, advisor to the Ukrainian president on international sanctions, told Swiss public broadcaster SRF that 95% of Russian drones and missiles contain mass-produced industrial parts from Swiss companies.
+ Russia’s killer drones still boast Swiss components
It is thought that many of the components find their way into Russian hands via Chinese intermediaries. Some of the Swiss companies manufacture in China.
Vlasiuk has called on Switzerland to better enforce international sanctions to prevent Swiss components from being used by the Russian military.
The Swiss State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) told SRF that Swiss companies are obliged to conduct due diligence on customers. They must contractually prohibit the re-export of goods to Russia when exporting or selling to third countries.
An effective and comprehensive enforcement of sanctions against Russia is a priority for the Swiss government, SECO told SRF.

The requests went to Lithuania, Latvia, and Estonia, among others, the agency’s sources said. It is unclear whether other countries received similar requests.
Elbridge Colby, head of the Pentagon’s policy directorate, was one of the officials who conveyed the requests. He cited public statements by Europeans describing Russia as “cornered like a rat” as an example of inappropriate rhetoric.

At another recent meeting, the Pentagon urged the Estonian delegation to be “measured” in its public statements, according to a source. It was not specified whether Pentagon officials objected to any particular statement.
Colby also recently told a representative of one of the Baltic countries that there should be no “poking” at Russia, according to another source.
The Baltic countries that border Russia have long worried about the Russian threat, particularly because of drones that regularly cross into their territory. European countries also accuse Russia of a series of sabotage acts. One of the most recent incidents occurred in Germany, where a drone carrying explosives was found at Leipzig Airport near a Ukrainian cargo plane.
Putin, for his part, claims Moscow does not want war with Europe and has no plans to attack NATO countries, but says it is prepared for one.

Voter turnout lower in runoffs in the last four presidential elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:49:41 UTC
17:49:41 KST

News
Voter turnout lower in runoffs in the last four presidential elections
Friday 30 October 2026 09:58
Friday, 30 October 2026, 09:58
PHOTO BTA
Font size
Voter turnout in the runoff has been lower than in the first round in each of the last four presidential elections, according to figures published on the Central Election Commission's website.
The first round of this year's presidential election, held on October 25, saw a record low turnout, with just 22.98% of eligible voters casting their ballots. A runoff is scheduled for Sunday to elect the country's next president.
The Central Election Commission recalls that in 2001, voter turnout stood at just under 42% in the first round, rising to nearly 55% in the runoff. The trend subsequently reversed, with fewer voters participating in the runoff than in the first round.
In the 2021 presidential election, turnout reached 40.5% in the first round and 34.8% in the runoff, a difference of 5.7 percentage points.
The figures for previous presidential elections show the following turnout rates:
2016: 57.5% in the first round and 51.6% in the runoff, a difference of 5.9 percentage points.
2011: 51.8% in the first round and 48% in the runoff, a difference of 3.8 percentage points.
2006: 42.5% in the first round and 41.2% in the runoff, a difference of 1.3 percentage points.

Electronic surveillance identified her as a Chinese intelligence asset and revealed her close relationship with Jensen Huang, according to the newspaper.

China criticizes proposed US telecom restrictions

"The US' practice seriously obstructs normal economic and trade exchanges between Chinese and US companies and does not serve the interests of any party, including US companies and consumers. China will take necessary measures to firmly safeguard its legitimate rights and interests," he added.

University finds plagiarism in Lithuanian PM’s doctoral thesis, gives 6 months to correct
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:47:00 UTC
17:47:00 KST

Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has been given six months to correct plagiarism and other academic writing violations in his doctoral thesis, but a university ethics commission has ruled against immediately revoking his doctorate.
The ethics commission at ISM University of Management and Economics identified five cases of plagiarism and two instances of improper text use that did not constitute plagiarism in Sinkevičius’ 2015 dissertation on alcohol consumption, according to its October 26 decision seen by BNS.
The commission concluded that the violations breached the university’s academic integrity principles and requirements for independent doctoral research.
It recommended that the university’s rector instruct the doctoral studies dean to establish requirements for a publicly available list of corrections and proper source attributions within 60 calendar days. Sinkevičius would then have six months from the approval of those requirements to make the corrections.
The revised dissertation would be reviewed by the doctoral committee and published alongside a correction supplement. If Sinkevičius refuses to address the shortcomings within the deadlines, the commission could recommend initiating proceedings to revoke his doctoral degree.
The commission said immediately pursuing revocation would be a disproportionate penalty. It found no violations in the procedures used to evaluate or defend the dissertation.
Sinkevičius acknowledged the findings and pledged to prepare the corrections.
“I conducted the data analysis and formulated the conclusions myself. Therefore, I have never doubted my work, but I do not dispute the violations identified,” he told BNS on Friday.
ISM rector Dalius Misiūnas said the commission had conducted a thorough and professional investigation in accordance with the principles of impartiality and objectivity. The university accepted its findings and would address the identified shortcomings, he said.
The investigation followed allegations of plagiarism that emerged in July. The commission began examining a complaint in August and later received two additional complaints.
Sinkevičius defended his doctoral dissertation at ISM in 2015.

Defense Ministry Chief Baram pushes munitions independence during visit to Covenant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:46:13 UTC
17:46:13 KST

Defense Ministry director-general Maj.-Gen. (res.) Amir Baram visited Covenant, one of Israel's fast-growing defense-tech companies on Thursday, as part of a series of visits to various defense companies.
According to the Defense Ministry, Baram’s visit “focused on strengthening Israel's munitions independence, expanding the production base, and preserving the State of Israel's qualitative and technological edge in the years ahead.”
The statement added that the visits are part of implementing the Ministry's strategy to strengthen Israel's defense-tech ecosystem.
"The ministry's policy is to encourage and strengthen both defense-tech companies and new start-ups, as well as the established industries. This balance is essential for fostering healthy competition, driving innovation and out-of-the-box thinking, maintaining our qualitative edge, and developing 'the next surprises,’” Baram was quoted as saying during the visit.
According to him, “We must look ahead to an intense security decade and adapt our plans to both global changes and the evolution of the battlefield. Defense exports are a critical growth engine and an enabling tool, not only for strengthening the economy, but also for building the IDF's force and delivering a critical mass of advanced systems to the warfighters on the front lines."
Recognizing the strategic importance of this ecosystem, the Israeli government launched a state‑backed investment initiative last year to strengthen early‑stage defense‑tech ventures. The Defense Ministry has also invested NIS 1.2 billion in start-ups alone, and small- and medium-size companies have signed contracts worth hundreds of millions each.
Last year, the Defense Ministry declared “munition independence” a strategic priority, pushing companies to boost their domestic munition production capacity. Since the outbreak of the wars that began with the deadly Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, Israel has used enormous quantities of munitions, and replenishing its stockpile has become one of the country’s highest priorities.
Anthem
Covenant, which has operations in the US, Germany, and Israel, emerged from stealth last month. Its flagship system, Anthem, is built to deliver heavy payloads at extended ranges while remaining affordable enough to produce in large quantities.
The company has disclosed relatively little about Anthem’s specific performance characteristics, including its precise range, payload, and unit cost. A report in the blog Missile Matters by expert Fabian Hoffman quoted reports saying that the missile has a range of 1,000-1,500 kilometers and has a payload of over 200 kilograms. The report also said that the missile may cost between $500,000 and $6,000 USD per unit.
According to the company, most of Anthem’s components are commercial‑off‑the‑shelf (COTS) parts, supported by long‑term agreements for critical parts. Covenant says this approach allows the missile to be produced quickly and reliably, even during wartime, by drawing on supply chains across allied nations.
The company aims to produce 1,000 Anthem missiles in 2027 in its German and American sites. The report by Missile Matters said that the sites in Israel and Germany “operate as quasi-independent entities with mostly localized supply chains, held under a unique corporate structure” that places them outside US export controls.
Earlier in the month, Denmark announced that it would be procuring the Anthem.

'A lot to do': US Congresswoman Aisha Wahab speaks with TNA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:45:53 UTC
17:45:53 KST

Breadcrumb
'Trying to do the right thing': US Congresswoman Aisha Wahab speaks with The New Arab
At a recent campaign event, US Congresswoman Aisha Wahab spoke with The New Arab about her race to keep her seat in California’s District 14, why many politicians fear speaking out, and how she has been able to build a broad coalition.
As one of the newest members of Congress, who won in a special election after Eric Swalwell resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct, Wahab is in the unusual position of campaigning immediately after taking office.
Though she comes to the 2026 midterms as an incumbent, she is not taking anything for granted, as she once again runs against Melissa Hernandez, the candidate she competed against during the primary.
According to ElectionsCALI, which publishes live prediction markets for California, Wahab is leading Hernandez 92 to 8 (in prediction market odds).
Wahab is the first Afghan American and one of the few Muslims to become a US Congress member. She is also one of a growing number of progressive Democrats speaking out on some of the party’s core issues, including Medicare for All (universal healthcare), taxing billionaires and getting big money out of politics–what many see as part of a new era of grassroots politics.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
You’ve said that some people are afraid of speaking up. What do you mean?
I think people have a lot of fear about talking about the real issues and holding people accountable. Not only holding people accountable, but also holding allies accountable, holding our own party accountable.
What do you think people have the most fear to talk about?
I think it depends on who you’re talking to, and I think that for me it’s always: why are we here? There’s no point in holding the seat if you’re not going to try to make change–on whatever issue you care about–whatever issue you think your community, your district, your constituents care about.
So, for me, you can take a look at my record in the [California state] senate, all of the bills that I’ve brought forward are from my district–some conversation I had, somebody shared a story, somebody shared a problem. Even just in this past week, we’ve had folks say: thank you for this bill at the federal level–you know, protecting women, protecting children, providing for our communities. There’s a lot of work to do.
Is it difficult to talk about things like Israel and Palestine?
I think that it’s definitely getting easier, being the only Muslim in the state legislature [referring to her recent time in the California State Senate], it was hard there. I think there’s this growing movement of accountability and where do our dollars go, and who’s being harmed and for what purpose. When we're talking about our international affairs across the board, there doesn’t seem to be a purpose that’s clear to the American people, and the harm being done does not contribute to a better quality of life over here. And so, as we hold ourselves accountable, our international policies, our dollars, we ask: Where does it go? Why does it go there?
Do you feel, with the person you're following in this seat, more of a responsibility to hold people accountable?
I've always believed in trying to do the right thing. I have several bills that focus on accountability, about going further to provide justice. Whether we're talking about my bill on survivor’s bill of rights, and sexual assault survivors, whether we're talking about closing the spousal rape loophole, whether we’re talking about the bill I did to ban child marriage. I have done a lot of work to not only educate my colleagues that these problems exist, that we have to do more. Even, for example, the Cornell case. I've always had a concern and problem with: why do these universities have their own policing, when it should be regular city jurisdiction law enforcement?
I believe that when we saw Representative [Eric Swalwell] the way we did, I think that there’s more to the story. And I think that by the resignation, it kind of [meant that] everyone in power felt like it absolved anybody of their engagement with him. The reality is that there's a lot of harm when you’re talking about sexual assault and sexual violence–whether it’s children or whether it’s women or whatever the case may be. It affects them mentally, emotionally, physically, spiritually for their entire lives. People don't really talk about the impact that these types of crimes have on victims. And as a daughter of an individual who was murdered, that one action sits with me for a lifetime; that one action affected the entire family. It wasn't just one person that got harmed. So, I think there's a lot to discuss when we’re talking about prioritising victims first; that's always been my goal.
Rhe ad campaigns that were against us–and I'm so glad the San Francisco Chronicle literally wrote that these were false and misleading and distorting her record–because my record is very clear. We have always prioritised victims first.
Even in our campaign, we have the support of people like Bernie Sanders as well as the chiefs of police, as well as sheriff, as well as the attorney general and so many people.
How did you build such a wide coalition?
It’s being able to talk to people directly, being honest, and listening and having an open door of communication. I may not always agree with anybody a hundred percent of the time. But being able to really understand where they’re coming from and find some middle ground is important for doing the best policy.
We had a bill regarding signal jammers. Law enforcement brought that forward to me–our own district, in fact. We worked on it, but we also realised teachers use it so kids don’t cheat in class, so they don’t text each other. So, how do we ensure that people who are using it in crimes get punished for it, but we don’t harm teachers and innocent people.
So, we made it in a way where we threaded the needle and the bill was written in a way that said: if you commit a crime, utlising this type of technology, it’s illegal. But if you use it for people taking tests, it’s not a big deal. I think threading the needle, building policy, writing it a certain way, working with people, understanding that there are multiple sides to a story, for even a tool, we need to prioritise.
I don’t think I’ve seen a coalition so wide. It really spans the spectrum.
We have everybody from Governor Gavin Newsom, Bernie Sanders. We have Adam Schiff, we have Pramila Jayapal–you name it. It's largely because I generally try to work with all people. I don’t really care for labels. I think that that puts you in a box. We want to make sure that we create policy that helps all people, not a specific type of person. Our policies last lifetimes. There's a lot of good you can do and there’s also a lot of harm. So, you need to be able to have those conversations to understand the full nuance of what you are really trying to do. I’m really honoured to be able to have this big, massive coalition. It shows the work that we have done and the conversations we have had. We’re going to try to work with all people.
Do you feel like you’re paving a path for people?
When I was first elected, there were a lot of firsts attached to the progress that I’ve made. I just want people to be able to know that they can do it. Even my own team, for example. My campaign manager has never run a campaign but mine. My team that does my video work had never done photography before. We're bound to make mistakes, we’re bound to fumble, we’re bound to fall down. But the effort is what’s true. If you can try your best, try your hardest, learn from your mistakes and have a goal and work towards that, that is what our efforts are.
I share this because in politics, you don’t need a specific degree. You don't need a specific background. You don’t need to speak a certain way to get elected. You are a representative of the people in your community. For all of them that have fear and doubts, you just want to make sure you persevere through that and also be able to bring people along. That has been genuinely what I've tried, and I may not agree with anybody a hundred percent of the time. But it’s like: where can we work together? That's the goal for me.
How would you feel if someone said that I got into this race because I saw what you were doing?
You know what's funny? We've had people say that and in fact I've had colleagues that ran for their local office because they saw me running for city council years ago. I always say the world is small and since that community, everyone you meet, when you’re able to make an impact, they make an impact on you. They make an impact on their community. You are able to also see where you can do more and be better. Nobody’s perfect, and so as long as people try, do their best, do the work for the people, that’s what I care about. So, when people are interested in running, they have to have the right reasons for why they’re running. I think there are a lot of people who have a lot of ego. A lot of people start to forget why they’re in office, especially with the fundraising component. We talk about that. You don’t want to sell out 'the American Dream'. For me, I try really hard to prioritise the 'American Dream' for everyone. Campaign contributions are not going to change that. In the state legislature, for example, I’ve pushed policies that were not popular among legislators.
For example?
My lobbying reform bill. Because they're so afraid. Their friends are all lobbyists, and I've had a lot of conversations where people were trying to lecture me on that. And I tell them: I appreciate your opinion, but my priority is the 40 million people who rely on the policies being created in this bill. The moment you say that, it kind of level sets them again. And it reminds them of who we really work for. And so even though it's very difficult to pass legislation like that–it gets watered down under the guise of this or that–the goal is to continue to help reform the institution, the work. That's what I care about.
Moving forward, how do you feel about the race?
We've heard rumblings where our opponent and her team met with people in the district and have stated that AIPAC may put in $4 million. I don't know if that’s true. I don't know if that’s them garnering support, or trying to establish more support. I don't know, so we can't assume that we have this in the bag because we’re elected right now. We work every single day. As you can tell, we had literally hundreds of people show up, stand in the burning sun to be able to be part of this. We just want to help, we want to be supportive, work hard for every vote, and see what happens.
How have you done both–run for office while holding office?
I'm very, very proud that we've done a lot of the groundwork ahead of time. I will say that I take my job very seriously. In fact, I voted on every single bill before I got sworn in–in the legislature for the [state] senate. We waited as long as we could before we resigned, and eventually 24 hours before we got sworn in, we resigned. And we started the work. We've just established and found our new district office. We got the short end of the stick in Congress in a lot of ways. They were supposed to have an office for us. That office already had a new tenant. We had to find our own office. There’s a lot of work to do.

China conducts combat readiness patrols around disputed shoal in South China Sea
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:45:33 CET
17:45:33 KST

BEIJING, Oct 30 (Reuters) - China’s military said on Friday its naval and air forces conducted combat readiness patrols around Scarborough Shoal in has long been a flashpoint in tensions between Beijing and Manila in the South China Sea.
The People’s Liberation Army Southern Theater Command, in a statement, said the patrols were “necessary countermeasure in response to the Philippines’ rights-violation and provocative acts” and it has strengthened such patrols this month.
The Philippine embassy in Beijing and the Philippine military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Tensions between China and the Philippines resurfaced at the close of a two-day Association of Southeast Asian Nations defence gathering on Thursday, with Beijing accusing an unnamed Philippine politician of obstructing its participation in the event. Manila said China had been given an opportunity at the meeting to state its position.
China claims sovereignty over almost the entire South China Sea via a nine-dash line on its maps that cuts into parts of the exclusive economic zones of Malaysia, Vietnam, the Philippines, Brunei and Indonesia. An international arbitral tribunal ruled in 2016 that China’s sweeping claims have no basis under international law, a decision Beijing rejects.
“Such patrols are aimed at further enhancing control and management over relevant waters and airspace, and serve as an effective countermeasure to cope with all sorts of rights-violation and provocative acts,” the Chinese military said.
Separately, the China Coast Guard also conducted law-enforcement patrols in the waters around the shoal on Friday, calling the activities “necessary countermeasure in response to the Philippines’ rights-violation and provocative acts.”
Neither the Chinese military nor the China Coast Guard gave details on which Philippine actions they were referring to.
(Reporting by Beijing Newsroom; Additional reporting by Nestor Corrales in Manila; Editing by Christian Schmollinger and Sharon Singleton)

“Growth has been missing for three quarters,” he said, describing the French economy as “at a standstill” in 2026.
“France is not heading for a crisis,” he stressed.
He warned: "Today, if we do not have the budgetary consolidation included in the budget, we will hit the wall.”
Lescure described Article 49.3 of the Constitution and government ordinances as “safety mechanisms” to ensure the country has a budget if parliamentary approval proves impossible. Article 49.3 allows the government to pass legislation with a parliamentary vote under certain conditions.
He also reported that 400 applications had been received for zero-interest loans from businesses affected by vandalism.
Between 1,000 and 1,500 businesses had been “truly vandalized,” while around 3,000 had been “affected,” though not necessarily vandalized, he said.
“We stand alongside business owners,” Lescure underlined, adding that he would visit affected businesses in Bordeaux on Friday.
