Binance freezes withdrawals after $6.3bn security breach
The crypto industry is reeling from a massive hack at Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange.
Digital assets worth more than $6.3bn (£4.7bn) have reportedly been taken from Binance by North Korean hackers, apparently after a laptop belonging to one of its engineers was hacked.
The company said its teams are “working around the clock” to resolve the issue.
“Rest assured that user funds are completely safe,” a Binance spokesperson said in a statement.
Binance said it had worked with partners to freeze the affected assets, with about $3bn located so far. It gave no update on the status of the remaining $3.3bn as Binance co-founder Yi He said the company would cover “all hacking losses”.
UK financial watchdogs monitoring fallout from Binance heist
Kalyeena Makortoff
The UK’s financial watchdogs are now monitoring for any potential fallout from the Binance heist.
A spokesperson for Britain’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) said:
“While Binance wasn’t registered with the FCA to provide crypto services in UK, we’re aware of the reported incident and engaging with them to understand the impact.”
While crypto firms are not regulated in the UK, the BankofEngland and FCA will be keeping an eye on any banks, insurers or fintechs that are exposed to Binance, and how that could ultimately hurt the UK’s wider financial system.
The BankofEngland is monitoring the Binance hack, according to a source familiar with the matter. However, it is understood there is no active concerns. The Bank of England declined to comment.
Justas Pukys, senior product manager at Surfshark, a cybersecurity company), reckons Binance customres shuold watch out for a potential second wave of scams targeting them.
That would involce criminals impersonating Binance representatives through fake security alerts and requests to transfer funds into “safe” wallets.
Pukys explains:
“The reported $6.3 billion Binance hack is alarming, but cryptocurrency holders should also be on high alert for a potential second wave of scams. Criminals could exploit the panic surrounding the incident to trick people into handing over their savings.
“Scammers may pose as Binance representatives, sending convincing emails or text messages warning that accounts are at risk or offering to help recover stolen funds. Some could even claim to be from Binance’s security team, urging users to transfer their cryptocurrency to a supposedly ‘safe’ wallet. In reality, following these instructions could mean handing your money directly to criminals.
Reminder: Binance’sRichardTeng reassured customers this morning that “your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss.”
Binance’s breach may show the “industrialisation of state-sponsored crime” is underwya, argues Keystone Law’s fraud & financial crime partner SyedRahman:
“The more important number in this hack may not be $6.3 billion. It may well be 20 minutes. The attacks had the advantage of preparation and coordination. Everyone responding had to establish what happened in real time. The challenge for the industry is where collaborative efforts in recovering those losses can ever match the speed of a pre-planned attack without sacrificing safeguards that make financial intervention legitimate.
“In essence, the real concern is not that the blockchain failed. It is that systems trusted to control billions of dollars may have been compromised. The weakest point in institutional crypto custody may no longer be the technology holding the assets, but the people and infrastructure authorised to move them.
“We may be witnessing the industrialisation of state-sponsored crime. If North Korean involvement is confirmed, this is not simply a criminal group exploiting a weakness within an exchange. It is a state-linked operation capable of extracting significant sums from global financial infrastructure in minutes.That demands a very different response from governments.”
Elsewhere in the financial world, NatWest has rounded out the Q3 bank earnings season with a bit of a whimper.
Pre-tax profits were up just 1.9% for the July to September period, hitting £2.2bn.
That’s despite an 8.9% rise in net interest income to £3.6bn, having been offset by an 81% jump in impairment charges - the sums they use for soured loans - from £153m to £277m.
However, NatWest said that impairment charge increase is a comparative issue, reflecting the one-off release of provisions last year, rather than any change in conditions for its borrowers, which has remained stable.
They’ve also reported higher operating costs, primarily linked to the integration of wealth management business, Evelyn Partners, which the bank bought earlier this year.
The Binance theft raises ‘serious questions’ for cryptocurrency exchanges, explains Jake Moore, global cybersecurity advisor at security firm ESET
“It is worrying just how quickly billions of dollars can disappear in a modern-day cyber heist, but it is unbelievable that a single laptop has enough privileged access to enable it. If a single device can authorise enormous cryptocurrency transfers, hackers can simply target systems and people until they find a weak link. And there is always one.
“While blockchain transactions can be traced, recovering stolen cryptocurrency is far more difficult, especially when attackers move funds across multiple wallets and blockchains extremely quickly using simple and well-known evasion tactics. North Korea has become increasingly sophisticated in using cybercrime to generate enormous sums of money, but this raises serious questions as to whether cryptocurrency exchanges are doing enough to protect customer assets and whether security and regulation is keeping up.
“Consumers who choose to keep cryptocurrencies should spread their digital assets across multiple reputable platforms and secure hardware wallets (such as their own USB) to reduce the risk of losing everything in a single attack.”
News of the Binance heist could knock confidence in crypto assets, suggests Cristiano Ventricelli, vice president of digital assets at Moody’sRatings
“The incident underscores the heightened cybersecurity risks associated with hot wallets, a component already exposed by the 2025 hack on Bybit cryptocurrency exchange. It also illustrates the risk concentration inherent in large, centralized intermediaries.
Stronger institutional controls can reduce some vulnerabilities, but the scale of assets under custody can amplify the impact of a successful breach.
The broader credit and industry implications will depend on the ultimate losses, affected counterparties, asset recovery, and importantly, whether the incident leads to wider disruption or loss of confidence across the digital-asset ecosystem.”
Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was probably conducted by North Korea’s TraderTraitor.
Chainalysis co-founder and CEO JonathanLevin wrote on X:
We live in unprecedented times. But DPRK are up to their old tricks. We assess @binance hack for $6.4B was likely done by DPRK group TraderTraitor due to links to previous hack.
Industry partners have already frozen ~$3B and we @chainalysis continue to follow all of the funds.
Ethereum accounts for about $3.79bn. That includes 200,630 ETH and 185 other tokens, among them 1.875 billion USDT, 823 million USDC and 88.5 million RLUSD.
Bitcoin outflows total 18,270 BTC, about $1.47bn.
Tron outflows total 612.7 million USDT and 46.4 million TRX, about $628m.
The XRPLedger lost 233.46 million XRP, about $296m.
Solana outflows total 970,500 SOL, about $96m.
Arbitrum, Optimism and Base combine to about $39m, including 74.6 million ARB taken on Arbitrum. Avalanche outflows total about $28m, and Polygon outflows total about $10m.
Richard Teng adds the Binance are ‘working closely’ with law enforcement.
He lists the actions which the digital exchange has taken since discovering the theft:
Temporarily suspended withdrawals while we complete a security revamp of the withdrawal service and its related addresses
Revoked the affected address authorizations
Engaged law enforcement and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds
Teng adds:
Our team hasn’t stopped. We’re working closely with law enforcement to ensure the matter is handled appropriately - and I’ll share what I can, as soon as I can.
Richard Teng, the co-chief executive officer of Binance, has pledged that customers money is ‘safe’, despite the hack.
Posting on X a few minutes ago, Teng confirms that it appears the break-in came via an employee’s laptop – but insists it was a ‘more complex’ attack than simply clicking on a rogue link.
Teng says:
I want to speak to you directly about what happened.
Bottom line - your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss.
Our initial investigation suggests this security incident may have started with a compromised DevOps engineer’s laptop. That gave an attacker access to a service container, where they submitted unauthorized withdrawal transactions.
To be clear: the attacker did not simply use one engineer’s permissions, and this was not a single “one-click” action. It involved a more complex attack process. Our investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual.
So far, we have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak.
Teng adds that Binance will share a detailed technical post-mortem once the investigation is complete and every fact is verified - and publish an updated Proof of Reserves once remediation is complete.
The hacker who swiped over $6bn of digital assets from Binance is in the process of switching stablecoins (which can be frozen) into etherium (which can’t), according to media company Decrypt.
Stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle moved quickly to blacklist the suspected attacker’s addresses in order to freeze a portion of the funds and make them inaccessible.
As centralized issuers, they each have the ability to blacklist addresses so their tokens cannot move, and more than $2 billion of those two tokens have been frozen so far by different stablecoin providers. ETH has no issuer, so every dollar converted before a freeze lands is out of their reach.
Jim Reid, market strategist at DeutscheBank, reports:
Crypto assets have come under pressure after Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, suspended deposits and withdrawals following a suspected hacking incident. Bitcoin is down -0.40% this morning, following a -3.03% slide yesterday.
Elite North Korean hackers blamed for Binance theft
TRM Labs, a blockchain intelligence firm that tracks the industry, has declared that an elite North Korean hacking unit called TraderTraitor was responsible for the security breach at Binance.
TRMLabs have also calculated that the breach is “the largest crypto theft on record”.
On October 29, 2026, an attacker moved approximately $6.36bn out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes starting at 20:05 UTC. That makes this the largest crypto theft on record, about four times the $1.5bn Bybit hack of February 2025. Binance has confirmed a security incident and suspended withdrawals on several networks.
TRM attributes the attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, based on robust on and off-chain intelligence. We make this judgment with high confidence. TRM is tracking the funds and alerting partners through the Beacon Network.

US stocks linked to cryptocurrencies fell in afterhours trading.

Feature: Ethiopian coffee firm eyes greater opportunities in China through CIIE
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:19:18 CST
16:19:18 KST

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- As the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) approaches, executives of Ethiopian coffee company AWO Coffee are making final preparations for the event, seeking to tap the potential of China's fast-growing coffee market.
Building on its successful debut at last year's expo, AWO Coffee is looking to further expand its presence in China, with the CIIE providing a platform to connect with potential buyers, promote its premium brand and establish business partnerships.
"Our participation at the CIIE last year was a successful experience for us. We achieved notable outcomes that exceeded our expectations," the company's General Manager Tesfaye Gebru told Xinhua in a recent interview. He noted that the debut participation enabled the company to gauge consumer reception and establish strong trade connections.
Kaleab Fekad, the company's marketing manager, described the CIIE as an important international trading platform connecting Ethiopian coffee producers and exporters with potential buyers and partners from China and around the world.
"We decided to attend this year's expo for the second time because our experience last year was very successful," said Fekad. "This year, we aim to further promote our brand and expand our market opportunities in China."
The 9th CIIE is scheduled to take place in Shanghai from Nov. 5 to 10. A total of 162 countries, regions and international organizations will participate, alongside 4,142 overseas exhibiting companies. The overall exhibition area will exceed 440,000 square meters for the first time, according to the organizers.
Launched in 2018 as the world's first national-level expo dedicated to imports, the CIIE aims to expand China's opening up and turn its vast market into a shared opportunity for the world.
"The Chinese market is entering the coffee business very rapidly and on a very large scale. Since the younger generation is getting more into coffee culture, the market has greater potential for the future, and we believe that we will be able to further expand our presence in China," Fekad said.
Named after the Amharic word for "Yes," AWO Coffee is one of Ethiopia's fast-growing coffee processors and exporters, supplying renowned coffee varieties to international markets.
"Since we began exporting raw coffee beans and later expanded into processed and powdered coffee, our export figures have grown rapidly over the years," said Fekad. "Our brand is also becoming increasingly well-known among Chinese consumers."
To meet changing consumer preferences in China, the company has diversified its product range to include roasted beans and packaged powdered coffee. Its products are sourced from its own farm and through partnerships with smallholder farmers in Ethiopia's major coffee-growing regions.
Since beginning its exports to China about 12 years ago, AWO Coffee has steadily expanded its trade ties with the market. Its annual shipments to China have grown significantly, with exports exceeding 200 tons in 2025.
Looking ahead, AWO Coffee plans to expand its operational capacity and further penetrate the Chinese market. The company also plans to establish a joint venture in China in the coming months to strengthen its marketing efforts and facilitate participation in more exhibitions across the country.
Beyond individual business ambitions, China's growing coffee market is becoming increasingly important to Ethiopia's broader coffee industry.
Industry observers attribute the rising demand partly to changing consumption habits, particularly among younger Chinese consumers, who are increasingly embracing coffee culture. The trend offers new opportunities for Ethiopian coffee producers and millions of smallholder farmers who depend on the sector for their livelihoods.
Widely regarded as the birthplace of Arabica coffee, Ethiopia is one of Africa's leading coffee producers and exporters. Its coffee is internationally renowned for its quality and diverse flavor profiles, ranging from wine-like and fruity to chocolatey. The sector is also a major pillar of the country's agriculture-based economy.
China, which entered the top 10 destinations for Ethiopian coffee exports several years ago, became the third-largest export market in the 2025/26 Ethiopian fiscal year, which ended on July 7, up from fifth place in the previous fiscal year, according to official data.
"China remains among the new market destinations for Ethiopian coffee, but we are witnessing increasing shipments of coffee to China, and we hope that the country will become the largest buyer of Ethiopian coffee in the coming two years," Ethiopian Coffee and Tea Authority (ECTA) Deputy Director General Shafi Umer told Xinhua recently.
Ethiopia exported 47,836 tons of coffee to China in the 2025/26 fiscal year, earning 347 million U.S. dollars, compared with 34,284 tonnes worth 219 million dollars in the previous fiscal year, according to the ECTA.
"We are trying to tap into the huge market potential for Ethiopian coffee in China through intensive promotion and exporting organic coffee to meet the growing demand of Chinese consumers, especially among the youth," Umer said. ■

Letter from China: The one-person company, the port and the shopping bag, snapshots from Hainan FTP
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
15:19:10 CST
16:19:10 KST

A reach stacker lifts a container at Yangpu Port in Danzhou City, south China's Hainan Province, Oct. 21, 2026. (Xinhua/Wang Teng)
by Xinhua writer Wang Teng
HAIKOU, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- At dusk, the salty sea air drifted over a beach on south China's Hainan Island, where a young man sat alone.
The man, Li Baihong, founded a one-person company (OPC) specializing in software development.
Unlike traditional ventures, an OPC is usually led by a single entrepreneur with AI tools handling tasks that would otherwise require a larger team.
His "employees" are three laptops loaded with AI assistants helping him develop software.
Now, he has earned about 200,000 yuan (about 30,000 U.S. dollars) in six months since the company was established.
In April this year, he resigned from a leading Chinese internet company in Shanghai and flew to Hainan with his belongings in three suitcases.
"I've explored several OPC communities in cities such as Hangzhou and Shenzhen. But I chose Hainan because the working environment here is like a forest park," said Li, adding that his happiest moment each day is the 10-minute e-bike ride to the seaside after work.
On the day he landed in Hainan, he submitted the documents to the local authorities online and received his business license seven days later.
Li's company is based in Hainan Free Trade Port Resort Software Community, just a 10-minute e-bike ride from the beach. The community offers entrepreneurship coaching, rent-free offices, and funding for entrepreneurs.
Under Hainan Free Trade Port (FTP) policies, eligible companies can benefit from a preferential corporate income tax rate of 15 percent. "I used to earn a high salary in Shanghai, but the taxes were high as well. So, the tax rate is one of the factors I consider when running my own company," he said.
To date, the community has attracted more than 400 AI-powered OPC enterprise entities and 700 makers, as well as entrepreneurs from overseas, said Si Xinying, director of Chengmai Digital Economy Research Institute, which is based in this community.
As the sun sank below the horizon, Li was still sitting on the beach. Lights came on at a port in the distance, and the sound of a ship's horn drifted in.
The next day, I took a bus along the western stretch of the Hainan Island loop road and reached Yangpu Port, the largest cargo port in the Hainan FTP.
When I arrived, customs officers were inspecting a shipment of coconuts imported from Thailand. Using intelligent inspection equipment, customs can complete inspection of a single shipment in under three minutes.
"If the machine detects abnormalities, the shipment will be sent for manual inspection," said Zeng Jie, deputy head of the supervision department of Yangpu Port Customs.
Since last December, the Hainan FTP launched island-wide special customs operations, a system that treats the whole island as a special customs area. As of Oct. 22, the Yangpu border inspection station has inspected 4,104 inbound and outbound vessels, up 11.95 percent year on year.
Among the goods unloaded from Yangpu Port are shipments sent to Hainan's duty-free shops. Currently, 12 offshore duty-free shops are located across Hainan Island.
Sanya City was the final stop on my reporting trip to Hainan. On the last day, after booking my departure ticket, I went to the Sanya International Duty Free Shopping Complex to buy duty-free goods for my family.
The sprawling mall offers a wide selection of international brands, attractive duty-free prices and convenient pickup services.
Tourists holding departure tickets from Hainan Island, including but not limited to train, ship or airplane tickets, may purchase duty-free goods in any duty-free shop on the island. After payment, they can take the goods with them or choose to have them delivered.
"Since the launch of special customs operations, foreign tourists who meet the requirements and plan to leave the island and the country can enjoy a tax exemption of 100,000 yuan per year to buy duty-free goods in Hainan, like other Chinese tourists," introduced Zhang Bin, general manager of China Duty Free Group Sanya Downtown Duty Free Store Co., Ltd.
There, I met a tourist from Russia carrying several shopping bags. She told me that it was her first time visiting China.
"It feels wonderful, because I can enjoy the island's tropical coastal scenery and buy international goods at such great prices," she said.
From January to September 2026, Haikou Customs supervised duty-free sales worth about 16.29 billion yuan in Sanya, with about 2.4 million shopper visits and about 12.59 million items purchased, up 16.48 percent, 6.29 percent, and 6.24 percent year on year, respectively.
After shopping, I headed to the airport. When the plane took off, I could see the golden beach and the cerulean sea outside the window. Although my trip has come to an end, the story of Hainan FTP continues. ■

Party to build links with emerging economic sectors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:18:17 UTC
16:18:17 KST

The Communist Party of China has stressed the need to promote party building in emerging sectors in a resolution adopted at a plenary session of the Central Committee, an official said on Friday.
The party will step up efforts to expand and deepen the coverage of party organisations and work in new types of economic and social organisations, as well as among groups in new forms of employment, so as to strengthen its appeal, cohesiveness and influence in emerging fields, said Huang Jianfa, deputy head of the organisation department of the committee.
New types of economic organisations encompass non-public-sector enterprises and businesses operating in emerging areas and cover a broad range of entities, including industry associations, chambers of commerce, social service agencies and community-based organisations.
New forms of employment have emerged alongside the growth of the internet and digital economy, including workers such as food-delivery couriers, ride-hailing drivers and online marketers, many of whom rely on digital platforms for their work.
China currently has around 84 million people engaged in new forms of employment, who play an important role in meeting people's daily needs, supporting livelihoods and keeping economic activity running smoothly. (Xinhua)

Knot for eating: Welcome to the Italian restaurant where every meal is knitted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:14:04 UTC
16:14:04 KST

From fluffy tiramisu to puffy ravioli, the food is as delicious as it is deceptive at 'Kate's Knitalian' — an immersive new art exhibition in London.
Layers of lasagna bursting with bolognese, pistachio-filled cannoli dusted in icing sugar, and a seductive slab of pillowy tiramisu.
These are just some of the mouth-watering dishes available at Kate Jenkins' new 'Knitalian' restaurant.
But here's the catch: none of them are edible.
Instead, Jenkins has knitted, crocheted, embroidered and sewed every single recipe, hand-crafting a feast of fiber art for her new exhibition at the Air Contemporary gallery in London, United Kingdom.
The gallery has been re-modelled accordingly, fitted with traditional trattoria-style gingham tablecloths, rustic wall art and a giant gelato fridge. If it weren't for a lack of baked dough wafting through the air, you could almost swear you've teleported from the bustling streets of Soho to a charming Italian deli.
This immersive element is an integral part of Jenkins' work, which has previously included knitted replicas of fishmongers, bakeries, supermarkets, bagel bars and more.
Her latest installation feels much more personal, however — inspired by frequent trips to Italy with her Italian partner.
"I always feel inspired [in Italy] because there's so much culture there in terms of food," Jenkins told Euronews Culture.
"There are all these amazing different parts of Italy and they're famous for different things. So, looking at the food culture in Venice, you've got cicchetti, which is like the equivalent of the tapas. And then there's Crotone, which is famous for its red onions."
The diversity of Italy's foods combined with Jenkins' interest in their subtle regional differences became a starting point for a year-long project that features more than a thousand fabric food and drink replicas.
Among them are slices of salami, various cheeses, bottles of Chianti, and hundreds of individual pasta pieces in bowls. No detail is left untouched, with Jenkins treating the process of knitting a lasagna as if she was actually cooking one.
"I was knitting the sheets of pasta, then making the Ragú, so that's crocheted, and then layering it all up, as you would when you're making your own cooked lasagna," Jenkins explains.
"It requires really looking at how things are constructed and then breaking it down and then rebuilding it, but knitted."
Getting the colours and textures correct also required endless experimentation, mixing yarns and trialling different stitch techniques to make it look as believable as possible.
"Making things like ravioli, it has to have a certain puffiness to it, and then it's got the little serrated edge and that has to be a certain stitch," she said.
"Or when I'm making an ice cream cone that's a 3D waffle structure, there's some things I use a crochet technique for and then others I'll use a knitting machine to get it to look right."
Ever since her grandma taught her how to knit as a child, the craft has been a major part of Jenkins' life.
She began her career as a knitwear designer in the late '90s, working with big fashion designers including Ralph Lauren, Marc Jacobs and Kate Spade before later founding her own label, Cardigan.
Then, while brainstorming ways to promote an accessories line, she started knitting foods — mostly for fun, but also as a way to get people to view things in a different way.
It proved so popular that Jenkins was able to open her first food-themed exhibition in 2007, 'Comfort Food', which ultimately changed the entire trajectory of her career.
"I think people love seeing food," she said, believing there's something universally joyful about seeing and creating replicas of pre-existing things.
"I find it very satisfying once I've set myself a goal and I go, right, I'm going to make a bagel and make it look identical to an actual bagel."
The exhibition also opens at a time when so-called "grandma hobbies" like knitting have soared in popularity among younger generations, with 86% of Gen Z now identifying as "crafters" or "makers", according to a survey by Mintel Group Ltd.
"The internet has opened the world up to people being able to learn online," Jenkins said.
"It's amazing and I can see why there's such a massive interest because it's more accessible and it's not too taxing. You don't need massive amount of tools or money to make something."
The communal nature of crafty hobbies has also allowed Jenkins to make her exhibitions more sociable and interactive, encouraging people to knit their own cakes at her 2022 'Cafe Kate' show in the Netherlands.
"It's nice to have that excitement, for people to go and just hang out and do a bit of knitting, or feel absorbed in the exhibition in that way."
There's a similar sense of conviviality at 'Kate's Knitalian', although guests can rest assured they won't need any knitting (or cooking) skills to visit the build-your-own-pizza station.
They will, however, need to exercise a lot of self-restraint not to take a bite out of anything...
'Kate's Knitalian' opens at Air Contemporary gallery in London, United Kingdom, from 30 October until 5 December 2026.

AI’s real bottleneck is electricity. Who will pay for it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:13:47 UTC
16:13:47 KST

AI’s real bottleneck is electricity. Who will pay for it?
As Big Tech turns to nuclear power to fuel its AI ambitions, the cost of keeping data centers running raises a question that extends far beyond Silicon Valley.
Within a week, two of the three largest cloud computing companies in the world signed 20-year contracts for nuclear electricity. Amazon has taken 690 megawatts from Constellation’s Calvert Cliffs plant in Maryland, including 190 megawatts of additional generating capacity expected between 2030 and 2032. Google has signed an agreement that will bring 890 megawatts of additional nuclear capacity into the United States. Constellation is investing more than $4.3bn to upgrade 11 reactors across Illinois, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey. Neither agreement, however, involves building a new nuclear reactor. Rather, they are paying to generate more output from reactors that already exist – some of which are even older than the companies themselves.
A few years ago, such agreements would have seemed inconceivable. Nuclear power had fallen out of favour following accidents at Three Mile Island in 1979, Chornobyl in 1986 and Fukushima in 2011. Germany phased out nuclear power, while Japan shut down its reactors after Fukushima, although it has since begun restarting them. In many democratic countries, advocating for nuclear energy became politically difficult.
Today, an undamaged reactor at Three Mile Island is being brought back into service, with Microsoft contracted to buy its output for 20 years. The US Department of Energy is providing up to $4.4bn in loans to support the restart of three shuttered plants, with the aim of restoring about 2.25 gigawatts. Palisades in Michigan, which was closed in 2022, is contracted to be generating again by March 2027. If successful, it would become the first US commercial nuclear plant to restart after entering decommissioning.
What has changed?
The quiet reversal
In the last decade, the industry’s answer to AI’s energy problem was efficiency – things such as better chips, smaller models and smarter cooling seemed appealing and feasible. Industry conferences featured discussions about performance per watt, with modern artificial intelligence (AI) chips performing more computation per unit of electricity than their predecessors.
Yet those efficiency gains did not reduce overall electricity demand. Instead, each gain was quickly put towards something larger. Even when DeepSeek demonstrated that a competitive model could be trained at a fraction of the computing cost many had expected, the result was not a reduction in industry spending. Instead, laboratories continued planning more training runs, models that reason for longer, agents that work continuously in the background, and video generation.
This would not be the first time something like this has happened in history. In 1865, William Jevons observed that more efficient steam engines made Britain burn more coal, not less, because cheaper power created uses that had not existed before. The International Energy Agency estimates that global data centre electricity demand will more than double to around 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, even assuming continued improvements in efficiency.
Hence, the industry has changed strategy – unable to shrink demand, companies are now buying up supply.
The arithmetic of waiting
Money, however, cannot solve every problem quickly.
A new large reactor takes a decade or more from decision to electricity. Tech companies are investing in small modular reactors to power their data centres, although many of these projects are not expected to deliver electricity until the early 2030s. So far, very few of these have been built anywhere in the world. Thus, while reactor restarts and upgrades are the faster option, the “fast option” still means 2027, 2028, 2029, or beyond.
AI capital expenditure, however, does not operate on that same calendar. The chips being installed this year could be overtaken by newer technology long before the 20-year electricity contracts powering them expire. This discrepancy underpins all of these announcements, yet the industry has not addressed the implications if demand weakens while contractual obligations remain.
Who pays in the meantime
This is where the story stops being about technology.
Most of these deals sit inside PJM, the grid operator serving roughly 67 million people across 13 American states and Washington, DC. PJM uses capacity auctions to secure sufficient electricity-generating resources for future demand, with the associated costs ultimately passed on to consumers through their electricity bills. Capacity prices have reached the regulatory price cap in three consecutive auctions. According to the grid operator’s independent market monitor, data centre demand contributed approximately $29.4bn in capacity costs across the four most recent auctions. In the latest auction alone, around $6.3bn of these costs were attributed to data centre demand, including forecasts for facilities that have yet to be built.
In effect, households are already paying higher electricity capacity charges, partly because of projected demand from facilities that may never become operational. The Natural Resources Defense Council estimates that, by 2028, the typical household within PJM could face an additional $70 per month in electricity costs if current trends continue. These rising costs are also having political consequences. Recent US polling shows growing public dissatisfaction with data centres, with electricity bills among the main concerns. In response, Virginia has established a separate electricity rate class for data centres, Ohio has introduced minimum billing requirements, and Illinois is debating legislation.
The aim of the Google agreement is to tackle this objection. Its underlying principle is that major new electricity consumers should bring additional generation capacity rather than compete with existing users for an already constrained supply. This approach represents a constructive step towards mitigating the pressure that data centres place on electricity systems.
However, the arrangement remains voluntary. In October 2026, US federal regulators rejected most of PJM’s proposal to require large new electricity consumers to provide their own generation capacity. As a consequence, the industry is voluntarily offering a commitment that regulators have so far declined to impose through PJM’s proposed rules. This poses the question: how long will such voluntary commitments remain viable if the costs of fulfilling them begin to rise?
What the Gulf should take from this
For Gulf countries preparing their own AI infrastructure expansion, the US experience offers a warning about the costs of getting these arrangements wrong.
For countries with abundant energy resources, the expansion of AI infrastructure presents a significant opportunity.
Qatar’s sovereign fund has committed to a $20bn joint venture with Brookfield for AI infrastructure, beginning with a first phase of roughly 300 megawatts and potentially expanding to near 1.5 gigawatts. Abu Dhabi is pursuing plans for up to five gigawatts of AI data centre capacity. Saudi Arabia is targeting almost two gigawatts through HUMAIN. The region’s competitive advantage is substantial. As demand for AI computing grows, access to electricity is becoming an increasingly important factor in determining where computing infrastructure is built. The Gulf is well positioned to capitalise on this demand.
However, the scale of the proposed developments warrants scrutiny. If the proposed 1.5-gigawatt build-out is completed in Qatar, it would represent electricity demand equivalent to approximately 12 percent of the country’s installed generating capacity. Electricity allocated to AI infrastructure cannot simultaneously serve other purposes, meaning the opportunity costs of these projects deserve serious consideration.
In the United States, the debate over AI infrastructure is becoming increasingly centred on who ultimately bears the cost of its electricity demands, with many of the major commitments already in place. The Gulf is in a rare position of being able to settle that question first: what the industrial tariff is, who funds the new generation, what happens to the contracts when the hardware ages, and what long-term economic benefits the country would see beyond energy revenues and a limited number of jobs.
While hosting AI infrastructure can generate considerable economic value, the greater strategic opportunity lies in determining the conditions under which that infrastructure operates. For Gulf countries, the opportunity to establish these terms exists now, before large-scale commitments constrain their options.

Qatari mediators return to Tehran to push for US-Iran deal, official says
Oct 30 - Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on Friday as part of efforts to reach a deal between the US and Iran, an official briefed on the talks told Reuters.
The mediation talks have been coordinated with the US, the official said.
Qatar presented a draft peace plan to Iran on Sunday, according to an official briefed on negotiations. But a senior Iranian official dismissed the proposals as unacceptable and said Tehran would maintain its nuclear position.
Washington wants nuclear issues included from the start of negotiations. Tehran demands that the US first end its port blockade and lift oil export sanctions.

Indonesia wildfire haze killed an estimated 3,560 people in September: report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:10:19 UTC
16:10:19 KST

Pollution from smoke emitted by months of wildfires across Indonesia caused an estimated 3,560 deaths in the vast Southeast Asian archipelago in September, according to a new study.
The same month, about 57.8 million people in Indonesia were inhaling unhealthy to hazardous air, said the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Helsinki-based think tank.
"Worsening air quality due to forest and land fires in Indonesia pushed the estimated death toll to 3,560 cases in September 2026, a twofold increase from the August estimate," a statement by CREA said on Thursday.
The CREA study estimated the number of deaths brought about by PM2.5 pollution in the short-term, meaning a matter of days.
PM2.5 particles are small enough to penetrate the lungs or bloodstream and the World Health Organization has linked exposure to a higher risk for illness and premature death.
Most estimated deaths occurred on Indonesia's part of Borneo island as well as on Java and Sumatra islands and in the country's east, said the report.
The researchers also looked at non-fire pollution from urban power generation, industry, and transportation, and found it had caused a further 1,750 deaths in September for a total of 5,310 in the country of about 290 million people.
"In September alone, exposure levels breached the WHO annual PM2.5 threshold... by over seven times nationally, 10 times in Sumatra, and an alarming 24 times in Kalimantan" in Borneo, said the report.
More than 330,000 cases of acute respiratory infection have been recorded countrywide.
'Predictable and avoidable’
Gripped by drought worsened by the El Nino weather phenomenon, Indonesia has for months battled wildfires that deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas says have consumed more than 1.9 million hectares in the nine months to September.
The government has not confirmed or rejected the number.
The resulting haze has sent pollution levels soaring as far afield as Malaysia, Singapore, the Philippines and East Timor, clouding Indonesia's ties with its neighbours.
Experts say the wildfires can be blamed in large part on slash-and-burn land-clearing practices, often by timber, palm oil or mining companies.
For the island of Java, the most populated and home to the capital Jakarta, the CREA report said between 73 and 80 percent of air pollution deaths, a total of 1,530 in September, were attributed to non-fire sources such as industry, vehicle emissions, and waste burning.
"These figures underscore the stark reality that non-fire air pollution sources are as dangerous as smoke from burning forests and peatlands," it said.
In the report, the CEO of Landscape Indonesia consultancy, Agus Sari, pointed to the government's "weak preparedness" for what he described as a "predictable and avoidable" disaster.
Agus pointed to budget cuts hampering the efforts of the BNPB national disaster management agency.
"Indonesia should be able to prepare for what is going to happen. The fact that we are not prepared at all is purely a matter of lacking the will," said Agus.
The CREA report argued the government needs to shift from wildfire response to the restoration of peatlands left fire prone by extensive draining.
"This step must be accompanied by firm law enforcement against illegal land clearing through burning, as well as strengthened legal accountability for concession holders to prevent damage," it said.
For regions battling non-fire pollution, such as Java, it said the government must enforce stricter emissions standards.
The government on Wednesday defended its approach to the fires, saying in a statement more than 72,000 people had been deployed in cloud-seeding and firefighting operations, more than 2,100 doctors and health workers activated in hard-hit areas, and 5.3 million masks distributed.

The average price of a litre of diesel in October hit its highest level in Finland since June 2022, according to figures published by Statistics Finland on Friday.
The average price per litre of diesel rose to 2.49 euros during October, exceeding the price in June 2022 by five cents.
Statistics Finland's report noted that the equivalent price of diesel this time last year was 1.67 euros, an increase of nearly 50 percent.
"It seems that oil is making it to the market despite the war situation, but the uncertainty related to transport is still reflected in supply and, as a result, is pushing up consumer prices," Kristiina Nieminen, Senior Statistician at Statistics Finland, stated in an agency press release.
Aside from diesel, the prices of 98-octane petrol and 95-octane petrol were also up.
The average price of 98-octane petrol this month was 2.38 euros per litre, while 95 came in slightly cheaper, at 2.28 euros.
"The annual change of the average price for petrol 95 was 33.3 percent and for petrol 98 it was 31.5 percent," Statistics Finland's report noted.

How Israel choked off Hebron at 10 entrances, as 5,000 forced to flee
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:07:36 UTC
16:07:36 KST

How Israel choked off Hebron at 10 entrances, as 5,000 forced to flee
An investigation by Al Jazeera’s Data Journalism Unit reveals the severe humanitarian and economic toll of the escalating Israeli military siege on Hebron.
Almost 5,000 people have been displaced as a result of Israel’s military siege on the southern West Bank city of Hebron, Al Jazeera reveals.
As the lockdown, which has choked the city off at 10 identified entry points, enters its second week on Friday, the number of people forcibly removed from their homes stands at 4,969. The displaced population includes vulnerable groups: 441 elderly people, 336 infants less than two years old and 312 patients with chronic diseases. More than 200 pregnant or nursing women are also included, as well as 44 people with disabilities.
Al Jazeera, which has analysed municipal data and statistics from human rights groups, reveals that 780 families are currently displaced, representing about 2 percent of the city’s 250,000 residents.
“Thousands of citizens were forced out of their homes, and the world watched children crying after midnight,” Hebron Mayor Yousef al-Jabari told Al Jazeera. He added in a statement to Anadolu agency that Hebron is “facing a severe, massive siege and collective punishment”.
On October 24, the mayor told Al Jazeera that about 2,200 people were displaced, meaning the number had more than doubled in just two days.
‘We will act to destroy this place’
The military siege began on Friday, October 23, after two Palestinians shot two Israeli soldiers dead in Hebron and injured three others, before the army killed the two attackers.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced on social media that he had ordered security forces to immediately close Hebron and “prepare for a full lockdown across all of Judea and Samaria [the Israeli term for the occupied West Bank]”.
“We will act to destroy this place, to change it completely,” he proclaimed.
The Israeli army said the operation aims to “thwart terrorism” by searching, arresting suspects, and confiscating weapons.
Defence Minister Israel Katz said Palestinians will not be allowed to return to their homes until Hamas’s “infrastructure” is dismantled.
However, the Israeli news site Ynet quoted the army as saying the search for weapons has had “limited accomplishments” and keeping residents away from their homes for a prolonged period faces “legal difficulties”.
The municipality noted that the targeted eviction zone spans 0.35 square kilometres (0.14 square miles) – the size of 49 football pitches and an area housing more than 500 families comprising at least 2,500 individuals.
Conditions remain precarious; among the families whose locations have been tracked, 283 are residing with relatives and 266 are in locations classified by the municipality as unsafe.
According to Al Jazeera’s findings, most displaced families have sought refuge with relatives or host families in nearby neighbourhoods such as Issa, and no one has resorted to official shelter centres, while only 23 families managed to secure rented homes.
Cordoning off a city
Al Jazeera’s analysis shows that Israeli forces have surrounded the city by closing off 10 entrances located between 2.4km (1.5 miles) and 7.6km (4.7 miles) from the centre.
These blockades include Halhul, Nabi Yunus and Ras al-Jora to the north; Beit Einun to the northeast; and Bir al-Mahjar to the northwest. The eastern and southern flanks are blockaded by closures at Jabal Juhar, al-Fahs, Qalqas, al-Harayiq and Dura.
The closed military operations zone lies about 2km (1.2 miles) west of the city centre, covering a documented area of at least 0.29sq km (0.11sq miles), or about 40 football fields.
In the Farsh al-Hawa area at the city’s western entrance, Israeli forces demolished a three-apartment residential building during the first two days of the operation – October 23 and 24 – targeted a ceramics company alongside car parts shops, and bulldozed approximately 7,000 square metres (75,000 square feet) of land.
Families were also evicted from the al-Jalda and Ein Deir Bahha neighbourhoods about midnight on Friday, October 23, when Israeli forces ordered residents via loudspeakers to leave.
During the first two days of the operation, forces converted several homes into military barracks and raised Israeli flags on them, according to Anadolu.
Raids, arrests and interrogations
Over the first six days of the operation, the Israeli military arrested approximately 110 Palestinians across the governorate, according to the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society (PPS).
The detainees include seven children, people with special needs, and dozens of former prisoners. Israeli forces also arrested three women, releasing two while keeping the third under interrogation at the al-Mascobiyeh detention centre.
Furthermore, the military continues to hold eight relatives of the two Palestinian gunmen who killed the Israeli soldiers, having transferred them to interrogation centres.
Beyond formal arrests, hundreds of citizens have been subjected to field interrogations during military raids.
The PPS reported that these interrogations, conducted on streets, at checkpoints and inside homes, have been accompanied by severe beatings and abuse.
The military has searched more than 500 sites in the city.
The Israeli army claims to have discovered a 15-metre- (50ft-) deep underground pit containing an electronic device near an attacker’s home, although the property owner has denied this. The owner said the excavation is a sewage cesspit for an area lacking infrastructure, adding that the property belongs to neither of the gunmen and is more than 100 metres (330ft) from their residences.
Economic paralysis
The Hebron Chamber of Commerce and Industry estimates daily commercial losses at 12 million shekels (about $3.8m) as a result of this siege.
Factory production capacity has plummeted by 40 to 60 percent, according to estimates by Adnan al-Natsheh, vice president of the Chamber.
The governorate houses about 3,500 industrial facilities, in particular plastics and dairy facilities, as well as 70 percent of the gold workshops for the Palestinian market.
The movement of commercial trucks has completely halted. The demolitions in Farsh al-Hawa alone have caused damage of more than two million shekels (about $640,000).
This recent escalation compounds an already heavy toll across the occupied West Bank.
In September alone, the Hebron governorate faced 272 attacks, including 122 perpetrated by Israeli settlers, and 19 demolition operations that levelled 91 structures, making it the most targeted governorate in the West Bank for demolitions.

Artificially heated reservoirs promote northbound movement of thermophilic mollusks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:07:21 UTC
16:07:21 KST

ARKHANGELSK, October 30. /TASS/. Artificially heated reservoirs, like, for example, those at thermal power plants, along with the climate warming, promote the movement of thermophilic freshwater mollusks species to the north. Among such mollusks is the river Dreissena polymorpha - an aggressive invasive species, threatening hydraulic structures as the mollusk can form fouling congregations even on submarines, Director of the Biogeography and Genetic Resources Institute at the Academician Laverov Federal Research Center for Integrated Arctic Studies (the Russian Academy of Sciences' Urals Branch) Yulia Bespalaya told TASS.
"Due to the climate warming, freshwater thermophilic mollusks can move closer to the Arctic borders. Not only that however. This process is facilitated by anthropogenic disturbed reservoirs with altered thermal conditions. The heated water dumping transforms natural habitats promoting the movement of invasive species towards the north. Among them is the river dreissena - one of aggressive invaders," she said.
Unlike insects, which often fly into the northern regions though still are unable to form a stable population due to insufficiently high temperatures for reproduction, the situation with mollusks is different. Heated reservoirs become a kind of refugium - those are shelters where alien species can gain a foothold and begin to reproduce.
Most bivalves are thermophilic. For many species, the breeding threshold is in the range between 12 and 15 degrees Celsius, for corbicula - between 6 and 15 - they can overwinter only in constantly heated water. However, some species, including the dreissen, feel quite comfortable and can breed even in the main watercourse.
"Dreissena was brought to the Arkhangelsk Region through the Severodvinsk Canal in the late 19th century - first finds date back to 1897. The mollusk had passed from the Caspian Sea through the Volga River. Since then, it has naturalized, formed a stable population and has been reproducing steadily. However, the density in our waters is much lower than, say, in the southern regions, where it may reach dozens of thousands of individuals per square meter, while our population is much more modest," the scientist explained.
The troublesome mollusk
Anyway, even in small quantities, the mollusk causes troubles, forming fouling congregations on fishing nets, hydraulic structures, ships and even submarines. When these structures additionally are heated by waste water, the fouling may become critical. Various methods are used to combat dreissena: mechanical cleaning, scraping, special paint coatings, and even chlorine treatment, although the latter is extremely harmful to the ecosystem.
"Dreissena is able to withstand salinity of up to 14 ppm, thus it colonizes marine objects, and also submarines, around which the water is not fresh," the expert said.
Scientists supposed the key to the invasive species' expansion may lie in genetics. Some of the local river dreissen individuals are of hybrid forms - they have fragments of genes, possibly, from other species of mollusks Dreissena rostriformis. Probably, it is this hybridization that gives them an advantage, allowing the mollusks to move further northbound and to adapt to harsh conditions.
"Right now, we are extremely interested in finding out the genetic structure of populations that live in warm discharge waters, for example, near nuclear power plants. We want to find out what kind of mutations or hybridizations allow them to survive in low winter temperatures and to reproduce actively," the scientist told TASS in conclusion.
In addition to the obvious climatic changes, such as warming, the thermal pollution of water bodies from industrial enterprises and energy facilities also contributes to the process. Discharges of artificially heated water from enterprises lead to periodic or prolonged increases in water temperature above the natural level. As a result, oxygen solubility decreases, the water's chemical and microbiological composition changes, the aquatic ecosystems' natural functioning gets disrupted. Consequently, the composition of aquatic organisms will change.
Thermosensitive species die, while thermophilic species, on the contrary, would appear to begin developing actively. Dreissena is a thermophilic species, as its native range is in the Ponto-Caspian and Aral basins. It has settled successfully in the Northern Dvina River long before the industrial development there.

Set to open on Paper Island in early December, KAI will have multiple pools, wellness facilities and also offer bathers access to the harbour’s waters for swimming.
Rain or shine (or even snow), nothing can get between Danes and going for a swim.
Soon, Copenhagen residents will have a new spot for doing so – and it’s seriously swanky.
Part of a wider project to revitalise Copenhagen Harbour, KAI will open on Paper Island on 5 December.
Designed by Japanese practice Kengo Kuma & Associates, the name is both a reference to the Japanese word for sea and the Danish word for quay (kaj), a nod to its location.
Described as a “water culture house”, the facility has 10 swimming pools plus direct access to designated swimming and dipping zones in the harbour and will host cultural experiences that “invite people to explore water in new ways”.
“It is part of the ongoing transformation of the city and its harbour from an industrial port into a cultural waterfront, where new functions have helped bring the surrounding areas of the Inner Harbour to life,” Yuki Ikeguchi, lead architect and partner in charge at Kengo Kuma & Associates, said.
“As Paper Island’s cultural cornerstone, the House is a civic institution dedicated to water and community, embraced by a public harbour bath.
“Open to all, it creates new settings for everyday life in Copenhagen, where physical and mental wellbeing can become a natural part of urban life.”
What to expect at KAI
Spanning some 5,800 square metres, the complex consists of five brick towers, each of which is shaped according to the outline of the pools beneath it.
The ground floor has a 25-metre fitness pool, a teaching pool and three children’s play pools, with access to the harbour bathing areas which include a swimming zone overlooking the Opera Park, and a plunge zone with views of the Royal Danish Playhouse.
The first floor is dedicated to wellness, with a therapy pool, a hot pool, and a cold plunge pool. It’s also where you’ll find the open-air valley pool, as well as the outdoor onsen, which boasts fantastic views of the harbour.
Able to handle 380 bathers at any given time, the facility also has three saunas, a heated stone and a steam bath.

In the United States, two helicopters collided in midair in Oregon, killing three people and closing a highway. Investigators carefully examined debris scattered across a field in the northwestern part of the state, officials said. UNN reports this, citing CNN.
Details
The crash killed 22-year-old Texas flight instructor Maddie Aasbo and 38-year-old Oregon pilot Tyler Sturdevant, as well as a student pilot from the United Kingdom, Yamhill County Sheriff Sam Elliott said during a press conference.
Aasbo was in one helicopter with the student pilot, while Sturdevant was the sole occupant of the other, the sheriff said.
The aircraft crashed onto a private agricultural field near McMinnville Municipal Airport, officials said. The red helicopter was left shattered into pieces, while the green helicopter lay upside down. McMinnville is southwest of Portland.
A section of nearby Highway 233 was closed because of the crash, the Oregon Department of Transportation said Thursday afternoon, offering no estimate for when it would reopen.
Leo Rodriguez said he called 911 after witnessing the crash while watching from his family vineyard.
"Suddenly I hear this loud rumble and this crunching of metal, I look up and just see these two helicopters had just collided in midair," he told KPTV.
"It took me a while for my brain to process what I was seeing. You don't see something like that every day. They twisted around and fell to the ground," the witness said.
The sheriff's office asked the public to avoid the area and "be patient while we respond to this critical incident."
The crash, which occurred at about 2:15 p.m. local time, is being investigated by the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said, adding that it is also investigating the incident. Federal investigators were at the scene Thursday evening, October 29, according to the sheriff.
The two helicopters were a Robinson R-22, which was conducting a training flight, and an Airbus AS350, which was performing a maintenance flight, the NTSB said. One of the helicopters was operated by Jerry Trimble Helicopters, a helicopter flight-training school and rental service for private flights, the company said in a statement. French centrists' feuding increases odds of Le Pen-Melenchon runoff
PARIS, Oct 30 - Infighting has broken out among centrist candidates for France's presidential race, splitting the mainstream vote and making a runoff between far-right Marine Le Pen and hard-left Jean-Luc Melenchon more likely.
Opinion polls before next April's presidential election show Le Pen is nearly certain to qualify for a second-round runoff in May and that Melenchon is consistently nudging ahead of mainstream candidates.
Centre-right Edouard Philippe, President Emmanuel Macron's former prime minister, has so far been the centre's torchbearer.

Philippe has also faced criticism over several awkward interventions — including suggesting in a podcast that ideally a newly elected president should have three months to rest before taking office — and political analysts say he is struggling to connect with voters at a time of rising political tensions.
"The terrible thing is that he isn't cutting through," Moreau-Chevrolet told Reuters. "They didn't understand that you have to campaign. There's a kind of dilettantism."
The anxiety has sharpened tensions between Philippe and his main rival, Gabriel Attal, another former prime minister. They are locked in a battle over who should step aside for the centrist ticket.
Philippe fell to 15% support in an IFOP-Fiducial poll for Le Figaro newspaper, a six-point drop since September. That is below the 16.5% for Melenchon, who would have enough to qualify for a runoff against Le Pen.
Attal stood at 13%, behind Melenchon and Raphael Glucksmann, a mainstream centre-left candidate.
Under pressure from lawmakers in his camp to abandon his presidential ambitions and rally to Philippe, Attal irritated many Macron allies this week by reviving the idea of a broad centrist primary, a proposal critics say risks fuelling division at a time when moderates can least afford it.
Still, Attal has leverage. As leader of Macron's Renaissance party, he controls the purse strings of the party machine.
CENTRIST VOTE FRAGMENTS
"It's catastrophic," said Jean-Baptiste Moreau, a former lawmaker from Macron's camp.
"They are attacking one another in the media and they are both collapsing in the polls. We're heading straight towards an RN-LFI second round," he said of Le Pen's National Rally (RN) and Melenchon's France Unbowed (LFI). "In the current state of opinion, I don't see how we avoid it."
The fragmentation stretches beyond the Philippe-Attal feud.
On the centre-left, Glucksmann has gained ground after winning the Socialist primary. On the right, Bruno Retailleau, a former interior minister, and David Lisnard, the free-market mayor of Cannes, are targeting the same moderate electorate.
Philippe's supporters say reports of his demise are premature. Laurent Marcangeli, a member of Philippe's party Horizons, acknowledged recent polling setbacks but said the former prime minister remained the only centrist candidate with a realistic path to the runoff.
"He's still in the race for the second round and to prevent a Le Pen-Melenchon duel," said Marcangeli, adding that in some polls Attal scored as low as single digits.
Some Macron allies, however, are openly questioning whether either man should carry on. They say any association with Macron, who is finishing his second term at record-low popularity, will weigh on a centrist candidate.
"The two of them are collapsing," said Perrine Goulet, a lawmaker from Macron ally MoDem. "Any candidate who has been in a Macron government is going to be struggling."
With Le Pen and Melenchon consolidating support at opposite ends of the spectrum, she said moderates needed to put aside personal ambitions and rally behind a single contender able to unite supporters of Glucksmann through to Retailleau.
"We're calling on everyone to put their egos aside and find the best candidate," Goulet said.
"If we keep Glucksmann on one side, Retailleau on the other, Edouard Philippe, Gabriel Attal, we'll end up with an LFI-RN second round. The danger is simply too great." REUTERS

Gold fell below $4,000 an ounce on Oct. 30 as rising oil prices and persistent U.S. inflation reinforced expectations of a Federal Reserve interest rate increase before the end of the year.
Spot gold was down 0.6 percent at $3,997.39 an ounce by 0255 GMT. U.S. gold futures for December delivery also fell 0.6 percent to $4,007.80.
The metal was heading for a second consecutive monthly decline, with traders pricing in about a 75 percent chance of a December rate increase, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool.
U.S. data released on Oct. 29 showed the personal consumption expenditures price index rose 0.5 percent in September, accelerating from 0.3 percent in August. The index was up 3.6 percent from a year earlier, above the Fed’s 2 percent inflation target.
Excluding food and energy, prices rose 3.1 percent from a year earlier, the Bureau of Economic Analysis said.
The Fed had kept its benchmark rate unchanged at 3.75-4 percent on Oct. 28, though two policymakers voted for a quarter-point increase. Its statement said inflation remained elevated.
Gold pays no interest, making it less attractive when returns on interest-bearing assets rise.
“Gold’s slide is asking serious questions of technical support around the $4,000 level,” said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade.
Buying on price dips had previously limited losses, but it was unclear whether that would support prices again, he said.
Oil was on course for a fourth consecutive monthly gain as attacks on Saudi Arabia raised supply concerns. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis said on Oct. 29 that they had attacked several Saudi oil facilities.
Higher energy costs threaten to sustain inflation through transport and production expenses, adding to pressure on central banks to keep monetary policy tight.
In Japan, Tokyo’s annual core inflation remained above the Bank of Japan’s 2 percent target in October.
Other precious metals also fell. Spot silver dropped 2.1 percent to $51.27 an ounce, platinum lost 1.9 percent to $1,458.85 and palladium declined 2 percent to $986.08. All three were heading for weekly and monthly losses.

Mahmood infuriates fellow ministers by failing to reveal impact of UK migration shake-up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:00:48 UTC
16:00:48 KST

Shabana Mahmood has infuriated ministerial colleagues by failing to share what they see as crucial information about the impact of her migration changes.
Sources say the home secretary has repeatedly refused to reveal how much she expects homelessness to rise as a result of changes to the asylum system.
Home Office ministers will meet their counterparts from other departments over the next few days to thrash out a compromise amid warnings about a potential staff crisis in the care sector.
One person with knowledge of the standoff said: “Shabana has been asked on multiple occasions what the Home Office assessment was of the impact her changes would have on homelessness and community cohesion, but she point-blank refused to engage with it.”
The Home Office says it cannot quantify the exact impact of the proposals because the detail has not yet been finalised. They insist the new system will be designed to minimise any impact on destitution and homelessness.
However, others in government believe the Home Office could give out more detailed information but does not want to admit how much disruption the proposals will cause.
“It has caused a huge amount of frustration among other ministers who are working on the government’s push to end rough sleeping,” said the source.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “This policy went through the normal cross-government process, with information shared through the formal collective agreement process.
“Ending asylum hotels will not leave people homeless. We are moving people into more suitable accommodation while delivering reforms that have already saved taxpayers more than £1bn since the election.”
Mahmood announced her changes to the asylum system last November, including ending permanent leave to remain and the government’s duty to support people who would otherwise become destitute.
The home secretary said her proposals would restore order to the immigration system and help puncture the appeal of hard-right parties such as Reform UK.
In an impact assessment released this month, however, her department admitted homelessness could rise.
“There is a risk that, if repayments materially reduce disposable income, some individuals could experience financial hardship or destitution,” the document said.
“This may increase demand for homelessness services and rough sleeping support, creating additional cost pressures for local authorities.”
The first requests for details about the potential impact were made by Ali McGovern and Miatta Fahnbulleh when they were ministers under Keir Starmer. They were supported by the then housing secretary Steve Reed, who was also understood to have been concerned about a possible rise in rough sleeping.
The three ministers already feared the push to move asylum seekers out of hotels could lead to more people sleeping on the streets.
They said the proposals made last November could prevent the government from hitting its target of halving rough sleeping by the end of the parliament.
McGovern and Fahnbulleh secured a meeting with Alex Norris, then a Home Office minister and now the justice secretary, but felt few of their questions were answered.
The pair were preparing to write a formal letter to the Home Office to demand the information when Fahnbulleh resigned from government in a move that helped bring about Starmer’s departure from Downing Street. The letter was never sent, sources said
An ally of Mahmood pointed to the Home Office’s impact assessment, which says: “Thresholds and repayment rates will be designed to … ensure individuals retain sufficient income to meet basic living standards.
“Given that the design of the recoupment mechanism has not yet been developed, it is not possible to assess the scale of the risk at this stage.”
Ministers say the row has only deepened since Andy Burnham came to power, not least because the prime minister has promised to give every rough sleeper a route off the streets by Christmas, committing hundreds of millions of pounds to do so.
Sources say Angela Rayner, Reed’s successor as housing secretary, also wants to see more details about the impact of Mahmood’s proposals.
The sources say she is particularly concerned about the possibility that moving asylum seekers out of hotels and into houses of multiple occupancy will reignite anti-immigration protests.
Rayner has argued against Mahmood’s proposals for changes to legal migration as well, arguing the government should exempt care workers from plans to make it harder for workers to achieve settled status.
The Guardian revealed this year that Burnham was considering intervening to make sure care workers were exempted and prevent a sudden exodus from the sector.
The issue is set to be decided over the next 10 days after a series of meetings between senior ministers.
A government source said: “The prime minister wants ministers to deal with the detail of this policy, but he has made it clear he supports Shabana but also wants to make sure sectors get the support they need.”

UK side-hustle tax-free allowance to rise to £3,000 next year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:00:47 UTC
16:00:47 KST

The amount Britons can earn from a side hustle without paying tax will rise to £3,000 next year in a fillip for those who make extra cash from hobbies or reselling.
Up to 1.4 million people could benefit from the change announced in the budget, with the chancellor confirming the tax-free “trading” allowance will increase from £1,000 to £3,000 in April 2027.
The number of Britons with a side hustle has exploded in recent years, with reselling clothes, tutoring and dog-walking among the popular avenues to create extra income at a time when household finances are under pressure.
Last year, 2.6 million people made money selling goods through platforms including eBay, Vinted and Etsy, according to data provided by HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) to accountancy firm Lubbock Fine. In 2024 the number was just 450,000.
Currently, people can earn up to £1,000 a year from a side hustle without paying tax but above this you may owe tax if your total income, including your main job, is above the £12,570 personal allowance.
Out of the 1.4 million people, an estimated 400,000 will see their tax bill go down, with an average saving of £380. Meanwhile, about 100,000 people will no longer have to report their trading income to HMRC.
Sarah Coles, the head of personal finance at AJ Bell, said that for people with a small side hustle, the more generous allowance “doesn’t just save tax, it also takes the hassle of admin off their plate”.
As a result, she added: “You can spend more time working for yourself and less doing paperwork for HMRC. It means you can make £3,000 before you have to think about doing a self-assessment tax return.”
Coles said people who were making more than £3,000 would have the choice to use the allowance or subtract business expenses and capital costs when calculating their profits for tax purposes.
Jane Hawkes, a consumer champion and the founder of the Lady Janey blog, said side hustles were a great way to turn hobbies, skills and spare-time activities into extra cash and “increasing the allowance should make this easier without wholly unnecessary red tape”.
But, she added: “It’s important that people understand their tax obligations, particularly the distinction between selling unwanted personal belongings and trading for profit, so they don’t inadvertently fall foul of HMRC rules.”
Selling your own clothes or other items is not taxable if you’re selling them for less than you originally paid as you are not making a profit.
Rules came into force last year requiring platforms to inform HMRC about their sellers and how much money they made. HMRC now receives data about every seller who made 30 sales or €2,000 (about £1,700) on any platform in the past year.

Biodiversity Cop17 seems to be stalling. Is it time to reform the process?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
07:00:46 UTC
16:00:46 KST

When things are not going well at an environmental summit, organisers often tell delegates that the “world is watching” in an attempt to focus minds. But spend any time at biodiversity Cop17 in Armenia and it is clear that the world’s attention is elsewhere.
The negotiating halls of Yerevan’s Meridian centre are subdued. Environment ministers have arrived from all corners of the world to plan their response to being so far behind the biodiversity targets they agreed four years ago. Right now, they appear on track to miss nearly all of them. They risk continuing the miserable record of never having met a biodiversity target they have set for themselves.
More from Cop17, after this week’s most important reads.
Essential reads
- The climate crisis will destroy our economies – we learned this 20 years ago. When will we act?
- Heat killed ‘staggering’ 50,000 people in Europe’s cities this summer, scientists warn
- Angry Labour MPs urge leadership not to overrule energy secretary on Rosebank
In focus
I write this during a good week for the environment. Lula’s incredible comeback in the Brazilian presidential election will probably guarantee four more years of low deforestation rates in their part of the Amazon rainforest, one of the most alive places on our planet. Serbia’s new Student List government could tackle the country’s dreadful environmental record. But these hard-won achievements have little to do with the increasingly fractured multilateral process.
In a side room on Wednesday, I sat down with Inger Andersen, the executive director of the UN environment programme, to discuss how the process could be reformed. The organisation is working with governments to streamline the sprawling set of agreements and bodies that make up the global environmental calendar, in an attempt to improve their impact.
“The process is delivering but it’s going too slowly. This is what the secretary-general [António Guterres] said when he was here: ‘Thank you. Good. Do more, but faster, because we are not where we want to be’,” she said.
Implementation has always been one of the most challenging parts of any Cop process. Painfully negotiated agreements lack ways to meaningfully highlight which countries are falling behind or punish bad behaviour. It will always be up to national governments to deliver on their promises.
During the climate Cop29 in Azerbaijan in 2024, leading policy experts called for a radical overhaul to climate summits, describing the process as “no longer fit for purpose”. They said they needed to shift from a focus on negotiation to implementation, and argued that only the most environmentally ambitious countries should host, although some in the group later walked back on that statement.
Even so, they are not alone in their calls for reform of the international patchwork of agreements and initiatives.
“Right now, the environmental agenda is very cluttered. There are lots of meetings, important as each one is. It will be very interesting for members states to look at the issue. Let’s begin with the easy stuff, like programmatic overlap between conventions, which has an energy-sapping effect,” said Andersen.
“We identified the illegal wildlife trade back in the 70s as a problem, then we identified migratory species, then broader biodiversity, then wetlands. Each of these conventions came along at the right time, but we now have a plethora of them. Maybe we should think about that,” she said.
By the end of Friday, governments are scheduled to sign off an action plan to get back on target with this decade’s biodiversity targets. Few in Yerevan are expecting major moves. But without change soon, calls to reform the Cop process will only grow louder. The health of the planet demands it.

Cop summits ‘no longer fit for purpose’, say leading climate policy experts

The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Facebook, according to Ukrinform.
“Over the past day, 211 combat engagements were recorded. Yesterday, the enemy launched one missile strike and 82 airstrikes, dropping 263 guided aerial bombs. In addition, the invaders deployed 9,576 kamikaze drones and carried out 2,478 shelling attacks on settlements and our troops’ positions, including 42 using multiple launch rocket systems,” the statement said.
