‘Historic milestone’ for Greenland as new international airport opens in Ilulissat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:59:08 UTC
15:59:08 KST

Greenland has completed its three-airport expansion, with Ilulissat’s new international gateway opening up direct access to Disko Bay and North Greenland.
A new international airport opened on Thursday in Greenland's third-largest town, Ilulissat, following approval by the Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority.
Built with the aim of better connecting the vast Arctic island to the rest of the world, it is the third new airport to open in Greenland since 2024. This puts the “final piece in place” in the country’s “historic airport expansion”, said operator Greenland Airports.
Ilulissat Airport is the last to open under the Danish autonomous territory’s expansion programme, following Nuuk in November 2024 and Qaqortoq in April 2026. Together, these airports “form a new backbone” for the country’s infrastructure, the operator said.
"The opening is a historic milestone for Ilulissat, for North Greenland, and for all of Greenland," said Jens Lauridsen, CEO of Greenland Airports.
“The three new airports in Ilulissat, Nuuk, and Qaqortoq fundamentally change how the country is connected internally and how Greenland is connected to the rest of the world.”
The new airport has a 2,200-metre runway capable of accommodating larger aircraft, enabling direct international services to Ilulissat, a hub for Disko Bay and North Greenland.
Air Greenland operates domestic flights between Ilulissat Airport and destinations including Nuuk, Aasiaat, Qaarsut and Upernavik. On the same day as the airport’s opening, Air Greenland launched a direct route between Ilulissat and Denmark’s capital, Copenhagen.
Following the launch, the regular winter schedule begins in November. The route between Copenhagen and Ilulissat will initially be operated by Jettime using a Boeing 737-800. Flights will primarily operate on Wednesdays, with selected additional Monday departures around Christmas and New Year, as well as in March.
Meanwhile, Icelandair will operate a seasonal service between Keflavík and Ilulissat from 3 June to 16 October 2027.
Operations at the airport will “ramp up gradually”, with opening hours and activity expanding in phases. “The goal is for the airport to be fully operational by the summer 2027 season,” Greenland Airports said.
The airport infrastructure upgrades, partly funded by Denmark, are intended to support the development of the local economy and tourism.
“Infrastructure is a long-term investment, and its real impact is measured in decades,” said Jens Wittrup Willumsen, chairman of the board of Greenland Airports.
“With the three new airports, Greenland has a foundation that future generations can build on.
“Now the task is to ensure that the new facilities benefit the entire country, including the towns and settlements around the airports, as part of the future development of business and tourism.”
Located on Greenland's west coast, about 250 kilometres north of the Arctic Circle, Ilulissat is situated next to Disko Bay, known for its enormous icebergs.
For tourism, the new airport means that international visitors can fly directly to Ilulissat to visit its UNESCO-listed icefjord. The airport also creates new opportunities for business, cargo, and regional development throughout North Greenland.

India news: National space agency ISRO to boost GPS alternative with new satellite launch

India news: Space agency to boost GPS alternative with new satellite
Published October 30, 2026last updated October 30, 2026
What you need to know
- The NVS-03 satellite will be carried into orbit by the GSLV-F18 rocket from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota
- It aims to boost NavIC, India's indigenous alternative to the US Global Positioning System (GPS) system
- Opposition leader Gandhi renews call for November 1 rally
Here are the top headlines from India on Friday, October 30:
Opposition leader Gandhi urges supporters to rally 'to save democracy'
Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi on Friday renewed his call for supporters of his Congress Party and other opposition groups to demonstrate this weekend at Ramlila Maidan in New Delhi, a large open space usually serving as a venue for religious festivals.
Gandhi and other senior opposition figures are seeking to capitalize on growing public discontent over alleged voter roll irregularities.
Gandhi encouraged people to turn out to protest on Sunday, despite recent clampdowns by police.
"This is not a march for any one political party, it's a march for the soul of India," Gandhi said.
"If you feel that India is under attack, you are under attack, your expression, your ideas, your way of thinking is under attack, come and join us."
Recent protests against alleged electoral fraud in India have seen protesters and police clash, with several protest leaders detained.
The largely youth- and student-led demonstrations have grown into one of the most serious challenges to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist government in years.
But Gandhi said: "Don't worry about the police ... the BJP will not have the guts to try any of their antics."
Uttar Pradesh MLC election result sends warning to BJP from Samajwadi Party
The Legislative Council elections results declared on Thursday in the northern Uttar Pradesh state has thrust the Samajwadi Party (SP) back in the limelight against the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) ahead of the state elections next year.
SP strengthened its position in Uttar Pradesh's Legislative Council after winning five of the 11 seats contested.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP retained its overall tally of six seats.
SP president Akhilesh Yadav described the results as a rejection of the BJP's policies on education, teachers and students.
"None of our candidates has actually lost, they just could not win in the face of the BJP’s manipulation," Yadav said, according to The Indian Express newspaper, without providing evidence.
West Bengal, Assam on flood alert after glacial lake outburst in Bhutan
Several districts in West Bengal, along with parts of Assam and Arunachal Pradesh, were placed on flood alert on Friday, media reports said.
The flood, triggered by a glacial lake burst at Sintaphu Lake in neighboring Bhutan, swept away infrastructure at the Gasa Tshachu natural hot springs in the Himalayan kingdom.
Indian authorities have stepped up monitoring along the Sankosh River, which flows from Bhutan through West Bengal and into Assam. Communities along the Brahmaputra River in Assam and Arunachal Pradesh have also been alerted over possible flooding.
In Bhutan, no casualties have been reported, state broadcaster BBS said.
According to Bhutanese media reports, two Bailey bridges, built in portable, pre-fabricated sections, may have been washed away, as well as a part of the road leading to Laya village, where the hot springs are located, had also been washed away.
India to launch new satellite to reduce reliance on US-owned GPS
India's space agency is set to launch a navigation satellite on Friday night to strengthen the country's indigenous alternative to GPS.
According to Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) the NVS-03 is "intended to augment the NavIC constellation and support continuity of navigation services."
The NVS-03 satellite, the third in ISRO's next-generation navigation series, will be carried into orbit by the GSLV-F18 rocket from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota at 11:51 p.m. (1821 GMT) on Friday.
According to ISRO, the satellite features an indigenous atomic clock alongside imported clocks, and adds the L1 signal to the existing L5 and S-band signals. It is designed to provide navigation coverage across India and up to 1,500 kilometers (932 miles) beyond its borders.
NavIC is seen as an alternative to the Global Positioning System (GPS) system owned by the United States government.
It was developed to reduce India's dependence on foreign navigation systems, however, according to the Hindustan Times newspaper, the program has faced repeated setbacks, including failing atomic clocks and satellite launch and deployment problems.
Last month, India had launched of its EOS-05 Earth observation satellite, its first ever imaging satellite in geosynchronous orbit.
Welcome to our coverage!
Hello! This is Shakeel from DW's New Delhi Studio bringing you the top updates from across India.
All eyes will be on the skies today as India prepares to launch a navigation satellite to strengthen its indigenous alternative to GPS, reducing the country's reliance on the US government-owned system.
Meanwhile, the results of the Legislative Council elections in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh serve as a warning from the Samajwadi Party to the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) ahead of the 2027 state elections.
Elsewhere, the states of Assam and West Bengal are on flood alert after a glacier burst in Bhutan.

Source: Ukraine's Air Force
Details: The Russians launched ballistic missiles – either Iskander-M, S-400 or KN-23 – from Russia's Voronezh, Kursk and Bryansk oblasts. The Air Force did not specify their number or the results of their interception.
Russian forces fired four Kh-59/69 guided air-to-surface missiles from Russia's Belgorod Oblast. Early reports indicate that as of 07:30, Ukrainian air defence had downed three of them.
The Russians also deployed 113 Shahed and Gerbera attack drones, as well as Parodiya decoy UAVs. These were launched from the Russian cities of Oryol, Kursk and Shatalovo, as well as from temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in occupied Crimea. Among the drones launched were 83 jet-powered Shaheds.
Quote: "Air defence downed or jammed 99 enemy targets:
- three Kh-59/69 guided air-to-surface missiles;
- 96 enemy UAVs of the Shahed type (71 of them jet-powered), Gerberas and other types of drones. Several attack drones are still in the air, and combat operations are ongoing."
Details: The main targets of the attack were Kyiv, Poltava and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts. Hits by drones were recorded at 17 locations, and fallen debris at five others.
Aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare assets, unmanned systems units and mobile fire groups from Ukraine's defence forces have been involved in repelling the attack.

Gazans doubt impact of Palestinian votes in Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:54:30 UTC
15:54:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Gaza's residents sceptical over impact of Palestinian votes in Israel's election
As Palestinian citizens of Israel voted and their political parties secured seats in the Israeli Knesset, many Gazans saw little reason to expect a change in Israel's genocidal policies towards Palestinians.
From tents and damaged homes, residents of the Gaza Strip followed Tuesday's Israeli elections, paying particular attention to turnout among Palestinian voters and the performance of Arab electoral lists.
Preliminary results released on Friday morning, with nearly all votes counted, showed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition securing 53 seats, compared with 48 for the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, while Arab parties won 19 seats, a historic record, according to Israeli media.
The results left the formation of the next government uncertain, with neither camp assured of securing a parliamentary majority, according to the Israeli media outlets.
Gazans, however, question whether Palestinian representation in the Knesset could translate into meaningful influence over Israeli policies affecting Palestinians.
Limits of Palestinian political influence
Gaza-based political analyst Tayseer Abdullah told The New Arab that the preliminary results reflected the continued dominance of hardline Zionist forces and the absence of an influential left-wing alternative offering a fundamentally different approach towards Palestinians.
"Israel's main political camps continue to prioritise military and security solutions while supporting settlement expansion, leaving little reason to expect a fundamental shift in policy," he said.
Commenting on the participation of Palestinian citizens of Israel, Abdullah said their parliamentary representation was important but remained limited in its ability to influence major political and security decisions.
He argued that the results should be assessed not simply by the number of seats won by Arab parties but by their actual capacity to influence government policies, particularly those affecting Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Even if Netanyahu lost power, Abdullah warned, a government led by other right-wing figures would not necessarily reverse the policies that have devastated Gaza or alleviate the humanitarian crisis facing its population.
He added that, in the absence of a political force committed to Palestinian rights and a genuine peace process, a change in Israeli leadership alone was unlikely to end the war or bring meaningful improvements to Palestinian living conditions.
Abdullah also pointed to the marginalisation of Arab parties despite their parliamentary representation, noting that major Israeli political forces remained reluctant to cooperate with them.
Excluding Arab citizens from political partnerships, he warned, could further weaken confidence in electoral participation as a means of influencing decision-making.
Another Gaza-based political analyst, Mustafa Ibrahim, told TNA that the preliminary results had complicated expectations of a clear opposition victory.
"Neither Netanyahu's camp nor its rivals appeared certain of securing the majority needed to form a government," he said.
The political deadlock could lead to prolonged coalition negotiations, another political figure being tasked with forming a government, or fresh elections if efforts to establish a coalition failed, he added.
However, Ibrahim cautioned that political uncertainty did not necessarily mean Netanyahu would lose power or that Israeli policies towards Palestinians would change.
Ramallah-based political analyst Esmat Mansour also said the final distribution of seats could affect the prospects of forming a government, depending on whether smaller parties crossed the electoral threshold.
"A prolonged stalemate or another election could follow if neither camp secured a majority," he said, adding that regional tensions involving Gaza, Lebanon and Iran could increase the risk of further escalation.
Fatah welcomes Arab participation, Hamas remains sceptical
Palestinian Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh described the Israeli elections as an internal Israeli affair but expressed hope that a political partner committed to a just peace would emerge.
In a statement on X on Thursday, he said implementing international resolutions was essential to achieving security, peace and stability in the region.
Fatah, meanwhile, views the participation of Palestinian citizens of Israel and the possible weakening of the Israeli far right as an opportunity to influence the country's political balance.
Its spokesperson, Maher al-Nammoura, told TNA that Palestinian participation reflected a desire to challenge the far-right government and its policies towards Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
He welcomed the support for Arab electoral lists, expressing hope that their stronger parliamentary representation would improve the opposition's chances of ending Netanyahu's rule.
"We hope these results will strengthen the opposition's ability to end Netanyahu's rule and weaken the far-right forces that have pushed the region towards further confrontation," he said.
Al-Nammoura added that Netanyahu's departure would be an important step towards changing the political climate.
However, he stressed that any meaningful change must be reflected on the ground, including an end to the war in Gaza, respect for Palestinian rights and a halt to measures undermining the prospects of a political settlement.
Hamas, however, remains sceptical that Netanyahu's departure would bring more moderate Israeli leadership.
A movement source, speaking anonymously, told TNA that Netanyahu was especially responsible for blocking ceasefire commitments, though other Israeli leaders also held positions harmful to Palestinians.
He said Hamas had repeatedly raised Israeli violations with mediators and Peace Council representatives, urging progress on the US president's plan and the roadmap discussed in Cairo.
Hamas remained committed to the agreements, including the roadmap presented by Nikolay Mladenov, the Peace Council's Gaza representative, and hoped election results could help advance implementation, he noted.
Little hope for change
The election results offered little reason for displaced Gazans to expect improvements in Palestinian lives, whether inside Israel or in the occupied territories.
Fawzi Abu Nasser, displaced from Beit Hanoun and now living in a tent in Gaza City, told TNA that he doubted the elections would bring meaningful change.
"Palestinians inside Israel have the right to vote, but they still struggle to live safely and secure their basic rights. Crime and violence are spreading in their towns, while the authorities are failing to protect them. So what can these elections really change?" he said.
Yazan al-Sharif, another Gaza City resident, believes that the problem extends beyond Netanyahu to the broader Israeli political establishment.
"Even Palestinians inside Israel face discrimination and violence. They participate in elections, but this has not stopped policies undermining their rights or the growing crime in their communities," he told TNA.
Al-Sharif said a victory by a genuine left-wing candidate might have opened the door to a different approach towards Palestinians.
However, he feared an Eisenkot-led government would be no better, citing his right-wing background and the deaths of his son and nephew in Gaza.
He also called for an end to the division between Fatah and Hamas, saying Palestinian political fragmentation had further compounded people's suffering.
Abdullah al-Helou, another Gaza City resident, highlighted the contrast between Palestinian citizens of Israel, who can vote in parliamentary elections, and Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank, who cannot elect their own national leadership.
"Palestinians inside Israel can elect representatives to parliament, but they still struggle for their rights. Meanwhile, Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank cannot even elect their own national leadership. This shows the limits of political participation," he told TNA.
For Gazans, the experience of Palestinian citizens of Israel illustrates the limits of electoral participation: the right to vote does not necessarily guarantee equality, protection or the ability to change policies that shape people's lives.

US general fired by Hegseth confesses to leaking classified information about Iran - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:54:09 UTC
15:54:09 KST

The Pentagon's top military planner was fired earlier this week after he admitted to leaking classified information regarding Iran and Ukraine to media outlets, Axios reported on Thursday.
Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia failed four polygraph tests before confessing to misconduct on camera, a US official told Axios. He was fired by US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
According to a report from the Pentagon, Sylvia was accused of making "unauthorized disclosures to the media," however, he "was cooperative with answering questions about interactions with the media to resolve this, and provided his personal phone for a forensics examination."
US officials told Axios that Sylvia started leaking information as early as June 2025, months before media outlets were officially removed from the Pentagon. He then continued to leak information via a secure messaging app, Signal, the report explained. Sylvia also held a secretive in-person meeting at a diner in Arlington, Virginia - roughly a 10-minute drive from the Pentagon.
"The meeting at the diner occurred because [redacted's] access to the Pentagon was revoked between meetings," the outlet reported.
"During the meeting at the diner, [Sylvia] relied on notes he took while reviewing a classified secret report to orally give [redacted] information on US assistance to Ukraine, the report says.
It adds that Sylvia did not coordinate the meetings with Pentagon officials or get the information verified before sharing it with the reporter, who was writing a book.
US Officials respond to Sylvia being fired
A reporter asked US President Donald Trump on Thursday about the situation and what proof the Pentagon had that Sylvia had leaked information to the press, the Washington Post reported.
"She's going to have big problems," he responded, apparently unaware that the general was a man. "Long-term problems."
Pentagon Spokesperson Sean Parnell put out a statement on X/Twitter shortly after the news broke, warning that "The Department of War has zero tolerance for the intentional, unauthorized disclosure of classified information."
"Following an extensive Air Force OSI investigation, the Department took necessary personnel action to protect sensitive information. To protect the integrity of the investigation, no further comment will be made regarding the individual or the circumstances of this action."
"Classified information is not personal property. Leaking it for personal, political, or professional gain is a betrayal of the trust placed in those responsible for keeping it," Parnell wrote.
"This matter, along with others, has been referred to the Justice Department for potential further legal action."
Although Parnell did not directly name Sylvia's case, a defense official familiar with the matter told the Washington Post that Parnell’s comments were related to the general’s removal.
Wider crackdown on information leaks
This comes as Hegseth's team takes a harsher approach to information leaks to the media, relying in part on the use and threat of polygraph tests, officials told the Washington Post.
Dozens of US military officers have been subjected to polygraph tests as concern within the Pentagon mounted over a wave of reports discussing classified information about the depletion of critical air defense munitions and other US weaponry.
The Defense Department announced a joint task force with the Justice Department in July, aiming to identify people within the Pentagon who were responsible for leaking information.
It also asked the Pentagon's Office of General Counsel to prioritize prosecutions against people who had made unauthorized disclosures to the media.

Shas's Deri rules out joining opposition bloc government without Likud as UTJ weighs talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:54:00 UTC
15:54:00 KST

Shas chairman Arye Deri has ruled out joining a government led by the opposition bloc without Likud, while United Torah Judaism (UTJ) is emerging as a potential coalition partner, ultra-Orthodox sources familiar with negotiations to form the next government said, following Tuesday's elections for the 26th Knesset.
The sources pointed to a fundamental difference between the two ultra-Orthodox parties' approaches. While UTJ is emerging as a possible negotiating partner for the opposition bloc's leaders, Shas has made clear it does not intend to join such a government without Likud.
According to the sources, Deri made clear in closed-door discussions that he is unwilling to join an Eisenkot-led government. The position comes as the ultra-Orthodox parties' coalition choices have become central to efforts to form the next government.
"The Oslo Accords were enough for him," they said. "He is not prepared for Shas to sit with the Left again and bear the public cost of such a move. As far as he is concerned, if a right-wing government cannot be formed, Shas would be prepared to participate in a unity government, but only together with Likud."
The divide between the two ultra-Orthodox parties has taken on particular significance in light of the 26th Knesset election results, which left neither bloc with the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.
Despite Shas's refusal, Maran Rosh Yeshiva Rabbi Dov Landau urged MKs from Degel Hatorah to consider joining the opposition bloc in coalition, Ishay Coen reported on Friday morning.
"We are not in anyone's bloc," Landau said. "We are in the bloc of the Torah world."
"Make every effort to regulate the status of yeshiva students."
Coalition arithmetic leaves both blocs short of a majority
According to the election results, Netanyahu's bloc holds 53 seats, the opposition bloc has 48, and the Arab parties hold 19.
The three main parties in the opposition bloc, Yashar, B'Yachad, and the Democrats, hold a combined 41 seats. Adding UTJ, which has seven seats, to the emerging coalition would bring it to 48 seats, 13 short of the required 61-seat majority.
Adding both ultra-Orthodox parties to the three opposition bloc parties would bring their combined strength to 54 seats, seven short of a majority.
By contrast, bringing both ultra-Orthodox parties into the entire opposition bloc, including Yisrael Beytenu, would produce exactly 61 seats.
However, given Avigdor Liberman's opposition to joining a coalition with the ultra-Orthodox parties and Deri's stated opposition to an Eisenkot-led government without Likud, this remains, at this stage, a purely mathematical possibility.
Another option is a minority government relying on outside support from Arab parties. Discussions over an Eisenkot-led government have also included the possibility of including Ra'am.
For example, the three opposition bloc parties, together with UTJ and Ra'am, would hold 56 seats. Additional support from the Joint List would raise that figure to 67, although such a move would require significant political agreements among parties with differing positions.
Nevertheless, forming a government does not necessarily require the support of 61 Knesset members in a confidence vote. A simple majority of those voting in favor over those voting against is sufficient.
For example, a government supported by 56 Knesset members could be formed if the Joint List's 11 lawmakers abstained and all 53 remaining MKs voted against it. In that scenario, the confidence vote would pass by 56 votes to 53.
By contrast, a government consisting solely of the three opposition bloc parties and UTJ, with 48 seats, would require at least 25 additional MKs to abstain or be absent from the vote, assuming all other lawmakers voted against it.
Netanyahu's bloc, which holds 53 seats, also needs eight additional mandates to reach a 61-seat majority. Numerically, that is exactly the number of seats held by Ra'am.
Military conscription law remains a major obstacle
On disagreements over the military conscription law, ultra-Orthodox sources expressed cautious optimism about reaching agreements with the opposition bloc's leaders, while stressing that the outcome would depend on their willingness to compromise. The issue has also sparked internal debate within Shas following the election.
"If replacing the government and removing Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir, and Smotrich from power are at the top of Eisenkot and his partners' priorities, we assume it will be possible to find common ground on the conscription issue," the sources said.
"If not, they will not have a government. They will have to decide what matters more to them and what they are prepared to give up to achieve it."
Thus, while UTJ is emerging as a potential negotiating partner, Shas's position narrows the options for forming a new government without Likud.
Even an agreement with UTJ on military conscription would not, by itself, be enough to form a government. The opposition bloc's leaders would still have to secure additional support or reach agreements that would allow the government to win a confidence vote.

Anti-corruption committee probes €200 million Turkish armored vehicle procurement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:54:00 UTC
15:54:00 KST

Anti-corruption committee probes €200 million Turkish armored vehicle procurement
The Riigikogu's Anti-Corruption Select Committee is investigating why the Estonian Center for Defense Investments procured wheeled armored vehicles from Turkey, rather than making a deal closer to home.
In 2023, Estonia purchased 230 armored vehicles from Turkish companies Otokar and Nurol Makina for €200 million, and the entire order has now been delivered.
In a report by the Riigikogu's National Defense Committee, experts say that by making the deal with the Turks, Estonia abandoned strategic cooperation with its neighbors and that, in wartime, our military equipment will not be compatible with theirs.
The Anti-Corruption Select Committee is now also awaiting answers from the Ministry of Defense and the Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK).
"Why did we leave a very strong, technologically advanced ecosystem that is geographically close to us and includes our strategic partners, and move to an ecosystem that is geographically distant from us and does not offer the same opportunities?" asked reserve Maj. Gen. and member of the Riigikogu's National Defense Committee Meelis Kiili.
RKIK was responsible for the procurement of the armored vehicles but did not want to comment to ERR on Thursday.
The state agency said the defense minister would explain the procurement decisions and the circumstances surrounding them.
Minister of Defense Martin Herem, the former commander of the Estonian Defense Forces, told ERR: "If we had wanted to get the same armored vehicles as those in the 1st Brigade, then, firstly, we would have paid more and, secondly, the battalions of the 2nd Brigade would not have been equipped with armored vehicles by today. There were two very important factors in the procurement of the Turkish armored vehicles: firstly, price and secondly, delivery speed. And in terms of delivery speed, they were the fastest. As for the quality of the equipment, there is actually nothing more to criticize about them than about any other equipment."
Former Ministry of Defense Secretary General Kaimo Kuusk said maintenance capabilities should also have been important alongside the criteria of delivery speed and price.
Herem said there have been no problems with the supply of spare parts so far, and a procurement process is also underway to find a maintenance provider in Estonia.
"In 10 years, we may say that it was all very foolish, that the war did not start and why did we waste money on it at all. Today, however, we must prepare our wartime units for a possible conflict and do so as quickly as possible. Any talk of waiting a little longer, developing something further and even obtaining something in our own country in three or four years' time with an economic profit is not entirely responsible," he noted.

06:53:00 UTC
15:53:00 KST

GDP flash estimate: Estonia's economy grew 2.2% in Q3 2026
The Estonian economy grew by 2.2 percent in the third quarter of 2026 compared with the same period last year, according to Statistics Estonia's preliminary estimate.
Robert Müürsepp, the agency's national accounts service manager, said several indicators point to broad-based strengthening, with growth faster both year on year and quarter on quarter.
SEB economist: Demand in export destination countries has helped
SEB economist Mihkel Nestor noted that 2.2 percent is roughly in line with the first and second quarters, when GDP grew 2.9 percent and 1.8 percent respectively. The flash estimate does not give more detailed sources of growth, but exports and domestic consumption probably both contributed.
"Demand growth in our main target markets has above all improved goods exports, which had long been in the doldrums. Household consumption has also clearly recovered this year, helped by wage growth of nearly six percent and the lowest inflation in recent times. On the other hand, rising energy prices are now accelerating inflation again, which will start to slow consumption growth. Investment has so far remained modest, but the growth in companies' borrowing activity suggests the coming quarters may bring better results in that area," Nestor said.
Nestor added that forecasts so far have predicted further acceleration of economic growth in 2027, but higher inflation and rising interest rates could trim those forecasts. On the other hand, the situation in the Estonian economy is certainly the best in recent years and moderate growth will continue next year.
A flash estimate is produced using statistical models rather than full accounting, drawing on trade, transport, manufacturing, tax and energy data, so it is not methodologically comparable to the official GDP figure.
Official third-quarter GDP data will be published by Statistics Estonia on November 30.
More detailed information is available from Statistics Estonia's website here and here.

UK denies entry to Swedish academic due to speak at Palestine event

UK denies entry to Swedish academic due to speak at Palestine event
Home Office cancels Andreas Malm’s planned travel to the UK, saying his presence ‘not conducive to the public good’.
London, United Kingdom – A pro-Palestine academic who was planning to travel to the United Kingdom has been denied entry because the government says his “presence in the UK is not considered to be conducive to the public good”.
The UK Home Office cancelled Swedish national Andreas Malm’s Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) on Wednesday, an email seen by Al Jazeera shows.
The decision came a week before Malm was due to appear on a panel organised by the British socialist magazine Tribune in London. Huda Ammori, cofounder of Palestine Action – which the UK has proscribed as a “terrorist” group – is also due to appear on the panel, which will be chaired by Hala Hanina of Palestine Deep Dive.
Malm, a climate activist and author who lectures at Lund University in Sweden, told Al Jazeera that he believes his ETA was cancelled because he was due to appear on the panel. He has contacted the Home Office for an explanation but is yet to receive a response.
“I have been going regularly to the UK for decades. My position on Palestine has always been public,” Malm said, adding that his latest visit to the country was in May.
“I haven’t said anything in public about Palestine during these intervening months or written anything about it. The only thing that could have caused this [latest UK decision] is that I was due to be on a panel on Wednesday evening, where I would talk to Huda Ammori of Palestine Action,” he said.
Malm used an ETA during his May visit to the UK, which allowed him to travel to the country again later in the year without seeking reauthorisation. He said he had received no indication from the Home Office that his ETA was at risk of being cancelled before receiving an email on Wednesday confirming that it had been revoked.
In its email, the Home Office told Malm that if he wishes to visit the UK, he needs to apply for a visa, after which the office will “consider your circumstances in more detail” before making a decision. However, the government website states that the processing time for a standard visitor visa is three weeks, meaning Malm would not receive it in time for next week’s panel even if his application were approved.
Travellers from countries whose nationals do not require a visa to visit the UK generally need an ETA. These include countries in Europe, the United States and Canada, among others.
Al Jazeera contacted the Home Office to ask for clarification on the cancellation of Malm’s ETA and whether it was connected to the event he planned to attend next week. They had not replied at the time of publication.
The cancellation of Malm’s ETA comes amid a wider crackdown on pro-Palestine activists by the UK government, something that began under then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
Tribune editor Oliver Eagleton said, “Andy Burnham’s government continues the authoritarian overreach we saw under Starmer. In this new dystopian Britain, it is now commonplace for authors and academics to be treated as terrorists because they support Palestinians facing genocide and the rights of people protesting that genocide.”
Starmer, a former human rights lawyer, was prime minister when the government proscribed Palestine Action last year.
The move classified the campaign group as a “terrorist” organisation under UK law, placing it on the same legal list as groups such as al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS). The proscription has been condemned by rights groups, including Amnesty International.
Most recently, Irish novelist Sally Rooney’s books were withdrawn from sale in the UK this month due to her public support for Palestine Action.
Rooney described Malm as a “brilliant and influential” intellectual.
“For the UK government to deny him entry to Britain is not only an outrageous attack on a respected climate expert, but a sad and frightening act of cultural self-harm,” she said.
Malm’s books include How to Blow Up a Pipeline: Learning to Fight in a World on Fire and The Destruction of Palestine Is the Destruction of the Earth.
‘A drift towards authoritarianism’
Since Palestine Action was banned, more than 3,850 people have been arrested for publicly backing the group, in largely peaceful protests.
“This is a drift towards authoritarianism that didn’t begin with me and it’s not going to end with me either,” Malm told Al Jazeera. “If I’m now being deemed a threat to the public good because I’m supposed to have a conversation with someone from Palestine Action, this is guilt by association. Where does it stop?”
Gareth Dale, reader in political economy at Brunel University of London, told Al Jazeera that the Home Office’s decision suggests the UK government intends to continue suppressing free speech under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.
“Andreas Malm is one of the world’s foremost campaigners on the two defining issues of our times – climate breakdown and the genocide in Palestine. Barring him from entry to the UK represents a monstrous attempt by the Burnham government to suppress free speech,” Dale said.
“Typical of bureaucratic tyranny, no reason was given for the ban; it is cynical and Kafkaesque. As Malm has committed no crime, we are left guessing as to the motives. Burnham cultivated the impression that his government would be turning a new leaf, but instead it is replicating Starmer-era authoritarianism.”

Stone fortress from time of the Prophets opened to public in central Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:49:37 UTC
15:49:37 KST

The remains of a 3,200-year-old stone fortress nestling in central Israel's Guvrin Forest were opened to the public Thursday following their excavation, conservation and renovation about eight years after the site's first public reveal.
Dating to the era of the Prophets, about the mid-12th century B.C.E., the Gal'on Fortress was only discovered in 2018. In the day, it had loomed above the main road between the coast and the Judean foothills. That road ran between the Canaanite city of Lachish and the Philistine city of Gath.
At the start of the 12th century B.C.E., Canaan was ruled by Egypt. But the Levant never has been the most peaceful of places, and the 12th century B.C.E. brought climatic and geopolitical upheaval, culminating in the "Bronze Age collapse" from about 1200 to 1150 B.C.E. that engulfed the Hittite Empire in today's Turkey and ended the Egyptian expansion into Canaan.
Forced back to the land of the Nile, the weakened Egyptian forces even had to fight against invaders known as the Sea Peoples.
Back here and before the implosion, in the early 12th century B.C.E. the fortified structure in what is today an artificial forest had to have been built by the Egyptians' local minions, the Canaanites – possibly to aid their combat against two new players in the region: the Israelites and the Philistines. Their advent led to a series of bloody territorial struggles, the Israel Antiquities Authority explains.
Let us merely note that to this day a debate rages over whether the Israelites hailed from further lands, as the Bible says, or if they emerged from the indigenous Canaanite population. The earliest known reference to "Israel" appears in the Egyptian "Merneptah Stele" carved in about 1208 B.C.E., which records Israel as a people in Canaan.
The fortress was apparently involved in either a Canaanite or Egyptian attempt to deal with the new geopolitical realities, suggest Saar Ganor and Itamar Weissbein, who excavated the site for the antiquities authority.
The restoration of the structure cost about 400,000 shekels ($128,000), the authority says. The work involved renovating the remains of the fortress and developing amenities for visitors, including parking, a new access road, a picnic area and signs. The authority adds that there is handicapped-accessible parking and an accessible path to the citadel.

'Star Trek', 'X-Men' star Patrick Stewart dead at 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:46:49 UTC
15:46:49 KST

Patrick Stewart, the British Shakespearean actor who became a Hollywood megastar through roles in the "Star Trek" and "X-Men" franchises, has died at his home in Los Angeles. He was 86.
His death on Wednesday came after a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to an official statement on his social media accounts.
"His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre," the statement said.
The actor, who hailed from the northern English region of Yorkshire, trod the boards in Britain with the Royal Shakespeare Company and the National Theatre in London, and worked on British television.
But he rocketed into the pop culture history books in his mid-40s when he was cast as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," and then again as Professor Charles Xavier in multiple "X-Men" and related Marvel films.
A proud Yorkshireman, Stewart "wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love," Ian McKellan said of his "X-Men" co-star and dear friend.
McKellan, 87, recounted meeting Stewart in London and hearing about his "Star Trek" offer, warning him he may get lost in Hollywood and to think of his stage career.
"Well, he took the risk and thank goodness for us all that he did."
Aboard the Enterprise
Stewart was 47 when he debuted as Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," the first live-action television spinoff of the trailblazing late-1960s sci-fi series.
He effectively filled the boots of William Shatner's Captain Kirk — to resounding success, both in the TV series and in several films.
Picard became known for a few catchphrases including "Make it so" and "Engage!"
But his move to America in 1987 was initially greeted with disdain by the Los Angeles Times, who wrote him off as an "unknown British Shakespearean actor."
Stewart later dubbed suggestions he was "slumming it" by moving into US television offensive.
He once called his Shakespearean bona fides "nothing but a preparation for sitting in the captain's chair of the Enterprise."
'Colossus of both stage and screen'
Stewart found further acclaim in the "X-Men" series, debuting in 2000 as Professor Charles Xavier, the founder and mentor of the mutant superhero team.
"For more than 25 years, he brought a gravitas and profundity to the role, earning fans across the globe," Marvel Studios said Thursday.
Longtime co-star Hugh Jackman, who played Wolverine, remembered Stewart as both "one of the greats of stage and screen" and "a tremendous friend and man."
Stewart is to make his final on-screen film appearance as Professor Xavier in "Avengers: Doomsday," set for release in December.
"What a heartbreaking week it has been," posted Shatner.
Stewart's death marked the second in days from the "Star Trek" universe, following that of Walter Koenig, who played Chekov in the original series.
Shatner said Stewart — who most recently played Picard in 2023 — brought "intelligence, grace and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did."
Stewart earned four Emmy nominations but never won. He did nab a spoken word Grammy, for his narration of "Prokofiev: Peter And The Wolf."
And even as he found success in Hollywood, Stewart's love of theater, and the bard in particular, never left him.
Between filming, he would return to the stage, winning two Olivier awards.
Shakespeare, Stewart said, "feels like a friend, someone who just went out of the room to get another bottle of wine."
The Royal Shakespeare Company called him "a colossus of both stage and screen and one of the finest classical Shakespearean actors of his generation."
Troubled start
Stewart was born on July 13, 1940 in the small West Yorkshire town of Mirfield, the third of three brothers in a working-class family.
His father, back from World War II and perhaps suffering from PTSD, would often beat Stewart's mother — which prompted Stewart to later work with the charity Refuge, which specializes in domestic abuse.
The actor left school at 15, and studied at Bristol Old Vic Drama School beginning in 1957, making his professional acting debut two years later.
Prematurely balding, Stewart missed out on many of the young romantic leads but quickly slotted into theater life, joining the RSC in 1966 and staying there until 1982.
Any misgivings Stewart had about taking the Picard role in the "Star Trek" universe were mollified by the thought it would be a one-season failure.
He was wrong.
"It changed my life," he said.
Knighted in 2010, Stewart married three times: to Sheila Falconer, with whom he had two children; briefly to "Star Trek" producer Wendy Neuss; and most recently to American singer Sunny Ozell, 38 years his junior.

Survivors of Spain’s worst train crashes urge action after latest disaster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:46:28 UTC
15:46:28 KST

Survivors of Spain’s worst train crashes urge action after latest disaster
As people still suffering post-traumatic stress watch history repeat itself, experts call for investment in the high-speed network.
Madrid, Spain – “I survived but the mental scars are still there all these years later. We must stop more accidents happening,” says Cristobal Gonalez.
Gonzalez suffered multiple injuries when a high-speed train, which should have been travelling at 80 kilometres per hour (50 miles per hour), hurtled off the line at 200km/h (125mph), killing 80 people.
The accident in 2013 at Angrois, near Santiago de Compostela in northwestern Spain, remains Spain’s deadliest rail crash.
On Wednesday, 13 years later, at least 69 people were killed when two trains collided near Urda, a town close to Toledo in central Spain. Only 10 months earlier, two other trains collided on the same line, in Adamuz near Cordoba in southern Spain, killing 46 people.
Survivors of Spain’s three worst rail disasters have said more must be done to avoid further tragedies.
“Now we have seen three dreadful crashes in Spain, at Angrois, Adamuz and Urda. They will keep happening if we do not act,” Gonzalez told Al Jazeera.
“At Angrois, the driver was going too fast; at Adamuz, an investigation said there was a problem on the track; and at Urda it might have been human error and a problem with the control system. Whatever, we must stop these crashes happening by investing more in safety.”
Gonzalez was travelling with a friend, Oscar, to Santiago de Compostela when the crash happened. He was in the front carriage when the train “flew” off the tracks and smashed into a bank.
He stayed inside the train trying to help others in their last moments. Years later, he struggles to talk about the events of that day.
“I will keep what happened to myself. It is very hard to share it, even if I wanted to – it is something that defies imagination,” said Gonzalez, who suffers from post-traumatic stress.
‘I cannot believe that this has happened again’
Santiago Rosendo, who was one of the passengers in the Renfe train involved in the Adamuz crash in January, spoke of the “panic” among passengers when the trains collided.
“There was a sudden stop – a very sudden stop – then following that, a loud crash. Then the train moved from side to side until the train slid onto its side and we were left entirely in the dark. The first thing I saw when I got off the train was a body,” he told Al Jazeera.
Rosendo, who was travelling on his own from Madrid to Huelva in southern Spain when the accident happened on a Sunday night, added: “I cannot believe that this has happened again on the same line. We have to do something.”
An initial investigation into the Adamuz crash found a broken rail had caused one train to veer off the line into the path of an oncoming train.
Experts have called for more investment in maintenance in the wake of this year’s crashes.
Between 2018 and 2022, Spain spent an average of about $1.67bn each year on high-speed lines, more than other European countries with similar networks. However, only 16 percent of that was spent on maintenance or repairs, according to European Commission data; the rest was devoted to the infrastructure.
In contrast, Italy, Germany and France spent an average of between 33 and 39 percent of their budgets on maintenance, even though each has smaller networks than the 4,000km (2,485 miles) in Spain.
Experts call for investment in maintenance
Jose Maria Goicolea, spokesman for the Spanish Association of Civil Engineers, told Al Jazeera that with the increase in use of the rail network, “there has to be more spent on maintenance.
“In 1982, when there was the first line, it was a very small network. Now it is much bigger with much more usage. It is a whole new ball game now. The emphasis cannot be only on building new lines but doing more maintenance.”
About 40 million people used the high-speed rail trains in 2024, almost double the figure for 2019. In the first half of this year, about 25 million travelled on the high-speed network, a year-on-year fall of 14 percent.
The line between Madrid and Seville, where both crashes happened this year, is the only one in Spain using a German-made LZB control system dating from the 1970s, which is being phased out.
“I would close the line between Madrid and Seville while the LZB system is phased out. It was only partly responsible for Wednesday’s crash. It failed. But the other reason was human error, it seems,” Goicolea said. “However, this is up to the politicians, not me.”
He added that the crash in January was caused by faults in the line.
Ramiro Aupin Lopera, an expert in infrastructure who lectured at the University Politecnica de Catalunya, said that since 2011, in the wake of the financial crisis, there had been a “ridiculous” fall in investment in maintenance on the Spanish high-speed railway network.
“At the same time that there has been growing use of the network, there has been less investment in maintenance. It is no surprise that we have had two crashes in less than a year. It may come from ignorance or disdain towards science and infrastructure on the part of the politicians,” he told Al Jazeera.
Apart from the state-run Renfe, Spain has two private operators, Ouigo from France and Iryo, which is part of an Italian consortium. They have voiced concern over the LZB system.
Helen Venezuela, then director of Ouigo Espana, told Spanish radio Cadena Ser last year: “This line (Madrid-Seville) is equipped with an obsolete system like LZB. It is like watching Netflix in black and white. We are Netflix and the system is still in black and white.”
Diego Martin, of SEMAF, the Spanish train drivers’ union, said blaming rail workers for the latest disaster would not prevent future crashes.
“Blame does not prevent accidents; identifying and determining the causes does,” he said.

Higher heating bills ahead for Riga residents – Rīgas siltums announces new tariff and warns of possible further increases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:37:20 UTC
15:37:20 KST

Riga's district heating company Rīgas siltums plans to increase its heating tariff by 19% from 1 December, the company announced.
Rīgas siltums has submitted a proposal to the Public Utilities Commission (SPRK) to revise its district heating tariff.
Under the proposal, the tariff would rise to 96.33 euros per megawatt-hour (MWh), excluding value-added tax, from 1 December.
This would represent a 16% increase compared with the previous heating season and a 19% increase from the currently applicable tariff of 80.96 euros per MWh.
Kalvis Kalniņš, Chairman of the Management Board of Rīgas siltums, explained that the sharp rise in energy costs is having a significant impact and that its effect on heating tariffs cannot be entirely eliminated.
Compared with the previous year, natural gas prices have already increased by 200%, biomass prices have risen by approximately 50%, and electricity prices have also climbed.
Together, these energy resources account for approximately 70% of the costs included in the district heating tariff.
The company had previously forecast that Riga's heating tariff could increase by 20% to 30% from December.
However, according to Kalniņš, measures taken by the company have helped limit the increase to 16% compared with the previous heating season.
He stressed that tariff adjustments are directly influenced by energy prices, particularly natural gas prices, which remain volatile and continue to rise.
Over the past six months, increasing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East have driven natural gas prices significantly higher, creating additional pressure on district heating production costs, Kalniņš noted.
According to the company, Rīgas siltums has implemented a series of measures this year, as it did before the previous heating season, to minimise the impact of energy price fluctuations on its tariff.
In line with its fuel procurement strategy, the company purchased natural gas gradually and in advance, diversifying risks and reducing the potential impact of developments in the Middle East on Riga's heating costs.
In cooperation with the Ministry of Climate and Energy, the company has developed a mechanism to separate the price of heat produced from biomass from fluctuations in natural gas prices within the market area by establishing a maximum heat purchase price.
The price cap has been introduced in accordance with amendments to the Energy Law.
A three-hour heat procurement mechanism has also been introduced, allowing cogeneration plants to use the heat they produce more efficiently during periods when electricity market conditions are favourable.
The measure is intended to support a more flexible district heating market, increase competition and reduce costs for consumers.
In preparation for the new heating season, the company has purchased natural gas and reached agreements with Latvenergo on heat purchases.
All these measures have helped reduce the impact of rising costs and keep the tariff increase below earlier forecasts, Valdovskis noted.
Kalniņš reiterated that Rīgas siltums has a strategic objective to gradually reduce its dependence on natural gas, whose price significantly influences heating tariffs.
Natural gas currently accounts for approximately 60% of the company's energy resources, and the goal is to reduce this share to 35% within five years.
Nevertheless, natural gas will remain necessary to ensure sufficient heat production during periods of peak demand and in emergency situations.
The company also noted that additional natural gas purchases will be required during the heating season.
The volume purchased will depend on the severity of the winter, while the price will depend on developments in energy markets.
As a result, the company cannot completely rule out the need to revise the heating tariff again during the season.
However, management stressed that it is too early to assess whether further changes will be necessary.
The company promised that any such decision would be based on economically justified calculations and that the public would be informed in advance.

Marko Mihkelson: Europe's decisive choice — appease Russia or repel aggression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:37:00 UTC
15:37:00 KST

Marko Mihkelson: Europe's decisive choice — appease Russia or repel aggression
Europe faces a decisive choice: give in to Russian pressure and accept a situation where aggression forcibly changes Europe's borders and calls into question our entire security order, or defend a united, free and expanding Europe, all at a time when authoritarian regimes around the world are increasing their influence, writes Reform Party MP and Riigikogu Foreign Affairs Committee chair Marko Mihkelson.
This is not merely a choice between various diplomatic approaches. It is a test of Europe's political will, strategic clarity and leadership. Do we have leaders capable of seeing beyond their own personal political agenda and understanding that peace is not born by giving in to an aggressor, but by creating conditions in which aggression no longer pays?
Europe needs a new strategic clarity: Russia's attempt to change borders by force must be thwarted, Ukraine must be given the military and financial aid it needs to prevail, and stronger economic pressure must be brought to bear on Russia than has been the case so far. A real peace process can start only when the preconditions needed have been created. A position of strength must be built for negotiations, not one's trump cards surrendered before talks have begun.
Another peace plan, same old concessions
Another supposedly Washington-originated peace plan to end Russia's war of aggression is doing the public rounds. Its details have not been officially confirmed, but the proposals outlined in the media again point to the possibility that significant concessions are being offered to Russia. It is possible that elements of the plan were also talked about at President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff's recent meetings in Oslo and St Petersburg.
According to the descriptions that have reached the public, consideration is being given to creating a demilitarized zone in the area of the current contact line, restoring trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the U.S., and Ukraine giving up its aspiration to become a NATO member. In return, Ukraine would be offered investment and continued integration with the European Union. At the same time, sanctions against Russia could be eased, U.S. investment in Russia restored, and even progress made on reopening the Nord Stream gas pipelines.
If these proposals correspond to what has been described publicly, this would be a solution highly amenable to Russia and requiring extensive concessions from Ukraine and from Europe.
The 28-point peace plan that reached the public after President Trump's meeting with Putin in Alaska last year, and which was later amended by European involvement, already contained similar ideas. There is consequently no fundamentally new approach visible in the current discussions. Instead, the question again arises as to whether, in order to end the war, there has been a willingness to sacrifice precisely those principles for whose defense Ukraine and Europe have been fighting for years.
Achieving peace is needed. But peace cannot mean recognizing the consequences of aggression, restricting Ukraine's sovereignty or weakening Europe's security architecture.
Thirty years of the wrong conclusions
A solution to Russia's aggression against Ukraine has been sought via negotiations since 2014. The Minsk agreements and the Normandy process helped, at times, to lessen the intensity of hostilities, but did not end Russia's aggression. Then in February 2022, Russia launched its full-scale invasion.
The Istanbul talks that followed brought no agreement, and later diplomatic initiatives have not succeeded in ending the war either. Between 2014 and 2022, ceasefire agreements were concluded repeatedly between Russia and Ukraine, but none brought lasting peace. Even the quietest periods remained short-lived.
Moscow has always blamed someone else for the failure of negotiations — the Ukrainians, the Americans or the Europeans. The Kremlin will not acknowledge its responsibility as the aggressor, but seeks to achieve the same goal via diplomatic and military pressure: to subjugate Ukraine and shape Europe's security order according to Russia's will.
To grasp this, one must look further back than 2014. Russia's imperial wars did not begin with the occupation of Crimea but gained new momentum soon after the collapse of the Soviet Union. An understanding took hold in Russia's leadership that restoring the empire and pushing back Western influence were unavoidable preconditions for restoring the country's great-power status.
Russia's foreign minister at the time, Andrei Kozyrev, who was part of President Boris Yeltsin's cabinet from 1990 to 1996, confirmed to me at our meeting in Miami that, by spring 1992, imperial-minded forces had gained the upper hand in the Kremlin leadership. This observation helps explain why the West's hopes for Russia's rapid democratization proved unfulfilled. The issue was not solely in the personhood of Putin's, but lay much deeper in Russia's political development.
The wars that began in the 1990s, including the Chechen wars, which cost tens of thousands of lives, neither attracted sufficient attention in the West nor led to decisive countermeasures. Nor did the apartment block bombings in Russian cities in the fall of 1999, in which more than 300 people died and which have been suspected of being organized by Russian security services, decisively change the West's attitude. Vladimir Putin's rise to power was greeted in many capitals with a somewhat cautious hope.
President George W. Bush, who met Putin in Slovenia in summer 2001, later summed up his impression in famous words: he looked Putin in the eye and saw in him a straightforward and trustworthy person. History has shown how costly the wish to see an authoritarian leader as that partner he is not can prove to be.
Putin has not hidden his goals. Since his rise to power, Russia has been heading in a direction in which changing borders by force, restricting the sovereignty of neighboring states and weakening NATO and Europe's collective defense have become central planks of Kremlin policy.
The West's mistaken assessments were repeated. After the 2001 terror attacks, Russia offered the U.S. support in the Afghanistan operation, sharing intelligence and allowing the use of Central Asian staging points. Western attention concentrated for a lengthy period of time on Afghanistan and the wider Middle East. The U.S.'s chaotic withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021 may in turn have reaffirmed in the Kremlin the understanding that Washington's appetite for a long confrontation is limited.
The war Russia fought against Georgia in August 2008 demonstrated Russia was prepared to carry out its geopolitical objectives by military force. After the war Russia continued to occupy a fifth of Georgia's territory, but the Western reaction remained limited. Soon there was talk again of resetting relations. NATO's 2010 strategic concept still saw Russia as a possible strategic partner rather than a growing security threat.
Also in 2014, when Russia occupied and annexed Crimea and began military operations in eastern Ukraine, the Western response initially remained modest. Only the shooting down of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 and the deaths of 298 people forced European countries to react more seriously. Sanctions and support for Ukraine were necessary, but they did not turn into a strategy capable of stopping Russian aggression.
Western disunity, Brexit, domestic political changes in the U.S. and the rise of Donald Trump deepened the uncertainty. By the fall of 2021, the Kremlin had taken the decision to prepare for full-scale war against Ukraine.
Five years later we are in a situation in which Russia has suffered enormous human losses but has retained the military initiative on important sectors of the front. The West's partial awakening and sanctions have so far not been sufficient to force Moscow to abandon its strategic objectives.
What is this stalemate we are talking about?
Lately it has gotten increasingly common to hear that, since no decisive breakthrough has been achieved on the Ukrainian front, diplomacy must again be given a chance. Others have emphasized that Europe must not be left on the sidelines while the U.S. and Russia talk about Ukraine's future. The latter position is in and of itself correct: Europe cannot be discussed without Europe, just as Ukraine's future cannot be decided without Ukraine.
But these arguments do not justify starting talks without a clear objective and a common strategy.
What is the stalemate we are actually talking about? Russia has not stopped its aggression. It continues to attack Ukrainian cities and infrastructure, is boosting its military production capacity and expanding hybrid activity in Europe. Russia is producing ballistic missiles and drones in large quantities, while Western production of air defense systems and interceptors is not growing fast enough. Russia's war machine is being kept running by goods, technology and components from China and other countries.
At the same time, warfare is changing technologically faster than the defense planning and production capacity of many Western countries can adapt. In addition to weaponry, Europe must develop air defense, counter-drone capability, intelligence and surveillance capability, and electronic warfare.
Most important, however, is that Russia has not abandoned its strategic objectives: to change borders by force, restrict Ukraine's sovereignty and shape Europe's security order according to Moscow's interests.
Negotiations are not a problem in themselves. What is dangerous is starting them in a situation where the aggressor retains the military initiative and the West is prepared to make concessions even before talks begin. Such an approach could give Moscow time to restore its military capability, deepen disagreements among Western countries and prepare a new aggression.
Nor must responsibility be forgotten. Negotiations must not mean setting aside the question of accountability for the war of aggression, for war crimes and for other violations of international law. The question of responsibility is not an obstacle to the peace process but part of the preconditions for a just and lasting peace.
Europe cannot permit talk of understanding Russia and of strategic stability to become a pretext for surrendering its interests and values.
A coalition of the willing must not turn into a coalition of the waiting
POLITCO has written about Europe's search for someone who could take on the lead role in engaging with Putin. But the question should not primarily be who sits at the negotiating table. What matters more is with what objectives and from what position of strength they will be going there.
After the strong confrontation between Trump and Zelenskyy at the White House in February 2025, several European countries coalesced into a coalition of the willing, to support Ukraine. That was a required step. But too much of the attention has focused on Ukraine's security guarantees after the war ends, rather than on how to shape the conditions in which Russia could be forced to end its aggression.
So the danger then arose that this coalition of the willing becomes a coalition of the waiting: instead of shaping the conditions for ending the war, it is preparing primarily for the situation after the war.
For Russia, talks often represent an opportunity to buy time, distract the other side and present new conditions. When Europe is first of all looking for a suitable person to engage with Putin but has not agreed on a common strategy, it is showing Moscow a weakness of political will.
Russia's public rhetoric towards European leaders has turned increasingly condescending and threatening. Moscow is trying to convince Europe that resisting its demands is pointless and that the cost of continuing the war is greater than the cost of concessions.
Pressure like this cannot be handled with diplomatic courtesy alone, or with new compromise proposals. Europe must first decide what it is defending and what outcome it considers acceptable.
Russia's strategic clarity — the restoration of empire and the political subjugation of Europe's security — must be met with an equally clear objective: to thwart aggression and prevent borders from being changed by force.
Europe must find strength in its own economy
Europe is economically superior to Russia, but economic superiority does not automatically translate into military capability. Europe is not one single state, and achieving unified political will and strategic clarity requires bold leadership and a readiness to look beyond member states' short-term budgetary interests.
The financial position of Europe's larger states limits their ability to increase defense spending rapidly. The large public debts, budget deficits and growing interest costs of the U.K., France, Spain and Italy mean that increasing defense investment requires some tough political choices.
At the same time, Ukraine continues to need extensive financial and military aid. Without European support, the resilience of Ukraine's state and society would be considerably weaker.
Europe cannot solve this dilemma with borrowed money or new budget targets alone. It also needs a rapid increase in defense industry production capacity, joint procurement, better coordination and decisive investment in technologies that meet the needs of modern warfare.
The increase in defense and security spending to 5 percent of GDP by 2035 agreed at NATO's Hague summit provides a framework, but it is not enough if the agreements remain on paper. Europe must turn its economic capability into real deterrent power.
Consistent economic pressure must also be brought to bear on Russia, restricting its access to technology needed for the war industry and strengthening secondary sanctions against those countries and companies that help Russia circumvent restrictions.
Europe must end the situation in which it supports Ukraine with one hand while with the other it enables Russia's war machine to earn money and procure the components it needs.
Europe must answer three questions
Before Europe starts looking for a suitable representative to hold talks with Putin, we will have to answer three basic questions.
Are we ready to accept borders being changed by force and aggression going unpunished? Are we prepared to weaken NATO's collective defense in the hope that Russia will leave us alone?
And do we have enough political will to defend Europe's freedom, unity and a security order based on international law, even when it requires short-term economic and political sacrifices?
These questions cannot be answered by a hope that Putin will change his objectives if he is offered sufficiently favorable conditions. His conduct so far gives no grounds to believe that new concessions would replace the need for credible deterrence.
Russia treats international politics as a zero-sum game in which one side's strengthening means the other's weakening. The Kremlin therefore interprets Western hesitation and internal disagreements as an opportunity to get closer to its objectives.
No diplomatic gesture will alter Putin's strategy if there is no readiness behind it to defend one's interests. Neither a compromise offered by Trump, Stubb nor anyone else can replace credible deterrence.
Finland and Norway's peace efforts must be assessed from the same starting point. Any initiative that contributes to a just and lasting peace deserves attention. But no diplomatic process can succeed if it proceeds from the assumption that Ukraine must give up its sovereignty, or that Europe must give up the principles of NATO membership and collective defense.
Rolling out the diplomatic red carpet to an aggressor without first forcing him to the negotiating table through pressure means weakening one's position before talks have even begun. Europe must not voluntarily surrender its most important trump cards or give Moscow reason to think that sufficient pressure can achieve concessions.
What should Europe's action plan be?
If Europe's objective is to restore a just and lasting peace, concrete steps and their sequence must be agreed.
First, Europe's strategic objective must be to thwart Russia's attempt to change borders by force and break up Europe's security architecture. This means that Ukraine's sovereignty and its right to choose its own future must not become a bargaining chip in negotiations between great powers.
Second, Ukraine must be given every possible military and financial assistance needed to repel Russian aggression. This requires a rapid increase in air defense, ammunition, drones, long-range weapons and defense industry production capacity, and Ukraine's integration into Europe's security and defense space.
Third, Russia's war machine must be weakened via economic measures. Sanctions must be tightened and their enforcement made more effective. Russia must lose the ability to use Western tech and economic ties to achieve its military objectives.
Fourth, Europe must transform its economic and political superiority into real security capability. This requires increased defense spending, defense industry development, joint investment and a greater readiness to take responsibility for Europe's defense.
Fifth, negotiations with Russia can give Europe the desired outcome only when they come from a position of strength. A just and lasting peace must ensure that Russia cannot repeat its aggression or impose its objectives by force. The precondition for this is Ukraine's ability to win its war of freedom and Europe's capacity to defend its own security.
A Ukrainian victory is not only in Ukraine's interest. It is Europe's opportunity to avoid a situation in which a temporary halt to Russian aggression turns into the starting point for a new war. Thwarting Russia's military and political expansion would also give Europe a stronger position in shaping a changing world order.
Europe must choose
In the spring of 2022, many of Europe's friends and allies acknowledged that Estonia and the other Baltic states had been right when we warned about Russia. We did not make a great number of it. We asked only that we be listened to in future.
Today that matters more than ever. Europe again faces a choice whose consequences extend beyond Ukraine's battlefields. The question is whether sovereignty, freedom and the inadmissibility of changing borders by force will remain the foundations of the international order, or whether a world will take shape in which great powers can impose their interests on smaller states at the threat of arms.
Europe cannot afford another concession to Russia that would merely postpone the next conflict and make it harder to avoid. We do not have to choose between war and peace, but between a short-term apparent peace and lasting security.
A just peace is born when the aggressor understands that he will not achieve his objectives by force. For that, Europe must end its hesitations, strengthen Ukraine and turn its common will into credible deterrent power.
Europe's security does not depend on how quickly we can reach an agreement with Russia, but on whether we can stop aggression and prevent its recurrence.
Europe's choice is not between surrender and war. It is a choice between a temporary silence bought with concessions and a just and lasting peace, one that defends freedom.

China seeks to strengthen cooperation with Iceland in Arctic affairs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:36:53 UTC
15:36:53 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
China’s Foreign Minister Wang Yi has called for “strengthening” cooperation with Iceland in trade, geothermal energy, green transition as well as Arctic affairs.
Wang made the remarks during a meeting with his Icelandic counterpart Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir in Beijing on Thursday, a statement from China’s Foreign Ministry said.
The two countries mark 55 years of diplomatic ties this year.
“China is willing to share development opportunities with Iceland, explore cooperation potential, strengthen cooperation in areas such as trade and economy, geothermal energy, green transformation, marine affairs, and the Arctic,” said Wang.
He called for enhanced exchanges in tourism, joint scientific research, and talent cultivation, and vigorously promote people-to-people exchanges between the two countries.
“Faced with the current turbulent international situation, both sides should strengthen cooperation, jointly uphold multilateralism, the rule of international law, and the core role of the United Nations in international affairs, promote the building of a more just and equitable global governance system, and make new contributions to maintaining world peace and stability,” he told Gunnarsdottir, who is on a visit to China since Monday until Saturday.
She will also lead a delegation of Icelandic enterprises to Qingdao, in eastern China's Shandong province, for a seafood expo.
After establishing ties in 1971, China has become Iceland's largest trading partner in Asia.
The two nations signed a free trade agreement in April 2013 – a first between the world’s second largest economy and a European country, which took effect on July 1, 2014.
In 2024, the bilateral trade volume between China and Iceland was $443 million, according to China’s Foreign Ministry.
