CEBU, Philippines (AP) -- The United States and Japan have agreed to establish a Japanese facility for the joint production of advanced medium-range air-to-air missiles, the Japanese defense chief said.
It is the latest move by the allies, which have repeatedly expressed alarm over China's growing assertiveness in Asia.
Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi made the announcement in a news conference Wednesday night in the central Philippine province of Cebu, where he met U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the sidelines of an annual meeting of Southeast Asian defense chiefs and their major Asian and Western counterparts.
Koizumi raised concern Thursday about China's increasing naval activity in southwestern Japan. He said that three Chinese destroyers and a coast guard ship together crossed the Osumi Strait south of the southern main island of Kyushu and headed east to the Pacific Ocean this week. It was the first such fleet configuration his ministry has spotted, he said.
Koizumi said he cited the incident as "an example illustrating the challenging security environment in the region" in his remark at a session Thursday. His ministry will keep watching the Chinese activity with high level of interest, he said. Japan has been accelerating a military buildup in southwestern Japan to deter China.
The annual meetings aim to avert a major regional conflict and strengthen defense cooperation. On the sidelines of the meetings, however, the U.S. and China and their allies have often traded criticisms.
The missiles that will be produced as part of a joint effort called "Operation Supercharge" are essential for the F-35 fighter jets, Koizumi said. The two sides agreed to build a final assembly and inspection plant for the Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, or AMRAAM, in Japan, he said. The U.S.-made F-35s are one of the world's most advanced aircraft and are also used by the Japanese military.
During his brief meeting with Hegseth in Cebu, Koizumi said he "shared a sense of crisis ... regarding the increasingly severe regional situation and we agreed to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-U.S. alliance with greater speed and intensity than ever before."
"We reaffirmed the importance of a free and open international order based on the rule of law, which rejects any attempts to unilaterally alter the status quo through the use of force, coercion or other means," Koizumi said.
Hegseth renewed the Trump administration's repeated assurances of commitment to help deter aggression in the region in a separate meeting on Wednesday with ASEAN defense ministers, who were led by the host, Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. Like Koizumi, Hegseth did not mention China by name in expressing his security concerns in the region.
"The approach we're taking, we describe as strong, quiet and clear," Hegseth told the ASEAN defense chiefs. "Strong enough to deter coercion and aggression, quiet enough to avoid needless escalation or public theatrics to let our actions speak for themselves."
His message is "clear enough that our friends, our partners and potential adversaries understand precisely where the United States stands and that we will defend our interests and the interests of our allies and partners," Hegseth said.
Hegseth has assured the Philippines, the oldest treaty ally of Washington in Asia, that the Trump administration will build a robust deterrence against China's increasingly aggressive actions in the disputed South China Sea. Beijing claims the busy waterway, a key global trade route, virtually in its entirety.
Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles said his country's forces, along with allies like the U.S., will press on with efforts to defend the rule of law despite China's increasing assertiveness, including in the South China Sea. Australia protested last year after a Chinese J-16 fighter aircraft released flares and passed within 30 meters of an Australian P-8 Poseidon surveillance jet over the disputed waters.
"That doesn't deter us from doing what we need to do, and that's essentially asserting the rules-based order here in the end of the Pacific," Marles told The Associated Press in Cebu on Wednesday. "Freedom of navigation on the high seas is profoundly important for Australia."
The Philippines, Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei, all ASEAN member states, along with Taiwan, also have overlapping claims in the South China Sea. Confrontations have particularly escalated between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and navy vessels in disputed shoals and outlying waters.
Washington has warned that it's obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces, ships and aircraft come under an armed attack, including in the South China Sea.
Beijing and Tokyo have a separate dispute over tiny Japanese-controlled islands in the East China Sea, with both sides often accusing the other of infringing on their maritime territory.

CTS News reported that the piano also drew attention after a man interrupted a high school student's performance by singing China's national anthem on Oct. 20. The student responded by shouting "Long live Taiwan, long live the Republic of China," referring to Taiwan's official name, and a video of the exchange sparked debate online.

The station posted a notice Thursday afternoon requiring prior approval for musical performances and banning commercial activities. It warned that people who disturbed public order or blocked walkways could be asked to leave, per Liberty Times.
The notice drew criticism from people concerned that ordinary piano performances could be restricted. Tainan City Government contacted railway officials, and the station removed the notice around 8 p.m. Thursday.
Under the revised approach, visitors can continue playing the piano without prior approval. The station plans to ban commercial activities, loudspeakers, and performances that obstruct passenger routes, per Taisounds.
The city government said it respected the railway's responsibility to keep passengers safe and ensure station announcements could be heard. However, it urged officials to clarify the rules so visitors would not mistakenly believe all musical performances were banned.

Japan moves forward with plans to establish a backup capital for Tokyo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
04:52:34 UTC
13:52:34 KST

Japan moves forward with plans to establish a backup capital for Tokyo
The law represents a key component of the coalition agreement signed a year ago between Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and its junior coalition partner, the Osaka-based Japan Innovation Party. The agreement includes plans to reorganize Osaka into a metropolis similar to Tokyo through the introduction of a special ward system.
The Japanese government is expected to announce its basic policy on the second capital designation in November, along with a proposed timetable for the selection process.
Under the new legislation, the second capital is intended to ensure the continuity of Japan’s national and social functions in the event of a major disaster, while reducing the concentration of economic activity in the Tokyo metropolitan region.
Prefectures granted the designation will also be eligible for regulatory exemptions and tax incentives aimed at attracting private investment.
The legislation authorizes the prime minister to designate a second capital based on applications submitted by prefectural governments. Notably, the law does not restrict the number of designated areas to one, allowing the possibility of multiple secondary capitals across Japan.
Several prefectures have already expressed interest in applying, including Hokkaido in northern Japan, Aichi in the central region, Osaka in western Japan and Fukuoka in the southwest.
On Tuesday, the government approved an ordinance outlining the eligibility requirements for second capital status.
According to the criteria, an applicant prefecture must account for at least 2.1 percent of Japan’s gross domestic product and include a city whose population represents at least 1.2 percent of the country's total population.
The administrative requirements stipulate that applicants must either reorganize a government-designated city into special wards or establish a cooperation agreement between the city and the prefectural government.
The ordinance also requires designated backup capitals to be located outside areas considered vulnerable to severe damage from a major earthquake affecting the Tokyo region or an eruption of Mount Fuji, Japan’s highest mountain, located between Yamanashi and Shizuoka prefectures west of the capital.

ADB approves first strategic business outlook, projects $104.5 billion in financing by 2029
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
04:52:30 UTC

ADB approves first strategic business outlook, projects $104.5 billion in financing by 2029
The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has approved its first-ever Strategic Business Outlook, outlining plans to provide $104.5 billion in financing commitments between 2027 and 2029 while introducing reforms to strengthen project preparation, implementation and delivery across Asia and the Pacific, Qazinform News Agency cites the bank’s press service.
ADB President Masato Kanda said the new framework brings together the bank’s strategic, operational, workforce and financial planning to improve its ability to respond to the evolving needs of its member countries.
“Building on our previous planning approach, this new outlook brings strategy, operations, workforce, and financial planning together in a single framework to help ADB respond with greater agility and flexibility to our members’ evolving needs,” Kanda said. He also emphasized the importance of maintaining high operational standards and improving efficiency to deliver the expanded financing program.
The new strategy comes amid growing demand for development financing, increasing economic uncertainty, rising disaster risks and rapid technological advancements. It also introduces sensitivity testing under different economic and operational scenarios, allowing the bank to better anticipate potential risks and adjust its plans accordingly.
Under its base-case projections, ADB expects to allocate $81.6 billion to sovereign operations, primarily supporting government-led initiatives, and $22.8 billion to nonsovereign operations, which mainly finance private sector activities.
As part of its efforts to improve development outcomes, the bank plans to place greater emphasis on project readiness, portfolio performance and the early identification of implementation risks. This will include expanding on-the-ground support, particularly in countries with limited institutional resources and implementation capacity.
ADB also intends to strengthen coordination between its public and private sector operations and mobilize additional private investment.
The Strategic Business Outlook reaffirms the bank’s commitment to poverty reduction and supporting vulnerable communities, including populations in fragile and conflict-affected areas and small island developing states.
Key priorities under the framework include strengthening food, water and energy security, improving disaster preparedness, promoting regional cooperation and supporting emerging industries, including critical minerals processing.
To assess progress, ADB will evaluate its performance based not only on financing commitments but also on measurable development outcomes. The bank will also pursue more efficient internal processes and expand the use of digital technologies to support the implementation of its broader program.
The Strategic Business Outlook will serve as the overarching framework guiding ADB’s operations through 2029. However, individual financing proposals and budget decisions will continue to undergo separate review and approval processes.

Finland launches criminal probe into Google data center project

Finland launches criminal probe into Google data center project
Finnish police have launched a criminal investigation into suspected environmental violations at a planned Google data center site, where hundreds of hectares of forest were cleared before the completion of mandatory environmental impact assessments.
The Oulu Police Department announced on Thursday that it is investigating suspected environmental damage at the site in Muhos, northern Finland, following complaints about the activities of Google’s local subsidiary, Tuike Finland.
According to Finnish public broadcaster Yle, police have received five requests for an investigation, including one from the Finnish Supervisory Agency (LVV), which oversees environmental permits and assessments.
Investigators identified possible irregularities in drainage and water management at the construction site. The authorities are examining whether the work violated environmental legislation and caused damage to surrounding waterways.
Google has acknowledged that it cleared around 330 hectares of forest in Muhos and nearly 200 hectares at another planned data center site in Kajaani, despite environmental impact assessments for both projects remaining incomplete.
Ecologist Mari Annala of the Finnish Association for Nature Conservation told The Guardian that Google cleared an estimated 250,000 trees in Muhos and another 150,000 in Otanmaki, bringing the total to 400,000.
Earlier this month, Finnish regulators ordered the company to suspend preparatory work at both locations, citing concerns about extensive logging, excavation, and drainage. The company confirmed on October 14 that it complied with the order.
The LVV has also warned that excavation and drainage at the Muhos site could release acidic, metal-contaminated water because of the area’s black shale deposits. The regulator has demanded a more detailed water management plan by November 5.
Google’s Finland country manager, Antti Jarvinen, apologized earlier this month for the extensive forest clearing but maintained that the company acted according to its understanding of Finnish law.
“I am extremely sorry that we are in this situation,” he told Finnish public broadcaster Yle.
Jarvinen said Google worked with the authorities and experts but declined to identify which officials were informed about the clearing.
The controversy comes amid growing opposition to data center construction in the US, where people have protested against the enormous electricity and water demands, potential environmental damage, and rising utility costs of the facilities. In Virginia, hundreds of demonstrators recently demanded a halt to new projects. In Arizona, people have opposed planned facilities over concerns about water shortages and electricity costs.

Interview: China's import expo offers showcase for "Made in Cote d'Ivoire," says Ivorian export promotion agency chief
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:41:19 CST
13:41:19 KST

ABIDJAN, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Cote d'Ivoire hopes to use its first official collective participation in the upcoming China International Import Expo (CIIE) to promote its products, expand access to the Chinese market and attract investment in local processing, the head of the country's export promotion agency has said.
In a recent interview with Xinhua, Kaladji Fadiga, director general of the Cote d'Ivoire Export Agency, said the West African country would showcase five strategic sectors and their value chains -- cocoa, coffee, cashew nuts, kola nuts and textiles -- at the ninth CIIE, scheduled for Nov. 5-10 in Shanghai.
"Cote d'Ivoire has quality products, recognized expertise and considerable potential," Fadiga said. "'Made in Cote d'Ivoire' represents excellence rooted in expertise, origin and history."
Cote d'Ivoire is a leading global producer of cocoa and cashew nuts. Fadiga also highlighted the potential of kola nuts among Asian consumers.
"Cote d'Ivoire aspires to position itself as an economic partner with a differentiated offering, combining unprocessed agricultural products and agro-industrial goods," he said, adding that the country aims to promote the "Made in Cote d'Ivoire" label through local brands ready to enter the Chinese market.
"Today, international trade is taking place in a particularly uncertain environment, marked by the resurgence of protectionism in markets," Fadiga said. "In this context, the resilience of the Chinese economy deserves particular attention."
He said this resilience offers significant opportunities for African countries seeking to diversify their trading partners. For Cote d'Ivoire, China's ability to sustain investment and honor its trade commitments despite global turbulence offers further opportunities to diversify its export markets and boost exports, he added.
He pointed to demand from Chinese buyers for Ivorian products, including cocoa, cashew nuts, rubber and cotton, as well as China's zero-tariff policy for all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic ties, including Cote d'Ivoire.
Calling the policy "much more than a simple adjustment," Fadiga said it could make eligible Ivorian goods, particularly cashew nuts, more price-competitive in the Chinese market.
Beyond tariff advantages, the expo provides Ivorian companies with a platform to meet Chinese importers and distributors, better understand market demand, identify potential business partners and pursue long-term export opportunities.
To support Ivorian exporters, the Cote d'Ivoire Export Agency and the Chinese Embassy in Cote d'Ivoire have established a bilateral working group called "Export to China."
The initiative seeks to connect Ivorian exporters with Chinese buyers, assist with customs clearance and help companies comply with sanitary and phytosanitary requirements. It also plans to organize study visits to China to familiarize Ivorian businesses with the Chinese market and its business environment.
Beyond trade promotion, Cote d'Ivoire hopes to leverage its economic ties with China to expand local processing and increase the value added to its exports.
Citing Ivorian customs data, Fadiga said the country exported 1 million tons of raw cocoa beans worth about 2.4 trillion CFA francs (4.1 billion U.S. dollars) in 2024, compared with 613,000 tons of processed cocoa products valued at approximately 2 trillion CFA francs (3.4 billion dollars).
"This is quantitative evidence of the strategic importance of increasing our local processing rate," he said.
"Our short-term objectives include signing several commercial contracts with Chinese importers and distributors, promoting Ivorian expertise among Chinese consumers, and identifying partners willing to invest in local processing," Fadiga said.
Looking ahead, he said Cote d'Ivoire hopes to strengthen its presence at successive editions of the expo, and deepen economic cooperation with China.
"Our role as a national export promotion agency is to ensure that 'Made in Cote d'Ivoire' finds its rightful place in global markets," he said. "With CIIE 2026, we are moving resolutely in that direction." ■

Xizang Story: Lighting up Lhasa's youth through Tibetan director's lens
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
12:41:10 CST
13:41:10 KST

LHASA, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- If Kangdrun were to pick a season to define her childhood, it would definitely be summer.
For the Tibetan director born and raised in Lhasa, capital of southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, summer means not only long school holidays and the traditional Shoton Festival, but also a season for linka, the beloved local tradition of gathering outdoors for picnics, songs, dances and laughter.
In mid-October, the 31-year-old filmmaker's first long film, "Linka Linka," a title drawn from that very word, hit the big screen.
Shot entirely in Tibetan, the 100-minute film dives into a summer night's linka party in Lhasa and weaves together three stories that trace the growth of its protagonist, Sangye.
"I deeply love my hometown. Bringing the Lhasa dialect and the modern lives to the screen is an instinctive and pure wish for me as a native," Kangdrun said.
The crew documented the young actress through four separate production stages from 2020 to 2024 as she grew from childhood into a youth. The film was supported by the region's literary and art funding program.
The film, notably, has reached audiences far beyond Lhasa. It has earned awards or nominations in Tokyo, Hong Kong, Sochi and Buenos Aires, such as the Firebird Award and FIPRESCI Prize at the 50th Hong Kong International Film Festival, and has been selected for other international film festivals in Shanghai, Udine, Barcelona and Vancouver.
Local audiences consider the film "very Lhasa," which is exactly the effect Kangdrun aimed for -- to document a real, living Lhasa and the youth in the city.
"In Lhasa, young people are just as comfortable recounting childhood in Tibetan as they are mapping out the future in Mandarin. They'll study anywhere the opportunity takes them, and return to lay out mats on the grass for a linka party in summer," she explained.
Like Sangye in the film, Kangdrun left her hometown to study and obtained a master's degree in film production at the Beijing-based Communication University of China.
While at university, Kangdrun began filming Xizang's veteran rock band NAMCHAK. Between academic terms, she kept returning to Lhasa to shoot and produce short films.
She said many of her peers had experiences pursuing study away from home and growing up amid diverse cultural influences, allowing them to look at the plateau more objectively.
"Culture flows, and it evolves as it moves," she said. "What we young people do today is quietly reshaping this city."
In Xizang, the Tibetan language is widely used in publishing, media, and daily life. Every year, more than 15,000 hours of radio programs, more than 80 movies, and 7,300 hours of TV programs are translated or dubbed from and into minority languages, according to a white paper issued last year.
Kangdrun is now busy completing her next piece, which is still focused on Lhasa. The work, "Orlo in the House," turns the lens on a Tibetan who works in a sweet tea house in the city.
"Filming has wrapped and the post-production is underway," she said. ■

SEOUL, Oct 30 (Reuters) - South Korea will respond firmly to protect the military border with North Korea despite claims by Pyongyang that it is conducting operations on its side of the line, Seoul’s national security adviser Wi Sung-lac said on Friday.
Tensions have spiked since a landmine blast inside the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ) border seriously wounded several South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission last month, which Seoul has said was caused by a North Korean mine.
The UN Command, which oversees the DMZ, has said a North Korean mine across the line violated the armistice. Seoul has demanded that Pyongyang immediately halt fortification work near the inter-Korean border, saying the activity has raised tensions.
Pyongyang has denied responsibility for the mine and Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on October 21 that North Korea will activate anti-South Korean propaganda loudspeakers along its entire border by the end of October.
South Korea’s spy agency said on Thursday that North Korea had not yet started any broadcasts.
Both Koreas have previously used such broadcasts as part of psychological warfare campaigns.

CPC outlines four areas in anti-corruption drive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
04:29:31 UTC
13:29:31 KST

The Communist Party of China (CPC) outlined four areas of focus for combating corruption in a resolution adopted at the fifth plenary session of the CPC Central Committee, a senior anti-graft official said on Friday.
The four areas are maintaining a tough stance against corruption, strengthening checks on and oversight over the exercise of power, fortifying the cultural-ethical foundations for championing integrity and disdaining corruption, and enhancing coordinated efforts to prevent corruption by rooting out audacity, opportunity, and desire.
"Conducts and discipline problems are long-term recurrent and stubborn, persistent efforts are needed to tackle them," said Zhang Fuhai, deputy secretary of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection of the CPC and deputy head of the National Commission of Supervision.
He made the remarks at a press conference on the guiding principles from the fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the CPC in Beijing.
Since the 18th National Congress of the CPC in 2012, discipline inspection and supervisory organs across the country have filed 8.105 million cases and punished 7.922 million people, including 963 officials registered at and supervised by the CPC Central Committee, according to Zhang.
"We will intensify anti-corruption efforts in areas with a high concentration of power funds and resources focus on corruption that involves both political and economic elements collusion between officials and business people, and capital infiltrating into the political realm dig deep into new and disguised manifestations of corruption and tackle on a regular basis misconduct and corruption that occurs at people's doorsteps," he said.
The plenum, which concluded on Thursday in Beijing, adopted the Resolution of the Central Committee of the CPC on Certain Major Issues concerning Persevering with Full and Rigorous Party Self-Governance. (Additional reporting from Xinhua)
Edited by Tony Sabine

Germany news: Friedrich Merz calls for global free trade alliance during Asia trip
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
04:25:00 UTC
13:25:00 KST

Germany news: Merz in Asia warns against weaponizing trade
Published October 30, 2026last updated October 30, 2026
What you need to know
- Chancellor Friedrich Merz is in South Korea on the last stop of a three-country Asia tour
- Merz calls for global trade to be strengthened and for a rules-based economic order
- President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping
- Berlin event set to mark the 65th anniversary of West Germany and Turkey's agreement on 'guest workers'
Here are the leading headlines from and about Germany on Friday, October 30:
IN DEPTH: 65 years on, many Turkish 'guest workers' in Germany face poverty
On October 30, 1961, West Germany and Turkey signed an agreement allowing the temporary recruitment of workers. Sixty-five years on, many so-called "guest workers" cannot live from their pensions.
Learn more about how "guest workers" are struggling as they reach retirement age in this in depth report by Oliver Pieper.
Merz at DMZ says he hopes Korea can reunify like Germany did
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday visited the Panmunjom truce village at the demilitarized zone (DMZ) separating North and South Korea, briefly standing on the North Korean side inside the barracks.
North and South Korea have been divided since the end of hostilities in the Korean War in 1953, with a border running across the peninsula.
In remarks to reporters, Merz recalled Germany's reunification 36 years ago.
"Let us hope that Korea too gets the chance one day to regain state unity," he said.
"You can also notice it here at this place, how much a country suffers from division and how strong the desire is for reunification, at least in this part of the Korean Peninsula," he said, adding that he had been asked about Germany's reunification experience while visiting Seoul.
North Korea, however, has backed away in recent years from diplomacy with the South, having officially removed language calling for reunification from its constitution while changing the South's status to that of a "hostile state."
German president in Beijing addresses trade tensions with China
While German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in South Korea on Friday called for a better rule-based trade order, President Frank-Walter Steinmeier was in the Chinese capital in a bid to smooth out trade disagreements.
In Beijing, Steinmeier called for preserving the "win-win principle" characterizing Sino-German relations, borrowing from the expression "win-win cooperation," one of the most frequently used phrases in Chinese foreign policy statements.
Germany's economic ties with China have gone through a shock in recent years, with Chinese manufacturing growing into sectors once dominated by German firms, and Chinese electric cars taking over market share.
At the start of a meeting with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, Steinmeier cited a recent deal limiting exports of Chinese hybrid cars to the EU in exchange for select tariff cuts on EU exports to China as an example of a "a way to find solutions."
Steinmeier also brought up Germany's growing trade deficit with China, which grew to nearly €90 billion ($100 billion) last year.
Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base.
Steinmeier said Germany would work to solve trade problems with China. "We are coming with the intention of maintaining and strengthening the framework for good economic exchange between our two countries," Steinmeier said.
Later in the day, the German president, who occupies a largely ceremonial role without policymaking power, was also recieved by an honor guard alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Merz in Seoul calls for new trade order, says supply chains cannot become 'political pawns'
During his final day of a whirlwind Asia tour this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told the Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul on Friday that Germany and Europe are ready to cooperate with Asian economies to foster a rules-based economic order.
Merz said the European Union is ready to take the lead in shaping a better deal for countries in Asia feeling the pressure of a destabilized rules-based trade order.
"Competition between the US and China is ramping up. Tariffs, technological decoupling strategies and a tough race for critical raw materials and new technologies are fundamentally changing the rules of our global economy," Merz said.
"These conflicts and systemic shifts in power patterns concern us all. They particularly concern economically aspiring partners in the Indo-Pacific, as well as in Germany and in Europe."
During stops in Singapore and Japan this week, Merz pushed for free trade partnerships and greater European cooperation with Asian economies.
In Singapore on Wednesday, Merz called for a free trade agreement between the EU and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), a sweeping multilateral free trade agreement connecting the Asia Pacific and the Americas.
The UK is the single European signatory, albeit outside of the EU bloc. The US pulled out during the first administration President Donald Trump in 2017, scuttling the original version, the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP).
"We want to offer opportunities beyond bilateral agreements,"he said in Seoul on Friday.
"We are resolutely joining forces against unilateralism, autocratic power politics and violations of international law," Merz added.
"When supply chains become political pawns, when access to key technologies is obstructed or when efforts to secure raw materials resemble displays of power rather than fair partnerships, this jeopardizes growth, prosperity and ultimately the security of entire regions."
Merz also tried to allay concerns about EU protectionism under the "Made in Europe" scheme intended to protect carmakers.
"There is a fear that we might be facing a new wave of European protectionism - that we are closing ourselves off from other nations," Merz said.
"I take these concerns very seriously. I will carry them back not just to Berlin, but also to Brussels, and I will certainly raise the fact that these concerns were expressed to me quite forcefully here," he added.
Citing Germany as an example, South Korean Prime Minister Han Seong Sook told the conference "German companies are using Korea as a central hub to expand their presence in the Asia-Pacific region."
Additional reporting by Nina Haase

Highlights From the Toasts at the 2026 TIME100 Next Gala
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
04:17:28 UTC
13:17:28 KST

A standout group of artists, innovators, politicians, athletes, and more came together at a gala in Manhattan on Oct. 29 to celebrate the 2026 TIME100 Next list.
The evening included a performance from Grammy-nominated singer Raye, whose recent hit singles, including “Where Is My Husband!’” have rocketed her into stardom after more than a decade of making music.
The evening also allowed a space for honorees to toast to what gives them hope for the future, and who helped them achieve success. Among those who spoke were Philadelphia 76ers guard Tyrese Maxey, actor Himesh Patel, singer-songwriter and content creator Alex Warren, Food4Education founder Wawira Njiru, and Saturday Night Live star Ashley Padilla.
Here’s a rundown of what each honoree said:
Tyrese Maxey
Tyrese Maxey gave the evening’s first toast, beginning his remarks by recognizing all the other 2026 TIME100 Next honorees in attendance.
“For me, it’s just an honor to be amongst all of you and be able to speak today,” Maxey said. “What motivates me, honestly, is y’all.”
Maxey shared a motto that he’s strived to follow since he was a kid: to get “1% better every single day.” He added that his father encouraged him that “the sky’s the limit.”
Maxey went on to highlight that his platform has enabled him to pursue other passions, including launching a nonprofit foundation to “give back” to the community.
The NBA All-Star closed out his toast by applauding all the honorees in the room.
“Shout out to all y’all,” he said. “I do really appreciate y’all because y’all are extremely inspirational to me, myself, and all of us around.”
Himesh Patel
During his toast, Himesh Patel spoke about how many of the people in the room “hold power and influence.”
“In these precarious times, I believe it’s imperative for each of us to think about where we hold it, and how we use it to do good in the world,” Patel said.
Patel went on to talk about his own story. He grew up in a village in Cambridgeshire, England, where his parents ran a corner shop, and he delivered newspapers. When he landed his first acting gig at the age of 16, he continued, his parents “made sure” that he kept up his paper route each day.
“As immigrants who built everything they had with their own hands, they know that nothing is certain except the fact that nothing is certain,” Patel said of his parents. He said that his story feels “unlikely because it’s sometimes been hard to believe I ever belong in rooms like this.”
Patel observed that when TIME was founded in 1923, his ancestors were living in a village in Gujarat, India, where they “were still subjects of colonialism.”
“103 years later, here I am, standing amongst you. I have those ancestors to thank,” he said. “Because they resisted their oppressors, they fought for their independence. In the face of fear, they chose to hope. Because my parents crossed oceans, defied the odds to build a new life in an unknown land. In the face of uncertainty, they chose to hope.”
Patel called hope “an act of defiance,” and ended his remarks by encouraging everyone in the room to “choose to hope.”
“All of us here are being told that we hold power and influence,” Patel said. “I’m using mine, standing here amongst all you incredible people to say: in these precarious times, in the face of fear and uncertainty—I choose to hope. Maybe you will too. Because imagine the power and the influence that act could hold.”
Alex Warren
Alex Warren opened his toast by sharing a story: when he was 7 years old, he climbed a tall tree and shouted down to his father, who was at the bottom and was prepared to catch him: “What if I fall?”
“Without hesitation, he responds, ‘What if you fly?’” Warren recalled. “That was my dad. He was always so quick to instill hope and question what you thought was impossible. My dad was a superhero, and I wanted to impress him. I performed talent shows in our living room, singing my heart out. No matter what lyrics I sang, wrong strings I would play, you couldn’t hear them over the cheers of a proud father.”
Warren said that he practiced performing every day, hoping to one day achieve his dreams of being a singer.
“I was too busy trying to show my dad how high I could fly that when I finally looked down, he wasn’t there to catch me,” Warren said. “I was 9 years old when I woke up to my mom asking me if I wanted to say goodbye to my dad, and the room that was filled with music and cheer the days prior was taken up by the deafening sound of silence.”
Growing up, Warren recalled being surrounded by people but feeling “so alone” much of the time. Music brought him comfort, he said, as he found people who listened to and appreciated his own work.
“I was never really alone, and now every night, no matter what lyrics I sing or wrong strings I play on my guitar, millions of people around the world are screaming these songs loud enough for anyone we have lost to hear,” he said. “So let’s raise our glass … and toast, but not to flying, but having someone there to catch you if you fall.”
Wawira Njiru
Njiru, the co-founder and CEO of Kenya-based nonprofit Food4Education, began her toast by reminding the room that while it often feels like the future is built by new inventions, technologies, and machines, it is actually built by people.
“The most valuable resource on this planet has never been the things we extract—oil, or gold, or data. It's the things we grow. The things we nurture,” Njiru said. “And right now, the world's largest reserve of it is sitting in African classrooms.”
Food4Education delivers over 600,000 meals each day to children across more than 1,500 schools across Africa. These are young people that we need to be investing in, Njiru said.
While artificial intelligence “promises to make our lives better,” she reminded the crowd that “somebody still has to do the physical stuff, the real stuff, the hard stuff, the human stuff.”
She spoke to her own experience growing Food4Education from a nonprofit that fed just 25 students to one that aims to feed 1 million children each day by 2027.
Though she and her staff grew their organization like a business, she said they did without “losing sight of the people [they] serve.”
When Njiru looks at the children who are in her nonprofit’s food line, she sees “the future.”
“The next scientific breakthrough, creative revolution, or great innovation could come from anywhere, from anyone,” she finished. “That's what gives me hope: what's possible when we invest in—and with—people.”
Ashley Padilla
Padilla, who captured hearts as a star cast member of SNL this past year, made the room laugh with a toast full of jokes and references to her most notable sketches.
“You may know me from a sketch where I fart in front of all my coworkers and then get very, very mad about it right after,” Padilla said, prompting laughs throughout the room. “And if you don't know me from that, then you don't know me at all.”
But soon, Padilla shared a vulnerable moment, saying it “is hard to give a toast when you know you should not be here.”
“There were so many chances to mess up my life along the way. I tried to quit comedy. I tried to quit on myself an embarrassing amount of times,” she said. “I told myself it was too hard, too painful, too impossible.”
But despite the negative self-talk along the way, Padilla said that there was always a voice in the back of her head telling her to “keep going.”
“I can viscerally remember hearing it in the backseat of my mother’s car, tears streaming down my face because I was failing school,” she recalled. “And there was that sound inside me that I should keep going.”
In the end, this was the message of Padilla’s toast, thanking that voice, “whispering inside all of us, pushing us all to keep going.”
The TIME100 Next Gala was presented by Rolex, Toyota, American Airlines, Danantara, Project Management Institute, and Target.

Rights Groups Links Cambodian Security Companies to Scam Compounds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
04:16:00 UTC
13:16:00 KST

From the outset, it must be said that Cambodia has delivered on promises to liquidate large-scale online scamming compounds, a key plank in the truce that ended last year’s border conflict with Thailand and a much-desired result ahead of its hosting the Francophonie Summit of French-speaking nations in mid-November.
Mopping up the smaller operations continues, with regular government updates including the arrests and deportation of foreign scammers and alleged organized crime figures, who during the COVID-19 years turned industrialized online fraud into a multibillion-dollar racket.
And the current broader attitude is a refreshing sea-change from the first three years of the scourge, when the public face of government was absolute denial of the allegations made by journalists and NGOs while tycoons and officials allegedly greased the wheels of the crime syndicates.
Therein lies the problem.
While the arrests and deportations of foreign tycoons like Chen Zhi and his cohorts within the criminal world made international headlines, their Cambodian counterparts remained hidden from view despite international sanctions, arrest warrants in Thailand, and Interpol Red Notices.
It’s a point that’s been driven home by the latest Amnesty International report, which ties five security firms to Cambodia’s scam compounds and the serious human rights abuses that were committed there. For the Cambodian government, it’s a matter of credibility.
Amnesty interviewed more than 150 survivors from 86 compounds and found guards were there not just to protect the premises but also played key roles in confining trafficked people, preventing escape, and enforcing forced labor. It also found that some directly participated in torture and other forms of ill-treatment.
More than 25,000 videos and photos from guards’ social media accounts, satellite imagery, and corporate records were used, tying the companies to politically connected businessmen and linking members of the Cambodian military and police in at least 22 scam compounds.
This, it says, raises concerns about official complicity and the failure of authorities to effectively dismantle the industry despite repeated crackdowns – and it called for an immediate investigation into the security companies and state officials linked to the compounds.
Amnesty named the five Cambodian registered companies as Leap Somnang Security, Security Response, ZD Security, Dara Security Service, and Best (Cambodia) Security Service.
At least three high-ranking military and police officers – Brig. Gen. Tek Bunthoeun, Col. Ban Sophat and Deputy Police Chief Lay Channy – had links to scamming compounds that indicated official involvement with the industry, Amnesty said in the 162-page report.
“At the heart of these connections are security companies whose guards controlled compound exits, hunted down people who escaped, and enforced compliance through fear and violence,” said Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General.
“Without them, this system of mass exploitation could not have functioned,” she said. “For years, survivors of these nightmarish compounds described encountering members of the Cambodian military or police inside. These accounts could not be independently verified – until now.”
The Amnesty report also follows a recent Al Jazeera documentary in which undercover journalists interviewed organized crime figures and met with senior government officials who also allegedly protected organized crime figures.
In short, the list of Cambodian companies, officials and tycoons who allegedly enabled the wholesale trafficking of humans and the crimes that were committed is long, public, and growing, with the latest Amnesty report adding another thick layer of evidence.
It’s a list that sits online, in every embassy that had a victim to extract or a citizen back home who was robbed, and in every major bank on the planet where international money transfers to and from Cambodia are judged on risk.
And it will serve as background for any foreign investor who ever considers spending a dollar in Cambodia where the economy is in dire straits and tourists have simply stopped coming.
Restoring Cambodia’s reputation and getting them back won’t be easy, but addressing global concerns like those raised in the Amnesty report would at least be a next step.

Ancient Martian meteorite discovered in Mali formed over 4.1 billion years ago: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
04:14:30 UTC
13:14:30 KST

Gizem Nisa Demir
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
A meteorite discovered in Mali in 2022 dates back more than 4.1 billion years, offering scientists rare insights into Mars' ancient crust and water history, according to a recent study.
NASA-funded researchers have determined that Teghaza 001, an approximately 800-gram (1.8-pound) meteorite found in the Sahara Desert, originated on Mars and is among the oldest Martian meteorites ever discovered on Earth.
Named after the salt plain in Mali where it was discovered, it is one of roughly 435 known Martian meteorites. The findings were published Thursday in the journal Science, according to NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL).
The study provides an initial characterization of the meteorite, which contains a distinctive combination of igneous, or volcanic, minerals. These minerals offer clues about how Mars' crust formed as magma cooled and was later altered by subsurface water. A separate study published in Science Advances in June examined the meteorite's water content and its implications for the planet's early surface.
"It was only after we started looking closely that we realized this meteorite is really unique," said Yang Liu, the study's lead author and a researcher at JPL in Southern California. "One of the paper's reviewers called it a Rosetta Stone for Mars."
Teghaza 001 is among the three most ancient Martian meteorites found on Earth. The others include ALH84001, which is composed almost entirely of one mineral and is of a similar age, and "Black Beauty," which formed about 2.1 billion years ago.
The meteorite's mineral composition resembles material observed by NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter in the planet's cratered southern highlands. Although its exact origin remains unknown, researchers identified several potential locations consistent with its mineralogy and chemistry.
"This is really our first piece of Martian crust from a part of Mars we've never had a sample of before," said Lee Saper, the study's second author, who conducted the research as a postdoctoral scholar at JPL and is now a scientist at NASA's Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley.
"It records interactions of water and rock and maybe even an imprint of the Martian atmosphere as it was losing water," Saper said.
Evidence of ancient water
Researchers at the University of New Mexico initially identified Teghaza 001 as Martian by analyzing its oxygen isotopes, which act as geochemical fingerprints. It appeared to belong to the shergottite class, the most common type of Martian meteorite.
However, Liu noticed unusual textures and minerals that warranted further investigation. Her team discovered zircon crystals, which preserve information about a rock's formation and help scientists determine its age.
Francois Tissot, a co-author from the California Institute of Technology, helped apply an in-situ rubidium-strontium dating technique developed by his team. The method analyzes individual mineral grains using a fragment smaller than a fingernail, preserving most of the rare meteorite for future research.
"Right now, we are one of very few labs in the world able to perform this kind of age-dating, and the first to date such an ancient Martian meteorite," Tissot said. "Our hope is to pave the way for dating even more Martian meteorites, or samples returned from other planets, their moons and asteroids."
The results showed that water altered the rock around 4.1 billion years ago, suggesting it originally formed even earlier. Evidence from its oxygen isotopes, texture and chemistry points to a dynamic water cycle on early Mars.
Researchers say further studies of Teghaza 001 could help clarify how water interacted with rocks and shaped the planet's early geological history.
"We've only scratched the surface," Liu said.

Kim Jong Un calls for rapid development of drone technology after North Korea launches ballistic missiles
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has called for the rapid development of drone technology in the country and watched tests of various weapons systems as tensions with South Korea continue to mount along the border.
Source: Associated Press, citing North Korea's state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA)
Details: Acquiring advanced drones is a key priority for Kim, who is seeking to strengthen both the country's conventional and nuclear capabilities. Experts believe that North Korean troops sent to Russia to support its war against Ukraine have likely gained valuable experience in drone warfare from the Russian Armed Forces.
KCNA reported that Kim visited an exhibition of various attack and other drones on Thursday 29 October, showcasing the latest advances in uncrewed aeronautical technology.
According to KCNA, in a speech at the exhibition, Kim stressed the need to achieve "absolute superiority in the drone technology" and announced unspecified measures required to "rapidly expand and strengthen the unmanned aeronautical technology".
KCNA also reported that North Korea later conducted test launches of various drones, missiles and munitions from 600mm ultra-precision multiple-launch rocket systems.
Photographs released by KCNA show Kim watching missiles in flight or clenching his fist, while his teenage daughter, standing beside him, applauds.
South Korea's military said earlier that it had detected the launch of around 10 short-range ballistic missiles from the North Korean east coast city of Wonsan on Thursday. These were North Korea's first ballistic weapons launches in 17 days.
AP noted that tensions between the two Koreas remain high following landmine explosions along the border last month that injured three South Korean soldiers. Seoul accused North Korea of laying mines south of the military demarcation line and demanded an apology. Pyongyang denied responsibility for the explosions and warned that it would take retaliatory measures in the event of provocation.
North Korea threatened last week to resume propaganda broadcasts over loudspeakers and deploy new weapons systems along the border.
North Korea withdrew from talks with the US and South Korea after Kim's high-stakes diplomatic initiative with US President Donald Trump collapsed in 2019. In recent weeks, North Korea has stepped up weapons testing, apparently seeking to strengthen its position in potential diplomatic negotiations with the US after Trump expressed a desire to resume talks with Kim.
Kim made an unexpected visit to a Chinese border city via a newly opened bridge on 24 October and pledged to develop bilateral relations. Kim has recently taken steps to strengthen ties with China, North Korea's economic partner, after prioritising relations with Russia for several years. This included sending thousands of troops and munitions, apparently in exchange for economic and military assistance.
Meanwhile, Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis arrived in North Korea on Thursday to attend a ceremony marking the reopening of Switzerland's diplomatic mission in Pyongyang and meet North Korean officials. He is due to travel to South Korea on Friday 30 October.
Background: North Korea conducted test launches of two types of submarine-launched strategic cruise missiles off its east coast in mid-October.

'Biggest hack in history': Crypto exchange Binance freezes assets after $6.3 b. security breach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
04:12:33 UTC
13:12:33 KST

North Korean hackers were behind a $6.3 billion raid on cryptocurrency exchange Binance, according to US blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs.
"An attacker moved approximately $6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," TRM Labs said in a blog post on its website.
"TRM attributes the attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea's elite hacking unit, based on robust on and off-chain intelligence. We make this judgment with high confidence."
Earlier in the day, Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said a security breach had resulted in an estimated $6.3 billion impact that analysts said could amount to the biggest crypto heist ever and might make investors rethink the risks of owning digital assets.
Binance said it had worked with partners to freeze the affected assets, with about $3 billion located so far. It gave no update on the status of the remaining $3.3 billion as Binance co-founder Yi He said the company would cover "all hacking losses."
An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of its engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and make unauthorized withdrawals, Binance said.
Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday.
Bitcoin dropped more than 3% to a six-week low of $76,368 and ether fell more than 3% to a two-month low of $2,178. BNB, a token originally launched as Binance Coin that can be used to pay Binance fees, was down 5% over the past 24 hours at $709.70, according to market aggregator CoinGecko.
Shares in crypto exchange Coinbase Global slid 4.8% while those of bitcoin buyer Strategy fell nearly 6% in extended US trading.
The incident could be the world's biggest crypto heist, according to analytics firm Chainalysis and other industry experts.
"It's the biggest hack in history," said Aravind Srinivasan, head of large crypto market maker GSR's systematic OTC business.
Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure lately due to higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.
"It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralized exchanges, as well as counterparty, solvency and liquidity risks," said Tim Sun, senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8 billion in assets under custody as of the exchange's 2025 annual report.
"User funds remain safe," Binance said in a statement. "As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our security teams conduct checks, secure wallet infrastructure, and trace affected assets, with the close support of our law enforcement and industry partners."
Binance has secure asset fund
Binance runs a secure asset fund for users, according to its website, which is a reserve held entirely in bitcoin that is intended to protect user assets in cases of security breaches.
"It's becoming very hard to counter hacks as AI can find vulnerabilities faster than you can fix them, said Bernardo Brites, CEO of Trace Finance, a payments and stablecoin infrastructure company.
"My view is that users will move away from smaller and medium-sized exchanges, (it is) becoming too risky to park your money somewhere that couldn't cover a hack of meaningful size."
Stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57 billion in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800 million.
World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to US President Donald Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack. Binance's Yi said $27 million in stablecoins and about $2 million worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen.
Crypto firm Ripple also froze roughly $200 million in funds, Yi said. Jack McDonald, senior vice president of stablecoins at Ripple, said the company was closely monitoring reports of a potential exploit involving Binance and was freezing affected funds and coordinating with relevant parties.
Incident adds to string of crypto thefts
Miguel Morel, CEO of blockchain intelligence firm Arkham, said data indicated that billions of dollars appeared to have been hacked from Binance by an unknown actor, though the exact cause had not been confirmed. Morel said the incident began around 4:30 p.m. EDT and appeared to be ongoing.
The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year, attackers stole $2.9 billion worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. In September, cryptocurrency exchange Bitget said roughly $350 million in crypto had been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry's vulnerability to hackers.
Authorities have warned that organized crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system.
Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident.
Coinbase said it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation.
In an unrelated incident earlier on Thursday, prediction market operator Polymarket temporarily halted trading after a security incident involving a third-party provider. It later resumed trading and said it would fully reimburse affected traders.

Israel’s coalition politics: How can you win an election and still lose power? - explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
04:12:26 UTC
13:12:26 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party appears to have won more votes than any other party in Israel’s October 27 election. Yet Netanyahu could still be out of office, replaced by someone whose party received far fewer votes. And the next government, whoever leads it, might include ministers from parties with very different political philosophies, perhaps even from opposite ends of the political spectrum.
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
For Americans, accustomed to seeing the winner of a presidential election take office and appoint a Cabinet, this may seem strange. But the explanation is easier to grasp when we consider how American political parties operate.
The Republican Party, for example, encompasses religious conservatives, libertarians, populists, fiscal conservatives, and moderates. These groups disagree over taxes, government spending, foreign policy, immigration, and the role of religion in public life. Some disagreements are so fierce that, in another political system, they might be separate parties.
The same is true of the Democrats. Progressives, democratic socialists, labor-oriented politicians, environmentalists, and business-friendly centrists coexist within the party, frequently fighting over its platform and direction.
In the United States, these factions generally compete for influence within two large parties. The parties themselves are broad coalitions, assembled before voters go to the polls. Their members may have little in common beyond preferring their own party over the other.
Israel approaches the problem differently. Rather than forcing so many political tendencies into two dominant parties, its electoral system lets many of those tendencies be represented by separate parties, each seeking its own share of parliamentary seats.
Imagine the Republican Party splitting into four or five parties, with religious conservatives, libertarians, moderates, and populists running separately. Now imagine the Democrats doing something similar, with progressive, centrist, environmentalist, and labor parties competing for votes.
After the election, these groups would have to negotiate which ones could work together, which policies they could agree on, and who would lead the resulting government.
That is roughly how Israeli politics work.
Winning seats not the same as winning power
Israelis vote for party lists rather than individual parliamentary candidates. The 120 seats in the Knesset, Israel’s parliament, are distributed roughly according to each list’s share of the national vote, provided it receives at least 3.25% of valid ballots.
In the 2026 election, 38 candidate lists were approved, although one withdrew before voting. Preliminary results indicated that 11 would enter the Knesset.
The parties represent a broad range of political, religious, and social interests. Some are secular, others religious. Some favor territorial compromise with the Palestinians, while others oppose it. Some represent the ultra-Orthodox community, some draw much of their support from Arab citizens, and others focus on economic and security policies.
With the votes still being counted Wednesday, Likud was projected to receive approximately 26 seats, or 21.7% of the Knesset. That would make it the largest party, but it would leave the other 94 seats in the hands of its rivals and potential partners.
For an American comparison, imagine Republicans holding 26 seats in a 120-member House of Representatives, Democrats holding 21, and nine smaller parties dividing the rest. Republicans would have the largest delegation but would be unable to govern without making deals.
Israel’s prime minister is not elected separately by the public, as an American president is. The prime minister heads a government that must command sufficient support in the Knesset to take office and remain in power. Usually, that means assembling a coalition with at least 61 of the 120 seats, although minority governments can sometimes survive with support from parties outside the coalition.
A party holding just six seats might determine whether a prospective government commands a majority. Its leader can demand substantial concessions to join the coalition, even if the party represents only a small fraction of the electorate.
Those concessions might involve religious education, military conscription, housing, economic policy, or the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. They can also involve Cabinet appointments.
In the United States, the president generally chooses Cabinet secretaries from among political allies, although presidents occasionally appoint members of the opposing party. In Israel, prospective coalition partners negotiate over which ministries their parties will control.
A small party might demand the Education Ministry or Finance Ministry as part of a coalition agreement. Another might insist on the Foreign Ministry, even if its foreign policy views differ considerably from the prime minister's.
A right-wing prime minister could therefore serve alongside a center-left foreign minister or a left-wing health minister. The coalition agreement sets out the broad compromises that let these parties govern together, though they may still disagree on key issues.
The prime minister whose party won seven seats
Israel provided a striking example of this system in 2021, when Netanyahu’s Likud won 30 seats, considerably more than any other party.
Yair Lapid’s centrist Yesh Atid party finished second with 17 seats. Yet neither Netanyahu nor Lapid became prime minister initially.
Instead, Naftali Bennett, whose right-wing Yamina party won just seven seats, took the job.
Bennett and Lapid reached an agreement that brought together eight parties spanning much of the Israeli political spectrum. Their coalition included right-wing parties, centrists, the left-wing Labor and Meretz parties, and Ra’am, an Islamist Arab party.
Few of these parties would ordinarily have chosen to govern together. Their common objective was to replace Netanyahu, who had dominated Israeli politics for years.
Under their agreement, Bennett became prime minister, while Lapid became foreign minister and alternate prime minister, with an arrangement for the two men eventually to exchange positions. Nitzan Horowitz, the leader of Meretz, became health minister.
Ra’am did not receive Cabinet posts, but it negotiated policy commitments and funding for Arab communities in exchange for participating in the coalition.
Despite leading the party that won the most votes, Netanyahu became leader of the opposition.
The outcome was entirely consistent with Israel’s electoral system. Bennett and Lapid had assembled enough parliamentary support to establish a government, something Netanyahu had been unable to do.
Their coalition lasted only about a year before collapsing under the weight of its internal disagreements. Netanyahu returned to power following another election in November 2022.
Bennett’s premiership remains a particularly instructive example for Americans: A politician whose party finished far behind the election's leading party became prime minister because he reached an agreement with other parties that together commanded enough parliamentary support.
When political rivals need each other
Personal relationships and political rivalries can matter as much in coalition negotiations as ideological differences.
Two parties might agree on nearly every major policy issue but refuse to govern together because their leaders distrust one another. Parties with substantially different views, meanwhile, might find common ground in their determination to remove an incumbent prime minister.
That helps explain the deadlock following this week’s election.
As of Wednesday afternoon, Netanyahu’s traditional right-wing and religious allies were projected to hold 53 seats, eight short of a majority. The four-party opposition bloc was projected to win 48, while two Arab-led lists were expected to win 19 combined.
On paper, the opposition and Arab parties would have enough seats to replace Netanyahu. In practice, some opposition leaders have firmly rejected governing with Arab parties or relying on their parliamentary support. The arithmetic allows for a government that the politicians involved may be unwilling to create.
American politicians are familiar with this problem, even if they encounter it in a different form. A president trying to pass legislation must often negotiate with members of the president’s own party whose views differ sharply. Congressional leaders spend considerable time keeping their party’s competing factions together, sometimes finding that a handful of members can frustrate the wishes of a much larger group.
Israeli coalition bargaining makes those tensions more visible because many of the competing factions have their own parties, leaders, and electoral mandates. Their negotiations over Cabinet positions, policy commitments, and the leadership of the government take place between separate political organizations.
Israel’s system gives voters a wider choice of parties and allows smaller religious, ideological, and minority groups to gain parliamentary representation. But those parties can exercise considerable leverage, and the compromises required to accommodate them may produce unstable governments.
America’s two-party system offers a different bargain. Its parties generally present voters with two broad alternatives, but the ideological divisions within them do not disappear after an election. Much of the political bargaining Israelis do between parties happens within the Republican and Democratic parties themselves.
Of course, there are limits to the comparison. America's president is elected independently of Congress through the Electoral College, while Israel's prime minister depends on parliamentary support. Even if American political factions broke away to form separate parties, they would not be choosing a president through congressional coalition negotiations.
Still, the comparison helps explain why the results of an Israeli election are often only the beginning of the struggle over who will govern.
Netanyahu's Likud appears to have finished first, but neither he nor his allies or opponents currently has a clear route to forming a government. The next stage will involve negotiations among parties that have spent months campaigning against one another, with decisions about the premiership, Cabinet appointments, and government policies all potentially on the table.
For Netanyahu, the question is whether he can attract enough partners to remain in power. For his opponents, the question is whether they can overcome their differences and agree on an alternative.
The 2021 election reminds us how surprising the outcome can be. Netanyahu's party won 30 seats, Bennett's won seven, and Bennett became prime minister. The party that finishes first on Election Day has an advantage, but the alliances formed afterward determine who governs Israel.

Without political renewal, Israel will remain stuck - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
04:11:50 UTC
13:11:50 KST

Three days removed from Israel’s pivotal election, many of the questions Israelis had going into the election remain unanswered.
The country is still caught in a political deadlock, with neither side able to secure a clear path forward. For many, the results look remarkably similar to those of Israel’s deadlocked elections in 2019 and 2020.
Unfortunately, so do many of the politicians.
Disappointing takeaways
After the October 7 massacre, years of upheaval, and an endless war that has reshaped Israeli society, one might have expected a greater appetite for political renewal. Instead, Israelis are once again left looking at familiar faces, familiar arguments, and a familiar stalemate.
Perhaps the most disappointing takeaway from this election is that, with the exception of Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party, new political forces have struggled to break into the conversation. Whether one agrees with their platforms or not, the failure of these parties to gain meaningful traction should concern anyone who wants to see Israel’s political system evolve.
The Haredi Public party, for example, offered haredi voters a genuine alternative to the established ultra-Orthodox parties. Yet, as of Thursday afternoon, it had received just 10,145 votes, leaving it far from parliamentary representation.
People of Israel leader Ofer Winter, who ran with an impressive list of fresh candidates, also fell short of the Knesset, attracting fewer than 100,000 votes before the double-envelope ballots were counted. His party’s performance was further undermined by Likud’s targeted campaign, although it appears he remained well short of the 3.25% electoral threshold regardless.
Yoaz Hendel’s attempt to appeal to reservists exhausted by years of service failed to cross the electoral threshold. His running mate, Yaron Zelekha, built his campaign around economic issues that other parties largely pushed aside. They, too, failed to translate their messages into parliamentary representation, according to the results counted so far.
These parties differed in their ideologies, constituencies, and priorities. Some offered a challenge to established political structures, while others sought to put neglected issues back on the agenda. Their failure does not necessarily mean their ideas lacked merit, or that their potential voters were wrong to seek alternatives.
It does, however, highlight how difficult it has become for new voices to establish themselves in Israeli politics.
There are some important caveats. Yashar is, after all, a new party, and its success in entering the political conversation demonstrates that renewal is still possible. The incoming Knesset will also include many new MKs within established parties. Political change does not always require the creation of an entirely new political movement.
Still, the broader picture is difficult to ignore. Former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who was absent from the previous Knesset, is back in the political arena. Yair Golan, another familiar figure from past Knessets, has returned to the forefront.
The other side
On the other side of the political spectrum, Moshe Feiglin may be presented as a fresh alternative, but he is hardly a newcomer, having already served in the Knesset a decade ago.
There is nothing inherently wrong with experienced politicians returning to public life. Experience matters, and voters are entitled to choose familiar leaders if they believe those leaders can deliver. Nor should novelty, by itself, be mistaken for competence.
New parties can disappoint, and new politicians can bring the same old habits into the Knesset. But the Israeli people, who have undergone such profound trauma since October 7, should be able to expect more from their political system than another contest between deeply entrenched camps.
Israel’s political deadlock will not be resolved by fresh faces alone. At the moment, divisions between the country’s political camps remain too deep, and any government that emerges from the current negotiations will have to find answers to the difficult issues that have divided Israelis for years.
But if one lesson can be learned from the election results, it is that without new voices and new ideas, the country risks remaining trapped in the same cycle of political instability that produced five elections between 2019 and 2022 and repeatedly prevented Israeli leaders from establishing a stable government.
After everything Israel has been through, that would be a missed opportunity at best, and a catastrophe at worst.
The country needs political renewal – not because every new party deserves a seat, but because a democracy that cannot make room for alternatives risks becoming stagnant.
Until Israel finds a way to break that pattern, the deadlock will remain – and the country will continue to struggle to find a way forward.
