How Saudi oil storage in Singapore could strengthen Asia’s energy security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
03:17:45 UTC
12:17:45 KST

How Saudi oil storage in Singapore could strengthen Asia’s energy security
Singapore plans to store Saudi crude oil in underground caverns on Jurong Island starting in the second half of 2027, as the city-state seeks to strengthen its energy security following disruptions to Middle Eastern oil supplies, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
Singapore's Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry and Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy announced the proposed arrangement on October 26. As an initial step, Singapore's Energy Market Authority and JTC Corporation exchanged a memorandum of understanding with Saudi Arabian oil giant Aramco during Singapore International Energy Week.
The crude would be stored at Jurong Rock Caverns, Southeast Asia's first commercial underground storage facility for liquid hydrocarbons. Located 150 meters below ground, the facility can hold approximately 9 million barrels of crude oil and condensates. The amount of storage capacity to be allocated to Aramco has not been disclosed.
According to the two ministries, the arrangement would allow Singapore to draw on stored crude during supply disruptions while providing Aramco with a storage base closer to its Southeast Asian customers. Singapore's Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry Tan See Leng said negotiations were expected to conclude within a few months.
Middle East conflict exposes Singapore's vulnerabilities
The agreement comes after months of turmoil in Middle Eastern energy markets, which highlighted the risks facing Asian economies dependent on imported oil.
In an April 7 statement to Parliament, Singapore's Coordinating Minister for National Security, K. Shanmugam said more than half of the country's crude oil imports came from the Middle East. He noted that Brent crude prices had risen by as much as 70% following the escalation of hostilities on February 28, while attacks damaged major oil facilities in Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and other countries.
Singapore managed to secure alternative crude supplies, but at considerably higher prices. Shanmugam warned that even the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz would not immediately restore normal export volumes because damaged energy infrastructure would take time to repair.
The government had already announced plans to increase its fuel reserves. "It will be costly but we think it necessary," Shanmugam told lawmakers. He also explained that Singapore does not publicly disclose the size of its reserves, arguing that doing so would reveal how long the country could withstand a supply disruption.
The proposed Saudi storage arrangement would address a related vulnerability by placing additional crude oil within Singapore itself. However, crude reserves are primarily relevant to the country's refining industry rather than its electricity supply, which relies on imported natural gas for approximately 95% of generation.
Singapore's role as a major oil trading and refining center has helped it maintain supplies despite the turmoil. Shanmugam described the city-state as the world's third-largest oil trading hub and sixth-largest refinery export hub. He argued that Singapore's ability to supply refined petroleum products to countries that provide it with crude had created commercial ties that helped preserve access to oil during the crisis.
The new arrangement would supplement those trading relationships with physical stocks of Saudi crude already held in Singapore.
Saudi Arabia expands its Asian oil storage network
For Saudi Arabia, the Singapore arrangement is part of a broader effort to position crude oil closer to major Asian markets.
Aramco already operates similar storage arrangements in Japan and South Korea. In Japan, the state-backed Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security leases 13 crude oil storage tanks in Okinawa to Aramco, providing capacity for approximately 8.2 million barrels. Under an agreement renewed for three years in November 2025, Japan receives preferential access to the stored oil during emergencies.
South Korea signed a comparable agreement in October 2023, allowing Aramco to store 5.3 million barrels of crude at facilities operated by the Korea National Oil Corporation in Ulsan. The arrangement gives South Korea priority purchasing rights during supply emergencies while allowing Aramco to use the facility to serve customers across Asia.
These agreements offer advantages to both sides. Aramco gains storage facilities near major buyers, reducing its reliance on shipments directly from the Gulf for every delivery. Host countries, meanwhile, can secure access to emergency supplies without necessarily purchasing and maintaining the entire inventory themselves.
Their geographical location has become particularly important following the 2026 Middle East conflict. Crude already stored in Japan, South Korea or Singapore lies beyond the Strait of Hormuz, through which much of the Gulf's oil exports normally pass.
If shipping through the strait is disrupted, inventories already in Asia can continue supplying local refiners without immediately requiring new shipments from the Gulf. For Saudi Arabia, overseas storage also provides greater flexibility in distributing crude among customers when export routes become unreliable.
Such facilities cannot eliminate the consequences of a prolonged supply disruption. Stored oil is finite, and replenishing inventories would remain difficult if Gulf shipping routes were blocked for an extended period. Nevertheless, having crude closer to customers can reduce the immediate impact of interruptions.
The Singapore agreement would extend this network into Southeast Asia, where the city-state already serves as a major center for refining, petroleum trading and regional fuel distribution.
Several important details remain unresolved. Unlike the agreements with Japan and South Korea, the proposed Singapore arrangement has not yet disclosed the volume of crude to be stored, its commercial terms or the precise conditions under which Singapore could access the oil in an emergency.
With operations expected to begin only in the second half of 2027, the agreement will do little to address current supply pressures. Its longer-term significance lies in a lesson reinforced by the 2026 crisis: access to international oil markets does not necessarily guarantee timely deliveries when major shipping routes are disrupted.

S Korea’s industrial output growth hits 15-year high, driven by semiconductor production
South Korea’s industrial production recorded its fastest monthly growth in more than 15 years in September, driven largely by a surge in semiconductor manufacturing. Retail sales and facility investment also increased, according to data released by the Ministry of Data and Statistics, Qazinform News Agency cites Yonhap.
Industrial output rose 3 percent month on month, marking the strongest increase since March 2011, when production grew by 3.4 percent. September also marked the first time since June that all three major economic indicators - industrial production, retail sales and facility investment - increased simultaneously.
Mining and manufacturing output surged 9 percent, largely supported by a 19.2 percent increase in semiconductor production. The growth in chip manufacturing was the highest since February, reflecting stronger production of memory chips, particularly dynamic random-access memory (DRAM).
Automobile production also recorded significant growth, jumping 39.9 percent as manufacturers increased output of auto parts and hybrid vehicles. The recovery followed the end of strikes at local carmakers and the summer holiday season. Meanwhile, production of medical, precision and optical instruments declined 8.8 percent.
Service-sector output increased 0.5 percent, supported by growth in wholesale and retail trade, as well as transportation and storage services.
Retail sales, an indicator of private consumption, rose 3.6 percent in September. Sales increased across all major categories, with durable goods recording the strongest growth at 4.4 percent, driven by higher demand for automobiles. Sales of nondurable and semidurable goods grew by 4.2 percent and 0.6 percent, respectively.
Facility investment also gained momentum, rising 5.3 percent month on month. Investment in machinery increased 4.7 percent, while investment in transportation equipment grew 7.4 percent.
Earlier, Qazinform reported South Korea’s births rose 13% in August to the highest level in seven years.

Hong Kong’s M+ museum, New York’s Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) and the Centre Pompidou in Paris signed an agreement on October 30 to establish a three-way cultural alliance, aiming to redefine how visual culture is collected, exhibited and shared globally.
The framework agreement, signed at M+ in the West Kowloon Cultural District, departs from conventional short-term blockbuster touring exhibitions and fee-based satellite franchises. With no money changing hands, the institutions will focus on collaborative curatorial research, conservation and extended loans spanning many years across their respective networks.
Under the partnership, MoMA is planning to open a dedicated gallery in New York in 2027 to promote the M+ collection, while M+ will begin to integrate MoMA and Centre Pompidou works into its exhibitions over the next 18 months. M+ also plans to showcase its LED facade commissions at the Pompidou’s new collection and exhibition facility in Massy, south of Paris.

Poverty plunges in India, but top 10% earn 13 times more than bottom 10%: World Bank

Amid heaps of trash, countless underprivileged children in India sort waste to earn a meager living, an invisible workforce fueling the country’s recycling economy.
NEW DELHI: India has lifted an estimated 496 million people out of poverty between 2011 and 2023, recording one of the world's fastest declines in poverty over the period. However, significant income inequality persists, with workers in the country's top 10% earning a median income nearly 13 times higher than those in the bottom 10%, according to the World Bank's October 2026 India Poverty and Equity Brief.The report highlights India's progress in reducing both extreme and multidimensional poverty but flags persistent challenges such as stagnant real wages, poor employment quality and unequal access to economic opportunities.Sharp decline in povertyThe share of India's population living below the lower-middle-income poverty line of $4.20 a day, measured at 2021 purchasing power parity (PPP), fell sharply from 57.7% in 2011 to 16.1% in 2023.Extreme poverty also witnessed a significant decline. The proportion of people living on less than $3 a day dropped from 27.1% to 2.6% during the same period.Rural poverty remains higherDespite the overall progress, poverty remains unevenly distributed across the country. Rural poverty stood at 19.3% in 2023, significantly higher than the 8.6% recorded in urban areas, based on the $4.20-a-day threshold.The report noted that households with lower educational attainment, fewer assets, limited access to stable employment and higher dependency ratios remain particularly vulnerable.
Geographically, states across a contiguous belt stretching from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal accounted for around 57% of India's poor population.The World Bank said further poverty reduction would increasingly depend on creating more productive employment opportunities in these regions, particularly through better-quality non-farm jobs.
More jobs, but wages remain stagnantIndia added around 134 million employed people between 2017 and 2023, nearly twice the increase in its working-age population. A significant share of this growth came from rural women entering paid employment, increasing the number of earning members in households.However, the rise in employment has not translated into comparable wage growth. The report noted that real earnings remained broadly unchanged, with much of the employment expansion concentrated in relatively low-productivity activities.It also flagged limitations in measuring inequality, noting that improvements in recent household surveys may account for part of the reported welfare gains, while wealthier households may not be fully represented, potentially leading to an underestimation of inequality.

Flash floods kill five in Syria
Four children drowned in bodies of water, while another man died in a car accident caused by the floods.
Heavy rains have been pouring over several Syrian provinces, leaving at least five people dead, including four children, in northern and eastern regions.
The four children all drowned in bodies of water across Raqqa and Deir Az Zor governorates, the Ministry of Emergency and Disaster Management said in a statement on Thursday.
A man also died when his car was caught in floodwaters near al-Salmani Bridge in the western Raqqa countryside.

Thursday marked the second day the ministry recorded responses to flooding across the country. It continues to issue situation updates on its X account.

State news agency SANA said al-Salmani Bridge, west of Tabqa, collapsed in the flooding, shutting the road linking Raqqa to Aleppo.
Emergency teams also reported rescuing 15 civilians whose vehicles were trapped by floodwaters. The ministry said it evacuated approximately 375 families from three camps on the rural outskirts of Raqqa.
This is not the first time the country has faced the threat of heavy rains and the flooding that follows.

At the time, the UN agency said 700 families had been displaced, including around 2,000 children, and that 49 water treatment plants in Deir Az Zor and Raqqa governorates had also gone out of service.

Bhutan glacial lake outburst triggers flash flood; North Bengal on high alert, thousands shifted to safety

A major Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) occurred on Thursday evening, October 29, 2026, at Shintaphu Lake (also known as Lemthang or Shintaphu Tsho) in the Gasa district of northwestern Bhutan.
NEW DELHI: Parts of West Bengal and Assam were placed on high alert after a glacial lake outburst in Bhutan triggered a flash flood, raising fears of a sudden rise in water levels along the Sankosh river. More than 10,000 people have been moved to relief shelters and safer locations in West Bengal, while authorities in Assam's Dhubri district have stepped up preparedness to deal with possible downstream effects.The outburst sent large volumes of water downstream through the Mo Chhu river towards the Sankosh river system, prompting authorities to activate disaster response mechanisms in vulnerable areas.The flood washed away infrastructure at the Gasa Tshachu natural hot springs in Bhutan's Gasa district. No injuries or loss of life have been reported, state broadcaster Bhutan Broadcasting Service (BBS) said on Friday.
The full extent of the damage from the late-night flood remained unclear. BBS said the assessment was hampered by “darkness and the strong flow” of floodwaters. Two Bailey bridges, constructed using portable, prefabricated sections, may also have been washed away.According to Bhutan's national newspaper Kuensel, parts of the road leading to Laya village, where the hot springs are located, were washed away, making the route impassable.
The road has been closed to traffic indefinitely. The area was evacuated before the floodwaters reached the hot springs.
West Bengal shifts thousands to safety
Authorities in West Bengal have alerted residents living along the Sankosh river and its tributaries following reports of the glacial lake outburst flood in Bhutan.Residents in the Darjeeling hills, Terai and Dooars regions have also been advised to remain alert and move to safer locations if they live in vulnerable areas.BJP MP from Darjeeling Raju Bista issued an alert through a post on X on Thursday, urging people living in the catchment areas of the Sankosh river and its connected tributaries to move to safer locations."A glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) has been reported at Lemthang in Bhutan. The overflowing water from the lake is flowing downwards through the Mofu River towards the Sunkosh River," the post read."Therefore, everyone living in the catchment areas of the Sunkosh River and all its connected tributaries have been informed to move to a safe distance immediately to protect their lives. Everyone in our Darjeeling hills, Terai and Dooars region are requested to stay alert," he added.State minister Nisith Pramanik said the government had received reports of the glacial lake outburst and that the overflowing water was moving towards the Sankosh river through the Mo Chhu river."Reports have just come in regarding a glacial lake outburst in Bhutan. Water from the lake is overflowing and flowing downstream into the Mo Chhu River, heading toward the Sankosh River. Residents living along the Sankosh River and its tributaries have been alerted; they are advised to move to a safe distance immediately to ensure their safety," Pramanik said.He said the water was expected to reach the plains within five to six hours, raising concerns about possible flooding."To manage the situation, the State Disaster Management Team has been activated, and the NDRF has also been notified. Disaster management volunteers have been instructed to be present on-site. The government is taking proactive measures and closely monitoring the situation to prevent any loss of life or property," he added.Alipurduar Superintendent of Police Amit Kumar Shaw appealed to residents not to panic, saying the administration was coordinating with Bhutanese authorities and disaster response agencies."First of all, I would like to tell the residents of the district that there is absolutely no need to panic. The situation is currently under control. We are in constant touch with the authorities in Bhutan. Our police team, the District Magistrate (DM) and the Block Development Officer (BDO) with their respective teams, along with all relevant agencies and stakeholders, are working together in close coordination," Shaw told ANI.He said the State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) had been deployed in the area, while a National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) team was also on its way. Civil Defence personnel had additionally been mobilised to assist with preparedness measures."We have already moved approximately 4,000 to 5,000 people into shelters, utilising school buildings as relief centres. Additionally, more than 6,000 people have been relocated to safe areas," he said.Shaw said the intensity of the water flow had decreased slightly, according to the latest information received, but the administration remained on high alert."The police, the DM's office, and the BDO's office have made arrangements for dry food and drinking water. We have also ensured that other necessities, such as toilet facilities, are provided. We will wait to see what the situation looks like in two hours. We are fully prepared and ready to handle any emergency that may arise," he said.He added that a red alert was in force for the Sankosh river system and warned that the approaching floodwaters could carry dead fish and debris, including large pieces of wood and concrete."We expect to see water flowing through the Sankosh River, likely accompanied by dead fish, as well as large pieces of wood and concrete debris," Shaw said.
Assam monitors possible impact in Dhubri
Meanwhile, the Assam government said it was closely monitoring the situation following the glacial lake outburst in Bhutan, with Dhubri district placed on alert over possible downstream effects.The Sankosh river flows through Dhubri district, and authorities have stepped up vigilance amid the possibility of a sudden rise in water levels."The situation arising out of the Glacial Lake Outburst Flood in Bhutan is being closely monitored by HCM Dr @himantabiswa," the Chief Minister's Office said in a social media post."Team @dcofficedhubri is on ground and prepared to effectively deal with the downstream effects," it added.
An Assam State Disaster Management Authority spokesperson said the water level of the Sankosh river was steady as of 6.30 am on Friday. The district administration and disaster response teams were on alert to tackle any eventuality.A special advisory issued by the ministry of Jal Shakti on Thursday for Assam and West Bengal said the Indian Embassy had reported a GLOF in Shintaphu Lake, located in Bhutan's Punatsangchhu river basin.Following reports of flash floods in the river's upper reaches, water levels in the Sankosh river could rise suddenly in Assam's Dhubri and West Bengal's Alipurduar districts, the advisory said.Local authorities in both districts were advised to remain alert, closely monitor the situation and take necessary precautionary measures.
What is a glacial lake outburst flood?
A glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF), also known as a jokulhlaup, occurs when the natural dam holding back a glacial lake fails or is breached, releasing large volumes of water downstream.
Such floods can cause sudden destruction of roads, bridges, settlements and other infrastructure, particularly in mountainous regions.Shintaphu Lake, located below Wakila Mountain in Lungo, Laya Gewog, in Bhutan's Gasa district, is among 17 glacial lakes in the country identified as potentially dangerous, according to local reports.Gasa Tshachu, a popular natural hot spring in northern Bhutan, was also hit by a flash flood in 2021 when the Mochhu river changed course and swept through the area.The latest incident has renewed concerns over glacial lake outburst floods in the Himalayan region. In August, a flash flood near Nepal's border with China killed more than 1,500 people and left over 5,000 missing, according to the supplied report.

Located within The Galleria on Abu Dhabi’s Al Maryah Island, Isabel Mayfair is a 580-sqm hospitality venue designed by Dubai-based practice DBM (Design by Mahsa), founded by artist and interior designer Mahsa Gholizadeh. Commissioned by BNF Hospitality, the interior establishes the London restaurant brand’s first international outpost. Above the central bar, a suspended brass-and-glass canopy redistributes light across the room, adjacent to an enclosed wine storage pavilion clad entirely in reflective brass panels. Realized on a compressed three-to-four-month construction schedule, the project by studio DBM balances large-scale fabricated metal installations with fine-gauge textile craft.

Venezuela: Opposition leader Machado says US backs 2027 election
October 30, 2026
Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado said on Thursday that the country was moving towards a US-prescribed presidential election in 2027, in her first public remarks since returning from 10 months in exile.
Calling the transition to democracy "irreversible," Machado said, "US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has laid out a sequence of steps for moving toward a democratic transition that includes presidential elections in 2027."
"The date of the election is the date of liberation," Machado said in Caracas after returning home following 10 months in exile.
Machado also reiterated that her priorities included dismantling the country's repressive system and securing the release of the thousands of political prisoners. She denied having had any contact with interim President Delcy Rodriguez.
Shortly before Machado's public statements, Rodriguez announced that there "will be elections" in Venezuela, without specifying a date.
Machado says Trump helped open 'floodgate to freedom'
Machado, who famously "presented" US President Donald Trump with her Nobel Peace Prize, thanked Trump for his actions on January 3, leading to "the floodgate to freedom" being opened in Venezuela.
The opposition leader was referring to the US capture of former President Nicolas Maduro, currently facing US drug trafficking and torture charges, which he denies.
Machado, however, criticized a major oil deal Washington and Caracas agreed to earlier this year, under which Venezuela is expected to supply 20% of its oil reserves to the United States.
"This agreement does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants," she said.
At the same time, she skirted questions that highlighted Trump's comments in January that she did not have sufficient support to immediately lead Venezuela, as well as his suggestion this week that the country could become the 51st US state.
US caught in a bind
Machado, who was barred from contesting the 2024 presidential election, backed opposition candidate Edmundo Gonzalez. His supporters said he had won by a wide margin, even though electoral authorities declared Maduro the winner.
Machado's recent return after nearly a year in exile complicates things for Washington which has said Machado has every right to be in Venezuela, but also praised acting President Rodriguez.

Taiwan hospital develops experimental treatment for lung fibrosis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
03:01:36 UTC
12:01:36 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taichung-based China Medical University Hospital said Thursday it developed a device that mimics breathing to train stem cells to produce vesicles for the potential treatment of pulmonary fibrosis.
The hospital said in a press release that it conducted experiments on rats to test the vesicles’ efficacy. The research findings were published in the journal Biomaterials.
Pulmonary fibrosis gradually scars and stiffens lung tissue. Symptoms include a dry cough and difficulty breathing, and advanced cases may require a lung transplant.
CMUH Superintendent Cho Der-yang (周德陽) said that although medications and rehabilitation therapies are available, they can only slow deterioration. He assembled a research team to investigate how to reverse the process.
Cho, chest surgeon Fang Hsin-yuan (方信元), Chen Chien-hsun (陳建勳), and clinical center deputy director Hsieh Ming-you (謝明佑) co-developed a 3D scaffold that subjects stem cells to movements resembling breathing. The cells respond by releasing vesicles enriched with miR-30.
Fang said miR-30, a type of microRNA carried by the vesicles, plays a role in tissue repair and inflammation.
According to the study, vesicles from rhythmically trained stem cells were 3.3 times more potent than those from conventionally cultured cells. The researchers examined how their contents could help repair damaged lung tissue.
Chen said the team administered the vesicles to rats through the nasal cavity and found reduced collagen buildup in their lungs. Cho said the team is conducting further tests in preparation for human clinical trials.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked seven Chinese naval vessels, one official ship, and six military aircraft between 6 a.m. on Thursday and the same time Friday.
Three of the aircraft crossed the median line of the Taiwan Strait and entered the country’s northern, eastern, and southwestern air defense identification zones. In response, Taiwan deployed aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems, according to the ministry.
So far this month, Taiwan has tracked Chinese aircraft 187 times and ships 345 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around the country.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

Who’s afraid of whom in Brussels?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

Night falls in the European capital. Everything’s quiet, but the nightmares are about to begin.
Viktor Orbán’s ghost haunts the Schuman roundabout; ash from the bonfire of red tape covers the Justus Lipsius building; Ursula von der Leyen’s chief of staff, Björn Seibert, chases after staffers demanding to know what “associate membership” for Canada actually means; and MEPs tremble at the prospect of construction workers uncovering the skeletons of political intrigues past during renovations.
Scared? You should be.
Advertisement
Here’s our guide to who is terrified of whom in the Brussels bubble.
Everyone is scared of Marine Le Pen
The person haunting EU diplomats, officials and lawmakers is French presidential front-runner Marine Le Pen. Will she really halve Paris’ contribution to the EU budget, as promised? Will she pull Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni away from the Brussels mainstream? And will she demand von der Leyen’s head?
The bubble had warmed (slightly) to the idea of Jordan Bardella in the Élysée Palace, after his years leading the National Rally’s European operation revealed a certain pragmatism toward Brussels — only for those hopes to be shattered when a Paris appeals court cleared Le Pen to be a candidate for the presidency.
The next ECB chief is scared of Jean-Luc Mélenchon
The European Central Bank president is the euro’s last line of defense against unorthodox national economic decisions — but that could be tested by French presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who is on course to reach the runoff after vowing to set billions of euros of French debt “on fire.” His incendiary plan calls on the Frankfurt-based ECB to waive interest payments on a vast tranche of French bonds — an unorthodox, perhaps impossible, maneuver that critics warn could even see France kicked out of the euro.
Now that we know Christine Lagarde will step down as ECB president in February, what France’s presidential candidates want to do about its monumental debt pile will haunt the race for her successor, with Dutchman Klaas Knot and Spaniard Pablo Hernández de Cos as the two frontrunners.
Lobbyists are scared of ChatGPT
The number of amendments lawmakers have filed has exploded since generative AI arrived, with key EU laws now facing thousands of proposed text changes. Parliament officials don’t think it’s a coincidence, with some pointing to amendments written in suspiciously bot-like language, and others saying sometimes amendments cite legislation that does not even exist.
Advertisement
The growing pile of amendments is haunting lobbyists, parliamentary assistants and officials forced to track and sort through it all — along with the fear that AI could eventually replace them. Spare a thought, too, for the MEPs who may have to vote through the amendments one by one, with hands raised in plenary.
Commission officials are scared of Austria’s Europe minister
Well-heeled Commission officials (and their families) are spooked by Austria’s Europe Minister Claudia Bauer, who has been leading a push to slash the Commission’s administration expenditure — which pays eurocrats’ salaries and offices — in the next seven-year budget. The campaign, backed by most EU capitals, resulted in an 8% cut to the admin budget in the latest budget proposal.
Bauer is so feared that EU officials joke they reduce their delegations’ size whenever they travel to Austria.
Jessika Roswall is scared of Stéphane Séjourné and Valdis Dombrovskis
Environment Commissioner Jessika Roswall and her department have reason to fear industry boss Stéphane Séjourné, who is taking the lead on the upcoming Circular Economy Act, despite Roswall’s official title of Commissioner “for a Competitive Circular Economy.” Making matters spookier, Roswall’s environment department now shares the Breydel building with Séjourné’s internal market and industry department, setting the stage for some chilling corridor encounters as Roswall pushes for greater environmental protection while Séjourné prioritizes industrial growth.
Roswall is also under pressure from EU simplification chief Valdis Dombrovskis to cut red tape on several environmental laws. The Latvian commissioner, who oversees the omnibus packages, wants a deal before year-end. Meanwhile, the center-right European People’s Party continues to press the Commission to reopen laws on birds, habitats, and water — the EU’s oldest nature protection laws — so they can be simplified too.
Alexander Stubb is afraid of Kaja Kallas and António Costa
Kaja Kallas has not publicly addressed the call that Finnish President Alexander Stubb made to Russia’s Vladimir Putin, but the EU’s top diplomat has made clear she dislikes such outreach. Still, if Putin offered serious talks and concessions, Kallas would be the obvious person to answer: as coordinating EU foreign and security policy is her job. “Of course I will talk if such an opportunity presents itself,” she told Estonian media in September when asked about speaking with Putin or his Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov.
Advertisement
Also reaching for the phone: António Costa. EU diplomats note that the European Council president represents the bloc at the leaders’ level abroad. That institutional turf war may explain why Stubb stressed that he and Norwegian Prime Minister Jens Støre spoke only for their own countries — not for Europe.
Manfred Weber is scared of his own group …
What keeps the leader of the European People’s Party — Europe’s largest political family — up at night? Divisions within his own ranks. So far, Weber has kept a tight ship and wants to reunite his troops ahead of the 2029 EU election, which he is casting as a battle against the far right. But that may prove tricky as the EPP’s national delegations increasingly clash over whether to work with the far right or isolate them.
… and the group is scared of Ouarda Bensouag
Central to Weber’s strategy is Ouarda Bensouag, the group’s secretary-general and his chief of staff. One of his most trusted lieutenants, she has a reputation as a smart but ruthless operator who EPP staffers fear when crossing paths in the Parliament’s labyrinthine hallways.
No one is scared of the Parliament … but they should be
Parliament’s attempts to spook capitals over the next long-term budget have been borderline tragic so far: It keeps threatening to kill the budget, but nobody seems to care or believe it will.
They should care. When it comes time to pass the budget, 361 of 720 votes will be needed, and the margin could be razor-thin in a fragmented chamber that’s hostile to plans to pool farm and regional funds. The louder MEPs protest — and the longer the Council ignores them — the more determined they become to prove the threat is real.
By Max Griera, Gregorio Sorgi, Kathryn Carlson, Nick Vinocur, Jakob Weizman, Fiona McNally and Eliza Gkritsi

====================================================================================================

Burnham tries to avoid a slavery reparations ‘disaster’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
03:00:00 UTC
12:00:00 KST

Prime Minister Andy Burnham will have an unofficial goal when he meets members of Britain’s former empire next week: Avoid a fight about slavery reparations.
Good luck, as they say, with that.
His predecessor Keir Starmer’s trip to the last Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, at a beach resort on the Pacific island of Samoa in 2024, is still the stuff of rueful mutters in parts of Whitehall.
Advertisement
Lined up in a semi-circle of armchairs — “like an Alcoholics Anonymous meeting,” as one person briefed on the gathering put it — leaders from many of the 56 Commonwealth nations negotiated live over a 16-page communique on laptops and tablets. Starmer, a barrister, found himself personally redrafting a key paragraph about reparations on a screen surrounded by other leaders, said two further people briefed on the meeting.
The unusually intimate format of the leaders’ retreat meant they had no officials with them on the veranda, and Starmer had just one civil servant — No. 10’s private secretary for foreign affairs — stationed in a tent close by. His chief of staff Morgan McSweeney was woken at 4 a.m. London time by a phone call to talk about the strategy for reparations.
That, however, was never clearly resolved. The retreat dragged on hours late; some leaders left before it was even over. Starmer was frustrated and felt he had been “ambushed,” said one U.K. official involved in the 2024 trip. A second said they had blocked the incident from their memory. A third said Starmer was left “furious,” adding: “He went in blind and it was terrible for him.” A fourth said simply: “It was a disaster.” All were granted anonymity to speak frankly.
The eventual communique agreed on a “conversation towards forging a common future based on equity.” This fudge kicked the issue of reparations down the road — where it now lands in Burnham’s lap.
Britain’s new prime minister will touch down at the biennial summit in Antigua and Barbuda next week to find the issue still firmly on some Caribbean and African leaders’ minds.
At the United Nations in May, 123 countries passed a motion calling for “inclusive, good-faith dialogue on reparatory justice.” The U.K. abstained. Barbados PM Mia Mottley announced a manifesto from Caribbean leaders on the “moral, ethical and legal case” for reparations in June. Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Botchwey said last week that an apology for Britain’s role in the slave trade “wouldn’t hurt.”
Advertisement
The visit will be a test of how Burnham — who has a reputation for speaking off the cuff, especially on issues of moral justice — maintains a delicate U.K. government line that reparations are not “the answer,” as Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told POLITICO last month. And Burnham will face that challenge in a unique spotlight: It will be his first overseas visit with King Charles III, who is the head of the Commonwealth.
POLITICO spoke to a dozen U.K. officials or politicians who were involved in the 2024 summit or the planning for Burnham’s upcoming visit. They painted a picture of acute anxiety in the British state over how to deal with calls for reparations from its former colonies; tensions between Downing Street and the Foreign Office over the handling of 2024; and serious questions in Whitehall about whether the summit is even useful for No. 10 — despite the king’s role leaving U.K. prime ministers little choice but to attend.
Burnham will not have to deal with the extreme jetlag and communications hurdles that dogged Starmer’s trip, which involved a 28-hour flight in each direction. But like Starmer, he will fly out at a time when his in-tray is crowded by other issues — not least the U.S. midterms happening at the same time and the domestic aftermath of his first budget, just unveiled this past Wednesday.
Keir Starmer attends a a state banquet during the CHOGM summit in Samoa, on Oct. 24, 2024. | Pool photo by Fiona Goodall via Getty Images
The first U.K. official quoted earlier in this story said: “There’s a sense that there can’t be a repeat of [2024] this time around.” The third U.K. official quoted above said: “I don’t understand why they’re making the same mistake. Does the prime minister really have to go?”
A No. 10 official, however, said Burnham made clear soon after taking power on July 20 that he was “very keen” to attend the summit. Miliband has “laid the groundwork so that things hopefully won’t be as tricky as they were in 2024,” this person added.
“Andy’s style is that he is an honest broker with people, and he will give an instinctive response to things,” the official said. “But the government’s position is clear that reparations are not seen as the right route. It’s a careful balancing act, but one that we’re well prepared for.”
Advertisement
Climate resilience fund in the works
One tactic for the current No. 10 will be to try to avoid talking about it public.
Downing Street has broken with recent precedent by deciding not to bring the usual “pack” of political journalists, taking a smaller media “pool” instead. This will limit the scope of questions that Burnham faces. (Political editors from news outlets, including POLITICO, have written to No. 10 to object to the arrangement.)
Timing could also allow the visit to slip under the radar. Burnham and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband will be there alongside counterparts including Anthony Albanese of Australia and Mark Carney of Canada, creating a rare opportunity for them to discuss the implications of the U.S. midterm results in private. The symbolism, as “middle power” nations deal with a drift in U.S. relations under Donald Trump, would be obvious.
British PM Andy Burnham, center, leaves the stage at the end of the Labour Conference in Liverpool on Sept. 30, 2026. | Ian Forsyth/Getty Images
Officially, the agenda is to build an alliance that can boost these middle powers, along with the developing states that global summits usually overlook.
The Commonwealth Secretariat — the London-based body that co-ordinates the summit — said the aim of next week’s gathering is “partnerships and investment,” including in climate and youth employment, and removing trade barriers.
Likewise, the U.K. Foreign Office has been working on a climate resilience fund for developing nations, two people with knowledge of the talks said. A third said conversations in the U.K. government had focused on mobilizing public and private finance, and improving access to finance for climate-vulnerable countries.
Advertisement
Three people with knowledge of the planning emphasized that this summit would be an opportunity to build on relations with countries that could discuss bilateral trade, though they did not name specific nations and no U.K. trade ministers are due at the event.
“There will obviously be trade and investment discussions with a range of partners,” said one of the three people, a U.K. government official, who also noted that the U.K. will raise the impacts of El Niño. “The bigger picture is that we want to use the Commonwealth network to deepen trade and investment links across its 56 members — that Commonwealth advantage is one of the reasons the grouping matters to the UK.”
‘Playing Scrabble with words’
But leaders at these events, known by the awkward acronym CHOGM, can raise whatever topics they wish — reparations included.
Denis O’Brien, the Irish telecoms billionaire who founded the Repair Campaign calling for financial reparations to the Caribbean in 2022, said: “The conversation has moved radically forward.” He urged Britain and other European nations to “start off with an apology and then have an engagement,” adding: “The Foreign Office and the prime minister’s office are playing Scrabble with words — and unfortunately they’re leaving King Charles, who is so highly respected in the Caribbean, in a very difficult position.”
Paul Boateng, the Labour peer who was Britain’s first Black Cabinet minister and now campaigns on the issue, said Caribbean nations “are going to be pressing it. This issue is not going to go away.” The recent UN resolution reinforced Caribbean and African nations’ argument, argued Boateng: “We can’t be seen to simply ignore it … We cannot hold the Foreign Office line that it changes nothing.”
That position cast a long shadow two years ago.
Advertisement
No. 10 flew to Samoa in 2024 insisting reparations were “not on the agenda,” even though the summit’s free-wheeling format meant the choice was effectively out of Downing Street’s hands.
This message “went down like a bag of sick” with Caribbean nations who saw it as “colonial” and “arrogant,” recalled one person involved in conversations at the time.
The handling created tension between Downing Street and the Foreign Office, then led by David Lammy, who also attended, according to six other people with knowledge of the 2024 trip.
King Charles and Queen Camilla attend the bestowing and farewell ceremony on Oct. 26, 2024. | Pool photo by Manaui Faulalo via Getty Images
One of the six people said No. 10 figures had expected the Foreign Office to better manage expectations among Commonwealth nations ahead of Starmer’s arrival. The person said: “No. 10 did not feel like they were well enough informed, and felt some of this could and should have been handled in advance. There was the feeling that both Lammy and the Foreign Office were institutionally pre-disposed to this sort of stuff and not shutting it down. The PM didn’t know what he was going into.”
A second person said: “The FCDO world does forget, sometimes, the politics of what’s going on in the U.K. It’s very institutionalized.”
A third person stressed that senior aides in No. 10 had blamed Foreign Office officials, not Lammy personally. Before Starmer left office this year, No. 10 had been drawing up plans for Starmer to skip this year’s CHOGM — and send Lammy as his representative. By then Lammy had been moved from the foreign office and was Starmer’s deputy prime minister.
Advertisement
Another of the six people countered that it was No. 10 that persisted, ahead of the 2024 summit, with a line that was too binary — reparatory justice, as campaigners prefer to call it, has a wide definition that includes support for climate adaptation and education — and failed to listen to Foreign Office warnings ahead of time about the strength of feeling among Commonwealth nations.
“The audit trail would completely exonerate David and the Foreign Office,” this person said. They argued No. 10 officials — who were keen to hold on to the mantle of fiscal responsibility ahead of Starmer’s first budget — had viewed the row too much through how it would be perceived by the right-wing Daily Mail newspaper.
Two other people with knowledge of the 2024 trip insisted they did not remember any significant friction between No. 10 and the Foreign Office. Lammy’s office did not immediately respond to an invitation to comment.
UK review mooted a scaled-back summit
More significantly, the 2024 summit also led to discussions in Whitehall about the set-up of CHOGM itself.
Lammy commissioned an internal review by Foreign Office officials on the Commonwealth in the wake of the 2024 summit, his former Special Adviser Ben Judah told POLITICO.
Judah said the review suggested reducing the frequency of CHOGMs to “every four or five years,” potentially aligned with the hosting of the Commonwealth Games, and seeking to remove the final communique and leaders’ retreat.
Advertisement
It suggested an investment conference in alternate years modeled on the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, which could keep the Commonwealth branding but with no organizational role for the Secretariat, said Judah.
Judah suggested this would improve attendance at CHOGM, which is often patchy; India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi does not plan to attend next week’s summit, for example, though there will be a delegation led by External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar. “The Indians think this thing is ridiculous and self-harming and just totally bizarre,” said Judah. “They’d be interested in a real investment conference, not this farce.”
A second former U.K. government official said they knew about the report, which has not been made public, adding that No. 10 figures under Starmer discussed similar concerns about the format of the Commonwealth summit after the Samoa visit.
Starmer sits with other leaders during the opening ceremony of CHOGM 2024 in Apia, Samoa. | Fiona Goodall/Getty Images
The Foreign Office declined to respond to questions about the report when contacted by POLITICO, including when it was finalized or whether any of its recommendations were pursued. One Foreign Office official, however, stressed that it was not the U.K. government’s position and that any decisions about future CHOGM arrangements would be for Commonwealth members collectively.
The U.K. government official quoted on trade and investment earlier in this piece said: “The Commonwealth is more important to our geostrategic position now than at any time throughout its 80-year history. In today’s more divided, unpredictable world, the Commonwealth has the potential to be a powerful, values-based force for good in the world.
“This gives us a huge opportunity to drive U.K. interests and priorities — Commonwealth relationships have helped to drive global support for Ukraine, and it is hugely important for our work on climate.”
Advertisement
Funding pulled from reserves
Judah, however, argued that the Commonwealth Secretariat is a “broken institution” and Britain should wind down its involvement to focus on an investment summit instead.
CHOGM has ended up as a “platform for the reparations campaign,” argued Judah: “There’s nothing else on the agenda because it’s not a real international organization, and it’s not a real summit with deliverables.” The Commonwealth and Secretariat, he said, has “essentially been taken over by the only countries that are still really invested in them, which are the Caribbean countries supported by a few African countries, to push the reparations agenda.”
For some, that extends to questions about the way the Secretariat spends its money.
Two people with knowledge of the situation said part of this year’s CHOGM summit is being paid for out of the Secretariat’s reserves. “There is a real sense of concern about the malaise and drift of the organization,” argued one of the two people. “Financially it’s in a dire, dire state.”
A Commonwealth spokesperson responded: “The Commonwealth Secretariat accesses reserve funds for the biennial Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting and always with member country approval.”
Back in 2024, Starmer’s most senior aides privately raised the question about whether he should attend the Samoa summit at all. “We were overruled,” said another person who worked under him.
Advertisement
Whitehall officials initially assumed that Burnham would not go either, until he said otherwise. “To a lot of the Caribbean countries, the word [from officials] was that he wasn’t going to show,” said O’Brien. “I think people were taken aback by that.”
But despite Starmer’s experience in 2024, Burnham will attend.
Among all other reasons, there is one very obvious one. “It’s very difficult for a prime minister not to go because the king goes,” said one person who worked under Starmer. “It’s important to him.”
Burnham’s ‘surer touch’
Once Burnham is in the room, campaigners hope he will at least be a listening ear.
Outside the prime minister’s Manchester office No. 10 North is a statue of Abraham Lincoln, commemorating the mill workers who refused to touch raw cotton picked by slaves.
Burnham referred to it in his first speech to the United Nations last month. “In 1862, people with little power used it to help those with none on the other side of the world,” he said. “The best change is change like that, bottom-up change led by people.”
Advertisement
The new prime minister “understands the importance of Manchester as the second great city of empire, and he has a surer touch than his predecessors,” argued Boateng. “We’ve got an opportunity to reset the relationship.”
What reparatory justice would look like is another matter.
Previous estimates have suggested Britain should owe as much as £18 trillion, but the conversation is far more nuanced than talking about a single big number.
Burnham departs Downing Street for prime minister’s questions on Oct. 21, 2026. | Leon Neal/Getty Images
While Boateng argues that no measures should be taken off the table, he would begin with reforming the International Monetary Fund and World Bank to give more Commonwealth countries a meaningful seat at the table, and returning historic artefacts such as the Benin bronzes that are displayed in London’s British Museum. “The British Museum holds loot, literally loot. These are stolen goods,” he said.
Britain is working on debt relief too. Chancellor John Healey plans to make international finance for developing countries a key theme when Britain hosts G20 finance ministers next year.
NGOs have urged Healey to make debt relief more generous by changing the G20’s common framework and UK domestic law, which sets the terms for 90% of debt that low-income countries owe to private lenders.
Advertisement
Maria Finnerty of Bond, the membership body for NGOs, said Britain “continues to play a role in enabling illicit financial flows through loopholes linked to the City of London and its overseas territories, amounting to the loss of billions from some Commonwealth countries.”
Miliband reflected all this in his POLITICO interview last month at the Labour Party Conference. While condemning the slave trade as “terrible,” he said his focus was on addressing current issues in countries “on the front line of the climate crisis, of the debt burden, of trying to reduce poverty in those countries.”
O’Brien is calling for monetary payments, however. Through the Repair Campaign, he wants to see the EU and U.K. make money available to the 15 Caribbean Community (CARICOM) countries — with a special case for Haiti — “each year for the next 75 years” for issues such as education, green energy and storm defenses to deal with climate change.
O’Brien would not be drawn on a single figure, but suggested payments should supplement the national budget of each affected country by around 10% a year.
Asked if he had had conversations with the Foreign Office, O’Brien replied: “What do you think?
“I mean, we would like to. We’re approaching this in a very friendly way, taking a very, very sensitive period of history and trying to get results. We have the highest respect for the British government, and particularly the King. But it can’t go on forever.”

Ayman Odeh is a member of the Knesset and chairman of the Hadash-Ta'al party
King of the algorithm: How Netanyahu enjoys the role of the undisputed ruler of Israel's social media feeds
To run into Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Facebook, Instagram or TikTok, you don't need to follow him. You don't need to like his posts, either. In fact, you don't even need to be interested in politics. All it takes is opening the app and scrolling. Netanyahu is the undisputed ruler of the feed – any feed. That's one of the most striking findings of a wide-ranging Haaretz investigation in which we created fictional personas representing six different Israelis and tracked their feeds for four months. Each persona saw a different reality, but the same man starred in all of them.
Nothing will change until Israelis realize: One side's victory doesn't mean the other's destruction
One of the deepest mechanisms of polarization is when a dispute shifts from what is actually correct to the question of what is truly motivating the person across from me. Factional identity becomes key when interpreting what the other person says. We attribute to them deliberate manipulation or assume that they have lost the ability to see reality for what it is. In this way, the "opponent" becomes a character in a book that we have already written about them. Differences in opinions inform the relations between people: That is, my reading of them carries greater weight than their own self-explanation.
The danger was never Netanyahu. It won't disappear even when he's gone
We are at a historic crossroads. An enormous wave of optimism swept millions to the polls, giving our politicians an unprecedented opportunity to change course just before we go over the cliff. Because one thing should be clear by now, after our 20,000th election in the past decade: In Israel, the person who forms a government is the one who can assemble a coalition of 61 Knesset seats. As things stand, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu doesn't have such a coalition. This moment offers a chance to settle it. We must not squander that chance. And the struggle must begin with a Jewish-Arab coalition.
Nearly 50,000 Israelis joined campaign calling for a government with Arab Parties
Nearly 50,000 Israelis joined a campaign calling for a government supported by Arab parties, amid growing efforts by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party to challenge the legitimacy of the Arab vote. Nearly half signed up after the election results were even announced, according to Zazim, the civic movement behind the initiative.
Arab citizens make up roughly 20% of Israel's population, but Arab parties have generally been excluded from governing coalitions. Their support could prove decisive in determining whether the parties seeking to replace Netanyahu can form a government.

"Likud itself previously held coalition negotiations with the United Arab List, an Arab party. Polls show that most opposition supporters favor cooperation with Arab parties, while most Arab voters want their representatives to participate in government."
"Arab citizens' votes carry the same weight as those of every other Israeli citizen. Arab parties must be treated as legitimate political partners. This election has shown that the future of Israeli democracy will be decided by the question of Jewish-Arab political partnership."

China expels a record number from Communist party amid Xi’s intensified purges of top officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:56:46 UTC
11:56:46 KST

China expelled a record number of officials from the Chinese Communist party (CCP) as it concluded a major political gathering, which saw an unprecedented number of empty seats indicating the scale of the purges under Xi Jinping.
A record 33 members were expelled at this week’s fifth plenum, a gathering of top officials that takes place roughly once a year.
Just 279 of the full and alternate members of the CCP’s Central Committee attended this week’s gathering, compared with the 376 originally named as members in 2022. That means that more than 25% of the original cohort were absent, many due to purges. It is the highest number of “empty chairs” at the plenum in modern Chinese history.
The confirmed expulsions included Zhang Youxia, the former second-in-command to China’s leader in the military hierarchy, and Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang. Other absences were unexplained.
“More empty seats underscores the plenum’s focus on Xi’s vision of strict internal discipline,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, in a post on X.
The theme for this week’s plenum was party governance. Since coming to power in 2012 Xi has focused on stamping out corruption in the party. But in recent years the campaign has intensified, taking out officials in the highest ranks of the party and the military, raising questions about if the campaign is also a tool to remove political rivals or punish disloyalty.
Xi appears to have grown increasingly frustrated with what he sees as a lack of discipline in the ranks of the party that wields absolute authority over the state and society in China. Earlier this year he said that the party must uproot “sick trees” and that the fight against corruption was a “never-ending journey”.
A series of purges has gutted the seven-man Central Military Commission, the ruling body of China’s People’s Liberation Army. There are now just two members left: Xi himself, and the military’s anti-graft tsar, Zhang Shengmin.
Zhang was promoted to the politburo of the CCP this week, the highest ruling body in the party. Zhang is now the only military member of the senior leadership body.
The plenum also laid the groundwork for the 21st Party congress, an event which happens every five years and is expected to next be held in the second half of 2027. Xi is expected to secure a fourth term as leader of the party, making him the longest ruler of Communist China since Mao Zedong.
The ranks of the Central Committee and the politburo will be refreshed at next year’s congress, but many analysts believe that recent purges have been so wide-ranging that there are few suitable candidates to be promoted.

Ex-Pentagon strategist accused of Iran and Ukraine leaks – Axios
The Pentagon’s former top military planner allegedly leaked classified information about Iran and Ukraine to journalists, Axios reported on Thursday, citing an internal investigation.
US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth fired Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia as head of strategy, plans, and policy on the Joint Staff earlier this week.
Without mentioning Sylvia by name, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said on Thursday that the department has “zero tolerance for the intentional, unauthorized disclosure of classified information.” He added that the Pentagon “took necessary personnel action to protect sensitive information.”
According to Axios, Sylvia admitted to leaking information as early as June 2025, before most media outlets were barred from the Pentagon. He allegedly continued communicating with reporters through the encrypted messaging app Signal and once met a journalist at a diner to discuss military aid to Ukraine without authorization.
“He had trouble passing multiple polygraph interviews,” the report said, according to Axios.
Officials reportedly suspect that the general deliberately deleted records of his communications with a reporter, though he claimed the deletion was accidental. Sylvia also allegedly admitted to being a source for another story criticizing Pentagon leadership.
Sylvia’s departure comes amid reports that the US and Israel are preparing to resume strikes on Iran following next week’s US midterm elections. US President Donald Trump has indicated that he may take military action if Tehran refuses to accept his terms for a peace deal.
Since returning to the White House in early 2025, Trump has sought to crack down on government leaks, accusing news outlets of conducting a smear campaign against him.
In July, Hegseth said the Pentagon and Justice Department established a joint task force to “identify and prosecute leakers.”
In April 2025, Hegseth fired three senior Pentagon aides – Dan Caldwell, Darin Selnick, and Colin Carroll – amid an investigation into alleged leaks of sensitive information to the media. All three denied wrongdoing, and none was subsequently charged with a crime. Caldwell later returned to the Trump administration in a position at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.

Kim Jong Un urges drone dominance as North Korea fires missiles, rockets
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
03:44:05 CET
11:44:05 KST

By Joyce Lee and Heejin Kim
SEOUL, Oct 30 (Reuters) - North Korean leader Kim Jong Un called for his country to seize “absolute superiority” in drone technology as he attended an exhibition and demonstration of unmanned aeronautical technology, state media KCNA reported on Friday.
The firepower demonstration featured tactical suicide attack drones, tactical cruise missiles, multipurpose drones and 600mm multiple rocket launchers, KCNA said.
The display highlighted Kim’s push to modernise North Korea’s armed forces by using drones and artificial intelligence as Pyongyang draws lessons from Russia’s war against Ukraine and other global conflicts.
It came amid heightened tensions between the two Koreas, with Seoul vowing to respond firmly to what it called North Korean breaches, and Pyongyang denouncing joint South Korea-US air defence drills.
KCNA photographs showed unmanned aerial vehicles bearing the North Korean Air Force’s emblem at the exhibition, attended by Kim.
Other images showed what appeared to be an unmanned aerial vehicle crashing into a military vehicle and exploding in a ball of flame during a weapons demonstration.
South Korea’s military said on Thursday that North Korea had fired around 10 projectiles, including short-range ballistic missiles.
Kim said that pursuing superiority in drone technology was “an indispensable option” given the changing nature of modern warfare, according to KCNA.
He also said using high-level AI in unmanned weapons systems should be a top priority for North Korea, KCNA reported.
Kim has repeatedly called for the development of drones and military AI. State media said Kim ordered mass production of suicide attack drones in November 2024, oversaw tests of AI-equipped versions in March 2025 and in September 2025 called AI a top priority in weapons modernisation.
DRAWING LESSONS FROM UKRAINE WAR
Since October 2024, North Korea has sent more than 16,000 personnel to Russia to aid Moscow in its war against Ukraine, and gained battlefield experience in drone, electronic and combined-arms warfare, according to South Korean intelligence.
North Korea is transforming its military with drones and AI, drawing lessons from the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea’s Kyungnam University.
By showing a comprehensive display of weapons, North Korea is trying to “shut off the possibility of dialogue or negotiations” with South Korea, Lim said.
North Korean state media also displayed for the first time what analysts described as a tailless, flying-wing stealth drone.
Photographs showed racks of small suicide drones and loitering munitions similar to the US Switchblade 600, suggesting an emphasis on cheap, mass-produced weapons, potentially drawing on lessons from the Ukraine war, analysts said.
Mock targets resembling South Korean K9 howitzers, M1 Abrams-type tanks and radar vehicles suggested the weapons were intended for use against South Korean and US forces, they said.
BORDER TENSIONS
South Korea will respond firmly to protect the military border despite Pyongyang’s assertion that it is conducting operations within its territory, Seoul’s national security adviser Wi Sung-lac said on Friday.
Separately, North Korea’s Defence Ministry said US and South Korean air defence drills were raising tensions on the peninsula and that there was “no limit” to its option for maintaining a strong deterrent posture, KCNA reported.
Tensions have escalated since a landmine blast inside the Demilitarised Zone seriously wounded several South Korean soldiers last month. Seoul said the blast was caused by a North Korean mine, which Pyongyang has denied.
Kim’s powerful sister, Kim Yo Jong, said earlier this month that North Korea would activate anti-South Korean propaganda loudspeakers along its entire border by the end of October.
(Reporting by Joyce Lee, Heejin Kim and Jack Kim; Editing by Nia Williams, Jamie Freed and Ed Davies)

====================================================================================================

John Turturro Gives a Career-Best Performance in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:44:04 UTC
11:44:04 KST

To paraphrase the old-school comedian Rodney Dangerfield, a pickpocket in 2020s New York gets no respect. Almost no one carries much cash anymore, and credit cards are useless unless you’re willing to commit fraud. What’s a poor guy with crackerjack observational skills and exceedingly dexterous fingers supposed to do when he can’t even pay for his diner breakfast with his morning’s earnings?
That’s where John Turturro’s Harry Lehman finds himself in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York, writer-director Noah Segan’s charming, nimble, and affecting drama about a guy who has seen his city, and his world, change drastically during his lifetime. For Harry, a typical workday involves boarding the subway and identifying the easy targets. In his soft, elegant tweed coat—a garment he might have bought 20 or 30 years ago, maybe at Barneys, when the dough was really flowing—he swirls through New York, his vision attuned to checked-out, earbud-wearing Wall Street dudes, or women who allow their purses to dangle precariously. He sees what others miss, though he’s living in a world where no one pays any attention to their environment. It’s a lonely life.
But there’s a bright spot in Harry’s world: Though his wife, Rosie (Karina Arroyave), has been stricken with an unnamed ailment and can neither move nor speak, his days revolve around her. He cares for her tenderly, as best he can, talking to her, laughing with her. At one point he puts Odyssey’s 1977 sequins-and-stardust disco hit “Native New Yorker” on the stereo and dances for both of them, in a kind of disco-salsa shuffle, his arms whirling as if the breeze itself were his dance partner.
Rosie’s care costs money, which means Harry needs to hustle harder than ever. Watches can still bring in the bucks, as long as they’re not fake. And to unload those, Harry has a close pal and longtime co-conspirator, the wily, wisecracking pawnshop owner Ben (Steve Buscemi). Ben will also take stolen phones, though they’re troublesome: they need to go to a guy in Chinatown, Kelvin Han Yee’s Frank, who knows how to scrub them, after which they’re packed into a container and shipped off to god knows where. When Harry boosts a USB crypto wallet from a brazen young criminal and spoiled rich kid, Dylan (Will Price), Ben has no idea what to do with it—plugging it into his circa-1995 desktop personal computer sends the machine into a tailspin. So he sends Harry downtown to see Frank—whose front is a herb shop, though it seems less like a front than a side hustle—and that’s where Harry’s troubles really begin.
The Only Living Pickpocket is part drama, part comedy, part thriller. It’s also a movie about a man reckoning with his past: We may warm to the sight of Harry caring so lovingly for Rosie, but there’s much more to his story, as we learn. And you can’t always tell where the movie is headed; its beats are wriggly, unpredictable. Until recently, writer-director Segan has worked mostly as an actor, often with director Rian Johnson (he appeared in Brick, Looper, and the Knives Out movies), and he has directed one previous feature, the 2022 horror movie Blood Relatives. The pickpocketty lightness of touch he shows is remarkable for a fledgling director.
It doesn’t hurt that he’s got Turturro as a star. In the early part of his career, as a favorite of Spike Lee and the Coen Brothers, Turturro, with his tightly coiled, jack-in-the-box energy, always looked like he might blow at any moment. But he’s become much subtler, and sexier, over the years. in the underappreciated 2013 comedy Fading Gigolo, which he also wrote and directed, he played a foxy florist who becomes a classy male escort, servicing sultry hotties (Sharon Stone, Sofia Vergara) before falling for a lonely Hasidic widow (Vanessa Paradis). Suddenly, he was a leading man, and a hot one.
Turturro still has some of his old combustibility; you occasionally catch an air of menace behind that snaggle-tooth smile. But he now has more softness, more range, and the performance he gives in The Only Living Pickpocket in New York is one of his finest, as well as one of the best of the year. In the first section of the film, you believe Harry is just a guy whose glory days have passed: He belongs to a dream New York, that of the 1970s and ‘80s, of strobe-lit dance clubs and independent cinemas seemingly on every block. (Cinematographer Sam Levy, who also shot Frances Ha and Lady Bird, is in tune with the old New York nestled within the current one; he captures the city, from the Bronx to Chinatown, in all its shabby-shiny glory.) At one point, Harry suggests to Rosie that the two hunker down for the evening and watch an old movie, maybe something with Barbara Stanwyck; he comes from a generation that was used to looking toward its past as well as its future.
The city wasn’t a safe place in Harry’s younger days—but we’re talking about something other than physical safety, a kind of creative vitality that, if you were attuned to it, could rub off on you like glitter. Harry still has some of that sparkle, but it’s tempered by melancholy, the aftermath of little mistakes and big ones he’s made along the way. Turturro captures all of it—and shows how Harry intends to do right by those he’s harmed—with the kind of lived-in ease you earn, if you’re lucky, over the course of a career. Whirling through the city in that tweed coat, he’s like Fred Astaire breezing through an obviously fake white-cardboard Venice or descending a staircase from nowhere. The grit of the city is his glamour, its noise his music. It’s all his for a song, or a watch deftly separated from its owner’s wrist. His city is a tough place and, as Odyssey sang, he should know the score by now. But at least he knows the dance steps, because as much as New York may change, those never do.

Vessel reported on fire in Strait of Hormuz: UK maritime agency

2026-10-30

Ilayda Cakirtekin
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) center said late Thursday that a vessel was on fire in the Strait of Hormuz.
"UKMTO has received a report of an incident 25NM Northeast of Khasab, Oman in the Strait of Hormuz. A third party has reported that a vessel transiting outbound is on fire, the cause is unknown at time of report," the agency said in a statement.
It later reaffirmed having received a verified report confirming that the crew were safe and there was no environmental impact.
"The report indicates that the tanker was approached on the port side by a small boat which attached two explosive devices to the hull above the waterline. The subsequent blasts resulted in a fire in the engine room which temporarily disabled the vessel," it noted.
UKMTO said the fire had been extinguished and the vessel continued to its next port of call. It further advised vessels to transit with caution and report any suspicious activity as authorities investigated the incident.
The incident comes amid rising tensions between Iran and the US about navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy and commodity supplies.
In February, the US and Israel launched a war against Iran. Tehran responded with attacks on Israel and US targets in the region before a ceasefire agreement was reached in April.
The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June concerning freedom of navigation in the strait, but its implementation stalled over disagreements related to security in the strategic waterway as tensions continued to escalate.

Bayer wins Roundup cancer trial after Supreme Court ruling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:40:00 UTC
11:40:00 KST

Bayer wins Roundup cancer trial after Supreme Court ruling
October 30, 2026
The German pharmaceutical giant Bayer won a trial on Thursday over claims the Roundup weedkiller, manufactured by subsidiary Monsanto, caused cancer in three women.
The Missouri jury sided unanimously with Bayer. It's the first trial since a US Supreme Court ruling that limits complaints over the product.
Bayer is waiting for a separate court ruling where the company is seeking a $7.25 billion (€6.5 billion) settlement in relation to tens of thousands of other Roundup cases.
What is the complaint against Roundup?
Thursday's court ruling follows a case brought to a St. Louis court by Theresa Aretino, Cynthia Fernandez and Betty Larkin in 2020.
The three women had said they were diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma after regularly using the weedkiller.
Their attorneys argued that Roundup was defectively designed and unreasonably dangerous, and that Bayer was negligent in selling it.
The three were not participating in the Bayer settlement. Some 65,000 other cases have been filed against the company, claiming Roundup gave them cancer.
What did the Supreme Court rule in regards to Roundup?
The US Supreme Court ruled earlier this year that plaintiffs could not argue that the Roundup label failed to warn users about the risk of cancer since the US Environmental Protection Agency had concluded the label does not require a cancer warning.
"We are pleased with the jury's favorable verdict for Monsanto validating our belief that there is no evidence to prove design defect, fraud or negligence claims in the Roundup litigation," Bill Dodero, the company's US general counsel and global head of litigation, said in a statement.
"This verdict should send a strong signal that plaintiffs who wish to pursue claims in the court system following the Durnell ruling will face significant challenges both in demonstrating they have viable claims and putting forth the necessary evidence to prove them in court," he added, using the name of the Supreme Court case.
The company has repeatedly defended the use of glyphosate, the active ingredient in Roundup, as safe, calling it "one of the most studied agricultural tools in history."
The EPA has previously concluded that glyphosate is probably not carcinogenic, but it is in the middle of a new review of its safety. The International Agency for Research on Cancer concluded in 2015 that the chemical was "probably carcinogenic" to humans, but Bayer has rejected the study's findings, calling it an outlier.

Salvadoran ex-president Saca released after 10-year sentence for corruption

Elias Antonio Saca, the former president of El Salvador, has been released after serving a 10-year prison term for corruption.
Saca, 61, arrived at court to formally report his release on Thursday after fulfilling the terms of a plea deal in which he confessed to diverting and laundering more than $300m from public funds during his 2004 to 2009 administration.
His lawyer, Mario Machado, said the former president had served his sentence in full without receiving early-release benefits.
Arrested at son’s wedding
Saca was first arrested during his son’s wedding in 2016 and was sentenced to five years for embezzlement and another five years for money laundering in September 2018.
A plea bargain allowed Saca to avoid a potential 30-year prison sentence.
In 2019, the former president was found guilty of offering $10,000 to a court employee to obtain information about a case against him, though a judge determined the second sentence to be part of his existing 10-year term.
Saca, a businessman and radio broadcaster, served as president as part of the right-wing Nationalist Republican Alliance (ARENA).
During the initial trial, prosecutors said Saca appropriated funds from the state budget for himself and others, including taking more than $7m for his former party.
Saca was also ordered to repay $260m to the state. He is one of four Salvadoran presidents who have faced corruption charges, including his successor Mauricio Funes, who escaped to Nicaragua in September 2016 and died there in 2025.

Trump pledges to push for IDF withdrawal from Lebanon if Beirut joins Abraham Accords - report

02:37:21 UTC
