New Analysis: Air Force Should Buy 250 Blended-Wing Tankers, as 2027 Demo Looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
01:41:16 UTC
10:41:16 KST

A new think tank analysis finds a hypothetical blended-wing body tanker could offer twice as much refueling performance as the KC-46A Pegasus and recommends the Air Force buy scores of them, as the service prepares to evaluate a BWB demonstrator next year and must juggle its future tanker plans with a host of other modernization priorities like fighters and bombers.
The report, released by the Hudson Institute on Oct. 27, makes the case that the Air Force needs a fleet of 250 advanced new tankers to meet the challenge of refueling operations in a potential conflict with China.
Traditionally during conflicts, the Air Force has launched tankers from uncontested airfields relatively close to bomber and fighter strike objectives. But the vast distances of the Western Pacific and the long reach of China’s missiles make that untenable, report authors Timothy A. Walton and Shane Dennin write.
By 2035, they note, Chinese forces will likely be capable of suppressing large-scale tanker operations from “the forward and many of the intermediate airfields that tankers normally rely on,” a capability that “could collapse U.S. air operations and heavily contribute to U.S. defeat in a war against the People’s Republic of China,”
The solution, they conclude, are tankers that can launch from farther afield and carry more fuel to the fight.
Blended-wing body aircraft blur the line between wings and fuselage for a design that is considered more aerodynamically efficient and has a large cabin/cargo space. The combination, the Hudson report concludes, means a “medium BWB can refuel more than twice as many force packages or refuel force packages more than twice as far as the KC-46A,” the report states. “At longer-ranges and higher offloads, the medium BWB can deliver up to five times as many operationally relevant increments of fuel as the KC-46A.”
Since 2023, the Air Force has been developing a BWB demonstrator/prototype program with startup JetZero, which is partnering with Northrop Grumman. That aircraft, dubbed Z4, is expected to make its first flight in 2027.
An Air Force spokesperson confirmed that the “blended-wing body project is currently active, on schedule, and meeting assembly milestones; the demonstrator’s first flight is scheduled for late 2027.”
JetZero has proposed a tanker variant, dubbed KC-Z4, though the demonstrator will not be a refueler.
The Air Force’s future tanker plans are not settled—the Eisenhower-era KC-135 fleet is showing its age, and officials have stressed the need for refuelers that can survive in contested airspace. At one point, they were exploring concepts through the Next-Generation Aerial Refueling System program, but they shifted gears in the 2027 budget request, saying they would focus on protection systems over a new aircraft.
Meanwhile, the service is still planning on buying up to 75 additional KC-46 Pegasus refuelers on top of the current program of record for 188. In May, the Air Force signed an agreement with Boeing to fix critical issues with the Pegasus, such as fielding an improved remote vision system that boom operators use to refuel other aircraft—a requirement that senior leaders have said must be resolved before the Air Force will sign the new contract extension to buy an extra 75 tankers.
The Hudson paper recommends the Air Force move forward with the KC-46 production extension contract. Then, assuming the BWB demonstrator evaluation goes well in 2027 and 2028, the service should direct fiscal 2027 research, development, test and evaluation funding to “mature medium-sized, long-range, high-offload capacity tanker designs, such as medium BWB,” the report states.
“Our proposed plan’s yearly tanker costs would require additional RDTE outlays in the late 2020s and early 2030s, but its total RDTE, procurement, and operations and support costs over 30 years could amount to $15.5 billion less than a plan that solely procured KC-46A,” according to the report, which compared acquiring and operating 250 Medium BWB tankers to the same number of KC-46s.
Retired Air Force Gen. Mike Minihan, who led Air Mobility Command between 2021 and 2024, said he saw the potential of the BWB demonstrator effort when it was conceived as a way to reverse the service’s neglect of tanker fleet modernization when compared to efforts to develop fifth- and sixth-generation bombers and fighters.
“One of my biggest concerns was the equilibrium of the strike force with the enabling force; I love B-21, I love F-15 EX, I love F-35, I love the [Collaborative Combat Aircraft], … but if we don’t invest in the enablers to make those things successful, we’re going to look silly on the modern battlefield,” said Minihan, who retired in 2024.
Minihan said his continued belief in the BWB design convinced him to become an advisor to JetZero earlier this year.
“It’s almost two times everything—two times fuel the efficiency, two times the amount of receiver service, two times quicker, two times the distance—I mean, it’s quite remarkable,” he said.
Douglas Birkey, Executive Director for AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, also noted the potential benefits of the BWB design.
“There is no question the Air Force needs new refueling capacity, and it needs to ensure that it can maximize offload range—you want to haul as much fuel as possible, not burn a whole lot on your way to the refueling track, offload as much as possible and then get back home,” Birkey said. “And the blended-wing body has definite, distinct aerodynamic advantages, being highly efficient to maximize that off-loader range.”
But Birkey said he is skeptical whether the Air Force can commit to a long-term funding plan for a next-generation BWB tanker in the current budget environment. The service’s $267.7 billion budget request in fiscal 2027 is $53 billion more than it 2026 budget, but even then, competing modernization priorities such as the sixth-generation B-21 bomber and F-47 fighter limited any investment in tanker fleet modernization. Buying a new fleet of BWB tankers would require even larger toplines of reliable funding over the next decade for the service.
“There’s got to be sustained long-term investment; this isn’t a one-year plus-up kind of investment. They need a decade’s worth of solid investment,” Birkey said. “They’re making up for so much underinvestment.”
For its report, Hudson evaluated the KC-46A, the Airbus A330 MRTT+, a medium-sized BWB design, a medium-sized reduced signature design, and a collaborative tanker aircraft—the latter two to theoretically shuttle tank from parent tankers such as the KC-46A at short-to-moderate distances. The KC-46A and A330 MRTT+ are medium-range, multirole designs while the Medium BWB is a long-range, high offload dedicated tanker. The medium BWB tanker is being designed to carry 300,000 pounds of fuel compared to the KC-46’s max capacity of 212,000 pounds of fuel. The A330 MRTT+ can carry 245,000 pounds of fuel.
Hudson concluded that the Air Force should take a holistic approach that includes:
- Prioritizing military construction and other funding to enhance capacity and resilience of its most important tanker airfields.
- Continuing to increase funding for command, control, and communications; self-defense; fuel transfer; and automation and autonomy mission systems for current and future tankers.
- Developing and procuring 250 medium-sized, long-range, high-offload tankers, such as the medium BWB, which could prove capable of standing in a moderate distance from threats.
The Air Force could begin fielding the new fleet of medium BWBs by the mid-2030s “for reasonable RDTE and procurement costs that align with projected budgets, and it could cost considerably less than simply buying more KC-46As,” the report states.
The report estimates that a mixed fleet with roughly 260 KC-46s and 250 medium BWB tankers would run $398 billion in totals costs over 30 years, while fielding an additional 250 KC-46s for a total fleet of 510 would cost $413 billion.
Both aircraft in the mixed fleet would complement each other, the report states: “Together, the force could succeed in its most stressing scenarios, as well as sustainably execute other operations across the world.”
Minihan said he agrees that the Air Force needs “bombers and fighters of fifth and sixth generation, but we generally don’t pay attention to the enabling force until it fails. … To think that we can take a four-generation gap between our strike force and our enabling force into combat with a near-peer adversary is a fool’s errand.”
Minihan said he was “on the record from my time in uniform as supporting” the medium BWB demonstrator effort. “It fits perfectly into the NGAS concept,” Minihan said. “Every pound of gas I save getting to the fight is a pound of gas I can give away to a fighter or a bomber.”

Player prepares for World Cup after career reshaped by injury
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
01:31:39 UTC
10:31:39 KST

The Physical Disability Rugby League World Cup is being staged alongside the men's, women's, and wheelchair tournaments.
It will be contested by Australia, England and New Zealand, with all games in Sydney.
What's next?
Australia faces England in the opening game tonight at Cabramatta Rugby Leagues Club.
There are many things to prepare for when playing a game of rugby league. How to break a line, gain an edge or pick a way through a defence.
You don't prepare for one unfortunate tackle to alter the course of your life forever.
In 2020, at the age of 18, while playing for the Narellan Jets in south-west Sydney, Bryce Crane was on the wrong end of a tackle and suffered permanent nerve damage and paralysis of his right arm.
Yet, there was only one thing on his mind.
"You don't really quite understand how much something means to you until it is ripped away," Crane said.
"It's weird to think about but I didn't think about my life, I just thought that I lost the game that I loved growing up playing."
For the love of the game
Crane was told not to worry about the sport. Now, he is preparing for a home World Cup as Australia's Physical Disability Rugby League (PDRL) star fullback.
Australia will host New Zealand and England in the three-team round-robin tournament which runs from October 30 to November 8 in Sydney.
"It's really exciting to get into the World Cup; we have had a few camps with the squad, so we are getting around knowing each other," Crane said.
It will be his second PDRL World Cup after he starred for Australia in the inaugural edition in 2022.
Despite Australia failing to win a game, Crane's performances earned him a spot in the Rugby League World Cup Dream Team, which also contained players from the men's, women's and wheelchair tournaments.
He was the only PDRL player in the team, and was named alongside fellow Australian internationals Josh Addo-Carr, Cameron Murray and Tarryn Aiken.
In the eyes of his teammates though, he does not just contribute to the team through his talismanic play.
Luke Vella, who is also an NRL assistant coach at the Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs, knows the hallmarks of a top-quality player.
"He is obviously very skilful and has a great ability to play the game, but he is very humble," Vella said.
"He is also very encouraging, there is times I know Bryce can make a break or make a tackle, but he puts others before himself quite often and encourages them and supports them along with their game."
Full circle moment
The final of the tournament will be held at the Sydney Football Stadium before one of the men's semifinals, the biggest stage the game has been played on so far.
Vella was injured at the ground while playing for the Bulldogs' under-20 side in 2014, and should Australia qualify for the decider, he will step onto that field for the first time in a playing role since then.
"It's funny, I haven't really thought about it too much to be honest," Vella said.
"Obviously the stadium got knocked down and rebuilt, it is a little bit different.
"I can't really describe what the emotions would be if we get there and I get the opportunity to play on the field again."
Vella's passion for the game quickly returned after his career-ending injury, and in 2019, he was named head coach of the Bulldogs' under-20s team, giving him a chance to push players to achieve dreams of making the NRL.
After coaching the team to the Jersey Flegg Cup in 2023, he earned his promotion to the first grade coaching ranks for the 2024 season, while balancing his return to playing.
He made his international debut for Australia against New Zealand in November 2024 in Auckland.
"When I got injured at 20, I fell back in love with it because it got taken away from me," Vella said.
"I love it because my thing for coaching is to develop players and help them achieve their goals, but then the competitive side, running around, throwing the ball around, a bit of contact too.
"All things rugby league, all come back to love."
For Crane and Vella, the pride in representing their country is palpable.
"At the end of the day, I'm not just representing myself, my family, my country, but I'm also representing people with all different types of disabilities," Crane said.
"I feel like that is a pretty cool thing to do."
This content was produced for the ABC's International Day of People with Disability coverage, which runs from November 19 to December 25, 2026.

SC said it is not inclined to completely ban firecrackers but warned authorities that orders are meaningless without ground-level enforcement
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Thursday said it was not inclined to completely ban firecrackers, but there was no point in passing orders and directions every year unless authorities implement them on the ground.“It concerns every living being,” a bench of Justices M M Sundresh and Prasanna B Varale observed while hearing a matter on the bursting of firecrackers in Delhi-NCR.Additional solicitor-general Aishwarya Bhati told the bench about the measures taken by Delhi govt and Commission for Air Quality Management to deal with air pollution.“There is no point in passing orders and directions unless you give effect to them on the ground, otherwise, it becomes a mockery,” the bench observed, while stressing enforcement.While saying that it was not an adversarial matter, the bench observed that authorities have to take up the issue seriously and take action. “You have to really regulate it. We are not inclined to completely ban, but don’t push us to take a very harsh stand,” the bench told Bhati.
Bhati said a series of measures have been taken which would come into effect from Nov, including curbs on older vehicles, construction and demolition activity and staggered office timings in Delhi. “We are geared up to deal with the pollution season which unfortunately happens,” she said.Centre also told the bench that its internal consultation on the issue pertaining to the use of barium in firecrackers was going on. Bhati requested the bench to grant three weeks to complete the consultation.The top court was hearing two petitions, including a suo motu case concerning air pollution in NCR covering issues like firecrackers, stubble burning and solid waste management. The other plea relates to a ban on manufacturing firecrackers.
During the hearing, an advocate, assisting the apex court as an amicus curiae in the suo motu case, said bursting firecrackers releases a huge amount of hazardous particulate matter (PM) which enters the human body and causes damage to lungs and other organs.She said during Dussehra last week, there was a spike in the Air Quality Index (AQI) in Delhi-NCR. Flagging the issue of enforcement, the amicus said there was no proper mechanism to assess whether the firecrackers which are being sold are actually green crackers.The bench had said that a middle ground would have to be found by specifying hours during which firecrackers could be used.

Trump administration renews bid to block Alaska election results
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
01:30:30 UTC

Trump administration renews bid to block Alaska election results
The updated lawsuit cites a new report that Democratic operatives recruited a competitor to confuse voters and unseat a Republican incumbent.
The United States Department of Justice has filed a revised lawsuit seeking to decertify the results of a Senate race in the state of Alaska if Republican incumbent Dan S Sullivan loses narrowly.
The updated lawsuit on Thursday comes just days before the November 3 midterm election, which will determine control of Congress.
The complaint accuses Democrats of trying to confuse voters by placing a candidate with the same name as Sullivan on the ballot.
Alaska’s Senate race is one of seven key toss-ups that will likely decide whether Republicans keep their majority in Congress’s upper chamber.
Democratic challenger Mary Peltola is seeking to unseat Sullivan, a Republican ally of US President Donald Trump.
But a New York Times report on Wednesday alleged that members of Peltola’s campaign helped recruit a retired teacher, Dan J Sullivan Jr, to run for the Senate seat as a spoiler candidate, designed to draw votes away from the incumbent.
The Times report prompted a renewed legal push under the Trump administration to bar Alaska from certifying its election results, should Senator Sullivan lose.
The Department of Justice issued 40 subpoenas and document preservation requests as part of the revised complaint, the Reuters news agency reported.
Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy also ordered a criminal investigation into the allegations. Peltola’s campaign has denied involvement in Dan J Sullivan Jr’s bid for the Senate.
Prosecutors, however, have accused the Democrat and her allies of playing partisan tricks – and undermining voters as a result.
“They orchestrated his sham campaign for the purpose of misleading Alaskan voters and getting Peltola elected,” Justice Department lawyers wrote in their amended complaint.
But the Justice Department’s lawsuit has raised concerns about election integrity and federal meddling.
Under the US Constitution, election administration falls to the states, not the presidency.
In June, Alaska’s Supreme Court ruled that Dan J Sullivan Jr could compete in the midterms, and the state’s election office has already taken steps to reduce confusion between the two Sullivans.
Recruiting candidates to split an opponent’s vote – a practice known as ballot stacking – is also generally considered to be legal and has been used by both parties in Alaska.
Critics have been sceptical of the Justice Department’s bid to pause the certification of Alaska’s Senate results if Senator Sullivan does not win re-election, noting it would be impossible to divine voter intent based on the final tally alone.
Justin Levitt, a former Department of Justice official under President Joe Biden, also questioned what legal authority the federal government had to get involved in the case.
“I don’t know what they’re putting out subpoenas to investigate because I don’t know what federal violations are implicated that DOJ would have jurisdiction over,” Levitt told the Associated Press news agency.
“Sure makes it seem like the point of the investigation is to become the story.”
Democrats and Republicans are locked in tight races nationwide that will determine which party holds a majority in the US Senate for the remainder of Trump’s second term in office.
Republicans currently hold a slim majority in the legislature’s upper chamber, with 53 out of 100 seats.
Democratic candidates are hoping to win seats by capitalising on Trump’s deep unpopularity and frustration over the cost-of-living crisis.
Trump has suggested he may not accept the midterm results if his party loses its majorities in Congress, and he has pushed false claims of widespread voter fraud.
The Justice Department has also attempted to challenge the voting process in several states, including California.

France’s protests, like Hong Kong’s in 2019, risk being defined by violence
It important not to let those seeking only confrontation take over the argument. A cycle of violence makes underlying pressures far harder to resolve
3-MIN READ3-MIN
6
 Listen
Bernard Chan, born in 1965, is a Hong Kong businessman. 
No protester sets out expecting a friend to be arrested, injured or caught in a confrontation with the police. Yet when that happens, the reasons for returning to the streets can change.
People may return not only because of the cause that first brought them out, but because they believe a friend has been treated unjustly. That is how anger becomes personal, and how a protest can move towards a dangerous cycle of action and reaction.
This is the risk confronting France. The student protests began over teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and deteriorating schools. But the central question is no longer simply why students took to the streets. It is whether further provocation, violence and forceful policing will allow others to define what their protests stand for.

WASHINGTON (Reuters) -- The U.S. economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter as resilient consumer spending and AI-driven business investment more than offset the impact of higher oil prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East.
Gross domestic product increased at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis said in its advance estimate of third-quarter GDP on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast GDP advancing at a 3.2% pace.
Estimates ranged from a 1.0% growth rate to a 4.2% pace.
The strength in growth is in stark contrast to households' downbeat assessment of the economy, reflected in President Donald Trump's record-low approval ratings and a sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment. The report was published less than a week before Tuesday's midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress.
The economy is expanding at a pace that is well above what some Federal Reserve officials regard as the non-inflationary growth rate of around 2%. The U.S. central bank on Wednesday left its benchmark interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated."
Economists expected the Fed to raise rates in December. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh told reporters "economic activity is expanding at a strong pace," noting that "while uncertainty remains, owing in part to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient."
Given the increasing dominance of AI-related spending, some economists said the strong GDP growth was probably not a true picture of the economy. Investors are increasingly focusing on the rising costs of long-term AI projects in which the payoff is uncertain. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, a potential downside risk to equipment spending. Still, economists did expect this pillar of support to weaken, though a pullback in spending was likely.
Consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, increased at a 3.8% pace in the July-September quarter after growing at a 3.8% rate in the second quarter. Historically low layoffs and moderate hiring are helping to underpin spending, though wage gains have at times lagged inflation.
But households also have been saving less and dipping into their nest eggs to fund spending. With average gasoline prices still above $4 a gallon as the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran drags on, economists anticipated a slowdown in consumer spending.

Why the US economy looks strong but feels bad to many
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
01:20:00 UTC
10:20:00 KST

Why the US economy looks strong but feels bad to many
The US economic expansion is in its seventh year, and there is no recession in sight.
Unemployment and layoffs are historically low. Consumer spending data suggests that Americans are splurging on things like live entertainment, travel and eating out. The economy is growing at its fastest pace in a year.
However, by many measures, people are miserable.
A significant portion of Americans say it feels like the economy is stacked against them.
Polls indicate that they are stressed out about the cost of living, anxious about job security and pessimistic about their economic future. And do not even get them started on petrol prices.
Economic issues keep showing up as voters’ top concerns ahead of the US midterm elections on Nov 3. 
But are things as shaky as many say?
How much have prices gone up?
Americans confronted the hottest inflation in more than four decades in the years immediately following the Covid-19 pandemic.
They are still struggling with sticker shock. 
Prices continue to go up, though at a slower pace than a few years ago.
The basket of goods and services measured by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics’ consumer price index was 3.7% higher in September than a year earlier. That is less than half the 9.1% pace of inflation reached as the US emerged from the pandemic.
But it is still high enough for people to notice.
The steady rise in prices comes on top of the post-pandemic spike. 
Since the end of 2019, overall consumer prices are up by about 30%.
Groceries are 32% more expensive. Eating out is close to 40% more. Rents are up by more than a third. Electricity costs are up by 43%. Auto maintenance jumped by more than half and car insurance by about 48%.
How unusual are the price increases?
Prices are almost always rising, but usually not this fast. In the decade before the pandemic, annual inflation averaged around 1.8%. Now it is roughly double that.
That is in part because the economy faced a series of shocks that accelerated price gains.
Supply chains stretched and broke in 2021 after the global economy reopened.
Then Russia’s invasion of Ukraine choked off fertiliser, wheat and oil shipments, sending food and fuel prices higher.
The Trump administration’s “Liberation Day” tariffs spooked markets, and subsequent levies raised prices on many goods.
The buildout in artificial intelligence technology fuelled business investment and construction hiring but also sent prices for computer software and components higher. 
And most recently the Iran war has led to higher energy prices and rising borrowing costs.
“Supply shocks have come more frequently, hit harder and lasted longer,” Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago president Austan Goolsbee said in a speech in London in September.
In an effort to tamp down inflation, the Fed in September raised interest rates for the first time since 2023, but left them unchanged at a subsequent rate-setting meeting in October.
How are Americans getting by?
Americans’ hourly earnings are, on average, up about one-third since the end of 2019. 
But adjusted for inflation, pay has barely kept up with rising prices.
And even the marginal gains Americans have made are beginning to evaporate. 
Inflation-adjusted pay was down from a year earlier for six straight months as of September. 
Even so, workers continue to spend – tapping a range of resources to do so.
Regular pay cheques are not the only source of income or wealth. 
Some people work in the gig economy.
The stock market hit a series of records in 2026, lifting investor portfolios.
Home values have grown substantially over the past few years, and big tax refunds in 2026 boosted household budgets.
But wages are the main contributor to income for most Americans up until retirement.
Sluggish wage growth alongside rising prices has forced many to save less – or not save at all.
What is happening in the job market?
On the good-news front, plenty of people are earning a pay cheque. 
The US economy is by many measures operating at or near full employment. 
The unemployment rate is historically low, though it edged higher, to 4.2%, in September.
Healthcare, construction and manufacturing have all been adding jobs in recent months.
And the labour force participation rate also rose in September, typically a positive sign that more people are looking for work.
But sector-specific strength and the low unemployment rate mask a sluggish job market.
Employers are not laying off many workers, but overall they are not hiring many workers, either.
That has left some people feeling stuck in place. 
Glassdoor’s employee confidence index, which measures how optimistic workers are about the business outlook of their employer over the next six months, fell in September to the lowest level in the survey’s 10-year history. 
Others are simply locked out. Entry-level college graduates have had an especially tough time cracking the job market, and the ranks of the long-term unemployed are growing.
So while there are pockets of strong demand, the overall job market is not hot enough to broadly lift real wages or create wide-ranging opportunities.
Who is feeling stuck?
A person who has a job is likely to keep it – layoffs are historically low.
US homeowners who bought before the pandemic have watched property values soar.
And investors have done well. An index fund tied to the S&P 500 has more than doubled in value since the end of 2019, even if the gains have not been reinvested.
But when these milestones do not apply, it might be a sign of falling further behind.
Home ownership is one area of frustration.
The median sales price of an existing home is up by about half since the end of 2019, and rates on 30-year fixed mortgages have climbed to more than 7%, from less than 4%.
Excluding taxes and insurance, that equates to a payment that is roughly double what it was before the pandemic.
What role is AI playing?
Investment in artificial intelligence is one of the economy’s bright spots.
But that has been cold comfort for many Americans who worry that the technology will eliminate their jobs while its data centres swallow up land in their communities.
Capital spending on data centres could total US$5.5 trillion (S$7 trillion) cumulatively by 2030, according to JPMorgan Chase & Co.
Some 54% of Democrats and 37% of Republicans said they oppose construction of new data centres in the US, according to a June survey by Reuters/Ipsos.
“People are very concerned, either directly or indirectly, around what this is going to mean for their jobs,” said John Leer, chief economist at Morning Consult.
“It’s another way in which the rules and the structure of the economy seem to be changing.”
What actually is shaping consumers’ outlook?
Americans’ views about their economic standing tend to be shaped by more than just their personal finances.
Indeed, surveys show that individuals generally feel more optimistic about the economy when their party holds the White House. 
When their party is out of power, they become more pessimistic, even when their own situation is stable.
After Donald Trump was re-elected president in 2024, for example, consumer sentiment surged among Republicans and dropped among Democrats, even before his inauguration.
But since the start of 2026, measures of sentiment have slumped across political affiliation, geography and income, suggesting a wide swath of Americans harbour concerns about the economy. BLOOMBERG

New Zealand household living costs up 3 pct annually
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
09:16:49 CST
10:16:49 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand household living costs rose 3 percent in the year to the September quarter, easing from a 3.2-percent increase in the year to the June quarter, as higher petrol prices drove inflation, official data showed on Friday.
The increase was mainly driven by a 19.1-percent rise in petrol prices, which accounted for almost one quarter of the increase in average annual household living costs, according to Stats NZ, the national statistics agency.
Electricity prices rose 9.3 percent over the year, while local authority rates increased 6.2 percent, also contributing to higher living costs, Stats NZ said.
Superannuitant households, or households receiving New Zealand's government retirement pension, recorded the highest annual inflation rate at 4 percent, while higher-spending households experienced the lowest annual inflation rate at 2.5 percent among all household groups, it said.
By comparison, consumer price index (CPI) inflation, which measures overall price changes, was 3.7 percent in the year to the September quarter, down from 4.1 percent in the year to the previous quarter, Stats NZ said, adding that falling interest payments helped keep household living-cost inflation below the CPI rate, with interest payments for the average household declining around 10 percent over the year.
Meanwhile, international airfares rose 12.5 percent during the period, mainly due to higher fares to Europe and Asia, the agency said. ■

Netanyahu bloc finishes in lead but short of majority: Official results

Netanyahu bloc finishes in lead but short of majority: Official results
JERUSALEM – Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s camp finished ahead of the opposition but remained well short of a parliamentary majority, according to final results from Israel’s general election released early on Oct 30.
Netanyahu’s coalition of right-wing and far-right parties won 53 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, with his Likud party remaining the largest single faction with 27 seats.
The opposition bloc, led by centrist Gadi Eisenkot secured 48 seats.
The results from the Central Elections Committee also confirmed a dramatic breakthrough by Arab groupings Raam and the United Arab List, which together won 19 seats and could emerge as kingmakers in coalition talks.
The two parties were targeted by unproven election fraud allegations circulated by Netanyahu’s camp on Oct 29.
Politicians and media reports claimed the parties were suspected of receiving Qatari funds to finance vote-buying.
The Arab parties and Qatar denied the allegations, while Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of seeking to “delegitimise” the election results.
Israel’s Shin Bet domestic security agency said it was investigating suspected irregularities but added it was not intended to “cast aspersions or place blame on an entire sector that went out to vote in a democratic and lawful manner”.
Without directly referring to the allegations against the Arab parties, the electoral commission said on Oct 29 that some information that had circulated was entirely unfounded.
The investigation is continuing alongside the process being conducted by the Central Elections Committee.
It will have no impact on the final results to be submitted to the president, it said.
The final results will be formally presented on Nov 4 to President Isaac Herzog, who will then begin consultations with party leaders before tasking one of them with trying to form a government, the commission said.
The absence of a majority bloc points to potentially difficult coalition negotiations that could last for weeks.
If no government can be formed, Israel could face another election, as it has several times in the past. AFP

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's camp has finished ahead of the opposition but remained well short of a parliamentary majority, according to final results from Israel's general election released.
Netanyahu's coalition of right-wing and far-right parties won 53 of the Knesset's 120 seats, with his Likud party remaining the largest single faction with 27 seats, according to results released early on Friday.
The opposition bloc, led by centrist Gadi Eisenkot secured 48 seats.
The results from the Central Elections Committee also confirmed a dramatic breakthrough by Arab groupings Raam and the United Arab List, which together won 19 seats and could emerge as kingmakers in coalition talks.
The two parties were targeted by unproven election-fraud allegations circulated by Netanyahu's camp on Thursday.
Politicians and media reports claimed the parties were suspected of receiving Qatari funds to finance vote-buying.
The Arab parties and Qatar denied the allegations, while Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of seeking to "delegitimise" the election results.
All eyes on Herzog now
Israel's Shin Bet domestic security agency said it was investigating suspected irregularities but added it was not intended to "cast aspersions or place blame on an entire sector that went out to vote in a democratic and lawful manner".
Without directly referring to the allegations against the Arab parties, the electoral commission said on Thursday that some information that had circulated was entirely unfounded.
The investigation is continuing alongside the process being conducted by the Central Elections Committee. It will have no impact on the final results to be submitted to the president, it said.
The final results will be formally presented on Wednesday to President Isaac Herzog, who will then begin consultations with party leaders before tasking one of them with trying to form a government, the commission said.
The absence of a majority bloc points to potentially difficult coalition negotiations that could last for weeks.
If no government can be formed, Israel could face another election, as it has several times in the past.

EU force helicopter crash kills four in Bosnia

EU force helicopter crash kills four in Bosnia
EUFOR confirms Chinook CH-47 helicopter crash in Bosnia, with four Italian nationals confirmed dead.
Four people belonging to the European Union Force in Bosnia (EUFOR) have been killed after an Italian military helicopter conducting a training operation crashed.
EUFOR said a CH-47 Chinook helicopter crashed during “routine training” in the Brcko region on Thursday, about 180km (110 miles) north of Bosnia’s capital, Sarajevo.
A total of 11 people were injured in the crash, EUFOR said, adding that all the injured are receiving treatment and are in stable condition.
The Italian government said in a statement that all those on board the military helicopter were its nationals.
The victims were two soldiers and two Red Cross volunteers, according to the Italian defence ministry.
“At this moment of immense grief, my thoughts go first and foremost to the families of our fallen, to whom I extend my personal condolences and those of the entire defence establishment,” Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said.
Wreckage
Bosnian media outlets published photos of the wreckage showing the helicopter overturned on the ground in a flat field.
A spokesman for Brcko hospital told the AFP news agency that there were 15 people on board at the time of the crash, which initially killed three people.
“Twelve people were transported to our hospital. Unfortunately, a fourth person succumbed to injuries in the hospital,” the spokesman said.
“EUFOR is conducting a full and thorough investigation of the incident and will release more information as it is verified, and when appropriate,” the force said in a statement.
EUFOR, which has between 1,000 and 1,500 personnel, has been deployed in Bosnia since 2004, when it replaced a NATO peacekeeping force that had been in the country since the Bosnian War ended in 1995. The mission oversees the implementation of the Dayton Peace Agreement, which ended the three-year war.

Trump DOJ issues subpoenas in California noncitizen voting probe, escalating pressure campaign

Unknown Publisher

09:56:21 KST

Trump Justice Department issues subpoenas in California non-citizen voting probe
- Trump’s Justice Department has subpoenaed Los Angeles County records in a criminal probe into alleged non-citizen voting, widening its fight with California before the Nov 3 midterm election.
- The DOJ says it has charged 156 immigrants and is using subpoenas to build cases, but studies say non-citizen voting is rare and has no effect on results.
- A judge rejected the DOJ bid to block California mail-in ballots, and California says the federal government lacks authority to interfere in state-run elections.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – President Donald Trump’s administration has demanded records from California as part of a criminal investigation into alleged voting by non-citizens – escalating its battle with the largest US state ahead of the midterm election on Nov 3.
The Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder’s office received federal grand jury subpoenas last week seeking information about the agency’s methods for detecting “unlawful voting by aliens” and preventing such ballots from being counted, according to copies of the subpoenas seen by Reuters on Oct 29.
The Trump Justice Department has heaped pressure on California over alleged non-citizen voting, filing a civil lawsuit against the state and sending a series of letters in October warning election officials that they risk criminal exposure if they do not verify voters’ citizenship status.
The subpoenas also seek records related to Los Angeles County’s response to those letters, according to the documents.
The demands are part of a nationwide effort by the Trump administration to identify cases of voter fraud, raising concerns among Democrats and other critics that Trump could use the issue to sow doubt about the results of the election, which will determine control of Congress.
“At every step, the US Department of Justice (DOJ) has taken a confrontational, adversarial approach,” Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan said in a statement on Oct 29.
“Election officials are acting in accordance with state and federal law.”
It was not immediately clear if Logan’s office was the focus of the investigation.
Legal battle
Though studies have repeatedly shown that voting by non-citizens is rare and has no impact on election results, the Trump administration has intensely focused on the issue.
The Justice Department has charged 156 immigrants with voting or registering to vote unlawfully in a pre-midterm push, Acting Deputy Attorney-General Trent McCotter told reporters on Oct 29.
The agency has used subpoenas to state and local election officials to build such cases.
A Justice Department spokesperson declined to comment on the latest subpoenas but said that California and the federal government “agree that non-citizen voting is properly addressed through criminal law”.
On Oct 28, a federal judge rejected a Justice Department request to temporarily block California from counting mail-in ballots from a list of 20,000 voters the administration alleges are likely noncitizens.
The DOJ has appealed the ruling.
Lawyers for California have questioned the reliability of the Trump administration’s immigration data and argued that the federal government does not have the authority to intervene in its elections.
Under the US Constitution, states administer elections and not the federal government.
Before ruling against the DOJ, US District Judge David Carter told agency lawyers at a hearing on Oct 27 that the “court believes that it would be wise that any threats to state and county election employees cease immediately”. REUTERS

Binance crypto platform suspends trades amid suspected hack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:55:00 UTC
09:55:00 KST

Binance crypto exchange suspends trades over North Korea-linked hack
October 30, 2026
Blockchain analysts said a North Korean hacking unit was likely behind the theft of more than $6 billion from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.
Binance temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals for security checks and said about $3 billion in affected assets had been frozen.
US-based blockchain intelligence firm TRM attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as an elite North Korean hacking unit.
"We make this judgment with high confidence," TRM said in a report published Thursday.
Why do analysts suspect North Korea?
TRM said attackers moved approximately $6.36 billion out of Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, most of it within about 20 minutes. It described the incident as the largest cryptocurrency theft on record.
"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," the firm said.
Bybit lost $1.5 billion in a hack in February 2025. The FBI attributed that attack to North Korea and TraderTraitor.
Jonathan Levin, co-founder and CEO of blockchain analysis company Chainalysis, also said the Binance attack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor.
Experts say North Korea uses cryptocurrency theft and other illicit cyber activities to obtain foreign currency and help fund its nuclear program despite international sanctions.
What has Binance said about the hack?
Binance did not confirm the attribution to North Korea, saying it was "working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice."
Binance said it worked to secure the affected assets and that it had located and frozen about $3 billion (€2.7 billion) so far. It did not provide information about the remaining $3.3 billion.
"Binance will cover all hacking losses," co-founder Yi He said, without providing more details about the incident.
"Rest assured that user funds are completely safe," a company spokesperson said.
Binance said its initial investigation suggested an attacker had compromised a software infrastructure engineer's laptop, gaining access to an internal service and submitting unauthorized withdrawals. The company said it had found no evidence that wallet private keys had leaked.
Tether froze around $1.6 billion in its USDT currency, according to CEO Paolo Ardoino, and Circle froze some $800 million-worth of USDC, boss Jeremy Allaire said.
The news of the possible hack sent Bitcoin's value tumbling by 3.2% on Thursday evening, dropping below $79,000.
Who is Binance ex-CEO Zhao?
Zhao, who founded the Binance platform in 2017, said "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."
He stepped down as CEO after pleading guilty in 2023. to failing to prevent money laundering on his platform. US President Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.
Zhao and Binance have been key supporters of cryptocurrency ventures by US President Donald Trump and his family.
Edited by Sean Sinico and Karl Sexton

Trump administration bolsters bid to block Alaska Senate certification
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
01:53:35 CET
09:53:35 KST

By Jacob Bogage, Luc Cohen and Bo Erickson
ROCK HILL, South Carolina, Oct 29 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump’s administration filed a revised lawsuit on Thursday seeking to block Alaska’s election results if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan narrowly loses and, according to a person familiar with the matter, issued more than 40 subpoenas and document requests in its probe.
The revised complaint by the US Justice Department cited a New York Times report that Democratic operatives recruited another candidate named Sullivan who could siphon votes from the incumbent. The Justice Department said the effort was intended to mislead voters and help elect Democratic candidate Mary Peltola.
The suit raises the prospect of a messy fight over a contest that could determine US Senate control in next Tuesday’s midterm elections. Republicans hold a 53-47 majority, while Democrats need a net gain of four seats.
Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy also called for a state investigation into the allegations.
“They orchestrated his sham campaign for the purpose of misleading Alaskan voters and getting Peltola elected,” lawyers for the Justice Department wrote in their amended complaint, referring to a retired teacher named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., who is on the ballot without a party affiliation.
Peltola’s campaign did not immediately respond to the amended complaint but has previously said it had “no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.”
The Times reported on Wednesday that Peltola aides worked with campaign lawyers and staff at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to recruit two candidates who could siphon votes from the incumbent Republican Sullivan, including Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.
Peltola’s former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, who was fired in August, told the Times that Peltola was aware of the effort.
The DSCC has denied involvement and accused Republicans of propping up candidates of their own in other races. Reuters was unable to independently verify the Times report.
Daniel J. Sullivan has previously denied in interviews with US news outlets that his aim is to cause confusion or divert votes from Dan S. Sullivan.
TRUMP HAD PUSHED THE CASE
Trump, who for years has sowed doubts about the fairness of US elections, had pushed the Justice Department to bring the Alaska case even before the Times report, seeking to preemptively block Alaska from certifying Peltola, a former congresswoman, if she were to win the election.
Trump told reporters earlier on Thursday: “It’s hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run. Frankly, I don’t know how you can allow somebody like that to run. It’s so unfair.”
Jessica Levinson, a professor who specializes in election law at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles, said that as long as Daniel J. Sullivan, the challenger to the incumbent, didn’t conceal financial support, his campaign likely didn’t break any laws and political parties are allowed to mislead the public.
Policing such behavior would open the door to the government investigating why candidates choose to run and why voters support them, she said. “To the extent that people are uncomfortable with two Sullivans, I would offer you’re probably going to be uncomfortable with a really high level of government intrusion into our elections as well.”
The Department of Justice has also escalated another legal campaign in California, where it has been investigating alleged voting by noncitizens.
The Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder’s office received grand jury subpoenas as part of the probe, according to copies of subpoenas seen by Reuters on Thursday.
The subpoenas, dated last week, seek records related to the county’s response to prior letters from the Trump administration warning of evidence that noncitizens are on the state’s voter roll. They also seek documents about the county’s efforts to prevent noncitizens from voting.
California has previously said the state’s safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust.
A Justice Department spokesperson declined to comment.
ELECTION DAY NEARS
As campaigning enters its final few days, the White House has shelved plans for Trump to appear on Saturday in Kansas, the site of an unexpectedly competitive Senate campaign, a Republican campaign official said.
“I don’t feel like I have to go to Kansas,” Trump told reporters.
Instead, the president will participate in more than 20 virtual campaign appearances before Tuesday, a White House official said.
Trump held a rally in Rock Hill, South Carolina, on Thursday, his second visit in two weeks to a state where opinion polls show an unexpectedly close Senate race between Republican Darline Graham and Democrat Annie Andrews.
Speaking about the hotly contested Michigan Senate race, where progressive Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed holds a small lead in most polls over Republican Mike Rogers, Trump continued his identity-based attacks on El-Sayed, a Muslim, by saying at the rally that “if you’re Black or if you’re Jewish, and if you vote for Abdul, you’re crazy.”
With control of the Senate at stake, both parties are deploying their biggest names in the closing days of the campaign, with Trump stumping for Republicans and former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigning for Democrats in competitive races.
Harris stumped in Macon, Georgia, at a get-out-the-vote effort. Democrats are aiming to reelect Senator Jon Ossoff, who leads in polling, and hope that Keisha Lance Bottoms, locked in a tight race, can become the first woman elected as governor in the state.
Trump’s approval rating stood at 32% in a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday, near a record low, as Americans sour on the high cost of living and the war with Iran.
More than 44 million Americans had already voted as of Thursday evening, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab. A total of 45.9 million voted early in the 2022 midterms.
(Reporting by Jacob Bogage in Rock Hill, South Carolina, Luc Cohen in New York and Bo Erickson in Washington, additional reporting by Andrew Goudsward, Richard Cowan, Nolan D. McCaskill, Ryan Patrick Jones, Tom Hals, Katharine Jackson; Writing by Brad Brooks and Costas Pitas; editing by Scott Malone, Howard Goller and Stephen Coates)

Polish Catholic bishop convicted of covering up for pedophiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Polish Catholic bishop convicted of covering up for pedophiles
A Polish court has found Catholic Bishop Andrzej Jez guilty of deliberately failing to report two priests accused of sexually abusing children, in a landmark ruling against one of the country’s senior Catholic clerics.
The District Court in Tarnow described Thursday’s verdict as “unprecedented,” noting that Jez is the highest-ranking Catholic official in Poland to have been convicted of such an offense.
The court found that the bishop had knowingly withheld information from police about abuse committed by two priests who served in his diocese.
Jez pleaded not guilty, arguing that he had first referred the cases to the Vatican and notified Polish authorities only after establishing the relevant facts. He also invoked the papal secret, a confidentiality rule governing sensitive Church matters.
The judge rejected his defense, ruling that Church regulations could not override Polish law. She stressed that investigating abuse allegations was the responsibility of law enforcement, not religious authorities.
Under Polish law, failure to report certain child sexual abuse offenses carries a maximum prison sentence of three years.
Jez avoided jail but received a two-year restriction of liberty, requiring monthly deductions of 25% of his salary to support a foundation assisting abused children. He was also fined the equivalent of about $5,000 and ordered to cover court costs.
The ruling is not final and can be appealed.
The case comes as the Catholic Church continues to face sexual abuse scandals and allegations of institutional cover-ups worldwide.
Earlier this month, former Australian Catholic Bishop Christopher Saunders was sentenced to six and a half years in prison for sexually abusing two young Indigenous men. A leaked internal Church investigation suggested that his misconduct could have been far more extensive.
In Spain, El Pais reported in April that its investigation had identified more than 3,000 people sexually abused within the Catholic Church since the 1940s. The newspaper accused Church authorities of responding with “opacity and denial,” reporting that some accused priests had been transferred to other parishes or sent abroad.
In the US, the Catholic Archdiocese of San Francisco agreed earlier this year to pay $395 million to settle more than 500 child sexual abuse lawsuits, following a series of costly settlements and bankruptcy filings involving other dioceses and archdioceses.

Using Claude at work? Your employer can now get AI-generated reports on those chats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:47:03 UTC
09:47:03 KST

Using Claude at work? Your employer can now get AI-generated reports on those chats
Anthropic has introduced new tools that let organizations analyze how teams use Claude, collect employee feedback and share AI budgets, according to an announcement published on October 28, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The features - smart reports, in-app surveys and pooled group budgets - are now generally available for Claude Enterprise, although availability varies by configuration.
Smart reports analyze a sample of a team’s conversations with Claude and group the work into categories. Administrators can review spending, outputs and common obstacles, including missing connections to other services or failed tool calls.
Reports also recommend recurring workflows that could be turned into reusable skills and rules to add to code repositories. Administrators can ask custom questions about model usage and costs, then save them as templates for future reports.
Team leaders who are not administrators can be given permission to generate reports for their own groups. Anthropic said the feature is intended to help organizations understand adoption and plan investments.
“Smart reports help admins understand adoption and inform investment planning, but they aren’t for evaluating individual performance or making employment decisions,” the company said.
The new in-app surveys collect employees’ views on the value Claude brings to their work. Default questions cover useful tasks, time saved and what would slow down or stop if access were removed.
Administrators can customize questions, select recipients and export responses to a spreadsheet. Anthropic said it accesses survey data only as necessary to operate the service.
Pooled group budgets give teams a shared monthly spending allowance, allowing heavier users to draw on funds that might otherwise go unused. Individual limits still apply, with access stopping when either the member’s limit or the group’s budget is exhausted.
Users who reach a limit can request additional spending from within Claude, subject to administrator review.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that Anthropic had announced early progress in using Claude to support drug development, including research into cancer treatments and food allergy therapies, as well as pharmaceutical manufacturing.

Trump cancels Iowa, Kansas midterm events, opts for ‘tele-rallies’

Trump cancels Iowa, Kansas midterm events, opts for ‘tele-rallies’
The Republican National Committee has announced broadcasts in at least 20 states after Trump nixes final rallies.
With only days left until the 2026 midterm elections, United States President Donald Trump has announced he will scale back his packed rally schedule, cancelling scheduled appearances in Iowa and Kansas.
The Republican National Committee (RNC) confirmed the cancellations in a statement on Thursday, unveiling a slate of “tele-rallies” to replace the nixed events.
RNC Chairman Joe Gruters argued that the virtual appearances will be more efficient, reaching more voters than Trump otherwise could with on-the-ground stops.
“Voters across the country want to hear from President Trump before Election Day, and this 72-hour sprint will be a huge boost in the closing days,” Gruters said.
The tele-rallies will be broadcast to nearly 20 states, including battlegrounds like Michigan, Alaska, Texas and Iowa, where competitive races are unfolding for the US Senate.
The RNC statement added that further events may be announced in the coming days.
Trump’s rally on Friday in Daytona Beach, Florida – some 320 kilometres (200 miles) up the coast from his Mar-a-Lago resort – will proceed as planned.
Less than five days remain until the midterm elections on November 3, which will decide the composition of Congress, as well as key state and local offices.
Whichever party wins control of Congress will exercise power over Trump’s legislative agenda during the final two years of his second term.
Trump has also expressed concern that the Democratic Party might push to impeach him for a third time if it wins majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate.
Currently, the Republican Party holds narrow majorities in both chambers. In the Senate, the party holds 53 seats out of 100. In the House, it has 218 seats, with all 435 offices up for grabs this election cycle.
The Senate, meanwhile, will see only about a third of its offices on the midterm ballot. Unlike in the House, where terms only last two years, senators are elected to six-year time spans, and their elections are staggered across different election years, to allow for greater stability.
Political analysts have predicted Democrats have an advantage this midterm election cycle, citing Trump’s slumping poll numbers and voter blowback over cost-of-living issues, foreign policy and other concerns.
Harvard University’s ElectIt election forecasting model, for instance, has estimated that Democrats have a 94 percent chance of taking control of the House.
The race for the Senate, however, will be more difficult, with fewer seats available to win. Harvard rates Democrats as having a 74 percent chance to win a majority there.
Trump has placed himself at the centre of the Republican strategy to defend the party’s congressional majorities. To motivate his base of support, he has repeatedly encouraged voters with the phrase, “Pretend I’m on the ballot.”
Midterm elections occur halfway through a president’s term, and they are often considered a reflection of a president’s popularity.
At 80 years old, however, Trump will be the oldest president by the time his term concludes, and his health has been a concern.
Since starting his second term, the Republican leader has been photographed with bruising on his hands, sparking speculation about any undisclosed medical conditions he may have.
After concluding a rally in South Carolina on Thursday, reporters inquired about his health.
“Mr President, you’ve been doing a lot of travel. We’ve been doing a lot of travel with you. How are you feeling? How’s your health?” a reporter from the news agency Reuters asked on the tarmac.
Trump, at first, dodged the question, focusing instead on his optimism about the Republican Party’s prospects in the election.
“We’re going to have a strong Tuesday night,” Trump said.
But the reporter continued with his line of questioning: “So you not going to Kansas has nothing to do with you being sick of travelling?” That prompted an irate reply from Trump, who lashed out.
“Oh, you’re sick to ask that question. You are sick,” Trump said, as he proceeded to insult the reporter’s weight.
“You’ve been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect. You are disgusting. Put yourself in shape. You look like hell.”
During his remarks to the reporter, Trump also questioned the need to visit Salina, Kansas, as he had planned to do on Saturday. “I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas,” the president said.
Kansas, normally a Republican stronghold, has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.
But this election cycle, Republican Senator Roger Marshall is facing a tight race with Democrat Adam Hamilton, the pastor of a megachurch.
On Thursday, the news outlet CNN released a poll showing Hamilton up by four percentage points, leading with 49 percent support to Marshall’s 45 percent.

Will Tai Po fire reforms wipe out collusion in Hong Kong’s building maintenance industry?
Experts say implementation will be a challenge, but changes signal a desire to shift deep-seated attitudes and take on longstanding systemic problems
A raft of reforms to overhaul Hong Kong’s building maintenance sector has been hailed as a bold first step in tackling bid-rigging and other deep-rooted problems, but observers said its success would depend on the determination and persistence to implement them to restore public trust.
They said the reforms signalled a departure from the government’s long-standing reliance on the self-discipline of industry professionals, but highlighted a notable absence of measures to tackle falsified authorisation letters and blacklist unscrupulous contractors via a transparent system.
Among the measures announced by the government on Thursday, several directly addressed calls from professional groups and lawmakers. These included setting up an independent body to support homeowners in renovation projects and criminalising bid-rigging. Other measures involve legal reforms and enhancements of oversight in the industry.
The government also finally addressed the question of political accountability that had lingered for 11 months after the deadly Tai Po fire, which claimed 168 lives. Secretary for Housing Winnie Ho Wing-yin resigned to take political responsibility, while authorities vowed to probe around 50 civil servants over potential administrative lapses within three months.

Thailand revokes citizenship of Chabad leader Rabbi Yosef Chaim Kantor as crackdown continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:34:14 UTC
09:34:14 KST

Thailand has intensified its measures against Chabad institutions in the country, after Thai Prime Minister and Interior Minister Anutin Charnvirakul signing an order revoking the citizenship of Rabbi Yosef Chaim Kantor, the head of Chabad in Thailand and a prominent figure in the country's Jewish community for more than three decades.
The decision comes amid a series of investigations and raids targeting Chabad institutions, including the site of a synagogue reconstruction project in Bangkok.
The official order, signed on Wednesday, October 28, alleges that Kantor continued to use his American citizenship after becoming a naturalized Thai citizen in 2013. According to an investigation by Thailand's Justice Ministry, Kantor used his American citizenship on 16 occasions when entering and leaving Australia, most recently on January 26 of this year.
Thailand's Interior Ministry maintains that Kantor's actions violated the conditions he agreed to when applying for Thai citizenship.
The order cites Section 19(2) of Thailand's Nationality Act, which addresses conduct that threatens national security, the economy, or society, or violates public morality.
The document states that Kantor knew the naturalization requirements when he submitted his application. It also warns that "if action is not taken promptly, serious harm could be caused to the public and the public interest."
Based on these findings, the interior minister ordered the revocation of Kantor's Thai citizenship.
Thai authorities investigate Chabad institutions in Bangkok
The decision follows a series of raids conducted in early October by Thailand's Department of Special Investigation (DSI), police, tax authorities, and other government agencies.
Authorities searched several institutions in Bangkok, including the Chabad Foundation, the offices of "Gan Chabad," and the Jewish Association of Thailand.
Among the locations inspected was the historic Beit Elisheva Synagogue complex, which is undergoing renovations and reconstruction.
Investigators seized documents, reviewed business registration records, and reportedly identified foreign workers without valid permits. Authorities also examined the registration of more than 60 companies at a single address.
The investigations focus on suspicions that Thai "nominees" were used to circumvent restrictions on foreign ownership of businesses and real estate. Authorities are also examining funding sources and donations.
However, the order revoking Kantor's citizenship does not accuse him of involvement in the alleged financial offenses under investigation. Instead, it is based specifically on his continued use of American citizenship.
Meanwhile, protests are being organized against the Chabad House in Patong, Phuket, with demonstrators using anti-Israel and, at times, antisemitic slogans.
The protests come amid allegations concerning land ownership and business activities that have not been substantiated.
Thai prime minister defends citizenship revocation
Anutin defended the decision in parliament, saying that "everything was done according to the law."
He said individuals granted Thai citizenship must comply with the requirements of naturalization and referred questions about further proceedings to the relevant authorities.
Kantor arrived in Thailand in 1993 and has since become a leading figure in religious and community activities serving Jews and Israelis throughout the country.
He has not yet issued an official response to the decision. Chabad Thailand previously said it was cooperating with the investigations and had nothing to hide.
Members of Thailand's Jewish community have expressed concern over the developments, viewing the revocation of Kantor's citizenship as another sign of growing pressure on Jewish and Israeli institutions in the country.

The Pentagon is quietly drafting a $1.1 trillion defense budget, Politico reported on Thursday, citing a defense industry official, two former officials, and another person familiar with the matter.
Such a budget cuts $400 billion from the “supersized” $1.5 trillion budget requested by US President Donald Trump.
According to Politico, the move could indicate what the political field will look like for the Republican Party after the midterm elections.
“The Pentagon can’t admit this,” one of the sources told Politico, speaking on the condition of anonymity.
The unprecedented budget is hinged on a process called reconciliation, Politico reported, which would allow Republican lawmakers to add $350 billion to a $1.15 trillion base budget.
The sources told Politico that Pentagon planners are considering what defense programs would be prioritized when faced with the reduced budget.
“None of them expect anywhere close to $1.5 trillion,” one of the former officials said. “They are absolutely developing plans [for less], and that is much more the expectation than anything close to $1.5 trillion.”
Budget cut could hinder US efforts to rebuild depleted weapons stockpiles
The reduced funding could disrupt the US Defense Department’s efforts to enter new defense agreements, continue with existing programs, and potentially affect the pace at which the US rebuilds its weapons stockpiles depleted during the war with Iran.
Citing the Pentagon’s latest estimates, the US’s cost of war with Iran sits at around $47 billion, some $29 billion of which is from critical munitions replacements.
White House budget director Russell Vought reportedly said earlier this month that the Trump administration has no developed alternatives to fund critical Pentagon programs if Congress doesn’t back the White House’s plan.
“Republicans are increasingly angry at the administration on the defense front,” the former official said. It’s “unlikely that anything drastic, a $1.5 trillion budget, would happen.”

Binance says $2.54bn in crypto funds frozen amid ‘potential security issue’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:29:24 UTC
09:29:24 KST

Binance says $6.3bn stolen in biggest crypto heist in history
Blockchain intelligence firm attributes attack to North Korean state-sponsored hackers.
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance has said that about $6.3bn in funds have been stolen in a “security incident” that looks to be the biggest crypto heist in history.
The world’s largest crypto exchange said on Thursday that it had suspended all deposits and withdrawals and that about $3bn in funds had been frozen following the apparent hacking.
Binance said an initial investigation suggested that a hacker had been able to make unauthorised transactions after gaining access to an engineer’s compromised laptop.
The company said it would cover all losses, adding that user funds were “safe”.
“Our teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly,” Binance said in a statement to Al Jazeera.
“We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice.”
The company added that it would share a “detailed” technical post-mortem once investigations were complete.
Changpeng Zhao, Binance’s founder and largest shareholder, said earlier that the exchange appeared to have been hacked.
TRM, a blockchain intelligence firm, said in a report that it assessed with “high confidence” that the attack was carried out by North Korea’s hacking unit TraderTraitor, which investigators have linked to the Lazarus Group.
Ari Redbord, TRM’s global head of policy, described the attack as “unprecedented” and a “watershed”.
“When North Korea steals at this scale, the money funds weapons proliferation and other destabilising activity. That makes this a global security issue, not just a crypto theft,” Redbord told Al Jazeera.
The price of Bitcoin, the world’s most popular cryptocurrency, fell about 5 percent following the heist, dropping below $77,000.
“Binance is one of the largest centralised exchanges, and so a blow to confidence in them risks shocking confidence to many retail investors, which could dampen prices of crypto assets,” Sean Foley, an expert in crypto markets at Macquarie University in Sydney, told Al Jazeera.
Foley said the attack highlighted the risks of centralised exchanges and could spur more traders to use decentralised alternatives.
“Any assets held at a centralised exchange are only as safe as the exchange itself, and the larger the exchange’s holdings, the larger a target it becomes,” Foley said.
The Binance hacking dwarfs the previous record for a crypto theft, set in 2025 when North Korean state-backed Lazarus Group carried out a $1.5bn heist on Bybit.
Cybercriminals stole $2.87bn in crypto assets in nearly 150 hacking incidents in 2025, according to the 2026 Crypto Crime Report produced by TRM.
Binance, founded in China by Zhao in 2017, has about $155bn in assets under management, more than any other exchange, according to CoinMarketCap.

What is celebrated on October 30 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:25:23 EET
09:25:23 KST

What is celebrated on October 30 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On October 30, the world celebrates the days of life and orthopedic nurses, while Ukraine marks Coach’s Day and Checklist Day. The faithful honor Saints Zinoviy and Zinoviya.
On October 30, the world marks International Orthopaedic Nurses Day and World Day of Life. According to the new style of the church calendar, Saints Hieromartyrs Zenobius and Zenobia are honored, while according to the old style, Saint Prophet Hosea and Saint Andrew of Crete the Venerable Martyr are commemorated, UNN writes.
International Orthopaedic Nurses Day
A global medical observance established in the United States in 1990 and supported by the National Association of Orthopaedic Nurses and international nursing communities.
The event is intended to recognize the important contribution of nursing staff to the treatment, care and rehabilitation of patients with injuries, musculoskeletal disorders, degenerative joint diseases and those recovering from complex orthopedic surgeries.
World Day of Life
An international human rights and humanitarian observance dedicated to the value of human life at all its stages.
The event emphasizes the importance of protecting fundamental human rights, ensuring access to quality healthcare and safe living conditions, countering violence and armed conflicts, and supporting the mental and physical health of people worldwide.
Coach Day
An unofficial professional holiday established in 1999 at the initiative of the Ukrainian Rhythmic Gymnastics Federation and sports organizations.
The day is dedicated to recognizing the key role of sports mentors, coaches at children's and youth schools, and professional teams in developing discipline, unlocking athletes' potential, achieving high sporting results and promoting a healthy lifestyle.
Checklist Day
An unofficial holiday that highlights the role of checklists in increasing productivity, minimizing human error and ensuring safety in critical sectors.
The date is associated with October 30, 1935, when the crash of the Boeing Model 299 prototype bomber demonstrated the need to introduce mandatory pre-flight checklists for pilots, which later became standard in civil aviation, medicine and management.
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers honor the memory of Saints Hieromartyrs Zenobius, Bishop of Aegea, and his sister Zenobia. They were born in Aegea, gave their inheritance to the poor and dedicated their lives to serving the Christian community.
Zenobius had the gift of healing illnesses through prayer, and during the persecutions under Emperor Diocletian, he and his sister openly professed their faith before the court, for which both were executed in 285.
According to the old calendar, believers honor the memory of Saint Prophet Hosea - one of the 12 Minor Prophets of the Old Testament, who denounced the apostasy of the people of Israel from God and prophesied the coming of the Savior.
They also commemorate Andrew of Crete the Venerable Martyr - a defender of the veneration of icons who suffered a martyr's death in Constantinople during the reign of the iconoclast Emperor Constantine V Copronymus.

New York signs law to protect children from AI chatbots
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:23:12 CST
09:23:12 KST

NEW YORK, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- New York State Governor Kathy Hochul has signed a law aimed at protecting minors from the growing risks of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots, the governor's office said.
The new legislation, signed by Hochul on Wednesday, prohibits companies from offering a range of chatbot features to users under the age of 18, which include pretending to be human, building emotional dependency, encouraging self-harm or engaging in sexually explicit conversations.
Under the new law, violations could result in a civil penalty of up to 25,000 U.S. dollars sought by the state's attorney general.
The bill also establishes a public website where New Yorkers could file complaints against chatbot companies for potential violations.
Several U.S. states have passed laws to restrict use of chatbots for children and enforce stronger safety requirements for AI companies.
In September, California Governor Gavin Newsom signed legislation requiring chatbot developers to conduct and publish annual child safety risk assessments and submit their products to independent audits.
Newsom also signed a law to ban social media platforms from deploying addictive features for users under the age of 16. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 30 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi held talks with Icelandic Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir in Beijing on Thursday.

In the face of the current turbulent international situation, the two sides should strengthen coordination to jointly uphold multilateralism, the international rule of law and the central role of the United Nations in international affairs, he added.
Wang also briefed his Icelandic counterpart on the fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Committee of the Communist Party of China.
China's success is highly significant to the world, Gunnarsdottir said, adding that Iceland attaches great importance to bilateral relations and stands ready to strengthen coordination with China.

North Korea tests attack drones as Kim calls for 'absolute superiority'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
