North Korea tests attack drones as Kim calls for 'absolute superiority'
North Korea has tested attack drones, cruise missiles and rocket launchers at a weapons demonstration, state media reported Friday, as Kim Jong Un called for faster development of military drone and artificial intelligence technology. The tests follow a series of weapons trials and rising tensions with South Korea.
North Korea has test-fired attack drones, missiles and a multiple rocket launcher at a weapons demonstration, state media reported Friday, as leader Kim Jong Un called for faster development of drone and AI technology for military use.
The event came a day after Seoul said Pyongyang had fired 'around a dozen' short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast, though it was not immediately clear whether the launches were linked to the demonstration.
At the event, Kim stressed the "aim to seize the absolute superiority in the drone technology is an indispensable option in the light of the ever-changing patterns of modern warfare", according to KCNA.
He added: "Strength precisely means peace and peace is guaranteed only by strength."
The demonstration featured suicide attack drones, multipurpose drones firing air-to-surface missiles, cruise missiles and 600mm multiple rocket launchers. KCNA said the drones and cruise missiles hit an island target with 100 percent accuracy.
The event follows a slew of recent weapons tests by Pyongyang, including a new precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile, both of which were said to employ AI technology.
Read moreNorth Korea fires 'around a dozen' ballistic missiles amid rising tensions with South Korea
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said its military detected "around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles fired from the Wonsan area of North Korea towards the East Sea", also known as the Sea of Japan.
The missiles flew about 250 kilometres (155 miles), and "South Korea and the United States are conducting a detailed analysis of their exact specifications", Seoul's military said, adding it had stepped up surveillance of possible additional launches.
Seoul's National Security Office, meanwhile, said the launches violated UN Security Council resolutions, labelling them "serious acts that do nothing to help manage the current situation".
Thursday's missile flurry comes against the backdrop of growing tensions over a landmine explosion along the heavily fortified border between the two Koreas that saw three South Korean soldiers wounded.
A joint Seoul-UN investigation earlier this month concluded that North Korea planted the landmines over a year ago.
Seoul accused Pyongyang of "a clear violation of the Armistice Agreement" and demanded an apology, something the North has mockingly dismissed.
Read moreNorth Korea test-fires submarine-launched cruise missiles amid rising tensions
'Show of force'
Last week, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, said the North would place loudspeakers on standby along the border "within days" and had put unspecified "new counter means" on alert.
Both countries have occasionally turned to loudspeakers blaring propaganda across their shared border and other psychological warfare methods.
South Korea days later proposed military talks with the North to "mutually confirm the precise location" of their border and discuss restoring communication channels, but Pyongyang has yet to respond.
The DMZ is one of the world's most heavily fortified frontiers, and landmine incidents have previously heightened tensions.
Seoul and Pyongyang remain technically at war, as the Korean conflict ended in 1953 with a truce rather than a peace treaty.
The ratcheting tensions come as US President Donald Trump's recent overtures to North Korea have raised concerns that Seoul – an ally of Washington – could be sidelined in potential nuclear talks involving Pyongyang.
In his most recent comments, Trump seemingly downplayed the possibility of a summit while insisting his relationship with Kim Jong Un was "very good".

Cuba's international visitors plunge 65.1 pct in first nine months of 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
08:22:41 CST
09:22:41 KST

HAVANA, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Cuba received 65.1 percent fewer international visitors in the first nine months of this year than in the same period of 2025, amid a deepening tourism crisis and tighter U.S. sanctions against the Caribbean island, official data showed Wednesday.
The island received 477,707 international visitors from January to September, down 890,140 from the same period a year earlier, according to figures released by the National Office of Statistics and Information.
Canada, Cuba's largest source market for international tourists, saw the steepest decline, with visitor numbers falling by 430,460. Arrivals from Russia decreased by 67,205, while visits by Cubans living abroad dropped by 60,081. The number of visitors from the United States fell by 42,984.
Tourism is one of the Caribbean country's main sources of foreign currency, but the sector is going through a crisis marked by suspended air routes, hotel closures and the withdrawal of international companies.
The Cuban government said in July that U.S. pressure had prompted seven international hotel chains to withdraw from the island, including Spain's Melia, Iberostar and Barcelo.
The crisis has been compounded by U.S. restrictions on oil supplies imposed since January, including threats of tariffs on countries supplying fuel to the island, as well as expanded sanctions introduced in May.
Cuba has been subject to a U.S. economic, commercial and financial embargo for more than six decades. In June, Cuba's National Assembly of People's Power approved a package of 176 economic and social reform measures aimed at liberalizing the economy, including provisions to attract new investors and expand private-sector participation in tourism. ■

How Netanyahu's bloc gained 83,000 votes but lost 11 Knesset seats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:18:23 UTC
09:18:23 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's political bloc, which won 64 seats in Israel's previous election, lost 11 seats in Tuesday's vote, despite receiving approximately 83,000 more votes than four years ago, an increase of 3.6%. The figure does not include supporters of Gideon Sa'ar, whose faction left the National Unity party and eventually joined Netanyahu's political camp.
By contrast, the bloc of parties seeking to replace Netanyahu and the Arab parties increased their support significantly. Unlike in 2022, no major party associated with the opposition bloc or the Arab parties failed to cross the electoral threshold. Another decisive factor was the sharp rise in voter turnout compared with 2022, particularly among Arab Israelis.
From 64 seats to 53
Likud increased its vote total to approximately 1,163,400, about 48,000 more than in the previous election. However, its share of the overall vote fell sharply, from 23.41% in 2022 to 20.51% this week. In other words, Likud gained votes, but only marginally, while the total number of ballots cast in the election for Israel's 26th Knesset jumped by nearly 20%.
Even when examining Likud's performance independently of its coalition partners, the numbers point to a relative decline. Its vote total increased by 4.3% over four years, compared with a 5.4% expansion of the electorate and a 19% increase in the number of people who voted. In both comparisons, the party lost ground relative to the broader voting population.
Netanyahu's bloc, which includes Likud, Religious Zionism, Otzma Yehudit, United Torah Judaism and Shas, received a combined 48.38% of the vote in the previous election. That share fell to 42.1% in Tuesday's election.
The most striking decline within the bloc was recorded by Shas, whose share of the vote dropped from 8.25% in 2022 to 5.26% in the election for the 26th Knesset. The party received approximately 95,000 fewer votes than four years ago, sending its representation plunging from 11 seats to just six.
Shas, which adopted an unequivocal position against drafting ultra-Orthodox men into the IDF, likely lost religious and traditional voters who shifted their support to other parties, including some within Netanyahu's bloc.
Rabbi Yitzhak Yosef, the party's spiritual leader, explicitly characterized Shas as an ultra-Orthodox party. In a message of encouragement to activists published Thursday afternoon, he wrote: "The community of those who revere God's word has always been the very finest."
United Torah Judaism, meanwhile, increased its vote total by approximately 31,700. Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism, which ran together in the election for the 25th Knesset, collectively gained nearly 100,000 votes compared with their previous joint showing. Some of those additional votes may have come from former Shas supporters.
Overall, Netanyahu's bloc gained approximately 83,000 votes, a relatively small increase compared with the growth recorded by the opposition bloc and Arab parties.
This time, no votes lost below the threshold
In the 2022 election, Meretz and Balad both failed to enter the Knesset. Meretz fell approximately 5,000 votes short of the electoral threshold, while Balad was about 17,000 votes away. Meretz received some 150,800 votes and Balad approximately 138,600, meaning nearly 290,000 votes cast for the two parties did not translate into parliamentary representation.
The parties associated with the bloc seeking to replace Netanyahu that crossed the threshold in 2022 received a combined 1,669,596 votes, excluding Meretz. That represented approximately 35% of all votes cast. Including Meretz, the center-left bloc's share reached about 38.2%.
In Tuesday's election, the four parties making up the opposition bloc received 37.76% of the vote, slightly below the comparable figure from 2022. However, unlike four years ago, every party in the bloc crossed the electoral threshold.
In absolute numbers, the bloc received approximately 2,141,700 valid votes, compared with around 1,820,000 in 2022 when Meretz is included. That represents an increase of more than 17%, helping lift the bloc's representation from 46 seats four years ago to 48 today.
Arab parties gain nine additional seats
The most dramatic gains, however, were recorded by the Arab parties. In cities such as Umm al-Fahm, where only about half of eligible voters participated in the previous election, turnout rose substantially. Sakhnin recorded the highest turnout of any city in Israel, reaching 86.4%.
These figures help explain why the Arab parties increased their combined representation from 10 seats in 2022 to 19 in Tuesday's election. In the previous election, Balad failed to cross the threshold, effectively leaving votes equivalent to approximately four Knesset seats without representation. The additional five-seat gain can largely be attributed to the dramatic rise in turnout among Arab voters.
In the previous election, the three Arab parties received approximately 511,000 votes. This time, the Joint List and Ra'am together won around 835,000 votes, an increase of more than 63%.
The bottom line is that Netanyahu's bloc increased its absolute vote total, but its growth was too modest compared with the expanding electorate and the gains recorded by rival parties. As a result, its parliamentary representation declined substantially.
The opposition bloc increased its vote total by more than 17%, and because none of its constituent parties failed to cross the electoral threshold this time, its representation edged upward.
The biggest winners in terms of increased representation were the Arab parties. With no major Arab party falling below the threshold and voter turnout rising sharply, their combined 19 seats in the 26th Knesset represent the highest number of lawmakers elected on Arab party lists since Israel's establishment.

Student-backed election winners demand sweeping resignations in Serbia
- Published
Serbia's victorious student-led movement has called for top figures in the police, intelligence and judiciary to stand down, days after ousting ex-president Aleksandar Vučić's party from power.
Standing in Pioneers' Park opposite parliament, newly elected MPs on the Student List demanded the immediate dismissal of all police officers who had broken the law, singling out the heads of the police, the BIA security agency and anti-terror unit.
It is not often a European country votes to fully reset its political system overnight, and Serbians have voted to hand the task to a group of novice politicians, made up of intellectuals, professors, artists, athletes and as many as 12 medical doctors and surgeons.
But the handover of power will take weeks, and the students' movement is concerned that evidence of possible wrongdoing could be destroyed in that time.
Just a few days ago, the park they were standing in on Thursday was a tent camp, filled with Vučić loyalists outside his office.
Within hours of him admitting defeat on Sunday night, the camp was dismantled, and a team of volunteers moved in on Monday morning to clean up the mess.
"This is just the first wave of spring cleaning, the new ones are coming now - we are very excited but ready to do it too," said Marija Milovanović, 25, as she scrubbed a park bench.
The student movement emerged from protests following the fatal collapse of a railway station canopy that killed 16 people in November 2024, in Serbia's second largest town Novi Sad.
Their desire was to bring those responsible to justice, and investigate widespread corruption claims blamed for one of the most tragic events in Serbia's modern history.
- How a movement of students brought down Serbia's Vučić 
  - Published3 days ago
They have made some bold promises.
Under their Student Plan, they promise to "halt the plunder, return stolen goods to the state budget, and invest directly in education and the economy".
The purge of Vučić loyalists has already begun at Serbia's state broadcaster RTS, where director Manja Grčić has stepped down.
Newly elected MP Mirjana Nikolić said Serbian citizens had the right to truthful information and RTS had served the interests of the government for years.
The new MPs have also set their sights on replacing the head of Telekom Srbija, Vladimir Lučić.
Vučić loyalist Ana Brnabić, who is currently Serbia's acting president, has accused her opponents of choosing "revolutionary justice, not rule of law," and of aiming to shut down "all of the media they dislike".
But one of the next government's best-known MPs, Dejan Šoškić, argues that key reforms need to be in place fast.
"In the first six months, I would like to see the media scene liberated, fighting against corruption on the way, the institutions operating as prescribed by laws and a lustration law introduced," said Šoškić, an economist who served as governor of the central bank between 2010 and 2012.
By lustration, he means banning from public office members of the Vučić government or party apparatus who are found to have violated the rights of Serbians.
That kind of purge will take time, as all of Serbia's main pillars of authority have been held by Vučić and his party for so long, warns Strahinja Subotić of Belgrade-based European Policy Centre.
Ultimately, he believes the new administration will have to "build bridges to the segments that have been operating well in the past".
All 141 successful candidates were chosen by students from universities across Serbia through a lengthy, secretive and carefully crafted process, and tasked with implementing the movement's plan for a complete rebuild of the country.
That political agenda took months for a highly diverse group of students to agree to. Now it is up to the equally disparate team of successful candidates to put the plan into practice, rather than the students themselves.
Another prominent figure on the Student List, is Radomir Saičić, a professor of organic chemistry at the University of Belgrade.
"While the practical mechanisms will be developed on the go, the new MPs will stick to the students' 1200-page long and detailed plan," he told the BBC.
"Parliament is making decisions, but since this change was led by students' efforts, we would highly value their opinion and work closely with them," he promised.
Not only are they newcomers to politics, but Serbia's election winners have no obvious leader and are faced with a series of complex challenges, including taking on the country's highly complex balancing act on the international stage.
Serbia is both a candidate to join the European Union and maintains close relations with Russia. Its bid to join the bloc has long been on the back-burner, while its Western Balkan neighbours press ahead.
The EU was quick to welcome the Student List victory and has promised to back their push for reforms to the rule of law, media freedom and fight against corruption.
But EU integration occupies a strikingly minor place in the students' election manifesto, which describes the bloc merely as Serbia's "most important economic partner".
For years, Belgrade has balanced its foreign policy between the EU and its eastern partners, Russia and China. Belgrade has managed to stand out in Europe by not imposing sanctions on Moscow since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In return, Serbia has been rewarded with preferential gas prices that have helped maintain domestic stability, and Vladimir Putin publicly endorsed Vučić's bid to remain in power.
That does not mean that the students have any plans to change course, and changing Serbia's foreign policy may not be high on their list.
"Serbia had it own experience with sanctions in the 1990s and we know that they mostly harm ordinary people and do not affect policies of a state," said Dejan Šoškić, referring to UN sanctions imposed during the wars in former Yugoslavia.
The new government's initial focus will most likely be on domestic reform, and the clock is already ticking before the next election campaign, with presidential elections due to take place in December.
Aleksandar Vučić is legally barred from running for a third term as president, but he has promised that his defeated Serbian Progressive Party will fight back: "We will beat them much faster than they can even imagine."

How elections worldwide are testing Trump’s influence abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:13:22 UTC
09:13:22 KST

In August, President Donald Trump claimed that 97% of Republican candidates he backed had won their primary races.
And it's true that Trump has shown an ability to influence races particularly in Republican primaries, picking off politicians he didn't like such as Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, and Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky.
But while he hasn't shied away from expressing his opinions on foreign leaders, his influence over other countries' elections is proving less strong.
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection on Sunday, defeating Trump-aligned Flávio Bolsonaro, whose father Jair had also been a Trump ally.
Also last weekend, a student-led movement in Serbia defeated the ruling party of Aleksandar Vucic, a populist leader who had cultivated ties with Trump and his circle. Vucic had served as Serbia's president from 2017, and as prime minister from 2014 to 2017.
During his concession speech, Vucic said that the loss was due to a "legitimization of a revolution carried out by the people with direct support from various European countries and the American deep state, the one that opposes President Trump."
Earlier this year, Vice President JD Vance had visited Hungary for two days and publicly backed then-Prime Minister Viktor Orban. However, Orban, who is also a staunch ally and endorsed by Trump, lost that election and was ejected from office after 16 years.
In October, Trump also endorsed Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection. While the results of the Oct. 27 election are not finalized yet, the Associated Press said that Netanhayu's Likud party had appeared to lose its majority in the country's parliament.
Still, Trump's influence on any one global election remains variable, experts said.
"Elections are always national first and regional or global a very distant second," Cas Mudde, professor of international affairs at the University of Georgia, told CNBC.
Furthermore, it is also not clear that Trump ever had a great influence over far-right actors elsewhere, said Stijn van Kessel, professor of comparative politics at Queen Mary University of London.
"Far-right parties and politicians like to celebrate each others' victories as it allows them to portray themselves as part of a successful global movement," he said, adding that those relationships can sour quickly when national interests collide and the foreign partner turns toxic in the eyes of the domestic electorate.
Van Kessel pointed to the fallout between Trump and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni earlier this year, which stemmed from Italy's refusal to allow U.S. aircraft to use one of the NATO airbases for its war on Iran.
Trump later claimed that Meloni "begged" him for a photo at the G7 summit, a claim that sparked a denial from Meloni.
Right wing strength
Still, right-wing movements remain strong in numerous places globally. In France, Marine Le Pen is currently the frontrunner to succeed President Emmanuel Macron, according to a compilation of polls by Politico. However, historically she has often started out leading a crowded field of hopefuls before support consolidates around a more moderate candidate.
In Germany, the far-right Alternative fur Deutschland, or AfD party won 20.8% of the vote in the country's February 2025 federal election, making it the country's largest opposition party. Trump ally Javier Milei leads Argentina, and Colombia's new President Abelardo de la Espriella was elected on a far-right platform.
Still, Mudde noted that most far-right leaders disassociate themselves from Trump when he becomes more unpopular in their country. Trump's poll numbers remain near a record low even in the U.S. over issues including the Iran war and the cost of living as energy prices soar.
"Voters are willing to give anyone a shot when they are economically frustrated, but when those experiments fail, they move on to something else," said David Barker, a professor of government at American University in Washington, D.C. At this point, Trump "undermines his allies' ability to maintain support."

Gadkari’s 140 kmph no-challan proposal faces legal, road safety hurdles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:08:16 UTC
09:08:16 KST

NEW DELHI: Road transport minister Nitin Gadkari’s recent announcement that he has asked authorities not to issue challans to cars travelling up to 20% above the prescribed speed limit on expressways — effectively allowing speeds of up to 140 kmph — cannot be implemented under the existing legal framework and may be detrimental to road safety, experts said.The announcement comes at a time when speeding remains the leading cause of road crashes and fatalities in India and globally. In India, more than 58% of road crash deaths (little over one lakh) in 2024 were attributed to speeding. Experts also pointed out that road infrastructure is not necessarily designed to safely accommodate cars travelling at 140 kmph.Speaking at a CII event on Tuesday, Gadkari said, “I was told that people are getting challans for speed violation on expressways for travelling little over 120 kmph. I have directed officers that no challans should be issued, if anyone is driving at speed that’s 20% more than 120 kmph. But if someone crosses that limit, issue challan.”
Under the existing Motor Vehicles Rules, maximum permissible speed for cars on access-controlled expressways is 120 kmph. The limit is 100 kmph on four-lane roads and 70 kmph on other roads. The prescribed limits for other categories of vehicles are lower.
The rules provide a limited relaxation for vehicles travelling up to 5% above the notified speed limit, beyond which the exemption from challans does not apply. This means the existing provision does not support a relaxation of 20% for cars on expressways.
Moreover, state govts and other local authorities are empowered to prescribe lower speed limits on roads falling under their respective jurisdictions, taking into account local conditions and safety requirements.Experts said any nationwide relaxation would therefore need to be examined in the context of these existing provisions and powers of relevant authorities.They said allowing higher speeds could increase both likelihood of crashes and severity of injuries when collisions occur. They added that any move to relax speed limits must be backed by a legal framework and scientific assessment of road safety, rather than a general exemption from enforcement.

Dramatic clifftop rescue of bride and groom-to-be
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:02:46 GMT
09:02:46 KST

Dramatic clifftop rescue of bride and groom-to-be
- Published
A couple who went for a beach walk shortly after getting engaged had to be rescued by the Irish Coast Guard after an incoming tide trapped them against a coastal cliff.
The bride and groom-to-be were hauled approximately 150m (490 ft) to the top of the cliff to safety because rescuers could not reach them by boat or by helicopter.
The dramatic rescue took place during gale-force winds on Achill Island, off the west coast of Ireland, on Monday afternoon.
Coast Guard volunteer Peter McManamon, who coordinated the operation, told BBC News NI: "They were two very lucky people."
It is believed the pair are originally from overseas but live in Ireland and were on a visit to Achill Island, off the County Mayo coast, when the incident happened.
McManamon said the couple had gone for a walk along Keel Beach when the tide began to come in behind them - at one point reaching above knee-level.
"They got engaged in Achill and they were just walking along [the beach] and they went out too far on the rocks," he explained.
"The weather conditions were atrocious there, and in that particular area the tide has come in very quick."
Unable to get off the sand because of the towering cliff behind them, the couple called 999 and asked for a coast guard rescue.
"It was too rough for a rib (rigid inflatable boat) to be tasked - it was blowing Force 8 to 10 at the time and the wave conditions wouldn't let us," McManamon said.
"We tried to walk out along the rocks to them but... the waves were just coming in and it was just too dangerous to put the crew in, so the helicopter was tasked."
'Hypothermia was beginning to set in'
Coast Guard helicopter R118, based in County Sligo, flew to the scene but the force of the winds meant its crew were unable to help the stranded couple.
"When the helicopter came, they tried to move in to winch them but there was too much down draft off the mountain for it to happen," McManamon explained.
So he then deployed climbers from Achill Island Coast Guard's cliff rescue team who abseiled down the cliff to pluck the couple out of the rising tide.
"The water was coming in around them - the water was roughly just above their knees," McManamon recalled.
The couple were taken to safety in stages. The woman was brought to higher ground first while her fiance waited with "waves crashing" around his legs.
Once they were both out of immediate risk, the climbers used ropes to separately haul both casualties a further 150m to the clifftop.
"They were very cold - hypothermia was beginning to set in," McManamon said.
However, the remote beauty spot could not be reached by vehicle so the casualties then faced a 2km (1.2 mile) walk down the hill to a waiting ambulance.
There, they were treated by paramedics before being taken to hospital for checks, but they did not need to be admitted.
McManamon said it is never a safe decision to walk along coastal cliffs in such weather conditions.
"It can be a dangerous spot, the locals don't really go near it at all," he said, explaining that other parts of the beach are more suitable for walking or swimming.
McManamon has been a member of the Irish Coast Guard for 20 years, the last seven of which he has spent at "officer in charge" at Achill Island Coast Guard Unit.
The role is voluntary.
Monday's rescue operation took more than seven hours, with his crew finally leaving cliff at about 21:30 local time.
"I didn't get a chance to talk to them [the couple] properly, I was too busy organising my own team," McManamon said.
"We were that wet and hungry, we just wanted to get tidied up and get our equipment back and to get to our own homes and families."
Popular site to pop the question?
McManamon agreed that it was one of the most dramatic engagement stories that he had come across.
Having celebrated his own 25th wedding anniversary earlier this month, he has some affinity with the couple - in fact Keel Beach was the setting for his own marriage proposal.
However, he was quick to point out that he popped the question "on the safe side of the beach".

Why is North Korea fortifying its border with South Korea?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:02:42 UTC
09:02:42 KST

A North Korean soldier sits on a self-propelled howitzer deployed along the border separating the two Koreas on 27 October. Photograph: Kim Hong-Ji/Reuters
A North Korean soldier sits on a self-propelled howitzer deployed along the border separating the two Koreas on 27 October. Photograph: Kim Hong-Ji/Reuters
Why is North Korea fortifying its border with South Korea?
A row over a landmine blast and a threat to resume loudspeaker broadcasts has highlighted Kim Jong-un’s military ambitions
Last week North Korea hit the headlines with a vow to fire up its loudspeaker systems to blare propaganda into the South, but the latest dispute comes against a backdrop of militarisation of the border by Kim Jong-un that has been years in the making.
Since April 2024, North Korea has been working on building a permanent fortified border through the demilitarised zone (DMZ) that divides the two sides, work that has led to a mine explosion that injured three South Korean soldiers and plunged ties to new lows.
Here’s a brief guide to what is being built, what Pyongyang says it’s for, and why even deciding where the border is has become such a fraught issue.
What is North Korea building at the border?
The 250km border is already fortified but not in the way many might traditionally think. It is more of a buffer than a barrier at the moment, in the form of a 4km-wide demilitarised zone (DMZ) which runs across the Korean peninsula.
Since 2024, the North is thought to have laid about 960,000 mines in the DMZ, close to half of all the mines thought to be in an area that is already one of the most heavily mined places on earth.
North Korea has also been constructing a continuous physical barrier on its side of the zone, along the full length of the line. It is made up of wire fencing, alongside minefields, tactical roads, and anti-tank barriers laid on ground stripped of vegetation. South Korea’s joint chiefs of staff say the ground-clearing is nearly finished while the construction work is 40-60% complete, and expect it to be finished by the second half of 2028.
Under the 1953 armistice that halted but did not end the Korean war, the DMZ was to be cleared of military forces and equipment.
North Korean workers are seen erecting barbed-wire fences at border areas in Hwanghae province on 25 October. Photograph: YONHAP/EPA
Why is Kim Jong-un doing this?
Kim Jong-un has abandoned the once-cherished goal of reunification. As recently as 2018, the leaders of the two sides met at the border, and their athletes marched together at the Winter Olympics. But in December 2023, Kim redefined the South as a separate, hostile state, and the construction began a few months later.
Experts in Seoul read Kim’s U-turn as removing the contradiction that lay in threatening nuclear war on people who the North had once called compatriot. When engagement with Seoul collapsed and Moscow emerged as a patron, Pyongyang was left free to press for recognition as a nuclear state.
They also say the construction achieves several goals: stopping North Koreans leaving, slowing any South Korean advance in the event of a return to warfare, and turning the frontier into something that works as an international border.
Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of the North Korean leader, has said the work will eliminate the danger of a conflict at the border. However, analysts argue the opposite: that the new artillery and missile units being installed make an accidental clash more likely to escalate.
Why are tensions rising now?
On 21 September, three South Korean soldiers were wounded by a landmine blast while clearing a path inside the DMZ. One soldier lost his foot.
South Korea’s military concluded the blast was caused by a North Korean mine placed south of the border, and Seoul has demanded an apology. Pyongyang denied any responsibility for the incident and called it a “self-staged farce”.
South Korea says North Korean troops have repeatedly crossed the border during the work to fortify their side of the line, leading to warning shots that Pyongyang says are provocations by “armed rogues”.
Kim Yo-jong has since issued about 10 statements in less than a month criticising the South, a frequency Seoul’s unification ministry called unusual. She recently said the North’s propaganda loudspeakers would be ready to blast across the border within days.
Does anyone know where the border actually runs?
No. The armistice drew the military demarcation line (MDL) on maps at a scale of 1:50,000, where a line just a millimetre wide covers about 50 metres of ground. A total of 1,292 numbered markers were then planted to fix it in place, but only about 200 are still identifiable.
So each side has reconstructed it following its own methodology. Seoul works from mapping aligned with the US National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency, while the US-led UN Command (UNC), which oversees the armistice, uses its own survey from a decade ago. North Korea is believed to simply connect the markers it can still see. South Korea’s defence ministry has found that its line and the UNC’s disagree at about 60% of the points they have compared, by tens of metres in places. It is unclear how differently the two Koreas read the line.
North Korean troops reportedly crossed the border about 50 times in August and September this year alone, compared with 17 instances in 2025.
Visitors in Gimpo, South Korea, look toward the North from an observation deck. Photograph: Kim Hong-Ji/Reuters
Is anything being done to resolve the border issue?
Seoul is trying. It has proposed talks to confirm jointly where the MDL runs, restore military communication channels severed in 2023 and agree how to avoid accidental clashes. It is the second such offer in a year. Pyongyang ignored the first.
South Korea’s defence ministry calls the work an armistice violation and has demanded that it stop. The UNC, on the other hand, has said that construction and fortification do not automatically constitute violations, and that each case has to be judged on its facts.

By Alasdair Pal
SYDNEY, Oct 30 (Reuters) - An Australian woman convicted of murdering three of her estranged husband’s relatives with a meal laced with deadly mushrooms lost an attempt on Friday to appeal her conviction, with a court also quashing her chances of parole.
Erin Patterson, 51, was found guilty last year of murdering her three elderly in-laws by serving them Beef Wellington contaminated with poisonous death cap mushrooms, in a case that captivated Australia.
She was sentenced to life in prison with a 33-year non-parole period, among the longest terms ever handed to a woman in the country.
Patterson has always denied wrongdoing, saying the deaths were accidental.
She had appealed on multiple grounds, arguing that certain evidence should have been kept from the trial, that her cross-examination was unfair, and that a mistake placing the jury in the same hotel as other parties to the case compromised the result.
A panel of three judges on Friday said those grounds were insufficient for an appeal.
A separate appeal by the prosecution, which argued giving Patterson a non-parole period was inadequate in light of the seriousness of her crimes, was successful.
“This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated, and stands to be denounced in the strongest terms,” Justice Stephen McLeish, speaking on behalf of a panel of three judges hearing the appeals, told the Supreme Court of Victoria in Melbourne.
“In all the circumstances, after anxious consideration, we have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period.”
Patterson’s lawyer did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
A jury last year found Patterson invited her mother-in-law Gail Patterson, father-in-law Donald Patterson and Gail’s sister Heather Wilkinson to a 2023 lunch at her home in Leongatha, a town of about 6,000 people, some 135 km (84 miles) southeast of Melbourne, and fed them the poisoned lunch.
She was also convicted of the attempted murder of Ian Wilkinson, Heather’s husband, who survived the meal.
The 11-week trial, held in the nearby country town of Morwell, attracted worldwide attention, and the case has since spawned several podcasts and books.
American streaming service Paramount+ this week announced New Zealand actor Melanie Lynskey would play Patterson in a six-part series dramatising the case.

The world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange has been hit by an industry-record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack, with experts identifying North Korea as the likely culprit.
Binance has scrambled to freeze the affected assets, with about $3bn located so far. The company gave no update on the other $3.3bn as Binance’s co-founder Yi He said the company would cover “all hacking losses”.
Analysts attributed the attack to North Korean state-backed hackers. North Korea has a history of crypto hacking and was behind the theft of approximately $1.5bn in virtual assets from a Tokyo cryptocurrency exchange last year, according to the FBI, in what was the previous record crypto heist.
TRM, a crypto analysis firm, blamed the attack with “high confidence” on TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit. Chainalysis, another analysis outfit, also attributed the heist to TraderTraitor.
Binance did not explicitly confirm that funds had been stolen, although TRM and Chainalysis claimed more than $6bn had been taken. The company said its teams were “working around the clock” to resolve the problem.
An initial investigation suggested the breach may have started with a hacked laptop belonging to one of Binance’s engineers, which let an attacker gain access to one of its systems and make unauthorised withdrawals, Binance said.
Binance, which allows users to buy, sell and trade digital assets, has 335 million registered users globally and had about $162.8bn in assets under custody as of the exchange’s 2025 annual report.
Richard Teng, a co-chief executive of Binance, said: “Bottom line – your money is safe, and we’re covering every loss.”
The company said in a statement: “As a precaution, all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while our security teams conduct checks, secure wallet infrastructure and trace affected assets, with the close support of our law enforcement and industry partners.”
Markets reacted immediately in early Asian trading on Friday, and bitcoin – the most popular crypto asset by far – dropped more than 3% to a six-week low of $76,368. Shares in the crypto exchange Coinbase Global slid 4.8%, while those of the bitcoin buyer Strategy fell nearly 6% in extended US trading.
Binance was founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao, who in 2023 pleaded guilty to a felony in the US related to his failure to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as CEO. Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.
Zhao posted to X on Thursday: “User funds are safe!” but added that the incident “does look like a hack on Binance”. He added that while he did not manage Binance any more, “as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered”.
If confirmed, the incident could be the world’s biggest crypto heist, according to Chainalysis and other industry experts. “It’s the biggest hack in history,” said Aravind Srinivasan, the head of the large crypto market maker GSR’s systematic OTC business.
Beyond the potential loss of assets, the security breach was likely to have wider ramifications for crypto, which had already been under pressure lately because of higher US interest rates and softer demand from exchange-traded fund buyers, analysts said.
“It may further dampen risk appetite and prompt investors to reassess the safety of assets held on centralised exchanges, as well as counterparty, solvency and liquidity risks,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, based in Hong Kong.
Binance runs a secure asset fund for users, which is a reserve held entirely in bitcoin that is intended to protect user assets in cases of security breaches, according to its website.
Bernardo Brites, the CEO of Trace Finance, a payments and stablecoin infrastructure company, said: “It’s becoming very hard to counter hacks as AI can find vulnerabilities faster than you can fix them. My view is that users will move away from smaller and medium-sized exchanges, [as it is] becoming too risky to park your money somewhere that couldn’t cover a hack of meaningful size.”
The stablecoin issuer Tether said it had frozen nearly $1.57bn in assets linked to the incident, while Circle froze more than $800m.
World Liberty Financial, a crypto company linked to Trump and his family, said on Thursday it had worked with the cryptocurrency custodian BitGo to freeze funds stolen in what it described as a Binance hack.
Binance’s Yi said $27m in stablecoins and about $2m worth of World Liberty tokens had been frozen.
The incident adds to a string of crypto thefts. Last year attackers stole $2.9bn worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 attacks, according to researchers at TRM Labs. In September the cryptocurrency exchange Bitget said roughly $350m in crypto had been stolen from its platform, underscoring the industry’s vulnerability to hackers.
Authorities have warned that organised crime groups are increasingly using cryptocurrencies to move funds across borders outside the traditional financial system.
Binance.US, a separate cryptocurrency exchange, said it was not affected by the security incident.
Coinbase said it was unaffected and was monitoring the situation.
In an unrelated incident earlier on Thursday, the prediction market operator Polymarket temporarily halted trading after a security incident involving a third-party provider. It later resumed trading and said it would fully reimburse affected traders.
With Reuters and the Associated Press

“Russia is deliberately hunting civilians: on trains, at stations, in residential buildings,” Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi said on the Telegram app.

A new missile attack hit districts of Kyiv just before 11 p.m. (2100 GMT) killing one person, the city’s military administration said. Warehouses were set ablaze and falling debris damaged a building on the east side of the Dnipro River.
A few hours earlier, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy had described the attacks as “very cruel” and “deliberate when everyone expects de-escalation steps”.
Zelenskiy warned that Ukraine had intelligence “about preparations by the Russians of new ballistic missile strikes. We need the means to take out all this Russian evil. We are expecting relevant decisions.”
The six-day truce brokered with US help applied only to southern Ukraine’s Kherson region, where a humanitarian mission was underway to provide relief to the Russian-held town of Oleshky, marooned in a war zone since the start of Moscow’s 2022 invasion.
Both sides issued virtually identical statements saying de-mining operations had been completed and the operation could begin to allow aid into the town and permit residents to head out if they wanted to leave.
Elsewhere, Russian drone and missile attacks on critical infrastructure including the rail network have upended civilian life and ravaged the economy. The strikes have exploited an acute shortage of air defence missiles.

Another attack on Dnipro hit a student dormitory, setting it ablaze, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. He added that a day of assaults had cut power to 350,000 households in the city.
Russia’s mounting bombing campaign against Ukrainian cities has regularly killed civilians. Moscow has denied targeting civilians.
NEW STRIKES ACROSS UKRAINE
Two teenage girls were killed on a central street in Chernihiv in northern Ukraine, and three people died in strikes on residential buildings in the central city of Kremenchuk.
In Chernihiv, in addition to the two dead teenagers, 23 people including four children were wounded in a drone attack on a busy downtown street.
“Ordinary, peaceful people were attacked who were just going to work, going about their daily business, making plans for the day,” said Dmytro Bryzhynskyi, head of the city’s military administration.
In Kremenchuk, strikes on a residential block and private buildings killed three people and wounded 32, the regional governor said. Russian drones also struck city buses in three separate attacks on southeastern Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia, wounding six, officials there said.
Thursday’s strikes came amid renewed efforts to revive US-backed peace talks to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War Two.
New three-way talks are expected to take place next month, with Ukrainian officials, including top presidential adviser Kyrylo Budanov, urging pressure on Moscow from Kyiv’s partners.

Policy paper: UK Offset Policy
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:01:00 GMT
09:01:00 KST

UK Offset Policy
Securing additional UK industrial, capability, and economic benefit from selected overseas defence and security procurements.
Documents
Details
The UK Offset Policy sets out how the Ministry of Defence will secure additional industrial, capability, and economic benefits for the United Kingdom from selected defence and national security acquisitions from overseas suppliers.
The policy will be applied selectively and proportionately. Where it applies, an overseas supplier will enter into a separate Offset Agreement and deliver additional activity supporting UK defence capability, industrial resilience, skills, innovation, supply chains and economic growth.
The policy forms part of the Defence Industrial Strategy and the Government’s wider approach to ensuring that defence investment strengthens national security and delivers long-term value for the United Kingdom.

Defence contracts to prioritise British jobs and skills
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:01:00 GMT
09:01:00 KST

Defence contracts to prioritise British jobs and skills
Overseas firms winning UK defence contracts to be required to invest benefits back into the UK under new Offsets policy.
- Major changes will require overseas defence contractors to invest benefits back into the UK up to the same contract value, such as jobs, skills and industry.
- Government backs British business by prioritising buying British defence contracts wherever possible, as part of changes outlined in the Budget.
- Comes after the government set a target of 3% GDP spend on defence in 2030, on the path to the NATO commitment of 3.5% in 2035.
British workers, businesses and apprentices will benefit from major changes which will see more defence work carried out in the UK thanks to the launch of a world-leading Offsets policy.
Under the new rules, overseas companies that win significant UK defence contracts will be required to invest back into Britain, through new British jobs and apprenticeships, opening UK factories, investing in domestic suppliers, transferring technology and innovation know-how.
This means contracts worth over £50 million will be considered for offsets. The contractors will be required to deliver such benefits to the UK that could reach the same value as the contract, for example a £100m contract could see new jobs, facilities, or skills training up to the same £100m value in the UK.
The government is prioritising buying British defence contracts wherever possible. Where it must buy defence equipment from overseas, this new approach will ensure British workers and businesses still benefit.
The move will encourage overseas defence suppliers to build enduring partnerships with UK industry, helping UK SMEs to access global supply chains and create new opportunities for growth.
Announced today by the Chancellor and Defence Secretary on a visit to BAE Systems Scotstoun, Glasgow, the policy applies to overseas defence contracts worth £50 million or more, delivered through the government’s Back British approach set out in the Budget.
Chancellor of the Exchequer, John Healey MP said:
  We are putting British jobs and British businesses at the heart of how Government spends taxpayers’ money.
When a big contract goes overseas, these changes will ensure 100% of the value creates new opportunities for workers and businesses here at home, strengthening our industrial base and supporting growth across Britain.
The defence economy in Scotland is worth £2.5 billion and directly supports 12,200 jobs, backed by the recent £10 billion Norway export deal for Type 26 Frigates supporting 2,000 local jobs and the £453 million Typhoon radar system supporting 300 roles in Edinburgh.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP said:
  Every pound we invest in defence should be judged by what it does for Britain. That’s why we are backing British by buying British wherever we can.
Even when that is not possible, we are acting to ensure that any investment brings jobs, skills and investment back home, strengthening our national security by boosting our domestic industry.
Since 2016, over £35.2 billion has been spent on defence contracts and services with industry overseas, representing 11 per cent of total MOD direct expenditure with industry and commerce between 2016/17 and 2025/26.
The new policy means future spending of this kind will also support jobs, skills and growth at home.
Companies that win qualifying contracts will be able to meet their commitment in several ways, including:
- creating British jobs and apprenticeships
- opening or expanding factories in the UK
- investing in British suppliers
- transferring technology and know-how to UK firms
- using more UK-made components
The UK joins allies who already use similar offset type polices to boost the economic benefit from defence procurement, such as Poland, Norway and the Netherlands.
Under the policy, overseas contracts worth over £50 million will be considered for offset. A new central Offset Authority will agree, value and monitor delivery through dedicated Offset Agreements, ensuring consistency across the lifetime of each arrangement.
Where the UK must buy defence equipment from overseas, this policy ensures Britain gets something back. The approach will be applied on a case-by-case basis by the MOD.
Last year alone, the MOD’s defence investment supported 274,000 jobs in UK industry, up 10 per cent on the year before, with £34.1 billion going to businesses based in the UK - and 85% of MOD expenditure already goes to UK firms.
The government’s fully funded Defence Investment Plan - backed by £298 billion over the next four years - will deliver stronger front-line military capability, supporting jobs, businesses and economic growth across the UK.
The policy delivers key commitments from the Defence Investment Plan and Defence Industrial Strategy, and forms part of the Government’s wider Back British approach through the Budget.
It follows the Chancellor’s announcements on Wednesday confirming a new commitment for the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank to deploy up to £5 billion over the next 4 years into defence, dual use and other sectors that support our national security alongside the commencing of treaty negotiations with the Netherlands, Poland, and Finland on the Multilateral Defence Mechanism to procure at scale and stockpile vital equipment which the UK has access to.
The Offset Policy is published today (30 October) and will apply to a select number of procurements from April 2027, with suppliers notified early and clearly where offset requirements will apply.

Samsung's Q3 net profit surges sixfold on booming AI chip demand
South Korean technology giant Samsung Electronics reported a more than sixfold increase in third-quarter net profit, driven by robust demand for semiconductors used in artificial intelligence infrastructure, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Yonhap.
According to the company's regulatory filing released Thursday, net earnings reached 75.13 trillion won (US$56.2 billion) in the July–September period, marking a 514.6% increase from 12.22 trillion won recorded a year earlier.
Samsung's operating profit climbed 783.1% year-on-year to 107.44 trillion won, while consolidated revenue advanced 126.9% to 195.25 trillion won.
The results made Samsung the first technology company worldwide to surpass 100 trillion won in quarterly operating profit. The South Korean chipmaker also extended its record-breaking streak, reporting all-time-high quarterly revenue and operating earnings for the fourth consecutive quarter.
The semiconductor division was the main contributor to the company's performance, generating 106.5 trillion won in operating profit, equivalent to approximately 99.1% of Samsung's overall operating earnings.
The company attributed the division's strong results to increased shipments of sixth-generation high-bandwidth memory (HBM4) chips and growing demand from AI data centers and server manufacturers.
Samsung, the world's largest memory chip producer, has benefited considerably from expanding global investment in AI infrastructure. The company was also the first in the industry to launch mass production and commercial shipments of HBM4 memory.
Looking ahead, Samsung anticipates continued growth in memory chip demand during the final quarter of 2026, supported by ongoing investment in artificial intelligence technologies.
The company also expects favorable conditions in the semiconductor market to persist into 2027, citing strong AI-related capital expenditure and constraints on chip supply.
However, performance across Samsung's other businesses was less favorable.
Its Device Experience division, which includes smartphones and consumer electronics, recorded an operating loss of 800 billion won, marking a second straight quarter in negative territory.
Despite the loss, the division registered higher sales compared with the previous year, supported partly by the introduction of premium smartphones, including the Galaxy Z Fold8. Rising component prices and difficult market conditions continued to weigh on profitability.
Separately, Samsung announced a quarterly cash dividend of 4,601 won per common and preferred share.
The company estimates that total shareholder returns in 2026 could reach between 90 trillion and 110 trillion won. With approximately 35 trillion won already distributed or committed, an additional 55 trillion to 75 trillion won may be returned through dividends, share repurchases and share cancellations.
Samsung's announcement followed another record-breaking earnings report from domestic rival SK hynix, which unveiled a shareholder return initiative exceeding 100 trillion won for 2026.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Samsung had forecast a nearly 1,800% year-on-year surge in second-quarter operating profit, driven by booming demand for AI memory chips.

2026-10-29

The Department of Justice on Thursday escalated its lawsuit targeting potential certification of the result of Alaska's Senate election, which it argues could be tainted by the candidacy of a man with the same name as incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.
The DOJ filed an amended version of its original complaint to add a new legal claim and details from Wednesday's New York Times article detailing alleged efforts by the people in the campaign of Democratic nominee Mary Peltola to recruit a retired schoolteacher named Dan J. Sullivan into the race.
The amended complaint in Anchorage federal court suggests that Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senate Campaign Committee misled Judge Sharon Gleason by saying in recent court filings they lacked knowledge about why the retiree Sullivan entered the race earlier this year.
The amended suit also notes that Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, late Wednesday ordered the state Department of Public Safety to investigate whether the alleged recruitment of the retired teacher violated criminal or civil laws. Dunleavy cited the Times' report as the reason for that probe.
"The New York Times has reported that Alaskans For Mary and the DSCC were well aware of the purposes of Daniel J. Sullivan's candidacy: they orchestrated his sham campaign for the purpose of misleading Alaskan voters and getting Peltola elected," the DOJ said in its amended complaint.
The DOJ, in a separate filing Thursday, said that the filing of the amended complaint with the new claim under the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution means that motions to dismiss the case by the state, Peltola's campaign, the DSCC and others are now moot. The DOJ cited precedent in the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals for that argument.
Gleason had given the DOJ until 5 p.m. Alaska Time Thursday to respond to the motions to dismiss, which have asked her to toss out the DOJ's original complaint before Election Day, Nov. 3.
The judge has yet to rule whether the dismissal motions are now moot.
Later Thursday, Alaska Division of Elections Director Carol Beecher and other state election boards blasted the DOJ in a motion asking Gleason to expedite consideration of a motion to dismiss the amended complaint.
"Rather than filing a substantive opposition to the Division's motion to dismiss, the United States has filed an amended complaint adding a second—but equally meritless— count (relying on the same underlying legal theory) and then opposed the Division's motion on the ground that it has been mooted by the amended complaint," the motion said.
"In the context of these expedited proceedings, the Court should not tolerate this gamesmanship," the motion said.
Peltola's campaign and the DSCC, in a subsequent motion to dismiss late Thursday, scoffed at the DOJ's new complaint and claim that it misled Gleason.
"In the portion of the proposed answer DOJ cites, Alaskans for Mary and DSCC stated that they did not have knowledge or information sufficient to admit or deny an allegation about Daniel J. Sullivan's mental state — whether he filed to run 'with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot's fairness or neutrality,' " the campaign and DSCC said in the motion.
"The only one who could possibly know Daniel J. Sullivan's true reasons for filing as a candidate is Daniel J. Sullivan, and Alaskans for Mary and DSCC's statement that they could not admit or deny that allegation was entirely proper."
"The Court should dismiss the Amended Complaint, with prejudice, before election
day," the motion said. 
"DOJ's choice to file the Amended Complaint, which adds nothing of substance to the original complaint, is a transparent attempt to keep this case alive for a few more days to cast a pall over the upcoming election and let the federal government continue to interfere in Alaska's elections."
The DOJ's lawsuit, originally filed on Oct. 23, seeks to block the state from immediately certifying any Senate election result "that may be impacted by voter confusion ... pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan."
President Donald Trump has said he ordered the DOJ to file the suit.
The political stakes in the Alaska Senate race are potentially momentous. The winner could determine the power balance in the Senate, where Republicans hold a six-vote majority.
The new DOJ filings came as NBC News reported that the department "has issued at least three dozen new subpoenas and document preservation requests" to Peltola's campaign offices and those of the former schoolteacher Sullivan.
Peltola's campaign and the DSCC, which have previously denied involvement in the retiree Sullivan's campaign to CNBC, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the amended DOJ suit.
Peltola's campaign, in a statement to CNBC on Thursday in response to Dunleavy's announcement, said, "Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any politician will keep her away from that fight."
"The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign," the campaign said.
Trump, before flying to South Carolina for a campaign rally Thursday morning, was asked by a reporter whether Senate Republicans should try to block Peltola from taking the seat in January if she wins Tuesday's election.
"Well, you're going to have to see what happens," Trump said.
"It's hard to believe that she can even be allowed to run. Frankly, I don't know how you can allow somebody like that to run," the president said.
Trump said the retired teacher Sullivan "was just put there as a fraud."
"But people aren't going to know that, so nobody's going to know what to do," Trump said.
Both Peltola's campaign and the DSCC have argued that Trump and other Republicans are being hypocritical in their claims about the Senate race.
"Republicans have a long history of recruiting and propping up candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns — including recruiting a prisoner with a New York address to run against Mary Peltola and spending nearly half a million dollars to secure a spot on the ballot in Alaska for an Arizona resident in the Senate race this cycle," a DSCC spokesperson said Wednesday.
The DSCC pointed to instances of Republicans promoting third-party and dark horse candidates in the current election cycle and past ones to increase chances of a GOP candidate winning a race.
Alaska election officials in a court filing have said the Division of Elections "has taken significant steps to distinguish" between the two Sullivans on the ballot, "so that voters can easily determine which candidate is which."
The retired teacher's name on the ballot is spelled out "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr." with no other words next to it.
Directly below his name, Sen. Sullivan is listed as "Sullivan, Dan. S." with the words "Registered Republican, incumbent" next to his name in parentheses.
Alaska election officials said in their court filing that "the United States lacks authority to intervene in state elections at all, much less in support of a favored candidate."

France braces for ‘very high risk’ of disorder at Halloween protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:52:30 UTC
08:52:30 KST

France braces for ‘very high risk’ of disorder at Halloween protests
Authorities vow firm action against violence as yellow vest and student movements announce widespread demonstrations.
France’s interior minister has announced the deployment of 70,000 police officers across the country in preparation for planned protests on Saturday, coinciding with Halloween.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Thursday that security measures, including the use of armoured vehicles and water cannon introduced last week, will be strengthened.
Nationwide protests over the rising cost of living have rocked France, with some degenerating into large-scale looting and riots.
“The day of October 31 presents a very high risk of public disorder,” Nunez said at a news conference.
About 70,000 police officers and gendarmes will be mobilised, matching the number deployed at last week’s protests, he said, calling the move an “exceptional measure”.
Demonstrations last Saturday drew about 410,000 protesters nationwide, according to the interior ministry, though unions put the figure at roughly double that. The ministry said more than 2,700 people were arrested a week earlier.
Warning on Halloween masking
The “yellow vest” movement and student unions have called for a new day of protests on Saturday.
Nunez warned demonstrators against using Halloween as “a legitimate reason to hide one’s face” to cause disturbances in public areas.
He told reporters demonstrations would be allowed, but “not in city centres, where there is a risk of public disorder”.
The interior minister issued a warning to far-right groups that clashed with left-wing protesters at rallies in about 15 French cities.
“We will tolerate no excesses,” he said, and pledged an “extremely firm” response.
Nunez accused the “ultra-left” movement and some yellow vest activists of circulating messages on social media promoting demonstrations on Halloween evening that called for a “revolution”.
“These gatherings will be banned,” he said.
The yellow vest movement has already announced a “third act” of its protests on Halloween and called for demonstrations outside the National Assembly and all town halls in the country.

Israel election results unaffected by foreign interference probe, committee says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:48:35 UTC
08:48:35 KST

Israel's Central Elections Committee said early Friday that the Shin Bet security agency's investigation into suspected election bribery and foreign interference would not affect the final results of Tuesday's parliamentary election. 
In a recorded statement released overnight, acting committee director general Dean Livne also stressed that the investigation does not concern any particular community and dismissed reports circulated throughout Thursday as entirely unfounded. Livne said the statement was issued with the approval of committee chairman Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg.
"Yesterday, the head of the Shin Bet presented classified intelligence to the committee chairman, which led to the opening of the investigation," Livne said. "With the chairman's approval, the main points were also presented to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, opposition leader Yair Lapid and Yashar! party chairman Gadi Eisenkot."
Livne emphasized that access to the intelligence was extremely restricted because of its high security classification. "No further details can be disclosed, but reports published throughout the day are entirely unfounded," he said.
"The investigation is taking place alongside the Central Elections Committee's ongoing work and will not affect the final results submitted to the president. Nor does it concern any particular community," Livne added. Once the investigation is completed, its findings will be submitted to Sohlberg, who will assess their scope and implications. The committee will update the public as quickly as possible, subject to the necessary restrictions.
Final election results confirmed
In a separate statement, the Central Elections Committee confirmed the final vote count for Israel's 26th Knesset, as announced earlier Thursday evening. Likud won 27 seats, Yashar! 21, Together 12, the Joint List 11, the Democrats 8, Ra'am 8, Yisrael Beiteinu 7, Otzma Yehudit 7, United Torah Judaism 7, Shas 6 and Religious Zionism 6.
The committee said the final voter turnout was 77.9%, with 5,716,665 votes counted. Of those, 5,690,778 were valid and 25,887 were invalid. The electoral threshold, set at 3.25% of valid votes, was 184,947 votes.
The committee stressed that the results remain subject to minor corrections over the coming days as part of its routine verification process, which includes reexamining a substantial number of polling stations, correcting data entry or transcription errors and reviewing complaints submitted by the public and candidate lists. "Subject to minor corrections, as in every election, these are the results that will be submitted to the president of the State of Israel on Wednesday, November 4," the committee said.
The Shin Bet issued its own statement Thursday concerning the investigation into suspected violations of election integrity, emphasizing that the inquiry was limited in scope and did not implicate any entire community. "An investigation of this kind is focused and limited, and does not cast suspicion on or accuse an entire community that exercised its democratic and legal right to vote," the agency said. "Only those who acted unlawfully will be dealt with."
The controversy began after Sohlberg sent a letter to Shin Bet chief David Zini instructing him to investigate suspicions involving foreign actors. According to reports, the intelligence concerns suspected transfers of money from Qatar, allegations Doha has categorically denied. Turkey has also rejected allegations of involvement.
"The integrity of elections is at the heart of democracy," Sohlberg wrote to Zini. Although he stressed that he could not assess the substance of the allegations, he said their reported connection to foreign actors made a thorough investigation essential. Such an inquiry, he wrote, was necessary to protect the integrity of Knesset elections and prevent unlawful activity intended to undermine democratic institutions or engage in subversion.
In its statement Thursday evening, the Shin Bet clarified that the intelligence underlying the investigation came from information gathered by the agency as part of its legal responsibility to detect foreign influence. It did not originate from any political party or political figure on either side of Israel's political spectrum. The agency also said that, apart from Sohlberg, no one outside the Shin Bet had access to the information before the elections concluded.
The Shin Bet stressed that the investigation was ongoing and cautioned against speculation about the nature of the allegations. "Any statement concerning the content or substance of the suspicions does not reflect the Shin Bet's position and should have been avoided," the agency said. The findings will be presented to the chairman of the Central Elections Committee, who is authorized to make decisions on the matter.
The agency said all relevant information would be submitted to election officials in full, transparently and without interpretation once the investigation was completed. It also confirmed that, at Sohlberg's request and with his approval, Zini had personally briefed Netanyahu, Eisenkot and Lapid over the preceding 24 hours on the main allegations being investigated. The Shin Bet emphasized that it is a state institution whose actions are carried out solely under its legal mandate, with oversight from its professional and legal officials.

Unknown Publisher

SBU detains driver suspected of directing Russian attacks on Kyiv' regions thermal power plants
The SBU said this in a statement seen by Ukrinform.
According to the SBU, one of the enemy's main targets was thermal power plants in the Kyiv region that were being brought back online after previous attacks.
"Under the guise of work-related trips, the suspect drove around the perimeters of power plants to assess the current state of energy infrastructure and photographed their exteriors with his phone. He then returned home, compiled the images, pinned their locations on Google Maps and added his own comments before preparing the files to send to his FSB handler," the SBU said.
SBU officers documented the suspect using a truck to scout the progress of restoration work on a power unit at a local thermal power plant. He was detained while preparing a report for the enemy, the agency said.
The investigation found that the driver had come to the attention of Russian intelligence after posting anti-Ukrainian comments in Telegram channels. After being recruited, he communicated with an FSB operative through a specially created chatbot, the SBU said.
According to investigators, he also monitored the locations of repair bases used by Ukraine's Defense Forces.
During searches, officers seized two mobile phones from the man. One of the phones had been damaged in an apparent attempt to destroy evidence of his cooperation with Russia, the SBU said.
SBU investigators notified the suspect that he was charged under Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (high treason committed under martial law).
The suspect is being held in custody without the right to bail. He faces life imprisonment and confiscation of property.

08:33:13 KST

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Amazon on Thursday reported that its third-quarter net sales rose 12 percent year on year to 201.94 billion U.S. dollars, driven in part by strong growth in its cloud computing business, while net income declined 2.4 percent.
According to the U.S. e-commerce and technology giant's financial results for the quarter ended Sept. 30, net income fell to 20.69 billion dollars from 21.19 billion dollars a year earlier. Diluted earnings per share decreased to 1.89 dollars from 1.95 dollars.
Amazon attributed the decline in net income primarily to the impact of pretax gains of 9.5 billion dollars in the third quarter of 2025 from its investment in artificial intelligence (AI) company Anthropic.
Amazon Web Services (AWS), the company's cloud computing division, reported net sales of 45.98 billion dollars, up 39.3 percent year on year, marking its fastest growth in nearly five years. AWS operating income rose 55 percent to 17.77 billion dollars from 11.43 billion dollars a year earlier.
Net sales from advertising services increased 11 percent year on year to 19.64 billion dollars.
The company's free cash flow turned negative in the 12 months ended Sept. 30, recording an outflow of 42.4 billion dollars, compared with an inflow of 14.8 billion dollars a year earlier, primarily reflecting increased investment in AI infrastructure.
Looking ahead, the company expects fourth-quarter net sales to range from 240 billion to 247 billion dollars, representing year-on-year growth of 12 percent to 16 percent. Operating income is projected to reach 28.5 billion to 33.5 billion dollars, up from 25 billion dollars a year earlier. ■

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- U.S. chipmaker Intel reported Thursday that its third-quarter revenue rose 21 percent year on year to 16.51 billion U.S. dollars, driven by strong growth in its data center and artificial intelligence business, while net income declined 18 percent.
According to the company's financial results for the quarter ended Sept. 26, net income attributable to Intel fell to 3.32 billion dollars from 4.06 billion dollars a year earlier. Diluted earnings per share decreased to 0.6 dollars from 0.9 dollars.
The company's gross margin increased to 43 percent from 38.2 percent a year earlier. On a non-GAAP basis, diluted earnings per share rose to 0.52 dollars from 0.23 dollars.
Revenue from Intel's Data Center and AI segment jumped 78 percent year on year to 7.3 billion dollars, marking the company's strongest data center revenue growth in 15 years.
Revenue from its Client Computing and Physical AI Group declined 5 percent to 8.1 billion dollars, reflecting continued challenges in the personal computer market.
Intel Foundry, the company's semiconductor manufacturing business, reported revenue of 6.7 billion dollars, up 58 percent year on year. The figure includes transactions with other Intel business units.
Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said demand for the company's central processing units remained robust despite near-term headwinds in the PC industry, adding that increasing supply to meet demand for Xeon server processors was an immediate priority.
Looking ahead, Intel expects fourth-quarter revenue of between 15 billion and 16 billion dollars. The company forecasts diluted earnings per share attributable to Intel of 0.10 dollars under GAAP and 0.25 dollars on a non-GAAP basis.
Intel also projects a GAAP gross margin of 37.1 percent for the fourth quarter, down from 43 percent in the third quarter. ■

Trump cancels weekend rallies, plans to phone in to other midterm campaign events
JOINT BASE ANDREWS, Maryland – President Donald Trump on Oct 29 cancelled planned weekend campaign stops in Kansas and Iowa, and his allies said he would instead phone in to rallies nationwide after four weeks of travel to boost Republicans’ election chances.
Trump told reporters he did not “feel like I have to go to Kansas”, a Midwestern state where Senator Roger Marshall, a fellow Republican, is in an unexpectedly competitive race with Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton.
“He is doing very well,” Trump said of Marshall. “We are going to have a strong Tuesday night.”
Later on Oct 29, the Republican National Committee said in a statement that it would also cancel a planned rally in Iowa, home to several competitive congressional races.
The cancelled in-person rallies were set for Salina, Kansas, on Oct 31, and Dubuque, Iowa, on Nov 1.
Since Oct 1, Trump has hosted 25 rallies in 19 states, often speaking for his party in rural areas of Republican-friendly states.
The Nov 3 midterm elections will determine whether Republicans retain narrow control of the US Senate and House of Representatives.
MAGA, a campaign funding group aligned with Trump, said on Oct 29 it would host a series of “tele-rallies” with the president in at least 19 states, including Kansas and Iowa, before Election Day.
The president is still expected to travel to rallies in several states before the Nov 3 election, including in Florida on Oct 30.
