Manosphere and online misogyny should be treated as public health issues, say UK experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:30:37 UTC
08:30:37 KST

The manosphere and online misogyny should be treated by the government as a public health issue, in the same way as obesity or smoking, experts have said.
Writing in the Lancet, the authors of a new report argue that a coordinated response is needed, involving governments, schools, health services and community organisations, similar to the public-health response to tobacco use and ultra-processed food.
“Men’s problems are framed [in the manosphere] as the result of feminism rather than structural conditions, and masculine identity is commodified through products and paid content that normalise and reinforce health-harming and performance-oriented masculinities,” the authors write.
The report defines the manosphere as “a diffuse commercial ecosystem and loose collection of online communities united by shared beliefs about masculinity, misogyny and male victimisation”.
It goes on to outline how the manosphere has evolved into a highly lucrative online industry that makes money by promoting “the most extreme expressions of misogyny and aggrieved masculinity”.
Prof Kent Buse, a co-author of the paper and co-founder of the social justice thinktank Global 50/50, said: “This is a business model, not a fringe. Outrage and grievance are good for business, so the system rewards the most extreme content. Expect the playbook that served tobacco so well: blame the individual, and call regulation an attack on freedom. Public health has a tested toolkit for commercial harms and we should use it.”
He added: “Boys and men are not the problem. The problem is the conditions that leave them isolated and without a secure future, and the companies that profit from their anger and insecurity.”
The authors also point to growing disengagement from education among boys around the world, as well as loneliness, money worries and social exclusion, which can leave young men searching for a sense of belonging. These problems, they say, can make them more vulnerable to online communities that offer simple explanations for their difficulties and often encourage them to blame women and feminism.
Prof Sarah Hawkes, the report’s other author, said: “The manosphere offers boys and young men belonging, identity and an explanation for why life feels hard.
“Those needs are real. A response that only removes the manosphere, without offering something credible in its place, will fail. We need to offer boys something better, not just tell them what to avoid.”
Mark Brooks, the policy and communications director at the Centre for Policy Research on Men and Boys, welcomed the report’s position that it was a public health issue and that men, boys, women and girls were all victims of this content.
“Far too often, the manosphere discussion has positioned all men and boys as a problem and not taken into account the broader economic, educational and cultural challenges that drive their engagement,” he said.
“Not all men and boys engage with this content equally. We are currently working on research to identify who is most at risk.”

US military movements don't signal decision to strike: Israel prepares, waits on Trump again
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:28:07 UTC
08:28:07 KST

Is the United States preparing to resume its war against Iran? When could another attack take place, and what would its objectives be? A series of military movements observed in recent weeks has raised these questions, but there is still no clear indication that President Donald Trump has decided to order renewed strikes. 
Israel's defense establishment is preparing for the possibility of another conflict, both offensively and defensively, while security officials stress that the developments remain preliminary and are intended, at least in part, to give the president military options should he decide to act.
One of the most significant developments involves the deployment of U.S. forces in the Arabian Sea, near Iran's coast. Twelve American destroyers have been operating in the area in recent weeks, up from approximately eight to 10 previously. Some may be involved in the naval blockade, but the increased presence is also being examined in the context of preparations for a possible military campaign. Two U.S. aircraft carriers are also stationed in the region, while a third is expected to complete its deployment near Japan. Washington will then have to decide whether to send it to the Arabian Sea as reinforcements or use it to replace one of the carriers already there.
Is overthrowing Iran's regime back on the table?
Alongside the naval buildup, preliminary indications of increased American air activity have also emerged. According to an analysis by Israel's Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), aircraft tracking data cautiously suggests that the United States is rebuilding its aerial refueling network in Europe, potentially providing a staging point for moving additional forces into the area covered by U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM). Between Wednesday and Thursday, an American RC-135 reconnaissance aircraft flew from the United States to Britain, while eight C-17 military transport aircraft landed in southern Israel. The assessment is that the aircraft were carrying air defense equipment and logistical supplies, potentially indicating preparations to reinforce defensive systems and offensive capabilities. The IDF has not commented on reports of the landings.
Security officials emphasize that the movements do not necessarily indicate a decision to attack. Trump could still pursue a diplomatic solution, and the scale of the preparations primarily reflects Washington's desire to keep the military option available. "The Americans are preparing options for the president, if and when he decides to launch an attack," a security official said.
The central question is what the objectives of another military campaign would be if one were launched. During Operation Rising Lion, Israel struck Iranian nuclear facilities, with the United States joining the campaign toward its conclusion by attacking the Fordow nuclear facility. During Operation Roaring Lion, which lasted 42 days, nuclear targets were largely avoided. Instead, the campaign focused on weapons manufacturing facilities, military and national infrastructure, Iran's navy and missile systems, alongside more limited strikes against symbols of the regime and the Basij paramilitary forces affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Another factor is Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's declaration ahead of Israel's elections that he had instructed the country's security agencies to advance a plan to overthrow the Iranian regime in cooperation with Trump. Netanyahu intensified his rhetoric on the issue in the days leading up to the vote and on Election Day itself. The IDF's Military Intelligence Directorate and Israeli Air Force are continuing to update their target lists, divided into categories including infrastructure, nuclear facilities, military buildup and missile capabilities. Any effort to overthrow the Iranian regime would also require a comprehensive operational plan developed by the Mossad intelligence agency in coordination with other Israeli security bodies.
Israeli defense officials are also considering the possibility that Iran could launch an attack of its own, driven by mounting economic distress and fears of another American-Israeli operation after having been caught off guard by major opening strikes on two previous occasions.
"In systems like the American military, preparing the available options takes time," a senior security official explained. "We are talking about weeks, certainly when it comes to a broad military campaign rather than a limited operation, even if it is a short one, as foreign media reports have suggested." The official said it remains difficult to predict Trump's decision. Even if the president authorizes renewed fighting, an attack would not necessarily follow immediately. Israel would prefer a short, intensive campaign, particularly after Operation Roaring Lion stretched to 42 days, considerably longer than initially planned.
Hezbollah prepares for possible confrontation
Military preparations are unfolding alongside diplomatic efforts. According to reports in recent days, U.S. Vice President JD Vance sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council and a figure considered close to Mojtaba Khamenei, to explore the possibility of renewing negotiations between Washington and Tehran. American officials said the initiative was undertaken with Trump's knowledge and at his direction. At the same time, the president continues to threaten a return to military action, potentially after the U.S. midterm elections. The simultaneous diplomatic contacts and military movements leave open the possibility that Washington is seeking to increase pressure on Tehran while preparing for potential military action.
Another concern is Israel's northern front. Israeli defense officials are preparing for the possibility that renewed fighting against Iran could expand into a confrontation with Hezbollah in Lebanon. During the past month, Israeli interceptor missiles have been launched near the Lebanese border. The IDF has not disclosed the targets of those interceptions, but Israeli assessments suggest that at least some may have involved Hezbollah reconnaissance drones attempting to gather intelligence on Israeli troop deployments. Hezbollah has also been moving weapons and preparing for the possibility of renewed fighting with the IDF.
Israel's Northern Command is working to reinforce defensive lines held by Israeli forces in southern Lebanon, establish positions offering greater control through observation and firepower, and prepare plans for capturing additional Hezbollah strongholds.
A renewed conflict could also affect Israel's political situation, with uncertainty continuing over the formation of a governing coalition following the elections. Another war against Iran could reshape the public agenda, alter the balance of power among political parties and place national security and relations with Washington back at the center of political debate. For now, Israel continues updating its military plans while Washington maintains both diplomatic contacts and threats of renewed action. Whether the preparations will lead to another military campaign, and what its objectives might be, remains uncertain.

Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson to spend rest of life in prison after losing appeal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:25:26 UTC
08:25:26 KST

in brief
- The Victorian Court of Appeal has resentenced Patterson to life without parole.
- Patterson had already been serving a life sentence for the murders of three family members she poisoned with death cap mushrooms.
Mushroom murderer Erin Patterson will likely die in prison after Victoria's Court of Appeal dismissed her conviction challenge and upheld a prosecution bid to impose a whole-of-life sentence without parole.
Delivering judgment from Melbourne's Supreme Court on Friday morning, justice Stephen McLeish confirmed the jury's guilty verdicts before setting aside the 33-year non-parole period imposed by the trial judge as inadequate for what he termed "shocking criminality".
McLeish said Patterson had calculated murdering all four of her lunch guests for nearly three weeks before the incident and that the sentence should reflect that.
"It represented a cruel breach of trust to members of the applicant's extended family," he said.
"In re-sentencing, it is necessary that the sentence vindicates unequivocally the primary value that our society places on each individual human life."
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
In its written judgment, the court described the offending as "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and said it "stands to be denounced in the strongest terms".
The court's ruling marks the latest chapter in a case that shocked the nation following a home-cooked family lunch in regional Victoria in July 2023.
Patterson was found guilty last year of murdering her former parents-in-law, Don and Gail Patterson, both 70, and Gail's sister, Heather Wilkinson, 66, after deliberately serving them beef Wellington laced with lethal death cap mushrooms at her Leongatha home.
Heather's husband, church pastor Ian Wilkinson, spent nearly two months in hospital with critical organ damage before eventually recovering. Patterson was found guilty of attempted murder alongside the three murder convictions.
Patterson, 52, was not in the courtroom when Friday's judgment was handed down.
She watched via video link from Dame Phyllis Frost Centre in Ravenhall as the bench stripped any prospect of future release, delivering one of the harshest penalties in Victorian legal history.
Defence challenge dismissed
Following a nearly three-month trial, Supreme Court Justice Christopher Beale sentenced Patterson in September 2025 to life imprisonment with a 33-year non-parole period.
However, Patterson's appeal barristers argued that significant issues at trial invalidated her convictions.
Primarily, her defence said the jury was insufficiently sequestered during deliberations, as it emerged that jurors were accommodated in the same hotel as the Crown's primary police investigator and two prosecutors.
However, McLeish dismissed the challenge, noting that the jury keeper had verified there was no communication between the parties.
"As against that assurance, there was only conjecture, guesswork, or surmise," McLeish said, ruling there was "no objective basis for a fair-minded person to reasonably apprehend that the jury might not have discharged its function."
They also argued that the Crown's five-day cross-examination of Patterson was needlessly aggressive and that the prosecution incorrectly changed its case by suggesting a fresh motive during closing remarks.
Whole-of-life sentence imposed
At the same time, chief crown prosecutor Brendan Kissane argued that the court should impose a harsher sentence and strip Patterson of her right to parole.
The prosecution maintained that the killings involved calculated premeditation, exacerbated by her failure to tell medical staff about the death caps her victims had consumed while doctors were still trying to save them.
McLeish agreed with the prosecution's argument, saying that a 33-year minimum term did not capture the calculating nature of her crimes.
"The applicant's intent to murder all four victims was sustained for nearly three weeks, from when she invited them to lunch, through to preparing and serving the poisonous meal, and then throughout the protracted suffering and ultimate deaths that resulted," McLeish said.
The bench highlighted an "elaborate series of deceptions", including Patterson's fabricated cancer claims used to explain why her children were absent from the lunch, persistent lies about where the mushrooms came from, and the deliberate destruction of evidence.
"This offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated, and stands to be denounced in the strongest terms," McLeish said.
"In all the circumstances, after anxious consideration, we have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period."
Active suppression orders remain strictly enforced for the media and the public.
Patterson's children and their schools cannot be named while rebroadcasting, photographing, or replicating any part of the court's live stream is a criminal offence.
Legal experts say her only remaining legal avenue is an application for special leave to appeal to the High Court of Australia.

Tributes Pour In for Patrick Stewart, Who Has Died at 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:21:50 UTC
08:21:50 KST

Tributes have poured in following the death of British actor Patrick Stewart, known for his decades of Shakespearean stage performances and his leading roles in the “Star Trek” and “X-Men” franchises.
Stewart, 86, died at his home in Los Angeles on Wednesday in the company of his wife, Sunny, after a “brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer's and dementia, according to a statement posted Stewart's official Instagram account announcing his death on Thursday.
“His sonorous voice and singular talent will forever be synonymous with indelible performances in every genre,” the statement read. “He explored the human condition in all its poetic complexity and brought hope not only to the far reaches of the Marvel Cinematic Universe, but into science fiction’s most iconic final frontier aboard the Starship Enterprise.”
Stewart's long and celebrated career spanned mediums and genres over more than six decades—from his first roles with the Royal Shakespeare Company to a variety of performances in television and film. He is set to make his final on-screen appearance in “Avengers: Doomsday,” which premiers in December, reprising his role as the X-Men’s Professor Charles Xavier.
In an interview with TV Insider in June, Stewart said that he couldn’t “imagine ever officially ‘retiring.’”
“I’ll always and forever be an actor,” he said at the time.
Patrick Stewart’s career took him from Shakespeare to ‘Star Trek,’ and beyond
Stewart was born on July 13, 1940, in the West Yorkshire town of Mirfield in England’s coal-mining country, where he later recalled growing up in poverty and a home marked by domestic violence. He described acting as a “safe space” and a “refuge from real life” that he discovered after a teacher first introduced him to Shakespeare.
Years before he made his big-screen debut, Stewart trained in classical theater and took on his first professional roles on the British stage in the 1950s and 1960s. He joined the esteemed Royal Shakespeare Company in 1966, going from smaller supporting roles to storied leading parts over the course of more than 15 years as a regular member of the company.
Beginning in the 1970s, Stewart appeared in television series including “Fall of Eagles” (1974), “I, Claudius” (1976), and “Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy.”
He reached a new level of international stardom with his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the “Star Trek: The Next Generation” series, which he played from 1987 to1994. In 2000, Stewart took on another career-defining part, that of Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” movies.
Throughout his career, Stewart received various accolades, including two Laurence Olivier Awards, recognized as the highest honor in British theater, and a Grammy for his recording of “Peter and the Wolf,”; as well as garnering nominations for the Golden Globes, Emmys, and a Tony. He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II for his service to drama in 2010.
Outpourings of praise and remembrance
The news of Stewart’s death quickly drew tributes from many within the “Star Trek” and Marvel worlds where he inhabited two of his most recognizable roles.
“We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days,” wrote the actor Hugh Jackman, who starred as Wolverine in the “X-Men” films alongside Stewart.
Marvel Studios also paid tribute to Stewart on Thursday.
“Sir Patrick brought Professor Charles Xavier to life with extraordinary grace, intelligence, and humanity, defining the character for generations of fans, from ‘X-Men’ to ‘Logan’ to ‘Avengers: Doomsday.’ He was a singular talent, a generous collaborator, and a true gentleman,” Marvel wrote in a statement shared on social media.
The studio's president, Kevin Feige, said in a statement to Variety that “after years of knowing him as the inimitable Captain Picard, I was in awe — and he turned out to be everything I had seen on screen and more: brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas.”
Feige added that “away from the cameras, he was even more remarkable, with a wonderfully sharp sense of humor.”
The “Star Trek” franchise remembered Stewart in a post on its official Instagram page as “a voice. A presence. A captain unlike any other.”
“Sir Patrick Stewart gave generations of fans an icon who inspired us to look toward the stars,” the post read. “Today, we celebrate an extraordinary life and an enduring legacy. Thank you, Sir Patrick.”
William Shatner, who played Captain James T. Kirk in the “Star Trek” franchise, said in a post on X that Stewart was “a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work.”
George Takei, who played Lt. Hikaru Sulu in the original “Star Trek” series, called Stewart on threads “a true and irreplaceable legend.”
“He inspired a whole next generation of star-gazers who looked longingly ahead to a brighter future for all humanity,” Takei said.
Stewart’s “Star Trek: The Next Generation” co-stars Wil Wheaton, who played Wesley Crusher on the series, and Jonathan Scott Frakes, who played William Riker, also shared tributes to the late actor.
“Godspeed, Captain,” Wheaton wrote in a message on Instagram, alongside a photo of himself with Stewart.
“Rest in peace, my friend,” Frakes wrote.
Rebecca Romijn, who like Stewart has played roles in both the “Star Trek” and “X-Men” franchises said in a video posted on social media: “I feel so grateful to have known him for the last 25 years, and to have been in his orbit … both as a fellow mutant and as a fellow member of Starfleet.”
“He was positively delicious, hilarious, naughty, incredible sense of humor, and that booming voice of his that always spoke to the very back of the room, as every classically trained Shakespearean great needs to master, has always been an inspiration,” she said. “I send my condolences to his family, and I’ll miss my friend dearly. Rest in peace, Patrick.”
Cary Elwes, who starred alongside Stewart in “Lady Jane” and “Robin Hood: Men in Tights,” recalled that he “first met Patrick on the set of Lady Jane back in 1984 and fell in love with him immediately.”
"Not only was amiable and kind with a great sense of humor, he was incredible to work with. His command of the screen with his sheer presence and that unmistakable voice was a sight to behold," Elwes wrote in a post on Instagram.

ASEAN Special Envoy Concludes Humanitarian Mission to Myanmar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:17:00 UTC
08:17:00 KST

Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro yesterday wrapped up a two-day humanitarian mission in Myanmar, potentially her last as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)’s special envoy to the country.
According to the Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), Lazaro began her mission with a visit to the city of Taunggyi in a military-controlled region of Shan State, to oversee the distribution of aid through the ASEAN Coordinating Centre for Humanitarian Assistance.
She then traveled yesterday to the capital Naypyidaw, where she met with Myanmar’s Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe. The two officials discussed “the humanitarian situation and hard-to-reach communities, as well as the overall implementation of the Five-Point Consensus,” ASEAN’s plan for managing the Myanmar conflict, the DFA said in a statement.
While in Naypyidaw, Lazaro also visited a school and monastery in Pyinmana Township that were granted Philippine humanitarian assistance after the devastating earthquake of March 2025. The DFA added that she concluded her mission in Yangon, where she held “consultations with ASEAN Embassies.”
Unsurprisingly, Myanmar’s Foreign Ministry characterized yesterday’s meeting between Lazaro and Tin Maung Swe differently, stating that the two envoys “held substantive discussions on ways to restore Myanmar’s original role and rights within ASEAN.” The Myanmar foreign minister informed Lazaro of the government’s efforts to promote peace and stability, address “terrorism,” and facilitate the delivery of humanitarian assistance, and “underscored Myanmar’s full cooperation under the ASEAN framework.”
The Five-Point Consensus, promulgated by ASEAN two months after the military coup, calls for an immediate cessation of violence, dialogue among “all parties” to Myanmar’s conflict, and access for humanitarian aid. However, the military’s failure to implement the most important terms of the Consensus prompted ASEAN to exclude Myanmar from its summits and foreign ministers’ meetings in late 2021.
Since taking office in April, the new military-backed administration headed by coup leader Min Aung Hlaing has pushed hard for normalization with ASEAN. Five ASEAN member states – Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam, and Malaysia – have rolled out the red carpet for the coup leader in recent months, with Indonesia and Brunei possibly to come.
At the same time, it has explicitly rejected the Five-Point Consensus and denounced ASEAN for its “discrimination.” While the Myanmar Foreign Ministry stated that Tin Maung Swe “highlighted the Government’s constructive cooperation towards implementing the ASEAN Five-Point Statement” – it now refuses to refer to it as a “Consensus” – he added that it would do so “without compromising its national interests and sovereignty in accordance with its own roadmaps and objectives,” some of which directly contradict the ASEAN plan.
It is thus unsurprising that Naypyidaw would seek to characterize Lazaro’s visit as a step on the road toward the current Myanmar regime’s relegitimization. Indeed, as one observer noted today on X, allowing Lazaro to preside over the distribution of humanitarian aid in Taunggyi, far from most of the active conflict zones in Shan State, allows the Philippines to claim progress on the Five-Point Consensus.
Notably, though perhaps not surprisingly, Lazaro, whose position as special envoy will end when Singapore takes over ASEAN’s chairmanship in 2027, concluded her mission without meeting detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
The 81-year-old has been in custody since the coup, but the military-backed government has loosened the terms of her detention somewhat over the last six months, in pursuit of its goal of regional normalization. After announcing her move from prison to house arrest in April, it has released photos of her meeting with a representative from the International Committee of the Red Cross. This month, it also allowed her to receive two books and a diplomatic package from Britain’s King Charles III and to hold a phone call with her son, Kim Aris.
As ASEAN chair in 2026, the Philippines has pressed Naypyidaw for access to the Nobel laureate. It made its first request for “brief access” after she was moved to house arrest in April and again in August after she was allowed to meet with the ICRC representative. The Myanmar administration refused both.
While Myanmar is keen to use Aung San Suu Kyi to extract concessions from its key partners, it is clear that this will stop short of recognizing her as a legitimate political interlocutor. Moreover, having rejected the need for an ASEAN special envoy at all back in August, the outcome of Lazaro’s mission is a sign that Naypyidaw will use ASEAN’s special envoys not to advance the Five-Point Consensus, but to support its chosen pursuit of political consolidation at home and diplomatic normalization abroad.

The broadcaster said the aircraft landed at Ovda and Nevatim air bases, while additional US military planes were reportedly dispatched to bases in Jordan, Saudi Arabia and Qatar.
According to KAN, the planes departed from Fort Bliss in the US state of Texas, which houses one of the US military’s largest air defense centers, including facilities associated with interceptor missiles and air defense batteries.
There was no immediate US confirmation of the reported deployments, and it remained unclear what cargo the aircraft were carrying or whether Washington had decided to launch an attack against Iran.
An Israeli official told the broadcaster that Israel and the US were closely coordinating their military preparations.
“Israel and the United States are coordinating closely, and although no decision has yet been made on the matter, the Americans and Israel are preparing for any decision President Donald Trump makes,” the official said.
The official did not specify the nature or timing of any potential decision.
Earlier this week, KAN reported that Washington had warned Gulf countries about the possibility of a short, limited military campaign against Iran.
According to the broadcaster, the US military has also transferred a Patriot missile defense system from Texas to reinforce its air defenses in the Gulf region.
The report said US troops stationed at bases across the region had been instructed to leave as a precaution against a possible military escalation.
It added that US forces were replenishing their weapons stockpiles, with an additional aircraft carrier and Marine Corps unit expected to arrive in November.
The reinforcements would reportedly join approximately 20 US warships already operating in the Middle East.
Separately, The Wall Street Journal reported earlier Thursday that US Central Command (CENTCOM) Commander Gen. Brad Cooper had briefed Trump on options for potential strikes against Iran.
The newspaper suggested that the briefing could indicate that Washington was moving closer to launching major military operations.
Democratic US Sen. Chris Murphy said he and several other senators had received a briefing on possible plans to attack Iran, describing them as “insane.”
Murphy warned that such an operation would lead to a devastating escalation and could undermine the US commitment to the rule of law.
The US and Israel launched attacks against Iran on Feb. 28, prompting Tehran to retaliate against Israel and US targets across the region before a ceasefire agreement was reached in April.
The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June concerning freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, but its implementation has stalled over disagreements related to the waterway’s security.
The latest reported military deployments come amid renewed concerns over a possible escalation between the US and Iran.

Russian President Vladimir Putin says he welcomed the rare phone call from the leaders of Finland and Norway, adding that Moscow has always supported efforts to normalize relations with European countries.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store spoke with Putin on Tuesday, breaking with the longstanding practice among European leaders of avoiding direct contact with Moscow since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022. The initiative drew criticism from Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, who questioned its effectiveness and said it was not coordinated with European partners.
At a press conference in the Kremlin on Thursday, Putin said he welcomes dialogue with Western countries despite their military support for Ukraine and sanctions on Russia.
“I believe it was the right thing to do. After all, there are people in Europe who, unlike some others, do not want to inflict a ‘strategic defeat’ on Russia but instead want to establish some kind of constructive dialogue,” he stated.
He added that Russia will support “any steps aimed at restoring full-fledged and comprehensive relations” with European countries, whether through the EU or on a bilateral basis.
Putin reiterated that Russia is not seeking a broader conflict with the EU or NATO. “We do not want any war with Europe. If some of them want one, let them prepare. But they have not achieved their goal of inflicting a ‘strategic defeat’ on Russia, and it is unlikely that this will be possible by 2030,” he said.
And if things go too far, there will be no winners at all. Let no one forget that.
The leaders of Norway and Finland said they sought to convey messages directly to Putin “regarding future negotiations to help to end the war,” ahead of US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks expected to take place in Abu Dhabi in the near future. They described the conversation as a follow-up to their meeting with Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky in Oslo on October 20.
Norway and the Kremlin disputed a report by the Financial Times claiming that Putin spent much of the call lecturing his counterparts on Russian and Slavic history.
Stubb has cultivated a close relationship with US President Donald Trump, with whom he has frequently discussed the Ukraine conflict, earning him the nickname ‘the Trump whisperer’ in the media.
The Finnish leader noted his country’s long experience of dealing with Russia. Finland shares a 1,340-kilometer border with its eastern neighbor and maintained peaceful, if sometimes uneasy, relations with Moscow throughout the Cold War.
The call came amid growing tensions between Kiev and Washington after Trump lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports and subsequently waived additional restrictions following Zelensky’s refusal to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Trump blamed for soaring fuel prices.
Moscow has accused European leaders of sabotaging the 2022 peace talks with Ukraine and seeking to undermine Trump’s ongoing efforts to broker a deal.

Analysis-Bukele’s gang offensive goes abroad as El Salvador rushes troops to Haiti
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:07:31 CET
08:07:31 KST

By Sarah Morland
Oct 28 (Reuters) - El Salvador’s deployment of thousands of troops to Haiti, days after four Salvadoran members of a UN-backed force went missing in a gang ambush, is the first major overseas test of President Nayib Bukele’s anti-gang tactics.
Around 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers were in Haiti as of Wednesday night, a security official told Reuters. Two sources with knowledge of the matter said these would for now be capped at 2,500. Yet authorities have not clarified the troops’ command, or rules of engagement, fueling concerns of more risks to civilians in a country with a long history of harmful foreign interventions.
Bukele billed the deployments as a rescue mission for four aircraft technicians who were part of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force in Haiti. They have been missing since they jumped from a burning vehicle during the ambush in a gang-controlled area on the outskirts of the capital Port-au-Prince.
Haitian and Salvadoran authorities have said the troops’ main mission is to rescue the missing technicians. But the deployment’s size - matching in 10 days what the UN-backed force struggled to deploy over more than a year - has prompted questions over whether the soldiers could be part of a broader and longer-term operation.
On Thursday, Bukele said the deployments were nearly finished and his government was covering 90% of the costs.
Bukele, in office since 2019, won huge popularity at home with tough-on-crime policies, including a gang crackdown that relied heavily on mass incarceration. Other governments have sought to replicate his approach, despite rights activists’ warnings over due process and innocent deaths.
Bukele would, however, likely encounter a profoundly different security environment in Haiti, analysts warned, as institutions have been whittled down by corruption and faltering funds, prisons are vastly overcrowded, the judiciary paralyzed and many gang recruits are underage.
“This could help increase support for Bukele if this helps his narrative of being an anti-gang force in the region and delivering results,” said Maria Fernanda Arocha, an analyst at conflict monitoring group ACLED.
“We don’t know if this will bring the results he is expecting.”
A CID Gallup poll on Wednesday showed 86% of Salvadorans approved of the Haiti mission, though 82% also expressed concern for their countrymen.
In El Salvador, security analysts said they were cautious of a risky mission without a formal agreement, UN backing, or support from the Shield of the Americas - a US-led anti-crime coalition the Trump administration launched earlier this year.
POINTS TO ESCALATION
Haiti’s unelected leaders have since 2022 called for international forces to help fight heavily-armed gangs that have expanded their influence beyond the capital and are responsible for massacres, gang rapes and widespread extortion.
But successive UN-backed missions were slow to deploy, leaving a fractured security response. Haiti hired a private military company run by Blackwater founder Erik Prince to fight the gangs, which nonetheless continued to make gains.
Sam Vigersky, a policy expert at the Council on Foreign Relations, said he believed the UN-backed mission - renewed for just six months in September - was under pressure to produce results but the Salvadorans’ arrival signaled more chaos.
“The overall security picture is not pointing towards one of stabilization, it’s pointing towards one of escalation,” he said.
Since the October 18 ambush, the area has been the site of continuous armed clashes. A security official said operations there were largely run by Haitian police.
Romain Le Cour Grandmaison, a security expert at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, said residents were skeptical of yet another foreign intervention and had reported heavy gunfire, drone strikes and possible civilian deaths.
He said he was not aware of humanitarian corridors to help people escape: “The gang leaders do not want people to leave the area because they probably want to use them as shields and make sure the population actually slows operations against them.”
Washington has not publicly supported the mission but a US military official said Pentagon C-130s helped it deploy.
Irwin Stotzky, a rights expert at the University of Miami, said the US administration, which ended immigration protections for about 350,000 Haitians, has reasons to be invested.
“We’ve got to make it appear as if it’s safe to send 350,000 people back to Haiti, when they actually are in great fear of their lives,” he said.
(Reporting by Sarah Morland in Mexico City, Harold Isaac in Port-au-Prince, Gerardo Arbaiza in San Salvador; Additional reporting by Simon Lewis in Washington; editing by Cassandra Garrison and Sanjeev Miglani)

Reddit shares sink on weak sales guidance and plans login requirement test as Google search traffic shrinks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:01:02 UTC
08:01:02 KST

Reddit plans to require all users to create official accounts to access the social media platform, marking a major departure for the site known as "the front page of the internet." 
The company revealed the change Thursday as part of its third-quarter earnings, in which it beat on the top and bottom lines, but provided weak fourth-quarter sales guidance. The company's shares dropped over 15% after its numbers were released.
Here's how the company did compared with LSEG estimates:
- Earnings per share: $1.40 vs. $1.35 expected
- Revenue: $895 million vs. $878 million expected
Reddit CEO Steve Huffman told CNBC in an interview that the company's shrinking search-referral traffic from Google went "down meaningfully in this quarter" due to the "shift to AI mode and AI overviews." The traffic decline played a big role in Reddit's planned efforts to require people to become logged-in users.
A previous Google search update designed to surface "authentic" content from internet forums helped Reddit grow its user base over the past few years, but the search giant's continued push on AI overviews and related chatting features has negatively impacted referral traffic.
"I think fundamentally that relationship between Google and the rest of the internet is evolving, and so for us, this means a continued focus on our core users that come to Reddit directly," Huffman said.
Previous Google algorithm changes would "kind of come and go," Huffman said, but the company's AI efforts represent "a fundamental shift in how the Google product works, from being a traffic driver to whatever's going on now."
The CEO didn't provide any specific timing on when Reddit plans for the platform registration change, saying only that implementing it through the site would involve a lot of complexity. The company will begin testing in the fourth quarter outside of the U.S.
He said that Reddit is still determining what parts of the service logged-out users will be able to see, and will iron out the details as part of its upcoming testing.
Reddit said that daily active uniques, or DAUq, rose 12% year-over-year to 130.3 million in the third quarter, trailing Wall Street estimates of 133.7 million. U.S.-specific DAUq dropped 2% year-over-year to 50.7 million, which was below analyst projections of 53.5 million.
Huffman said that "search referral traffic is down meaningfully in this quarter" and that the trend will continue in the fourth quarter.
He said that Reddit is continuing its effort to make its platform "a daily habit" for users. "So that's where our focus is: growing those app users and logged-in users," Huffman said.
Reddit, which derives the bulk of its overall sales from online advertising, is able to monetize logged-ln users better than logged-out users, because those registered users are more active and valuable to advertisers itching to deliver more targeted ads.
"The vast majority of our revenue comes from our app users and logged-in users are direct traffic, and both of those are up Q. over Q. and so that's where our focus is," Huffman said.
The company's third-quarter sales grew 53% year-over-year, marking an end to the eight-straight quarters of revenue growth eclipsing 60% that it reported in July as part of its second-quarter earnings.
Reddit said that fourth-quarter sales will come in a range of $1 billion to $1.03 billion, which was below Wall Street estimates of $1.05 billion.
"It's still a strong guide," Huffman said about its revenue guidance. "We are still growing at an industry leading rate, and that's despite the headwinds from search referrals."
Reddit's third-quarter average revenue per user, or ARPU, came in at $6.87, which was higher than the $6.50 that analysts were expecting.
The company's "other revenue" segment, which includes its data-licensing business, jumped 35% year-over-year to $48 million in the third quarter. Reddit's two biggest data-licensing partners are OpenAI and Google.
Huffman said that Reddit remains "in negotiations" with Google over its data-licensing agreement, and said that it is "only going to do a deal that makes sense for Reddit," if it chooses to continue the partnership.
"I think there's a lot of strategic considerations that goes into that," Huffman said.
Huffman called the required registration plan a "big change" for himself, considering he "grew up on the open Internet."
"Reddit is the last platform to provide basically unfettered logged-out access, and that's largely because of me, I've been holding that line," Huffman, a Reddit co-founder, said. "I think users will probably go through the same understanding that I have, which is that it's a sign of the times. It's an evolution of how these platforms work."
Huffman later expanded on the significance of AI's impact on Reddit's user growth in an earnings call with analysts, and explained that the company plans to continue spending on marketing efforts intended to offset search-referral declines. 
"This is a consequential time for Reddit, and this period does remind me of about 11 years ago when I came back to the company," Huffman told analysts, referring to when he rejoined Reddit in 2015 following it's then-chief Ellen Pao stepping down. "We had a lot of conversations then about what is Reddit and what is Reddit for, and what is our place in this ecosystem. And we've been having those conversations at Reddit recently." 
"Reddit's mission is to create community and belonging for everyone in the world, and while there's overlap between Reddit and other players in the ecosystem, whether we're talking about social media or AI search, fundamentally, Reddit is communities and conversations," Huffman said.

Youth theatre raises more than $68k to carry forward 50-year legacy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

Sydney theatre Shopfront Arts Co-Op has empowered young people for 50 years
Joining Shopfront Arts Co-Op changed Paul Capsis's life.
Fresh out of high school, the writer and performer — known for the 1998 movie Head On — was dragged by a friend to watch a show at the youth theatre in southern Sydney in 1983.
Seeing performers his own age on stage was "remarkable", he recalls.
"It was a magical experience," he says. "I was like, 'What have I been missing out on all these years?'"
After the show, Shopfront's co-founder, director Errol Bray, invited him to get involved in its upcoming production of A Midsummer Night's Dream.
The theatre became a refuge after Capsis's difficult school years.
"I was severely bullied," he says. "You start to think that is how the world is going to be outside."
At Shopfront, Capsis began writing and performing in his own shows, created in collaboration with other young people in the company.
"It was a major thing to be with people that liked me," he says. "We laughed and we performed and we hung out.
"It was healing after my horrific years at high school."
The youth theatre that shaped Capsis's life turned 50 this month.
Over the past five decades, it has kick-started the careers of artists including Olivier Award-nominated performer Trevor Ashley, former Sydney Theatre Company artistic director Andrew Upton, and playwright Hilary Bell.
It also continues to empower young people as performers, writers and decision-makers, and has also been acknowledged by the wider industry at the Sydney Theatre Awards.
Making big things happen
One of its award-winning shows, The Lies We Were Told, created with Australian Theatre for Young People, was remounted at the Sydney Opera House this month in celebration of the company's 50th anniversary.
It followed a youth conference, featuring Heartbreak High star Thomas Weatherall and musician Dobby, and a 50-hour act-a-thon fundraiser, which aimed to raise $50,000 for the theatre. It raised more than $68,000.
The act-a-thon was a fitting tribute to the company's punk past, not only bringing together alumni with the current ensemble, but replicating its successful fundraiser of 1978.
That year, to avoid eviction, the young people of Shopfront resolved to buy the building and raised a $43,000 deposit through an act-a-thon, raffles and government support.
It is a history Shopfront's Young Leader, Liv Tsigaropoulos, who works as a conduit between the theatre's staff and young people, knows well.
When she was in Year 9, she made a mini documentary about the theatre for the National History Challenge, which won her the national Democracy Matters award.
By then, she had already been part of Shopfront for a couple of years, having started when she was 13.
Now 19, she's thrilled to be a custodian of the company during its anniversary year.
"It's the best time to be Young Leader," she says.
"It's such a full-circle thing. I remember reading about the act-a-thon when I was doing my research."
The performance of The Lies We Were Told is part of that full-circle feeling; Tsigaropoulos auditioned for that show when she first joined Shopfront in 2021.
"Since that, I never left, and they could never get rid of me," she says.
Over her six years with the theatre, she has participated in its drama workshops, made short films, learned about technical production, and joined one of its five advisory panels.
For Tsigaropoulos, the special thing about being part of the theatre is the lengths it will go to bring a young person's ideas to life.
She recalls how that gave her the "confidence to stand by [her] ideas".
"In a space like Shopfront, you can say a crazy, big, unrealistic or impossible goal, and the Shopfront staff make it happen," she says.
"You're gonna see your words expressed on stage, what you think expressed on stage, and that's so special … People watch it and laugh and cry."
For example, she suggested she start a show stuck outside.
"It was so silly," she says. "I was like, 'I've missed the show.'
"It's small things I think are funny or cool and would want to see. Getting that put in a show is really fulfilling."
Now, it is up to her as Young Leader to help make those things happen for the next generation of young people.
"The only thing more beautiful than [your idea being brought to life] is working at Shopfront, and a young person tells you an idea, and you make it happen," Tsigaropoulos says.
The next 50 years
The money from the fundraiser will help Shopfront keep bringing young people's ideas to life at a time when funding for arts companies can be precarious.
It is something Shopfront knows all too well, having lost multi-year funding from the federal government alongside many youth arts companies in 2016, and again in 2021.
Shopfront is currently receiving funding from Creative Australia and Create NSW.
The money raised will also help the theatre stay open to everyone, through scholarships and free tickets to performances.
"We never turn young people away if they can't afford it," Tsigaropoulos says.
"We'd rather lose money and let a young person come for free and get to experience Shopfront."
Capsis recalls his own fundraising efforts for Shopfront, standing on a box outside Hurstville Station, singing Janis Joplin.
"We're raising money, we're making shows, and that became my blueprint," he says.
"The big world of professional theatre and musical theatre didn't see me as somebody they wanted, so I made my own work."
It was his training ground, which saw him tour shows to the UK and Canada, and sing on stage for the first time.
"Some people go to NIDA [National Institute of Dramatic Art] and they do three years intensive," Capsis says. "I did Shopfront theatre one night a week and every weekend."
It also helped him make connections, including with Hilary Bell and Julian Meyrick, who collaborated on his award-winning one-man show about his Maltese grandmother, Angela's Kitchen.
"It all comes from Shopfront," he says.
For Capsis, what sticks out is how the theatre empowered him and the young people around him.
"I think it's extremely important young people have a place to voice how they feel, and to learn," he says.
That centring of young people may be what's behind the longevity of Shopfront Arts Co-op, Australia's longest-running and only youth-owned and led theatre company.
"[That longevity is] a testament to all the people who have ever come through Shopfront and the determination, the belief they have in amplifying young people's voices, and that has stayed at its centre since the very beginning," Tsigaropoulos says.
She adds empowering young people remains important, even if they don't want to pursue careers in the arts.
"We're not an acting school pumping out mini DiCaprios and Margot Robbies," Tsigaropoulos says.
"[But] it gives a lot of people a place where they feel they belong and feel welcome and feel accepted."

US agency votes to ban all Chinese labs from testing US electronics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:56:00 UTC

US agency votes to ban all Chinese labs from testing US electronics
- FCC votes to bar Chinese labs from testing US electronics, including phones, cameras and computers, over national security concerns and lack of reciprocal access.
- Chair Brendan Carr said 82% of electronics were tested in China in 2025, and warned labs could expose sensitive data, admit insecure gear, or steal intellectual property.
- The ban starts in December 2028. It adds to wider US action against Chinese tech, including restrictions on drones, routers, and firms such as Huawei and ZTE.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) on Oct 29 voted to bar all Chinese labs from testing electronic devices including smartphones, cameras and computers for use in the US, expanding a previous agency action targeting Beijing.
The FCC said it will prohibit test labs and certification bodies in countries including China that deny reciprocal treatment to US-based test labs. The FCC prohibitions are slated to take effect in December 2028. FCC Chair Brendan Carr said that in 2025, 82% of electronics were tested in China, which does not have an agreement with the US.
“These labs are a critical gateway into American communications infrastructure – and their privileged role gives them access to sensitive and confidential information about electronic products often months before the devices enter the market,” Carr said, adding they could “allow insecure gear into the US market, disrupt communications networks, or even steal intellectual property”.
The Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In 2025, the FCC banned testing of US electronics by labs owned or controlled by the Chinese government, and several dozen labs were barred.
About 4% of all electronic devices are tested in labs inside the US, Carr said.
Separately, the FCC streamlined its approval process for devices tested in US labs or labs from countries not posing national security risks.
This is the latest move by Washington to crack down on China over technology issues and equipment.
In December, the FCC banned the import of all new models of Chinese drones and also has banned imports of new models of Chinese-made consumer routers, the boxes connecting computers, phones and smart devices to the internet.
In July, the FCC voted to bar sales of devices in the US that contain key hardware from Chinese companies deemed to be national security risks.
The FCC maintains a list of firms, including Chinese telecom company Huawei and ZTE, whose equipment is barred for sale in the US due to national security concerns.
In June, the FCC banned the import of more equipment from a group of Chinese manufacturers including Huawei and ZTE and has proposed to ban the import of most military-grade drones. REUTERS

NCLT, NCLAT hijacked by corporate affairs ministry: SC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:55:05 UTC
07:55:05 KST

SC slammed the corporate affairs ministry for "completely hijacking" NCLT and NCLAT, citing infrastructure failures, large vacancies and contractual hiring that undermine the tribunals' autonomy.
New Delhi: In an outburst sure to embarrass the govt, Supreme Court Thursday slammed the ministry of corporate affairs for “completely hijacking” the two most important quasi-judicial financial adjudicatory bodies – National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) and the appellate NCLAT.The stinging remarks came from a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana while hearing petitioners who have been complaining for the last few months about the shoddy infrastructure, lack of support staff and large vacancies hampering the work in NCLT, which in the financial year 2024-25 had approved resolution plans worth Rs 55,000 crore. The tribunal adjudicates corporate civil disputes, company law violations and insolvency proceedings.“The system, the tribunals, we are compelled to observe, has been completely hijacked by the ministry of corporate affairs. That is the problem. And that is impinging on the autonomy of these institutions. These are the things we must look into. The ministry wants to have a complete whip over these tribunals. That is what is most unfortunate,” said the CJI.
The bench has sought detailed proposals on infrastructure and staffing from the presidents of NCLT and NCLAT in four weeks.
Contractual employees harassing judicial members, let past and present staff go: SC
Appearing for NCLT Bar Association, senior advocate Sanjiv Sen said the roofs of certain floors in the building housing NCLT are collapsing and have become unusable. A large number of posts of judicial and technical members are lying vacant, he said, adding that the most unfortunate part is that out of 320 regular posts in NCLT, 253 are vacant.At this juncture, senior advocate Meenakshi Arora said the ministry has outsourced recruitment of contractual employees to a foreign firm and that could jeopardise the integrity of the important financial adjudicatory body. She said the existing contractual employees have already rendered service for eight years and must not be displaced.CJI Kant said, “We are not approving contractual recruitment of employees. It must be done through the Union Public Service Commission or Staff Selection Commission.” When Arora said termination of contractual employees must be stayed, the bench said, “We will not do any such thing at the behest of contractual staff. We would like to give full autonomy to the presidents of NCLT and NCLAT on this issue. The only thing is how soon it should happen.”The CJI said, “Contractual employment means backdoor entry. In Bombay for instance, I know how these contractual employees ran away with original files and FIRs had to be registered. They do not care about the judicial members or technical members. Some technical members are still manipulating certain things.”
“But these contractual employees are harassing the judicial members. So let the past and present contractual employees go. Let the autonomy of recruitment be with the president of the tribunals.... The heads of these tribunals are the most suitable persons to assist us in suggesting ways and means to smoothen and strengthen the day-to-day functioning of these two important tribunals, including requirements of land and buildings and safekeep of records.”

Trump inspired Putin to escalate the war in Ukraine — Le Monde
Kyiv • UNN
The first tanker carrying Russian diesel set sail for New York after Trump and Putin reached an agreement. The supplies did not lower prices in the United States.
Russia’s return to the global diesel fuel market, which was agreed during a phone call between U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian dictator Vladimir Putin, took shape on October 23, when the first Russian tanker departed the Gulf of Finland for New York, where it is expected to arrive in approximately 20 days. This is reported in a Le Monde article, according to UNN.
Details
It is noted that the cargo of more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel proved insufficient to reduce fuel prices in the United States, which reached record highs on the eve of the U.S. midterm elections. But that does not matter, since the “deal” is, above all, a political gesture.
It does not matter that the diesel fuel deal will not deliver the expected economic benefits; the effect of the announcement is what matters. Trump and Putin must send signals
The publication states that, emboldened by the deals with Trump, Putin “is planning to escalate the war in Ukraine.”
“As the United States announces an increasing number of energy deals with Russia, the prospect of consensus-based peace talks between Kyiv and Moscow continues to fade,” the publication writes.
We remind you
The agreement between U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian dictator Vladimir Putin on the supply of Russian diesel fuel practically had no impact on the U.S. fuel market. Despite the announced deliveries, diesel in the United States continued to become more expensive.

Opposition People's Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo visited the scene, while King Felipe VI travelled to a hospital in Toledo treating survivors of the disaster. The monarch was greeted by hospital staff and other people waiting outside before entering the building.

In January, 46 people were killed in another collision involving Renfe and Iryo trains on the same line. The latest crash, just four weeks before a national election, has also disrupted rail travel, with the high-speed route between Madrid and Seville closed and thousands of passengers seeking alternative transport.

Bukele's gang offensive goes abroad as El Salvador rushes troops to Haiti
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:46:19 UTC
07:46:19 KST

Bukele's gang offensive goes abroad as El Salvador rushes troops to Haiti
Oct 29 - El Salvador's deployment of thousands of troops to Haiti, days after four Salvadoran members of a UN-backed force went missing in a gang ambush, is the first major overseas test of President Nayib Bukele's anti-gang tactics.
Around 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers were in Haiti as of Wednesday night, a security official told Reuters. Two sources with knowledge of the matter said these would for now be capped at 2,500. Yet authorities have not clarified the troops' command, or rules of engagement, fueling concerns of more risks to civilians in a country with a long history of harmful foreign interventions.
Bukele billed the deployments as a rescue mission for four aircraft technicians who were part of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force in Haiti. They have been missing since they jumped from a burning vehicle during the ambush in a gang-controlled area on the outskirts of the capital Port-au-Prince.
Haitian and Salvadoran authorities have said the troops' main mission is to rescue the missing technicians. But the deployment's size - matching in 10 days what the UN-backed force struggled to deploy over more than a year - has prompted questions over whether the soldiers could be part of a broader and longer-term operation.
On Thursday, Bukele said the deployments were nearly finished and his government was covering 90% of the costs.
Bukele, in office since 2019, won huge popularity at home with tough-on-crime policies, including a gang crackdown that relied heavily on mass incarceration. Other governments have sought to replicate his approach, despite rights activists' warnings over due process and innocent deaths.
Bukele would, however, likely encounter a profoundly different security environment in Haiti, analysts warned, as institutions have been whittled down by corruption and faltering funds, prisons are vastly overcrowded, the judiciary paralyzed and many gang recruits are underage.
"This could help increase support for Bukele if this helps his narrative of being an anti-gang force in the region and delivering results," said Maria Fernanda Arocha, an analyst at conflict monitoring group ACLED.
"We don't know if this will bring the results he is expecting."
A CID Gallup poll on Wednesday showed 86% of Salvadorans approved of the Haiti mission, though 82% also expressed concern for their countrymen.
In El Salvador, security analysts said they were cautious of a risky mission without a formal agreement, UN backing, or support from the Shield of the Americas - a US-led anti-crime coalition the Trump administration launched earlier this year.
POINTS TO ESCALATION
Haiti's unelected leaders have since 2022 called for international forces to help fight heavily-armed gangs that have expanded their influence beyond the capital and are responsible for massacres, gang rapes and widespread extortion.
But successive UN-backed missions were slow to deploy, leaving a fractured security response. Haiti hired a private military company run by Blackwater founder Erik Prince to fight the gangs, which nonetheless continued to make gains.
Sam Vigersky, a policy expert at the Council on Foreign Relations, said he believed the UN-backed mission - renewed for just six months in September - was under pressure to produce results but the Salvadorans' arrival signaled more chaos.
"The overall security picture is not pointing towards one of stabilization, it's pointing towards one of escalation," he said.
Since the October 18 ambush, the area has been the site of continuous armed clashes. A security official said operations there were largely run by Haitian police.
Romain Le Cour Grandmaison, a security expert at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, said residents were skeptical of yet another foreign intervention and had reported heavy gunfire, drone strikes and possible civilian deaths.
He said he was not aware of humanitarian corridors to help people escape: "The gang leaders do not want people to leave the area because they probably want to use them as shields and make sure the population actually slows operations against them."
Washington has not publicly supported the mission but a US military official said Pentagon C-130s helped it deploy.
Irwin Stotzky, a rights expert at the University of Miami, said the US administration, which ended immigration protections for about 350,000 Haitians, has reasons to be invested.
"We've got to make it appear as if it's safe to send 350,000 people back to Haiti, when they actually are in great fear of their lives," he said. REUTERS

Starbucks Q4 revenue falls 4.5 pct, net income surges 408.8 pct
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
06:46:00 CST
07:46:00 KST

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- U.S. coffee giant Starbucks reported Thursday that its revenue fell 4.5 percent year on year to 9.14 billion U.S. dollars in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, while net income surged 408.8 percent, partly reflecting a sharp decline in restructuring and impairment costs.
According to the company's financial results for the 13-week quarter ended Sept. 27, net income attributable to Starbucks rose to 677.2 million dollars from 133.1 million dollars a year earlier. Diluted earnings per share increased to 0.59 dollars from 0.12 dollars, while non-GAAP adjusted earnings per share rose 53.8 percent to 0.8 dollars.
Operating income jumped 256.5 percent to 991.8 million dollars from 278.2 million dollars a year earlier, while operating margin expanded to 10.8 percent from 2.9 percent.
Starbucks said the decline in quarterly revenue was primarily attributable to the conversion of its retail operations in China to a licensed joint venture model.
Global comparable coffeehouse sales rose 7.2 percent, driven by a 5.2 percent increase in average ticket and a 1.8 percent rise in comparable transactions.
In North America, comparable sales increased 7.9 percent, including a 7.7 percent rise in the United States. Revenue from the North American segment grew 6 percent to 7.33 billion dollars.
The international segment recorded a 37 percent decline in revenue to 1.31 billion dollars, largely reflecting the restructuring of Starbucks' China operations. International comparable sales increased 0.9 percent.
Starbucks opened a net 303 new coffeehouses during the quarter, bringing its global store count to 41,607 at the end of September.
For the full fiscal year 2026, Starbucks reported revenue of 37.91 billion dollars, up 2 percent from the previous year. Net income attributable to the company rose 36.1 percent to 2.53 billion dollars, while diluted earnings per share increased to 2.21 dollars from 1.63 dollars.
Looking ahead, Starbucks expects revenue to decline approximately 1 percent in fiscal 2027, primarily reflecting the transition of its China operations to the licensed joint venture model.
The company projects approximately 4 percent growth in North American comparable sales and plans to open a net 1,200 new coffeehouses worldwide. ■

Indian man suspected of faking Bondi Beach mass shooting injury to receive victim compensation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:44:20 UTC
07:44:20 KST

Australian police in New South Wales announced Wednesday that a 46-year-old man had been arrested and charged with allegedly attempting to defraud authorities by fabricating an injury sustained in the Hanukkah terror attack at Sydney’s Bondi Beach.
He is suspected of doing so to obtain substantial financial compensation intended for victims of the attack.
According to a police statement, the man falsely claimed that he had been injured in the shooting on December 14, 2025, in which 15 people were killed. He subsequently filed fraudulent compensation claims. The amount he sought has not been disclosed.
The Australian newspaper The Daily Telegraph identified the suspect as Simaxwell Cyril, an Indian citizen who claimed he had been struck by shrapnel during the attack. However, he is suspected of having fabricated the injury.
The Australian federal and New South Wales state governments operate a special assistance program for victims of the massacre. Under the program, eligible victims wounded by gunfire or shrapnel can receive a one-time payment of 35,000 Australian dollars, plus recognition grants and assistance covering medical expenses and financial losses.
The suspicions against Cyril came to light by chance during an investigation by detectives from the New South Wales Police Homicide Squad into police actions during the attack.
This investigation is separate from the terrorism investigation targeting the perpetrators of the massacre. While gathering evidence, detectives became suspicious that Cyril had provided a false account of his injury and used it to submit compensation claims.
Police arrested Cyril on Tuesday morning at a police station in Parramatta, western Sydney. He was charged with offenses of “publishing false or misleading information to obtain a benefit” and “making a false representation that resulted in the commencement of a police investigation.”
He was released on bail on restrictive conditions and must appear at Parramatta Local Court on November 18.
Cyril expected to be deported from Australia
However, his legal troubles did not end there. According to The Daily Telegraph, after his release on bail, Cyril was arrested by Australian immigration authorities on suspicion of remaining in the country beyond the expiration of his visa.
He was transferred to the Villawood Immigration Detention Centre and is expected to be deported from Australia.
The allegations prompted strong reactions within Australia’s Jewish community, which is still grappling with the aftermath of the attack. Alex Ryvchin, co-chief executive of the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, condemned the alleged attempted fraud. He told the Nine Network that diverting police resources to investigate false claims when the community needs protection from security threats is an “abhorrent act that we should all condemn.”
What is the Bondi Beach massacre?
The massacre took place on December 14, 2025, when two attackers, a father, Sajid Akram, 50, and his son, Naveed, opened fire on hundreds of people attending a Hanukkah celebration at Bondi Beach.
Fifteen people, aged between 10 and 87, were killed, and approximately 40 were injured. The father was shot dead by police, while his son was wounded, arrested, and charged.
Meanwhile, a further hearing in the case against Naveed Akram, now 25, took place Wednesday, as the alleged compensation fraud case came to light. Akram faces 78 charges, including 15 counts of murder, 43 counts of attempted murder, and committing a terrorist act.
Judge Karen Stafford granted the prosecution’s request to postpone the hearing until February 2027 to allow time for consultations with victims and their families to be completed.
Police clarified that the investigation into the suspect accused of compensation fraud would not affect the proceedings against Akram.

An Italian military helicopter operating with the EU peacekeeping mission in Bosnia and Herzegovina crashed on Thursday, killing four people and injuring 11 others, Italy's defense ministry said.
Two of those killed were members of the Italian army and two belonged to the Italian Red Cross's Volunteer Military Corps, the ministry said. It added that all 11 injured were receiving treatment and none was in a life-threatening condition. A total of 15 people were on board.
"At this moment of immense grief, my thoughts go first and foremost to the families of our fallen, to whom I extend my personal condolences and those of the entire Defense establishment," Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said.
ANSA news agency reported the helicopter came down in the village of Gorice in Brcko district. Images carried by local media showed a military transport helicopter overturned on the ground and shattered into pieces.
"There are no words capable of easing such a profound loss," Crosetto said.
Reason for crash under investigation
The aircraft had been deployed as part of Operation Althea, run by the European Union Force, which oversees the implementation of the Dayton Peace Agreement.
Italy's defence ministry said the cause of the crash was under investigation and that inquiries were underway to establish the circumstances of the accident.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni also expressed her condolences, writing on X: "My thoughts are with the victims, their families, and all those who, as part of the mission to promote peace and stability in the region are experiencing hours of anguish."

According to N12, Norden called senior police officials and provided details that initiated the investigation and led to the arrests. Lahav 433 now has jurisdiction over the case.

Unlike you, with us this is the truth and not another lie."
The Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) launched an investigation into suspicions that foreign entities, potentially including Qatar and Turkey, funneled money into Israel to influence voting in Arab communities.
