True Zionists should welcome Arab participation in Israel’s government - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:43:28 UTC
07:43:28 KST

Israel’s Arab citizens have given our country an extraordinary democratic opportunity. Their turnout in this election should be a source of national pride. Bringing willing Arab partners into government could strengthen our democracy, help repair our society, and change how Israel is seen around the world.
Millions of Israelis went to the polls, including thousands who flew home to vote. Their commitment deserves our respect. After years of war, loss and division, our citizens deserve leaders prepared to use the opportunity they have created.
In these pages on October 12, I argued that politicians who exclude Arab citizens from government because they are Arab hand Israel’s enemies a weapon. The election has made that question immediate. Gadi Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett, Yair Lapid and Yair Golan now face a decision whose consequences extend far beyond the formation of another coalition.
With counting still underway, the reported result gives Netanyahu’s bloc 53 seats, the Zionist opposition 48 and the Arab parties 19. These numbers do not constitute a governing agreement. They demand serious negotiations among those who believe our country needs a different government.
Not welcoming Arab voters would make mockery of equal citizenship
Our Arab fellow citizens sought change through Israel’s democratic institutions. We should welcome their participation and recognize its significance. Celebrating their votes while refusing to consider their representatives as governing partners simply because they are Arab would make a mockery of equal citizenship.
Eisenkot, Bennett, Lapid and Golan: each of you has asked Israelis to trust you with our future. You now have a responsibility to examine every credible path to a government that can defend the country, restore its institutions and serve its citizens. Campaign pledges cannot relieve you of the duty to exercise judgment.
I write as an Israeli who believes in the Jewish state and fears for its future. I respect those who have carried the burden of defending it, including leaders with whom I disagree. I ask them now to challenge the prejudices that prevent us from building a stronger country.
There must be clear obligations for every governing partner. Each must reject terrorism, respect democratic institutions, and undertake to protect Israel and its citizens. Apply those standards equally to Jewish and Arab parties, then negotiate over the differences that remain.
Some differences may prevent agreement. A party’s policies or conduct may make cooperation impossible. But being Arab cannot be a disqualification, and no leader committed to Israel’s founding promise should defend such a position.
In 1948, as our country faced war for its survival, Ben-Gurion proclaimed a Jewish state committed to equal political rights for all its citizens. The Declaration of Independence called on Arab inhabitants to participate in building the state and its institutions. These commitments belong to the core of the Zionist dream.
True Zionists should have the confidence to honor them. A Jewish state in which Arab citizens share responsibility for governing fulfills a promise made at its birth. Excluding them because of their identity betrays it.
Bennett and Lapid have already governed with Ra’am, and Arab ministers have already served Israel. They know cooperation is possible and understand its difficulties. The task now is to build an agreement in which willing Arab partners exercise meaningful authority and accept the responsibilities that accompany it.
Arab leaders must also be prepared to compromise. Those seeking a place in government must help develop a workable program and accept responsibility for difficult decisions. They cannot expect their partners to take political risks while declining to take any themselves.
The international consequences could be profound. Palestinian citizens of Israel already elect representatives to our parliament in competitive national elections. Seeing those representatives exercise authority in the government of the Jewish state would provide a powerful answer to those who insist that Zionism necessarily means racial exclusion.
A cabinet in which Jewish and Arab ministers govern together would confront that claim with an uncomfortable reality. These would be Arab citizens making decisions, directing ministries and sharing responsibility for Israel’s future. Their authority would come from the same democratic process as that of their Jewish colleagues.
That would directly challenge the allegation that Israel’s Jewish identity makes equal political participation impossible. It would not resolve the conflict in the West Bank and Gaza or settle accusations concerning Israeli rule there. Those questions require decisions of their own, and our argument gains strength when we are precise about what shared government would demonstrate.
Netanyahu, extremists does not get to define Zionism
Netanyahu and his extremist partners have repeatedly weakened that argument through rhetoric that treats Arab political participation as a threat. When they suggest that a government supported by Arab votes lacks legitimacy, they give substance to the very charge of exclusion that Israel’s defenders are asked to rebut.
They do not get to define Zionism for the rest of us. Their insistence on distinguishing between the legitimacy of Jewish and Arab votes violates the equality promised at Israel’s founding. We should reject that rhetoric openly and build a government that gives practical effect to our principles.
The first test would be what that government delivers. Organized crime terrorizes Arab communities and weakens the state. Housing, education, public services and confidence in the police demand sustained attention. Jewish and Arab ministers who tackle these problems together would begin repairing the relationship between citizens and their government.
This could be the fastest credible way to begin restoring Israel’s standing after years in which the current government has deepened our divisions and damaged trust in our institutions. A new coalition alone will not repair that damage. A government that shares authority and addresses neglected social problems would show that the country has begun to change.
It would be the political equivalent of pressing Control-Alt-Delete on a system that has become stuck. The problems would remain, but we would have a chance to make government function again, with different partners and a renewed commitment to the citizens it serves.
Such a government could also improve the conditions for diplomacy with Saudi Arabia. Riyadh’s demands concerning Palestinian statehood would remain, and Arab participation in our cabinet could not substitute for addressing them. Yet a government prepared to build trust with Arab partners at home could bring greater credibility to negotiations abroad.
For Israelis, and for Jews defending Israel around the world, this would be a change worth fighting for. We could point to a Jewish state whose Arab citizens help govern it, with shared obligations and real authority. Our answer to those who deny the possibility of such a state would be visible in the government itself.
Eisenkot and his colleagues should begin serious negotiations now. Establish common obligations, test where agreement is possible and bring willing Arab partners into government. Our voters have created an opportunity to renew Israel’s founding promise. Those who claim to defend that promise must now act on it.
Jeremy M. Levin is an Israeli-American physician-scientist and biotechnology executive, an elected member of the American Zionist Movement and a participant in the most recent World Zionist Congress. He is a former CEO of Teva Pharmaceutical Industries and former chairman of the Biotechnology Innovation Organization.

AI generated
NEW YORK – Nvidia’s chief executive Jensen Huang said the chipmaker’s dealings with Megaspeed International were “normal and not unusual” following a New York Times report that one of the Singapore-based firm’s executives is under investigation for spying on behalf of China.
Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed’s officials was proper, and the chipmaker has checked to ensure that Megaspeed didn’t illegally send its artificial intelligence processors to China, Huang said in an interview on Oct 29.
That country is barred from buying Nvidia’s powerful AI chips – known as graphics processing units, or GPUs – under US export rules.
“We’ve studied all their deployments of our GPUs and counted every one,” he said in the interview. “And I think the US government also has as well.”
The remarks follow a Times story that the US government is investigating an executive from Megaspeed for allegedly providing information to the Chinese government.
Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, has previously been pictured with Nvidia’s leader on social media, and the story reports that she may have been serving as a Chinese agent aiming to evade chip export controls.
In the interview, Huang said that his interactions with her were typical of those with Chinese customers and executives.
She is no longer with Megaspeed, he said.
“Our relationship, our interactions, have been related to Megaspeed, and it was all completely normal and not unusual,” Huang said.
The CEO said he had not been informed by the US government of its suspicions about Huang Le.
The growing geopolitical rivalry between the US and China has led to increasing clamp-downs by Washington on exports of key American technology.
That has cut off Nvidia from a lucrative source of revenue in China, the largest market for chips.
The company has received some latitude to ship a limited amount of older artifical intelligence-related products to the Asian country under the Trump administration.
That approval has not resulted in a material amount of shipments, at least in part because Beijing has sought to limit the deliveries itself in an effort to foster its own chip industry.
Nonetheless, the restrictions on exports have led to investigations and charges of smuggling of Nvidia’s best products to China – something the company has said is an insignificant issue.
Megaspeed is one of a group of companies that Bloomberg News and others have reported may have tried to illegally divert shipments of chips intended for data centres outside of China into that country. BLOOMBERG

Why are Israelis surprised Arab voters showed up? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:38:53 UTC
07:38:53 KST

Oops. Look, there are Arabs in Israel.
Israelis woke up on Oct. 28 to realize that the Arab vote could change the picture, and many of them reacted as if they had only just discovered that Arab citizens live here. The Joint List and Ra'am won 19 seats between them, up from 10 in the outgoing Knesset, on an Arab turnout of about 80%. Those are the facts. The surprise is the story.
This is not new. Israelis have always had a talent for not seeing the Arabs who live among them. In May 1967, weeks before the Six-Day War, when Jordan ruled East Jerusalem, Naomi Shemer wrote "Jerusalem of Gold" for the Israel Song Festival. Looking across the border at the Old City, she described its market square as empty. It was not. Arab Jerusalemites lived there, traded there and prayed there. They simply were not in the song.
Amos Oz once told Shemer as much. The square was not empty, he said, and "we are not alone in this land." Shemer answered with a marriage analogy: another man's presence does not make a wife any less yours. The others are not denied. They are simply noticed only when they seem to threaten what is "ours." The rest of the time, they are scenery.
Arab citizens make up about a fifth of Israel's population. Nearly half of Israel's pharmacists are Arab, and Arab nurses and doctors fill hospitals and clinics across the country. We trust them with our bodies. We rarely think of them as voters.
Part of it is the way we live. Most Jews and Arabs in Israel live in separate towns, send their children to separate schools and, until university or the hospital ward, rarely share a room. Part of it is language. Arabic is the mother tongue of one in five Israelis, yet only about 10% of Jewish Israelis understand some Arabic. And part of it is the words we use. In Hebrew, Arab citizens are "the sector" (HaMigzar) or "the minorities," terms that keep them at a polite distance. Arab towns make the evening news when there is a murder, rarely when there is a vote.
None of this belongs to the right alone. In fact, the surprise was loudest among those who see themselves as liberal, open and democratic.
Israel's center-left likes to think of itself as the camp of coexistence. It praises the Arab doctor in the COVID ward and speaks warmly of a shared society. But when it comes to power, it keeps Arab citizens at arm's length. Its leaders ruled out Arab partners in advance and, in the words of a TheMarker analysis this week, dug their own pit by turning their backs on Arab voters. The Arab parties reached out. So far they have been ignored.
For much of the center-left, the Arab public is not a partner but a reservoir: votes that should turn out against Netanyahu, quietly, and then disappear from the conversation. Arab citizens are welcome to tip the balance, as long as they do not ask for a seat at the table. TV presenter Lucy Aharish put it bluntly on her program: “In the last elections, the Israeli center complained that the Arabs didn’t show up and so brought the extreme right-wing government to power. Now that they have shown up, the parties reject them.” When Arab citizens turned out in force, many liberal Israelis were as taken aback as anyone. They had hoped for help. They got a public with its own parties, its own leaders and its own demands.
Israel's founders saw it differently. The Declaration of Independence, signed on May 14, 1948, by the 37 members of the People's Council, calls on the state's Arab inhabitants to take part in building it "on the basis of full and equal citizenship and due representation in all its provisional and permanent institutions," as Naama Lazimi recalled. On the right, Ze'ev Jabotinsky went further. In The Jewish War Front, published in 1940, he wrote: "In every Cabinet where the Prime Minister is a Jew, the vice-premiership shall be offered to an Arab, and vice-versa." The founders of the Labor movement's state and the father of the Israeli right agreed on this much. It is their heirs who are surprised.
To be precise, Arab citizens have always voted. In Israel's first decades, turnout was even higher than today, reaching 90% in 1955, according to the Israel Democracy Institute, but under military rule those votes went mostly to Mapai and its affiliated lists, not to parties of their own. In the last 20 years, Arab turnout has never come close to this year's 80%. What is new is not that Arabs vote, but that they voted as a public with a voice of its own.
That is the paradox. For years, right and left alike have asked whether Arab citizens are integrating into Israeli society. This week they did the most integrated thing a citizen can do: they stood in line at a polling station, in an Israeli school, and dropped a ballot into an Israeli box. And that is what startled us.
There are real arguments to be had with some of the parties they voted for, as there are with many parties. But an argument with a party is not the same as discomfort with its voters.
"The Arab citizens are not guests in the country," Nimrod Dvir, founder of the Darkhenu movement, wrote in Ynet this week. That this still needs to be written, by a liberal, to liberals, says it all.
The “market square” was never empty. It was full in 1967, it is full today, and on Oct. 27 its people showed up in numbers that made them impossible to overlook. We can keep acting surprised every few years, or we can finally look at the square as it is.

Patrick Stewart, ‘Star Trek’ Captain Picard and ‘X-Men’ actor, dies at 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:36:06 UTC
07:36:06 KST

Patrick Stewart, ‘Star Trek’ Captain Picard and ‘X-Men’ actor, dies at 86
Stewart died in Los Angeles after battling Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia.
Patrick Stewart, the acclaimed British actor who played Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” films, has died. He was 86.
Stewart died on Wednesday in Los Angeles following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said in a statement on Thursday.
Although best known for his film and television roles, Stewart spent much of his career onstage, performing Shakespeare and other classics.
His career included performances as Claudius and Macbeth, a one-man adaptation of “A Christmas Carol”, and West End and Broadway productions of Harold Pinter’s “No Man’s Land” and Samuel Beckett’s “Waiting for Godot” alongside longtime friend Ian McKellen.
Stewart earned some of the best reviews of his career for his 2007 portrayal of Macbeth, including his only Tony Award nomination. The Times of London described his Macbeth performance as “an enthralling creation of frailty, appetite, egotism and grim humour”.
“Nearly 50 years I’ve waited,” Stewart told the Associated Press news agency in 2008. “I learned it when I was 14. I memorized all the soliloquies just because I thought they were great. And they stuck, so I didn’t have to learn those bits of the play, which is a blessing, because learning lines has now become the one curse of this job.”
From working-class Yorkshire to Shakespeare
Raised in Mirfield, West Yorkshire, a working-class corner of northern England, the future 24th-century commander of a starship grew up without a bathroom in his house.
He joined an amateur drama group at 12 and, as a teenager, memorised Shakespeare for fun. A scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School helped launch his acting career.
Stewart, who developed alopecia at a young age, had been bald since he was 19.
His childhood was also marked by domestic violence. His father, a former regimental sergeant major in the British Army, was prone to outbursts of “repeated violence against my mother,” as Stewart wrote in a newspaper piece. “Violence is always a choice a man makes and he alone is responsible for it.”
Stewart later became a patron of Refuge, a charity supporting survivors of domestic abuse.
From Shakespeare to Captain Picard
Stewart spent 14 years with the Royal Shakespeare Company, playing everyone from Mark Antony and Henry IV to Shylock and Oberon.
“People who were not in the company would say to me, ‘Give it a break. Why don’t you go somewhere else?’ And I would say, ‘To do what?'” he told the AP. “Telly?”
He eventually left and appeared in the 1981 film “Excalibur”. In 1987, shortly after performing in “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?”, he was offered a role in a science fiction series.
“I found myself in Hollywood shooting a syndicated science fiction series, which I was assured would fail,” he said.
But “Star Trek: The Next Generation” ran for seven seasons and 178 episodes. Stewart became known worldwide as Captain Jean-Luc Picard, whose command, “Make it so”, became one of the show’s best-known lines.
Stewart also played Professor Charles Xavier, the leader of the X-Men, beginning with the 2000 film “X-Men”. He returned to the role in several sequels, including 2017’s “Logan”, alongside Hugh Jackman as Wolverine.
Stewart died just days after Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov in the original “Star Trek” series, which aired from 1966 to 1969.
Queen Elizabeth II knighted Stewart in June 2010. He also served as an ambassador for the International Rescue Committee.

The General Staff of the Ukrainian Armed Forces reported this on Facebook, according to Ukrinform.

Russia's average daily losses in October currently stand at around 1,750 personnel.
"Losses in the Russian army continue to rise steadily: 26,090 personnel in February 2026, 46,230 in September, and 49,040 in October (as of October 29)," the General Staff said.
This is significant because the enemy's rate of losses exceeds its ability to replenish its units, meaning that each month of the war is costing the Russian army increasingly more, the military said.

World’s largest crypto exchange investigates suspected multibillion-dollar hack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:30:10 UTC
07:30:10 KST

World’s largest crypto exchange hit by cyberattack
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, has estimated the impact of a cyberattack at $6.3 billion, saying hackers may have exploited an employee’s compromised laptop to make unauthorized withdrawals.
In an update on Friday, the company said its preliminary investigation suggested that an attacker gained access to a service container through a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer, allowing unauthorized withdrawal transactions to be submitted.
Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked and pledged to cover all losses using its Secure Asset Fund for Users and company funds.
“The estimated total impact sits at around $6.3B. We have worked with blockchain partners to freeze affected assets, with ~$3 billion frozen on-chain so far,” the exchange said in a statement.
The company stressed that customer funds are safe and said it would publish a detailed technical report once its investigation is complete.
As an immediate precaution, Binance temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals, and conducted security checks. It also revoked the affected address authorization and enlisted law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms to trace and recover funds and identify those responsible.
The incident follows reports of suspicious transactions involving billions of dollars in digital assets transferred from wallets linked to Binance on Thursday.
Blockchain researchers initially estimated the outflows at $2.77 billion across five blockchains. Binance subsequently confirmed that $2.54 billion in affected assets were frozen.
Stablecoin issuers Tether, Circle, and Ripple were among the companies that moved to freeze assets linked to the suspected attack.
The suspected attack comes amid a series of major cryptocurrency thefts this year. In September, hackers stole around $388 million from the Bitget exchange. Attacks on the Drift Protocol and Kelp DAO platforms in April resulted in losses of $285 million and $292 million, respectively. In February 2025, suspected North Korean hackers stole around $1.5 billion from Bybit in what was widely described as the largest cryptocurrency heist on record at the time.
Binance co-founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao pleaded guilty in 2023 to violating US anti-money-laundering laws and stepped down as head of the exchange as part of a settlement in which Binance agreed to pay $4.3 billion in penalties. He subsequently served a four-month prison sentence.
US President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in October 2025. The White House defended the decision, saying he was unfairly prosecuted under former President Joe Biden as part of a broader crackdown on the cryptocurrency industry.

The museum building, designed by Pritzker Prize-winning Japanese architect Fumihiko Maki and Studio Opolis, an architectural practice located in Mumbai and Pune, is quite striking too.On X, industrialist Anand Mahindra called it "a seminal moment of recognition", adding that it has the potential to be a game changer for the museum-going experience in India.

An armored capsule instead of an open platform: Ukraine develops an evacuation module for the Murakha UGV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:25:10 UTC
07:25:10 KST

Ukrainian company Robotic Complexes is developing CASEEVAK, an armored module that lets the Murakha unmanned ground vehicle carry wounded soldiers off the battlefield, the company told Militarnyi on 28 October. The casualty rides in a closed capsule with ventilation, heating, lighting, and a first-aid kit, and side and rear doors let medics load and reach the soldier from any side.
Drones that can fly long distances pose a threat to both wounded soldiers and the crews evacuating them, making transportation the main challenge, said Ukrainian military medic Daryna Boiko, The Independent reported. Developers are looking for new ways to counter this threat. The current Murakha model is being equipped with passive anti-drone protection elements, the developers say.
An armored capsule that keeps the wounded connected
After a wounded soldier is loaded onto an evacuation platform, it is important not only to transport them to a safe location but also to protect them and monitor their condition during transit.
The module is built around a closed armored capsule made of 3.5 mm-thick Armox 500T steel with an inner lining of HDPE 1000, the media outlet reports. Side and rear doors allow the wounded to be loaded from different directions and accessed during evacuation.
To enable the operator to monitor the person inside and maintain contact with them, the capsule is equipped with a camera with day and night channels and two-way audio communication. The system can be controlled via ELRS, LTE, Starlink, or fiber-optic communications. Militarnyi reports that even if the capsule is detached from the main platform, it retains two independent communication channels.
The developers are also working to integrate vital-signs monitoring systems intended to provide medical personnel with information about the wounded person’s condition during transport.
An electric platform and protection against FPV drones
The evacuation module requires a platform capable of carrying it as it moves through dangerous areas. The Murakha is equipped with two electric motors, delivering a combined torque of 1,600 N·m, and a 35 kWh battery. The system’s stated range is up to 80 km, according to the media outlet.
Another area of development is protection against drones. Measures intended to protect the system include net launchers and electronic warfare (EW) equipment. However, work on a protective cage against FPV drones is still ongoing, according to the report.
The company has already conducted ballistic tests of the armor steel at a distance of 50 meters, using ammunition of various calibers, Militarnyi reports.
The Murakha-Mini logistics platform
The same company previously developed the Murakha-Mini logistics platform. Ukrainian military personnel began using it on the front line to deliver equipment, provisions and other supplies, Militarnyi reported on 24 October 2025.
The UGV can carry up to 250 kg and travel up to 40 km on a single charge, the media outlet reported. During one combat mission, it transported 150 kg of cargo and towed a six-metre platform carrying another drone and provisions, covering 16 km in one direction, Militarnyi reported.

Amazon posts negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion, holds 2026 capex unchanged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:24:49 UTC
07:24:49 KST

Amazon shares plunged more than 6% in extended trading Thursday after the company reported disappointing third-quarter results and ballooning negative free cash flow, reflecting its swelling AI investments.
Here's how the company did, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG:
- Earnings per share: $1.89 vs. $1.96 estimated
- Revenue: $201.94 billion vs. $202.31 billion estimated
Wall Street was also looking at other key revenue numbers:
- Amazon Web Services: $45.98 billion vs. $45.29 billion, according to StreetAccount
- Advertising: $19.64 billion vs. $20.82 billion, according to StreetAccount
The company held steady on its capital expenditure forecast for 2026, saying it continues to expect spending will reach $220 billion this year.
Tech's hyperscalers have been on a blistering spending run to meet the surge in demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure, but signs have begun to emerge that the capex splurge is moderating. Earlier this week, Microsoft lowered its capex forecast for the year to $170 billion from $175 billion, while Alphabet maintained its guidance at $195 billion to $205 billion.
CEO Andy Jassy said on a conference call with investors that the company expects to "spend meaningfully more in 2027," and that Amazon has a "clear line of sight to attractive financial returns."
The aggressive AI spending has eaten into Amazon's cash flow. The company posted negative free cash flow for the second consecutive quarter, recording an outflow of $42.4 billion for the trailing twelve month period, a swing of 386% year over year. In the prior quarter, the company reported negative free cash flow of $7.6 billion.
The company said the shortfall was primarily due to an increase in purchases of property and equipment as a result of AI investments.
Capital expenditures reached $77.3 billion during the quarter, ticking up from $35.1 billion one year earlier, and coming in well above analysts' estimated $58.7 billion, according to FactSet.
Amazon said it expects fourth-quarter revenue to be in the range of $240 billion and $247 billion. The midpoint of its guidance was below Wall Street's expectations of $244.5 billion, according to LSEG. The fourth quarter is typically one of Amazon's biggest by revenue, due to the peak holiday shopping season.
Sales in Amazon's cloud segment soared 39% year over year to $45.98 billion. That topped the consensus forecast for $45.29 billion and growth of 38%, according to StreetAccount.
Jassy highlighted AWS acceleration in the earnings release, saying the company expects revenue growth rates of "over 40%" next year and in 2028. He added, "Our AWS investment in functionality and infrastructure is working."
Jassy told investors on the call that he expects AWS will be a $1 trillion revenue business in the next five to 10 years.
Amazon is facing pressure from Wall Street to show that its AI investments are lifting its revenues. The company pointed to growing traction for Bedrock, its AI model marketplace, along with its Trainium and Graviton AI chips.
Jassy said Amazon's chips business "continues to grow triple-digit percentages year over year." He added that the company plans to make its Trainium chips available externally "late in 2027," assigning a timeframe to comments Jassy made earlier this year suggesting such a move.
Third-quarter net income came in at $20.69 billion, or $1.89 per share, vs. $21.19 billion, or $1.95 per share, a year ago. The company said the decrease was driven primarily by a $9.5 billion pre-tax gain from its investment in the AI startup Anthropic, which was recorded in the 2025 third quarter.
While the AWS segment continues to hum along, results weren't as bright in Amazon's retail business, which remains its largest unit by revenue, or its advertising segment.
Online sales gained 2% year over year to $68.47 billion, which fell short of analysts' projected $69.68 billion, according to StreetAccount. It marked a slowdown from one year ago, when sales increased nearly 10%.
Advertising revenue rose 11% year over year to $19.64 billion. That missed StreetAccount consensus estimates of $20.82 billion.
Both units were impacted in part by Amazon's decision to pull its annual Prime Day sale forward in several countries from its typical third quarter timeframe into the second quarter so as to not conflict with the FIFA World Cup in July.

Germany's Alexander Zverev clinches tennis No. 1 ranking
October 29, 2026
Germany's Alexander Zverev is set to become the new world No. 1 in men's tennis, capping a year in which he won two Grand Slams.
Zverev is the second German man, after Boris Becker, to clinch the top spot in the sport. Becker reached No.1 some 35 years ago.
Zverev replaces Italy's Jannik Sinner, who previously held the world's No. 1 spot.
Zverev got there by reaching the quarterfinals of the Erste Bank Open in Vienna this week.
The 29-year-old is the second-oldest first-time No. 1 ranked player after Australian John Newcombe achieved the feat at age 30 in 1974.
"(It is) very special. To have the feeling to be on the top of the world is amazing," Zverev said.
"It is different than winning a tournament or a title, but it's such a special feeling to know that the No. 1 is going to be next to your name when the new rankings come out."
Among German female tennis players, only Steffi Graf and Angelique Kerber have achieved this in the WTA rankings.
Two Grand Slams in 2026
Zverev's career had long been defined by getting close to Grand Slam titles but never quite reaching the pinnacle, facing stiff competition from Sinner and Spanish talent Carlos Alcaraz.
But he finally had its broke through this year, when he won the Grand Slam at both the French and US Opens.
Known for his consistency, he was just the ninth man to reach at least the semifinals at all four majors in the same season.
The Hamburg-born Zverev also won a gold medal in the 2021 Olympics.

What next for Erin Patterson?
Patterson now must apply to the high court for leave to appeal should she wish to continue fighting her conviction or new sentence.
She is one of only a handful of Victorian offenders sentenced to life without parole, and one of the only women in Australian history to be given the sentence.
When the judges left court, Patterson also stood, took a book from beside her, and walked off-screen.
In court, family members hugged and were emotional, and detectives involved in the case looked elated. Nobody commented outside court.
You can read our full report here:
Patterson showed no emotion on the video feed as McLeish outlined why her appeal had failed, and how the director of public prosecutions had succeeded in seeking a longer sentence.
Patterson’s actions mean it is ‘inappropriate’ to fix non-parole period, justice says
McLeish said the court had found Patterson’s actions “carefully planned and deliberate”, saying she had engaged in an “elaborate series of deceptions”.
 The applicant’s murderous intent dated back to the invitations to lunch, it persisted through the lunch that the poison was administered …
We have concluded that the case involved such calculated criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period.
Erin Patterson fails in her bid for a retrial
Erin Patterson has lost her bid to overturn her convictions, with the court finding unsuccessful or rejecting all seven grounds her lawyers had argued.
The director of public prosecution has succeeded and Patterson will be resentenced to life without parole. She was sentenced last year to life imprisonment, with a non-parole period of 33 years.
Justice Stephen McLeish said Patterson’s “offending was extraordinarily cold and calculated and stands to be denounced in the strongest terms”.
Erin Patterson can be seen on a video link from the Gordon unit of the Dame Phyllis Frost Centre, the state’s women’s prison, wearing a royal blue jumper and staring out a window to her right.
She is on mute, but was asked by court staff whether she could hear proceedings in the court and raised her right thumb in the air in response.
Ian Wilkinson not at court for appeal decision
We’re still waiting outside the Victorian supreme court room where the appeal decisions will be heard.
Unlike during the appeal hearings themselves in August, there are only a handful of representatives from the victims’ families in court.
Ian Wilkinson, the only surviving victim of the beef wellington lunch, is not at court.
Homicide squad detectives, including Stephen Eppingstall, the informant in the case, are among those waiting for the appeal.
There’s a dozen or so members of the public here too, including some who attended every day of the trial in Morwell.
The appeal decisions will be handed down in the Banco court, the supreme court’s ceremonial court.
Director of public prosecution argued Patterson’s initial sentence inadequate
During the hearings, Brendan Kissane KC, the director of public prosecution, appealed against Patterson’s sentence, arguing that it was manifestly inadequate.
He said that even though Patterson would be aged in her 80s by the time she was eligible for parole, her sentence was still too lenient.
When asked whether a longer non-parole period would essentially damn Patterson to dying behind bars, and had “some artifice of it being life with life”, Kissane told the court:
 It has its harsh aspect to it, of course, we accept that.
But in our submission that is not a matter that is outweighed by the seriousness of the offending.
A note on the proceedings today
The court of appeal is due to make its decision at 10am today. Our reporter, Nino Bucci, will be there and we’ll bring you updates as soon as they happen.
It could be a very quick ruling and over in a matter of minutes.
Patterson is not expected to attend the appeal decision in person.
Patterson’s lawyers argued seven grounds for appeal
In August, the court heard Erin Patterson should have been given no possibility of ever being released from prison, or a non-parole period so lengthy that she was likely to die behind bars.
Her lawyers argued seven grounds for her appeal, including that allowing jurors to stay in the same hotel as police and the prosecution while they deliberated over their verdicts in the triple murder trial represented a “catastrophic” failure of the justice system.
Patterson sentenced last year
Erin Patterson, 52, was last year sentenced to life imprisonment, with a non-parole period of 33 years, for the murders of her estranged husband’s parents, Don and Gail Patterson, and his aunt Heather Wilkinson, after she hosted them for lunch.
Patterson was also convicted of the attempted murder of Heather’s husband, Ian Wilkinson, who survived the beef wellington laced with death cap mushrooms after spending weeks in hospital.
Welcome
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Erin Patterson’s bid for a retrial.
Patterson is set to find out if she could face a longer prison sentence or a new trial this morning, as Victoria’s highest court hands down its decision on two appeals regarding her triple murder case.
The court of appeal is set to rule on the two appeals from 10am, after justices Lesley Taylor, Stephen McLeish and Peter Kidd heard arguments from her legal team and prosecutors in August.

Putin says Moscow seeks better European ties, conflict will produce no winners
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:18:12 CET
07:18:12 KST

MOSCOW, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Russia supports any steps aimed at restoring relations with European countries, President Vladimir Putin said late on Thursday, adding the outbreak of any conflict would leave a situation with no winners.
Commenting on his phone call this week with the leaders of Norway and Finland, Putin said Russia was prepared for a potential war with Europe, though it did not want one.
“We support any steps…we support any actions aimed at restoring full-fledged and complete relations with European countries,” Putin told reporters after hosting a summit with African leaders.
“First of all, we are ready, but we want no war with Europe. And if anyone wants it, let them prepare, but right now they have not achieved their goal — to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia. And if things go too far, there will be no winners at all. Let no one forget that.”
Putin said Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere had been right to make the call despite criticism from some European capitals that the two were breaking ranks by initiating contact with Moscow.
He said Russia wanted no impediments to navigation in the Baltic Sea and added that restricting communication could lead to a situation similar to that in the Strait of Hormuz since the outbreak of the US-Iranian conflict in February.
“Does someone want the same situation in the Baltic as in the Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz?” Putin said. “I don’t know. We don’t want that, but we will respond to any challenge.”
(Reporting by Olesya Astakhova; Writing by Maxim Rodionov; Editing by Andrew Heavens, Ron Popeski and Jamie Freed)

Kim Jong Un urges drone dominance as North Korea fires missiles, rockets
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:18:00 CET
07:18:00 KST

By Joyce Lee and Heejin Kim
SEOUL, Oct 30 (Reuters) - North Korean leader Kim Jong Un called for his country to seize “absolute superiority” in drone technology as he attended an exhibition and demonstration of unmanned aeronautical technology, state media KCNA reported on Friday.
The firepower demonstration featured tactical suicide attack drones, tactical cruise missiles, multipurpose drones and 600mm multiple rocket launchers, KCNA said.
The display highlighted Kim’s push to modernise North Korea’s armed forces by using drones and artificial intelligence as Pyongyang draws lessons from Russia’s war against Ukraine and other global conflicts.
It came amid heightened tensions between the two Koreas, with Seoul vowing to respond firmly to what it called North Korean breaches, and Pyongyang denouncing joint South Korea-US air defence drills.
KCNA photographs showed unmanned aerial vehicles bearing the North Korean Air Force’s emblem at the exhibition, attended by Kim.
Other images showed what appeared to be an unmanned aerial vehicle crashing into a military vehicle and exploding in a ball of flame during a weapons demonstration.
South Korea’s military said on Thursday that North Korea had fired around 10 projectiles, including short-range ballistic missiles.
Kim said that pursuing superiority in drone technology was “an indispensable option” given the changing nature of modern warfare, according to KCNA.
He also said using high-level AI in unmanned weapons systems should be a top priority for North Korea, KCNA reported.
Kim has repeatedly called for the development of drones and military AI. State media said Kim ordered mass production of suicide attack drones in November 2024, oversaw tests of AI-equipped versions in March 2025 and in September 2025 called AI a top priority in weapons modernisation.
DRAWING LESSONS FROM UKRAINE WAR
Since October 2024, North Korea has sent more than 16,000 personnel to Russia to aid Moscow in its war against Ukraine, and gained battlefield experience in drone, electronic and combined-arms warfare, according to South Korean intelligence.
North Korea is transforming its military with drones and AI, drawing lessons from the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea’s Kyungnam University.
By showing a comprehensive display of weapons, North Korea is trying to “shut off the possibility of dialogue or negotiations” with South Korea, Lim said.
North Korean state media also displayed for the first time what analysts described as a tailless, flying-wing stealth drone.
Photographs showed racks of small suicide drones and loitering munitions similar to the US Switchblade 600, suggesting an emphasis on cheap, mass-produced weapons, potentially drawing on lessons from the Ukraine war, analysts said.
Mock targets resembling South Korean K9 howitzers, M1 Abrams-type tanks and radar vehicles suggested the weapons were intended for use against South Korean and US forces, they said.
BORDER TENSIONS
South Korea will respond firmly to protect the military border despite Pyongyang’s assertion that it is conducting operations within its territory, Seoul’s national security adviser Wi Sung-lac said on Friday.
Separately, North Korea’s Defence Ministry said US and South Korean air defence drills were raising tensions on the peninsula and that there was “no limit” to its option for maintaining a strong deterrent posture, KCNA reported.
Tensions have escalated since a landmine blast inside the Demilitarised Zone seriously wounded several South Korean soldiers last month. Seoul said the blast was caused by a North Korean mine, which Pyongyang has denied.
Kim’s powerful sister, Kim Yo Jong, said earlier this month that North Korea would activate anti-South Korean propaganda loudspeakers along its entire border by the end of October.
(Reporting by Joyce Lee, Heejin Kim and Jack Kim; Editing by Nia Williams, Jamie Freed and Ed Davies)

El Salvador frees ex-President Saca after 10-year corruption sentence
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
23:17:46 CET
07:17:46 KST

By Gerardo Arbaiza
SAN SALVADOR, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Elias Antonio “Tony” Saca, a former Salvadoran president imprisoned for corruption, was released on Thursday, his lawyer said, standing alongside the politician as they exited a courthouse.
Saca, 61, served a reduced 10-year sentence after pleading guilty to diverting and laundering more than $300 million from the state budget during his 2004-2009 administration.
His lawyer, Mario Machado, said the former president had served his sentence in full without receiving early-release benefits. “The 10 years were completed,” Machado said.
“We have come to the court to formally report the release. This was requested just yesterday.”
Although Saca was sentenced in 2018, his prison term was backdated to 2016, when he was arrested during his son’s wedding. A plea deal allowed Saca to reduce a potential 30-year sentence.
Saca is one of four Salvadoran presidents to have faced corruption charges, although the other former leaders avoided the prospect of jail time. Mauricio Funes and Salvador Sanchez Ceren fled to Nicaragua, and Francisco Flores died before his trial could begin.
Saca, a businessman and radio broadcaster, served as president as part of the conservative Nationalist Republican Alliance (ARENA).
In 2014, after his expulsion from the party, he sought to return to the presidency with the Grand Alliance for National Unity (GANA), but the Supreme Court ruled his candidacy unconstitutional.
Prosecutors had alleged that Saca diverted state funds for personal use and to benefit his allies, including by funneling large sums of money to his party. Saca was ordered in separate civil proceedings to repay millions of dollars to the state.
(Reporting by Gerardo Arbaiza; Writing by Raúl Cortés Fernández and Diego Oré; Editing by Daina Beth Solomon)

The star of "X-Men" and "Star Trek," Patrick Stewart, has died
Kyiv • UNN
British actor Patrick Stewart died at the age of 86 at his home in Los Angeles. He was known for his roles as Picard and Professor Xavier.
British actor Patrick Stewart, known for his roles as Professor Charles Xavier in the "X-Men" franchise and Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the series "Star Trek: The Next Generation," has died at the age of 86. This was reported by his longtime representative, Kelly Bush Novak, UNN reports.
Details
It is reported that Stewart passed away on October 28 at his home in Los Angeles.
He was surrounded by the warmth of family and friends, live music, prayers, tears, laughter, and those profound feelings that only he could evoke—a man who devoted his entire life to all of us
Background
Patrick Stewart was born on July 13, 1940, in Mirfield, Yorkshire, England. The actor said that in childhood, theater became a way for him to escape a difficult situation at home.
After several roles in British film and television, Stewart made his American film debut in "Excalibur" (1981). He later played Gurney Halleck in David Lynch's science-fiction film "Dune" (1984).
The actor achieved worldwide fame for his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in the series "Star Trek: The Next Generation," which premiered in 1987.
In 2000, the actor was cast as Professor Charles Xavier in the film "X-Men," based on Marvel comics.
Among the actor's other notable works are the films "Robin Hood: Men in Tights," "Conspiracy Theory," "Green Room," "Charlie's Angels," and "Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness." Stewart also worked on voice acting for animated films, including "The Prince of Egypt," "Bambi II," and "Gnomeo & Juliet."
In 2010, Queen Elizabeth II knighted Stewart.

Trump administration attempts to take down leak of ICE personnel data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:16:51 UTC
07:16:51 KST

Trump administration attempts to take down leak of ICE personnel data
An Icelandic web company, FlokiNET, has defended the data’s publication as satisfying a ‘legitimate’ public interest.
The United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has asked an Icelandic web hosting company to take down a site with information about tens of thousands of its employees.
On Thursday, the Icelandic company FlokiNET posted a letter it received from the cybersecurity firm ZeroFox, on behalf of DHS.
The letter accused FlokiNET of violating its terms of service by publishing a “stolen” employee dataset and asked it to “remove or disable” the information.
“The content is live and places more than 40,000 identifiable individuals at risk of harassment, stalking, and physical harm,” the letter said.
FlokiNET said the letter concerned one domain, icepi.cx, which has compiled information about employees from a range of DHS agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP).
Those agencies have come under intense scrutiny since the start of President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign in 2025.
But the Trump administration has often refused to identify DHS agents involved in specific operations, citing safety risks.
Though FlokiNET said it refused to comply with DHS’s request, it noted that the website’s registrar ultimately suspended the domain. The employee information has since moved to a different domain.
In a statement posted online, FlokiNET defended its decision not to remove the site.
“Federal officers carrying out an enforcement programme are not private individuals while they are carrying it out,” the company said. “The public has a legitimate interest in knowing who is doing that work, under whose authority, and in which office.”
The database was first posted online on Wednesday by Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), a group that showcases leaked government data.
In the past, DDoSecrets has released emails from convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, as well as information from the Israeli Ministry of Justice and police departments in the US.
A hacker group calling itself the “Department of Peace” has claimed responsibility for obtaining and sharing the DHS data.
Since the database was first published, other groups have spread the information elsewhere, including on sites like icepi.cx. As a result, the information is unlikely to be entirely scrubbed from the internet.
The Trump administration, however, has taken an aggressive approach to online platforms purporting to contain information about ICE employees and other agents involved in immigration operations.
Last year, for instance, the US Department of Justice pressured tech giants like Apple to remove apps that track ICE agents, including one called ICEBlock.
The move sparked backlash from Democrats and free-speech advocates, who argued that the public has a right to report on ICE’s movements.
“Blocking access to these apps at the request of the federal government raises the distinct possibility that Apple is working with government to violate its customers’ First Amendment right to record and report on the activities of their government,” Democratic Representative Jamie Raskin wrote in a letter last year, asking Apple to review its decision.
Immigration agents, meanwhile, have taken several steps to conceal their identities during operations, including wearing face masks or street clothes.
That lack of transparency has spurred criticism from human rights groups and immigration advocates, who argue that they have little recourse to pursue allegations of excessive force or impropriety during ICE raids.
Since Trump was sworn in for a second term, at least 25 people have faced gunfire from immigration agents. Six of the shootings have resulted in deaths.
Other cases have involved alleged violations of civil liberties – including unlawful arrests and racial profiling – as well as controversial tactics like car ramming and tackling.

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Oct 30, 2026
Nations said to be undermining science at UN nature talks
Political tensions are mounting in the final days of the United Nations biodiversity talks with a handful of countries accused of trying to weaken the science that underpins global nature policy.
The growing feud over the role of science has alarmed veteran negotiators and follows recent efforts by fossil fuel-reliant nations to delay reports by the IPCC, the global authority on climate change.
“The same thing is happening here as what is taking place with the IPCC,” said a French government delegate at the COP17 summit in Yerevan, Armenia.
He said four countries – Saudi Arabia, Russia, Argentina and Brazil – were frustrating progress.
Brazil’s Bolsonaro isolated, ridiculed after self-exile
In a viral wave of mockery, Brazilian popstar Anitta declared herself free of cellulite, one influencer declared himself the “true president” of Twitter, and another social media user proclaimed himself the winner of the next lottery.
The target of the taunts was Flavio Bolsonaro, who – after fleeing to the United States following his election defeat – proclaimed himself the leader of Brazil on Oct 28 in a confusing series of revised statements.
The moves by the 45-year-old senator have been met in Brazil with a mixture of derision, disbelief, and disapproval, even from within his own camp.
2 dead as ‘fairy chimney’ rock spires collapse in Turkey
A landslide triggered by heavy rainfall caused a rock spire to collapse in Turkey’s Cappadocia tourist region on Oct 29, killing at least two people, the local governor said.
Turkey’s Cappadocia region, a magnet for tourists from around the world, is home to rock formations known as “fairy chimneys”, created by ancient volcanic activity.
“According to initial findings, two people were killed and five others injured in the incident,” Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said on X.
Ex-factory worker crowned China’s richest woman, again
A factory worker-turned-entrepreneur who made her fortune producing glass screens for Apple’s iPhones has reclaimed the title of China’s richest woman on the back of her foray into high-end manufacturing.
Zhou Qunfei, 56, founder and chairman of Lens Technology, is worth 127 billion yuan (S$24.4 billion) today. This is up 15% from a year ago, according to the Hurun Richest Women in China 2026 list released on Oct 28.
She overtook Zhong Huijuan, founder of drugmaker Hansoh Pharmaceutical, whose estimated wealth stands at 124 billion yuan, to take the top spot for the second time. Zhou was first crowned China’s richest woman in 2015.
Star Trek and X-Men star Patrick Stewart dies at 86
Patrick Stewart, who rose from poverty in England to become an accomplished Shakespearean stage actor and then achieved global stardom as the erudite Captain Jean-Luc Picard in TV’s Star Trek: The Next Generation and the telepathic Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men movies, has died at the age of 86.
Stewart, knighted in 2010 by Queen Elizabeth II for his contributions to drama, died at his home in Los Angeles, according to a statement on his X account.
“We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” it said.

Putin says Moscow seeks better European ties, conflict will produce no winners
MOSCOW – Russia supports any steps aimed at restoring relations with European countries, President Vladimir Putin said late on Oct 29, adding the outbreak of any conflict would leave a situation with no winners.
Commenting on his phone call this week with the leaders of Norway and Finland, Putin said Russia was prepared for a potential war with Europe, though it did not want one.
“We support any steps... we support any actions aimed at restoring full-fledged and complete relations with European countries,” Putin told reporters after hosting a summit with African leaders.
“First of all, we are ready, but we want no war with Europe. And if anyone wants it, let them prepare, but right now they have not achieved their goal – to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia. And if things go too far, there will be no winners at all. Let no one forget that.”
Putin said Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere had been right to make the call despite criticism from some European capitals that the two were breaking ranks by initiating contact with Moscow.
He said Russia wanted no impediments to navigation in the Baltic Sea and added that restricting communication could lead to a situation similar to that in the Strait of Hormuz since the outbreak of the US-Iranian conflict in February.
“Does someone want the same situation in the Baltic as in the Gulf or the Strait of Hormuz?” Putin said.

Philadelphia appoints new rat control manager

Philadelphia appoints new rat control manager
Philadelphia has appointed a new Rat Abatement Manager to tackle its rodent problem, following approximately 4,000 rat-related complaints each year, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to the city’s Department of Public Health, Adrian Jordan will lead a team of health inspectors conducting door-to-door visits in neighborhoods most affected by rat infestations. The team will assess the scale of the problem, carry out control measures and advise residents on preventing further infestations.
According to the department, Philadelphia receives around 4,000 complaints about suspected rat activity annually. Inspections confirm approximately 2,000 cases, prompting treatment and follow-up prevention efforts.
Jordan will also coordinate efforts between five municipal agencies, including the Water Department, Sanitation Department and Streets Department, to address problems that require cooperation across city services.
The city has a long history of battling rodents. In the early 1900s, Philadelphia’s health authorities paid residents five cents for every dead rat delivered to a designated collection station.
Today, officials emphasize prevention rather than financial incentives. Residents are advised to store garbage in tightly sealed metal containers, remove potential rodent hiding places and seal openings larger than half an inch (1.27 cm) around their homes.
The department also encourages residents to report rat sightings so inspectors can investigate and take appropriate action.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency explained how rodents can spread plague.

The identity and location of seven Russian tankers transporting 288,000 metric tons of diesel to the U.S. were announced by Greenpeace Ukraine on Oct. 29.
Following U.S. President Donald Trump suspending sanctions on Russian oil exports, a live tracker map developed by Greenpeace, an international environmental organization, shows Russian tankers currently moving across the Atlantic Ocean, with one vessel approaching the U.S. East Coast.
“Every shipment of Russian diesel comes at a human cost," Polina Kolodiazhna, energy campaigner at Greenpeace Ukraine, said in a statement. "Every dollar flowing into Russia risks fueling more attacks, more destruction and more deaths. These shipments also undermine the international sanctions regime and send a dangerous message that business with Russia can continue as usual, even as its war against Ukraine rages on."
Greenpeace Ukraine identified the tankers as the Taurus, Pvt Azura, Agioi Fanendes, Talisman, Leruo, Iblea, and Primorye. Three of these vessels, the Talisman, Leruo, and Primorye, are currently sanctioned by multiple countries as part of Russia's "shadow fleet" illegally exporting oil, according to Ukraine's war sanctions portal. The Talisman has been under U.S. sanctions since January 2025.
The ships are expected to arrive in the U.S. in early November, though it is not known at which ports they will arrive.
Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree on Sept. 28 restricting access to data on the country's oil refineries and energy exports amid Ukrainian campaigns against Russia's oil infrastructure. The decree added another layer of secrecy to Russian exports, helping shadow fleet vessels evade sanctions.

Attack of the clones: Alaska has a ‘black PR’ moment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:05:29 UTC
07:05:29 KST

Attack of the clones: Alaska has a ‘black PR’ moment
US President Donald Trump has accused Democrats of fraud over an alleged plot to field a namesake candidate in Alaska’s Senate race.
An electoral trick familiar to Russians who remember the political free-for-all of the 1990s, the tactic involves recruiting a candidate whose name matches that of an established politician in the hope of confusing voters and siphoning off votes.
In Russia, such contenders became known as “clone candidates” and were a hallmark of the country’s notoriously ruthless election campaigns, forming part of the political “black PR” playbook.
In Alaska, Republican incumbent Senator Dan S. Sullivan now faces a namesake challenger, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher who is also running in the November 3 election.
According to a New York Times investigation, operatives linked to Democratic candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee allegedly helped recruit the namesake candidate as part of a broader effort to undermine the incumbent. The newspaper cited interviews, text messages and documents detailing the operation, which reportedly began in 2025. Both Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic committee have denied involvement.
Following the report, Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, ordered an investigation into whether any laws had been broken and whether criminal charges or civil action was warranted. Trump has branded the alleged scheme “voter fraud at the highest level” and called for Peltola and the namesake candidate to be removed from the ballot and prosecuted.
@Odinsraven66 @StephenM To be precise, there is no indication what party "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.” might be affiliated with on the Alaska bingo card. https://t.co/TWjsD2dWtT
— DougS (@doug_swartout) October 24, 2026
US black PR that came to Russia
Russians know the playbook. During the 1998 elections to the St. Petersburg Legislative Assembly, namesake candidates appeared in multiple constituencies. At least two challengers sharing the surname Mironov ran against Sergey Mironov, then acting speaker of the regional parliament. He nevertheless secured a decisive victory with around 70% of the vote.
In a 2000 State Duma by-election in Sverdlovsk Region, Yekaterinburg police chief Nikolay Ovchinnikov faced Vladimir Ovchinnikov, who appeared above him on the alphabetically arranged ballot. The namesake reportedly secured more than 5% of the vote, although the police chief ultimately won.
An isolated example of the practice surfaced in St. Petersburg as recently as 2021, when opposition politician Boris Vishnevsky faced two rivals who had legally changed their names to Boris Vishnevsky, adopting similar hairstyles and beards for their election portraits.
This is not the first time the practice has appeared in the US. In the 2020 Florida state Senate race, a little-known candidate named Alex Rodriguez received more than 6,000 votes, while Democratic incumbent Jose Javier Rodríguez lost to Republican Ileana Garcia by just 32 votes.
The namesake candidate subsequently pleaded guilty to campaign-finance offenses connected with the scheme, which involved a former Republican state senator.

PROFILE - Patrick Stewart, Star Trek and X-Men star, dies at 86
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:03:24 UTC
07:03:24 KST

Sir Patrick Stewart, the acclaimed British actor who achieved worldwide fame as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films after decades on the Shakespearean stage, has died at the age of 86.
Stewart died Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles following an illness involving Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, his spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, confirmed Thursday to the Hollywood Reporter.
He spent his final hours surrounded by family and friends, including his wife, singer-songwriter Sunny Ozell, according to a statement released by his representatives.
His death marked the end of a career spanning more than six decades across theater, television, and film, becoming one of the world's most internationally recognized actors.
From Yorkshire to Shakespeare
Born on July 13, 1940, in Mirfield, West Yorkshire, Stewart grew up in a working-class household with limited financial means.
His father, a British Army veteran of World War II, struggled with the psychological effects of his military service and was physically abusive toward Stewart's mother, an experience the actor would later discuss publicly.
Stewart discovered acting while still at school and briefly worked as a newspaper reporter before pursuing the stage professionally.
He trained at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School and spent his early career performing in regional theaters across Britain.
In 1966, he joined the Royal Shakespeare Company, beginning an association that would establish him as a leading classical actor.
Over the following decades, he appeared in productions of Macbeth, Hamlet, King Lear, Antony and Cleopatra, and numerous other works by Shakespeare.
He also performed on the London stage and Broadway, earning recognition for his commanding voice, disciplined performances, and ability to portray complex characters.
From the stage to global stardom
Despite his established reputation in British theater, Stewart's international breakthrough came in 1987 when he was cast as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation.
The series, which ran until 1994, introduced a new generation of audiences to the science fiction franchise.
Stewart's portrayal of Picard, a thoughtful and diplomatic Starfleet commander who often relied on reason and negotiation rather than force, became one of the franchise's defining performances.
He reprised the role in several Star Trek feature films before returning decades later in the television series Star Trek: Picard, which ran from 2020 to 2023.
His popularity grew further in 2000 when he took on the role of Charles Xavier, the powerful telepathic leader of Marvel’s X-Men superhero team, a role many fans saw him as perfectly suited for.
As Professor X, as the character is also known, Stewart appeared in multiple installments alongside fellow British actor Ian McKellen, who portrayed Xavier's adversary and frenemy Magneto.
His performance in the critically acclaimed 2017 film Logan brought another major chapter of the character's story to a close.
He also appeared in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness in 2022 and is expected to appear posthumously in the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday.
Beyond his dramatic roles, Stewart demonstrated his comedic abilities through appearances in television productions including Extras and voice work on the animated series American Dad.
Theater, honors, and advocacy
Despite his Hollywood success, Stewart remained closely connected to theater throughout his career.
He frequently performed a one-man adaptation of Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol and appeared alongside McKellen in acclaimed productions of Waiting for Godot and No Man's Land.
His performances earned him two Laurence Olivier Awards, a Grammy Award, and nominations for several Emmy and Golden Globe Awards.
In 2010, Queen Elizabeth II knighted him for services to drama.
Stewart also became an outspoken advocate for survivors of domestic violence and military veterans experiencing mental health difficulties.
Drawing on his own childhood experiences, he supported organizations including Refuge, which assists domestic abuse survivors, and Combat Stress, which works with veterans.
In his 2023 autobiography, Making It So: A Memoir, Stewart reflected on his upbringing, career, relationships, and the lasting impact of witnessing violence in his childhood home.
The book traced his journey from a modest Yorkshire household to international stardom and explored the personal challenges behind his public success.
Stewart is survived by his wife, Sunny Ozell, whom he married in 2013, and two children from his first marriage.
His career leaves a legacy spanning classical theater and popular entertainment, with his portrayals of Picard and Professor Xavier remaining among the most recognizable characters in modern science fiction.

Hegseth reportedly fires high-ranking army strategist over alleged leaks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
22:01:56 UTC
07:01:56 KST

The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has reportedly dismissed Lt Gen Brett Sylvia, a high-ranking army strategist serving on the Pentagon’s joint staff, following allegations that he disclosed classified information to the public.
The Pentagon announced on Thursday that it had referred an alleged information leak case for criminal investigation, maintaining that the removal of the senior general was essential “to protect sensitive information”, the Washington Post reported.
Sylvia had served as the director for strategy, plans and policy on the joint staff.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell acknowledged the dismissal in a statement on social media, though he did not mention Sylvia by name.
“Following an extensive Air Force OSI investigation, the Department took necessary personnel action to protect sensitive information,” Parnell wrote. “To protect the integrity of the investigation, no further comment will be made regarding the individual or the circumstances of this action.”
“This matter, along with others, have been referred to the Justice Department for potential further legal action,” he added.
A spokesperson for the Department of Justice said in a statement that it “has ongoing investigations related to possible leaks of classified information”.
“We work closely with our government partners, which includes the Department of War,” the spokesperson added, using the Trump administration’s name for the Pentagon.
Sylvia’s removal represents one of the most significant actions so far in Hegseth’s extensive campaign to identify officials suspected of sharing information with journalists, as the unpopular US war on Iran moves into its ninth month.
In July, Hegseth announced that the Pentagon and the US Department of Justice had created a joint taskforce “to identify and prosecute” what he called the “unauthorized disclosure of sensitive” information to the press.
Last year, Hegseth implemented new restrictions governing media access that prompted legal concerns from press organizations.
Dozens of journalists surrendered their press badges rather than agree to the new media policies, which have been subject to legal challenges.
A senior Pentagon official told Reuters that Sylvia failed three separate polygraph tests, in which he was asked whether he had disclosed classified material.
“The extent of his leaking became so critical that Secretary Hegseth took immediate action and fired Sylvia in order to protect national security. Urgent action was needed and could not wait another second,” the official said, according to Reuters.
However, a colleague of Sylvia told the Washington Post that the general had consistently rejected accusations that he leaked classified information, while also acknowledging that he had previously communicated with members of the press.
In August, three journalists fired by the Pentagon from the US government-funded news outlet Stars and Stripes sued the department in federal court, arguing their dismissals were illegal and violated their first amendment rights to free speech.

Ahmad Tibi, head of the Joint Arab List's parliamentary bloc in Israel's Knesset, has alleged that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is seeking another election to cling to power, urging opposition parties to thwart his plans by forming a government led by Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot.
In an exclusive interview with Turkish news agency Anadolu, Tibi said he believes Netanyahu intends to remain at the helm of a caretaker government while preparing to launch another war against Iran in coordination with US President Donald Trump.
"I think Netanyahu wants another election. For now, he wants to remain prime minister of the caretaker government," he said.
"Netanyahu wants to launch a war against Iran in cooperation and coordination with Donald Trump after the US midterm elections, then hold another election," he added.
Tibi urged opposition parties to move swiftly and decisively to prevent Netanyahu from carrying out that scenario.
"The opposition must block Netanyahu by announcing that a government will be formed under Eisenkot as prime minister. We, as the Joint Arab List, are ready to help," he said.
He stressed that the Joint Arab List does not intend to join a new government but is prepared to facilitate its formation through understandings with opposition parties.
"We in the Joint Arab List do not want to enter a government. We have spoken about providing a safety net for our community and making it possible to bring down Netanyahu’s government and establish an alternative government through understandings with the opposition," he said.
Tibi said Arab lawmakers would seek commitments addressing the needs of their communities in exchange for providing parliamentary support.
"The most important thing for us now is to bring down this government," he added.
He expressed hope that opposition leaders would overcome their differences and end internal disputes following Tuesday’s parliamentary elections.
Arab turnout 'blocked Netanyahu's plans'
Tibi described the high turnout among Arab voters as a major political achievement that prevented Netanyahu from securing another parliamentary majority.
"Netanyahu is deeply disturbed by the high turnout among Arab voters because it blocked and disrupted his plan to form another government under his leadership," he said.
"Netanyahu cannot form a government. Itamar Ben-Gvir will never be police minister again," he added.
Tibi said the participation of Arab voters had also prevented far-right politicians, including Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, from returning to power.
"This is an achievement for our politically aware Arab public, which acted with great political wisdom and responsibility," he said.
He urged Arab lawmakers to use their electoral gains to help establish an alternative government.
"We all want to use this trust, these votes and these seats to contribute to bringing down Netanyahu’s government and making way for another, less harmful alternative government," he said.
Rejects allegations of election fraud
Tibi accused Netanyahu and his political allies of conducting a campaign against Palestinian-Israeli voters following the election.
"Netanyahu is conducting an open campaign against Arab voters for all to see," he said.
He rejected allegations from Netanyahu’s political camp that Palestinian-Israeli voters had engaged in election fraud.
"The only address for thieves is Netanyahu’s Prime Minister’s Office. Benjamin Netanyahu is the last person who can lecture us on honesty and integrity," Tibi said.
He pointed to the corruption charges against Netanyahu and criminal investigations involving other government officials.
Tibi said Palestinian-Israeli voters had participated in large numbers despite physical difficulties, citing elderly people and people with disabilities who made their way to polling stations.
He accused Netanyahu’s political camp of seeking to discourage Palestinian-Israeli participation to remain in power.
"They want Arabs not to vote so they can continue governing. Our votes brought down their plans," he said.
Tibi also alleged that the campaign was intended to delay the publication of official election results and prevent the replacement of Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana.
He said he was reassured by the Central Elections Committee’s position that the allegations would not affect the publication of the results.
Responds to Netanyahu over Qatar visit
Asked about a social media post in which Netanyahu questioned why he had traveled to Qatar two days before the elections, Tibi dismissed the criticism.
"Netanyahu posted a tweet asking why Ahmad Tibi traveled to Qatar and published a picture of me at Al Jazeera," he said.
"It is clear to everyone that I gave an interview watched by millions on Al Jazeera and returned quickly. If I am invited again, I will go and participate. Anyone who does not like that can deal with it."
He reiterated that Netanyahu was "the last person" qualified to lecture others about honesty and integrity.
Open to coordination with other Arab parties
Tibi said the Joint Arab List was open to coordinating with the United Arab List (Ra’am) led by Mansour Abbas to facilitate the formation of an alternative government.
"We have a common goal: bringing down this government. Of course, there is nothing wrong with coordinating with our brothers in the United Arab List," he said.
He also dismissed the possibility that Avigdor Lieberman, leader of the Yisrael Beiteinu party, would abandon the opposition bloc.
"I don’t think so, but this is always Lieberman’s behaviour after elections. He is trying to pressure Eisenkot and the change bloc to secure a period as prime minister," Tibi said.
He criticised Lieberman’s apparent distancing from the opposition following the election as irresponsible.
"I heard him say he does not want to sit with Bibi (Netanyahu) or Tibi. I say that’s right, because I don’t want to sit with Lieberman either," he added.
Election leaves blocs short of majority
The interview came after Tuesday’s parliamentary elections left neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition parties with enough seats to form a government independently.
According to the latest results, Netanyahu’s bloc secured 53 seats, opposition parties 48 and Arab parties 19 in the 120-member Knesset.
A parliamentary majority requires at least 61 seats, placing Arab parties in a potentially pivotal position in negotiations over forming the next government.
Israel’s Central Elections Committee announced on Thursday that counting of special ballots had been completed, with the official final results to be released later.
President Isaac Herzog is expected to consult parliamentary factions after receiving the official results before assigning a lawmaker the task of forming a government.
