Patrick Stewart, Shakespearean actor turned Star Trek and X-Men star, dies at 86
- Sir Patrick Stewart has died at 86 in Los Angeles after a brief journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, his X account said.
- He rose from poverty in Yorkshire to acclaim with the Royal Shakespeare Company, then became famous as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Professor X in X-Men.
- Stewart said acting was his “safe space”; he was knighted in 2010, acted into his 80s, and left a lasting mark on stage and screen.
AI generated
LOS ANGELES – Patrick Stewart, who rose from poverty in England to become an accomplished Shakespearean stage actor and then achieved global stardom as the erudite Captain Jean-Luc Picard in TV’s Star Trek: The Next Generation and the telepathic Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men movies, has died at the age of 86.
Stewart, knighted in 2010 by Queen Elizabeth II for his contributions to drama, died at his home in Los Angeles, according to a statement on his X account.
“We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” it said.
Stewart became an actor at age 18 and gained acclaim on the stage as a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company beginning in the 1960s. But it was not until after he was hired at age 47 for Star Trek: The Next Generation – a TV series that ran from 1987 to 1994 as a sequel to the original 1960s Star Trek – that he gained mainstream fame, acting into his 80s.
“Make it so,” his character Picard often said, instructing a subordinate to carry out a command, or sometimes deploying the similar catchphrase: “Engage.”
It was a role he had debated even taking after his longtime friend and fellow Shakespearean Ian McKellen advised him to spurn Star Trek and remain in theatre.
Stewart did take the role and became both a fan favourite and an indispensable part of a lucrative sci-fi franchise, playing Picard not only in 176 episodes over seven seasons of that series but also in several Star Trek films and in the later streaming series Star Trek: Picard that began airing in 2020 when he was 79.
“As the seven seasons of TNG (The Next Generation) went by, the distinction between Jean-Luc Picard and Patrick Stewart became thinner and thinner, until it was impossible for me to know where he left off and I began. So much of what I believed and felt went into that show,” Stewart told the Guardian newspaper in 2022.
Stewart also initially baulked at being cast as the wheelchair-using mutant Professor X in the X-Men movies, based on the popular Marvel comic book character.
“I said, ‘Look, I know this isn’t science fiction, but it’s fantasy, and I’ve done that.’ But they persuaded me that it wouldn’t be like Star Trek, so I did it. And yet again I was proved wrong,” he told the Guardian.
He became a critical part of another big-money franchise, starting with the first entry X-Men in 2000 and followed by several more, including the 2002 Marvel movie Doctor Strange In The Multiverse of Madness.
He appeared alongside McKellen, who played the villain Magneto, in some of the X-Men films.
Stewart, playing Charles Xavier, took part in the filming of the highly anticipated Avengers: Doomsday and will appear in the Marvel film that is due to hit theatres in December.
Marvel Studios paid tribute to Stewart on Oct 30 in a statement, calling him “a singular talent, a generous collaborator and a true gentleman”.
Acting was safe space
Stewart was born on July 13, 1940, in the English town of Mirfield in Yorkshire. He was raised in poverty, with a father who he said returned from World War II an alcoholic who suffered from post-traumatic stress syndrome and physically abused Stewart’s mother. Stewart recalled putting his body between his father and mother to try to protect her.
As a child, Stewart said, acting became a “safe space” after a schoolteacher introduced him to Shakespeare, specifically The Merchant Of Venice, during a class when he was 12. He started losing his hair at age 17 and was bald by 19. He was embarrassed at the time, but eventually embraced it.
Star Trek, created by Gene Roddenberry, presented a hopeful vision of the future, with humankind venturing into the cosmos in spaceships exceeding the speed of light and encountering alien races. The enduring popularity of the original series and the success of spin-off films prompted Roddenberry to create The Next Generation sequel series.
The Picard character was the opposite of the swashbuckling and sometimes unintentionally buffoonish Captain James T. Kirk, played by William Shatner, of the original series – envisioned as more cerebral and disciplined, though sometimes coming across as stuffy, humourless or self-important.
Stewart recalled being a little bit too serious towards his cast mates early on.
“I tell the story of calling a meeting of my principal fellow cast members and telling them that I thought we were not disciplined enough, that we should not be fooling about on the set as much as we were, but taking everything seriously,” Stewart told The New Yorker magazine in 2023.
“And one of the cast members said, ‘Oh, come on, Patrick, we’ve got to have some fun.’ And I thumped the chair and said, ‘We are not here to have fun’ – which they have never let me forget. They taught me so much about loosening up and being freer,” Stewart added.
Stewart also felt the series improved as it went along, faulting his own portrayal of Picard in the first two seasons.
“I found it lacking intimacy. It was very authoritative, but there were few other qualities in him,” Stewart said, adding that his work got better in subsequent seasons.
In fact, the finest work for the entire cast may have been the two-part, time-bending series finale.
He became Sir Patrick Stewart when he was knighted by the queen at Buckingham Palace in 2010. He told reporters that his heroes were British actors Laurence Olivier, John Gielgud and Alec Guinness, who had also been knighted, adding that being “in that company is the grandest thing that has professionally happened to me”.
Stewart was married three times and had two children. His third marriage, in 2013, was to American musician Sunny Ozell. REUTERS

Ukraine’s Navy said on 29 October that it destroyed two Russian Su-34 fighter-bombers in a Neptune missile strike on Marinovka airfield in Russia’s Volgograd Oblast.
The reported strike targets aircraft Russia uses to launch guided aerial bombs against Ukrainian cities, military positions, and frontline communities. Destroying the two jets would reduce Russia’s capacity to carry out these attacks.
Neptune strike hits Russian military airfield
According to the Ukrainian Navy, its units struck the site where Russian aircraft were stationed at Marinovka airfield using a Neptune coastal missile system.
The Navy said the strike destroyed two Su-34 fighter-bombers belonging to Russia’s 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment, based near the settlement of Oktyabrsky in Volgograd Oblast. The regiment is part of the 4th Mixed Aviation Division of Russia’s 4th Air and Air Defense Forces Army.
The Ukrainian Navy did not provide further details about the strike.
Su-34s are key to Russia’s guided bomb attacks
Russia uses Su-34 fighter-bombers to launch guided aerial bombs, known as KABs, against Ukrainian military positions and settlements, particularly in frontline areas. These attacks threaten both Ukrainian troops and civilians in communities near the front.
According to Ukrinform, Russia’s Aerospace Forces had approximately 140 Su-34 aircraft of various modifications in service as of 22 October.
The Ukrainian Navy said it would continue striking Russian military targets to weaken Moscow’s ability to wage war against Ukraine.

European energy giants declare record profits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

European energy giants declare record profits
As European households struggled to pay their energy bills, the continent’s oil companies more than doubled their profits over the last quarter, reaping the benefits of the US-Israeli war on Iran.
Eight months to the day since American and Israeli forces began bombarding Iran, Brent crude prices sat at $115 on Thursday, up from $72 pre-war. Dated Brent, the actual on-the-spot price that purchasers are paying for Brent cargoes in the North Sea, was even higher, at $120.
This price spike has driven the cost of petrol, diesel, and heating oil to record highs across Europe. However, it’s been a windfall for Europe’s largest oil companies, according to quarterly profit statements compiled by Germany’s Der Spiegel on Thursday.
British oil and gas giant Shell recorded a profit of $12.1 billion between July and September, a more than twofold increase on the previous quarter, and on the same quarter last year. Between July and September 2025, Shell made $5.43 billion in profit.
France’s TotalEnergies increased profits by 127% to $9.1 billion in the same period, while Spain’s Repsol recorded an almost fivefold increase, from $640.7 million to $3.1 billion. Austria’s OMV, meanwhile, increased profits by 68% to $2.36 billion.
German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil and his counterparts in Austria, Italy, Poland, Portugal, and Spain, have called for an EU-wide windfall tax on the oil giants, similar to the “solidarity levy” imposed by Brussels after the escalation of the Russia/Ukraine conflict in 2022.
“The Commission has been very reserved on this issue, although several member states have been calling for models to be presented for a long time,” Klingbeil said after a meeting of EU finance ministers in Ireland last month. “This must happen by the next [finance ministers’] meeting in October at the latest,” he added.
The European Commission shot down Klingbeil’s proposal, and October passed with no action from Brussels. “It is in the hands of member states,” EU Economic Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis told reporters. “Member states can go ahead and take those decisions on the taxing of windfall profits.”
Despite Gulf exports reportedly recovering to 80% of pre-war levels, Houthi attacks on Saudi energy facilities and shipping, the threat of naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, and warnings of an “intense” new US military campaign against Iran have all played a role in keeping oil prices nearly twice as high as they were at the beginning of February.

'Extremist right-wing ideologies' an increasing threat in France & 'across much of democratic world'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:06:36 UTC
05:06:36 KST

'Extremist right-wing ideologies' an increasing threat in France & 'across much of democratic world'
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
François Picard is pleased to welcome Dr Joseph Downing, Senior Lecturer in International Relations and Politics at Aston University. In modern France, the politics of insecurity increasingly extends beyond questions of crime and public order to encompass deeper struggles over national identity, disappearance of the political centre and erosion of democratic values. The emergence of far-right extremist violence, alongside the persistent stigmatization of ethnically diverse working-class suburbs, raises urgent questions about the relationship between fiery and divisive political rhetoric and far-right radicalization. Downing examines these interrelated challenges against the backdrop of a deadly shooting in the Paris suburbs, allegedly motivated by racist and anti-Muslim hostility.
For Downing, the attack illustrates a broader shift in Europe's extremist landscape, in which the rise of far-right political violence demands greater public and institutional attention: "This is really one of the first and one of the most serious right-wing nationalist, nativist-inspired terror attacks that you see in France."
Yet Downing's analysis reaches beyond the horrific attack. He challenges the political representation of France's working-class suburbs as centres of Islamist radicalism, describing such portrayals as a divisive rhetorical strategy that stigmatizes communities whose residents are overwhelmingly engaged in ordinary civic and economic life.
His central political concern is the weakening of the democratic centre. Amid rising living costs, social insecurity and the circulation of polarizing identity narratives through digital media, he argues that political movements on the ideological fringes gain an advantage by offering apparently simplistic, and often divisive solutions, to deeply complex problems. "The centre of politics in France, as in many other democracies, is struggling to hold."
Perhaps most revealingly, Downing identifies the deliberate or careless conflation of racial identity, migration status and religious extremism as a particularly damaging feature of contemporary political discourse. By treating French citizens of African or Arab heritage as perpetual outsiders, political commentators risk reinforcing the very divisions that undermine national cohesion.
The interview therefore opens onto a wider question at the heart of contemporary democratic politics: what happens when narratives of national insecurity become more politically influential than the social realities they claim to describe?
Downing's reflections illuminate not only the challenges facing France but also the wider vulnerabilities of democratic societies confronting political polarization, economic anxiety and the normalization of exclusionary rhetoric.

'The city is alive': A brief peace in Kherson, but residents fear what comes next
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:05:57 GMT
05:05:57 KST

'The city is alive': A brief peace in Kherson, but residents fear what comes next
- Published
The Ukrainian city of Kherson has known its first two days of quiet after many years, as a US-brokered temporary ceasefire has allowed residents rare moments of respite from the constant Russian aerial attacks that plague the front line region.
Videos posted on social media showed people strolling down streets covered in anti-drone nets and gathering in the city's squares - ordinary activities that usually mean keeping one eye on the sky and one ear out for incoming drones.
"Ever since the ceasefire was announced, there's been total silence," said Olga, 42, speaking by phone from Kherson. "We are all, of course, overjoyed."
"I don't even know what to call it," she added, her smile coming through in her voice. "It's as if everything has finally come to an end."
Since Tuesday, Kherson has "literally come back to life," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
"People are calmly going out, walking, enjoying the autumn sun. What for some is ordinary everyday life, for residents of the Kherson region today is the greatest desire."
The temporary pause in hostilities - due to end on Sunday - is the result of efforts by US First Lady Melania Trump to broker a safe passage out of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which lies on the other side of the Dnipro river from Kherson.
For several days, Russian forces have been working to clear the road of mines, ahead of a planned evacuation of Oleshky's civilians on Friday.
But there are fears that, alongside carrying out the well-publicised "humanitarian operation" – which some American journalists will be invited to witness – the Russians are using the truce to bolster their forces in the area ahead of a renewed onslaught of Kherson from next week.
"They are... using this lull to strengthen their positions, bring in more military supplies, weapons, ammunition, and drones, and carry out some redeployment of their forces," an anonymous source working in local government told the BBC.
Petro Andriushchenko, Director of Ukraine's Center for Studying the Occupation, says Kherson locals have told him that they witnessed a military build-up around Radensk, some 20km (12 miles) from Oleshky.
Its residents will be saved but "we are simultaneously giving the enemy an opportunity to exploit the ceasefire for its own military purposes," he said. Once the ceasefire ends, the situation may be "worse than we saw before, because Russia's units will be stronger. They have enough time to prepare to prolong this action."
Though Kherson residents are clear-eyed about what lies ahead, for a brief period this week the city caught its breath.
No violations have been reported on either side since Tuesday. There have been other ceasefires in the past, but these were generally not respected, Kherson resident Dima said.
"This is the first time the shelling has stopped, people don't quite believe it," he told the BBC. "They are going to the shops, drinking coffee, walking around... The city is alive."
On social media, a woman named Yulia wrote about her unusually uneventful trip to the supermarket with an edge of disbelief. For once, she said, she returned home from the shops "whole and calm, not as usual - scared, sweating from the horror and with a lump in my throat."
This week, dozens of people were also able to access their belongings and homes in the so-called "red zone" of Kherson – an area so exposed to drones and artillery attacks that it has become unlivable.
"Some are venturing into places where nobody has dared to go for years, filming areas where simply being present has meant - and will once again mean - almost certain death," said Denisa Bohackova, a Czech volunteer who lives in Kherson.
Dima described scenes of "girls, boys, parents, grandmothers" walking down the streets of the red zone carrying suitcases and bags, returning to their flats to see what they could retrieve.
Some of those who returned to the red zone found buildings reduced to charred, empty shells; in other cases, homes had been looted. The scale of destruction in some of these places, Bohackova said, is "breathtaking".
Others were rushing back for reasons beyond material concerns. Angela Dobrovolska's husband Serhiy was killed two years ago by a grenade dropped by a piloted Russian drone - an instance of a "human safari" attack of the kind that Kherson has become sadly infamous for.
On Thursday, Angela headed back from Kyiv to Kherson to visit his grave for the first time in months. "They say that all the people have rushed to Kherson," she said. "And I'll be going to the cemetery to my husband."
The population of Kherson has dwindled from over 250,000 to about 65,000 since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which will enter its sixth year in February.
Though civilian life in the city never stopped, Bohackova said, it also carried on under the conditions of an active battlefield, with schools, theatres, kindergartens and hospitals moved underground.
"An ordinary civilian from Kherson has experienced more of this war than many soldiers," Bohackova said.
Olga, who is raising two children, described regular blackouts, mines dropped by drones and concealed by fallen leaves, drone fragments ricocheting, and a city that typically shuts by the afternoon.
But since silence fell on the city, Olga has been able to live a normal life. She drove to a different town and took the bus to another district to visit her grandmother with her son. Around her, the shops were full, as were the cafes. After years of quiet streets, "there was even a small traffic jam," she smiled.
But the clock is ticking.
The evacuation of nearby Oleshky is due to be completed by Sunday, after which the ceasefire will be over. "The concern is that, starting Monday, things could turn truly chaotic," Olga said.
"We know the strikes will resume, and that they will increase," said Dima, as he and his wife prepared to visit their flat in the red zone for the first time in several months.
"These few days showed us how it could be if it all finally ended."

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. Russia’s FSB has released new details about Ukraine luring Russian teenagers into committing terrorist acts through the popular youth dating chatbot Divinchik.

Ukraine's recruitment of teenagers through the Divinchik dating chat
- The FSB has reported new cases of teenagers being recruited by the special services of Ukraine to commit terrorist attacks through the popular youth dating chatbot Divinchik / Leo - Dating, Communication, New Friends.
- It said that in August-September 2026 alone, eight minors aged 14 to 17 and two adult Russian citizens (19 and 24 years old) were detained in Moscow, St. Petersburg and the Leningrad Region, Nizhny Novgorod, Omsk, Ryazan and Sverdlovsk regions.
- According to the FSB, the detainees planned or had already committed arson attacks on law enforcement vehicles, gas stations, energy and transport infrastructure facilities on the instructions of the Ukrainian special services.
- They also served as couriers for transferring funds received from defrauded citizens to crypto exchange offices.
- It said that since July 2025, 56 Russians aged 12 to 24, users of the Divinchik Telegram service, who committed crimes under the psychological influence of the special services of Ukraine, have been detained in various regions.
Testimony of detainees
- The FSB showed a video recording of the detention of several teenagers involved in terrorist attacks through the popular youth dating chatbot Divinchik.
- In the footage, the young people said that they had met with young women in the chat, after which they were contacted by unknown people and forced to commit illegal acts through deception, blackmail and threats.
- As a result, several detainees set fire to gas stations, another photographed a relay cabinet, after which he was ordered to set it on fire to allegedly close his criminal case.
Involvement of minors in terrorist attacks in St. Petersburg
- The special services of Ukraine have involved two underage St. Petersburg schoolgirls in committing terrorist attacks through Telegram chatbot Divinchik /Leo, Svetlana Petrenko, an official representative of the Investigative Committee of Russia, told TASS.
- As a result, one of the schoolgirls set fire to a gas station in September 2026.
- Also in September, the second schoolgirl, while at a police station, poured flammable liquid over official cars, after which she set them on fire.
- After that, she went to another police department but was detained.
- In addition, a teenager has been brought to criminal responsibility in the Leningrad Region.
- A young man purchased flammable liquids and set fire to a gas station in St. Petersburg and the Leningrad Region, recording his actions on video.
- He acted on the instructions of a person who contacted him after meeting a young woman in the chatbot Divinchik and threatened negative consequences for him and his family members.
- They were all placed under house arrest.

Healey backs away from cutting welfare cost despite warnings of public finance shortfall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:02:16 UTC
05:02:16 KST

John Healey has backed away from cutting the cost of welfare this parliament, amid dire warnings his first budget could lead to brutal spending cuts because of a £28bn shortfall in public finances.
Experts rounded on Healey’s steady-as-she-goes budget on Thursday, with the Institute for Fiscal Studies saying he had left himself a mountain to climb by ducking big tax and spending decisions.
In a damning analysis, the IFS said Healey would need to have set aside an additional £28bn a year, to offset the impact of inflation on future spending plans and hit the target of spending 3% of GDP in defence by 2030.
Instead Helen Miller, the IFS director, said Healey had opened the way to “a spending review that looks pretty brutal for some departments” – including real-term budget cuts.
“Public service spending plans look extremely tight. They don’t look to me like plans that this government would want to deliver,” she said, adding that meant Healey could face “another season of damaging speculation about tax rises”.
The welfare bill will not be part of the spending review, which focuses on departmental budgets. But in a bid to underline his determination to balance the books, the chancellor pointed to plans for reform, telling BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “We have to bring the benefits bill down.”
He had earlier appeared to say cuts would be made in this parliament, when asked if there would be a reduction in the bill before the next election. “There will be. There will be a reduction in the benefits bill,” said Healey. “We’ll do that in a Labour way and we will do that because it is simply not good for Britain or progress to have a bigger and bigger benefits bill.”
However, Treasury officials clarified that he had not meant to give a timeline and Healey later told Channel 4: “It’s not correct to say that we are going to bring this welfare bill down in this parliament because we’ve not set a timetable for that.”
Instead, he pointed to forthcoming reviews from Alan Milburn on employment support for young people, and from Stephen Timms on disability benefits.
Milburn is expected to recommend additional spending upfront, aimed at bringing down costs over the longer term by helping more young people into employment.
The Office for Budget Responsibility has said total welfare spending will grow from £334bn last year to £431bn by 2030 – with about half of that being spent on pensioners and a quarter on sickness and disability benefits. The overall forecast spending has risen by £8bn since March.
With a tough global economic backdrop, Healey has said the single biggest driver of better prospects for the UK would be an end to the Iran and Ukraine wars.
But in his interviews, Healey appeared to take a more cautious view than the prime minister on the potential for growth from rejoining Europe or the single market. Asked by LBC if growth would be stronger if the UK were in the EU or the single market, Healey replied: “Well, I don’t actually accept that. Brexit has certainly hit our level of growth. It’s certainly hit our level of trade. But we had a referendum. We’re out of the European Union. The challenge for me now is how do we make the best of an economy which this year has proved remarkably resilient.”
Asked later by Channel 4 if he, like Andy Burnham, hoped for the UK to re-enter the bloc in his lifetime, Healey said: “I’m older than Andy Burnham. I don’t expect to see that.”
The chancellor put measures to ease the cost of living at the heart of his first budget, including a £100 winter cost of living payment for most households. However, critics lined up on Thursday to accuse him of taking a “scattergun” approach – and of not hitting Britain’s banks hard enough to fund the package.
The Resolution Foundation thinktank said Healey had failed to target energy support to the households that need it most ahead of a difficult winter, with bills expected to rise sharply in January and the Bank of England to raise interest rates next week.
Ruth Curtice, Resolution’s chief executive, said: “Faced with a tough backdrop amid global economic turmoil, the chancellor delivered a scattergun budget that did little to address the sharp challenges facing Britain.
“Cost of living support is being spread far too thinly and will leave even those families receiving help facing higher energy bills than they did during the last energy price shock.”
Paul Nowak, the TUC’s general secretary, has strongly advocated for a bank windfall tax to fund energy support. He said he welcomed Healey’s approach, but would be pushing for him to go further.
The chancellor has doubled the surcharge banks pay on their profits from 3% to 6% for 15 months. Novak said: “It was right to tax banks to help people with their energy bills, but I think banks could have been asked to pay a fairer share. He’s going to review it in 15 months. We’re going to be looking as part of that review – if banks are still making windfall profits – for him to extend and increase the bank tax.”
As well as casting doubt on whether Healey’s future spending plans are realistic, the IFS said the £15bn headroom, or buffer, he has left himself against Labour’s fiscal rules could easily be eroded by higher than expected energy costs.
The chancellor allowed the buffer to absorb some of the impact of the Iran war, which has driven up the government’s cost of borrowing. At the time of the spring statement, Rachel Reeves had built up headroom of £24bn.
Miller said that was a “reasonable” decision to make, but “a lower buffer leaves the chancellor more exposed to future bad news”.

Man targeted Muslims, Africans and North Africans, French prosecutors say
Prosecutor Olivier Christen said suspect admitted that he chose the location because it was ‘a hotbed for Islamists’.
A man in France charged with murder and attempted murder has admitted he targeted individuals “who appeared to be Muslim, African, or North African”, prosecutors have said.
France’s anti-terrorism prosecutor’s office confirmed on Thursday that the 39-year-old, identified as Kevin T, had been formally charged in connection with a “terrorist” enterprise. Prosecutor Olivier Christen said Kevin admitted he chose the location because it was “a hotbed for Islamists”.
Before changing his position on Thursday, Kevin had disputed the racist nature of the attack.
One person was killed and seven others were injured last Friday when a man fired at people from his car as he drove through the towns of Trappes and La Verriere, west of Paris. He was arrested later that day. A child was among the victims, most of whom had foreign heritage.
The prosecutor said Kevin had stated that he felt “no regret” but that he did not intend to “kill children”. However, he added that he “might have been mistaken due to their size”.
Pengo Bossio Wangi, a 26-year-old French citizen with Congolese heritage, was killed in the attack.
During a search of Kevin’s home, authorities found “weapons or weapon components, specifically a magazine, two pairs of brass knuckles, a steel bayonet, and a silencer”, officials said.
Police also found a copy of Adolf Hitler’s book Mein Kampf, along with a Quran, a Bible and stickers celebrating Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally party. Kevin T had displayed a “very high level of preparation” ahead of the attack, according to prosecutor Christen.
He explained that in September, Kevin acquired “several weapon components designed to enhance the tactical effectiveness of a Sten submachine gun, as well as a police armband and handcuffs”.
The suspect said he was neither a member of nor a sympathiser with any political party, Christen added.

====================================================================================================

Social media use ranks among the top predictors of depression in a study of 183,000 adults
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:00:03 UTC
05:00:03 KST

An analysis of more than 183,000 American adults surveyed over an 11-year span indicates that higher daily social media use is consistently linked to an elevated likelihood of reporting depression. Using machine learning models to evaluate demographic and media habits from 2014 through 2024, researchers found that social media use ranked among the strongest predictors of self-reported depression, with its contribution to predicted risk rising once use exceeded about two and a half hours per day. The findings, published in npj Mental Health Research, suggest that the connection between heavy social media use and self-reported depression is not limited to teenagers and has remained stable across a decade of shifting digital trends.
Social media encompasses online platforms built for interpersonal communication, content sharing, and public commentary on community life, services, or products. Over the past decade, the rapid adoption of platforms such as Instagram, Snapchat, and TikTok has reshaped how people socialize, express themselves, and compare their lives to the lives of others. Alongside this expansion, public health experts have raised questions about whether heavy engagement with these apps contributes to depression, a mood condition characterized by persistent sadness, low energy, and a reduced interest in everyday activities.
Some early studies suggested that heavy use of social platforms might take an emotional toll. In a 2016 experiment involving 1,095 adults in Denmark, participants who took a one-week break from Facebook reported higher life satisfaction and more positive emotions than those who kept using the site, particularly if they were heavy users or prone to envying others online. Similarly, a study covered by PsyPost in 2018 found that teenagers who spent more free time on screen-based activities reported lower happiness than peers who spent more time on in-person activities, with the happiest teens using digital media for less than an hour a day.
Other studies complicated this picture by questioning whether social media actually triggers mental distress or whether people who are already struggling simply turn to their screens more often. For instance, a 2018 study of university students tracked 125 undergraduates seven times a day for two weeks and found that feeling lonely or tired predicted more passive scrolling later on, whereas scrolling did not predict subsequent increases in depression symptoms or stress.
Meanwhile, some researchers analyzing large time-use diaries argued that overall screen time had little negative impact on youth well-being, while critics countered that combining television, gaming, and social media into a single screen-time measure can hide risks specific to interactive social platforms, particularly among women and girls.
Most of the debate surrounding digital media and mental health has centered on teenagers and young adults or relied on data from a single point in time. That narrow focus has left open whether the association between social media time and depression extends across the broader adult lifespan and whether it has held steady as smartphone habits evolved. Martin Block of Northwestern University, Vikram Suresh and Hans Breiter of the University of Cincinnati, and their colleagues examined 11 years of national survey data from American adults aged 18 to 70, building on Block’s earlier analysis of the 2014 survey data, which linked media use to depression.
The researchers analyzed data from the Media Behavior and Influence Study, an annual survey conducted each January and February from 2014 through 2024 by the market research firm Prosper Analytics. Participants were recruited through corporate customer databases, social media, and direct mail, with each yearly sample balanced to match U.S. Census benchmarks for age and gender. After screening out incomplete responses and people who finished the questionnaire in under two minutes, the analytic sample included 183,300 adults across the 11 annual waves, with between 15,410 and 17,869 participants surveyed each year.
To measure self-reported depression, the survey presented participants with a list of 31 health conditions and asked them to indicate with a yes-or-no answer which conditions they experienced. Participants also estimated the likelihood, from 0 to 100 percent, that they engaged in different media activities during each hour of a typical weekday and weekend day. From these hourly ratings, the authors calculated each person’s average daily minutes spent on social media, general internet browsing, television viewing, video gaming, email, and news consumption.
The team first used logistic regression, a statistical technique that estimates how strongly each type of media use relates to the odds of reporting depression while holding demographic factors constant. They then trained machine learning models known as balanced random forests for each survey year, combining 15 demographic and media-use variables: personal income, age range, gender, ethnicity, marital status, education level, occupation, household size, number of children under 18, and daily minutes spent on social media, internet use, television, gaming, email, and news.
A balanced random forest builds many decision trees using equal-sized samples of depressed and non-depressed individuals, which keeps the larger non-depressed group from overwhelming the computer’s predictions. To understand how the models reached their classifications, the researchers calculated Shapley Additive Explanations, a method grounded in economic game theory that measures how much each individual variable pushes a person’s predicted probability of depression up or down.
Across the 11-year study period, both daily social media time and the share of adults reporting depression climbed steadily. The proportion of respondents reporting depression rose from 15.1 percent in 2014 to 22.0 percent in 2024, following an upward trajectory both before and after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic. After adjusting for demographic characteristics, every additional minute of daily social media use was associated with a 0.26 percent increase in the odds of reporting depression, which translates to roughly 17 percent higher odds (not the same as a 17 percent higher chance) for each additional hour spent on social media per day.
Comparable positive links emerged across all 11 years for daily time spent playing video games, browsing the internet, watching television, and using email, with gaming and internet use showing per-minute associations as strong as or slightly stronger than social media, whereas news consumption showed a weak relationship in only two of the 11 survey waves.
In the machine learning analyses, the balanced random forest models showed moderate ability to distinguish adults with and without self-reported depression. On a standard measure of this ability, where 0.5 reflects chance and 1.0 reflects perfect sorting, scores ranged from 0.66 to 0.74 across the 11 annual datasets, and the models correctly flagged roughly 40 to 53 percent of adults who reported depression. To test whether patterns learned in earlier years remained relevant later on, the researchers trained a model exclusively on surveys from 2014 through 2018 and used it to predict depression in the 2019 through 2024 datasets. The model performed similarly in those later years, with scores of 0.68 to 0.72, indicating that the relationship between media habits, demographics, and depression remained stable over time.
Additional sensitivity tests showed that removing the 2020 and 2021 survey waves or accounting for the COVID-19 pandemic as a separate factor did not alter the link between social media use and depression. When the authors ranked the 15 predictors across three different importance measures over the entire decade, personal income had the strongest overall influence on predicted depression, followed by social media use, general internet use, and age range.
Social media use grew more prominent as a predictor over the course of the decade, rising from ninth place in the game-theory rankings in 2014 to consistently place among the top four predictors from 2019 through 2024. While social media use is a daily habit that people can change more easily than demographic traits like income or age, the authors caution that high importance rankings can reflect how much a behavior varies across a population rather than showing that changing the behavior will reduce depression.
Examining how different amounts of daily social media time affected the machine learning predictions pointed to a consistent pattern across multiple survey years. Below roughly 150 minutes per day, time spent on social media had a nearly neutral effect on whether the model classified a participant as depressed, but beyond two and a half hours per day, additional social media time increasingly pushed predicted depression risk upward. The authors describe this 150-minute mark as a hypothesis for future studies to test rather than an established safe limit.
Subgroup analyses also highlighted notable demographic patterns. Among young adults aged 18 to 25, self-reported depression prevalence ranged between 24 percent and 40 percent for women across the decade compared to between 15 percent and 25 percent for men, while the machine learning models performed better among adults aged 45 and older than among the youngest age group.
The link between heavier social media engagement and depression aligns with research covered by PsyPost in 2019, which tracked symptom severity longitudinally in adolescents rather than self-reported depression across the adult lifespan and similarly found that higher social media and television use predicted more severe depression symptoms over four years, although video gaming was not linked to depression in that teen sample. The results also echo a meta-analysis covered by PsyPost earlier in 2026, which examined longitudinal data in children and teens rather than repeated surveys of adults and found that higher social media use was consistently linked to increased depression and anxiety.
At the same time, the new findings stand in tension with a longitudinal study covered by PsyPost in 2020, which tracked individual adolescents over an eight-year period into young adulthood rather than analyzing population-level data in adults aged 18 to 70 and found that increases in daily social media time were not associated with increases in depression or anxiety. They also contrast with a study covered by PsyPost in 2025, which used objective smartphone screen-time tracking in a small sample of mostly young adults rather than self-reported usage across a broad adult population and found no meaningful association between social media use and depression.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. Because the study relied on repeated cross-sectional surveys that sampled a new group of adults each year rather than following the same individuals over time, the analysis cannot establish whether heavy social media use causes depression. It is possible that adults who are already experiencing depressive symptoms spend more time online seeking distraction, social connection, or relief from low mood when in-person interactions feel difficult. The relationship could also work in both directions, with heavy social media exposure contributing to distress through social comparison or disrupted sleep while depressive feelings simultaneously encourage more time online.
Depression was assessed through a single self-reported yes-or-no question rather than a clinical interview or a multi-item diagnostic scale. That approach may overlook milder symptoms or include inaccurate self-diagnoses. Daily media time was also estimated from self-reported hourly probabilities collected exclusively in January and February. The sample also came from a commercial survey panel recruited through company customer lists, social media, and direct mail rather than a random national sample, and it was balanced only on age and gender, so it may not fully represent American adults.
In addition, the survey did not separate passive scrolling from active interactions such as messaging friends or sharing original posts, leaving open which specific online habits account for the link with depression. The authors suggest that future longitudinal and experimental studies should track individuals over time, incorporate psychological measures of how people weigh rewards and negative experiences, and test whether keeping daily social media use below the 150-minute mark offers a meaningful benefit for mental health. Recruiting partly through social media could also tilt the sample toward heavier users.
The study, “Social media use and depression across 11 years of U.S. adult data,” was authored by Martin Block, Vikram Suresh, Johnathan Avant, Sumra Bari, Nicole Vike, Felix Zhan, and Hans Breiter.

====================================================================================================

Powderfinger announce more shows, discuss split and joyful reunion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
20:00:00 UTC
05:00:00 KST

Powderfinger's joyful reunion was inspired by their kids and Cold Chisel
When Powderfinger broke up in 2010, their farewell tour sold 220,000 tickets.
Sixteen years later, their reunion tour has become Australia's hottest ticket. All 300,000 tickets for the Brisbane band's initial 26 shows sold out in six days.
"The response was genuinely overwhelming," guitarist Darren Middleton tells the ABC's Zan Rowe.
"As soon as tickets went on sale, we were like: 'Holy shit!'
Today, they've added nine more dates, including stops in Hobart and Canberra, to supply the intense demand.
Ticket requests have come from some unlikely places.
"It was pretty nuts," frontman Bernard Fanning says. "Not just the public response but privately.
"Like, plumbers that fixed a drain 15 years ago and still have my phone number."
Among the most beloved and best-selling Australian acts of the 90s and 2000s, Powderfinger's return was kept under wraps over 18 months of "white lies" and clandestine meetings.
In May last year, Fanning, Middleton, guitarist Ian Haug, bassist John "JC" Collins, drummer Jon Coghill and long-time manager Paul Piticco conferred to "seriously" discuss the prospect fans had longed for since the group's 2010 split.
"We got together and said, 'Let's think about if we want to do it. Is this the right time for everyone?" Middleton says.
"One idea put around was: 'No-one in the band owes Powderfinger anything.' If someone doesn't want to be a part of it, we don't do it. That's OK."
After a month away to deliberate their reasons for reuniting, they reconvened. "We got on the Zoom [call] and went, let's do it!"
Why now? Family and falling in love with the band
One of Fanning's "main reasons" for getting back together was "for my kids".
"Because they haven't seen [us perform], they'd love to be part of it … and every one of us said exactly the same thing."
"We're never very cool in our kids' eyes," Middleton adds.
Each member has taken a different path over 16 years: from raising families to pursuing solo projects, politics and other careers.
"We've all gone through different experiences, learned to stand on our own two feet again and discover who we are," Middleton reflects.
"And actually fall in love with music and with the band again."
Fanning says time apart has deepened the bonds of their friendship.
"By the end of the band, there was tension, which is natural after 21 years [together].
"But now, all those petty differences have completely disappeared in a sea of nappies and teenage angst and whatever else.
"In the last 16 years, we've had time to think about how much fun and joy there was … try and bring that into the equation again."
It's a rare opportunity whose significance isn't lost on Middleton.
"We're still alive," he enthuses. "It sounds silly, but I've lost friends in the music industry … their bands no longer have the chance to do what they did. We're super lucky."
Cold Chisel, community and nostalgia
Powderfinger's choice to headline concerts outdoors under stadium-sized tents was inspired by attending Cold Chisel's "Big Five-O" anniversary shows.
"It feels like a festival but it's indoors, it's the best of both worlds," says Fanning, who never saw Chisel the first time round, but was thrilled when he got the chance to see them reunite.
That people feel the same way about Powderfinger "makes sense," he reasons.
The group's chart-topping, award-hoovering anthems were the soundtrack to people's lives in the pre-streaming era, ruled by CDs, TV and radio, not algorithms.
"There's a warmth of feeling for that time when Powderfinger was doing well [and] people want to recapture that a little bit," Fanning acknowledges.
"I think nostalgia gets a bad rap. Because it generates good feelings amongst people, which are seriously lacking in our society at the moment.
At a time of "so much difficulty and division in the world", harnessing live music's power to foster community was a driving force for the reunion.
A multi-generational moment
Powderfinger's cross-generational popularity was evidenced by last year's Hottest 100 of Australian Songs, where the majority of voters (aged 18–29) voted in three songs.
"It's crazy," Middleton remarks.
"My 25-year-old daughter, her friends are pumped about coming. It makes me feel young again.
"People coming to see us are parents with kids who are teenagers or above. What a great experience! 'Dad, take me to see that band that you used to love …'"
Since the band bowed out in 2010, "society has devalued music incredibly", Fanning says.
Particularly Australian music, with homegrown music accounting for just 8.4 per cent of local streaming, according to a recent APRA AMCOS report.
In response to increasing festival cancellations, venue closures and declining live attendance, the frontman says there needs to be a "concentration on the arts and how important it is for our stories to be told by us".
"And that comes from musicians, from artists, authors, journalists, from whoever. It's really important to encourage that Australian storytelling to continue."
To that end, Powderfinger are committing to an all-Australian line-up of support acts for their tour, including partnering with triple j Unearthed to give emerging acts a platform to perform for tens of thousands of people. Stay tuned for details.
Will there be new music?
All five members always voted on every major career and creative decision.
Is Powderfinger still a democracy in 2026?
"Yes, unfortunately," Fanning deadpans to hearty laughter.
"It has to be. We wouldn't be able to function any other way.
"It's part of [our] DNA … sometimes there's some late-night lobbying" with JC serving as "the whip", he continues.
Beginning rehearsals in December, each member will have a say on figuring out which tunes will make the cut.
Fanning experimented with writing a set list "of what I thought were essentials".
"There were 22 songs, which is too long."
Don't expect epic four-hour long shows.
"No way. I want the quality to be really high the whole way through," Fanning says.
Middleton counters: "We'll craft a few different set lists [that] we'll revolve."
And the burning question: Will These Days and My Happiness find new company?
"I'll happily accept criticism that it's a nostalgia tour, because we're not making new music," Fanning says.
"The one thing Jimmy Barnes said to me: 'If you ever get the band back together do not make a record.'"
That said, "the chemistry of the five of us being together is very unique … [we're] never closed off to the idea of a new song, from anybody," Fanning says.
"That's what I'm excited about again. That chemistry you cannot manufacture."
But the reunion marks a new adventure.
"All of us are approaching it with so much excitement," Fanning says.
"We know it's different now, the way that we relate to each other is different.
"We obviously have to step up to a really high level or else we will disappoint a lot of people."
But Powderfinger are intent on putting in the hard work. For them, it's about proving some chemistry, between band members, between artists and audiences, between generations, is irreplaceable. And sharing that with 300,000 people and counting.
"I don't want to anticipate how it's going to feel," Middleton says.
"All I know is it's going to be an amazing end to 2027."

Russia and Ukraine have completed demining along routes designated for a humanitarian mission to Oleshky, a Russian-controlled city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, the two countries’ human rights commissioners said on Thursday.
Russian commissioner Yana Lantratova and Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets announced in separate Telegram statements that the humanitarian convoy was ready to depart for the city’s central district hospital.

The completion of demining marks a key step towards enabling the planned aid delivery and providing civilians with an opportunity to leave the city safely during the agreed ceasefire.
Temporary ceasefire enables aid and evacuations
A ceasefire brokered by US President Donald Trump between Russia and Ukraine in Oleshky took effect at 0100 GMT on Tuesday.
The arrangement is intended to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations in the city, which Moscow took control of in 2022.
The ceasefire is scheduled to remain in force until 1059 pm GMT on Sunday, giving humanitarian operations a limited window to proceed.

Quick hits: Marnus caught in ugly exchange after all-time send off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:54:18 UTC
04:54:18 KST

Marnus Labuschagne was involved in an ugly moment of DRS drama after giving a retaliatory send-off, as Temba Bavuma threw his wicket away in the shadows of stumps.
Here are the quick hits from day three of the third Test between Australia and South Africa.
1. DRS drama and Labuschagne's ugly exchange
It was one of the most contentious moments of the series when, midway through the evening session, with South Africa 2-95 and still five runs behind, Mitchell Starc collected Marques Ackerman with a steepling, searing bouncer.
The South African lost his balance as the ball thudded into what looked to be a mixture of helmet and bat before flying to Cam Green behind the wicket.
The Australians went up and so did the umpire's finger.
Undoubtedly dazed from the contact, the batter regained his composure and met with partner Temba Bavuma.
Eventually, a referral was called for, but only as the DRS timer ticked to zero.
It was touch and go, but the officials deemed Ackerman had taken too long, despite the severity of the hit.
With the South Africans pleading their case to the umpires, the ever-vocal Marnus Labuschagne could be heard giving his own opinion over the stump mic.
"The timer's up, oh no, see you buddy!" Labuschagne said from his position at the other end of the wicket.
Meanwhile, Travis Head had made his way over to the South African camp.
"Heady, what are you doing mate? He's off!" Labuschagne could be heard saying.
Head, hands outstretched towards batter and umpire in what appeared to be a peace offering, turned back towards his team and replied.
"I'm just checking if he's alright," Head said.
Reluctantly, Ackerman made his from the middle, but spent some time at the boundary in the futile hope of being called back.
Thankfully, the replays showed the ball had collected a thick edge before crashing into visor, meaning Ackerman was doomed to be out for 62 even if the review had been permitted.
2. Bloodied Harmer keeps South Africa in the game
With an advantage to press home at the beginning of day three, the set Australian pair of Alex Carey and Josh Inglis would have been hoping for at least another full session of batting.
The conditions were perfect, the pitch was flat, and things looked very promising as Inglis reverse-swept his way to a hugely impressive second Test century.
However, neither wicketkeeper-batter would see the other side of the first drinks break, with off spinner Simon Harmer once again doing the damage.
Only moments after ripping a nail and bloodying his fingers while attempting a low catch with his non-bowling hand, Harmer had Inglis caught behind for 102.
It was a brilliant delivery; drifting away, spinning in and kissing the outside edge of the Western Australian's blade.
Four overs later, a similarly exquisite off break had Carey (80) nudging to Aiden Markram at slip, and Harmer, a fingernail down, had dragged his side back into the game.
Australia's tail proceeded to eke out a 100-run first-innings lead, eventually dismissed for 429.
3. Marnus gives it to Bedingham
Labuschagne was in quite a mood on day three.
Before the DRS drama in the evening session, the Queenslander took quite some pleasure in giving it back to Proteas batter David Bedingham.
On day two, Matthew Breetzke had joyously celebrated Labuschagne's five-ball duck by leaping over the pitch and shouting directly at the Australian.
And when Bedingham holed out to Josh Hazlewood during the middle session on day three, Labuschagne responded in similar fashion.
The Queenslander had his chest puffed out as he ran towards the South African, face red and fist pumping, screaming what you can only imagine was something entirely considered and reasonable.
Loading Twitter content
Bedingham was out for 11 and South Africa's second innings was already beginning to teeter at 2-31.
4. A strange moment on the hill
It was a strange morning on the hill.
During the first session, the broadcast cameras found a man holding a sign that read: "Ryan Rickelton, is your mum single?"
The middle-aged gentleman received a good amount of screen time, which he used to blow kisses and adjust his sunglasses in a performance that probably wouldn't have endeared him to anyone in the Rickelton family.
Loading Twitter content
Rickelton, South Africa's wicketkeeper-batter, was stony-faced in response, before pursing his lips and shaking his head solemnly.
The commentators were lost for words at what was an uncomfortable moment for everyone involved — and especially, you'd imagine, for Ryan Rickelton's mother.
5. Bavuma throws it away in the shadows of stumps
Stumps were in sight for Bavuma and Breetzke.
The South African pair had so diligently rebuilt South Africa's innings after Ackerman's dismissal, and had just eight more balls to survive.
But with shadows lengthening at Newlands and with the pitch offering more and more for the slower bowlers, Nathan Lyon conjured a little bit of magic.
It was the perfect off spinner's delivery; drifting, turning sharply and bowling a swinging Bavuma clean through the gate.
However, it was a wildly inappropriate shot from the usually so-considered Bavuma, and the South African captain couldn't quite believe what had happened.
He grimaced and shook his head as he made is way from the middle for 35, with South Africa finishing the day on 4-140 and just 40 runs in front.

California, feds continue election war after courts rebuke challenge to 20,000 ballots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:53:07 UTC
04:53:07 KST

California, feds continue election war after courts rebuke challenge to 20,000 ballots
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Courts have twice rejected the Trump administration’s bid to block the counting of 20,000 ballots that it says may be from noncitizens; the Justice Department is appealing.
- The ongoing battle is part of a multifront election battle between the administration and the state that has also seen L.A. County officials subpoenaed.
- Gov. Gavin Newsom says California is deploying election lawyers to protect voting, while county officials have rebuffed Justice Department threats.
Soon after a federal judge in Los Angeles sharply rejected a Trump administration effort to block 20,000 California ballots from voters it alleged may be noncitizens, the U.S. Justice Department appealed — leaving attorneys on both sides preparing Thursday for yet another court battle.
That was despite the lower court judge calling the request an unlawful threat to eligible voters in Tuesday’s midterm election and to free and fair American elections moving forward, and the same appellate court having already rejected the plan days before.
“Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution,” wrote First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli, the lead prosecutor in L.A.
Early Thursday, Gov. Gavin Newsom swiped back at the Trump administration, writing, “A warning to Donald Trump: I’m deploying election lawyers to key battleground districts in California to protect every vote. And I just made it a FELONY to illegally seize ballots.”
With just days to go until polls close, the heated election war between California and the Trump administration is showing no signs of slowing down despite multiple court orders rejecting the administration’s central effort to interfere in the midterms by accusing state and county officials of willfully turning a blind eye to voter fraud.
That’s in part because lawyers within the U.S. Justice Department have been unrelenting in their pursuit of such control, both through court orders and threats to state and county officials — including through criminal grand jury subpoenas issued to at least three officials in Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan’s office.
The subpoenas, reviewed by The Times, demand that the officials appear before prosecutors the day after the election with a slew of internal documents and testify as to how their office handled the Justice Department’s demands to set aside the ballots.
It’s also because those same state and county officials have refused to yield, denouncing the threats as unconvincing and illegal in recent letters back to the Justice Department.
“Be aware that we consider DOJ’s efforts to threaten California election officials with criminal sanctions for following federal and state law to be an effort to unlawfully intimidate both election officials and California voters, which can undermine voters’ faith in the election process,” Susan K. Blitch, counsel for Monterey County, wrote in one.
U.S. District Judge David O. Carter ruled that the administration’s allegations were “not credible” and that the intervention it sought would violate a host of federal laws.
Several election experts warned that Trump administration officials are trying to sow confusion and suspicion about an election in which the Republican Party is poised to lose ground, in part so they can reject the outcome. But they also said the courts have consistently rebuffed the Trump administration and will continue to do so through Nov. 3 and after — with the recent rulings over the 20,000 flagged ballots a perfect example.
“The federal government lost in every way it could possibly lose. It lost on the law, and it lost on the facts, and it lost on the equities — [or] weighing the harms to the various parties,” said Rick Hasen, director of the Safeguarding Democracy Project at UCLA School of Law.
Appeal, rebuke, appeal
Last week, Trump administration attorneys decided that U.S. District Judge David O. Carter was not ruling quickly enough on their emergency request for a temporary restraining order to block California, Secretary of State Shirley Weber and Logan from counting the 20,000 ballots the administration asserted were from “likely noncitizens” — so they appealed to the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals.
On Monday, a three-judge panel there — including two appointees of President Trump and one of President Biden — denied the appeal for a lack of jurisdiction, because Carter hadn’t weighed in yet. However, two of the judges — Mark J. Bennett, a Trump appointee, and Gabriel P. Sanchez, the Biden appointee — wrote separately to make clear that they also would have denied the administration’s request for being likely unconstitutional and in violation of federal law.
On Wednesday, Carter, an appointee of President Clinton, ruled that the administration’s allegations about noncitizen voters were “not credible” and that the intervention it sought would violate a host of federal laws, sow chaos in the ongoing midterm election, likely lead to the disenfranchisement of legitimate voters and foster future political meddling in elections.
“This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,” Carter wrote. “If [the Trump administration’s] last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process.”
Carter wrote that never in American history “has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch.”
The ruling — forceful, unequivocal and based on several of the same arguments made by Bennett and Sanchez — was cheered by state officials and voting rights groups. Election experts said it squared directly with their understanding of the law and was appropriate in the face of the Trump administration’s unprecedented, legally baseless effort to intervene in an ongoing state-run election.
Justice Department lawyers filed a sparse appeal back to the 9th Circuit on Thursday, arguing the ongoing counting of ballots constitutes an emergency the court must intervene to stop, and asking it to do so by Friday. The same panel that previously rejected the request took the case back up, and gave the state, L.A. County and several voting rights groups until Friday morning to respond.
War of words
On Wednesday night, Newsom appeared on “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” and predicted Trump will take sweeping steps to “literally suppress the vote, to set the conditions where he will then express doubt in the electoral outcome, and suggest that it was rigged.” But he also said California is fighting back and prepared.
“Right now, I am focused on getting over 1,000 poll workers, folks out there to monitor the DOJ monitors that Trump’s gonna send to try to steal this election,” Newsom said. “We have been running tabletop exercises. We have 1,000 volunteers. We have 134 election law attorneys that we’re sending out.”
On Thursday, Essayli replied to the latter deployment, writing, “You’re going to protect every legal or illegal vote? What about California citizens whose votes are being diluted by ineligible voters. Do their constitutional rights matter.”
Everything you need to know about how to vote in the 2026 California general election, including how to register, where to vote and how to check the status of your ballot.
Trump, meanwhile, asserted with no evidence that “there are hundreds of thousands of bad ballots, bad votes, in California. Millions, in my opinion.” He said that California has “very corrupt elections,” and that if it had honest ones, he “would have won it by a lot.”
The remarks were just the latest in a swirling and highly public war of words between state and federal officials.
Federal prosecutors have issued three grand jury subpoenas to officials in Logan’s office. One dated Saturday and addressed to the office’s records custodian seeks internal emails, text messages, guidance and discussions related to the Trump administration’s demands that Logan’s office investigate alleged noncitizen voters. It orders the custodian to appear in Santa Ana on Wednesday, the day after the election, or provide the records and a signed certification beforehand.
Prosecutors are also seeking records describing how the county screens for unlawful voting, prevents noncitizen ballots from being counted and handles evidence that noncitizens voted in federal elections or that others helped them to do so.
A Justice Department spokesperson said it doesn’t comment on grand jury subpoenas, but noted Carter had “explained that voting unlawfully results in criminal exposure.”
Carter did say that a “clear remedy” to the administration’s concerns already existed, in that prosecutors could criminally charge individuals committing voter fraud. But he also explicitly denounced what he called the administration’s “threat” to charge election officials, writing that “these threats must stop.”
Logan, in a statement, said Carter’s “admonishment about threats directed at election officials on Tuesday was well placed and appreciated. At every step, the U.S. Department of Justice has taken a confrontational, adversarial approach. Election officials are acting in accordance with state and federal law.”
In Carter’s courtroom Tuesday, Essayli claimed the federal government has maintained a collaborative “tone” since it first demanded the state set aside ballots, and said he was surprised at how “adversarial” state election officials had been. But Essayli and other Justice Department officials have been engaged for weeks in an aggressive back and forth with California officials online — which is highly unusual for prosecutors actively litigating related cases.
When Newsom’s office recently wrote that “Trump’s DOJ is so desperate to invent ‘widespread voter fraud,’ it sent California counties lists of people who NEVER voted — and voters from the WRONG COUNTY. Absolute clown show!” Essayli shot back, “Hey Fraud King,” with a crown emoji. “We’re not waiting for them to vote.”
Also unusual have been the threats Justice Department attorneys have been sending to county election officials in California, including in a series of letters Friday in which they asserted varying numbers of “likely aliens” per county, set a 48-hour deadline for the counties to cooperate with federal authorities to prove those voters are citizens.
In one letter to Kristin Connelly, head of the Contra Costa County registrar’s office, U.S. Atty. Craig Missakian flagged 407 potential noncitizens in the county and said he was writing “to make unmistakably clear the legal implications” of processing any ballots from those voters.
On Wednesday, Thomas L. Geiger, Contra Costa County counsel, responded with his own letter, questioning the accuracy of the noncitizen claims and saying it would be “legally unsound” for Connelly to “disregard both California and federal law” in order to comply with Missakian’s demands.
Other California officials have signaled a willingness to work with federal authorities. San Luis Obispo County District Atty. Dan Dow said Thursday that his office is investigating “63 federally identified suspect registrations” off a list also provided to the county clerk-recorder.

Trading has resumed on Polymarket’s flagship international platform after a hack that drained money from the wallets of some traders.
A third-party vendor based in the United Kingdom was breached, not the prediction market’s website itself. Law enforcement in the UK have been notified of the incident, the company said. Trading was initially paused while the company investigated for several hours.
On X, prominent traders complained that they had lost money; blockchain analytics firm Bubblemaps reported that around 700 users appeared to have been affected, with approximately $2.7 million stolen. This is not the first time that Polymarket traders have experienced security woes. In June 2026, Polymarket experienced another breach, which resulted in over $2 million in losses for impacted traders.
The company has been a lightning rod for controversy since its 2020 launch. In the past few years, it has been the center of several high-profile alleged insider trading incidents resulting in arrests. One case involved a Special Forces soldier accused of wagering on the capture of Venezuela’s former leader; another involved a Google employee who allegedly used confidential information to make millions. Polymarket recently raised $1 billion in August 2026, with a fundraising round led by 1789 Capital, the venture capital firm where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner. It is now valued at $21 billion.
