No seat at the table: Israel’s post-election message to its Palestinian citizens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:25:17 UTC
03:25:17 KST

Israel’s dilemma over its identity as a state couldn’t be clearer, and its leaders have set their priorities straight after the long-awaited election day on Tuesday. According to the Israeli Central Elections Committee, some four million Israeli citizens cast their vote, representing around 77.7% of voters, the highest turnout in over 20 years. Described as the most heated in Israel’s history, the 2026 elections centered around one question: Should Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stay in power?
As of Thursday morning, after counting nearly 90% of votes, the Netanyahu camp takes the prize, with 55 out of the 120 seats in the Knesset, followed by the opposition camp with 49 seats, and the Arab Palestinian parties with 19 seats, the most seats won by Palestinian citizens of Israel in the state’s history. Neither the Netanyahu camp nor the Eisenkot camp has reached the 61-seat majority required to form a government, and the Arab camp seems to be the key to solving the deadlock. However, the majority of the Eizenkot camp refuse to ally themselves with Palestinians, despite fiercely wanting to oust Netanyahu. This makes the achievement of the Palestinian vote essentially irrelevant, despite representing 20% of Israel’s population, and leaves the central question of forming a new government unresolved.
There are multiple possible scenarios ahead, and somebody will have to make some strategic concessions with deep political implications for the identity of Israel. The coming weeks may be the most politically significant since Israel’s establishment in 1948 — for Israel as a state, for its Palestinian citizens, and for Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, who remain subject to Israel’s rule, despite not having citizenship. In order to understand the significance of this political moment, and the possible scenarios to come, we need to look back at the elections process within a larger context.
Voting on what?
Israelis voted on Tuesday for the first time since the October 7 attacks in 2023, widely considered as the largest security failure in Israel’s history, for which Netanyahu, under whose watch it happened, hasn’t taken any responsibility. But it is also the first vote sinceIsrael unleashed a genocidal military campaign on Gaza, which has earned a world-wide concensus for the crime of genocide, including a charge from a UN special investigation commission, all major international human rights organizations, the International Association of Genocide Scholars, and Israel’s leading human rights group, B’Tselem. The Gaza genocide has turned global opinion against Israel, pushing it into an unprecedented political isolation. Meanwhile, neither its official stated goal of destroying Hamas, or its unofficial goal of expelling Palestinians out of Gaza, has been achieved.
Under Netanyahu’s government, Israeli settlers in the West Bank have launched their largest ever offensive, ethnically cleansing more than 100 rural Palestinian communities and attacking the heart of Palestinian towns, which invited international condemnation and even sanctions, albeit limited, on Israeli settlers in the West Bank.
It is also the first Israeli election since Israel’s two-round war with Iran, which has seen Israel receiving missile strikes like never before, wear out the U.S. deterrence in the region, giving Iran full control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz, boosting its position in the region, and deepening the U.S. opposition to Israel’s influence in American politics, including amongst the Republican party. Meanwhile, Netanyahu’s own promise of “regime change” in Iran has become a distant dream.
This election also arrives with a backdrop of Netanyahu’s campaign to change the decades-old established state institutions in Israel, giving the extreme ideologically-driven para-state pro-settler movements a way into controlling state institutions, and concentrating power in the executive branch, polarizing Israeli society along ideological and social identity lines. The peak of this crisis culminated in 2023, with the mass protests in Israel against Netanyahu’s attempt to diminish the power of the Israeli Supreme Court, shortly before the October 7 attacks. Moreover, the Tuesday vote comes in the midst of the unresolved Haredi drafting crisis, as the religious ultra-orthodox Jewish community demands to put its exemption from military drafting into law, while more Israelis demand that Haredis serve in the army like the rest, especially with the exhaustion of reservist forces, and the Israeli army’s crisis of manpower. In an attempt to maintain support from both sides of the crisis, Netanyahu dragged it on until the very end of his term.
By opening multiple fronts of war, deepening Israel’s military presence in Lebanon, and escalating campaigns on Palestinians in the West Bank, Netanyahu succeeded in keeping Israel in a constant state of emergency, fostering a ruthlessnationalist war-time atmosphere. Last week, media reports revealed that Israeli war planes were sent to the edge of Iran’s borders, in an attempt to provoke a new round of fighting, which would have forced the postponement of the elections. According to reports, the Israeli army’s Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir refused to go through with an attack on Iran at Netanyahu’s demand, setting a new precedent in the dynamic between the army’s chief and the Prime Minister. If he stays in power, Netanyahu has promised new military offensives in Gaza, in the West Bank, and against Iran.
Netanyahu’s setback
Two main camps are confronted. On the one hand, the Netanyahu camp includes his Likud party and other smaller right-wing, nationalist, religious, and anti-Arab parties, such as the far-right Jewish Power party led by Itamar Gvir and the far-right Religious Zionism party led by Bezalel Smotrich. On the other hand, the opposition anti-Netanyahu camp is led by former chief of the Israeli army staff, Gadi Eizenkot, and his Yashar party. Eizenkot himself is considered to be center-right, institutionalist, and pragmatic, joined by other key figures of the Israeli opposition: Avigdor Liberman, leading the Israel Beitenu far-right party, representing Russian-origin Jewish Israelis, Neftali Bennet, former Prime Minister, leading the B’Yachad far-right pro-settlers party, Yair Lapid, running the Yesh Atid center-right secular party, and Yair Golan, running The Democrats party, described as the left of the Zionist spectrum, secular, institutionalist, and pragmatic.
Shortly after voting posts closed at 10:00pm local time, media estimations showed that the opposition camp, led by Gadi Eizenkot, had won a majority of votes, making up between 52 to 54 seats out of the 120 seats in the Knesset, followed closely by the camp of the Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with 49 to 52 seats.
Netanyahu’s Likud party, the main force in his camp, was estimated to have won 24 to 25 seats, becoming the largest single party, followed by the Yashar party, led by the main opposition leader, Eizenkot, with 21 to 24 seats. Netanyahu’s main allies in his now-expired cabinet, Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party and Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party, were estimated to have won seven and six seats respectively. However, without the required majority, Netanyahu appeared to be far from forming a cabinet and staying in power. Although Eizenkot’s camp, with less ideological common ground, appeared to have come on top, it didn’t reach the required majority either.
The surprise of the night came from the two Arab lists, representing the Palestinian minority, who, according to initial estimates, won 17 to 18 seats, far more than their goal of 15 to 16 seats prior to the voting day. These seats were won by two forces. First, the Joint Arab list, including the Palestinian nationalist, liberal, pro-citizenship Balad party, whose leader, Sami Abu Shehadeh, quit the race in early October to avoid being disqualified by the Israeli Supreme Court, the Ta’al nationalist pro-citizenship Palestinian party led by Ahmad Tibi, and the Hadash anti-Zionist Arab-Jewish leftist party. This alliance was estimated to get 11 seats. Second, Ra’am, representing a branch of the conservative Islamic movement led by Mansour Abbas, which was estimated to have won six to seven seats.
The voting rate in the Palestinian community in Israel reached 80% according to Palestinian media outlets in Israel, a historical voting rate unseen since the mid-1990s, securing the highest number of seats for Arab parties in the history of Arab representation in Israel. The high Palestinian turnout affected how the vote-to-seat ratio is calculated, making it impossible for either of the two main camps to reach the 61-seat majority and positioning Palestinian representation in the Knesset as a key player capable of determining who forms the next Israeli government. However, in the hours that followed, this numerical victory proved not to be a guarantee of Palestinian citizens of Israel’s capacity to influence Israeli politics.
In the early hours of Tuesday night, Palestinians celebrated in the headquarters of the Joint Arab List in Nazareth, where the head of the list, Yousef Jabarin, said in a speech that “our people sent Ben-Gvir home.” Jabarin later told the media that the Arab parties’ priority was to oust Netanyahu’s government and ensure that “there will be a change in policies, not only in faces.”
In Tel Aviv, Israeli opposition supporters also celebrated at the headquarters of Eizenkot’s campaign. The opposition leader offered what was described as a victory speech, saying that Israelis “had demonstrated that they lost trust in Netanyahu.” Eizenkot called upon the Israeli security forces to “remember that Netanyahu is now the head of an interim cabinet, and no longer the Prime Minister,” in a clear call to refuse any attempt by Netanyahu to start a war with Iran in the remaining transition weeks of his term. Netanyahu, for his part, remained silent until 3:00 am, when he declared, from the Likud party’s headquarters in Jerusalem that his party was the largest, and called for a “right-wing, strong, government,” and that Israel must “not form a government with anti-Zionist Arab parties.” Meanwhile, Netanyahu’s allies, including foreign minister Gideon Saar and finance minister Bezalel Smotrich, dismissed the opposition celebrations as premature.
In 2022, Netanyahu formed the government which ended its term on Tuesday, the 6th that he has led so far, with a 68-seat coalition in the Knesset. For years, Netanyahu has been seen as the sole leader of the overwhelmingly growing Israeli right and far-right camp. For him, falling short of securing a stable majority and forming a government is a clear setback. Despite this, his chances of staying in power proved to be far from over, after the official vote count began to be published on Wednesday morning. The first announcements indicated a comeback of Netanyahu’s camp on top, with 54 seats, with Eizenkot’s camp falling to 49, and later 47 seats. By Wednesday night, 77% of votes had been counted, confirming Netanyahu’s camp as the largest block in the new Knesset, although still short of the 61-seat majority required to form a government. Arab lists, for their part, were announced to have won up to 19 seats, making them the determining factor.
The final result is yet to be announced on Thursday night, after counting the votes of Israeli serving soldiers and foreign diplomatic missions, which take longer to register due to a special procedure. These make up more than 600,000 votes, representing 10 to 12 seats, which could change the entire equation. Given that these votes do not include Palestinian citizens, they are expected to go to both Netanyahu’s and Eizenkot’s camps, probably along the same lines as the other votes.
The Arab dilemma
The Arab lists, representing the Palestinian national minority in Israel, have established themselves as the determining factor, sharing the same goal as Eizenkot to put an end to Netanyahu’s 18 years in power. All of Eizenkot’s allies have expressed their willingness to oust the current Prime Minister, and they have the chance of doing that by building an alliance with the Arab lists. However, Eizenkot’s allies, except for Yair Golan, have pledged not to form a government with Arab support.
The Joint Arab List’s leaders have stated that although they wouldn’t join a government coalition, they are ready to provide an Eizenkot-led government with a “safety net” by supporting it with their vote of trust, without joining the coalition or subscribing to all its decisions.
The Ra’am Palestinian party, led by Mansour Abbas, on the contrary, is ready to join an Israeli government. It even has a Jewish candidate on its list, Yoav Segalovitz, a former Knesset member for Lapid’s Yesh Atid party, now occupying the second slot of Ra’am’s list, under Abbas himself, just to make it easier for the Israeli opposition to make an alliance with Ra’am, without having to put an Arab face in the cabinet. By all measures, the Israeli opposition has the possibility of ousting Netanyahu and ending his political career. It is only a difficult choice because it requires some form of alliance with the Palestinian component.
This is a difficult choice, because of the overwhelming anti-Arab sentiment in Israel, growing since before October 7, 2023. Since 2015, Netanyahu has referred to the Arabs’ participation in elections as a “national security threat,” arguing that Arab citizens “have 22 other Arab countries.” In 2015, on election day, Netanyahu addressed his supporters, warning that “Arab voters are coming out in droves to the polls,” and repeated the same threat last Tuesday. To the exception of Yair Golan, and non-Zionist Jewish leaders who are part of the Arab lists, Israeli opposition leaders never pushed back against Netanyahu’s logic. None of them attacked him for discriminative or inflammatory language, nor did any of them take the advantage to come out as more moderate or morally higher. Opinion polls, and Tuesday’s voting results have shown that bigotry against “the Arabs” is the most unifying political message in Israel.
Accepting an alliance with Arab lists would mean a loss of public support and, therefore, instability for the incoming government. Eizenkot, Lapid, and Bennet have stressed that they want to form a Zionist government, which means the exclusion of both Arab and Haredi parties, the latter of which are considered non-Zionist for religious reasons. However, without the support of Arab lists or Haredis, Eizenkot’s camp remains unable to form a government, as is Netanyahu.
What’s next?
There is no possible scenario ahead in which the solution to the current political deadlock in Israel comes from Netanyahu’s camp. It is monolithic, fanatic, and laser-focused on an extremist agenda on domestic issues, Palestinians, and surrounding countries that Netanyahu refers to as “Greater Israel.” For this camp, any cooperation with Arab lists is not only a political taboo, but also an accusation that it throws at its opponents to discredit them.
At the same time, there is no possible scenario without any concessions. The opposition camp, at least, has obvious concessions to choose from: accepting Netanyahu’s continuity in power, or accepting cooperation with the Arab lists. If Eizenkot and his allies lean towards Netanyahu, the current Prime Minister might have to drop his alliance with the Haredis and begin drafting them into the Israeli army.
These concessions might come in the form of one of four scenarios. The first of these scenarios is the ousting of Netanyahu, if Eizenkot, with the support of at least one of his allies, Yair Golan, decides to cooperate with Arab lists, especially the Joint List, by accepting their offer of a safety net. This would allow Palestinian candidates to discuss the terms. Among these are, according to statements made by the head of the Balad party, Ahmad Tibi, changing the speaker of the Knesset for a more moderate one, drafting legislation to improve the conditions of Palestinian citizens of Israel, especially in terms of house demolitions and fighting organized crime, and de-escalating tensions in the West Bank and Gaza.
The second possibility is a unified government between Netanyahu and Eizenkot’s camp, making Palestinian citizens and the seats that they won completely irrelevant. The Haredi community might find itself sidelined as well. This scenario is the one favored by the Trump administration, according to Israeli media reports, which said that Trump is planning to mediate between both Israeli camps to form a stable government that can participate in a possible upcoming round of war on Iran. In this scenario, Palestinians’ hopes of de-escalating the situation in Gaza and the West Bank, and improving conditions for Palestinian citizens of Israel, would all fade away.
The third scenario is the continuity of the political deadlock, and setting a new date for elections, which would be in March. This would give Netanyahu at least five more months n power, during which he can start a new war with Iran to boost his popularity and force a war-time atmosphere on his opponents, and go further in the escalation in the West Bank. The Israeli president Yitzhak Herzog, who is tasked with choosing who receives the delegation to form a government, said that he wants to prevent this scenario.
The fourth and final scenario is that Netanyahu would use the remaining time he has as interim Prime Minister to start a war with Iran, possibly after the US midterm elections, when such a war would be more favorable for the US president. This would impose a war-time state of emergency in Israel, in which Eizenkot and other opposition leaders would find themselves forced to join a national unity war government under Netanyahu.
As it stands today, one thing has been made clear: Despite the fact that the anti-Netanyahu camp has won an overwhelming majority, a feat that should make the path to a post-Netanyahu government clear, this is not the case, and the only reason is that this camp includes a major Arab, Palestinian component.
The incapacity of the Israeli opposition to form a government with Arab lists immediately stems only from the anti-Arab sentiment in the Israeli political scene and society. This is despite Palestinian citizens of Israel showing every possible flexibility, asking for nothing more than recognition of their status as a national minority as equal citizens. In the case of Mansour Abbas, leader of the Ra’am party, he even stated his disposition to recognize the Jewish character of Israel. But it is for their Palestinian, Arab identity that Netanyahu has delegitimized any political cooperation with them, without any significant pushback from his opponents.
In practice, Israel is clearly defining itself as a democracy only when its Palestinian citizens are made absent, and that despite being the original, indigenous people of their own country, they are still not allowed a seat at the table.

‘A clear alliance’: Nations accused of undermining science at UN nature talks
- Four countries, Saudi Arabia, Russia, Argentina and Brazil, are accused of weakening UN biodiversity science at COP17 in Yerevan, Armenia.
- The dispute centres on whether nations should “welcome” or only “take note” of two IPBES reports on nature, climate and the economy.
- Delegates and experts warn this could set a harmful precedent and leave nature policy without a strong scientific base.
AI generated
YEREVAN - Political tensions are mounting in the final days of the United Nations biodiversity talks with a handful of countries accused of trying to weaken the science that underpins global nature policy.
The growing feud over the role of science has alarmed veteran negotiators and follows recent efforts by fossil fuel-reliant nations to delay reports by the IPCC, the global authority on climate change.
“The same thing is happening here as what is taking place with the IPCC,” said a French government delegate at the COP17 summit in Yerevan, Armenia.
The delegate requested anonymity to discuss ongoing negotiations.
The delegate said four countries – Saudi Arabia, Russia, Argentina and Brazil – were frustrating progress.
The pushback is directed at two scientific assessments by the UN-backed IPBES biodiversity panel on the overlap between the nature and climate crises and the economic forces driving them.
Nearly 200 nations were due to agree how these landmark findings should guide efforts to protect nature but some countries “did not want to acknowledge them”, the French delegate added.
A negotiator from another developed nation told AFP these four countries were also leading this push.
“There is a clear alliance of Russia, Saudi, Argentina and, to some extent, Brazil, all working together to try to water down IPBES reports, not welcome them, or use them as bargaining chips in other negotiation items,” the negotiator said on condition of anonymity.
Setting precedent
Much of the dispute boils down to a few paragraphs of text in a draft agreement and whether countries should “welcome” or “take note” of the IPBES findings.
The latter phrasing is considered far weaker in the language of UN negotiations, where every word is closely scrutinised.
The current draft was “a text without ambition”, said the French delegate.
“If we no longer have a scientific basis to work from, then everything we discuss here is merely a matter of opinion,” the delegate added.
Academics and civil society activists at COP17 have already issued a joint statement of concern at the state of negotiations.
When approached by AFP in Yerevan, IPBES chair David Obura declined to comment as the talks were still ongoing.
Although the summit is due to end on Oct 30, a number of outstanding matters – including around the science – remain unresolved.
The dispute echoes a growing pattern in consensus-based global negotiations, where oil-producing countries are accused of frustrating efforts to tackle fossil fuels, plastic trash and other environmental harm.
Climate science has long been a flashpoint and the IPCC is currently deadlocked, as countries including Saudi Arabia and India push to delay publication of its next set of benchmark reports on global warming.
In an unprecedented decision in 2025, a crucial summary of the Global Environment Outlook, a flagship UN scientific report, was torpedoed as nations rowed over fossil fuels.
“We’ve pretty much always seen IPCC reports being politicised...,” said the negotiator from the developed country.
“But in the biodiversity world they’ve been much less contentious until the last few years, and this COP in particular.”
“They’re never easy, no decision is. There’s always nitpicking over language – but it’s gotten far worse.”
Bethan Laughlin, a senior policy specialist for the Zoological Society of London who observed the COP17 negotiations firsthand, said the trend was worrying.
“The point really isn’t this particular text, although it is highly significant. The point is the precedent it sets,” she told AFP in Yerevan. AFP

Finland launches criminal probe of suspected environmental damage by Google

Unknown Publisher

Finland launches criminal probe of suspected environmental damage by Google
The US tech giant is investing $15bn in a huge new data centre project in northern Finland.
Finnish police have launched a criminal investigation into suspected breaches of environmental law at the construction site of a planned Google data centre in northern Finland.
The project is part of a $15bn deal announced last month by Alphabet’s Google to invest in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure in Finland, which the US company described as its largest investment in Europe.
Authorities have said Tuike Finland, a local subsidiary of Google, conducted forest clearing and drainage at a planned site near the town of Muhos, before the environmental impact assessments required under Finnish law had been completed.
“We are investigating whether the company’s operations have breached the Water Act and resulted in environmental damage,” Detective Superintendent Kari Pakanen told the Reuters news agency on Thursday, adding that a guilty finding could lead to a corporate fine.
Pakanen declined to say whether any individuals could become a target of the investigation, and a Google spokesperson said the company would cooperate with the police investigation and continue to focus on maintaining compliance at its sites.
Tree felling prompts local anger
Videos and photographs showing the scale of the forest clearance at the site of the data centre, and Google’s initial reluctance to address the issue in the days after the news broke, have prompted widespread anger in Finland, where there is a high level of respect for the natural environment among the public.
“All the outrage and dismay directed at Google, I can very much share that, especially when we are talking about the parent company valued as the third-largest in the world,” Finnish Green MP Oras Tynkkynen told Al Jazeera. “There is just no excuse. You have to know the legislation of the country you are operating in; you can afford to hire the best legal experts to help you navigate the local legal requirements.”
Finnish authorities ordered Google to stop work at the data centre site at the start of October, and the latest information from the police highlights shortcomings in the drainage and water management at the site.
Tynkkynen called Google’s actions “unforgivable”, but cautioned that while the anger being directed at the US tech giant was justified, it was also diverting scrutiny away from legacy Finnish forestry companies, which he says are “by far the biggest contributors to biodiversity loss in this country”.
What is Finland’s appeal for data centre construction?
Finland’s cool climate, low-carbon electricity and government endorsement of AI projects have contributed to making the country one of Europe’s main destinations for data centre investments in recent years.
Finland, similar in size to Germany – but with one-seventh of the population, less than six million people – has had less vocal opposition to data centre buildouts than other places, including in the United States.
AI data centres are among the main drivers of a projected rise of up to 40 percent in Finland’s electricity consumption in the coming years, if all agreed grid connection projects go ahead, grid operator Fingrid has said.
Google’s planned investments in Finland include data centres, electricity grid improvements and clean energy and battery projects to power services such as Gemini, Search, Maps and YouTube.
Supporting Google’s plan, Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in September that the deal would be a boost for the economy, playing down concerns that it would suck up energy and push up power prices.

We Now Have Intel About the Russians Preparing New Ballistic Missile Attacks; We Need the Capabilities to Shoot Down This Russian Evil – Address by the President

US Jews urge Israel opposition to partner with Arab parties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:21:12 UTC

Breadcrumb
US liberal, progressive Jewish groups urge Israel opposition to ally with Arab parties
Liberal US Jewish leaders are urging Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot and his allies to work with parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel to oust incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, after Tuesday’s closely contested election left both major blocs short of a majority.
Several Jewish-led organisations in the US, including liberal pro-Israel lobby group J Street and activist group Israelis for Peace, have called on the opposition to embrace Arab-led parties as partners in political change.
The Joint List secured 12 seats and the United Arab List (Ra’am) seven, bringing Palestinian parties’ combined representation to a record 19 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
The election also saw a surge in participation among Palestinian citizens of Israel, with turnout among Palestinian voters reportedly reaching a historic 80%.
J Street president Jeremy Ben-Ami welcomed their participation, saying that “their voices and votes are a vital part of Israel’s democratic fabric”.
“This is a moment for the Jewish opposition parties to demonstrate genuine leadership by reaching out to the Arab parties and working together to form an alternative government,” Ben-Ami said in a statement.
“Israel cannot build a stronger, more inclusive democracy while treating the political representatives of one-fifth of its population as illegitimate governing partners.”
New York-based Israelis for Peace also praised the high turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel, describing it as “a victory to the anti-Netanyahu bloc” for helping dislodge the ruling coalition led by Netanyahu and the far right.
However, the group criticised the opposition bloc for “refusing to accept this gift, out of no other reason but deep-rooted, unexamined and systemic racism”.
The criticism comes as Eisenkot pledged to “do everything in my power to form a Zionist government” on Wednesday.
His bloc’s projected 48 seats, compared with 53 for Netanyahu’s camp, mean the opposition may need support from Arab-led parties, including the Joint List.
Formal alliances between Jewish-led parties and Arab parties have long faced resistance in Israeli politics, including since the establishment of Israel and the Palestinian Nakba in 1948.
Eisenkot’s own pre-election rejection of Arab backing could add to uncertainty following an inconclusive result, particularly amid Netanyahu’s repeated attacks on the opposition.
The prime minister warned his right-wing Jewish supporters that voting for the opposition would put Arabs in power.
Daniel Levy, political commentator and president of the US/Middle East Project (USMEP), told The New Arab that a growing minority within the Israeli diaspora, particularly in the US, as well as within Israel, was calling for a coalition that included Arab parties.
However, he argued that the decisive test would be whether opposition parties were prepared to accept Palestinian Arab parties as political partners.
He added that the issue could test whether liberal Zionism could translate its stated principles into meaningful political change in Israel.
“The question is now in the courts of the Zionist opposition, and the question is as follows: You have been telling everyone that Netanyahu is an existential threat to Israel. The continuation of his government is a disaster,” Levy said.
“Now you have the opportunity to remove it. It means partnering with the non-Zionists of the Palestinian Arab community. It means, in the words of [Democrats chairman] Yair Golan, if you like, not playing Netanyahu.”
With the election producing no clear winner, Levy said the extent to which Arab-led parties gain greater recognition, and whether attitudes towards them are shifting, would become clearer during what could be weeks of protracted negotiations over the formation of a new government.
“Even if Eisenkot can be convinced, can [Avigdor] Lieberman, who built his career on racist rabble-rousing against the Arab population, and [former prime minister Naftali] Bennett, who is a former settler leader, will they get on board with it?” Levy told The New Arab.
“Maybe the opposition bloc do go for it, or at least maybe they cooperate inside the Knesset without even forming a government. Maybe they just cooperate in the Knesset to swear in a new Knesset speaker, new committees, and to make some changes there.”
He continued: “I think many people are looking at this and saying, ‘Okay, are you going to show us all that ultimately your belief in the Jewish ethnostate and your racism towards the Palestinians is stronger than your willingness to get rid of Netanyahu?’”

Al Jazeera marks 30th anniversary with network overhaul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:20:07 UTC
03:20:07 KST

Al Jazeera marks 30th anniversary with network overhaul
Marking three decades, Al Jazeera unveils a new structure: three channels, 33 programmes, and tech-driven innovation.
Al Jazeera is marking its 30-year anniversary with a transformation of the network, introducing a three-channel structure for its Arabic-language broadcasting operation and 33 programmes aimed at providing audiences with more in-depth coverage and analysis.
Since its launch on November 1, 1996, the Qatar-based network has helped reshape Arab journalism, challenging dominant political narratives and providing a platform for political debate rarely seen on television in the region at the time.
Reflecting on this enduring legacy during a special anniversary episode of the network’s Arabic-language Baad al-Bath podcast, veteran anchor Khadija Benguenna detailed the foundational shifts the network brought to the Arab news industry.
Benguenna said that Al Jazeera had popularised practices such as breaking news alerts, continuous live coverage, and exclusive reporting, which were subsequently adopted by other Arab broadcasters.
Former Al Jazeera news director Ahmad al-Sheikh echoed that sentiment during his appearance on the same broadcast. He described the Arab world’s media environment as previously devoid of independent voices, and credited Al Jazeera with providing an example for other Arab broadcasters to improve standards across the board.
A new era
The anniversary brings a significant restructuring of the Al Jazeera Media Network’s Arabic-language news services, separating rolling breaking news coverage, live event broadcasting, and more in-depth reporting across three channels.
Speaking to the Qatari newspaper Al Raya, Asef Hamidi, the managing director of Al Jazeera Arabic, described the changes as a “new renaissance” for Al Jazeera. “We are talking about numerous paths undergoing significant development that the audience will notice,” Hamidi said.
Hamidi, who was appointed to his current position in September 2025, said the restructuring was intended to address the growing volume and complexity of news and the need to offer audiences different ways of following events.
In an interview with Qatari newspaper Al Watan, Sheikh Nasser bin Faisal Al Thani, Al Jazeera Media Network director general, explained the philosophical necessity behind the expansion.
“From the very beginning, Al Jazeera was more than just another television channel,” Sheikh Nasser said. “It was a broader project to deepen public understanding.”
He said the strategy for the network’s fourth decade would be guided by three principles.
“Our fourth decade will be defined by three priorities: immediacy, understanding and the human dimension,” he said.
Three channels, three approaches
Under the new structure, each of Al Jazeera’s three Arabic-language news channels will have a distinct editorial focus.
Al Jazeera Mubasher, which began broadcasting in 2005, will continue its concentration on uninterrupted live coverage of events, without commentary from presenters or correspondents.
For breaking developments, the new Al Jazeera Now service will focus on developments as they unfold. But unlike a conventional news channel, it will operate without scheduled bulletins or a fixed programme grid.
Meanwhile, the flagship Al Jazeera Arabic channel will retain its news bulletins while pivoting more towards in-depth analysis and investigative journalism, as well as other programmes.
The restructuring is accompanied by plans for 33 programmes, promoted under the slogan “Your questions are our questions”.
Sheikh Nasser said the expansion was intended to provide more context on news events to Arab viewers.
“The real competitor today is not another channel, but noise – the flood of information that makes understanding harder, not easier,” he said, adding that Al Jazeera wanted to fill that gap in understanding.
Hamidi said the new programming would include investigative documentaries, discussions of political and social issues, and programmes examining the historical roots of current conflicts.
Deepening the context
The network’s ambitions extend beyond television broadcasting to strengthening Al Jazeera’s local and regional reporting through dedicated digital platforms covering Palestine, Egypt, Sudan, the Gulf and other parts of the Arab world.
The Syria Now platform, which offers documentaries, investigations, and field reporting focused on Syrian affairs, has quickly emerged as one of the primary digital outlets for news on the country.
Looking ahead, the network is also planning a project called Al Jazeera Cultural, provisionally scheduled for launch in late 2027.
The initiative will serve as a space to foster sustained debate about the Arab world’s cultural and intellectual life.
Technological integration
The expansion also forms part of a wider technological transformation, including the development of The Core, an artificial intelligence initiative announced in December 2025 in collaboration with Google Cloud.
The initiative aims to integrate AI into newsroom operations, helping journalists manage information, coordinate coverage and make better use of the network’s reporting archives.
One component, Orbit, is being designed to coordinate newsroom workflows, including monitoring developments, commissioning stories, organising interviews, translating material and managing reporting assignments.
Sheikh Nasser said the first phase of The Core is scheduled to launch on November 1.
Despite the increased use of AI, Sheikh Nasser insisted that human oversight would remain primary.
“Artificial intelligence enables the human and does not replace him,” Sheikh Nasser said. “The main standard for us is conscience and editorial judgement, and editorial judgement is human.”

apple breaks a 16-year design rule with its first touchscreen macbook pro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:19:00 UTC
03:19:00 KST

apple breaks a 16-year design rule with its first touchscreen macbook pro
after years of reserving touchscreens for its mobile devices, apple allows creatives to create digital content directly on the display.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
Apple brings touch to the MacBook Pro after years of resistance
Apple has unveiled its first touchscreen MacBook Pro in Cupertino, California, ending a 16-year position on how people should interact with a laptop. Announced on October 28th, 2026, the new 14- and 16-inch models allow users to work directly on the display, reaching past the keyboard and trackpad to manipulate content with their fingers. It is a familiar gesture on an iPhone, though one Apple has long resisted bringing to the Mac.
Back in 2010, Steve Jobs argued that vertical touch surfaces were uncomfortable to use for extended periods. Speaking at Apple’s Back to the Mac event, he joked that eventually ‘your arm wants to fall off,’ explaining why the company had concentrated its efforts on developing multi-touch trackpads instead. For Jobs, the horizontal surface offered a more comfortable way to interact with a computer.
Apple maintained this thinking for years. In 2018, software chief Craig Federighi again questioned the ergonomics of reaching toward a laptop screen, suggesting that the existing trackpad offered a better experience. With the new MacBook Pro, the company has revisited that position, introducing touch as an additional way to work while retaining the familiar laptop configuration.
designers can now work directly on the screen
For designers and artists, the change opens up some interesting possibilities. Graphic designers can draw directly onto their work in Pixelmator Pro, while 3D artists can interact with digital models using their fingers. Photographs can be enlarged with a pinch, and windows can be moved across the desktop with a swipe. The screen itself becomes another working surface, allowing certain tasks to move beyond the trackpad.
Apple has integrated the touch sensor directly into its new OLED panel, reducing the distance between a finger and the content beneath it. The hinge has also been redesigned to provide greater stability when the screen is pressed. Meanwhile, macOS 27 translates touches into mouse clicks in existing applications, allowing much of the current software library to respond to the new interaction.
The MacBook Pro still operates as a conventional laptop, with a fixed screen and the familiar keyboard below. Apple Pencil support is absent, and the device has no convertible tablet mode. Touch instead joins the existing controls, allowing users to move between methods depending on what they are doing. For creative work, that could mean switching from precise cursor movements to directly adjusting something on screen.
a brighter OLED display changes the visual experience
The touchscreen arrives alongside Apple’s new PROLED XDR display, which uses two layers of light-emitting pixels to produce deeper blacks and brighter images. The screen reaches up to 2,000 nits of brightness, according to Apple, and supports both P3 and Adobe RGB color spaces. These capabilities are particularly relevant for photographers and graphic designers working across digital and printed media.
Another familiar feature has made its way over from the iPhone. Apple’s Dynamic Island now sits at the top of the MacBook display, replacing the previous camera notch with an interactive area for notifications and controls. Music playback and incoming calls can be accessed from this small section of the screen, which expands and changes according to the activity.
The physical design has also been slimmed down, with the 14-inch model now weighing 3 pounds and the 16-inch version weighing 4 pounds. Narrower screen borders create more room for the display, while a revised cooling system accommodates the smaller enclosure. Despite these changes, the overall silhouette remains recognizably MacBook Pro.
apple’s illuminated logo returns after a decade
There is also a small return to Apple’s earlier laptop designs. The illuminated Apple logo, removed from the MacBook Pro in 2016, is back on the rear of the display. For years, the glowing mark was one of the most recognizable features of Apple’s portable computers. Its reappearance brings a familiar detail to a machine introducing one of the company’s biggest changes in laptop interaction.
Inside, the new models use Apple’s M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, with battery life rated at up to 24 hours. The technical upgrades extend across processing power and storage capacity, though the most immediately visible changes concern the display and the ways people can interact with it.

U.S. inflation accelerates in September on higher energy prices
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
02:17:22 CST
03:17:22 KST

This file photo taken on Sept. 15, 2026 shows the gasoline price at a gas station in New York, the United States. U.S. inflation accelerated in September as consumers paid more for gasoline and other energy goods, according to data released by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) on Oct. 29, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Fengguo)
NEW YORK, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- U.S. inflation accelerated in September as consumers paid more for gasoline and other energy goods, according to data released by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) on Thursday.
The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, rose 0.5 percent month on month in September, the largest gain since March. Year on year, PCE inflation climbed to 3.6 percent, the highest since May. Both readings were in line with economists' expectations.
Prices for gasoline and other energy goods surged 9.2 percent from August, as the Iran war and restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz kept fuel costs elevated. Goods prices rose faster than in August, while services prices increased at a steady pace.
Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the core PCE price index rose 0.3 percent month on month in September, the same pace as a revised reading for August. Core PCE inflation rose 3.1 percent year on year, up from 3 percent.
Inflation has now run above the Fed's 2 percent target for more than five years, and September's data kept it moving further away from that goal.
U.S. consumer spending rose 0.5 percent in September, slowing from August, the BEA said. Adjusted for inflation, spending was unchanged, as higher prices absorbed the gain.
Personal income rose 0.2 percent, slower than in August and short of the increase in prices. With households still spending, the personal saving rate fell to 3.8 percent, the lowest in nearly four years.
The report came a day after the Fed left its benchmark interest rate unchanged at a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent, while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated." The decision followed a quarter-point rate hike in September.
Financial markets continued to expect another move this year. Traders were pricing in an over 80 percent chance of a rate hike at the Fed's December meeting, according to CME's FedWatch Tool. ■

Along the Black Sea coast, it will be mostly cloudy, with light rain in isolated areas, mainly along the southern coast. Light to moderate north-northwesterly winds will blow. Maximum temperatures will range from 14°C to 15°C, while sea water temperatures will be 16°C to 17°C. The sea will be around force 3 on the Beaufort scale.
Cloudy weather will prevail over the weekend. Rain is expected in many parts of the country, with snow in the mountains above 1,600 metres. Winds will be light to moderate from the southeast. Minimum temperatures will range from 4°C to 9°C, while maximum temperatures will be between 9°C and 14°C.
Across the Balkans, it will be predominantly cloudy, with rain in many areas. Precipitation will generally be light in the northern half of the peninsula, while further south it will be accompanied by thunderstorms.
Temperatures will reach 19°C in Athens, 16°C in Istanbul, 14°C in Bucharest and 12°C in Belgrade.

'Deeply regressive': How the French government plans to make protesters pay for riots and looting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:15:38 UTC
03:15:38 KST

'Deeply regressive': How the French government plans to make protesters pay for riots and looting
As France continues to pick up the pieces after riots and looting broke out on the fringes of nationwide peaceful demonstrations on October 17, the government is pushing forward a bill that would make protesters have to pay up to €10,000 in reparations for damage caused during public unrest – even if they were not directly responsible for the vandalism.
You’ve seen the images by now. The grey husks of cars staining the asphalt with soot. The gutted boutiques spilling their wares onto the street to be snatched up by eager hands. The fires licking the ribs of burning barricades, reaching higher and higher into the skies over Paris. The charred belfry of the Limoges town hall falling into the building’s blazing bowels.
Although the overwhelming majority of the public demonstrations against the rising cost of living that swept France on October 17 unfolded peacefully, the riots and looting that broke out on the margins of many of the street marches left the country reeling.
While the costs are still being tallied, France’s Chamber of Commerce and Industry has said that almost 2,500 businesses were damaged over the weekend, with more than a thousand of those ransacked, looted or set on fire. The free-market IFRAP Foundation has estimated the nationwide costs at not far short of a billion euros.
Hammered on all sides by accusations that it had badly bungled its role in ensuring public order in the face of mass demonstrations, the French government has brought forward a draft bill that would make protesters liable to pay up to €10,000 for damage caused during public demonstrations – even if they were not the people responsible for it.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
The “make rioters pay” law passed through the right-wing-dominated Senate on Wednesday, and will now be debated in the more divided National Assembly. Although its final form has yet to be determined, the draft law has already raised an outcry from human rights organisations, workers unions and France’s left-wing political parties, who say the bill as it stands today would be an all-out assault on the fundamental right to hold peaceful demonstrations.
Other legal experts have also questioned the need for such a law.
Laurent Caruso, a criminal defence lawyer and a member of the National Bar Council’s Liberties and Human Rights Commission, said that the French criminal justice system already had ways of making people pay for the damage they’d caused during riots.
“If you’ve committed an offence, you may face criminal penalties, or you may have to pay a fine, and the fact that you’ve committed an offence may mean that you may be required to pay for the damage you’ve caused, the destruction and all the resulting consequences,” he said. “So this mechanism already exists – when you’re responsible for something, you pay.”
But putting a name and face to the individuals responsible for the worst property damage after rioters have been driven from the streets is no easy task. To this end, the draft law targets not just individuals found guilty of theft or destruction of property, but people who have “knowingly taken part in” a group formed expressly to carry out acts of vandalism.
The law would also apply to people who have remained in public gatherings even after they have been ordered twice by police to disperse.
“Under this proposed law, the idea is to broaden out the group of people who could be held liable – people who, although they may not necessarily have taken part in something, are nonetheless liable for it,” Caruso said. “And the aim seems to be that as it is sometimes difficult to identify the people responsible, we’re going to broaden the circle of people who could be held responsible, and we’re going to make someone or other pay. Never mind if you’re not actually responsible – you’ll still pay for what the others did, because you shouldn’t have been there in the first place.”
Read more'I didn’t know it was theft': Trials begin in Paris following October 17 violence
The draft bill as it stands raises uneasy questions. If the person next to you in a peaceful march starts scrawling slogans on the nearest bus stop, are you now considered part of a group of vandals? How far would you have to walk away from them before you’re no longer financially liable for their actions? Would you have to leave the protest altogether?
For that matter, how much time do you have to leave a demonstration once police have given the order to disperse before you’re legally on the hook for everything that follows after? As anyone who has struggled to push their way through a crowd of people kettled in on all sides by armed riot police can tell you, it’s not always as easy as the draft law would suggest.
It’s for these reasons that the draft law has come under heavy criticism from rights groups. Amnesty International warned that the law would be “a deeply regressive step” for France. Two of France’s major workers unions, the General Confederation of Labour and the French Democratic Confederation of Labour, on Thursday condemned the draft bill as a profound threat to the fundamental right to non-violent protest.
Caruso said that the uncertainty engendered by the bill seemed specifically designed to make potential demonstrators think twice before joining a peaceful street march.
“The direct consequence is that this is a freedom-destroying law that infringes upon civil liberties, because it is a direct assault on the freedom to demonstrate,” he said. “And the aim is precisely to discourage people so as to avoid having to deal with this sort of situation – given that the state is, after all, a little overwhelmed at the moment.”
Read moreFrance faces reckoning with public order policing after violent protest weekend
He warned that the law’s broad wording left it open to arbitrary enforcement or even abuse by the police tasked with applying it.
“There’s a risk of discrimination too – if you’re a white man in a suit and tie participating in a march, you might not risk much, but if you’re a young person from the housing estates, you might be more easily picked out of the crowd,” he said. “So there’s a risk that this will be arbitrary, and this is what’s murky about the law – and that’s dangerous.”
Those who fear the draft law amounts to little less than collective punishment also point to provisions that would see people’s social benefits seized to cover the cost of damages caused during outbursts of street violence. Financial assistance for low-income households, housing assistance and the minimum income that France’s poorest people are entitled too could all partially be taken away to cover the costs of damaged property.
Caruso said that social benefits had long been off-limits under French law.
“Tomorrow, if we take away a family’s benefits, your whole family could end up paying for something you may not even have done,” he said. “And here, I think we’re taking things too far in the way we approach this issue. Legally, it’s not possible – it’s not fair to begin with, it’s not morally right, but on top of that, it’s completely out of keeping with the law.”
As the Senate heating grew more heated, French Communist Party senator Fabien Gay pointed out that deducting €57 every month from a family receiving the minimum income as proposed would take 14 years to reach the €10,000 threshold set by the draft law. If the far-right National Rally’s (RN) threshold of €30,000 passed into law, it would take families 44 years to pay the damages.
RN senator Edwige Diaz was unperturbed.
“To those who tell us that we are taking money from disadvantaged people, I say: don’t worry,” he said. “We’ll give them the chance to pay it back over the rest of their lives.”
The once unheard-of suggestion of stripping social benefits from families whose members have been judged responsible for the shop windows that other people have broken also rests on an uncomfortable truth: that many of those found guilty of property destruction during social unrest simply don’t have the means to pay for the damages they’ve caused.
“It’s difficult to take money from someone who doesn’t have any – and in that situation, there aren’t many options,” Caruso said. “From a criminal law perspective, there are penalties such as carrying out community service without pay; this benefits the community and is a way of making some sort of social amends for offences, provided they aren’t too serious, of course. But otherwise, with someone who has no money, it’s still difficult to make them pay, apart from pursuing them through the legal system until they have money, they’re in work, and we can take money to compensate for what has happened.”
But he stressed that opposition to the draft law was spurred not by a desire to shield looters from legal consequences, but the very opposite: to ensure that those consequences didn’t instead fall on the shoulders of people who had played no part in the kind of riots that erupted on October 17.
“As lawyers, we are not in favour of leniency or impunity,” he said. “It’s only right that people are punished for breaking the law, but it has to be done in accordance with the most basic legal principles, without undermining the civil liberties as they stand in our country – and that, from our point of view, is a red line that must not be crossed.”

The Promise and Pitfalls of Nvidia’s Venture in Kazakhstan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:15:00 UTC
03:15:00 KST

Nvidia co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang had an unmistakable air of confidence about him on October 23 as he took to the stage in Astana, Kazakhstan, before an eager audience of business executives, tech workers, political figures, and journalists.
In a nearly hour-long fireside chat with Kazakhstan’s Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev, Huang waxed effusive about the “incredibly visionary” President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, praising his foresight in declaring AI development to be a “national priority.”
After Madiyev announced that Nvidia had invested an undisclosed sum in Higgsfield, an AI video-generation company that became Kazakhstan’s first unicorn in September 2025, Huang also heaped praise on the startup and its founders.
But above all, the microchip engineer-turned-billionaire executive was most bullish in describing the upward trajectory of the global AI industry and Kazakhstan’s potential to position itself at its center.
“Kazakhstan has a fundamental advantage because you have so many natural resources already. Instead of just exporting energy in the future, you could transform this energy into intelligence and export intelligence,” Huang said. “You’re going to be a hub, a computing hub, an AI factory hub for all of Europe.”
On one level, Huang’s visit to Kazakhstan was just the latest stop on the barnstorming world tour the Nvidia boss first began in 2024 to sell the idea of “sovereign AI” to national leaders and statesmen.
But at another, it marked a meeting of minds and ambitions. The venerable chipmaker seeking to extend the global reach of its technology by powering next-generation data centers meets a resource-rich country hoping to turn its energy reserves into a competitive advantage in the AI economy. It’s a match made in heaven – or so it would seem.
Beyond this storybook partnership, however, lie significant challenges. Kazakhstan’s far-reaching AI plans call for billions of dollars in investment, expanded computing infrastructure, and a shift from supplying raw materials to producing higher-value digital services.
But experts say building and operating energy-intensive data centers will require not just abundant natural resources, but also a reliable electricity supply, the infrastructure to deliver it, and customers willing to pay for faraway computing capacity.
Coded in the Stars
For Nvidia, Kazakhstan is in some ways the ideal case study for its “Sovereign AI” strategy, which encourages governments to build domestic AI ecosystems around data centers, homegrown LLMs and local AI entrepreneurs, all powered by Nvidia chips.
Thanks in part to pitches like the one delivered by Huang in Astana, the strategy is quietly flourishing. In February, Nvidia’s chief financial officer said sovereign AI revenue had more than tripled to over $30 billion, and industry estimates suggest the company’s hardware underpins the overwhelming majority of sovereign AI language models.
But few countries have embraced Nvidia’s vision as fully as Kazakhstan. Since Tokayev pledged in 2025 to make the country a “fully digital nation” within three years, Astana has created an AI ministry, enrolled more than 650,000 students in AI training, and passed a comprehensive AI law, which entered force in 2026 amid the government’s “Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence.”
This convergence was on full display in Astana last week, as Huang approvingly noted that Kazakhstan was “the first country that I’ve been to where the president declared the country to be an AI nation.” Madiyev, for his part, framed the government’s strategy in Nvidia’s terms, calling Huang’s “five-layer cake” AI economic model “the main pillar” of Kazakhstan’s digital strategy, and pitching the country’s mines and factories as a testing ground for Nvidia’s advancements in “physical AI.”
The more substantive partnership between the two, however, centers around the planned Data Center Valley in Ekibastuz, in northeastern Kazakhstan. There, beside the coal-fired Ekibastuz GRES-1, the country’s largest power plant, the government broke ground in January on Data Center Valley, a campus it hopes will eventually reach one gigawatt worth of computing capacity. (It was this project Huang had in mind when he called Kazakhstan a future “AI factory hub for all of Europe.”)
In June, Astana announced a $10 billion package of agreements with Firebird, a U.S. cloud operator, and state-owned Kazakhtelecom to develop the site using Nvidia technology. Under the arrangement, Kazakhtelecom will provide power, cooling, and telecommunications infrastructure, while Firebird is set to finance the computing hardware.
More details about this investment became public last week, when Firebird signed an investment agreement with the government at the Akorda presidential palace, according to which the Data Center Valley site will be primarily used to generate computing power for international clients, with 10 percent of Firebird’s total GPU capacity to be allocated to Kazakhstani companies and government agencies. Under the agreement, the site will be powered by 45,000 high-end Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs, for which U.S. export licenses were announced last week.
For some experts, like Dr. Rustem Bigari, an AI and digital governance expert, this collaboration’s mutual appeal is apparent.
According to Bigari, Kazakhstan can offer globally competitive electricity prices, while data centers across the country are running low on capacity, meaning additional computing power is needed to fulfill the country’s AI ambitions, including developing Kazakh-language language models.
“We are offering the basic foundations that Nvidia needs,” Bigari told The Diplomat, adding that further investment in computing power would help Kazakhstan “become the main AI and cloud computing hub in the whole region.”
Similarly, Asad Bokhari, an assistant professor at Nazarbayev University’s Graduate School of Public Policy, sees Nvidia’s arrival as vindication of the government’s broader digitalization campaign, and a signal that Amazon, Microsoft or Google “may also follow in its footsteps” by investing in the country.
“If the government of Kazakhstan was not prepared, all of the country’s resources would be useless for Nvidia’s data center plans,” Bokhari said, crediting the government’s institutional readiness. “But it is, so it’s a win-win for both sides.”
Critical Error!
But not everyone in the expert community was so impressed by Astana’s Nvidia-themed festivities last weekend.
“We looked at Jensen’s visit as basically just PR and marketing,” said Marat Beksultanov, a New York-based geospatial consultant who has studied the Data Center Valley project. “We weren’t expecting any breakthrough announcements.”
This is significant because, according to Beksultanov, the most important questions about the Data Center Valley remain unanswered. “There’s actually two extremely big issues,” Beksultanov told The Diplomat. “One is power, and then the other one is customers.”
Since 2023, Kazakhstan has consumed more electricity than it generated each year, typically making up the shortfall by importing power from Russia. Last winter, during a record peak, national grid operator KEGOC reported that the country had no spare generating capacity, leading to nearly 1,000 megawatts having to be imported on December 27.
The government had previously expected to achieve a modest power surplus by 2027. But the Data Center Valley’s first phase alone would see it consume more electricity at full capacity than that entire increased figure, according to Beksultanov’s analysis. Moreover, in mid-October an energy ministry official pushed back the energy self-sufficiency target to early 2028, months after the Data Center Valley is supposed to open.
“There’s a mismatch in the timeline,” Beksultanov said, adding that new data centers will also have to compete for power with the government’s existing industrial projects, including expansions in aluminum, steel, ferrosilicon and copper smelting capacity.
Yet even if Kazakhstan can ramp up its electricity generation, a potentially thornier question remains: who will actually use the Data Center Valley?
As Nazarbayev University’s Bokhari said, the announcement that 10 percent of the site’s computing capacity would be reserved for local universities, businesses, and public institutions offers some clarity on how Kazakhstan intends to benefit from the project. Bokhari said he expected the government to prioritize domestic users over exporting computing capacity abroad.
Nevertheless, the lion’s share of the Data Center Valley’s computing power is supposed to go to international customers, none of whom have been publicly identified yet. Russia and China, the geographically closest potential clients, seem likely to remain semi-permanently off-limits due to U.S. export controls, and – despite Huang’s confident predictions to this effect – Europe may not represent a realistic customer base, either.
Roughly 95 percent of Kazakhstan’s outbound internet traffic currently runs through Russia, raising questions of security and sanctions. And about three-quarters of the country’s electricity is generated by coal-powered plants.
“Maybe European customers will come en masse to Kazakhstan and start using their data centers tomorrow, but the [environmental, social, and governance] risks will likely pose a very strong barrier to business,” Beksultanov said.
The Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable, inaugurated by Tokayev and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev in October, offers Kazakhstan an alternative route for international internet traffic to Europe via the South Caucasus. But with the cable’s commercial rollout and integration into wider networks still underway, how much traffic — if any — has already shifted away from Russia remains unclear.
The issue, ultimately, is that none of these problems stand to impact Nvidia’s interests or its approach. The company’s preferred business model is selling tools around the world to power the global AI revolution, which might explain its enthusiasm to partner with Kazakhstan’s government.
“Think about the gold rush,” Beksultanov said. “Nvidia is the guy who’s selling shovels. Would you expect that guy to say, well… this is a risk, you might not find gold? No, he would say business is good – go for it.”
Representatives from the AI ministry, Data Center Valley, and Nvidia did not respond to multiple requests for comment regarding the Data Center Valley project, its financing, power supply, future customers, or expected timeline of operations.

Hong Kong’s leader apologises for residential fire that killed 168 people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:14:21 UTC
03:14:21 KST

Hong Kong’s leader has apologised for government shortcomings that contributed to a fire that killed 168 people in the city last year, a rare sign of public contrition that nevertheless failed to impress some victims’ families.
The chief executive, John Lee, and seven other officials bowed in apology at the release of a report that pointed to “decades of failure” by government bodies.
Four departments “should bear part of the responsibility” for the high casualties, the report said. So far one official, housing secretary Winnie Ho, has resigned.
Last November, a small fire probably started by a cigarette grew into an inferno that enveloped seven of the eight towers in Wang Fuk Court, a housing complex that was shrouded in bamboo scaffolding and netting for renovations.
Former residents and victims’ families have been waiting to see how the government will address who is to blame for the ignored warnings, substandard building materials and disabled fire alarms that made the fire the world’s deadliest in a residential building since 1980.
Authorities have filed charges, including manslaughter, against seven individuals and two companies over their roles in the fire. At least 35 people have been arrested.
The independent report released on Thursday found the “main culprits” of the fire were private contractors but also accused officials of “lax enforcement”.
Had the four departments better recognised the risks and acted accordingly, “there was a real possibility that the misconduct of the private-sector parties and the fire hazards in WF Court could have been rectified or removed before the fire”, it said.
Lee said a three-month investigation would now begin into the government’s role.
“I am deeply saddened. I would like to apologise to the affected residents and the general public,” Lee said on Thursday, adding that housing minister Ho should “bear political responsibility”.
But Yip Ka-kui, who lost his wife and home in the fire, told reporters he did not consider the government’s acceptance of accountability adequate. “All the secretaries for the departments named should step down,” he said, according to AFP news agency. “Administrative responsibility falls short” and political accountability even more so, Yip added.
Phyllis Lo, whose mother died in the fire, told AP news agency that progress had been made but that justice had yet to be served.
She added the officials’ apology was late, though it was better than nothing.
Hong Kong’s government has previously been accused by critics of being more concerned with clamping down on criticism than addressing the causes of the disaster.
Since a national security law was imposed on the city in 2020 by Beijing, the city’s once vibrant civil society groups and political opposition have been all but quashed.
In the weeks after the fire, authorities warned against crimes that “exploit the tragedy” and reportedly arrested at least three people for sedition.
China’s national security agency in Hong Kong also summoned international media representatives, saying they had smeared the government in their reports on the fire.
On Thursday Lee promised that “similar incidents will never be allowed to happen again”.
Some observers had called for a more legally powerful inquiry commission to be set up, rather than the judge-led independent review committee that compiled Thursday’s report.
Lee told reporters that authorities had proposed “systematic reforms”, including criminalising bid-rigging and overhauling the complaints system.
The report stated: “The fire has been put out, but the reform has only just begun.”

Criminal Probe Launched in South Africa Over Contraband Baobabs Bound for Georgia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:12:00 UTC
03:12:00 KST

South African authorities have opened a criminal investigation into the attempted illegal export of five baobab trees to Georgia, halting a massive shipment at the coastal port of Durban after discovering the exporter lacked required environmental permits.
The five trees, estimated to be between 200 and 300 years old and weighing up to 30 tons each, remain impounded at a Durban logistics warehouse while investigators build a case under the country's forestry laws.
Under South Africa’s National Forests Act, the indigenous baobab is a protected species. It is illegal to cut down, harvest, transport, or export live specimens without explicit authorization from environmental regulators. While South Africa permits the commercial trade of processed baobab derivatives—such as fruit powder, seed oil, and cosmetic extracts—under strict licensing, the live specimen trade is tightly restricted to protect the slow-growing trees from international exploitation.
According to the Daily Maverick, the shipment was intercepted this summer at a facility operated by Africa Global Logistics, a subsidiary of the maritime shipping firm MSC Group. Officials discovered that the exporter lacked the mandatory permits required to export the specimens. Days after the seizure, the exporter submitted a retrospective permit application, which environmental authorities rejected.
“The department refused to issue a license retrospectively to regularize allegedly illegal criminal activities,” South Africa’s Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment said in a statement to OCCRP, confirming that a criminal case had been opened under the National Forests Act.
Department officials declined to publicly identify the exporter or the intended recipient in Georgia, citing the active investigation. However, a conviction carries severe penalties under South African law.
“A person who contravenes the prohibition in the National Forests Act commits a first category offense and may upon conviction be sentenced to a fine or imprisonment for a period of up to three years, or to both,” Sello Molekwa, chief director of communication and advocacy at the department, told OCCRP.
To botanists and conservationists, the uprooting of the trees—extracted from the Waterberg District in South Africa’s northern Limpopo province—represents a devastating loss of irreplaceable natural heritage.
Dr. Sarah Venter, a baobab expert and founder of the Baobab Foundation in South Africa, explained that removing the trees required approval under two distinct pieces of South African legislation.
“They didn’t have either,” Dr. Venter said, expressing hope that the impounded giants could still be saved. “I am hoping that the trees will be returned to Limpopo Province, where they came from, and replanted into their natural environment.”
Although South African authorities have not officially named the buyer, the seizure coincides with reports in Georgian media indicating that a private residence linked to the country’s billionaire former prime minister, Bidzina Ivanishvili, is preparing for a major tree delivery.
Ivanishvili has a documented history of importing ancient African trees for his personal estates and a public dendrological park on Georgia’s Black Sea coast. Between 2022 and 2023, eight massive baobabs were exported from Kenya to his park in Georgia. All eight trees withered and died last year, prompting the park’s management to issue an official statement blaming critical media coverage for extended procedures that then caused the demise of the trees.
The appetite for live specimens appears to continue. On Sept. 15, Georgia’s independent Formula TV reported that a new private residence being built for Ivanishvili outside Tbilisi was undergoing a “special landscaping project,” with a new baobab expected to arrive by late October.
The park is owned by a Georgia-registered firm ultimately controlled by Ivanishvili's wife, while the residence is owned by its subsidiary. The director of the firm that owns the residence did not respond to requests for comment regarding whether the South African shipment was destined for the property.
Meanwhile, the five uprooted trees remain held at the Durban facility. Africa Global Logistics stated that it acted solely as a logistics agent, halted the shipment as soon as regulatory concerns were raised, and is cooperating fully with authorities without facing criminal charges.

Several people died and many others were injured after a helicopter with the European Union peacekeeping force in Bosnia crashed Thursday in the country's north.

Albanian opposition storms parliament, sets off flares and smoke bombs

Sali Berisha and other opposition members stormed parliament in the capital, Tirana, on Thursday in support of demonstrators, who are demanding Prime Minister Edi Rama’s resignation. Berisha and his colleagues unsuccessfully tried to prevent a vote on a new law governing the country’s central bank.

The student-led protest movement has since evolved into something far bigger, with demonstrators citing economic stagnation, alleged corruption and poor education standards, coupled with high tuition fees.
The anti-government protests are Albania’s largest in decades and have turned violent, injuring hundreds of people, including police officers. Government buildings, banks and private buildings have also been attacked and set on fire.
Rama has been in office for 13 years and has refused to resign after winning a fourth term last year.
As Berisha addressed parliament on Thursday, his colleagues surrounded him while holding photos of protesters allegedly injured by rubber bullets.
Rama has introduced fines of more than $6,000 for anyone who attends a protest that turns violent, even if they did not participate in such acts. That is six times Albania’s average monthly salary of around $1,000.
Rama has announced a series of measures aimed at easing the protests. These include increasing the monthly scholarship stipend for students from low-income families, according to Albania’s public broadcaster, Radio Televizioni Shqiptar. Scholarships have also been extended to master’s degree students. Rama has also announced subsidised rent for students, the broadcaster reported.
