Municipal Association of Victoria demands data centre moratorium as planning approvals rise
In short:
The Municipal Association of Victoria has demanded the state government impose a moratorium on data centres.
The peak body for all 79 councils in Victoria passed a resolution at its state council meeting calling for a moratorium on approvals for all new or expanded data centres until a "comprehensive" planning and environmental framework is established.
What's next?
The move by councils places pressure on the major parties to respond to mounting community opposition ahead of next month's election.
Councils across Victoria have banded together to demand the state impose a moratorium on data centres, putting pressure on the major parties to respond to mounting community opposition ahead of next month's election.
The Municipal Association of Victoria (MAV), the peak body for all 79 councils in Victoria, passed a resolution at its October state council meeting calling for a moratorium on approvals for all new or expanded data centres until a "comprehensive" planning and environmental framework was established.
A second motion calling for better regulation of the social, economic and environmental impacts of data centres was also passed, amid ongoing concerns over land, energy and water use.
MAV president Jennifer Anderson said the resolutions "added weight" to local government concerns around data centres, with the peak body now able to advocate on behalf of all Victorian councils to the state and federal governments.
"If you're elected or now that you're in government, this is what our 79 councils are telling us they want done around data centres,"
Ms Anderson said.
"They have clearly told us this is important to them; this is what they want."
Eight Victorian councils brought data centre motions to the MAV's October State Council, including Melbourne, Geelong, Maribyrnong and Hume, reflecting the sector's increasing concern over the facilities' impact on local communities.
The City of Greater Geelong's submission said large-scale data centres could delay residential and industrial development "needed to support growing communities."
Data centre giant NextDC this year purchased 169 hectares of land in Lovely Banks in the Northern Geelong Growth Area — land that had been earmarked for more than 2,000 new homes as part of a plan to help solve the city's housing shortfall.
In nearby Corio, one of Geelong's largest suburbs, construction of a NextDC data centre is already underway.
With the Victorian government entering caretaker mode next Tuesday, Ms Anderson acknowledged there was "limited capacity to do much", but said the MAV would engage in advocacy both before and after the election with all parties.
"Once the government of the day is decided, then we will go pretty hard at getting all elected state officials — regardless of whether they're the government of the day, the opposition, crossbench et cetera — to know what these priority motions were," Ms Anderson said.
"Let's have a proper partnership. Let's look at what the impacts could be on the ground to our communities.
"We all look after the same communities. It's about having those conversations early before things get legislated."
The cities of Melton, Brimbank, Maribyrnong and Hume had separately called for an immediate moratorium on data centre approvals earlier this year.
In a submission to a recent Senate inquiry into artificial intelligence and data centres, the MAV said local government sat on the "frontline" of the impacts of AI infrastructure, increasingly tasked with balancing housing growth, infrastructure strain and community expectations.
The peak body criticised the government's Development Facilitation Program for allowing data centre companies to lodge planning applications directly with the planning minister rather than local councils, for projects considered to be a "significant economic development".
"What it's doing is taking powers away from council and community," Ms Anderson said.
The Victorian government announced new data centre regulations last month, including banning them near homes and schools, and mandating the use of renewable energy and non-drinking water.
"In Victoria, we set the rules — data centres must bring their own supply to protect our energy costs — and they can't be built near homes," the government spokesperson said.
An opposition spokesperson said under a Liberal and Nationals government, data centres would not be built in or next to residential areas, or green wedges.
"They will be located in designed Data Centre Precincts, appropriately distanced from homes," the spokesperson said.
The Greens have called for a moratorium on all new AI data centres and compensation for affected communities.
The party's spokesperson for AI and data centres, Sarah Mansfield, today said the government had "run out of excuses for letting big tech corporations railroad our communities".
"Victorians shouldn't have to sacrifice housing, water and energy security for Labor's reckless obsession with turning Victoria into a playground for big tech billionaires chasing a quick economic sugar hit," she said.

As Ukraine clears over 300,000 explosives in Kherson Oblast, UN appoints Russian diplomat to oversee mine action
Unknown

UN appoints Russian diplomat to oversee mine action, as Ukraine clears over 300,000 explosives in Kherson Oblast
The United Nations has appointed a Russian diplomat to a senior position overseeing mine action, drawing criticism from Ukraine as the country continues to clear hundreds of thousands of explosive devices left behind by Russia's war.
U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres announced the appointment of Gleb Desyatnikov as assistant secretary-general for mine action and police in the Department of Peace Operations on Oct. 27.
Desyatnikov has served as Russia's ambassador to Jordan since 2018, including throughout Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. According to the U.N., he has more than 35 years of experience in international relations and security affairs, including previous positions at Russia's Foreign Ministry.
"Moscow has mined the United Nations," Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi wrote on X on Oct. 29, criticizing the decision.
"Entrusting this responsibility to a representative of the aggressor state is deeply troubling and undermines trust in the United Nations," he added.
The appointment comes as Ukraine faces one of the world's largest demining challenges, with Russian mines and unexploded ordnance threatening civilians and complicating the recovery of agricultural land and infrastructure.
In southern Kherson Oblast, demining teams have neutralized 300,691 explosive devices on the Ukrainian-controlled right bank since the start of clearance operations, according to the regional military administration.
Between Oct. 22 and 28 alone, specialists surveyed 602.8 hectares (1,490 acres) and neutralized 471 explosive devices, the administration reported on Oct. 29. Authorities said 74.5% of the territory designated for clearance on the region's right bank has now been cleared.
In December 2022, Human Rights Watch (HRW) confirmed that Russia was using 13 models of anti-personnel and 13 models of anti-vehicle landmines in its invasion of Ukraine, and that approximately 30% of the country — an area twice the size of Austria — had been "contaminated" with mines.
Among them are also PFM-1 "Butterfly" anti-personnel mines. The mines are green or olive in color, and recognizable by their distinctive shape, similar to the "propellor" seeds that spiral down from maple, ash, and sycamore trees. During the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, they became better known for their injurious effects on the curious children who would find them while out playing.
Speaking to the Kyiv Independent nine months later, HRW Associate Director Mark Hiznay, explained the near impossibility of keeping that figure current. What is known is that Russia, at the beginning of the full-scale invasion, had a stockpile of 26 million mines —the largest in the world, according to various estimates.

NATO–Ukraine AI Forecasts Russian Drone Threats 24 Hours Ahead, 50 Kilometers Behind Front
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:09:44 UTC
03:09:44 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
NATO–Ukraine AI Forecasts Russian Drone Threats 24 Hours Ahead, 50 Kilometers Behind Front
NATO and Ukraine have developed an artificial intelligence system capable of predicting Russian drone activity up to 24 hours in advance across areas extending 50 kilometers behind the front line, Business Insider reported on October 29.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The system, known as Initiative 13 or Model 13, generates predictive maps to help Ukrainian commanders anticipate Russian drone operations and position troops and equipment. A spokesperson for NATO’s Joint Analysis, Training, and Education Center (JATEC) explained that the technology "turns an array of disparate data into a clear map of expected activity."
Initiative 13 covers Ukrainian territory between 5 and 50 kilometers behind the line of contact, dividing the area into geographical cells. For each cell, the system forecasts the intensity of Russian reconnaissance and strike drone activity, threat levels, potential changes, and possible variations in drone operations.
The AI analyzes historical battlefield data, including previous Russian drone activity, aircraft types, deployment patterns, weather conditions, terrain, and proximity to the front line. Its forecasts identify high-risk areas for the following day, allowing commanders to adjust deployments and potentially reduce exposure to Russian strikes.
However, JATEC emphasized that the system is intended to support military planning rather than replace real-time intelligence or commanders' decisions.
Ukraine's Ministry of Defense announced on October 13 that Model 13 had been validated using real-world battlefield data and was ready for integration into the Armed Forces' situational-awareness systems. The ministry described its ability to predict Russian drone operations as highly probable, although no specific accuracy figures were disclosed.
Ukrainian forces already operate the Delta battlefield management platform, which consolidates frontline intelligence into an interactive map accessible through computers, tablets, and smartphones. Model 13 was developed jointly by Ukraine's Armed Forces and NATO's Allied Command Transformation, with support from JATEC.
The push toward data-driven warfare is also reshaping how Ukrainian units record and reuse combat results. Between March and October 1, drone operators logged more than 3 million strike missions through Mission Control, a Delta module that feeds completed mission data back into future planning.
In September alone, troops entered more than 1.8 million mission results, a more than ninefold increase over monthly usage at the start of 2026. By July, the system was already recording more than 6,600 confirmed enemy targets hit each day.

Automated air-defense turrets have destroyed dozens of Russian drones over Kyiv in the past month alone, including fast jet-powered Geran-5 and Banderol UAVs, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry reported on October 29.
The Defense Ministry and Ukraine’s Brave1 defense innovation cluster have been developing and integrating automated gun systems into the country’s air-defense network, giving Kyiv another relatively low-cost layer for intercepting Russian aerial threats.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Brave1 began working on automated turret technology in 2024. Since then, the systems have moved beyond the development stage and are now operated by the Ukrainian Air Force.
Among the Russian targets already destroyed by the turrets are Banderol and Geran-5 jet-powered drones—a growing threat as Moscow introduces faster UAVs capable of placing greater pressure on conventional mobile fire groups and interceptor drones.
According to the Defense Ministry, automated turrets deployed as part of Ukraine’s private air-defense initiative have already destroyed more than 60 aerial targets.
“This is the result of systematic work that proves that the latest Ukrainian developments are capable of effectively countering aerial threats both on the front line and over cities, protecting critical infrastructure,” the ministry said.
The private air-defense initiative allows Ukrainian companies to establish additional protection for employees, industrial facilities, and energy infrastructure rather than relying solely on state-operated air-defense units.
The United States is supplying Ukraine with only 12 Patriot air-defense interceptor missiles per month—roughly four times fewer than under former President Joe Biden—while withholding approval for additional weapons Kyiv has already paid for as Russia intensifies attacks against civilians and civilian infrastructure.
Previously, reports emerged that Ukraine’s largest express-delivery company has built its own private air-defense capability—and says it has already shot down Russian Shahed attack drones.

====================================================================================================

INSS outlines recommendations for US, UK to set independent oversight, enforceable 'red lines'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:09:07 UTC
03:09:07 KST

A new study by the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) published on Wednesday urges US political parties to establish binding definitions, independent review mechanisms, and enforceable red lines to address antisemitism among political candidates and elected officials.
The analysis entitled "Partisan Antisemitism in the United Kingdom and the United States: Response Mechanisms and Red Lines" was authored by INSS researchers Ariel Cohen and Ofir Dayan, head of the INSS Antisemitism and Delegitimization Research Team.
The authors examined how political organizations determine who is qualified to represent them and what consequences should follow when ideological boundaries are crossed. The researchers noted that while political parties grant candidates campaign funds, legitimacy, and institutional infrastructure, responses to antisemitism in the US often remain ad hoc and contingent on political calculations.
The authors explored the British Labour Party under Jeremy Corbyn's leadership as a primary case study. In the UK, an accumulation of antisemitic statements by party members, including formal complaints submitted between 2016 and 2018 by the Jewish Labour Movement (JLM) and Campaign Against Antisemitism (CAA), culminated in a formal investigation by the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) in 2020.
The EHRC found Labour responsible for unlawful acts of harassment, discrimination, and political interference in complaints handling, shifting the issue from individual misconduct to institutional failure.
The authors highlighted that public pressure, including the March 2018 "Enough Is Enough" protest outside Parliament organized by the Board of Deputies of British Jews (BoD) and the Jewish Leadership Council (JLC), a poll showing 55 percent of respondents viewed Corbyn unfit to be prime minister, and an unprecedented pre-election intervention by Chief Rabbi Ephraim Mirvis, turned antisemitism into an electoral crisis. Britain's centralized party structure, combined with EHRC regulatory oversight, allowed Labour to establish an independent complaints process and candidate vetting under Keir Starmer. The authors noted that this framework could serve as a model for parliamentary systems like Ireland, Australia, and New Zealand.
In analyzing the United States, the authors found a distinct dynamic shaped by a decentralized party network, primary elections, and First Amendment protections. Because state governments run primaries and no central party organ approves ballot access, US party leadership cannot directly disqualify candidates or prevent them from running.
The authors observed that US party leaders often limit themselves to public condemnation without taking concrete action, disavowing candidates only when separate, electorally dangerous scandals emerge. As an example on the Democratic side, the authors cited Graham Platner, a Senate candidate in Maine who maintained party support despite possessing a tattoo associated with the Nazi SS, with senior figures withdrawing support only after he faced unrelated sexual assault allegations. On the Republican side, North Carolina Lieutenant Governor Mark Robinson faced criticism for Holocaust denial statements, but senior party figures distanced themselves only after a report linked him to explicit posts on a pornography website.
The authors also pointed to incumbent figures who expanded their political standing despite public controversies over antisemitic rhetoric, noting that when Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar made controversial remarks in 2019, the resulting House resolution was broadened into a general condemnation of hate without censuring her, naming her, or addressing antisemitism as a standalone issue.
On the Republican side, Minnesota Senate nominee Royce White and Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene maintained political standing despite promoting antisemitic conspiracy theories. Furthermore, the authors raised concerns regarding political boundary-setting with influential outside figures, citing Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed's collaboration with online influencer Hasan Piker, as well as Republican figures and Jewish groups warning against the influence of Tucker Carlson, Candace Owens, and supporters of Nick Fuentes infiltrating conservative activist training institutions. A Politico investigation exposing antisemitic messages exchanged by young Republican leaders was cited as evidence of extreme rhetoric seeping into youth pathways.
Examining existing US response mechanisms, the authors noted that while parties can withhold funding, endorse primary rivals, or strip elected officials of committee assignments, these tools carry limited impact against candidates with independent fundraising bases, Super PAC support, or strong online followings. Post-election sanctions like committee removal or expulsion require congressional votes that parties are often reluctant to pursue due to tight voting margins and fear of political retaliation.
Condemnation alone fails to define political legitimacy
The authors highlighted 'The Front Line,' a political organization launched in July 2026 affiliated with Republican Senator Ted Cruz as a potential vehicle for change. The group seeks to make antisemitism a "disqualifying factor" in Republican primaries by running targeted campaigns against candidates, such as spending $400,000 against Florida gubernatorial candidate James Fishback following his statements on "white genocide" tropes.
Authors Cohen and Dayan told The Jerusalem Post that public condemnation alone fails to define political legitimacy unless linked directly to structural consequences within political parties.
“Both major American parties condemn antisemitism in principle, but too often fail to translate that condemnation into meaningful consequences. On both sides of the aisle, candidates continued to advance after antisemitic remarks surfaced, and were dropped only when a separate scandal made them an electoral liability, signaling that antisemitism alone does not disqualify one from being a public servant,” said Cohen and Dayan.
“The British Labour Party's experience demonstrates the importance of treating antisemitism as an institutional challenge rather than a series of isolated incidents. While American parties cannot simply replicate the British model, they can establish clear standards and enforce them through endorsements, campaign funding, and committee assignments. Without consistent enforcement, condemnation remains a statement, not a true commitment to protect Jews, ” Cohen and Dayan told the Post.

Paris shooting suspect admits targeting Muslims and people of African origin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:08:43 UTC
03:08:43 KST

The shooting left one dead and seven injured. The national anti-terrorism prosecutor's office highlights the premeditated nature of this racist attack.
The suspect in the shooting in Trappes and La Verrière, on the outskirts of Paris, has admitted specifically targeting people he perceived to be Muslim or of African or North African origin, anti-terrorism public prosecutor Olivier Christen announced on Thursday.
Known only as Kévin T., the 39-year-old is accused of killing one man and injuring seven other people during the attack, which was carried out both from a car and on foot on 23 October.
"He admitted having specifically targeted people who are of a Muslim or African, North African type," the prosecutor said at a press conference. The suspect is also said to have explained that he chose Trappes because he regarded it as "a hideout for Islamists".
An attack prepared over a long period
The prosecutor stressed what he described as the "very extensive preparation" of the attack.
During questioning, Kévin T. acknowledged premeditation and said he had fired "in bursts". Investigators established that from September he had bought several items intended to improve the effectiveness of his weapon, a Sten-type submachine gun dating from the Second World War. He had also bought a police armband and handcuffs.
On the day of the attack, the suspect drove between Trappes and La Verrière, shooting at several people. The man killed, Pengo Bossio Wangi, was 26 and originally from the Democratic Republic of Congo. Among the seven injured was an 11-year-old girl whose life is no longer in danger. As of Thursday, three victims remained in hospital, one of them in a life-threatening condition.
A search of the suspect's home in Plaisir, also on the outskirts of Paris, uncovered an arsenal that included magazines, two brass knuckles, a steel bayonet and a silencer. Investigators also found a Quran, a Bible and a copy of Adolf Hitler's "Mein Kampf".
Stickers bearing nationalist slogans were also discovered. Many bore the words "Long live France, RN, proud to be French", referring to the far-right National Rally party, while others carried phrases including "100% French, long live France" and "Support for the security forces". The suspect admitted having designed and ordered them online, while insisting that he was neither a member nor a supporter of any political party.
Despite these admissions, he denied intending to commit a terrorist act and considered his actions "legitimate", according to the prosecutor.
He also denied having intended to kill children, saying he may have misjudged the height of the 11-year-old victim. He nevertheless said he felt "no regret".
The suspect had reported psychological and psychiatric problems. However, according to the prosecutor, a medical examination found no acute psychiatric decompensation or signs of hallucinations or delusions that would justify compulsory hospitalisation.
The National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office has opened a judicial investigation into murder and attempted murder in connection with a terrorist act, with an aggravating circumstance linked to the presumed origin or religion of the victims. Prosecutors have requested that the suspect be placed in pre-trial detention.
Emmanuel Macron points the finger at the far right
Appearing on the YouTube channel HugoDécrypte on Wednesday, President Emmanuel Macron denounced what he called "a racism of atmosphere" and "a disinhibition of violence".
Macron blamed far-right political movements for helping create that climate, citing National Rally and groups close to it.
The RN reacted sharply on Thursday on television channel TF1. Party MP Jean-Philippe Tanguy described the president's comments as "very problematic", accusing him of having allowed "hateful ideologies" to flourish during his time in office.
A national tribute to the victims
A national tribute will be paid to the victims of the attack. The announcement was made on Wednesday 28 October by the government, the day after a request at the National Assembly by the leader of the Green MPs, Cyrielle Chatelain.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu will preside over the ceremony, minister responsible for combating discrimination Aurore Bergé told the Senate.
A date and location have not yet been announced.

Bangladesh nuclear plant gets power generation nod
Bangladesh’s Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant has received the final regulatory clearance, paving the path to commence electricity generation.
Rooppur, the country’s first nuclear power plant, was given the nod to advance to Stage C by the Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA), the Daily Star reported on Thursday.
During this stage, the reactor’s power will be increased to produce steam, boost the turbine, and generate electricity. Capacity will gradually be increased in phases.
“Now Unit 1 will proceed with the power startup to begin the generation process,” BAERA Chairman Mahamudul Hasan was quoted as saying by the news outlet. He added that the authority would determine the startup date.
Rosatom head Alexey Likhachev earlier this month told media that the plant is on track to be connected to the national grid by end of next month.
The Rooppur plant, located 160 kilometers from Dhaka on the banks of the Padma River, was built at a cost of $12.65 billion, with Russian financial and technical support. With two VVER-1200 Russian-designed reactors, it will have a combined capacity of 2,400 megawatts. Moscow is financing $11.9 billion in state loans for the project.
Rosatom, which is providing equipment, nuclear fuel, and engineering assistance, expects to commission the second unit in 2027.
Once fully operational, the plant is expected to deliver 12% of Dhaka’s power demand.
Likhachev recently disclosed that Moscow is in talks with Dhaka to build a new phase of Rooppur’s high-capacity units.
“We are primarily talking about a possible additional phase of large units,” Likhachev said on the sidelines of the Russian Energy Week forum, adding that Dhaka was also exploring the possibility of small-capacity units and a research reactor.

IDF may scale back Hebron presence by weekend after evacuating thousands of Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:08:23 UTC
03:08:23 KST

The IDF may exit or reduce its presence over this coming weekend from the Hebron neighborhood it has occupied since last weekend, The Jerusalem Post has learned.
None of this is certain and the situation is highly dynamic, since to date pre-elections, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rejected the clear recommendation from IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir to leave the area and allow the at least 2,000 evacuated Palestinians to return to their homes.
But there is some increased expectation that Netanyahu may show more flexibility to IDF recommendations now that the election has passed and he feels in a stronger political position than expected.
The IDF occupied the area in response to last Friday morning’s deadly Hamas terrorist attack and noted that the terrorists were connected to a broader Hamas clan in the neighborhood in question, though the IDF never presented concrete evidence of how most of the 2,000 evacuees could be connected to any specific crime.
Already by Sunday-Monday, the IDF was recommending it allow the evacuated Palestinians to return, saying that it had inspected all of the relevant areas, and there was no clear military reason to remain.
Why IDF's evacuation of Hebron is different
The forced evacuations from Hebron appear to be different from other recent incidents.
Although in early 2025, Israel cleared areas of Jenin, Tulkarm, and Nur al-Shams in the West Bank, evacuating close to 40,000 Palestinians, those areas had experienced well-documented mass terror incidents dating back to early 2022.
The IDF carried out multiple temporary evacuations at that time and even sent in the Palestinian Authority to fight large and organized terror groups before undertaking the mass evacuation and destroying several structures in those areas.
In contrast, this time, the IDF provided little information about the offenses of the 2,000 evacuated Palestinians, other than to say that they were familially connected to the Hamas-linked Gaza clan.
While during the 2015-2016 stabbing intifada and in earlier years, Hebron had been one of the most violent and unstable areas – and there have been some terror incidents emanating from Hebron over the past three years of war – generally, it has not been one of the leading problem spots.
In addition, the IDF said it destroyed illegally built structures that could make security operations harder to carry out. However, the military was extremely vague about what those operations were and why entire buildings needed to be destroyed to carry them out.
Pressed about how many of the 2,000 hamula (“clan”) members have records linking them to terror (or at a minimum, to rock throwing), multiple IDF sources did not appear to have any specific information on the topic.
Rather, the operation seemed to be motivated by public statements made by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz about clearing or destroying the neighborhood of the two men involved in the terror incident on Friday – apparently a collective punishment measure.
While Israel has placed closures on terror-emanating areas in the past, it has not carried out mass evacuations and building demolitions to such an extent without a specific connection to those being impacted.
Petition alleges IDF soldiers turned Palestinian homes into military positions
Meanwhile, Adalah petitioned the High Court of Justice on Thursday on behalf of Hebron’s municipality and seven residents, seeking to halt what it described as forced evacuations and demolitions during an IDF operation, and secure the return of residents ordered out of their homes.
The petition asks for an immediate order barring further evacuations and the demolition of homes, businesses and other civilian buildings while the case is considered. It also seeks safe passage for medical teams, emergency vehicles and municipal workers, arguing that sweeping movement restrictions are cutting residents off from essential services.
According to the petition, troops ordered families in the Ein Deir Baha and al-Jalda neighborhoods of western Hebron to leave their homes around 12:30-1 a.m. on the night of October 23-24. Orders were announced over loudspeakers, leaving residents insufficient time to prepare, the petitioners said.
Residents were told they could not return until further notice, without being given a timetable or conditions for their return, the petition alleges. It says some families spent the night outside and some residents were unable to take their vehicles with them.
Municipal figures cited in the petition put the number of families affected by the operation at 780, which could reach much higher than the original 2,000 estimate, up to 4,969 people, which itself was up from 488 families and 3,171 people earlier.
The petition alleges that troops took over some homes and turned them into military positions, while demolishing civilian buildings and requiring traders to remove goods from their businesses at short notice.
It says restrictions also affect residents who remain at home, hindering access to medical treatment and the movement of ambulances and emergency vehicles. According to the municipality’s figures cited in the filing, blocked access routes had prevented rubbish collection and left approximately 1,200 tons of waste accumulating across the city by Wednesday.
Adalah argues that the scale and open-ended nature of the evacuations violate international humanitarian law. Article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention permits temporary evacuation where civilian safety or imperative military reasons require it, and requires evacuees to be returned once hostilities in the area have ended.
The petitioners contend that no specific justification has been provided for evacuations on this scale. They argue that barring residents’ return indefinitely, while damaging or taking over their homes, risks making their displacement lasting.
They also invoke the convention’s prohibition on destroying property unless military operations make it absolutely necessary, arguing that a general reference to security needs cannot justify demolitions across residential neighborhoods.
The petition further alleges collective punishment, citing both the measures imposed on residents and statements by Israeli officials presenting the operation as a means of exacting a price for the shooting. The convention prohibits punishing protected civilians for offenses they did not personally commit.
Adalah said it approached the authorities on Sunday and sent a reminder the following day, but had received no substantive response by the time it filed the petition.
The case names the defense minister, the head of IDF Central Command, the military advocate-general and the attorney-general as respondents. Alongside an urgent hearing, the petitioners seek immediate protection against further evacuations and demolitions, followed by orders lifting the challenged restrictions and ensuring residents’ safe return.
Already on Sunday, the Association for Civil Rights in Israel (ACRI) demanded that displaced residents be allowed to return, movement restrictions be lifted, and demolitions carried out as punishment be halted. It also requested the orders authorizing the measures already taken.
It argued that public statements by ministers indicated a punitive purpose, including Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s description of demolitions as serving as deterrence and as exacting a price for the attack.
“No attack, however grave, gives the military license to punish an entire city,” ACRI executive director Noa Sattath said.
In an initial decision last Friday, Justice Gila Canfy Steinitz directed the state to respond and said she expected it to refrain from changing the existing situation, or demolishing addition buildings, pending a further decision.

Hold your nose: a £1.25bn subsidy for rich Rolls-Royce’s new engine had to happen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:07:27 UTC
03:07:27 KST

It wasn’t a “nothing” budget for engine-maker Rolls-Royce. The company was handed £1.25bn from public coffers to part-fund the development of a next-generation engine for single-aisle commercial planes.
The chancellor buried this giveaway in two short sentences in the stodgy middle of his speech, presumably because it would look too much like a case of corporate welfare just after he had grumbled about the £14bn extra we’ll be paying in debt interest this year.
And it’s not as if Rolls is on its uppers. The pride of Derby is the UK’s most radically improved major company of the past few years. It sits in fifth spot in the FTSE 100 index, sporting a market value of £105bn, and has enough spare cash to spend up to £9bn on share buy-backs this year.
But there had been an air of inevitability about this subsidy ever since the company’s chief executive, Tufan Erginbilgiç, talked earlier this year about how he would “appreciate” financial support from the government in developing the UltraFan engine. Appreciate? What he meant is that other governments would cough up if the UK didn’t.
That, unfortunately, is how life works in the global aerospace business. Subsidies are a down payment on the jobs and factories that can follow. Germany, reeling from the woes of its carmakers, would love to have a bigger slice of the hi-tech UltraFan action (and has a role in the gearboxes anyway). The US aerospace industry is a study in how generous defence contracts subsidise civil operations. Healey couldn’t ignore those facts of aerospace life.
What’s more, one can see how the possible long-term return on the £1.25bn could turn out very well. “The single biggest opportunity in aerospace over the next 50 years is to secure a UK engine position on next generation narrow body programmes,” said the government’s strategy document for advanced manufacturing. Aircraft engines are high-value products. About 80% would be exported, doing wonders for the national balance of payments. Projections of “tens of thousands of highly skilled jobs” eventually are credible.
The big “if” is that Rolls hasn’t yet got a slot on a narrow-body programme. The company exited that market a couple of decades ago; its civil aircraft side currently only supplies engines to the smaller wide-body long-haul market. Rolls needs to get on to either the Airbus or Boeing narrow-body programmes, and success or failure won’t be known until some time around 2030.
Thus the government is only contributing to a joint 10-year £2.5bn research and development programme, including a “demonstrator” engine to show off the gas turbine tech. There will be spillover benefits for defence capability but, ultimately, UltraFan needs to be on a civil project. It is a big bet – and Rolls, even if it wins, will need a corporate partner at a later stage.
The point, though, is that the UK government had to get behind the UK runner in this race. One trusts the guarantees on UK jobs and investment, beyond the 3,300 roles supported initially, will be written in triplicate in the final agreement. That must be a fundamental condition of support on this scale.
But this is an occasion to hold your nose. Rolls is plainly not a corporate pauper but, yes, it is justifiable to shove £1.25bn its way. Andy Burnham’s “reindustrialisation” talk would otherwise ring very hollow.

Third-quarter U.S. GDP increases a better-than-expected 3.4% as September inflation accelerates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:06:31 UTC
03:06:31 KST

The pace of price increases stepped up in September, keeping inflation well above the Federal Reserve's target, while the economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, according to Commerce Department reports Thursday.
The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.5% for the month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.6%. The monthly increase was the largest since March but in line with the Dow Jones consensus, while the annual rate was 0.1 percentage point below.
Excluding food and energy, the core PCE posted respective readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, in line with the consensus. While the Fed follows both measures closely, officials generally see the core reading as more indicative of longer-term inflation trends.
While inflation continued to run ahead of the Fed's 2% target, the Commerce Department also reported that gross domestic product was strong in the third quarter.
GDP increased at a seasonally adjusted annualized pace of 3.4%, better than the 3.1% estimate and well ahead of the 2.2% in the second quarter.
Also, in September consumer spending proved resilient, climbing 0.5%, a bit below the forecast for a 0.6% gain, while personal income rose 0.2%, compared with the estimate for 0.3%.
The reports come the day after the Fed voted to hold its benchmark interest rate in a range between 3.75%-4%. Despite elevated inflation readings, central bank officials insist they can afford to evaluate incoming data before deciding on their next move.
"The period right in front of us is information rich. There is a lot that's happening in the world. My colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it," Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday.
However, the data deluge from Thursday shows the Fed could have more work to do.
A Labor Department report also released Thursday showed that layoffs remain low. Initial jobless claims edged lower to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 24, below the estimate for 200,000 and near levels last seen in the late 1960s.
Stock market futures were negative following the releases while Treasury yields also fell.
"Net, net, economic growth is powering ahead despite the uncertainty of geopolitical risks and the damage posed to many sectors of the economy by higher energy costs," said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at Fwdbonds. "The economy was thought to have been a lost cause during much of the current Administration's time in office, but real GDP has bounced back above a 3 percent run rate in Q3 2026 for the first time in a year."
Economic growth has been driven by higher levels of investment from the artificial intelligence build-out, as well as high levels of consumer and government spending.
Consumer spending rose 3.8% in the third quarter, the same pace as the prior period. Gross private domestic investment soared 19.4%, driven by a 20.9% surge in equipment spending and an 8.4% jump on intellectual property products.
Real sales to private domestic purchasers, a proxy that Fed officials use for underlying demand, rose 4.9%, compared with a 4.6% increase in the second quarter.
There was some good inflation news for the period: On a quarterly basis, PCE prices rose 2.1% on the headline number and 2.5% for core, down respectively from 5% and 3.3% in the second quarter.
September's price increases were driven largely by a surge in energy costs that economists fear could be spreading to other parts of the economy. Gasoline and other energy goods saw a 9.2% rise for the month while energy goods and services broadly jumped 5.4%.
At the same time, services prices excluding energy and housing rose 0.4%, and housing costs increased 0.3%.

Russian publisher Eksmo alters Joe Hill’s ‘King Sorrow,’ removing a reference to Putin and replacing Russia’s invasion of Ukraine with ‘war in Europe’

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:06:03 UTC
03:06:03 KST

Russian publisher Eksmo alters Joe Hill’s ‘King Sorrow,’ removing a reference to Putin and replacing Russia’s invasion of Ukraine with ‘war in Europe’
Several passages in the Russian translation of American author Joe Hill’s novel “King Sorrow” were rewritten to avoid censorship problems, changing the author’s meaning. Nikolai Karayev, who runs the speculative fiction Telegram channel Zvezdnye Mayaki Kapitana Norta, drew attention to the changes by sharing several passages from the original alongside their Russian translations.
Hill, Stephen King’s son, writes fantasy and horror. “King Sorrow” is about students who summon a dragon from another world. The Russian edition, translated by Dmitry Starkov, was published in August 2026 by Fanzon, part of the Eksmo publishing group.
Here are a few examples of changes in the Russian translation:
- In one passage in the original, a character says he has “reliable information that the Russians are farming them. They grow trolls like potatoes in the permafrost of Siberia.” Eksmo’s version reads: “I have reliable information that the Ukrainians are breeding trolls. Raising trolls like little pigs.”
- In another passage, the characters watch footage of the war in Ukraine as the novel describes a strike on a maternity ward in Mariupol. In the translation, Mariupol became Donetsk: “On March 9, something like that hit one of Donetsk’s maternity hospitals. A deafening explosion, a column of flame… One of the expectant mothers was killed in the explosion, and her baby was stillborn.”
- A reference to “Russian oligarchs who vacationed in Italy with Vladimir Putin” became simply “Russian oligarchs who vacationed in Italy.”
- Instead of “Russia invaded Ukraine,” the translation says “that night war broke out in Europe.”
After media coverage of the changes, Eksmo CEO Yevgeny Kapyev promised to “look into the situation thoroughly” and criticized Hill, writing:
So I’m wondering, this thing in Western popular culture that started with James Bond, where the bad guys are Russians or Asians, is it ever going to end? Russia could be portrayed as a wonderful country everywhere… at least in the future… Self-fulfilling prophecies are a thing, after all…
And I’m asking authors not to put “Easter eggs” about the current fraught political and military situation into their books… At this rate, they’ll be putting them in recipes soon. There are tons of other ways to get your point across…
In the spring, Kapyev was detained along with other senior Eksmo executives in the “publishers’ case.” The case concerned allegations by law enforcement authorities that Popcorn Books, another Eksmo-owned publisher, had engaged in the “distribution of LGBT literature.”

Sara won a prized place to study medicine in Glasgow. Why is the Home Office blocking her?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:02:31 UTC
03:02:31 KST

For the last decade, Sara (not her real name), 25, has dreamed of becoming a doctor. She secured a highly sought after place to study medicine at Kabul University in February 2021, but in a matter of months the Taliban returned to power and imposed a ban on women studying for degrees. Sara had been searching for other options. Then the University of Glasgow offered her a lifeline.
Her visa application was made just days before the Home Office introduced a visa brake in March 2026 for students from Afghanistan, Sudan, Myanmar and Cameroon. Her teachers consider her to be an exceptionally able and dedicated student, she had secured funding and the university was waiting to welcome her on to a gateway course at its school of medicine, dentistry and nursing – a route to a full degree course to become a doctor. So why have the UK’s home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, and her officials gone to such extraordinary lengths to bar her?
Sara says her life has been “challenge after challenge”. She survived a suicide bomb attack on her school, swerved her father’s attempts to force her into early marriage, as well as the omnipresent Taliban who patrol Kabul’s streets. Then she made a nail-biting escape from her country and avoided capture by police in Pakistan who were searching for her. But it is the UK’s Home Office, which champions women’s rights, that has inflicted the deadliest blow.
Sara grew up in a poor household in Kabul in the period before the Taliban regained power. Against the wishes of her violent father, who wanted to see her follow the traditional path of teenage marriage and a life of enforced domesticity in service to a husband, she fought to continue her education, encouraged to aim high by inspirational female teachers at her single-sex school.
“The community I come from is a particularly traditional one,” she says. “Even among my relatives I couldn’t find any girl who has been educated. While boys were free, my mum, who has always supported me, was told by relatives that rather than pursuing an education I needed to go somewhere where I could be taught to cook. After a relative’s daughter got married I was told I was next in line.”
But at school, she saw that life could be different. “I was about seven years old when one of my teachers first encouraged us girls,” she says. “Later, my physics teacher was also very supportive. She said that we would face challenges but should never give up in pursuing our dreams.”
Sara says that she is still in contact with some of the girls she was at school with, who were similarly inspired by their female teachers. Some of them are now flying high in other countries, having been granted full university scholarships.
But there were others whose ambitions were thwarted. “I can still see the face of one 15-year-old girl who was like a supportive older sister to me at school. She wanted to continue her education but she was full of tears when she came to school one day and told us her family was forcing her to leave school and get married.”
When Sara was 15, a much-loved uncle died after his heart disease was misdiagnosed. At that moment, she vowed to become a doctor. “My uncle was such a kind soul. He always supported me when my father was being harsh. ‘It’s OK. Whatever your father is doing, I’m with you,’ he used to say to me.”
Sara always put everything into her studies at school, getting marks close to 100% in her tests and exams. Along with her love of science, she speaks multiple languages. She is Hazara and along with Hazaragi speaks Dari, Pashto, Urdu, English, as well as some Spanish and Arabic.
Somehow, despite her father’s disapproval, she continued her studies and attended an educational centre to prepare for Afghanistan’s university entrance exam, the Kankor, so she could secure a place at Kabul University to begin her medical studies. In October 2020, it was targeted by a Taliban suicide bomb attack. She was feeling unwell that day so did not go to school. Many of her friends were killed.
Against the odds, in February 2021, she passed her exam, secured her place at the Kabul University’s medical school, and was overjoyed – until she and other women at the university had their right to study brutally terminated when the Taliban came to power in August 2021.
Devastated, but undeterred from pursuing her dream, she began volunteering at medical clinics in Kabul, taken there and back by clinical staff who supported her, ducking down and hiding in the car when they approached Taliban checkpoints. When Taliban members came to the clinic for treatment, she was bundled into the staff room to hide until they had left. She continued her medical studies at home, begging friends who were studying to send her PDFs of medical textbooks because she couldn’t afford to buy them. She devoured the medical bible Gray’s Anatomy.
Despite the Taliban obstacle, she was determined to keep studying any way she could. “I was at the clinic one day in 2023. I wasn’t allowed to perform medical procedures on patients but wanted to learn as much as I could. I asked a friend to teach me how to do sutures and then practised the technique on a banana. The head surgeon came in and asked what we were doing, saw how enthusiastic I was and allowed me to observe an operation.”
By 2024, life at home with her father was becoming increasingly violent and dangerous and the pressure on Sara to marry was increasing. “The situation was deteriorating so much that we had to find a way to get out,” she says.
Sara hoped she could pursue her medical studies in Pakistan, so before she left Afghanistan she went to the medical school in Kabul to try to get her course records to prove that she had started a medical degree. “Taliban guards wouldn’t let me through the front gate and were very abusive to me so I couldn’t get them,” she says.
Sara was later able to get a reference from one of her lecturers at the university which described her as a “highly dedicated and capable student.”
“She demonstrated strong academic performance, critical thinking and a deep passion for medicine. She is a resilient, compassionate and motivated individual,” the lecturer said.
Sara, her mother, her siblings and other relatives had to leave Afghanistan in a hurry when things reached crisis point with her father. “I could only pack a few clothes,” she says. “But I took my white medical coat with me, hoping that even if I was unable to continue my medical studies in Afghanistan, I would be able to qualify to be a doctor somewhere else.”
The family managed to get together the money to escape to Pakistan by plane. Their cover story was that Sara’s mother needed urgent medical treatment. Their male escort was Sara’s brother-in-law. At Kabul Airport, they were stopped by the Taliban and taken into a room for questioning.
“We arrived at the airport at 12.30pm for a 2pm flight. We were questioned in that room until 1.50pm. My hands were shaking so much. I didn’t think they would let us go. They wanted to know why my father was not accompanying us to Pakistan. When they finally released us at 1.50pm, we all had to run to make it on to the plane before it took off. When we sat on the plane my mum said to us; ‘Our life is full of challenges. If we overcome one, another one comes.’”
Life in Pakistan was not much better. The family overstayed their visa because they had nowhere else to run to and Sara was unable to continue her medical studies. “Sometimes the police came to look for us at the place where we were staying. I hid in the kitchen cupboard when they knocked on our door so they wouldn’t find me,” she says.
A London-based English teacher, Jane Conway, became another lifeline. She taught English to refugee students and became involved in a group called Save Afghan Women. After the Taliban regained power, Conway helped with online English classes for women no longer able to physically study in Afghanistan, and got to know Sara and other members of her family who she supported as they continued their higher education.
It was Conway who found that the University of Glasgow had a gateway course for female students from Afghanistan who wanted to pursue a degree in medicine, and helped her apply. “It was teacher Jane who found this option for me,” says Sara.
She applied for the scheme and was accepted after finding, with Conway’s help, sources of funding to support her with bursaries to cover fees and living expenses. Hope was restored. All she needed now was for the Home Office to grant her a visa to take up the course in Glasgow. She thought that after everything she had been through this would be the easy bit. But three rejections citing contradictory reasons followed.
She was told in one rejection that the Home Office was satisfied she had appropriate funds in place to support her study in the UK although they deemed her not to be a genuine student. She cried and cried at that accusation, after all the years of doing everything possible to pursue her medical studies. “I would like to ask the home secretary what is her definition of a ‘genuine student?’ I wish I had the opportunity to visit her in person and ask her this question face to face, eye to eye.”
Then, in another refusal, they said she didn’t have suitable funds in place, but accepted she was a genuine student.
Sara underwent a phone interview with a Home Office official. “The interview was very tough. It lasted about an hour and a half and the man asked me lots of questions about my mother, my father, my background. After the interview he told me to keep checking my email and I was hopeful I was going to be granted a visa.”
But once again her hopes were dashed. She is now pursuing a degree in accounting and finance in another country, undisclosed for safety reasons, because it is more affordable than a medical course. “I don’t have any other option,” she says.
In London, Conway despairs about the inconsistent decision making by the Home Office. “Sara is a good and wonderful person who wants to do good in the world,” she says. “It would seem that the Home Office is so obsessive in its target seeking that it has become blinded to exceptional cases like Sara’s, denying the UK of the benefits that such motivated and talented people could bring.
“In spite of all the obstacles Sara encountered pursuing her dream to become a doctor, she never gave up. Then, when that wonderful new door of opportunity was opened up to her by the University of Glasgow, instead of walking through it with hope and excitement, it is our British Home Office that unequivocally slams the door shut in her path. I feel a deep shame that the government is cutting off a life-changing opportunity for a truly exceptional person, who has already been persecuted in her own country simply for being a woman.”
On 28 September, Mahmood delighted the audience at the Labour party conference by announcing she was reactivating a refugee resettlement route, albeit a small one, highlighting Afghan women and girls as one of the groups who would benefit. It later emerged that there will be significant restrictions to the scheme for some eligible nationalities (it is only open to Palestinian refugees who have already escaped Gaza and are registered as refugees with the UN, for instance), while the much larger refugee family reunion scheme remains suspended after more than a year.
Sara refuses to give up on her dream of qualifying to become a doctor. She tries to keep up with the latest scientific developments in medicine.
“In Afghanistan, so many people don’t have arms or legs because of all the fighting,” she says. “If I can qualify as a doctor I would like to help people in my country. My ambition is to become a cardiac surgeon because as far as I know there are no female cardiac surgeons in Afghanistan and I would like to be the first.” If she achieves this, she says, “my goal is to use my experiences to inspire other Afghan girls to pursue education and overcome the obstacles in their lives”.
If she can’t ever return to her country, she wants to work with Doctors Without Borders. “They work with people in difficult-to-reach places. I believe that people in those places deserve to have a good doctor to treat them. From my perspective, doctors are superheroes. They are the best for people. Whatever happens, I will always keep my white coat with me. It is the history of my struggle.”

More prisoners recalled to jail than released in England and Wales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:00:33 UTC
03:00:33 KST

More people were recalled to jails in England and Wales in the first half of this year than were released, despite government efforts to reduce the prison population, according to figures released on Thursday.
Ministry of Justice (MoJ) data shows that 12,338 people were recalled to custody between the beginning of April and the end of June, while 12,278 people were released. It continues a trend set between January and March, when 13,193 people were returned to prison and 12,977 released.
A total of 52,716 prisoners were put back behind bars in the year to June after breaching the terms of their licence – 27% up on the previous 12-month total.
The high recall rate is a key contributor to the prison capacity crisis and helped to prompt early release schemes earlier this month.
The MoJ figures also show 79,274 inmates were freed early from prison between September 2024 and June 2026 under emergency measures brought in by the government to try to tackle the overcrowding crisis.
The move, known as the SDS40 early release scheme, cut the proportion of sentences some prisoners must serve in England and Wales from 50% to 40%. It is one of several policy changes that are likely to have contributed to the rise in recalls, the MoJ said.
The emergency measures were replaced with a permanent scheme for early releases from 1 October under the Sentencing Act 2026.
The Howard League for Penal Reform said the “alarmingly high rate of recalls is making a terrible problem even worse”, as it called on the government to find a “lasting solution” to the overcrowding crisis.
Rob Preece, the head of communications at the Howard League, said: “The prison system is under enormous pressure, with chronic overcrowding, staff shortages and awful conditions that make it close to impossible to rehabilitate people effectively. Imposing ever longer sentences has led us to this crisis, but the alarmingly high rate of recalls is making a terrible problem even worse.”
Enver Solomon, the chief executive of the social justice charity Nacro, said the number of recalls must be urgently addressed to avoid prison spaces being filled up again by people sent back to jail.
“A significant proportion of those released immediately go back to chaotic lives involving addiction, mental health problems and homelessness. Without adequate support and stable accommodation in place as soon as they step outside the gate, it is very difficult to break the revolving cycle of going back into prison too many are caught up in,” he said.
The MoJ said it was “vital those who break the rules can be hauled back to prison”. The department said the rise in recalls amid SDS40 releases was also likely to have been influenced by policy changes that result in most offenders being taken back into custody for 56 days before being released again – known as a fixed-term recall – instead of being held until the end of their sentence.
Incidents of self-harm and violence have remained high as pressure on the prison system has grown. Safety in custody statistics showed that 360 people in prison died in the 12 months to the end of September 2026, including 66 people who died in circumstances recorded as “self-inflicted”.
Prisons recorded 68,231 incidents of self-harm in the 12 months to the end of June 2026, at a rate of one every eight minutes. Self-harm incidents fell by 12% in men’s prisons and fell by 3.8% in women’s prisons.
A separate dataset showed that the number of serious offenders on probation who were charged with a serious further offence had increased for the third successive year, to a record number.
Of 281 serious offenders charged, 119 were registered sexual offenders, 128 were murderers, and four were terrorists or posed a terror risk, according to figures on multi-agency public protection arrangements.

Why jet lag throws even foraging seabirds off course
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:00:27 UTC
03:00:27 KST

Seabirds returning from foraging trips can be thrown hundreds of miles off course by a form of jet lag that arises when their body clocks get out of sync with local time, researchers say.
Tracking data from Manx shearwaters on the west coast of the UK revealed that when the birds returned home to their colonies after trips over the Atlantic, their rapid eastward flights disrupted their sense of time and navigation.
The impact was limited on adult shearwaters because the birds were able to correct their bearings in flight. At most, the birds veered off course by about 15 degrees. After correcting their course, this added only an estimated 3 miles to a 600-mile journey.
But less experienced birds were likely to have a tougher time, the study found, with first-time foragers at risk of flying off course by hundreds of miles.
Most studies on birds’ biological clocks have been conducted under laboratory conditions but Dr Patrick Lewin, a behavioural and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford, set out to investigate wild birds with the help of his colleagues.
Their analysis of 20 years of GPS tracking data revealed a clear effect when the Manx shearwaters flew east across lines of longitude as they returned home, leading their clocks to run up to an hour or so behind local time. “The bird’s internal clock can be subject to a jet lag phenomenon, manifesting as birds flying off course,” Lewin said.
Like many animals, shearwaters use the sun as a compass. Because the sun moves across the sky as the Earth rotates, reading its position correctly relies on the birds adjusting their heading relative to the sun, using their body clock to keep track of the time of day. Sunset and sunrise keep the bird’s body clock in sync, helping them adjust to changes in local time.
Writing in Science, Lewin said the mismatch between local time and the birds’ internal clocks could make them drift off course when the sun lay farther around the sky than expected. Surprisingly, the errors remained when birds followed the coastline, where landmarks could have guided them, further supporting the idea that the sun plays a central role in anchoring their sense of direction.
“For adult shearwaters, this lag has very limited impact on their overall journey, with errors adding a calculated 5km to a 1,000km journey,” Lewin said. “However, for first-time migrant birds, such orientation shifts due to sun compass errors could result in deviations of hundreds of kilometres as they lack a map sense to help reorient them when they lose their way.”
Prof Richard Holland of Bangor University, who was not involved in the study, said it was a significant finding: “It seems to confirm in wild animals what more controlled experimental studies have shown: reliance on the sun compass for animals that move during the day, even when it is not accurate.”
Manx shearwaters spend most of their lives far out at sea. They cover enormous distances but return each year to islands off the west coast of the UK to breed in burrows.
“It’s not clear from the study what the consequences of these errors are, since the birds return to their colony and the errors are small,” Holland said. “Nonetheless, it highlights the importance of understanding the role of biological rhythms across multiple contexts in animal behaviour, as more and more we are starting to realise just how important these are for numerous biological functions.”

People in interracial relationships tend to be more politically liberal, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:00:02 UTC
03:00:02 KST

An analysis of data from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health found that people with a romantic partner of a different race had 37% greater odds of holding more liberal political views than people with a same-race partner. However, the size of this difference varied depending on people’s race, sex, and marital status. The paper was published in The Journal of Race, Ethnicity, and Politics.
Romantic relationships and political beliefs may seem like separate aspects of life, but research suggests that they are closely connected. In the United States, people with conservative political views tend to place greater importance on traditional family structures and are more likely to prefer romantic partners of the same race. Those with liberal views, on the other hand, tend to be generally more accepting of interracial relationships.
Over the past several decades, interracial relationships have become increasingly common, reflecting broader changes in American society and attitudes toward racial diversity. Since the U.S. Supreme Court struck down laws prohibiting interracial marriage in 1967, public acceptance of such relationships has increased substantially. Recent estimates suggest that roughly one in five newlyweds and cohabiting adults in the United States has a partner from a different racial or ethnic background. However, relatively little is known about the political beliefs of people who are actually involved in such relationships.
One possibility is that people in interracial relationships are more politically liberal because they are generally more open to relationships across racial boundaries and may have greater awareness of racial discrimination. At the same time, political preferences differ considerably according to race, ethnicity, sex, and marital status, making the relationship between romantic partner choice and political ideology more complex than it might initially appear.
Study author Byron Miller and colleagues wanted to compare the political beliefs of people in interracial relationships with those of people in same-race relationships. They expected people in interracial relationships to be more liberal on average, but they also hypothesized that this association would depend on a person’s race, sex, and marital status.
They analyzed data from wave 4 of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Add Health). This is a large-scale, longitudinal study in the United States that began in 1994–1995 with adolescents in grades 7–12 attending 80 high schools and 52 middle schools. Since then, researchers have followed participants into adulthood, collecting data on their physical and mental health, social relationships, behaviors, and socioeconomic circumstances. At the time of wave 4, in 2008, participants were approximately 24 to 32 years old.
The analysis included 12,603 participants. Their political beliefs were measured with a single question: “In terms of politics, do you consider yourself very conservative, conservative, middle-of-the-road, liberal, or very liberal?” The researchers classified participants as being in an interracial relationship if their current or most recent romantic partner’s race differed from their own, and they also took into account participants’ race/ethnicity (white, Black, Hispanic, or Asian), sex, marital status, age, and education.
About 15% of participants were in interracial relationships. People in interracial relationships were much less likely to be white than those in same-race relationships (34% versus 74%), and more likely to be Hispanic or Asian.
After accounting for demographic characteristics, people in interracial relationships had 37% greater odds of holding more liberal views than those in same-race relationships. But this association differed across groups. It was weaker among Asian and Hispanic participants than among white participants, and weaker among married participants than among those who were unmarried, while it was stronger among women than among men.
When the researchers looked at combinations of these factors, they found that among married participants, interracial relationships were more strongly linked to liberal views for Black and Asian adults than for white adults. Combinations of race and sex showed no statistically significant differences. The authors suggest that some Asian and Hispanic adults with conservative views may prefer partners from the white majority, while the pattern among married Black and Asian adults may reflect people choosing partners who share their political views.
“Interracial relationships are a catalyst for major changes in racial/ethnic relations and diversity in the United States, especially as children from these romantic relationships contribute to the biracial baby boom,” the study authors wrote. “[A]s this demographic continues to grow more prevalent as the United States becomes more racially/ethnically diverse, the political beliefs of biracial families are likely to have an increasingly greater influence on the policies, processes, and representatives that shape racial and ethnic politics.”
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the political views of people in interracial relationships. However, the design of this study does not allow any causal inferences to be derived from the results. Because of this, it remains unknown whether liberal individuals are more likely to start a relationship with a person of a different race, whether a relationship with a person of a different race makes an individual more liberal, or whether other factors influence both political attitudes and relationship choices.
The data were also collected in 2008, before Donald Trump’s presidency, which some researchers argue has reshaped the political views of men and women, so the findings may not reflect current patterns. Political views were measured with a single question, and the study did not examine specific racial pairings within couples, such as Asian-white or Black-Hispanic partnerships.
The paper, “Biracial at the Ballot Box: Exploring the Association Between Interracial Relationships and Political Beliefs,” was authored by Byron Miller, Madelyn Chandler, and Nico Allen.

One Nation might not win Victoria, but NSW is where the real fight is
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

analysis
Labor battles against One Nation insurgence while feeling inflation pain
New South Wales Premier Chris Minns delivered an attention-grabbing prediction this week.
"By any poll, by any measure, [One Nation leader] Mike Newman will either be the premier or the opposition leader after March 13," Minns said on Sydney radio.
While the immediate focus is on One Nation's performance at the Victorian election in late November, next year's NSW contest will be a more important test for the insurgent party.
On present indications, the best One Nation could do in Victoria would be to prop up a Coalition minority government, although there seems a fair prospect Opposition Leader Jess Wilson could get to a majority. There's no chance of One Nation Victorian leader Warren Pickering becoming opposition leader.
A good performance in Victoria obviously would be a fillip for One Nation, but the NSW election will be the big pointer for the future.
The latest Resolve Political Monitor NSW poll, published in September, has Labor on 29 per cent, One Nation 25 per cent and the Coalition 24 per cent.
The Minns government, although in minority, should be in a strong position to win a second term. A pragmatist from Labor's right, and a leader with a relatable style, Minns has distanced himself from the Albanese government, which is still bogged in the problems from its controversial budget, with a now deeply unpopular prime minister.
High inflation adds to the problem
The NSW opposition is weak. On current assessments, the Liberals are considered likely to lose metropolitan seats to Labor. The Nationals could face a near wipe-out, with One Nation well placed to grab regional seats.
Newman, formerly a trade bureaucrat who spent many years working in Japan, is a more credible figure than Pickering.
If One Nation did become the official opposition in NSW, the most populous state, that would be a serious shock to, and realignment of, the political system in this country.
It would have sweeping implications federally, notably diminishing both the Liberals and Nationals. It would surely shake the leadership of Angus Taylor, who is from NSW.
One question, as NSW moves towards its election, is whether voters, who usually distinguish between state and federal issues, might, if the Albanese government is still in the doldrums, use the opportunity to give the feds a kick over the cost of living.
This week's high inflation figures — with the headline figure at 4.3 per cent in the year to September (up from 4 per cent in the year to August) and the underlying rate at 3.7 per cent — have homebuyers bracing, given the high market expectations of another interest rate rise on Tuesday. That would be the fifth rise this year.
The government is feeling ever more sharply the blow back from a disgruntled electorate to which it can't afford to give relief.
While it continues to reject the argument that its own spending has contributed significantly to the high inflation, it is also responding to that argument. Treasurer Jim Chalmers this week was at pains to emphasise the mid-year budget update due in December would contain a savings package.
But both he and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese refused to commit to these amounting to net savings.
"We'll continue to have those discussions … in the cabinet, in the ERC (Expenditure Review Committee). That's what we do," Albanese said.
Loading
Government still ahead on economic management
Reserve Bank officials, who have been out and about in recent days including at Senate estimates hearings, have been walking a delicate line.
They are trying to get across the message that spending needs to be contained, while keeping within their own lane, which requires they are not seen to be telling the government how it should act.
Of course, government spending (which also includes state spending) is not entirely responsible for the inflationary problem. Although there was an issue before the Middle East conflict, the war is a major factor in accelerating inflation.
The biggest increase in Wednesday's inflation figures was in the cost of fuel. More generally, a surge in private sector investment from the AI boom, combined with supply constraints, adds to inflation.
But spending is part of the problem. And for the government, it is the present actual and political pinch point.
In the latest Essential poll, released this week, when people were asked (from a list) what was most responsible for the rising cost of living, 32 per cent said government spending, while 24 per cent opted for global events, and 19 per cent for supermarket price gouging.
A frustrated Chalmers said early this week, in a podcast with Nine: "So for people who think we should cut much harder, they should nominate, I think, those areas that should be cut more substantially. But we have been finding savings, many more savings than our predecessors, and that's because we take the hard yards of budget sustainability seriously."
Meanwhile, responding to calls of "What would the Coalition do?", the opposition this week listed $31 billion worth of cuts and other savings, focused on the climate bureaucracy, "corporate welfare", the housing bureaucracy, and changes to the tobacco excise. It said these cuts would more than fund its promise to index income tax brackets.
The Essential poll showed the disquiet among voters continues to grow. More than six in 10 voters (61 per cent) said they thought the country was on the wrong track, compared with 54 per cent in January and 46 per cent in October 2025.
Despite this unease, the government was still ahead on economic management, with 32 per cent of voters selecting Labor when asked which party they would trust to "ensure the economy works in the interests of everyday Australians". But One Nation followed, on 29 per cent, with the Coalition, which sees the economy as its favoured ground, on just 18 per cent.
Albanese won't be on hand when the Reserve Bank delivers its decision on rates on Tuesday. He'll be at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua and Barbuda. It had been thought the PM might skip it, given how many international meetings he has to attend during summit season. But King Charles made it clear he hoped to see him there.
On Thursday, Albanese was asked if he could give people "a sense of when their lives are going to get easier and not harder".
"These challenges won't be solved overnight," he said. It was a grim message.
Michelle Grattan is a professorial fellow at the University of Canberra and chief political correspondent at The Conversation, where this article first appeared.
