Labor warns against 'overcorrection' on student visas as universities face $2b revenue hit
In short:
Labor has acknowledged fears that its tougher student visa rules are putting off genuine applicants and hurting Australia's universities.
The federal government says it will make the system easier to navigate without weakening its crackdown on student migration.
What's next?
Universities will be consulted on revised financial requirements and changes to how student visa applications are assessed.
Labor will recalibrate its international student crackdown with an overhaul of visa requirements to ensure the tough rules do not deter quality applicants from Australia.
The federal government will review financial requirements for international students from South Asia amid concerns that high refusal rates are dissuading genuine applicants and damaging Australia's education sector.
Visa rejections have soared in the two years since a ministerial direction was introduced to strengthen assessments of whether education is the primary purpose behind a student's application.
Assistant Minister for International Education Julian Hill will use a speech in Sydney today to defend Labor's reforms to the sector as necessary for restoring integrity but will warn against an "overcorrection".
New international student commencements at public universities are projected to fall about 18 per cent this year, wiping about $2 billion from revenues over three years.
Mr Hill will say tighter visa rules are only partly responsible for those losses, with competition from other countries and cost-of-living pressures among the other factors.
But he will acknowledge Labor's crackdown is having unintended consequences, with high refusal rates discouraging the very students Australia wants to attract.
"They are terrified of a visa refusal that hurts their chances of studying elsewhere," Mr Hill will say.
New financial guidance for students
Home affairs and education officials are developing new financial standards for South Asia and a replacement for Ministerial Direction 106, with universities and education agents to be consulted in November.
The direction was introduced in 2024 to help immigration officials assess whether student visa applicants genuinely intended to study in Australia, including scrutinise their financial circumstances.
Student visa rejections subsequently soared, with more than 24.2 per cent of applicants knocked back last financial year.
More than 51 per cent of all student visa applications from Nepal were rejected over that period, while than 40 per cent of Indian applicants were refused.
The changes now under consideration are designed to provide greater certainty for prospective students about their chances of securing a visa.
Mr Hill will flag the possibility of raising financial thresholds, arguing clearer requirements could improve visa approval rates even if fewer prospective students qualify.
"Even if this means raising the financial standards and a smaller pool of prospective students, I want grant rates to improve and greater certainty for everyone," he will say.
Labor does not want to 'tank' universities
The government is also considering a New Zealand-style system allowing students to deposit funds covering their tuition and living expenses to demonstrate their financial capacity, although Mr Hill will caution this would be a longer-term reform.
He will insist Labor has no intention of abandoning its efforts to rein in student migration, arguing the changes are necessary to protect the integrity of the system.
Mr Hill will say the government's intention is not to "tank" the international education sector as other nations, such as Canada, have done.
International education is Australia's fifth-largest export sector and supports about 250,000 jobs.
But Mr Hill will take aim at private education providers he says "harvest" profits, while public institutions reinvest surpluses into teaching, research and facilities.
"In a sector where overall customer numbers onshore have to be limited, then the highest value for Australia — as a nation and for taxpayers — comes from students at public institutions, studying with diverse cohorts of young Australians and international peers," he will say.

====================================================================================================

Economist delivers 'worst-case scenario' on interest rates as inflation fails to cool
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Up to three interest rate hikes and a recession on the cards as inflation woes persist
Australia has a dirty little secret.
Despite four Reserve Bank interest rate hikes, supposed fiscal restraint, and a recent small improvement in productivity, inflation is rising.
At face value, it makes no sense. Millions of households continue to struggle to make ends meet.
Dig a little deeper, though, and the logic of why the country continues to struggle with inflation is painfully simple.
There's simply too much money chasing too few goods and services.
There appears to be only one solution: Lower demand until the economy breaks.
While there were some whisperings that Australia could move into recession, now the case is growing with a second leading economist today adding his voice to concerns the worst could still be ahead. More about that later.
Moving pieces of economic puzzle
To understand Australia's inflation problem, look no further than the Reserve Bank's commentary.
Following its most recent decision to raise the cash rate, the RBA's statement began by saying inflation was already too high.
It went on to say "… and some of the upside risks flagged in August are materialising".
"The conflict in the Middle East has broadened, and global energy prices are now much higher than had been assumed in the August forecasts," it wrote.
"AI-related demand is driving rapid growth in global prices for technology-related goods.
"And there remains pressure on domestic capacity."
Put simply, the economy is struggling to supply the goods and services to meet current demand, and higher energy prices are adding to the cost-of-living pain.
The solution then is to boost the nation's ability to meet demand.
Failing that, demand needs to come down.
Inflation slipping away from us
Better news on the supply front came in the most recent national accounts, where GDP per hour worked (one measure of productivity) moved out of negative territory, albeit to zero.
But over the year, it sits at -0.2 per cent.
Lacklustre productivity means the only near-term option is for demand to fall.
Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers said on Wednesday the government was doing its bit.
"We've been able to manage the budget in a much more responsible way than it was being managed by our predecessors … we accept our part in the fight against inflation," he said.
And while private (or business) investment did not contribute to GDP in the June quarter, it was driven by household consumption (+0.2 percentage points).
It has put a target on the back of households as the ones to blame for the "excess" demand.
Iran war making inflation sticky
And this is the critical point. The Iran war is squeezing oil supplies and forcing fuel prices higher.
The Reserve Bank says its liaison program shows businesses are passing higher production costs on to customers.
Worse still, as RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser said this week, is that businesses don't really see an end in sight to elevated costs.
"There's just some sign that some companies might be thinking, 'You know what? Maybe prices aren't going all the way back. And if they're not, we're going to have to take that into account with the pricing decisions.'"
This paves the way for his "nightmare" central banker scenario of unanchored inflation expectations.
Sledgehammer to demand
One way to reverse this vicious cycle is to ensure consumers don't have money in their pockets to spend, or at least not as much.
Hence, interest rate rises take money out of consumers' pockets.
So, rather than supply not meeting demand, demand can't meet supply.
Economic theory tells you prices then stop rising and actually fall.
Why? Because business owners are forced to lower prices to bring customers back into their stores.
To be fair, the Reserve Bank has tried to set this path in motion but its "cautious" approach has proved too cautious.
But if households spend so little that the corner store doesn't replace a leaving staff member, the person who would otherwise have landed that job buys fewer items and saves more … and so on.
This environment could push the unemployment rate beyond 5 per cent, former NAB chief economist Alan Oster says.
But interest rates need to rise higher for this to occur.
"My worst-case scenario would be two or three further rate rises, which I think would clearly cause you recession,"
Mr Oster said.
"And I think you're probably going to struggle anyway.
"Certainly, I'd expect, I'll wait until they've actually done it before I review my forecast, but I would expect to see lower growth and higher levels of unemployment and probably unemployment with the five in front of it," he said.
HSBC chief economist Paul Bloxham forecasts the damage to demand this year and next will see the unemployment rate hit 5.1 per cent.
He also has updated his economic growth forecasts and now sees the chances of an Australian recession in 2027 as a coin toss.
"We see a recession as a 50:50 chance," he said.
So will rates keep rising?
Betashares chief economist David Bassanese does not think the RBA will need to hike interest rates beyond November, but concedes Australia would likely enter a recession if it did.
"All up, my base case is that RBA will raise rates next week but then leave rates on hold at the last meeting of the year in December, providing households at least a small pre-Xmas reprieve," he said.
Loading
"Given gathering signs of weakness in the economy, particularly the very weak outlook for house prices, my expectation is the RBA won't need to raise rates further in 2027, though the risk still lay firmly to the upside.
"Should rates need to rise even further next year, the risk of recession would no doubt intensify."
The number of interest rate hikes from here, says State Street Investment Management economist Ma Krishna Bhimavarapu, will depend on how much weaker the economy gets in coming months.
"We still expect the cash rate to ultimately have a five handle, but the path from here will depend on how quickly the economy slows," he said.
The nation faced two options 12 months ago: improve productivity or else.
The exogenous shock of an oil-sensitive war made improving productivity urgent, but we've missed the boat.
The Reserve Bank is now left with the unenviable task of taking a sledgehammer to demand for the greater good.
Let's be honest, it's positively sinister, as are most dirty little secrets.

3 reported dead in Italian military helicopter crash in Bosnia
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:58:43 CET
02:58:43 KST

An Italian military helicopter
crashed in Bosnia Thursday and three people have been reported
to have died in the crash.
                                    
The Mayor of Brčko said there were three dead and 12 injured. He
did not say what nationality they were.
                                    
Siniša Milić told ANSA that all had been treated at a hospital
in the city.
                                    
"Three people have died and twelve have been injured" following
the crash of a European Union Force (EUFOR) helicopter in
Bosnia, Milić told ANSA.
                                    
"All of them have been treated at a hospital in Brčko. Medical
staff are on high alert," he added.
                                    
EUFOR subsequently confirmed the news of the crash and said
"several" crew members had died.
                                    
The CH-47 chopper, deployed as part of Operation EUFOR Althea in
Bosnia and Herzegovina, crashed for reasons currently under
investigation.
                                    
Rescue teams responded immediately.
                                    
The Ministry of Defence stated that, at this time, "it is not
possible to provide further details, pending more precise
information—particularly regarding the health status of the
personnel involved."
The European Union Force in Bosnia and Herzegovina (EUFOR) has
announced that an incident occurred today during a routine
operation near the town of Gorica—located in the Brčko district,
close to the Serbian border—involving the crash of an aircraft
belonging to the international military mission.
                                    
It remains unclear whether the three individuals on board have
died, nor has their nationality been confirmed.
                                    
According to unofficial reports, all three people on board
perished in the crash. "EUFOR is conducting a full and thorough
investigation into the incident and will provide further
information once the facts have been established and it is
appropriate to do so," stated the EU mission, which includes an
Italian contingent. According to the mayor of Brčko, Siniša
Milić, there are three fatalities and 12 injuries.
                                    
EUFOR has urged the public to refrain from spreading unverified
information or disinformation, and to seek updates on the
incident exclusively through official channels.
                                    
The news was confirmed to the ANSA news agency in Sarajevo by
Brčko Mayor Siniša Milić.
                                    
"Three people have died, and twelve have been injured. All have
been treated at a hospital in Brčko. Medical staff remain on
high alert," Milić added.
                                    
Further details regarding the identities of those on board, as
well as the causes of the crash, will be released once the
authorities have completed the necessary checks and published
the findings of the investigation.

The Trump administration is trying to persuade businesses in the United States to accept Russian diesel fuel
Kyiv • UNN
U.S. officials are urging companies to accept discounted Russian diesel fuel. Businesses fear sanctions and reputational damage.
Officials in U.S. President Donald Trump's administration are privately urging American companies to accept Russian diesel fuel bound for the United States. At the same time, businesses fear legal consequences and reputational damage. The Washington Sun reports this, according to UNN.
Details
American companies fear the risks associated with purchasing Russian fuel. In particular, Democrats in Congress claim that President Donald Trump's executive order violates sanctions law. Despite this, administration officials are urging companies to accept cargoes that are still en route to the United States.
It is reported that both moscow and Washington are very forcefully encouraging them to accept these cargoes, including by offering significant discounts, but they are facing a wall of resistance because of reputational and legal risks.
A Treasury Department representative told the publication that the license to purchase Russian diesel "is consistent with actions the department has taken in the past," and that the Department "complies with applicable laws and regulations." According to an industry analyst, the cargo owners had been trying to "sell" them for several weeks but had found no buyers among American companies. Several sources confirmed that, when the tankers were loaded, there were no confirmed buyers in the United States.
Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, the senior member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, urged shipowners in letters to change course and not deliver Russian diesel to American ports.
Any company or individual considering purchasing Russian diesel fuel should understand that they are committing a crime and that Congress is watching. In addition, they could be held accountable by a future administration, even if the current one is turning a blind eye
Blumenthal also called for the disclosure of information about the sellers, buyers, terminal operators, and insurers involved in the transaction, as well as any instructions from the Treasury Department.
According to industry analysts and officials, tankers heading to U.S. ports will likely change their final destination to Brazil. It has been purchasing significant volumes of Russian diesel since the United States imposed sanctions in 2022.

Emergency stockpiles are a luxury that not everyone can afford | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:55:15 UTC
02:55:15 KST

The Be Ready campaign may offer sensible advice in principle (Every Briton should stockpile water and food supplies, government advises, 22 October), but as a midwife working in Tower Hamlets, one of the poorest boroughs in London, I can see first-hand that its practical recommendations risk excluding precisely those families who are already most vulnerable.
For families living in a single room in a shared house, storing nine litres of water per person alongside three days’ worth of essential supplies may simply be unrealistic. When families are already struggling with the cost of food, heating and everyday necessities, buying additional emergency provisions may also be financially impossible.
Perhaps local councils could create a stockpile hub where those in need could access the recommended supplies, free of charge. Being prepared should be a public health measure, not a privilege reserved for those who can afford it.
 
Keira Callaghan
 
London
While it flies in the face of just-in-time principles, I think the initiative to improve resilience is sensible in the current situation (Andy Burnham says he has emergency stockpile of beans, soup and Twiglets, 23 October). However, due to health issues, I rely on a monthly repeat prescription of several life-preserving medications. It used to be normal practice to request a new prescription when I opened the last box, but now the policy at my GP surgery appears to be that they will not issue a new prescription until a week before I need them.
The pharmacy then requires up to a week to process the prescription, meaning that my medications are always dispensed at the last minute. Localised shortages and periodic mistakes have caused me problems in the past, and I suffer from prescription anxiety every month. This policy is also incompatible with the latest government advice to stockpile essential medication. When the inevitable catastrophe strikes, I will find myself without my essential medication, and I doubt that 75 tins of beans and a packet of Twiglets will be much consolation.
 
Chris Rotheram
 
Thornton-Cleveleys, Lancashire
 The government is urging us to stock up enough supplies to survive for 72 hours. People might be wondering if it is time to dust off their copies of Protect and Survive from the 1980s. That document advised us to ready ourselves for nuclear war by preparing a bucket of sand for a toilet, and laying in some jigsaws to keep the kiddies amused. I feel pretty sanguine that such precautions won’t be needed today, because here in Hexham, where there used to be a nuclear bunker (for the use of officialdom, not for us, of course), there is now a McDonald’s. So, just keep calm and carry on.
 
Caroline Westgate
 
Hexham, Northumberland
You tell us the new government guidance for stocking up on supplies to survive for three days in an emergency, but nowhere does the advice tackle effluent. If we need three litres of bottled drinking water per person per day, the assumption is that mains water is not available.
Could the government please provide advice on where and how we will be expected to do our ablutions in a sanitary way when the toilets will not flush? We do not all have the luxury of a garden in which we can dig a hole. Some of us live in a block of flats, and dealing with three days’ worth of shit is something that needs planning.
 
Peter Slessenger
 
Reading, Berkshire
 We are beginning to see the elements of a Labour survival kit. Andy Burnham has gone for Twiglets, while John Healey is carrying a bottle of HP Sauce (Harold Wilson’s gravy). To complete it a flask of tea is required (Tony Benn).
 
Keith Flett
 
Tottenham, London
 Regarding Wes Streeting’s advice to stock up on essential food items in the event of food shortages and power cuts, can he please now advise on how to heat up tins of beans, soup, peas, etc when the electricity/gas is off?
 
Jane Kilsby
 
Countesthorpe, Leicestershire
 Call me a cynic, but might the government’s call to stock up on emergency supplies have been an attempt to increase economic activity before the budget?

Save Hammersmith Bridge – but keep it free of cars | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:54:56 UTC
02:54:56 KST

Simon Jenkins is a great defender of our national heritage, having produced many books on the subject and frequently written in the Guardian against aggressive modern architectural horrors. How shocking, then, to find him arguing for the replacement of Hammersmith Bridge simply to provide for yet more cars on the roads (Hammersmith Bridge is a symbol of our dysfunctional times. The money is there, the joined-up thinking isn’t, 23 October). He claims that the principal cause of congestion is “London’s epidemic of roadworks”, when actually it’s the fact that there are just too many cars trying to use a road network that isn’t designed for them.
Furthermore, he says that, in its present state, the bridge “merely allows pedestrians and cyclists to cross it” – and yet between 12,000 and 15,000 people use it every day. Reopening it to motor traffic (and increasingly heavy cars have massively contributed to the current state of degradation of the bridge) would bring little benefit. Well over half the households in Hammersmith and Fulham don’t have access to a car, and there are very good public transport links in the area; there is even a well-thought-out plan put forward by the Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light Transit group to run driverless electric “pod” vehicles to provide for those who are unable to walk across Hammersmith Bridge.
And quite apart from the huge difficulty involved in enabling the tearing down of a Grade II* listed structure (where’s our doughty defender of national heritage now?), there is no effective business case for replacing it at enormous cost to provide for yet more cars, when for both environmental and health reasons (particularly because of the pollution they cause), the whole emphasis should be on reducing our reliance on cars. If only someone in authority would summon up the courage to tackle the motoring lobby.
 
Dr Richard Carter
 
Putney, London
Simon Jenkins is right to castigate the different London authorities that have failed to replace Hammersmith Bridge over a period of seven years. No other capital city in Europe would allow such a prolonged truncation of a major transport artery, preventing vehicles from crossing the river. London is not a unitary authority and its mayor does not have the powers of his peers in other capitals to raise the finance to pay for the cost of a new bridge. The lack of joined-up thinking appears to be baked in to the planning processes of the different relevant authorities.
This sorry state of affairs in south-west London has led to permanent traffic chaos along the Upper Richmond Road and the hell that is Putney High Street during rush hour. Were it not for the British obsession for so-called “heritage” projects, we could have had a temporary bridge capable of carrying traffic years ago. Instead citizens are obliged to walk or pedal their way across a wonky bridge in order to get to the other side for the sake of a misplaced nostalgia for Victorian engineering feats.
 
Julian Heddy
 
East Sheen, London
The outdated photograph published with Simon Jenkins’s off-beam article on Hammersmith Bridge suggests decrepitude, when the reality is quite different. Thanks to £55m of investment by Hammersmith and Fulham council, this iconic, Grade II* listed bridge has found a successful new purpose as an active travel crossing, with 15,000 people a day walking and wheeling across its reopened main carriageway.
I know of no “growing body of opinion” calling for its replacement. On the contrary, the settled local preference has moved to build on this success with a proposal to introduce a fleet of lightweight, autonomous electric shuttles to fill the public transport gap to ensure all residents can cross comfortably and safely. Community-led Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light Transit is working with Ohmio UK and partners to deliver this vision.
Traffic on neighbouring bridges and the wider road network is down compared with before the bridge closed to motor vehicles, while Barnes’s local economy is booming, aided by the ebike revolution.
There is no credible business case for spending hundreds of millions bringing back polluting, dangerous and exclusionary through traffic. With the mayor targeting a 27% reduction in car traffic by 2030, the priority must be to build on this success, not undo it.
 
Charles Campion
 
Chair, Barnes Hammersmith Electric Light Transit
Simon Jenkins is a respected commentator on London’s heritage and built environment, with a deep understanding of the costs of maintaining historic infrastructure. We share his commitment to London’s bridges, but not his views on how the City Bridge Foundation’s charitable funds should be used.
We maintain five Thames bridges: Tower, London, Southwark, Millennium and Blackfriars, spanning centuries of engineering history. Their upkeep requires sustained investment and commitment, demonstrated by our current £15m Blackfriars Bridge refurbishment, repairing more than 2,000 cast-iron balusters and repainting the entire structure.
Our endowment exists to meet these responsibilities in perpetuity. It is not a general fund for London’s infrastructure, nor is its value a measure of money freely available to spend.
Alongside maintaining and supporting our bridges, where there are funds available, we make grants to charities tackling inequality and disadvantage across London. These funds are made for charitable purposes and governed by the legal and regulatory arrangements that apply to our work. They cannot simply be redirected to pay for the restoration or replacement of a bridge outside our remit.
We recognise the importance of London’s bridges to the people who rely on them every day, but other Thames crossings are the responsibility of other organisations. We share knowledge and experience with those responsible through industry groups.
For nearly 900 years, the legacy of Bridge House Estates has helped keep London’s bridges standing while supporting charitable work across the city. We are proud of this legacy and the charity partners working alongside us to build a fairer London.
 
Paul Martinelli
 
Chairman, City Bridge Foundation

8 of the most atmospheric Christmas markets worth visiting
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:54:43 EET
02:54:43 KST

8 of the most atmospheric Christmas markets worth visiting
Kyiv • UNN
Strasbourg, Dresden, Vienna and other cities preserve unique Christmas traditions. This selection tells about the markets and the main festive dishes.
European Christmas markets have long since evolved from simple winter markets into a large-scale cultural phenomenon, with each city preserving its own centuries-old secrets. Every market is special, with its own fairytale atmosphere and traditions. UNN has selected for you 8 of Europe's most spectacular winter destinations, their unique traditions, and the main gastronomic symbols that everyone should try.
Strasbourg
This French city is deservedly called the "capital of Christmas." The market was first established here in 1570 under the name "Christkindelsmärik." Before that, the city had hosted a Saint Nicholas market, but when Alsace became Protestant, Catholic holidays were abolished and the market was renamed in honor of the Christ Child. You should definitely try the local bredele cookies, which are baked exclusively for the holidays, and instead of ordinary mulled wine, try hot white Alsatian wine or spiced apple juice with cinnamon.
Interestingly, Strasbourg has an entire "Christmas tree guard service." The main tree in Place Kléber is selected for months in the surrounding forests: it must be perfectly symmetrical and taller than 30 meters.
Dresden
The local Striezelmarkt is Germany's oldest market; it has been officially mentioned in documents since 1434. At first, it was simply a single day of trading, when townspeople were allowed to buy meat after the strict Christmas fast. Be sure to try authentic Dresden stollen. Today, only a few dozen local bakeries have the right to place an official quality mark on it.
The market got its name from the word "Striezel"—the term once used for a festive cake. It is also here that the world's tallest wooden Christmas pyramid stands: a 14-meter structure from the Ore Mountains.
Nuremberg
The Christkindlesmarkt in Nuremberg is a place of strict traditions. You will not see plastic garlands or loud modern pop music here. The city council closely monitors that all stalls are made exclusively of natural wood and decorated with fresh fir branches. The market is famous for Nuremberg sausages. They are very small, about the length of a finger, and are traditionally served three at a time in a sliced, crispy roll. The market's main symbol is not Santa Claus, but the Christ Child. A girl is chosen for this role by the townspeople once every two years, and she opens the festival by delivering a speech from the balcony of the Frauenkirche.
Vienna
Vienna's markets are pure classic. The very first "December Market" here was authorized by Emperor Albert I as early as 1298. It is important to note that Vienna has not just one market, but more than a dozen different locations throughout the city. Every year, the markets issue signature cups shaped like boots or hearts, which you can keep as a souvenir after paying a deposit. They are used to serve the signature hot punch. It is here, near City Hall, that the most romantic market takes place: hundreds of illuminated figures are lit up on the trees in the park, while a huge ice rink is set up among the wooded paths.
Prague
The Czech winter fairytale is centered around Old Town Square. While steam rises from stalls serving grilled sausages, the Gothic Orloj clock counts down the hours to Christmas. Prague's markets are famous for trdelník—rolled dough with cinnamon and nuts—as well as fried hermelín cheese. Traditionally, a live nativity scene with real sheep, goats, and a donkey is installed in the center of the Prague market every year, and children are happily allowed to pet them.
Tallinn
The market on Tallinn's Town Hall Square is small but incredibly cozy. The northern winter atmosphere can be felt here like nowhere else—old stone buildings, snow, and lamplight. Tallinn will surprise you with blood sausage served with lingonberry jam, cinnamon-roasted almonds, and hot mulled wine with the famous Vana Tallinn liqueur added. According to local legend, it was in Tallinn, in 1441, that the Brotherhood of Blackheads erected Europe's first public Christmas tree, around which dances were held.
Wrocław
The Wrocław Christmas market on Market Square is now considered one of the largest in Central Europe. The historic center transforms into a real fairy-tale town with two-story wooden mills. Oscypek — smoked goat cheese from the mountains, grilled and served with cranberry sauce — is a delicacy no market is complete without. If you pay close attention, you may spot the famous local bronze dwarfs hiding throughout the Wrocław market. During the holiday season, some of them are even given tiny winter hats and scarves.
Zagreb
If you thought the best markets could only be found in the north, Zagreb easily disproves that. For several years in a row, the Croatian capital won the title of Europe’s best Christmas market. Here, you should try fritule — mini doughnuts with chocolate, cinnamon, or powdered sugar, served hot in cups. The market encompasses not just one square but literally the entire city: from Zrinjevac Park with its classical music pavilion to the historic underground Grič Tunnel, which is transformed into a light tunnel with musical accompaniment.

“I know how technically the evacuation to Ukraine can take place, but I don’t know what will really happen,” Zelensky said.
Rights advocates warn of ‘human shield’
Ukrainian human rights advocates have warned that Moscow may try to keep part of the population in place.
Oleksandr Pavlichenko, executive director of the Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union, told Ukrainian Radio that Russia sees civilians in frontline Oleshky as a human shield against Ukrainian fire, Ukrinform reported earlier on Thursday, Oct. 29.
According to Pavlichenko, there was no information available yet on whether Russian forces would subject evacuees to filtration, but warned that the risks existed. So far, he said, further details about international observers, including their number and access, remain unclear.
Saving the children from what Ukrainian senior authorities previously called a “death trap” remains a priority.
Petro Andriushchenko, head of the Center for the Study of Occupation, said Russian forces would almost certainly use the truce to move and rotate their units, adding that such activity could also take place on the Ukrainian side of the Dnipro River.
Human-made catastrophe
Oleshky, located on the left bank of the Dnipro River in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region, roughly 5 kilometers (3 miles) southeast of Kherson city, has faced severe shortages of food, clean water and medicine for months, with the last food delivery reported on May 26.
According to Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha’s estimates, roughly 1,700 people remain in the city from a prewar population of 24,000, including 47 children.
Ukraine’s human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets, who leads the humanitarian operation, earlier said that about 6,000 people, including some 200 children, remain across Oleshky and the surrounding settlements. In his view, up to 2,000 people could remain in Oleshky itself.
However, neither figure could be independently verified, particularly because Russian occupation authorities narrowly restrict access to information from the area.
Lubinets said on Sept. 16 that the residents had started escaping on foot independently across mined fields and under threat of constant Russian drone attacks, simply because they saw no other way out.
Before the truce was officially announced, Pope Leo XIV held a telephone discussion with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 16, urging him to agree to an immediate ceasefire and allow the delivery of food and medical assistance to the city.
The pontiff then spoke to Zelensky on Monday, Oct. 19, reiterating his earlier request for a humanitarian ceasefire.
On Oct. 20, European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno declared a hunger strike in protest over the starvation of civilians in Oleshky.

Beskrestnov: Russia produces more ballistic missiles than the entire world produces Patriot interceptor missiles
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Russia is producing ballistic missiles in volumes that exceed the global production capacity for Patriot interceptor missiles, stated Serhiy Beskrestnov (Flash), an advisor to the President of Ukraine on defense technologies.
"Russia produces more ballistic missiles than the number of Patriot interceptor missiles produced globally to counter them," he told reporters on Thursday, according to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent.
According to Beskrestnov, Russia continues to manufacture Iskander and S-400 missiles, with production capacities in these segments exceeding current requirements. Furthermore, Russia has partially shifted production away from Kinzhal missiles toward ballistic missiles, Beskrestnov noted.
He emphasized that the increase in Russian ballistic missile production exacerbates the shortage of interceptors. He added that this imbalance is further compounded by the introduction of missiles from North Korea and Iran.
Beskrestnov noted that countering this threat requires an increase in the global production of PAC-3 interceptor missiles. At the same time, this process faces limitations, and scaling up production volumes takes time.

Six lanes and metro line under fire: Kyiv prepares about $22 million for backup river crossings after Russian strike on Southern Bridge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:52:25 UTC
02:52:25 KST

The Ukrainian government has instructed Kyiv to establish alternative routes after Russian attacks stopped traffic on one of the capital’s main bridges. The city authorities will bear the cost of the new crossings, with Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko saying the city needs an additional $22 million.
This year, Russia has launched tactics to spread panic among civilians and trigger more people to leave the country. In the latest attack, several Russia's ballistic missiles struck the Southern Bridge, used for vehicle and metro traffic, breaking a huge hole and paralyzing all the pathes. The bridge was closed. Now, there is a fear that more bridges can be targeted this way, dividing Kyiv in two parts.
The situation is urgent, as Ukrainian Transport Minister Mykola Kalashnyk says about 600,000 vehicles cross the Dnipro in Kyiv every day.
What is Kyiv’s response to the winter terror?
According to Klitschko, Kyiv convened the capital’s Defense Council on 28 October to find an answer to this difficult question.
The agenda included implementing a project to build combined water crossings over the Dnipro River and access roads to them.
“The military command will determine the locations, with approval to be granted, among others, by the Kyiv City Military Administration,” Klitschko said.
Under the government’s recommendations, the Kyiv city authorities must find $22 million for the project.
Klitschko had previously faced heavy criticism after it emerged that the city lacked sufficient shelters and last winter exposed serious shortcomings in preparing infrastructure for Russian attacks. These included a lack of alternative energy supply routes, poorly distributed energy, burst heating pipes that flooded apartments, and the inability of people with disabilities to reach shelters without elevators.
The mayor himself said the problems stemmed from the central government withholding funding, which had stalled numerous energy resilience projects and delayed their implementation.
The latest announcement also indicates that Kyiv has once again taken on the financial burden itself.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has been working with Japan on backup crossings. Tokyo has already delivered 720 meters of prefabricated bridge structures to Ukraine. The two sides are currently exploring how this equipment could be used to establish alternative crossings.
Step two: strengthening existing infrastructure
Another option is to reinforce existing bridges. City specialists are developing additional technical solutions to protect bridges across the Dnipro River, Klitschko said in his statement on 27 October, adding that proposals from the military had also been heard.
The issue of installing mobile shelters was also raised on the same day, the mayor of Kyiv said in a separate statement on his Telegram channel on 27 October. Despite intensifying Russian attacks and about, as Radio Svoboda reported in its article on 30 September, $11 million set aside in 2025, Kyiv still has only a handful of mobile shelters: LB reported in December 2025 that district tenders failed. Donors paid for the first one at a bus stop, the Kyiv City State Administration said on 15 October.
Klitschko raised the issue of shelters again after a court on 12 October ruled that local authorities must urgently install mobile shelters in public areas, including near public transport stops, parks, and squares, according to Kyiv’s Prosecutor’s Office.
Russia hits the Southern Bridge again
On 2 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an interview with the Financial Times that Russian ruler Vladimir Putin had ordered the lifting of previous restrictions on airstrikes. Among new targets, according to him, were bridges, data centers, internet, mobile networks, hospitals, kindergartens, schools, and universities.
The night of 26–27 October showed what that looks like. Russia launched ballistic missile attacks in a few waves, and the second of them hit the Southern Bridge and the metro infrastructure on it, Klitschko said. The structure carries six lanes of road traffic and two metro tracks.
Zelenskyy put the night’s total at 16 ballistic missiles and blamed delays in deliveries of Patriot and NASAMS interceptors: “Every such delay is a new Russian hit on one target or another.”

Turkey and Israel's growing rivalry in the Horn of Africa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:51:20 UTC
02:51:20 KST

Breadcrumb
Turkey and Israel's growing rivalry in the Horn of Africa
The Horn of Africa is where strategic maritime corridors, fragile states, and regional ambitions converge - and it is emerging as a new front in Middle Eastern geopolitical competition.
Israel’s 26 December 2025 recognition of Somaliland’s independence added new dimensions to these tensions, intersecting with Turkey’s expanding military, economic, and diplomatic footprint in Somalia and broader partnerships across the Horn of Africa.
From Turkey’s perspective, Israel’s Somaliland move and its broader regional engagement challenge Ankara’s strategic interests. Tel Aviv, for its part, views Somaliland as a potential gateway to projecting influence near Houthi-controlled territory in Yemen and along one of the world’s most important maritime corridors.
Somaliland’s longstanding quest for international recognition risks becoming further entangled in the rivalries of Middle Eastern powers, transforming a local sovereignty dispute into a wider contest over the future of Red Sea security.
As Turkey and Israel deepen their engagement, and other external actors pursue their own agendas, the Horn of Africa might end up an increasingly crowded arena of geopolitical competition. The implications for regional stability could be serious.
Israel's Somaliland gambit and the rivalry with Turkey
Situated alongside busy maritime routes, the Horn of Africa links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, occupying a position of much geostrategic importance.
Egypt, Iran, Israel, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) increasingly view the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, and the surrounding territories as a single security environment. Instability in one part of this interconnected region can disrupt commercial shipping, threaten energy security, and intensify rivalries among states far beyond its shores.
Israel’s decision to recognise Somaliland’s independence and to invest in deeper ties with the self-declared breakaway republic is very much about securing a strong position in a territory situated in close proximity to Yemen.
This land can provide Tel Aviv with the means to closely monitor Houthi activity, improve intelligence collection, and strengthen surveillance of maritime routes that have become increasingly vulnerable to disruption.
“Israel’s interest in the Horn of Africa is not new but has sped up amid regional shake-up in the aftermath of [7 October 2023],” Dr Burcu Ozcelik, Senior Research Fellow for Middle East Security at the London-based Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told The New Arab.
“Israel sees Somaliland mainly through a defence cooperation lens, and as a possible staging ground for future offensive military activity against the Houthis. The strategic value of access near Yemen for Israel spans intelligence, surveillance, and potentially military operations,” she added.
Ankara and Tel Aviv’s rivalry and maritime security interests are “mutually reinforcing” motivations, argued Cameron Hudson, an independent analyst with expertise on African peace, security, and governance, who previously worked on Africa at the Central Intelligence Agency, State Department, and the US National Security Council.
“They are two sides of the same coin and cannot be disaggregated,” he told The New Arab.
However, Omar S. Mahmood, a Senior Analyst for Somalia and the Horn of Africa at International Crisis Group, offers a more qualified interpretation. He suggests that the immediate motivation for Tel Aviv is mostly related to security, while competition with Ankara is a secondary consequence, not necessarily the driving force.
“I don’t think Israel’s relationship with Somaliland is driven by a broader rivalry with Turkey per se. But there are local ramifications as Somaliland itself is seeking external allies as it is uncomfortable with growing Turkish military support to Somalia, viewing it as a potential future threat,” explained Mahmood in an interview with The New Arab.
“So, in this sense the middle powers can get drawn into supporting opposite sides in local rivalries, even if that was not the primary factor driving their engagement in the first place,” he added.
Turkey's foothold in Somalia
Turkey’s presence in Somalia is a product of many years of sustained investment and political commitment.
In 2011, Somalia faced a devastating famine which claimed approximately 250,000 lives (half of them children) amid an unprecedented humanitarian crisis. At that time, Mogadishu did not have many reliable partners around the world.
That was when Ankara’s engagement with the country gained momentum, beginning with humanitarian assistance and reconstruction before developing into a much wider relationship across multiple domains, from investment to military training and security cooperation to state-building.
Central to Turkey’s military partnership with Somalia has been its TURKSOM facility in Mogadishu. This training establishment has been at the heart of Turkish efforts to help build up the Somali government’s ability to fight al-Shabaab.
Ankara and Mogadishu signed a 10-year defence agreement in 2024, extending their cooperation into naval development and the protection of Somalia's coastline, alongside growing Turkish interests in maritime security and offshore oil and gas exploration, underscoring Turkey’s stakes in Somalia achieving greater stability.
Bilateral ties also strengthened when Somalia sought international support following Ethiopia's agreement with Somaliland concerning access to the sea in exchange for recognition - a deal which infuriated officials in Mogadishu.
Ankara subsequently helped mediate between Somalia and Ethiopia, illustrating how Turkey’s influence has gone beyond military and economic cooperation and entailed effective regional diplomacy.
In late 2025, Turkey joined many other countries around the world in strongly denouncing Israel’s recognition of Somaliland. Ankara feared that recognition of the breakaway republic gravely threatened Somalia’s territorial dignity.
Turkey also has concerns about the potential creation of openings for external actors to establish a presence for themselves in territories situated near maritime routes where Ankara has vested interests.
Rather than reacting with an immediate escalation of its military presence, Ankara seems to find its most effective response to be based on reinforcing its relationships and institutions that serve to underpin Turkish influence in Somalia. This measured approach appears to be aimed at protecting the investments which Turkey has made in the country without setting Ankara up for any overt confrontation with the Israelis in Somalia.
However, Ankara’s efforts to preserve its position in Somalia could have unintended consequences. Somaliland may interpret deeper Turkish-Somali security cooperation as a threat to its political ambitions, prompting Hargeisa to seek stronger external backing and, in the process, potentially deepening regional tensions.
The Emirati factor
No analysis of Turkish-Israeli competition in the Horn of Africa is complete without taking stock of the UAE’s role. Abu Dhabi’s support for Somaliland, even if short of formal recognition, places the UAE broadly on the same side of this sovereign dispute as Tel Aviv.
The UAE has vast strategic and commercial interests across the Red Sea, giving Abu Dhabi high stakes in the Horn of Africa’s evolving security order, while its normalised relationship with Israel continues to be an important feature of the Middle East’s geopolitical landscape more than six years after the Abraham Accords’ signing.
On the other side, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Qatar, and other regional actors have expressed support for Somalia’s territorial integrity, a position that connects their interests in the Horn of Africa to their wider security cooperation in the Middle East.
Hudson sees the UAE and Israel as a “powerful and mutually reinforcing duo in the Red Sea” which are both willing to challenge established power structures and intervene in disputes in the Horn of Africa to further their national interests at the region’s expense.
“They are happy to pick winners and losers, unsettle established power dynamics, and actively intervene in regional politics and conflicts in ways that benefit them even if that means unsettling regional dynamics,” he told The New Arab.
Hudson contrasts this with “Turkish or Saudi efforts to stabilise and reinforce established power dynamics as a way of limiting destabilising outside influences.”
Clearly, Abu Dhabi’s role is important not only due to Emirati ambitions but also because external backing can make local leaders less willing to compromise by reducing the perceived costs associated with confrontation.
The local stakes of a wider geopolitical contest
Despite the growing involvement of Middle Eastern states in the Horn of Africa, and the risks of this region becoming more of an arena for external competition, it is necessary to note that Somalia and Somaliland are not passive actors victimised by a giant game of geopolitical chess.
Both have agency and are actively seeking non-African partners to strengthen their positions and advance their political objectives.
For the government in Mogadishu, Turkey's military, economic, and diplomatic support is critical to strengthening state institutions, improving security, and protecting Somalia’s territorial integrity.
Meanwhile, Somaliland has long sought international recognition and has strong incentives to cultivate relationships with countries such as Israel and the UAE, which might advance that goal or at least provide greater protection against perceived threats.
In this sense, “you have a layer of local rivalries that now intersect with regional rivalries, creating a potentially dangerous situation,” explained Mahmood, who emphasised that this permits “Horn of Africa actors to take on more maximalist, aggressive and less compromising positions, knowing that [they] have…external support to fall back on.”
Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, Israel, and maritime targets have done much to help explain why regional powers see the Horn of Africa as increasingly important to their foreign policy calculations.
As Houthi-Saudi hostilities escalate, Riyadh is focused on growing stronger security partnerships with regional actors, while governments in the Horn of Africa are likely to view closer cooperation with the Kingdom as a way to secure higher levels of assistance and bolster their own military capabilities. Meanwhile, the conflict in Sudan adds new layers of complication as it draws regional actors into overlapping security and political calculations.
Yet a greater military presence does not necessarily translate into greater stability. While competing powers expand their security footholds with the aim of countering one another, mistrust can deepen, territorial disputes can intensify, and local actors will probably pursue greater support from external powers.
Therefore, the Horn of Africa is increasingly likely to become exposed to conflicts in and around the Red Sea even if not directly involved in their initial escalation. Within this context, heightened insecurity means that further militarisation of the Red Sea risks undermining, rather than enhancing, security.
An evolving security arrangement around the Red Sea
On 7 August, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement - a trilateral alliance which is defensive in nature and aimed at containing the chaotic instability unleashed by the war centred on Iran.
This security configuration has potentially significant implications for the balance of power around the Red Sea and Horn of Africa. It was hardly surprising that the leadership in Mogadishu hailed the pact in the immediate aftermath of its announcement, especially given Somalia’s close ties with the three signatories and shared threat perceptions of Israeli aggression.
For Somalia, the pact’s significance extends beyond its endorsement and raises important questions about regional realignments and Ankara’s position in the Horn of Africa within the wider context of an emerging security architecture.
Escalating Houthi-Saudi hostilities prompt a broader recalibration of regional security alignments, bringing Turkey and Pakistan closer to Saudi Arabia through the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. For Ankara, this partnership offers an opportunity to connect its longstanding presence in Somalia with a wider strategic role in Gulf and Red Sea security.
Dr Ozcelik told The New Arab that the hostilities have “crossed red lines that were deemed unthinkable not long ago,” setting in motion a realignment among Riyadh’s allies. Ankara’s growing institutional engagement with the Kingdom therefore extends beyond diplomatic rhetoric, highlighting a more formal commitment to regional defence and security cooperation.
There are implications of this emerging Turkish-Saudi alignment for the rivalry between Ankara and Tel Aviv. As Dr Ozcelik stressed, Ankara is “institutionalising its partnership with Saudi Arabia beyond rhetoric and through defence commitments, minilateralism, and regional diplomacy.”
This closer Turkish-Saudi relationship will not escape Israeli strategists’ attention, particularly as Ankara expands its regional security role while Riyadh remains firm in its support for Palestinian statehood.
In Dr Ozcelik’s assessment, these parallel developments risk “fuelling a greater gulf between Israel and Turkey,” further complicating an already tense relationship that has significantly deteriorated since 7 October 2023.
While commentators sometimes toss Somalia around as a possible Mecca Joint Defence Agreement candidate, Hudson considers formal Somalia membership in the pact unlikely in the near term. He noted that Somalia remains a recipient of security assistance rather than a country capable of contributing meaningfully to a mutual defence arrangement.
“Given the high level of instability still emanating from Somalia, external countries would be foolish at this point to enter into a mutual security agreement with them now. Somalia can’t provide for its own security, let alone contribute to the security of others,” Hudson told The New Arab.
Similarly, Mahmood does not expect Somalia to formally join the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. But he does think Mogadishu is likely to deepen security relations with the pact’s three signatories, noting that this is a development already underway. “Somalia prefers to align with this bloc of countries and sees them as a future source of support as it continues to build up its military capabilities,” he observed.
The risks of an expanding geopolitical contest
The internationalisation of the Horn of Africa’s political disputes and security crises entered a new chapter after Israel became the first UN member-state to officially recognise Somaliland ten months ago.
What started as a dispute over Somaliland’s recognition and Somalia’s territorial integrity has transformed into a larger contest over maritime security, military access, and regional influence.
A dangerous risk is an exacerbating security dilemma in which competing alliances deepen mistrust, undermine compromise, and expose the Horn of Africa to conflicts originating elsewhere.
Preventing further escalation will require Middle Eastern powers and their regional partners to exercise restraint while recognising that lasting stability depends on addressing the disputes that drive Somalia and Somaliland to seek competing external allies.

Egyptian man who fire-bombed pro-Israel rally in Colorado pleads guilty to federal hate crimes

Egyptian man who fire-bombed pro-Israel rally in Colorado pleads guilty to federal hate crimes
DENVER, Oct 29 - The man who lobbed gasoline bombs at a pro-Israel rally in Colorado last year, injuring several people including a woman who later died, pleaded guilty on Thursday to federal hate-crime charges, the US Department of Justice said.
Mohamed Sabry Soliman, 47, an Egyptian national, is already serving a life sentence for his guilty plea in May to more than 100 state charges, including first-degree murder.
Soliman pleaded guilty to nine counts of hate-crime offenses and three explosives charges in federal court in Denver, according to the DOJ. The charges are punishable by life in prison after federal prosecutors declined to seek the death penalty.
The plea deal asks that Soliman be sentenced to life in prison plus 50 years. Soliman will be sentenced on January 7.
"The defendant admitted that he committed the attack because of the actual or perceived Jewish religion and Israeli national origin of the group he targeted," the DOJ said in a statement.
David Kraut, a federal public defender listed as Soliman's lawyer, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Soliman has admitted tossing two Molotov cocktails at people taking part in a rally in downtown Boulder on June 1, 2025, held in solidarity with hostages seized by Hamas militants who stormed Israeli villages from the Palestinian enclave of Gaza on October 7, 2023.
Prosecutors said Soliman yelled "Free Palestine" as the gasoline bombs he lobbed at the crowd burst into flames outside a municipal courthouse in the heart of Boulder's popular Pearl Street shopping district.
Admitting his guilt in state court nearly six months ago, Soliman denounced his own crimes as contrary to "the teachings of Islam" and insisted he bore no ill will toward Jewish people. He went on to lament the "thousands of families who have lost their families in Palestine and Gaza," and said the "enemy is Zionism."
Authorities in Colorado identified 29 victims from the attack, including 14 who were burned or injured while fleeing and 15 who were close enough to be considered targets of attempted murder. One victim, 82-year-old Karen Diamond, died of her injuries later that month. Her husband suffered severe burns and survived.
The firebombing came amid heightened tensions over the 2023 Hamas raid and Israel's military assault in Gaza, which sparked a surge in anti-Jewish and anti-Muslim hate crimes across the US and a wave of pro-Palestinian protests that many Israel supporters branded as antisemitic. Pro-Palestinian protesters reject accusations their support of Gazans amounts to antisemitism.
FAMILY'S IMMIGRATION DETENTION
According to affidavits filed in court by prosecutors, Soliman told investigators after his arrest that he had planned his attack for a year, but delayed going through with it until after his daughter had graduated from high school.
Soliman, who had lived with his wife and five children in Colorado Springs, also has asserted that his family members were unaware of his intentions beforehand.
The family was taken into immigration custody in June 2025 after his arrest and transported to a detention facility in Texas. They were held until a court-ordered release on April 23, 2026, more than 10 months later.
The children and their mother, who subsequently divorced Soliman, were rearrested on April 25 of this year just after returning to Colorado. They were freed again when attorneys intervened a day later, according to court documents.
Court records entered at about the time that Soliman reached a plea deal with federal prosecutors earlier this month showed that he had withdrawn motions seeking to preclude any further attempts at removing his family. REUTERS

UN special rapporteurs on Thursday warned of the systematic destruction of education and the media in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Anadolu reports.

She said that “98% of the schools and all 13 universities have been destroyed,” adding, “Almost 21,000 Palestinian students have been killed. A classroom of children every day during the war on Gaza.”
Saying that the destruction aims to uproot Palestinian society, Shaheed said: “Scholasticide is multigenerational; it aims to dismantle the very foundation of Palestinian society, erase their history and destroy a sense of collective self.”
She said 13 libraries, the central archives of Gaza holding 150 years of history, 195 heritage sites, 227 mosques and at least three churches were also destroyed or targeted.
In the occupied West Bank, Shaheed said, “Last September, 10 out of 48 schools were demolished in East Jerusalem.”
She noted that some schools had to close after failing to obtain licenses, which often depend on curriculum changes that delete references to Palestinian history and culture.
“In the first half of the year, there were 224 security incidents, which affected 152 schools, 20,450 students, and at least 859 educational personnel,” she said. “Settler violence has also displaced at least 1,700 children from school.”
Francesca Albanese, the rapporteur on the situation of human rights in the Palestinian territory occupied since 1967, addressed the briefing virtually and said her latest report examines the role of the media.
“Since October 2023, Israel has killed nearly 300 journalists and media workers in Gaza,” she said.
She said when witnesses are silenced, “the crime is not only committed; it is concealed, and impunity becomes part of the plan.”
Albanese said more than 74,500 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza, which “has the highest number of child amputees per capita in the world.”
Pointing to the ceasefire announced last year, she said, “I wish I could tell you the so-called ceasefire had brought relief. It has not,” she said, adding that more than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed since it was announced.
Albanese said thousands of Palestinians were forcibly displaced from Hebron in the West Bank after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to destroy the neighborhood of those behind the Oct. 23 checkpoint attacks.
“Gaza might be the breaking point, not because of the United Nations’ lack of tools, but because its members chose not to use them,” she said. “It is not too late.”
Urging states to act, she said: “Suspend arms transfer and trade that sustain unlawful occupation and genocide. Fund and protect UNRWA. Protect the journalists.”
“History will ask what each of us did. Let our answer not be that we just watched,” she added.

Unknown

Ukraine should not agree to limits on size of its armed forces – Admiral Bauer
He made the remarks in an interview with Ukrinform on the sidelines of a special event hosted by the Brussels office of the Kyiv Security Forum.
"I think there's two elements that are extremely important when it comes to a just peace. One is that Ukraine remains a truly sovereign state, which can decide its own future and its alliances. And that means credible Armed Forces. That means the ability to run the country as the people of Ukraine want. All these demands from Russia that there shouldn't be credible Armed Forces in Ukraine are unacceptable," Bauer said.
He added that, second, there must be credible means of deterring the aggressor from invading again.
"People often talk about security guarantees, but there should be credible deterrents to make sure that Russia understands that, if they try again, they will fail," the Dutch admiral said.
In his opinion, unless these two conditions are met, it is highly unlikely that Ukraine will be able to accept any peace settlement proposal.
He believes that even territorial concessions could form part of a settlement, but only if the two conditions outlined above are met.
"Also, it's not about giving away lands. You could say that you are accepting that you have no control over these territories, but you're not accepting that they are Russian. No de jure recognition. It's only accepting the situation only to end the war," he said.
At the same time, drawing on the experience of the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Bauer believes it is unlikely that anything short of a mechanism as close as possible to Article 5 of the NATO Treaty would be an acceptable option.
Speaking about the security of the entire European continent, the admiral also said that Ukraine must genuinely become "part of our security in the larger sense, when it comes to Europe."

Data analysis firms Polysights and Bubblemaps have also flagged the activity as suspicious and are investigating, the report said.

Representatives for Polymarket and Polysights did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Bubblemaps said its analysis shared with Bloomberg was recent and that it had no further updates.

IDF soldier indicted for allegedly spying for Iran, leaking sensitive military intelligence

2026-10-29
17:49:36 UTC
02:49:36 KST

A soldier has been indicted for providing information to Iran, the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), Israel Police, and the IDF Spokesperson's Unit, announced in a joint statement Thursday.
The soldier was arrested in September in a joint operation by the Shin Bet, the Ayalon District Police Investigations Unit, the Military Police Criminal Investigation Division (MPCID), and the Defense Ministry's security authorities.
The official charges filed by the prosecution are providing information to the enemy with intent to harm state security, providing information for the benefit of the enemy, and contact with a foreign agent.
The soldier's alleged espionage activities involved encrypted communications, coded messages, cryptocurrency payments, and a cover story designed to conceal his contact with Iranian intelligence. His handler also reportedly offered him a substantial financial incentive to travel to Iran.
According to investigators, the soldier maintained contact with Iranian intelligence operatives for approximately a year, fully aware of whom he was communicating with. During that period, he allegedly disclosed sensitive information about his unit's activities, IDF operational readiness, and emergency mobilizations, including details of his own call-up at the outbreak of Operation Roaring Lion.
IDF soldier allegedly shared military base coordinates, photos of US aircraft with Iran
The information he allegedly provided included the locations and coordinates of military bases, along with photographs of interceptor missiles, military vehicles, and US refueling aircraft stationed at an Israeli airport.
Investigators also found that the soldier supplied his handler with personal information about fellow soldiers and commanders in his unit, despite knowing that the Iranian operative intended to use those details to recruit additional individuals for espionage.
In exchange, the soldier received payments through cryptocurrency wallets, following instructions from his Iranian handler.
The investigation further revealed that the soldier gave his handler access to a Telegram group called "Kal Bakrav," which serves Israelis preparing for military service. The Iranian operative subsequently joined the group.
The handler also instructed the soldier to install malicious communications applications that would allow them to exchange encrypted messages. He reportedly suggested that the soldier purchase a basic mobile phone and a handgun.
IDF soldier, Iranian handler allegedly used coded messages and cover story to evade detection
To avoid detection, the two allegedly agreed to communicate using coded language and devised a cover story in case Israeli security authorities uncovered their activities.
The Iranian handler also offered the soldier $200,000 to travel to Iran, according to investigators.
A military court extended the soldier's detention until November 12, 2026.
In their joint statement, the Shin Bet, Israel Police, and IDF described the case as an extremely serious threat to national security and urged the public to remain vigilant against suspected foreign intelligence recruitment attempts.
"We call on the public to exercise the utmost vigilance. Any suspicious approach by an unidentified individual, request to provide information, or offer of payment in exchange for 'services' must be reported to the security authorities," the agencies said.
The security agencies added that they would continue working to prevent espionage and terrorism and pursue legal action against individuals suspected of assisting enemy operatives or endangering Israel's security.

Israel extradites Israeli-Russian citizen to US over alleged USD 2.8 million crypto theft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:49:34 UTC
02:49:34 KST

Israel extradited Alexander Block to the United States early Thursday to face charges over the alleged theft of about USD 2.8 million in digital assets from cryptocurrency platform Nomad, the State Attorney’s Office announced.
Block, an Israeli-Russian citizen formerly known as Alexander Gurevich, was transferred to American authorities after extensive legal proceedings in Israel, including an unsuccessful Supreme Court appeal and a subsequent request for a further hearing.
The case concerns allegations that he exploited a security flaw in August 2022 to obtain digital tokens - without depositing the assets that were supposed to back them - and then moved the proceeds between digital wallets to conceal their origin.
According to the Supreme Court judgment, US authorities indicted Block in the Northern District of California in August 2023 on eight counts involving computer offenses, transferring stolen property, and money laundering. The US requested his extradition in December 2024.
Block was arrested at Ben-Gurion Airport in May 2025 while preparing to travel to Russia. He had changed his surname from Gurevich to Block and obtained a passport in his new name shortly before his arrest.
Block identified flaw in crypto platform, withdrew about 2.8m in tokens
Nomad, the cryptocurrency platform, operated as a bridge between blockchain networks, allowing users to lock digital assets on one network and receive corresponding tokens on another.
According to the American extradition request, Block identified a flaw that allowed him to bypass the check confirming that the original assets had been locked. Prosecutors allege that, after testing the vulnerability, he withdrew about USD 2.8m. in tokens on August 1, 2022, without supplying the corresponding assets.
He then allegedly converted the tokens into other cryptocurrencies and transferred them between wallets to obscure the source of the funds.
The Jerusalem District Court approved his extradition in July 2025. His appeal challenged whether the alleged conduct constituted criminal offenses under Israeli law and whether the evidence was sufficient to support extradition.
Block argues transactions used Nomad functions
Block argued that the transactions used functions available within Nomad’s automated system and that the public record of blockchain transfers undermined the money-laundering allegations.
The Supreme Court rejected those arguments, holding that exploiting a programming flaw could constitute unlawful computer intrusion, even where the software technically permitted the action. It also explained that publicly visible transactions did not necessarily identify the people controlling the wallets or rule out efforts to conceal the source of funds.
The State Attorney’s Office said Supreme Court President Isaac Amit subsequently rejected his request for a further hearing. Thursday’s transfer was coordinated by the prosecution’s International Department and the Israel Police’s operational coordination and Interpol units.

The results of Israel's elections have raised concerns within the Iranian regime, particularly over the possibility that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will remain in power, although continued political instability in Israel could ultimately serve Tehran's interests, Iran expert Beni Sabti of the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS) said.
Sabti discussed how Iran is analyzing the election results, its fears of Netanyahu, and its preparations for another military confrontation. He also criticized the Trump administration's handling of the Islamic Republic.
According to Sabti, political divisions in Israel and the United States provide Iran with a significant advantage.
"The Iranians are mainly hearing multiple voices. That is the biggest problem on the Western side when facing Iran, and it is what serves Iran the most. We are in a state of instability, with questions about the government and whether an order will be given or not. This greatly strengthens the Iranians. They don't understand democracy. That's the problem. It's not that we're doing something wrong. They don't understand it."
Addressing the possibility that Netanyahu will continue serving as prime minister, Sabti said: "The Iranians' worst nightmare has come true. From their perspective, the best thing would have been for Netanyahu to leave the political scene and for a new coalition to emerge, one that would take time to understand Iran. As far as they are concerned, Netanyahu is the strong man, and he can attack."
"To their credit, they analyze everyone and understand everyone. They see them all as demons. They understand that one was a chief of staff (Gadi Eisenkot), while another was prime minister for a short time (Naftali Bennett). But during that short period, I remember that every two or three weeks, an Iranian officer or scientist would disappear. That was during Bennett's time."
He continued: "They do analyze these people, but Netanyahu is the one credited with the wars, and that is why he frightens them the most. They compare it to their own mentality. When the Iranian leader has ruled for 37 years, and Netanyahu has been around since 1996, that's also 30 years. In the Iranians' eyes, he is someone like them, and that is why he scares them more.
"I'll say it again, this is all from their perspective. The very possibility of a change in leadership is already better for them. Incidentally, a second election would be the best thing that could happen to Iran. Instability, chaos."
The American side
Sabti also addressed contacts between Washington and Tehran, arguing that divisions within the US administration are sending the wrong message to Iran.
"On the American side, there are also disagreements. The worst thing that happened last night was the American misunderstanding. The vice president is sending what amounts to a plea, which is how the Iranians are describing it this morning."
"JD Vance sends a message to the secretary of Iran's National Security Council and says, 'Let's agree on various things,' 'We'll open the straits,' 'You'll receive medicine.' The Iranians see this as the enemy's surrender."
"There is no such thing as a humanitarian gesture in Iran. It's like the trucks going to Hamas. When you want to help the other side's poor, they interpret it as you not wanting to destroy them. To this day, we are still sending trucks and money to Hamas."
Turning to Iran's economic and social situation, Sabti described worsening conditions and growing tensions.
"The situation is very bad. Yesterday, they raised the price of bread. In a single day, the price of bread jumped by 55%. People are lining up for fuel, and the sounds of war are growing louder.
"The voices coming from the US are voices of despair. The Iranian public sees a letter from the American vice president saying, 'Let's talk.' The Iranians are at a point where another medicine or another Acamol [painkiller] won't help them. They need surgery to actually remove the regime.
"There are millions of Iranians who want to overthrow the regime. That sentiment is there. It's a shame the Americans started something and then seemed to lose faith in it. That is the most ridiculous thing that has happened here. There is no benefit to an attack if they are not going to see it through to the end."
Finally, Sabti addressed the possibility of renewed protests against the Iranian regime, pointing to the symbolic significance of the birthday of Cyrus the Great.
"Today is the birthday of King Cyrus. Iranians are desperate to go out and demonstrate against the regime on such a day. Nobody is calling on them to do so; nobody is talking to them about it. October and November are protest months in Iran, and there is real potential right now.
"If President Trump had called on the Iranian people, perhaps we would be in a different situation. Unfortunately, President Trump has done half the job on many things."

The aircraft was involved in Operation Althea. The causes of the accident still have to be established.
An Italian helicopter taking part in an EU peacekeeping operation has crashed near the town of Brčko in northern Bosnia and Herzegovina.
The European Union's EUFOR military mission confirmed the CH-47 Chinook helicopter had crashed on Thursday afternoon. A spokesman said four crew members had been killed and 11 were injured.
A spokesman for Brčko hospital, said three of the 15 crew members on board the helicopter were killed in the crash and a fourth died in hospital.
"Twelve people were brought to our hospital. Unfortunately, a fourth person died from his injuries in hospital," said the spokesman, Salih Ibrahimbegovic.
EUFOR also said no civilians had been injured and no civilian infrastructure, property or vehicles were damaged in the crash.
The crash happened in Gorice, about 180 kilometres (110 miles) northeast of Sarajevo.
"As a result of this crash, a number of EUFOR personnel tragically lost their lives, and others were seriously injured," EUFOR said in a later statement.
Bosnia's Defence Ministry said "it is not possible to issue further statements, while awaiting more precise information, above all about the state of health of the personnel".
EUFOR has urged people not to spread unverified information or disinformation and to rely on official channels for updates on the incident.
Brčko district mayor Siniša Milić said three people had died and 12 had been injured, with one of those injured in a critical condition.
"All have been treated in a hospital in Brčko. Medical staff are on alert," he said.
Further details about those on board and the cause of the crash are expected to be released once the authorities have completed their investigation.
EUFOR’s roughly 1,200-strong mission has operated in Bosnia since 2004, when it took over from NATO. It works under a UN Security Council mandate to help maintain security and oversee the military provisions of the peace agreement that ended the 1992–95 war.

Senior US general fired, accused of leaking classified information
Italy
