By Phil Stewart
WASHINGTON, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired US Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia, a senior military planner on the Pentagon’s Joint Staff, over accusations he leaked classified information to the public, officials said on Thursday.
Sylvia’s firing is one of the highest-profile consequences to date from Hegseth’s sweeping hunt for officials suspected of leaking information to the news media as the unpopular Iran war enters its ninth month.
Hegseth’s effort includes a Pentagon task force to identify the source of leaks and the widespread use of polygraph exams on senior officials as part of these investigations.
Last year, he introduced a media policy that raised legal concerns among press organizations, and revoked the press credentials of journalists who refused to sign it.
A senior Pentagon official, speaking on condition of anonymity, accused Sylvia of failing three polygraphs questioning him about leaking classified information.
“The extent of his leaking became so critical that Secretary Hegseth took immediate action and fired Sylvia in order to protect national security. Urgent action was needed and could not wait another second,” the official said.
US President Donald Trump, who misidentified Sylvia as a woman, said the senior US general has “got problems.”
“We’re very much looking for leakers, and she’s going to have big problems, long-term problems,” Trump told reporters.
Sylvia could not be immediately reached for comment.
KEY POSITION
Sylvia led the Directorate for Strategy, Plans, and Policy at the Joint Staff, known inside the military as the J5, a key position that helps advise the top US military official, General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
He previously led the US Army’s 101st Airborne Division. His dismissal was first reported by The Atlantic magazine.
His removal comes as the US military plans for a potential resumption of intensive bombings in Iran, something Trump has called “another little Epic Fury.” The Pentagon has fumed about leaks during the Iran war, including about its planning and the expenditure of munitions.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that an internal US military analysis estimates it would cost more than $29 billion in munitions alone to restock weapons used against Iran so far. That’s the bulk of the more than $47 billion spent on operations in the war.
Sean Parnell, the chief Pentagon spokesperson, said the decision followed an extensive investigation by the Air Force Office of Special Investigations.
“This matter, along with others, have been referred to the Justice Department for potential further legal action,” Parnell said, without identifying other officials who may also be targeted.
Parnell added: “Our commitment was not an empty promise. We vowed to find you, and we meant it.”
A spokesperson for the Joint Staff withdrew an initial statement expressing gratitude for Sylvia’s 32 years of service, saying “we determined the statement did not appropriately reflect the full circumstances.”
“Out of respect for the service member and the ongoing personnel process, we will not comment further,” the spokesperson said.
(Reporting by Phil Stewart; additional reporting by Ryan Jones; Editing by Don Durfee and Sanjeev Miglani)

Israel's election results are in: How a government is formed or new elections are triggered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:41:57 UTC
02:41:57 KST

Israel's Central Elections Committee completed the vote count Thursday, leaving the country facing a familiar political dilemma: Neither of the main blocs has secured the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
Despite the inconclusive results, political consultations are already underway, with parties on both sides seeking to assemble a governing coalition and avoid another election. The next stage will place President Isaac Herzog at the center of the process, as party leaders prepare to recommend their preferred candidates for prime minister.
How does Israel form a government after an election, what happens if the first candidate fails, and when could voters be sent back to the polls?
Step by step: What happens after Election Day?
The first step is the official publication of the election results by the Central Elections Committee in Reshumot, Israel's official gazette. Under the law, the committee has eight days from Election Day to publish the results, making Wednesday, November 4, the final deadline.
The 26th Knesset is scheduled to be sworn in on Tuesday, November 10, exactly two weeks after the October 27 election. But the race to form a government will begin before the new parliament formally convenes.
Once the Central Elections Committee submits the official results to President Herzog, he will summon representatives of the parties elected to the Knesset to the President's Residence. Each party will recommend the lawmaker it believes should be tasked with forming the next government.
Herzog is expected to begin consultations on Wednesday, November 4. The meetings are expected to continue Thursday and could extend into Friday.
Under Israeli law, the president has seven days from the publication of the official election results to complete consultations and assign the task of forming a government. If the results are published on November 4, that gives him until November 11, although he may make his decision earlier.
The president generally gives the mandate to the lawmaker he believes has the strongest chance of assembling a governing coalition. In most cases, that is the candidate who receives the largest number of recommendations from parliamentary factions.
The first attempt: 28 days, with a possible extension
The first lawmaker entrusted with forming a government has 28 days to complete coalition negotiations and present a government.
The president may grant additional time, but extensions cannot exceed 14 days in total, giving the candidate a maximum of 42 days.
If the candidate fails, Herzog has two options. He can assign the task to another member of Knesset, potentially the leader of the opposing political bloc, or inform the Knesset speaker that he sees no prospect of forming a government.
A second candidate would receive 28 days to form a coalition, without the possibility of an extension.
The last chance: 61 signatures in 21 days
If the president concludes that no candidate can form a government, or if the second candidate also fails, a final parliamentary mechanism comes into play.
A 21-day period opens during which at least 61 of the Knesset's 120 lawmakers can submit a written request asking the president to assign the task to a specific member of Knesset who has agreed to accept it.
If the required majority of lawmakers signs such a request, the designated candidate receives 14 days to form a government.
If that effort also fails, or no candidate secures the necessary 61 signatures within the allotted period, the Knesset is automatically dissolved and Israel heads to another election.
For now, the election may be over, but the political contest is far from settled. The coming weeks will determine whether the parties can negotiate a coalition capable of securing the Knesset's confidence or whether Israelis will once again be asked to return to the ballot box.

What Ceuta’s border crisis reveals about Frontex’s role in European security
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:39:29 UTC
02:39:29 KST

A rare visit by Spain's King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia to Ceuta earlier this month has brought renewed attention to a migration crisis that continues to strain the Spanish territory on North Africa's Mediterranean coast, nearly three months after an unprecedented influx of migrants from Morocco.
Around 70,000 people crossed into Ceuta in late July, with humanitarian organisations estimating that at least 141 people died during the crossings.
Although most migrants have since left, thousands remained in the territory in October, many sleeping rough as local authorities struggled to provide shelter and essential services.
The royal visit, the first in nearly two decades, also came amid renewed tensions between Spain and Morocco, which maintains a longstanding sovereignty claim over Ceuta.
The crisis has exposed the pressures facing one of Europe's most sensitive external borders, where migration management still relies heavily on physical deterrence, cooperation with neighbouring countries, and emergency measures.
But Ceuta is neither an isolated incident nor an exception. It raises a broader question about the European Union's approach to border management: How does the bloc control its external frontiers, and who is accountable for the machinery behind them?
Part of the answer lies in the dramatic evolution of Frontex, the Warsaw-based European Border and Coast Guard Agency.
Over the past two decades, Frontex has evolved from an agency that primarily coordinates member states' border operations into a heavily funded institution with its own armed standing corps and expanding surveillance capabilities.
Yet, this technological militarisation has not delivered structural stability.
Its expanding use of aerial surveillance and cooperation with third-country authorities have also raised concerns about indirect pushbacks at sea and the division of legal responsibility between Frontex and national authorities.
Investigations into alleged pushbacks, oversight failures, and the agency's response to maritime emergencies have intensified scrutiny of whether Europe's expanding border security system is compatible with its fundamental rights obligations.
The rise of Frontex
As European integration deepened, migration and border management increasingly became matters of security policy.
The 1992 Maastricht Treaty marked an early step towards intergovernmental cooperation on migration, while the 1997 Amsterdam Treaty established the Area of Freedom, Security and Justice (AFSJ) as a central element of EU policy.
The 1999 Tampere European Council summit subsequently laid the foundations for the Common European Asylum System (CEAS).
Population movements following the collapse of the Soviet Union, the EU's eastward enlargement and the September 11, 2001 attacks further reinforced the association between migration, terrorism and border security.
Although a 2001 German-Italian proposal for a joint border police force stalled over concerns about national sovereignty, the 2003 Thessaloniki summit agreed to establish an operational mechanism to manage the EU's external borders.
The Council subsequently established Frontex under Regulation (EC) No 2007/2004, based on Articles 62 and 66 of the EC Treaty. Headquartered in Warsaw, the agency began operations on 1 May 2005.
Initially responsible for coordinating border operations among member states, conducting risk assessments and providing training, Frontex has gradually evolved into a large operational border force with armed personnel.
Its budget, approximately €6 million in 2005, has grown to more than €900 million annually, while successive regulatory changes, notably Regulation (EU) 2016/1624 and Regulation (EU) 2019/1896, have expanded its powers.
Under the 2019 regulation, Frontex aims to reach an operational capacity of 10,000 personnel by 2027, comprising 3,000 statutory Frontex staff and 7,000 personnel contributed by member states.
Equipped with uniforms, operational equipment and the authority to carry firearms under specified conditions, the standing corps represents a significant departure from the agency's original coordinating role.
Europe's expanding border security framework
The EU's increasingly security-oriented approach to migration was further reinforced by the adoption of the New Pact on Migration and Asylum in 2024.
The pact introduced a seven-day screening procedure at the EU's external borders, along with accelerated asylum and return procedures for certain applicants.
Under the framework, some asylum seekers may be treated as not having formally entered EU territory while their applications are processed, raising concerns about access to asylum procedures and legal safeguards.
The pact also expanded the Eurodac biometric database, lowering the minimum age for collecting fingerprints and facial images from 14 to six.
Its solidarity mechanism allows member states to contribute through relocation, financial payments or other forms of support, while the broader framework places greater emphasis on cooperation with third countries in managing migration.
Yet as Frontex's operational powers have expanded, questions have persisted over who bears responsibility when alleged rights violations occur.
The agency operates alongside national border authorities, creating a complex division of responsibilities between Frontex, host member states and other participating countries.
While national authorities retain responsibility for many operational decisions, Frontex provides personnel, surveillance capabilities and intelligence support.
Critics argue that this arrangement can complicate efforts to establish responsibility for alleged violations and make it more difficult for affected individuals to seek legal redress.
Pushbacks and the accountability question
Investigations by European oversight bodies and journalists have raised serious concerns about Frontex's involvement in unlawful pushbacks and how it handles evidence of alleged rights violations.
A European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) investigation found that then-executive director Fabrice Leggeri and senior agency officials were aware of illegal pushbacks carried out by the Greek Coast Guard in the Aegean Sea.
The investigation documented failures to report incidents and attempts to conceal evidence of alleged violations, including deleting records and diverting surveillance flights. It also raised concerns about interference with the agency's fundamental rights monitoring mechanisms.
Leggeri resigned in April 2022. The European Parliament subsequently refused to grant discharge for Frontex's 2020 budget, citing concerns over the agency's management and accountability.
Questions about Frontex's responsibilities also emerged following the Adriana shipwreck off the coast of Greece in June 2023, in which hundreds of migrants and asylum seekers died.
An investigation by the European Ombudsman found shortcomings in Frontex's response to maritime emergencies and raised questions about its ability to act independently when vessels are in distress.
The agency detected the overcrowded vessel by aerial surveillance before it sank, but the disaster exposed gaps in communication, coordination, and responsibility between Frontex and national authorities.
Such controversies have fuelled calls for greater oversight and, in some cases, the agency's dismantling.
The Abolish Frontex movement, a coalition of civil society organisations and activists across Europe, has campaigned to abolish the agency, citing alleged rights violations, biometric surveillance, and its role in enforcing restrictive border policies.
Frontex's growing reliance on aerial and satellite surveillance, alongside its maritime operations, has raised concerns that its border-monitoring practices could facilitate interceptions that circumvent international maritime law and search-and-rescue obligations.
Operating from bases in Malta and Pantelleria, unmanned aerial vehicles developed by Israel Aerospace Industries and Elbit Systems, alongside the EU's Copernicus satellite network, are used to detect migrant boats in the Mediterranean.
Critics argue that surveillance information can be shared with the Libyan Coast Guard or Tunisian authorities rather than civilian rescue organisations, enabling third-country forces to intercept migrants and return them to countries where they may face abuse.
Because such interceptions can occur without direct physical involvement by EU personnel, questions have emerged about whether Frontex is facilitating what critics describe as “refoulement by proxy”.
Human Rights Watch has accused Frontex of complicity in abuses against migrants intercepted and returned to Libya, raising concerns about the agency's responsibilities under the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning people to places where they face serious threats to their safety or fundamental rights.
The paradox of fortress Europe
Events along Ceuta’s perimeter and unmanned patrols tracing the central Mediterranean are two sides of the same coin.
On the periphery, frontline states rely on ad hoc physical barriers, bilateral appeasement of authoritarian transit regimes, and immediate pushbacks.
Meanwhile, at the institutional core in Brussels and Warsaw, billions of euros continue to pour into an autonomous surveillance and security architecture designed to insulate the European mainland from the human reality at its gates.
As Frontex marches toward its 2027 goal of a 10,000-strong armed standing corps under the codified framework of the 2024 New Pact on Migration and Asylum, the central paradox remains unresolved.
Advanced surveillance drones, automated biometric screening, and outsourced interception do not eliminate the root causes of forced displacement; they can instead shift difficult questions of legal responsibility into a fragmented jurisdictional space.
Unless subject to enforceable judicial oversight by the Court of Justice of the European Union, independent scrutiny by civil society, and uncompromising operational transparency, Frontex will remain what the Ceuta crisis so starkly laid bare: a multibillion-euro “security illusion” that continually undermines the foundational human rights norms upon which the European Union was built.

====================================================================================================

World Stroke Day: how to recognize dangerous symptoms, save a life, and prevent the disease
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
19:37:16 EET
02:37:16 KST

World Stroke Day: how to recognize dangerous symptoms, save a life, and prevent the disease
Kyiv • UNN
Stroke symptoms occur suddenly: call 103 or 112 immediately. In Ukraine, diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation are covered by the NHSU.
On October 29, the world observes World Stroke Day—a disease that can cause disability or death within minutes. Its first signs are sometimes mistaken for fatigue or stress, resulting in precious time being lost. UNN explains how to recognize the symptoms, help the affected person, and receive free treatment in Ukraine.
Details
The World Stroke Organization’s campaign in 2026 is being held under the slogan Every Minute Counts ("Every minute matters"). Its aim is to teach people to recognize the danger in time and call emergency services.
What a stroke is and why it occurs
A stroke is an acute disruption of cerebral blood circulation. Without sufficient oxygen, brain cells begin to die. Consequences may include impaired movement, speech, vision, memory, and coordination. An ischemic stroke occurs because a blood vessel is blocked by a clot and accounts for the majority of cases. A hemorrhagic stroke is caused by a vessel rupturing and bleeding. Treatment for these conditions differs, and it is impossible to determine the type based on external signs: urgent diagnosis using CT or MRI is required.
Contrary to everyday myths, a stroke does not occur only in older people. If a young person has problems with high blood pressure, heart disease, heart rhythm disorders, diabetes, or vascular damage, they are just as likely to suffer a stroke as older patients.
How many strokes are recorded in Ukraine and worldwide
According to WHO estimates, 11.9 million new strokes occurred worldwide in 2021. Approximately one in four adults is at risk of experiencing a stroke during their lifetime. In addition, stroke is one of the leading causes of death and disability both in Ukraine and in most countries worldwide.
According to the Ministry of Health, 128,075 Ukrainians were diagnosed with a stroke in 2024. A statement by the Kyiv Regional Military Administration dated October 29, 2026, says that more than 90,000 cases of acute stroke were treated in Ukraine during the first eight months of this year. In turn, Ministry of Health expert Professor Yuriy Flomin reported that 68,116 hospitalizations for acute stroke were recorded during the first half of 2026. The share of hospitalizations at facilities with a contract with the National Health Service of Ukraine increased from 86% in 2021 to 96.5% in the first half of 2026.
Speaking about strokes in Ukraine, it is worth emphasizing that, despite the war, access to specialized care for people suffering from this condition is improving. According to the data cited by Flomin, thrombolysis was used in 18% of hospitalizations for ischemic stroke during the first half of 2026, while mechanical thrombectomy was performed in 3.7%. CT, MRI, or angiographic examinations were recorded in 98.1% of hospitalizations for acute stroke.
How to recognize a stroke: five warning signs that should not be ignored
Signs of a stroke usually appear suddenly. Ukrainian doctors advise remembering them using the acronym MOZOK, where
-  M - speech. The person speaks unclearly, confuses words
or does not understand the other person; 
-  O - face. The corner of the mouth droops, and the smile becomes
asymmetrical; 
-  Z - dizziness. Balance and
coordination are impaired; sometimes a sudden, very severe headache occurs; 
-  O - eyes. Vision suddenly deteriorates, and objects appear double; 
-  K - limbs. An arm or leg becomes weak or numb,
more often on one side of the body. 
You can also ask a person suspected of having a stroke to smile, repeat a sentence, and raise both arms. Difficulty performing even one of these actions is a reason to call an ambulance immediately.
A severe headache, vomiting, or sudden drowsiness also requires attention, especially if it occurs simultaneously with other signs. Sometimes the symptoms disappear quickly. This may be a transient ischemic attack—a short-term disruption of blood flow to the brain that warns of the risk of a stroke. Even if the person feels better, emergency examination is necessary.
How to recognize a stroke: Ukrainians reminded of dangerous symptoms28.10.24, 15:57 • 13579 views
First aid for a stroke: what to do before medical professionals arrive
First of all, you should immediately call 103 or 112. The dispatcher needs to be told the address, the symptoms, and that a stroke is suspected. It is also important to remember when the person was last known to be well, as the choice of treatment depends on this.
Until the medics arrive, ensure that the person remains calm and loosen any tight clothing. If the patient is conscious, help them assume a comfortable position. If the person is unconscious but breathing normally, place them on their side. This is done to prevent stomach contents from entering the lungs if the patient begins to vomit. This position also reduces the risk of choking on their own saliva.
If normal breathing is absent, begin cardiopulmonary resuscitation according to the dispatcher’s instructions.
A person suspected of having a brain hemorrhage or thrombosis of the brain’s blood vessels must not be given water, medication, or food. Because of impaired swallowing, they may choke. Aspirin is particularly dangerous among medications. It can harm the person because it thins the blood. This is life-threatening in the case of a hemorrhagic stroke.
Before the medics arrive, prepare the person’s documents, a list of the medications the patient takes, and information about any comorbidities so that dispatch to the hospital is not delayed because of this.
How to receive free stroke treatment in Ukraine
Acute stroke care is covered by the Medical Guarantees Program at hospitals that have the relevant contract with the NHSU. In August 2026, the service reported that there were 179 such facilities.
Free services include an examination by a neurologist, a CT or MRI scan, tests, round-the-clock monitoring, medications, inpatient treatment, food, and early rehabilitation. When indicated, thrombolysis (dissolving a clot with medication), mechanical thrombectomy (removing a clot through the blood vessels), or neurosurgical intervention is performed. The treatment method depends on the type of stroke and when the symptoms began. Thrombolysis is possible only under certain conditions and within a limited time, and it is not used in cases of hemorrhage.
According to international recommendations, emergency neuroimaging should be performed as soon as possible. In Ukraine, the standard provides for aiming to perform a CT or MRI scan no later than 30 minutes after the patient is admitted. The NHSU emphasizes separately that patients should not have to pay for a CT or MRI when a stroke is suspected as part of inpatient care. You can clarify the list of facilities or complain about demands for payment by calling 16-77.
Who is at risk and how to prevent a stroke
The main risk factor in this situation is high blood pressure. It may cause no symptoms while gradually damaging the blood vessels. Smoking, high cholesterol, diabetes, obesity, physical inactivity, alcohol, and heart rhythm disorders are also dangerous.
To prevent stroke, the WHO recommends monitoring blood pressure, blood sugar, and cholesterol; not stopping prescribed treatment; quitting smoking; limiting salt and alcohol; and eating more vegetables and fruit. At least 150 minutes of moderate physical activity per week is beneficial if there are no contraindications.
For heart rhythm disorders, a doctor may prescribe medications to prevent blood clots. However, taking such medications without medical supervision is dangerous.
Ukraine also has the "Health Screening 40+" program for the early detection of risks, while under the "Affordable Medicines" program, certain medications can be obtained free of charge or with a co-payment.
Life after a stroke: is recovery possible?
Although many strokes still end in the patient’s death at home or in hospital, many patients overcome this condition with the help of medical professionals and survive. However, the consequences of the illness may include impaired movement, speech, memory, or swallowing, as well as anxiety, fatigue, and depressive symptoms. Some patients require long-term—and sometimes lifelong—assistance from others. The prognosis depends on the severity of the stroke, the timeliness of treatment, and rehabilitation.
Rehabilitation begins as soon as the patient’s condition allows. A physical therapist, occupational therapist, speech and language therapist, and psychologist help restore movement, communication, and self-care. The process may take months and requires family support.
After discharge in Ukraine, a person may receive inpatient or outpatient rehabilitation, as indicated. At facilities that have a contract with the NHSU, it is covered by the Medical Guarantees Program. A doctor refers a patient for an inpatient course; transfer from another facility is also possible. The sessions are tailored to each individual: one person may need to learn to walk again, while another may need to restore swallowing or the ability to form words. It is important for relatives to help the person follow the specialists’ recommendations, but not to force them to do exercises beyond their capabilities.
To prevent a recurrent stroke, it is necessary to monitor blood pressure, glucose, and cholesterol and follow the doctor’s instructions. Unfortunately, a stroke cannot always be prevented. However, knowing the signs of a stroke according to the B.E.-F.A.S.T. formula, promptly calling 103, and managing risk factors can help save lives and reduce the likelihood of severe consequences.
Let us remind you
The Ministry of Health warns that recently more and more middle-aged people have been suffering strokes: as of 2019, more than 62% of stroke cases occurred in people under the age of 70.

Russia still hasn’t found an effective way to curb VPNs. Now officials are considering limits on all foreign internet traffic.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:36:19 UTC
02:36:19 KST

Russia still hasn’t found an effective way to curb VPNs. Now officials are considering limits on all foreign internet traffic.
What happened?
On October 27, Forbes reported that Russia’s Digital Development Ministry is considering routing all foreign internet traffic through TSPU filtering equipment (TSPU is the Russian acronym for “technical means of countering threats”), effectively separating the Russian internet from the global internet at a technical level.
The measure could primarily affect people who use VPN services to bypass blocks. The plan is to cap the amount of foreign data each user can consume. The proposed limit is not yet known.
Several sources told Forbes about the proposals, which will likely be included in a bill to overhaul the telecommunications industry. The authorities have been preparing changes to telecommunications laws since the spring and are discussing specific proposals with major industry players. The Digital Development Ministry stressed that all the proposed measures “are being examined, but it is premature to say which will make it into the final amendments or in what form.”
Haven’t there been proposals like this before?
Not quite. First, in the spring, the Digital Development Ministry wanted to limit foreign traffic only on mobile networks. Now, the proposal apparently also covers home internet connections.
Second, the earlier plan called for telecommunications providers themselves to identify and limit foreign traffic. The ministry asked them to charge users extra if they used more than 15 gigabytes of foreign data a month. BBC News Russian reported that each additional gigabyte would have cost 150 rubles. Now, the ministry plans to impose the restrictions itself using TSPU equipment.
What would the authorities gain from this?
The Digital Development Ministry intends to use this approach to combat VPNs that allow users to bypass Russian internet blocks. These services are generally based abroad, as are most of their servers. So when users connect to one of these VPNs, all their traffic becomes foreign traffic, even when they visit Russian websites.
VPN services could try to rent servers inside Russia to get around the data cap. But this summer, the authorities banned Russian hosting providers from serving them.
There are also plans to create a register of violators who have used servers in Russia to run VPNs. If caught bypassing blocks, they will be barred from signing contracts with hosting providers in Russia for a full year. In other words, using Russian hosting infrastructure will become even harder in the future.
But for now, too much about the proposal remains unknown, Sarkis Darbinyan, a digital rights lawyer and expert at RKS.global, told Meduza:
It’s unclear what exactly the ministry will consider a foreign domain, whether there will be exemption allowlists, and what will happen once the quota runs out: disconnection, slower speeds, or an extra charge. These details will determine whether the measure specifically targets VPNs or affects everyone.
How does the ministry plan to identify foreign traffic?
We don’t know. Most likely, by IP address. Since 2019, Russia’s communications regulator, Roskomnadzor, has required Russian holders of autonomous system numbers, which identify networks, to report their network addresses and notify the agency of any changes within three business days. Roskomnadzor can use those addresses to determine whether a given data packet came from Russia or abroad.
But under this approach, even people who don’t use VPNs could find that some traffic from Russian websites is technically classified as foreign. Much depends on whether individual components of a webpage — fonts, images, or videos — load from foreign sources and exactly how the data is routed. Even traffic from a site with an IP address registered in Russia can pass through nodes abroad. This could happen, for example, because of the particular terms of traffic-exchange agreements between telecommunications providers or because traffic takes alternative routes during network outages.
How would TSPU equipment limit an individual user’s foreign traffic?
We don’t know this for certain, either. The difficulty is that TSPU equipment filters data packets that don’t explicitly identify the user they belong to. Only the source and destination IP addresses are visible. That information is not enough to limit a particular person’s foreign traffic: Different subscribers can use the same IP address at different times.
Telecommunications providers, however, have the missing information. In the spring of 2025, they were required to give Roskomnadzor comprehensive information about their subscribers, including their assigned IP addresses and the number identifying the specific TSPU device through which each user’s traffic passes.
Since December 2025, telecommunications providers have been subject to fines of 300,000 to 500,000 rubles for each failure to provide this information.
If the ministry’s proposal is adopted, how will it affect ordinary Russians?
For now, we can only speculate. But requiring all foreign traffic to pass through a filter that tracks quotas would clearly make it easier to slow and ration that traffic. This would be another major step in the authorities’ campaign against independent VPNs, and users of those services would be hit hardest, Darbinyan said. Besides finding a working VPN, they would have to decide how best to use their allotted gigabytes of foreign data, choosing between videos, games, social media, and other sites and services unavailable in Russia.
Darbinyan said there could be several other consequences:
- There will be problems with updates. Updates for iOS, Windows, and games can run to tens of gigabytes. A single file could eat up a month’s allowance. “And then,” Darbinyan said, “if you can’t afford an extra international data package, you’re stuck without up-to-date software.” That creates an additional risk: Devices without updates are more vulnerable to scammers and malware, both of which are proliferating with the AI boom.
- Developers, IT workers, and remote workers will suffer. Using GitHub, Docker Hub, cloud services, Zoom, and Microsoft 365, or working with foreign clients, means using lots of foreign data. “For freelancers, students taking international online courses, and scientists, the restrictions will become an obstacle to their work. Online gaming will probably become a pastime only for the wealthy, who can afford to pay for extra gigabytes, since gaming requires enormous amounts of data,” Darbinyan told Meduza.
Still, Darbinyan believes the authorities are unlikely to impose a strict, very low cap on everyone at once:
Technically, it’s very difficult, and politically, it’s costly — because it would upset users opposed to the government as well as businesses, the IT industry, and gamers. Most likely, they’ll start with mobile networks, a generous cap, and extensive allowlists, then gradually tighten the restrictions.
This measure is also unlikely to make foreign services disappear entirely. The aim, apparently, is to make access to foreign services inconvenient, slow, and expensive so that people switch to Russian alternatives on their own, rather than to cut off access to everything abroad.

Analysis: Kevin Warsh is keeping Wall Street guessing. It may be his most powerful tool
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:32:34 UTC
02:32:34 KST

Kevin Warsh is done proving himself.
The Federal Reserve chairman's news conference Wednesday was sharply different from his early appearances in the job, when he often seemed backed into a corner. He's shown he is willing to let the markets guess where he is going — at least to a point. And he has started using his authority to reshape the institution.
Warsh was appointed by a president who said cutting interest rates was a litmus test for his choice for Fed chair. When the Federal Open Market Committee opted to hold rates flat in June and July, even with inflation well above the Fed's 2% target, a swarm of commentators questioned the new chairman's credibility. The FOMC's subsequent decision in September to raise rates came with such a hawkish reading of the economy by Warsh that the markets swung sharply in the opposite direction. Investors thought the Fed might be locked into a rate hike this week until a pair of top officials came out and appeared to deliberately temper market expectations.
This week, Warsh put all that behind him. He disavowed any expectation that the Fed is on a set course: "If we had a firm conclusion about the conduct of monetary policy, we'd announce it to much fanfare today," he said.
But Warsh also gave a strong signal that his current lean is toward higher rates. "While overall financial conditions are tighter, I'm unwilling and unable to call them tight," he said.
He was preserving his options while laying the intellectual groundwork for a hike in December, should inflation remain stubborn.
Warsh declined to confirm the widespread assumption in the markets that the officials who had talked down the markets had done so at his direction. Fed insiders have said that the central bank's vice chairs usually coordinate messaging with the chair.
"To suggest somehow that I am some kind of all-knowing person sending messages out, that's not the committee of the FOMC that I know," Warsh said. And yet the market got the message that the Fed wouldn't hike this week. If Warsh wants to give otherwise taboo forward guidance through his lieutenants, he now has plausible deniability.
This is Warsh's MO: He is intellectually flexible and highly focused on achieving his goals.
For instance, one of the goals of the task forces he has assembled to kick-start policy changes is to change the way the Fed measures inflation. But that was impossible while his commitment to fighting it was in question. September's rate hike does a lot to answer the skeptics who said he wasn't serious about slowing price increases, and he is willing to deliver more rate increases, if necessary.
"If you think that we're tolerating some inflation target somewhere in the twos, let us disabuse you of it," Warsh said Wednesday. The target is 2% flat. His remarks are a recipe for higher rates as long as the economy stays strong.
Warsh and the FOMC will have a raft of new data before the next meeting, in December, to make their case. That could, alternatively, help him make the case that productivity is rising, allowing for more growth without inflation.
Meanwhile, Warsh's other changes at the Fed are starting to take effect. He announced a plan Wednesday to reduce the number of times the FOMC is scheduled to vote on interest rates over the next two years. The Fed will keep meeting eight times a year, but will skip a vote on whether to change rates at one meeting in 2027 and two in 2028. That move has the effect of devaluing a good chunk of Fedspeak. The market won't pay much mind to a marginal regional Fed president's comments when they come as much as three months ahead of a rate decision. Regional presidents also get one fewer scheduled vote in their yearlong rotations as decision-makers on the FOMC.
The Fed chairman retains the authority to call an impromptu meeting at any time should he see the need to change rates.
But there are risks to Warsh's way of doing business, especially as he recedes further behind the curtain. The advocates for Fed transparency believe that sunlight adds more rigor to officials' arguments.
That could already be a problem, said Robert Sockin, chief U.S. economist at asset manager PGIM. He is in the camp that thinks inflation is running too hot to justify the Fed's decision not to raise rates this week.
"While more data is always better, Warsh did not sufficiently explain why this backdrop did not justify a rate increase, particularly given his comment that while he thinks financial conditions have tightened, he would not say they are tight," Sockin said.
It was a "policy mistake" to hold, "and a gradual Fed likely means one that has to hike higher, mechanically raising recession risk," Sockin said.
The full consequences of Warsh's approach may not become clear for months. That gives him room to maneuver as he reshapes the Fed. But it also means the consequences of waiting to tighten may not become apparent until it's too late.

Israel election: Authorities dispute Netanyahu’s fraud claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:32:00 UTC
02:32:00 KST

Israel election: Authorities dispute Netanyahu's fraud claims
October 29, 2026
Israel woke up on Thursday to allegations by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party that foreign actors may have sought to influence voter mobilization efforts in Arab communities during this week's legislative election.
No'am Sohlberg, the Supreme Court judge who heads Israel's Central Election Committee, sent a letter to Israel's internal security agency Shin Bet to look into the Likud's claims.
According to Likud's statement, Arab parties Ra'am and the Joint List — which received a record share of the vote, mostly due to unprecedented turnout in communities of Arab and Palestinians with Israeli citizenship — allegedly used "severe criminal offenses" to spur voters to go to the polls, including bribery, threats and other forms of election fraud.
"Severe suspicions were brought to my attention about improper intervention in the elections by foreign funding by outside actors that act against the Israeli interest," Sohlberg wrote in the letter, adding that he was "unable to testify" as to whether the allegations are true.
"The elections in the State of Israel were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the elimination of the Jewish state," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's party claimed in a statement. His own coalition lost seats, leaving both the prime minister and his opponents short of a majority — unless they were to work with one or both of the Arab parties.
Likud and other right-wing figures pointed to the unusually high turnout in Arab communities, reports of organized transportation to polling stations and concerns over foreign-funded voter mobilization campaigns as grounds for requesting an investigation. They argue that a formal review is necessary to maintain public confidence in the electoral process, regardless of whether wrongdoing is ultimately found.
Authorities refute allegations
Israel's elections are administered by the Central Election Committee, a body comprising representatives of parliamentary parties and chaired by a Supreme Court justice. Large-scale election fraud has historically been rare, although disputes over campaign conduct and voting procedures regularly arise.
Israeli police said there is no evidence to support Likud's claims, neither "investigative” nor "informative.”
"Election day went with a minority of irregular incidents in the area of election integrity, also compared to other elections," it said in a statement.
A high-ranking Central Election Committee official, too, denied the allegations.
"We don't have any basis for claims of 'stolen elections,'" Dean Livne, the Committee's acting director general, told Israeli public broadcaster Kan 11, adding that the committee received "claims rather than evidence" from Likud and other parties.
Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main competitor and the head of the Yashar party, blamed the Israeli leader for leading an "improper influence operation" to cast doubt on the elections and create what he called "a fictive delegitimization" for the next parliament.
However, Eisenkot, also called for Likud's allegation of electoral fraud to be investigated.
The religious Muslim Ra'am party denied any involvement and said it would cooperate with any investigation.
Qatar released a statement denying any involvement in the Israeli elections, calling them "false propaganda aimed at dragging Qatar's name into Israel's political conflicts."
The controversy comes against the backdrop of growing polarization in Israeli politics and increasing public distrust between rival political camps.
Likud's motivation could be to decrease the Arab influence on Israeli politics, according to Amira Halperin, a senior fellow at the Palm Beach Center for Democracy and Policy Research. "The Arab votes were very, very important in this election," she said.
Such allegations could also hurt the public's trust in the election process Halperin argued: "We need to be cautious about predicting a failure of the democratic system."
Shin Bet head in focus
Israeli media reports have suggested that some of the concerns cited by Likud were based on intelligence assessments examined by the Shin Bet, though the agency has not publicly confirmed the details of any such findings.
Public broadcaster Kan reported the suspicions' extent as "relatively small," citing sources familiar with the Shin Bet investigation. Israeli daily Ha'aretz, too, quoted sources familiar with the allegations as saying the reports are "being blown out of proportion.”
David Zini, the head of the agency, said on election day that the elections in Israel are "safe, sound and supervised," adding that the Elections Committee and Israeli police are "successfully" preventing anyone from hurting it.
Zini's appointment earlier this year was criticized by opposition figures, who questioned both his qualifications for the role and Netanyahu's motives in selecting him. Supporters of the appointment rejected those criticisms, arguing that Zini's military experience and security background made him suitable for the position.
Separately, the Shin Bet, has been involved in investigating several of Netanyahu's closest aides on allegations of undisclosed ties to Qatar. Those investigations are unrelated to the current election allegations.
Pre-planned tactics?
Israeli outlet N12 has reported that in the weekend before the elections that Likud officials were discussing potential election-integrity complaints ahead of voting, although no evidence of actual irregularities had been presented at that stage, with a focus on Arab and Palestinian communities .
"They sat and brainstormed to find creative ideas of how to complain about this issue," said Daphna Liel, the reporter who broke the story.
Historic turnout
Arab and Palestinian participation in this week's election was unprecedented, with turnout jumping from around 50% in 2022 to about 80% in 2026, according to reports in Israel.
Arab voter participation has fluctuated significantly in recent decades. Turnout has often been influenced by debates within Arab society over whether participation in national elections can effectively advance the interests of Arab citizens, who comprise roughly 20% of Israel's population. The exceptionally high turnout in this election was widely seen as a sign of renewed political mobilization.
This resulted in huge success forthe Joint List and Ra'am, with 11 and eight parliament seats, respectively, in comparison to six and four in the 2022 election. Both parties have already voiced their willingness to cooperate with Israel's Zionist opposition to replace Netanyahu.
Most parties in Israel's Zionist opposition promised not to join a coalition with Arab parties ahead of the elections, with the exception of left-wing Zionist party "The Democrats” (HaDemocratim).
On election day, there were also allegations over "systematic delays" in voting in Arab and Palestinian polling stations, according to Adalah, an Israeli-Palestinian NGO for the legal rights of the Arab minority in Israel.

His removal comes as the U.S. military plans for a potential resumption of intensive bombings in Iran, something Trump has called "another little Epic Fury." The Pentagon has fumed about leaks during the Iran war, including about its planning and the expenditure of munitions.
Reuters reported on Wednesday that an internal U.S. military analysis estimates it would cost more than $29 billion in munitions alone to restock weapons used against Iran so far. That's the bulk of the more than $47 billion spent on operations in the war.
Sean Parnell, the chief Pentagon spokesperson, said the decision followed an extensive investigation by the Air Force Office of Special Investigations.
"This matter, along with others, have been referred to the Justice Department for potential further legal action," Parnell said, without identifying other officials who may also be targeted.
Parnell added: "Our commitment was not an empty promise. We vowed to find you, and we meant it."
A spokesperson for the Joint Staff withdrew an initial statement expressing gratitude for Sylvia's 32 years of service, saying "we determined the statement did not appropriately reflect the full circumstances."
"Out of respect for the service member and the ongoing personnel process, we will not comment further," the spokesperson said.

Sylvia's firing is one of the highest-profile consequences to date from Hegseth's sweeping hunt for officials suspected of leaking information to the news media as the unpopular Iran war enters its ninth month.
Hegseth's effort includes a Pentagon task force to identify the source of leaks and the widespread use of polygraph exams on senior officials as part of these investigations.
Last year, he introduced a media policy that raised legal concerns among press organizations, and revoked the press credentials of journalists who refused to sign it.

The morning after: Israel’s election leaves more questions than answers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:30:13 UTC
02:30:13 KST

Israelis went to the polls expecting clarity. What they got instead was a political puzzle no one seems able to solve. On the latest episode of The Deep Dive, host Jacob Laznik and Knesset correspondent Keshet Neev unpack a whirlwind week in which months of polling were overturned almost overnight.
With more than 97% of votes counted, Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud emerged as the largest party at around 27 seats, and his bloc leads the opposition 53 to 48, yet neither side has a path to 61.
Arab parties make the difference
The kingmakers in this deadlock are the Arab parties, which won a record 19 seats on the back of turnout above 80%, well past their previous high of 15. That surge also raised the electoral threshold and wiped out every small party that had dominated months of pre-election speculation.
The conversation moves quickly through the scenarios now being whispered in the Knesset corridors. Could a unity government bring together Netanyahu, Gadi Eisenkot and Naftali Bennett? Laznik floats a provocative “200 IQ” scenario for how it might play out, and both hosts explain why the parties’ policy promises may make such a coalition unworkable, pointing to the Gantz precedent as a cautionary tale. They also examine the Arab parties’ unusual new posture, now focused less on longstanding red lines and more on ousting Netanyahu, alongside Avigdor Liberman’s role as the opposition’s wild card.
Then there is the story that broke publicly later: a Shin Bet investigation into possible foreign interference, with Qatar and Turkey reportedly under scrutiny. Qatar has denied involvement, and the Central Elections Committee says the integrity of the vote remains intact.
The hosts also look beyond Israel’s borders. They discuss how next week’s US midterms could reshape Washington’s approach to Iran, why reports of Donald Trump’s views on far-right ministers might push Netanyahu toward a broader coalition, and what it means that Netanyahu used election night to name toppling the Iranian regime as his first priority. They also reflect on what these first post–October 7 elections reveal: a Netanyahu bloc still in the lead, but noticeably weaker than before the war.
Neev offers viewers a practical guide for cutting through the deliberate noise of the coming weeks. As Laznik puts it, anyone claiming to know what happens next is lying.

Israel’s exit polls may have ‘fundamental problem’ after Netanyahu bloc surprise, pollster says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:29:56 UTC
02:29:56 KST

Israeli pollsters significantly underestimated Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's political bloc in the latest election, Dr. Menachem Lazar, CEO of Lazar Research and Maariv's pollster, acknowledged in an interview with Nissim Mishal and Anat Davidov on 103FM, as he attempted to explain the discrepancies between the polls and the election results.
According to Lazar, there is no room for doubt.
"The pollsters were wrong, all of them. Some more than others, but there was a mistake. A serious mistake. I could argue that the last poll I conducted was on the Thursday before the election and that things happened between then and the election, but that is not really the reason. We were wrong. We saw a picture that ultimately turned out to be different. We gave the opposition a majority, and we saw that the Netanyahu coalition had a majority."
Lazar elaborated on the extent of the polling failure.
"We will have to conduct a full assessment of what happened once we see the final results. We need to wait another day. We underestimated the Netanyahu bloc, underestimated Benjamin Netanyahu's strength. We saw more or less the same thing in the 2015 election, how on the final day of the election he managed to increase Likud's strength."
He then explained how election polling is conducted and what the discrepancies might indicate about Israeli voters.
"There are two things that need to be done correctly with an exit poll: correctly distribute the polling stations, thoroughly examine how the exit poll polling stations were selected, look at the difference between the nationwide distribution and the distribution of those polling stations, and conduct another examination of the gap between the exit poll ballot box and the actual ballot box next to it.
"The exit poll ballot box is supposed to represent the actual ballot box beside it. This is not the first time. There may be a fundamental problem here, either with the polling stations and how the exit polls are positioned and constructed, or with how the Israeli public behaves ahead of elections."
'Neither side won'
Addressing accusations that the polls were intended to manipulate public opinion, Lazar said:
"Clearly, everything will head in that direction. There are more serious things we will need to examine. We examine ourselves after every election campaign. There is no election in which we produce results that match the parties' results exactly. Generally, we produce much better results when it comes to the blocs. There was the 2015 election, when there was also a similar discrepancy. We corrected ourselves in the election campaigns that followed. We will examine, correct, and hope that in the next rounds it will work better."
Lazar also addressed the issue of double-envelope ballots and the changes they could bring to the final distribution of Knesset seats.
"In my assessment, apart from the fact that the Arab parties have a smaller share of the overall vote, this should reflect what we are seeing in the Jewish sector. It could push the Reservists' Party and the Economic Party above the electoral threshold. They are short by around 40,000 votes, and they may reach that number.
"There is a certain chance that it could instead go to the Jewish Home party and Naftali Bennett, who were short by 1,400 votes, or Meretz, which was short by several thousand votes. Once again, a party could be on the threshold. We need to wait."
Lazar explained that the remaining ballots could also affect the balance between the political blocs, although he believes the overall election picture is relatively clear.
"The Arab parties could lose one or two seats, and there could be movement between the blocs. There are also the surplus-vote agreements. I think the overall picture looks fairly clear. Neither side won, and the entire argument is about who lost less. Now the question is how to form a government with this situation, or whether to go to new elections, where there are also assessments of what might happen."

Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg directed Shin Bet Director David Zini to investigate the suspected foreign funding and election interference.
The integrity of the vote at polling stations had been maintained, the Central Elections Committee said.
The official vote count announced on Thursday included the remaining double-envelope ballots, which were the last to be counted.
How many seats does each party have?
Netanyahu’s Likud is projected to enter with 27 seats, making it once again the largest party in the Knesset. United Torah Judaism and Otzma Yehudit are expected to enter with seven seats, and the Religious Zionist Party and Shas are expected to enter with six seats.
Most TV channel polls before the elections showed Likud receiving significantly fewer seats, while other parties in Netanyahu’s bloc, including Shas and Otzma Yehudit, were projected to gain more.
The opposition bloc, comprising Yashar, B’Yachad, Yisrael Beytenu, and The Democrats, is expected to enter the Knesset with 48 seats.
Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar is projected to enter the Knesset with 21 seats. B’Yachad, led by Naftali Bennett, is expected to enter with 12 seats. Yair Golan’s The Democrats is expected to enter the Knesset with eight seats. Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beytenu is expected to enter with seven.
The Joint List was projected to win 11 seats, while Ra’am was projected to secure eight seats in the next Knesset.
Most TV channel polling before the elections had shown the opposition bloc in the lead, and Yashar was projected to be the largest party in the Knesset.
Ofer Winter’s People of Israel party and Yoaz Hendel’s The Reservists-Economic party both fell short of the required 3.25% threshold.
The prospect of a unity government involving Netanyahu and Eisenkot remains possible, although Eisenkot had previously rejected serving under Netanyahu, including in a rotation government. Other opposition leaders have also ruled out joining a coalition led by Netanyahu.
The political deadlock could also ultimately lead to another election, although the parties may still reach an agreement through coalition negotiations.

Belgium to vote on 'ICE-style' undocumented migrant home raids
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:29:27 UTC
02:29:27 KST

Breadcrumb
Belgium to vote on 'ICE-style' home raids targeting undocumented migrants
Belgium’s parliament is set to vote on controversial legislation that would allow police to enter private homes to arrest undocumented migrants facing deportation, in a move campaigners have likened to tactics used by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
The bill, due to be put to a vote on 5 November, would allow authorities to enter homes between 5am and 9pm with authorisation from an investigating judge. It would apply to foreign nationals who have received an enforceable order to leave Belgium. The measure could also include the homes of people suspected of accommodating undocumented migrants.
The proposal has faced widespread opposition from civil society organisations, lawyers, judges and local authorities, with critics warning that it threatens constitutional protections of the home, privacy and family life, while placing children and vulnerable households at risk.
They argue that the measure would allow authorities to enter private homes outside the framework of criminal investigations.
"The Belgian government may call them 'home visits', but that doesn’t change what they are: police forcibly entering private homes and traumatising families and children to arrest people who simply lack the right papers," Chiara Catelli, advocacy officer at the Platform for International Cooperation on Undocumented Migrants (PICUM), said in a statement.
"We've all seen the devastating consequences of home raids in the US, where they fuel fear and violence and tear families apart. It’s deeply alarming that an EU member state is now moving in the same direction," she said.
The legislation was introduced by Belgium’s Asylum and Migration Minister Anneleen Van Bossuyt and Justice Minister Annelies Verlinden. It was approved by the Chamber of Representatives' Interior Committee in a second reading on 7 October and is now awaiting a vote in the full parliament.
PICUM has also raised concerns about the level of judicial oversight and the ability of those affected to challenge the legality of a raid before its consequences become irreversible.
Although an investigating judge would have to authorise entry, PICUM said the judge might not have access to the entire case file before making a decision. It also warned that people whose homes are searched could be left without an effective remedy to contest the authorisation.
Sotieta Ngo, executive director of the Coordination et Initiatives pour Réfugiés et Étrangers (CIRÉ), described the proposal as an attack on fundamental rights and solidarity.
"It's an attack against human dignity. It's an attack against solidarity. This proposal is a major violation of the constitutional principle of the inviolability of the home. From a democratic standpoint, there is nothing acceptable about this text," she said.
Under amendments approved by the parliamentary committee, an investigating judge would be able to determine how an operation is carried out and impose additional protections where children are present. However, opponents argue that these safeguards do not remove the risk of psychological harm to children and other household members.
Noor Ketels, policy officer at Vluchtelingenwerk Vlaanderen, said the consequences could extend well beyond the households directly targeted.
"The harm of this bill goes far beyond any single raid. Fear can stop undocumented people from seeking help and make those offering shelter afraid to open their doors. People already in precarious situations could be left with nowhere safe to turn," she said.
"Everyone’s fundamental rights must be protected, regardless of their residence status. We urge the Belgian Parliament to reject this bill."
More than 60 municipalities across Belgium have reportedly adopted motions opposing the proposal, while the Brussels regional parliament also passed a resolution against it on 2 October.
Protests against the legislation are expected across the country on 4 November, a day before the parliamentary vote.
The Belgian government has rejected comparisons between the proposal and ICE, arguing that the legislation is a narrowly defined measure intended to enforce existing deportation orders rather than target undocumented migrants generally.
Van Bossuyt has said the measure would apply to people who refuse to cooperate with their return and pose a threat to public order or national security, citing convicted sex offenders and people involved in terrorism as examples.
She has also stressed that police would need authorisation from an investigating judge before entering a private residence.
In the United States, ICE has faced heavy criticism over its conduct.
A tracker by US investigative outlet The Trace identified nine people killed in shootings involving federal immigration agents since President Donald Trump began deploying agents as part of his enforcement operations in June 2025. The figures include agents from ICE and other federal immigration agencies.

Pakistan rights activist Imaan Mazari and husband jailed for 10 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:28:18 UTC
02:28:18 KST

Pakistan rights activist Imaan Mazari and husband jailed for 10 years
Couple say they are ‘prisoners of conscience’ being made into an example by Pakistan’s military-backed authorities.
An antiterrorism court in Pakistan has sentenced prominent human rights lawyers Imaan Mazari and her husband, Hadi Ali Chattha, to 10 years in prison on terrorism-related charges.
Judge Tahir Abbas Sipra announced the verdict on Thursday, following their trial inside Adiala prison in the garrison city of Rawalpindi.
The couple were found guilty of putting “the security of [the England and Wales Cricket] team at risk”, the judge wrote, adding that it “clearly shows the intentions and objective of the accused to create a sense of terror”, according to a copy of the court judgement obtained by the AFP news agency.
At the same time, the ruling conceded that the security breach was “a very common nature ordinary type of incident apparently of removal of a barrier”.
The case relates to an October 2024 incident in which the couple removed road barriers in the capital, Islamabad, along a route designated for the touring England cricket team.
The couple were indicted on October 7, accused of obstructing police and inciting public interest, and pleaded not guilty.
In statements seen by the Reuters news agency, the couple denied the charges, while calling themselves “prisoners of conscience”, adding that they were being targeted for their human rights work.
In their defence document, the couple had earlier said they were “being made an example to further cement the chilling effect against those who stand (or want to stand) against tyranny, oppression and injustice”.
Relatives criticise judicial process
Shireen Mazari, who is Imaan Mazari’s mother and served as Pakistan’s human rights minister under incarcerated former Prime Minister Imran Khan, said it was a “sham trial without any due process”.
Mazari told the Reuters news agency the couple “were not permitted to defend themselves through their own lawyer, and were not provided with key legal documents”, adding that the defence would file a petition against the verdict in the Supreme Court.
Amnesty International called the convictions “an indictment of Pakistan’s justice system.”
“It was a test of the judiciary’s ability to uphold the principles of justice and the right to fair trial. It has failed that test miserably,” said Amnesty’s Yasmine Ahmend.
“It is clear that these ‘anti-terrorism’ charges are being used to punish Imaan and Hadi for their human rights advocacy,” she added.
Mazari and Chattha have been in custody since January 23, in a separate case over their social media posts.
A lower court sentenced them each to 17 years the next day under Pakistan’s Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, which critics have said is designed to quash antigovernment dissent online.
Although the Supreme Court later suspended those sentences, police re-arrested the couple the same day in the security breach case.
“Imaan and Hadi’s re-arrest dispels any pretence that the charges against them are anything other than a politically motivated attempt to punish them for their human rights work”, said Babu Ram Pant, Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director for South Asia, adding that the case demonstrates once again the authorities’ willingness to weaponise the legal system against critical voices.
Pakistan’s law minister, Azam Nazeer Tarar, has repeatedly said the country’s judiciary is independent.

Europe's total debt hits record high above $95T in H1
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:26:29 UTC
02:26:29 KST

Sevgi Ceren Gökkoyun
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Total debt across 32 European nations topped $95 trillion in the first half of 2026 to reach a record high, the Institute of International Finance said on Thursday.  
Rising borrowing costs and political uncertainties are making it increasingly difficult to stabilize debt levels across the region, according to the institute's European edition of the Global Debt Monitor report.
Europe's debt pile accounted for approximately 25% of global debt during the six-month period, while the region's debt-to-gross domestic product ratio stood at around 325%.
The ratio remained more than 45 percentage points below levels seen at the onset of the eurozone debt crisis, the report noted.
France posted Europe's largest debt stock at $15.5 trillion, followed by the UK at $14.7 trillion, Germany at $13.5 trillion and Italy at $7.2 trillion.
Across economic sectors, financial institutions held the largest share of outstanding debt at $30.4 trillion, followed by non-financial corporations at $26.4 trillion, public debt at $22.5 trillion and household debt at $15.7 trillion.
France experienced the sharpest rise in borrowing costs among EU members this year, with its five-year credit default swap spread rising above 100 basis points to its highest level since late 2012, while Italy's spread stood near 75 basis points.
The report warned that persistent budget deficits, higher borrowing costs and shrinking fiscal buffers in a difficult political climate make stabilizing debt trajectories harder for European governments.
Heavy reliance on foreign investors to fund fiscal shortfalls leaves regional governments vulnerable to shifts in global risk sentiment and cross-border capital flows, the institute said.
Political gridlock could reignite market tensions as debt concerns increasingly concentrate in Europe's largest economies, raising the risk of broader financial spillovers, the report added.

Israeli leader Netanyahu accused of using ‘ugly’ smear tactics to cling to power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:26:06 UTC
02:26:06 KST

Benjamin Netanyahu has been accused of using smear tactics to cling to power, after he claimed that Arab Israeli parties had used foreign backing to “steal” Tuesday’s election, in which the prime minister’s coalition lost its parliamentary majority.
Netanyahu and his allies called on the internal security service, Shin Bet, to investigate alleged vote buying and other irregularities in Palestinian communities in Israel, supposedly funded by foreign money.
Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the main opposition bloc, accused the prime minister and his Likud party of trying to derail the election results.
“It’s already clear that Likud and Netanyahu have embarked on a coordinated, organised campaign seeking to delegitimise the results of the election,” Eisenkot said in a video message.
The prime minister’s allegations were quickly disowned by a range of government officials, including police officers and members of the election committee. Netanyahu was also rebuked by the president for “tarnishing an entire community”.
On Wednesday night, the prime minister posted a statement by Likud online, which described the claimed violations as “an attack on democracy whose purpose is to lead to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamisation of Israel, and the overthrow of rightwing rule”.
Tuesday’s elections led to Netanyahu’s far-right coalition losing its majority after four years in power. The main Jewish opposition bloc also fell short, however, leaving two Arab Israeli parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, holding the balance of power.
Final results released early on Friday local time showed the pro-Netanyahu bloc winning 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset and Eisenkot’s bloc taking 48 seats. Joint List and Ra’am won the remaining 19 seats, a historic high for the Arab Israeli community, which makes up about a fifth of Israel’s population.
The prime minister’s attack appeared aimed at stopping the Jewish and Arab opposition from voting together in the new Knesset to oust the incumbent speaker, Amir Ohana, a Likud politician and former Shin Bet official, and advancing their own legislation.
The Likud statement posted by Netanyahu on X said: “It is clear that no Zionist party should cooperate with Ra’am and the Joint List, replace the Knesset speaker through votes bought for cash, and form a government that is dangerous to Israel.”
Opposition leaders lambasted the claims of Netanyahu, 77, who has run Israel for 19 of the past 30 years.
Yousef Jabareen, the Joint List leader, accused the prime minister of incitement. “Netanyahu was defeated at the ballot box,” Jabareen said, adding that he “refuses to come to terms with the fact that the Arab public voted and decided”.
Eisenkot said any investigation should be conducted “without fear or favour,” and with “the utmost caution”, but insisted it could not be used as a reason to delay the convening of the newly elected Knesset, due to be sworn in within 14 days of the election.
The acting director general of the central elections committee, Dean Livneh, said there appeared to be no basis for the claims. Police officials quoted across the Israeli press said the allegations were groundless, adding that voting had been relatively trouble-free.
The president, Isaac Herzog, called for political leaders to “avoid tarnishing an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy”.
It was not specified in Likud statements, but press reports said Qatar was the foreign power alleged to have funded vote-buying and voter mobilisation. Majed al-Ansari, an adviser to Qatar’s prime minister, said its government “categorically” denied any involvement in the elections.
The record turnout among Arab Israelis (Palestinians with Israeli citizenship) appeared to be driven by outrage at routine discrimination and fear that it could become far worse if extremist and openly racist members of the government, such as the national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, and the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, secured another term in office.
On Thursday, Ben-Gvir called for the arrest of Arab party leaders, and Smotrich demanded they be subjected to Shin Bet interrogation.
Voting in Nazareth, the biggest majority-Palestinian town in Israel, was brisk on Tuesday, with few signs of irregularities, other than apparent ploys by the government and coalition parties to suppress the Arab vote.
Some packets of ballots sent to Nazareth polling stations were in Hebrew alone, rather than in Hebrew and Arabic. Election workers said that monitors sent by far-right parties had attempted procedural ploys to slow down voting but had been largely unsuccessful.
The leaders of the Joint List and the Zionist “Change” bloc have ruled out a formal coalition, but officials from both have discussed the possibility of tactical voting in the Knesset to unseat Ohana, the speaker, and to pass some consensus legislation.
One proposed bill would establish a commission of inquiry into the security failures that helped lead to the Hamas attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, something Netanyahu has blocked over the past two years.
Ahmad Tibi, a party leader on the Joint List, said Netanyahu was trying to subvert the election results by trying to sabotage a common front between the Eisenkot bloc and the Arab Israeli parties.
“This entire campaign is directed against Eisenkot, to prevent him, intimidate and scare him off forming a government that relies on external support from the Joint List or Ra’am,” Tibi told the Reuters news agency.
Naftali Bennett, a former prime minister who is a partner in the “Change” bloc, pointed out the irony of Netanyahu denouncing Qatar for election meddling while the Israeli leader’s own political advisers are being accused of taking Qatari money for promoting the Gulf monarchy’s image.
“This morning, suddenly, when it serves his interests, Netanyahu remembered Qatar and is using it to sow chaos and undermine public confidence in the democratic process,” Bennett wrote on X.

UAE sentences eight people to life over arms supplies to Sudan’s army
Defendants handed life sentences amid tensions between Khartoum and Abu Dhabi over Sudan’s war and the RSF.
A court in the United Arab Emirates has sentenced eight people to life imprisonment over arms trafficking and money laundering to Sudan’s army, state media report.
The individuals supplied weapons and military equipment to the Sudanese army and were part of a money-laundering network connecting the two countries, the Emirati state-run news agency WAM said on Thursday.
It said the Abu Dhabi Federal Court of Appeal concluded on Thursday that the convicted individuals had participated in an integrated scheme for the illicit trafficking of weapons, ammunition and military equipment.
The accused were also found to have forged documents using companies and bank accounts in the UAE to channel funds relating to the arms deals and “conceal” their sources and destinations.
The court ordered the confiscation of ammunition and communications devices used in the crimes and the deportation of those convicted from the UAE after serving their sentences, WAM reported.
The “arms deals, money laundering endangered UAE interests”, the court order said.
Ties between the UAE and Sudan have deteriorated as the Sudanese military has accused Abu Dhabi of supplying arms to its rival in Sudan’s civil war, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group, which it has been fighting since April 2023. The UAE has denied the allegation.
The war has displaced more than 14 million people and created severe poverty and food shortages.
This week, more than 100 people – mostly women and children – were killed when military drones hit a busy city market frequented by RSF fighters in the city of Nyala in the western region of Darfur.
Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, said a second attack hit a civilian neighbourhood. MSF said a hospital it supports in Nyala received 36 bodies in the hours after that attack, 21 of them wearing civilian clothing, and its teams saw more than 150 wounded in the emergency room.
The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights has previously accused the RSF of carrying out war crimes and a possible crime against humanity in its takeover of el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur state, after forcing Sudan’s army to withdraw from its last stronghold in the Darfur region.

Rights groups petition Israeli court over Hebron expulsions
