Items found in Pompeii home hint at life before volcanic explosion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:59:11 UTC
01:59:11 KST

Ancient cosmetics, coins, mouse skeletons found in Pompeii home shed light on life before deadly eruption
Ancient items found in a sealed closet in Pompeii hint at what life was like in the historic Roman city before it was destroyed in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in A.D. 79.
The closet was located in a home in the central area of the city, the Pompeii Archaeological Park said in a news release. The house had previously been excavated in 1912, but an investigation of the surrounding areas is just now underway.
Inside, archaeologists found cosmetics, an incense burner, a bronze lantern and a balsam jar. Weights, likely used for commercial activity, were also found inside a wooden chest of drawers. The researchers also found vases and pots made of materials such as bronze, glass and ceramic, and a "refined snuff bottle" decorated with pine.
A necklace representing multiple deities and made of several materials was also found. The piece of jewelry might have been considered "magical" during the Roman era, the park said. Now these pieces are known as "crepundia," or rattles. The necklaces have amulets, meant to protect the wearer as a child. Many carried them into adulthood as mementos of childhood, the park said.
There were high levels of "geographical mobility" in the Roman world, the archaeological park said, explaining that many people, from slaves to wealthy merchants, lived far from relatives and the places they were raised.
The necklace found in the closet contains at least 20 miniature objects and materials including bone and crystal.
The wardrobe also held 38 bronze coins, preserved in a container made of plant material. The presence of the coins has led researchers to believe that the owner or owners didn't have time to recover valuable items.
It's impossible to know what happened to the people who owned these items, the archaeological park said. They may have escaped the eruption of Vesuvius and been unable to return to the site and dig for their belongings. They may have died in the disaster, along with about 15% to 20% of Pompeii's population, or afterward, without heirs who could reclaim the objects.
Little is known about the residents of the house. The items in the closet, including the paintings, and the location of the home on one of Pompeii's main streets suggest "a certain standard of living." But mouse skeletons found inside the home cast some doubt on this belief. However, such skeletons have been found in other spots of Pompeii, showing the city contended with "unwelcome guests," the park said.
The home has previously been attributed to a person named Cornelius Maximus, the archaeological park said. That identification was based on the discovery of inscriptions that are no longer visible. The newly found items likely won't bring researchers closer to identifying the home's owner, but they allow archaeologists to study "the various traces of a life," said archaeological park director Gabriel Zuchtriegel in the Facebook post.
"We cannot reconstruct with certainty the identity of those who lived in the house, but these fragments bring us closer to their daily lives," said Zuchtriegel.
Pompeii is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and popular tourist attraction. Archaeologists are also constantly exploring the ruined city, searching under heaps of volcanic ash and pumice to peer into its preserved remains.
In January, the archaeological park announced that researchers had found a 2,000-year-old love note and illustrated gladiator fight scene inscribed on a city wall. In December 2025, archaeologists found evidence suggesting that some Pompeii residents returned to live in the city after the eruption.

US uncovers alleged $49 million mental health fraud
A Virginia mental health provider allegedly used hotel stays and false signatures to bill Medicaid millions. Its co-owner now faces federal fraud charges, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to the US Justice Department, Mikia Antoneice Noble, 37, was arrested on October 28 following her indictment earlier this month. She co-owned Advancing Communities Everywhere LLC (ACE), a mental health provider near Richmond.
The company offered care for people experiencing mental health crises. Prosecutors say its bills told a different story from the care patients received.
ACE allegedly charged Medicaid for services delivered by teams that included licensed mental health professionals. Instead, a single, less-qualified worker provided the care, according to the indictment.
The alleged scheme also involved more than $2 million spent on hotel room rentals. Prosecutors say ACE offered rooms to entice Medicaid beneficiaries into receiving services they did not need.
Medical records allegedly carried signatures of licensed professionals who had never participated in the care. Some records claimed Noble herself provided services while she was outside the country.
Prosecutors also accuse Noble and her co-owner of misleading organizations auditing ACE’s services.
Between January 2022 and April 2026, Noble allegedly helped submit over $49 million in fraudulent claims.
She faces one conspiracy charge and three counts of health care fraud. Each carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison if she is convicted.
The FBI and Virginia’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit are investigating.
The charges remain allegations. Noble is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

Sacha Baron Cohen publicly apologizes to Kazakhstan for ‘Borat,’ 20 years after the film’s release
British actor Sacha Baron Cohen has publicly apologized to the people of Kazakhstan for his portrayal of Borat in the 2006 film of the same name. “Borat” follows Borat Sagdiyev, a fictional journalist from Kazakhstan who travels to the United States to make a documentary, encounters American culture, and finds himself in all sorts of comical situations.
“I want to apologize to the people of Kazakhstan for the first time ever because Borat has got nothing to do with Kazakhstan,” the actor said on the podcast “Happy Sad Confused.”
Baron Cohen said he had developed an earlier version of the character for the BBC, with a different name and Albanian nationality. His name and nationality later changed depending on which television channel was paying for the show. “I would just say, ‘Oh, that character already belongs to the BBC. I’ve got a completely new character, this guy’s called Alexi Krickler, he’s from Moldova,’” Baron Cohen said.
The actor reiterated that at some point he had chosen Kazakhstan as a place “that no-one knows anything about.” He emphasized that he doesn’t even know what a Kazakh accent sounds like. Before recounting a complaint from the Kazakh Embassy, he apologized for being unable to imitate a Kazakh accent and said he would use Borat’s accent for the anecdote because his knowledge of Central Asian accents was limited.
Baron Cohen described the apology as his first for the character he created, though he has had to defend Borat ever since the film came out. “The joke is not on Kazakhstan. I think the joke is on people who can believe that the Kazakhstan that I describe can exist,” the actor said in a 2006 interview with Rolling Stone.
Over the years, Kazakhstan’s authorities have shifted from hostility toward “Borat” to acceptance. In 2005, the country’s Foreign Ministry threatened to sue Baron Cohen and claimed his show had been commissioned for political ends to tarnish the international reputation of Kazakhstan and its people.
In 2006, shortly before the film’s release, the country’s authorities paid for a four-page advertising supplement in The New York Times and the International Herald Tribune touting Kazakhstan’s achievements in the 21st century.
Although “Borat” was not officially banned in Kazakhstan, it never screened in the country’s movie theaters after its world premiere. The film also did not receive a theatrical distribution license in Russia.
Over time, attitudes toward Borat in Kazakhstan softened. In 2017, Czech tourists in Astana got off with a small fine for walking around dressed as Borat (Baron Cohen himself offered to pay it). In 2020, Kazakh Tourism, the company responsible for promoting tourism within Kazakhstan, adopted his catchphrase “Very nice!” as the country’s official tourism slogan.
By then, a sequel to “Borat” had been released worldwide, and the Kazakh diaspora in the United States continued to oppose it. In November 2020, the Kazakh American Association called for “Borat 2” to be excluded from consideration for Oscar, Golden Globe, and other award nominations.

Netanyahu or not, Israel’s settler colonialism will continue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:56:48 UTC
01:56:48 KST

Breadcrumb
Netanyahu or not, Israel’s settler colonialism will continue
On Tuesday, Israel went to the polls. By the next morning, both Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot had claimed victory. Exit polls put Likud first, with 53 seats to 48 for Eisenkot’s Yashar, but left both blocs short of the 61 seats needed to govern.
The question now is who will form the next government and whether the two men may end up sharing one.
For many Palestinians, this election matters less for who wins than for what the result reveals to the world and what it conceals.
Mask off
Likud has governed Israel for most of the period since 1977. Netanyahu has held the premiership longer than anyone, outlasting even David Ben-Gurion’s roughly 13 years.
Netanyahu and the parties to his right are the most honest expression of the Israeli state: a state founded on ethnic cleansing and sustained through racism, apartheid, and genocide. Others dress this reality in the language of democracy, coexistence, and peace. Netanyahu does not bother.
In 2019, he said it plainly: “Israel is not a state of all its citizens,” but “the nation-state of the Jewish people and them alone.” That year, his campaign ran on “Bibi or Tibi,” casting Palestinian lawmaker Ahmad Tibi and the Palestinian citizens of Israel he represents as the threat voters had to defeat. His official Facebook page urged Israelis to stop a government dependent on “Arabs who want to destroy us all women, children and men.” This year, one of his central campaign slogans is “The right or Palestine.”
The 2018 Nation-State Law, passed under Netanyahu, declared that the right to national self-determination in Israel belongs exclusively to the Jewish people and enshrined Jewish settlement as a “national value.” His government did not invent this principle; it gave legal form to the principle on which the Zionist project was founded.
Since then, Israel has approved dozens of new settlements and retroactively legalised unauthorised outposts. In February 2026, it went further, reopening West Bank land registration for the first time since 1967. In Area C, land that Palestinians cannot prove they own under Israeli procedures can be registered as Israeli state land and made available for settlement.
Meanwhile, state-backed settler violence has reached record levels. And then there is Gaza.
Netanyahu’s unfiltered colonial politics have forced both the Israeli public and world leaders to confront what they have spent decades refusing to see.
A “liberal” or “centrist” government would not undo this. It would launder it. We have seen this before: settlements expanded under Labour governments, including through the Oslo years, while the world applauded a peace process.
Mask on
A friendlier face in Tel Aviv would give many in the “international community” the excuse they have been waiting for to look away.
Consider Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main challenger and leader of the “centrist” Yashar party. He was a central decision-maker in the Israeli occupation army, rising to chief of staff and later sitting in Netanyahu’s war cabinet after 7 October. He publicly articulated the Dahiya Doctrine: the strategy of overwhelming force against civilian areas used in Lebanon and Gaza.
Eisenkot’s party promises a “Jewish and democratic” state- ethnonationalism, but made to look democratic. He rejects the two-state solution that Washington and Brussels still present as the road to peace. His objection to Ben-Gvir and Smotrich is not what they do, but how it looks abroad.
The West, the EU included, has hoped an opposition victory would whitewash Israel’s image. The election results point the other way: over 77% of Israelis voted for right-wing and far-right parties, around 15%, largely Palestinian citizens of Israel, backed the Arab parties, and just 6.51% voted for the Zionist left.
The result also exposes the limits of framing opposition to Netanyahu as an awakening to the horrors committed by the state. Given a choice, most Israeli voters did not opt for a fundamentally different agenda; they endorsed the same core project of Jewish supremacy and Palestinian dispossession, and they backed the Israeli genocide in Gaza.
Across the political spectrum, Israel has shed any pretence of democratic equality. Arab citizens are delegitimised: their parties were banned before the vote and reinstated only by the courts, and their turnout was branded an “emergency” on election day.
Their record result has been met with cries of a stolen election and demands that their leaders be interrogated and arrested, and a further crackdown on their rights now looks all but certain. Even the “centrist” opposition refuses to govern with them.
The difference between “moderate” and “extremist” Zionism lies less in its goals than in how it presents them to the outside world.
Both currents seek to preserve Israel as a state that privileges Jewish nationality and control over historic Palestine. “Moderate” Zionism speaks the language of democracy, security and a negotiated settlement while continuing settlement expansion, military occupation and the structural exclusion of Palestinians.
“Extremist” Zionism says the same things openly: annexation, transfer, Jewish supremacy, making the underlying reality harder for Western allies to ignore.
Eisenkot and figures like him do not oppose the system so much as manage its image. Their objection to Ben-Gvir and Smotrich is not that Palestinian rights are being denied, but that the denial has become too visible, too crude and too damaging to Israel’s standing abroad.
The “moderate” opposition offers a more presentable version of the same political order: one that Washington and Brussels can still call “Jewish and democratic,” even as that democratic claim becomes impossible to sustain.
Every Israeli election, regardless of the outcome, offers Palestinians, whether those eligible to vote or not, the same choice: one settler-colonial project, with or without the mask.
I would rather see it without.
It is a grim truth that we live in a world where people and leaders often wait for Palestinians to suffer visibly before they speak or act against Israel’s colonial occupation. And it is crueller still that Palestinians are expected to choose between those who kill us brutally and those who would kill us just as surely, only more slowly, and in a manner more acceptable to the international community.
Tamam Abusalama is a Palestinian-Belgian communications professional, born and raised in the Jabalia Refugee Camp. She is currently leading the strategy for the European Citizens’ Initiative Justice for Palestine, which calls for the full suspension of the EU-Israel Association Agreement.

The Ukrainian Navy destroyed two Russian Su-34s in a Neptune strike
Kyiv • UNN
The Ukrainian Navy struck two Su-34s at the Marinovka airfield in Russia's Volgograd region. The aircraft were used to carry out attacks on Ukraine with guided aerial bombs.
For the second time this month, the Ukrainian Navy, using the "long Neptune," destroyed two Russian Su-34s at the site of the 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment in the Volgograd region. The Ukrainian Navy reports this, as UNN reports.
Units of the Ukrainian Navy launched a missile strike with the Neptune coastal defense missile system on the location of enemy aircraft at the Marinovka airfield in Russia’s Volgograd region. As a result of the strike, two Su-34 frontline fighter-bombers were destroyed at the site of the 11th Mixed Aviation Regiment (the settlement of Oktyabrsky, Volgograd region) of the 4th Mixed Aviation Division of the 4th Air and Air Defense Army
The Navy noted that the Su-34 is one of the main platforms of Russian tactical aviation for deploying guided aerial bombs against Ukrainian cities, Defense Forces positions, and frontline areas.
Supplement
On October 15, the Ukrainian Navy destroyed four Russian Su-34 bombers, and two more were damaged at the Borisoglebsk airport. This aircraft is a deeply modernized version of the basic Su-34 frontline bomber, which Russia began mass production of in 2020. Thanks to its new hardpoints, this aircraft is the primary carrier of guided aerial bombs and precision-guided missiles with which the enemy attacks Ukraine’s frontline regions.
The Main Directorate of Intelligence of the Ministry of Defense reported that the Russian Aerospace Forces have approximately 140 Su-34 fighter-bombers of various modifications in service. Intelligence officials also noted that since the beginning of the war, the Defense Forces had managed to destroy 43 aircraft and damage another seven.
According to data from OSINT analysts, based on confirmed information, it has been established that Ukraine’s Defense Forces destroyed 42 Russian Su-34s, while another five were damaged. It has also been visually confirmed that Russia lost only one Su-34M aircraft. This occurred in July 2022. At that time, the bomber was shot down near Alchevsk in the Luhansk region, and it was done by the Russians themselves as a result of "friendly fire."

Pharma companies continue to pay millions to doctors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:52:47 UTC
01:52:47 KST

Pharma companies continue to pay millions to doctors
The flood of money poured into doctors, hospitals, networks of doctors, professional bodies and patient groups by pharmaceutical companies remains substantial.
In 2025, these payments – in the form of conference attendance fees, accommodation expenses, fees and consultancy fees – totalled CHF234 million ($283 million).
This figure is CHF28 million lower than in 2024, but the decline is mainly due to the lower number of major research collaborations, explains Der Beobachter in Thursday’s issue, which, along with other publications in the Ringier Group, tracks these payments via the platform www.pharmagelder.ch.
Currently, over 60 companies disclose these payments on the basis of an internal industry self-regulatory scheme, agreed in 2014 to improve transparency in a sector that some consider opaque. In total, the payments disclosed since then amount to CHF2.1 billion.
The concern with these payments is potential conflicts of interest, points out the fortnightly magazine, which champions consumer interests. It has been shown that doctors who receive sponsorships tend to prescribe expensive brand-name medicines more often than cheaper generics containing the same active ingredient.
+ Pharma pushes for higher European drug prices, Trump or no Trump
Furthermore, they write prescriptions for a greater number of medicines and, statistically, deviate more often from official, impartial medical guidelines.
In theory, according to medicines legislation, the choice of treatment must not be influenced by financial incentives but rather a course of treatment must be based on scientific and objective criteria. However, neither the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) nor professional associations or other trade organisations monitor compliance with these rules, the magazine emphasises.
For the past two years, the most generous company has been the Anglo-Swedish group AstraZeneca. The company, which aims to bring 30 new cancer treatments to market by the end of 2027, has more than doubled its payments over five years, bringing them to CHF27.4 million. Swiss firm Novartis ranks second with CHF26.4 million, followed by Roche, which contributes CHF25.6 million.
The American giant Pfizer, which last year ranked fourth among funders with CHF21.3 million, has halved its payments in Switzerland to CHF11.3 million; however, the company has scaled back its involvement almost exclusively in the area of major research collaborations, while payments to individual doctors have increased in recent years.

Ukraine heads for first economic decline since 2022 as Russian strikes take their toll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:51:28 UTC
01:51:28 KST

Ukraine heads for first economic decline since 2022 as Russian strikes take their toll
Intensified Russian attacks on Ukrainian businesses have pushed the economy into decline for the first time since 2022’s invasion shock, choking key industries as inflation hits a three-year high.
Ukraine’s National Bank said on Oct. 29 that the country’s economy will shrink by 0.4% this year, after revising its previous forecast of 1.8% growth. The last time Ukraine’s economy contacted was the year of Russia’s full-scale invasion, which saw its gross domestic product (GDP) plummet by an astonishing 30% before gradually recovering the following year.
The bank said the decline was caused by Russia’s months-long blockade of seaports and escalating attacks on logistics and production facilities. The metallurgy industry has particularly suffered, with steel production shutting down across the country amid the heightened risk of deadly Russian strikes.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's Agriculutral Ministry said that farmers wont see any profits from crop production this year, as they cannot export goods via the Black Sea, while costs for autumn sowing, fuel, fertilizers, and land rental payments have increased.
The attacks, combined with the fuel crisis caused by the war in the Middle East, have also caused inflation to surge to double digits, jumping to 10% in September, the bank said.
The NBU predicts that annual inflation will reach 12.5% by the end of 2026 — a three-year high. To help cool the economy, the bank hiked its benchmark interest rate from 16% to 16.5%, the highest level since October 2023. The rate is expected to remain in place until spring 2027, the NBU said.
"Taking the consequences of the destruction into account, the NBU forecasts a slow recovery in economic growth in 2027-2028," the bank said.
"Economic activity will be supported, in particular, by public and private investment in the defense industry, the localization of weapons production financed through the Ukraine Support Loan, and projects to restore critical infrastructure."
The bank predicts that next year, Ukraine’s foreign partners will provide $52 billion in direct budget support and $37 billion for defense needs through the EU’s Ukraine Support Loan program, after the country passed several laws this month to unlock funding from the EU and the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
The funding will help Ukraine cover core budgetary needs, although the country faces a projected deficit of nearly Hr 1.7 trillion ($37 billion) next year.
This year has been one of the hardest for Ukraine’s economy, with businesses expected to lose some $10 billion in the wake of the attacks, creating a Hr 70 billion ($1.5 billion) tax shortfall.
As Russia shows no sign of slowing its attacks, the country is adapting to a new phase of the war. Ukraine’s Economy Ministry is developing support programs for companies, including a multibillion-dollar war risk insurance fund to help cover businesses starting in January.

Israel completes vote count, Netanyahu bloc retains 53 seats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:50:22 UTC
01:50:22 KST

Şahin Demir
29 October 2026•Update: 29 October 2026
Israel’s Central Elections Committee has completed counting votes in Tuesday’s parliamentary elections, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc securing 53 seats, opposition parties 48 and Arab parties 19, the Ynet newspaper reported Thursday.
The committee said it had completed counting special ballots, known as double envelopes, but would release the final results later.
Results from 12,644 polling stations have been entered into the system, totaling 5,589,836 votes, including 5,564,764 valid votes and 25,072 invalid votes, it said.
The special ballots include votes cast by soldiers, prisoners, diplomats, and hospitalized voters who could not vote at their regular polling stations.
The overall distribution of seats among the three political groupings remained unchanged from Wednesday’s results, despite changes in individual parties’ seat allocations following the counting of special ballots.
Netanyahu’s Likud party rose from 26 to 27 seats, while the ultra-Orthodox Shas party fell from seven to six.
Among Arab parties, Ra’am gained one seat, increasing its representation to eight, while the Joint List dropped one to 11.
Netanyahu’s bloc includes his Likud party and allied far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.
The opposition bloc, led by former Israeli Army Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, includes his Yashar party, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett’s Together alliance, Yair Lapid’s Yesh Atid, Yair Golan’s Democrats and Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu.
The two Arab parties, the Joint List and the United Arab List (Ra’am), secured a combined 19 seats, potentially putting them in a pivotal position in negotiations to form the next government.
Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition bloc reached the 61 seats required for a majority in the 120-member Knesset.
Voter turnout reached 77.7%, the highest since 1999 and up 7.1 percentage points from the 2022 elections, according to the Central Elections Committee.
The official results are expected to be announced Nov. 4.
President Isaac Herzog will then consult parliamentary factions before appointing a lawmaker to form the next government.
The new Knesset is expected to be sworn in Nov. 10.

USA: GMLRS Missile Successfully Redirected in Flight and Hit Moving Target for the First Time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:50:20 UTC
01:50:20 KST

Lockheed Martin, in collaboration with the U.S. Army, successfully tested the ability to re-target a GMLRS guided missile after launch from a HIMARS rocket system, striking a moving target.
This was reported by Lockheed Martin’s press office.
The tests took place at White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. During the test, a GMLRS rocket was launched from a standard M142 HIMARS launcher, after which updated target data was transmitted to it directly during flight.
The Strigo data link and the Remote Interceptor Guidance-360 (RIG-360) system were used for this purpose; the company funded the integration of these systems at its own expense.
After receiving the new data, the missile adjusted its guidance and successfully destroyed the moving target.
According to the developers, implementing this capability does not require a fundamental redesign of the GMLRS missile itself. Instead, the technology involves integrating existing reconnaissance assets, launchers, and target-acquisition systems into a single network.
Lockheed Martin notes that the data transmission system used can also be adapted for the ER GMLRS long-range rockets and the operational-tactical Precision Strike Missiles (PrSMs).
Lockheed Martin has been working on the capability to update target coordinates in flight since at least 2023. At that time, the company first demonstrated the transmission of new coordinates to an experimental GMLRS communication channel using the RIG-360 system.
During the test, the equipment was mounted on an aircraft that simulated the missile’s flight path.
The next phase consisted of the current tests, during which the technology was tested using an actual GMLRS missile and against a moving target.
In August 2026, Lockheed Martin also unveiled the Strigo family of technologies, which includes radio-frequency sensors, data links, and guidance heads for missiles of various types.
Technologies from this family are already being used in the development of the PrSM Increment 2 missile guidance system, designed to engage moving ground and sea targets. In September, the U.S. Army ordered PrSM Increment 2 missiles from Lockheed Martin worth $1.2 billion.

Bolsonaro’s leadership claim fails to win support from allies in Brazil
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
17:50:07 CET
01:50:07 KST

By Isabel Teles
SAO PAULO, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro’s decision to declare himself the country’s rightful “leader” has failed to garner support from key figures in his political camp, leaving the right-wing lawmaker increasingly isolated in Brazilian politics.
Bolsonaro made the claim in a letter he posted on social media after arriving in the United States on Wednesday, having left Brazil following his defeat to leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva by more than 4 million votes in Sunday’s runoff.
Bolsonaro has cited the fact that a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice extended voting by two hours due to Lula campaign allegations of voter suppression in left-leaning northeastern states, though Bolsonaro’s campaign had also sought a voting extension due to rain in conservative southern states.
He alleged he was a victim of an electoral coup, but did not provide evidence for electoral fraud.
Lula’s victory has been recognized by Brazil’s electoral authority, global leaders, international observers, and Bolsonaro’s own party.
“I did not like it,” the head of the senator’s Liberal Party, Valdemar Costa Neto, told reporters on Thursday when asked about the letter.
“Flavio went through a difficult situation — we understand that — but we do not approve of it. We want to move the country forward,” he said later.
Sao Paulo Governor Tarcisio de Freitas, a prominent Bolsonaro ally who campaigned vigorously for the lawmaker, told newspaper Estadao that Brazil’s election results must be respected and that it was time to move forward.
US President Donald Trump, who confirmed his administration had allowed Bolsonaro to enter the country, declined to comment on Thursday when asked who he thought was the legitimate winner.
“I watched the election. I didn’t take sides. I let it be. I was asked not to take sides by the president, the current president,” he said.
PARTIES RECOGNIZE LULA’S WIN
Aecio Neves, head of the center-right Brazilian Social Democracy Party and a vocal critic of Lula’s Workers’ Party, described Bolsonaro’s behavior as “incomprehensible” in a statement, adding that opposition politics must be conducted from within the country.
Center-right party Uniao Brasil, which backed Bolsonaro in the second round, said it was essential that institutions “remain greater than any individual.” The election was conducted with integrity and its results must be respected, it added.
The centrist Brazilian Democratic Movement (MDB) party, which also supported Bolsonaro in the runoff, struck a similar tone.
“The MDB reaffirms its total confidence in the Brazilian electoral system and, therefore, in the legitimacy of the result of the election last Sunday,” it said.
‘FLAVIO IS VENTING’
In his letter, Bolsonaro pledged to lead the opposition from abroad and “assume the risks” that local politicians could not, adding he would support a potential bid by Senator Rogerio Marinho for Senate president in 2027.
Marinho, who served as Bolsonaro’s campaign manager, told reporters that Bolsonaro remains “a leader” and ”the most prominent figure on the right” in Brazil, given the support he received from nearly 60 million voters.
But Marinho also rejected allegations of electoral fraud.
“The Liberal Party cannot make that claim, nor can I make that claim, because there is no evidence to support it,” he said. “Flavio is venting in response to the second-round election results, which were unexpected for all of us.”
(Reporting by Isabel Teles; Additional reporting by Jacob Bogage in Washington; Editing by Gabriel Araujo and Aurora Ellis)

Oct 23 (Reuters) - The first Russian diesel bound for the US following a surprise agreement reached between Moscow and US President Donald Trump is aboard a tanker heading for New York, ship-tracking data showed on Friday.
Trump announced the deal this month as part of his efforts to bring down soaring diesel prices ahead of November 3 US midterm elections.
Trump also waived parts of a new US sanctions law against Russia and threatened Europe with a US diesel export ban unless countries released more from their emergency reserves to help ease prices.
The Malta-flagged medium-sized tanker Agioi Fanendes was loaded with 40,000 metric tons of ultra-low sulphur diesel in Russia’s Baltic port of Primorsk on October 22, according to LSEG shipping data. It is expected to arrive in the United States on November 7. The identity of the buyer and seller were not immediately known.
Post publication, Eastern Mediterranean Maritime Limited (EASTMED), the manager of the Agioi Fanendes tanker, said that the vessel was awaiting orders while sailing towards the North Atlantic but its destination had not been determined as New York.
“The discharging port or country is not yet nominated and finalised,” an EASTMED official told Reuters.
The cargo will be the first imported by the US since former President Joe Biden announced a ban on US imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in 2022.
Trump announced on October 9 that Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, to the US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter”.
A Kremlin spokesperson on Friday confirmed a first ship under the deal had departed, but did not specify whether it was bound for the US market or elsewhere.
“As far as I’m aware, there have already been reports from the Ministry of Energy that the first tanker has, in fact, set sail for its recipients, its buyers. Further shipments will continue at a steady pace from here on,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on a daily conference call.
The deal with the US involved Russia lifting a self-imposed ban on diesel exports.
RUSSIA RESUMING GLOBAL EXPORTSSince the EU imposed a full embargo on imports of Russian oil products in February 2023 over the war in Ukraine, Russia has exported diesel mainly to Turkey and Brazil, as well as to African countries.
It also supplies Central Asia by rail.
Shipping data from LSEG and Kpler published this week showed Russian diesel cargoes resuming voyages to their traditional destinations after Moscow lifted its own ban, with at least two tankers signalling trips to Turkey and Brazil.
It was unclear where other tankers were destined for, with cargoes loaded in Primorsk signalling Gibraltar, the Atlantic Coast or Port Said, LSEG data showed.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak has said additional US shipments would follow as companies from the two countries work out the necessary contracts.
Putin envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who also heads Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, said last week that the US Treasury had asked the fund to help sort out tricky payment issues relating to the agreement.
That account was not accurate, a source familiar with the matter said.
Novak has said that Russia would be able to increase its diesel exports to its usual levels of 3-3.5 million tons per month by year-end.

HEALTHCARE SYSTEM ‘AT BREAKING POINT’

Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Tuesday that three tankers carrying Russian diesel to export markets were already under way and that a fourth would sail on October 28.

Under the current diesel export ban, the government permits limited exports through a quota system. Those quotas will quadruple from October levels to 2 million metric tons, or about 0.5 million barrels per day, in November, the sources said. Shipments under existing intergovernmental agreements will also continue.
The Energy Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
The current ban on diesel exports is due to expire on October 31.
In October, the government exempted several refiners from the ban and granted them export quotas totalling 0.5 million tons, the sources said. A new government order expected in early November would expand the list of exempt refiners and set new export limits. If the quotas are used up quickly, the government could consider increasing them further, the sources added.
Nominal diesel production in Russia exceeds domestic consumption by about 40%. As refineries return to normal operating rates, they will need export outlets to prevent a domestic glut.

The 21.3 billion euros ($23.8 billion) on the table is part of the Security Action for Europe (SAFE) instrument, which includes 150 billion euros ($167.5 billion) in favorable loans freed up in May 2025 that EU countries can draw on to help them beef up their defense and support to Ukraine.
The scheme proved quite successful, with 19 countries submitting proposals for the loans.
However, the full 150 billion euros was not used, chiefly because Italy and Hungary scaled down their borrowing plans, allowing the Commission to issue its new call.
"Along with their needs and national defense priorities, member states are also encouraged to use the funds from this second call to strengthen cooperation with Ukraine," a European Commission press release reads.
For the Commission, that means EU countries engaging in joint defense procurement with Ukraine and spending to address Ukraine's "urgent needs," for example, in "air and missile defense systems, drones and counter-drone systems, and ammunition and missiles."
That new call for submissions also comes as Ukraine-EU defense cooperation has gained momentum.
Among the spending plans already foreseen for the SAFE loans are many plans for joint production with Ukraine, even for countries seen as less pro-Ukraine in the bloc, such as Bulgaria, which has a plan to co-produce drones.
The EU has since then also launched its EU-Ukraine drone alliance, which brings together manufacturers from both sides to deepen cooperation, and the bloc has moved forward on five pan-continental defense projects, in which Ukraine has been deeply embedded.
The same day the European Commission issued the new call for SAFE proposals, EU-Ukraine defense cooperation was a key topic at Brussels' annual defense and security conference, organized by the consultancy Logos.
Panu Routila, CEO of Finnish defense manufacturer Patria, told the Kyiv Independent he is excited about a new joint venture between his company and Ukrainian drone producer General Cherry.
For Routila, the cooperation will allow the two companies to advance together on first-person view (FPV) drones and interceptor technology.
Patria is now looking for "direct collaboration" with Ukrainian companies across a range of "emerging capabilities," following that first positive collaboration, Routila told the Kyiv Independent.
Former Prime Minister and head of the Kyiv Security Forum Arseniy Yatsenyuk told the Kyiv Independent at the same event that his message for defense manufacturers in Europe is simple.
"Press your national governments to support Ukraine and to provide more," Yatsenyuk said.
He characterized the situation as a win-win, because if countries provide financial support to Ukraine, it can continue to procure from European defense manufacturers.
The SAFE loans are a concrete line of funding through which national governments could boost financial support at low borrowing costs.

Anger in Syria over government 'inaction' after deadly Jordanian airstrikes

Jordan’s military said Monday that its air force had struck what it described as terrorist sites in the southern Syrian province of Daraa, targeting groups it said were linked to a deadly shooting at a church in southern Jordan which killed nine people on 23 October, a rare incident in the kingdom. Jordanian authorities said they arrested three suspects behind the shooting.
The Islamic State (IS) group later claimed responsibility for the shooting. Jordanian officials subsequently claimed that the attack in southern Syria had killed more than 20 IS members and targeted a major weapons depot, while acknowledging unintended civilian casualties.
While Jordan has carried out repeated airstrikes in southern Syria in recent years, primarily against drug-smuggling networks operating near its border, Monday's operation has fuelled particular outrage because of the civilian toll and questions over whether Damascus had agreed to the strikes.
Amman said the operation was coordinated with the Syrian government, a claim Damascus rejected, saying the strikes were carried out without prior notification or coordination.
The Syrian Foreign Ministry condemned the attacks as a violation of the country’s sovereignty, said an investigation had been launched and called for coordination over security operations along the shared border.
However, criticism intensified after Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and his Jordanian counterpart, Ayman al-Safadi, issued a joint statement on Wednesday following a telephone call to discuss the consequences of the strikes.
The statement said Safadi had explained that the operation was based on field intelligence and aimed at "neutralising confirmed threats and imminent terrorist operations targeting Jordan's security." He also expressed regret over civilian deaths.
The two sides agreed to establish a joint security committee to examine the circumstances and repercussions of the strikes and strengthen coordination along the border.
Although Damascus had separately condemned the operation and summoned Jordan’s ambassador to deliver a formal protest, many Syrians have viewed the joint statement as accepting Jordan’s account.
Comments online, including under the Syrian Foreign Ministry’s statement on X, have reflected widespread anger over what users described as the government’s failure to defend Syrian sovereignty and adequately respond to the civilian deaths.
"Are these the ISIS members, Minister? And are these ISIS weapons depots, Your Excellency?" one user wrote, questioning Jordan’s account while referring to images showing the aftermath of the strikes and child victims.
Others argued that accepting Jordan’s justification for the operation could provide Israel with further excuses to widen its occupation in southern Syria under the pretext of fighting extremist groups.
After Assad’s fall, Israel invaded Syria’s Quneitra and Mount Hermon regions, claiming its military presence there was needed to prevent extremist militants from reaching its border.
"You are completely unfit for this position. How can you allow the Jordanian king to use you to push this narrative, while you repeat it so blindly?" one user wrote, addressing Syrian officials.
"Do not complain when Israeli forces invade Daraa under the pretext of rooting out ISIS. You are officially acknowledging that ISIS is present there, and you have now given Israel the green light," the user added.
Another comment accused the government of accepting Jordan’s account at the expense of the victims.
"A statement full of humiliation, submission and acceptance of the Jordanian narrative. It also betrays the blood of those killed by describing the massacre as a strike against terrorists. Were the children terrorists?" the user wrote.
The criticism reflects wider sensitivities and concerns in southern Syria, where residents have faced years of conflict, repeated Israeli incursions and security operations. Many remain under threat of foreign military action in Syria, which often kills civilians.
IS controlled large swathes of Syria before its territorial defeat in 2019, but the group continues to operate clandestine cells, particularly in desert areas, and has claimed attacks against security forces and civilians.
The group's continued activity has raised concerns about the future of counterterrorism operations as the US reduces its military presence in Syria.

Here's what Eli Lilly reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
- Earnings per share: $7.48 adjusted vs. $6.26 expected

Everyone's afraid, but they're pressing on: how the local ceasefire in Oleshky became a test for a broader deal
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
18:46:00 EET
01:46:00 KST

Everyone's afraid, but they're pressing on: how the local ceasefire in Oleshky became a test for a broader deal
At 03:00 on 27 October 2026, something happened in Kherson Oblast that local residents had grown unaccustomed to after years of full-scale war: silence fell.
Ukraine and Russia had agreed to a temporary cessation of hostilities in part of Kherson Oblast in order to allow a humanitarian mission to reach Russian-occupied Oleshky. Since then, attacks have stopped in Kherson and its outskirts, drones have disappeared from the skies, and the sound of artillery explosions has ceased.
Local residents and soldiers alike are surprised by this new – or rather long-forgotten – reality. After years of continuous hostilities, peace has become an unfamiliar experience.
Occasional detonations can still be heard, mostly during mine clearance operations. The danger, however, has not disappeared: people continue to come across landmines even in Kherson itself.
Valeriia, a local resident, told Ukrainska Pravda that there has been noticeably more traffic – buses and cars – on the roads in recent days.
Yet not everyone has welcomed the unusual silence with relief. For some residents, the ceasefire has brought fresh anxiety. They fear that once it ends, Russian forces will bring new weapons into Oleshky and resume its attacks on Kherson with even greater intensity.
"Some people say, 'Oh, it'll be bad after the ceasefire, and Kherson will take a beating.' So what? Shouldn't we save people? Should we just let them suffer?" Valeriia says with feeling.
The pause in hostilities, which is due to last from 03:00 on 27 October until 22:59 on 1 November, means far more than a temporary lull along one section of the front line.
First and foremost, it is a humanitarian operation intended to open up access to Russian-occupied Oleshky, deliver aid, and enable civilians to evacuate.
But at the same time, it's also an important military and political experiment: the first attempt to test whether Ukraine and Russia can not only agree on a ceasefire but also ensure that political decisions are implemented on the ground, directly along the front line.
Ukrainska Pravda has examined how the preparations were made for the Oleshky ceasefire and what we can expect from it.
The Pope and Melania Trump step in to save Oleshky
In September 2026, the humanitarian catastrophe in Russian-occupied Oleshky began to turn into an issue of international diplomacy.
Ukrainian religious organisations were among the first to sound the alarm. On 19 September, the All-Ukrainian Council of Churches and Religious Organisations appealed to Pope Leo XIV, the World Council of Churches and other influential religious bodies, urging them to intervene.
The appeal described the de facto humanitarian blockade of the city, which had received no regular food supplies since late May.
Representatives of international organisations began responding to the appeal almost immediately. They included Heinrich Bedford-Strohm, moderator of the Central Committee of the World Council of Churches, and Michael O'Flaherty, the Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights.
In mid-October, Pope Leo XIV personally joined the international efforts. On 16 October, he called Vladimir Putin and proposed a temporary ceasefire to allow food and medicine to be delivered and civilians to evacuate voluntarily.
Three days later, the Pope discussed the proposal with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
On 20 October, Pina Picierno, an Italian politician and vice-president of the European Parliament, joined the campaign to draw attention to Oleshky. She began a hunger strike to highlight the situation of those living in Oleshky and press for a humanitarian corridor to be set up.
A pivotal moment in the international efforts came on 23 October, when the White House unexpectedly announced that US First Lady Melania Trump had helped secure an agreement between Ukraine and Russia on a local ceasefire in Oleshky.
According to CNN journalists, Oleshky first came to Melania Trump's attention in September. At an event she hosted during the week of the UN General Assembly, someone told the first lady about the tragedy unfolding in the Ukrainian city. Melania immediately set to work.
The White House's official statement referred to a temporary halt in hostilities, the delivery of humanitarian aid and the establishment of safe passage for the evacuation of civilians.
The White House's initial announcement said the ceasefire would begin on 29 October. However, on 23 October, both Ukraine and Russia confirmed that preparations were underway for an operation to begin what was called the "silence regime".
On the Ukrainian side, the Office of Ukrainian Parliamentary Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets coordinated work with Russia and international partners. Behind the scenes, Davyd Arakhamiia, who is also a member of Ukraine's negotiating team, handled communications with the White House and Russian institutions.
Melania Trump's statement made no mention of this, but it was Arakhamiia who persuaded her to make a public announcement.
"Once again, the Russians had started backtracking on the agreement," a source in Ukrainian diplomatic circles told Ukrainska Pravda. "Through Davyd, our side arranged with Washington for Melania to issue a statement, effectively cutting off the Russians' opportunity to back out."
At 03:00 Kyiv time on 27 October, the ceasefire came into effect.
That same day, Melania Trump announced that the parties had not only managed to bring the ceasefire forward by two days, but had also extended it beyond Oleshky itself to provide safe passage for humanitarian convoys.
A test of peace: the other side of Oleshky
The ceasefire agreement in Oleshky has implications that go beyond the humanitarian situation, extending into the broader military and political sphere.
The organisers intend the local ceasefire to serve as a test of whether the Ukrainian and Russian military command structures can implement political agreements to halt hostilities.
A source involved in organising the ceasefire told Ukrainska Pravda that putting even such a limited agreement into practice has proved an extremely difficult task.
Problems have arisen not only on the Russian side, but also within Ukraine's own military system.
"Halting the hostilities has turned out to be an extremely difficult task," a source in Zelenskyy's team told Ukrainska Pravda. "Even when the military have reached an agreement, they keep backtracking and pulling out. We've already reached an agreement with our own military three times, but they backed out on all three occasions, saying: 'Have them call us again and guarantee that nothing will go wrong after we stop fighting.'"
According to sources, the problem is that a political order to cease fire does not automatically translate into a halt in hostilities on the front line.
Military commanders must learn not only to issue the relevant orders, but also to ensure that every unit in the designated area complies with them.
A source from Zelenskyy's inner circle explains: "We want to get the military – both our General Staff and the Russian one – used to the idea that if the political leadership decides that we're going to stop and freeze hostilities along a particular section of the front line, with neither side opening fire, the military can manage the process. They can guarantee it. Rather than the political leadership reaching an agreement and the military saying, 'Sorry, we can't stop, we've got something going on there.'"
Paradoxically, however, sometimes it's just as hard to get Ukrainian forces to implement such agreements as to get Russian forces to.
"Over the years, the Russians have stamped out internal resistance. They have a rigid military hierarchy. Our army, by contrast, is decentralised. And someone – some well-known military blogger – can go on air and say something that causes the whole thing to fall apart," the source says.
If the experiment in Oleshky is a success, its organisers hope to repeat a similar operation on another section of the front line some time later.
"We want to try it now, and if it works, then after a short interval, we want to organise a humanitarian corridor on another section of the front line as well," a source involved in organising the truce explains. "The idea is to teach the military how to do this – how to stop, guarantee safe passage and so on – so that later, if a major agreement is reached, we can implement it straight away."
Oleshky residents prepare to leave
Meanwhile, in Oleshky itself, preparations are underway for the evacuation, which is due to begin on 30 October.
For those willing to evacuate, the biggest concern is the route out. The Ukrainian authorities have not officially announced it, and two possible routes are being discussed among local residents: to Ukrainian-controlled territory or through Russia.
According to the terms of the agreement posted by Fox News, the route to Ukraine will be via Russia. The Ukrainian delegation, together with those wishing to leave, will travel from Oleshky to the Russian city of Anapa in Krasnodar Krai under escort from Russia's Dnepr military grouping. From there, on 31 October, they will be flown to Homiel (Gomel) in Belarus on a military transport aircraft operated by Russia's Ministry of Defence. Dmytro Lubinets and representatives of his office are also due to travel on this flight. The agreement was signed by Lubinets and Russia's Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova on 23 October.
A volunteer who spoke to Ukrainska Pravda said that so far several hundred people have signed up for evacuation. As previously reported, around 1,500 people still remain in Oleshky.
Volunteers are compiling lists of those wishing to leave, although people had previously been told to register at the local hospital, which is controlled by the Russians and has become the city's main hub during the occupation.
"Those lists at the hospital are being drawn up by the orcs. Who'd go to Russia? People should register through our people," Mariia, a local resident, told Ukrainska Pravda.
At the hospital, the Russians are resorting to intimidation and fear-mongering, telling people in Oleshky that they will only be allowed to take one bag with them during the evacuation. The occupying forces are also insisting that everyone will be taken to Russia, where they will have to go through filtration camps and other checks.
The volunteers who spoke to Ukrainska Pravda said the filtration rumours are just the latest Russian fake news, intended to make people base their evacuation decisions on fear.
Many people in Oleshky have no communications. Locals say the Russians are also deliberately jamming communications, making it increasingly difficult to organise the evacuation. Residents of Oleshky who know about the evacuation lists are trying to pass information on to those who cannot access it.
"There are elderly people who can't leave their homes and are cut off from the rest of the world. Their neighbours come over and tell them all about the evacuation," Mariia said.
Lists of people wishing to leave are being compiled by volunteers and representatives of the Ukrainian authorities. Lubinets' office is collecting information about those who need to be evacuated. Family members are signing up as well as Oleshky residents themselves: often, people who have already left for Ukrainian-controlled territory or Europe are adding their parents to the lists remotely.
People are trying to find relatives who are still in Oleshky and have been out of contact for a long time by reaching out through acquaintances.
Animals are also being prepared for evacuation from Oleshky. Even people who left their pets behind in Oleshky earlier are contacting volunteers and asking them to collect the animals.
Four-legged friends can be evacuated, but there is one complication when it comes to dogs: they have to wear muzzles.
"We found a bag of muzzles in Oleshky. People are now trying to work out how to pass them on to other pet owners," another local resident, Sofiia, told Ukrainska Pravda.
"There's an elderly couple – the woman has a severe form of diabetes, and they can't make it to the place where the bag is. They want to evacuate their dog, which weighs 40 kg. It's a calm dog, and intelligent, but it has to have a muzzle."
"Everyone knows what to expect from the Russians"
Oleshky residents have little faith that the evacuation can be carried out successfully. People are fearfully imagining various scenarios, including the possibility of a strike on the convoy.
"Everyone knows what the Russians are like. No one trusts them an inch. How many times have they declared truces along different sections of the line of contact? And how many times have they broken them?" says Mariia.
Statements by the occupying forces are also fuelling the distrust. Russia has promised to deliver humanitarian aid to Oleshky itself, and the news has triggered a fresh wave of fear among local residents. There have been cases in the past when Russian forces have delivered ammunition under the guise of "humanitarian aid".
"It's terrifying. They could bring in more than just aid. A lot more… We've been through this before. Everyone knows the Russians are f**king liars," Mykhailo, an Oleshky resident, told Ukrainska Pravda.
***
While some Oleshky residents are looking for any way to leave, others have become so disillusioned that they have decided to stay – in a place where not only normal life but even existence itself is impossible.
These people are hoping that humanitarian aid will be delivered, enabling them to hold out for a little longer.
"One man I know says he can't take it any more," Mykhailo said. "He doesn't care any more; he doesn't have the strength to leave. I've offered him the chance to leave so many times, but he says no. I told him, 'Mate, look, it's your choice, but think it through carefully…'
And there are a lot of people like him who simply won't leave."
People have split into two camps: those who have lost hope after repeated failed attempts to "rescue" them, and those in whom even the tiniest glimmer of hope for a new life has begun to flicker.
Ultimately, it's up to everyone to make their own choice and take responsibility for it. After all, it cannot be ruled out that after a few days of this "first truce", fighting on the Kherson front could escalate to unprecedented levels.
"There's going to be some serious ping-pong," one local volunteer told Ukrainska Pravda. "Everything will be wiped out. The Russians will bring in ammunition supplies now. Locals are already watching the Russians move in equipment and ammo and prepare to attack Kherson."
But one of the organisers of the mission in Oleshky told Ukrainska Pravda that he still believes the operation could succeed and have positive consequences.
"If everything works out, this will be the first example of a genuine truce across a fairly large section of the front line. It's been such a struggle – the military, the FSB and Lord knows who else are doing nothing but trying to sabotage the whole thing. But we believe it will work out and set a precedent."

Deadly train crash puts Sánchez on the ropes a month before elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:44:21 UTC
01:44:21 KST

Wednesday's accident happened in the middle of the pre-election campaign, adding pressure to Sánchez's government. With a month to go, parties are locked in a blame battle.
Wednesday's train crash near Toledo has added pressure on Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez ahead of the early general election he called for next month.
His government has already faced a succession of crises this year, including another deadly rail accident in Adamuz in January and the migration crisis in Ceuta in July. The latest accident represents another political shock in the middle of the pre-election period and comes as the government's handling of public services faces renewed scrutiny.
Although the main parties suspended their pre-campaign events after the tragedy, with the exception of Vox, political confrontation has continued.
The Partido Popular has questioned the government's management of the rail network. Far-right Vox has filed a criminal complaint for homicide against Transport Minister Óscar Puente while Frente Amplio has demanded that he appear before parliament to explain what happened.
The investigation still has to establish what caused the collision and whether human, technical or coordination failures were involved. But the political debate is already moving faster than the investigation.
While investigators try to reconstruct the minutes leading up to the crash, the parties are already disputing the narrative of what happened and, above all, who should bear its consequences.
One crisis after another
The crash is the latest in a series of crises that have shaped public debate in Spain in recent years and are now feeding into the election campaign. These include protests over housing, migration tensions in Ceuta, the nationwide blackout, devastating floods in Valencia, the handling of the COVID-19 pandemic, and corruption cases involving figures close to Sánchez and the PSOE.
For the public, the more immediate questions are what happened, why it happened and what will be done to prevent it from happening again.
The tragedy in Urda has once again put rail safety at the centre of the national debate, barely nine months after the Adamuz accident, which killed 46 people. The two incidents have renewed questions about infrastructure oversight, safety protocols and accountability.
What were the polls saying before the Urda tragedy?
Even before this week's train crash, polls were already pointing to a difficult electoral landscape for Pedro Sánchez, although some showed signs of recovery for the PSOE.
According to a poll published by El Mundo on 26 October, the Partido Popular was on 30.6% of the vote and between 125 and 131 seats, compared with 26.1% and between 103 and 109 seats for the Socialists. Vox was on 19.9% and between 66 and 69 seats.
Another poll published by El Español around the same time put the Partido Popular at around 32% of the vote and 135 seats, the PSOE at 27% and 108 seats, and Vox at 18.6% and 63 seats.
Both polls suggested that the PP and Vox together could secure an absolute majority.
The Centre for Sociological Research (CIS), however, has presented a very different picture, placing the PSOE well ahead of the PP in its latest barometer.
The sharp differences between polls add further uncertainty to a pre-election period already dominated by political and management crises, with the Urda rail tragedy now added to the debate barely a month before the general election.

Interim President Delcy Rodriguez ruled out on Thursday calling immediate presidential elections, insisting that Venezuela must undergo comprehensive institutional reforms before setting a definitive electoral calendar.
Rodriguez emphasized that elections governed by the Constitution will take place, but the timing must prioritize political stability over strict timelines.
"The election should not be a problem, and we will not go back until there are times when there is no confrontation," Rodriguez told the nation in an address. "The political future of the country is not measured by a date on the calendar."
Rodriguez outlined a broader roadmap required before Venezuelans head to the polls, including legislative overhauls, participation guarantees across the political spectrum, and a complete renewal of the electoral authority.
She said the reform process must produce "an electoral power accepted by all" to ensure elections serve as "a solution and not a generator of irreconcilable conflicts,” urging an orderly "political, economic, cultural, spiritual, democratic and verifiable" transition and warning against sudden political shifts.
"Venezuela is not going to jump into a void. Let's employ existing laws and institutions to make them better," she added.
In a notable policy shift addressing long-standing complaints from human rights organizations regarding arbitrary detentions, Rodriguez also announced new directives for domestic law enforcement and instructed police agencies to ensure that "no person is detained" without a formal court order.
The address came ahead of opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Corina Machado’s first scheduled news conference since returning to Venezuela.
According to her party, Vente Venezuela, Machado is slated to address the media around midday. The appearance follows a recent visit to the northern coastal state of La Guaira, where she met communities affected by the June 24 double earthquake.
Anticipation remains high regarding Machado’s response to the government’s proposed electoral conditions and her vision for the opposition's strategy.
On Wednesday, when asked about Machado, Rodriguez dismissed claims of state intimidation, asserting that "there is no political persecution" in Venezuela and suggesting Machado "could avoid the show."

Climate change had also made classrooms in Saint Lucia increasingly hot, making more comfortable school environments an urgent priority, he said, adding that his government is modernizing and diversifying agriculture and developing renewable and alternative energy sources amid rising living costs, while hoping to continue exchanging expertise with Taiwan in those areas.
Education is highly valued in Taiwan and Saint Lucia, and the Saint Lucian public is grateful for Taiwan’s continued scholarship support, he said.
“This is why the people of St Lucia are so appreciative of the scholarships you continue to offer our students,” he said.
“In this regard, we look forward to the expansion of our scholarship programs and the construction of a modern cultural and creative arts center,” Pierre said.
More than 400 young people from Saint Lucia have so far received scholarships from Taiwan to pursue higher education, he said.
Pierre stressed that people are a country’s most valuable asset, thanking Taiwan for its assistance with training, scholarships and infrastructure.
He also expressed hope that more Saint Lucian doctors, young academics, students and professionals would move to Taiwan to study.
Pierre said he hopes closer ties between Taiwan and Saint Lucia would bring greater benefits to their people through concrete projects.
“As we look to the future with great optimism and our desire to make Saint Lucia one of the best places to live and work in the Caribbean, I thank you,” he said.
Lai thanked Pierre for his continued support for Taiwan, adding that official and private-sector exchanges between the two countries have grown closer over the past two years.
Lai added that the Taiwan External Trade Development Council would hold the 19th Taiwan-Saint Lucia trade exhibition in Saint Lucia next month, with more than 70 local companies expected to participate alongside Taiwanese businesses.
Meanwhile, he also thanked Pierre for publicly supporting Taiwan’s bid for full membership of the UN at the recent UN General Assembly session and called for continued cooperation on global challenges, including climate change and public health.

Growing share of Taiwanese tax dependents are elderly: Ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:43:05 UTC
01:43:05 KST

In a sign of Taiwan’s aging population, the proportion of tax dependents over age 70 has risen by 8.2 percentage points over the past 10 years, the Ministry of Finance said yesterday.
In a report on trends in Taiwan’s consolidated income tax revenues, the Department of Statistics said income tax revenues had reached record highs each year since 2021, rising to NT$873.7 billion (US$26.8 billion) last year.
The report attributed the steady increase to higher salaries, stock market gains and rising interest rates.
Photo: Taipei Times
Overall, consolidated income tax revenue accounted for 23.1 percent of Taiwan’s total tax revenue last year, compared with 30.1 percent in Japan, 28.8 percent in South Korea and 18.3 percent in Singapore, the ministry said.
Following Taiwan’s 2018 tax reforms, the proportion of income tax-exempt households rose considerably.
By 2024, 45.3 percent of tax filings, or 3.17 million tax-filing units, were not required to pay any income tax, the report said.
Meanwhile, the top 20 percent of earners accounted for 60 percent of all income earned in 2024, but 97 percent of the total income tax burden, the report said.
The ministry highlighted increases in both the proportion of single tax filers and filers with elderly dependents.
These trends reflect a growing proportion of people remaining unmarried, smaller household sizes and an aging population, the ministry said.
In 2024, single-person tax filings reached a record high of 57.4 percent of the total, while eight in 10 new tax filing households were single individuals with no dependents, the report said.
Meanwhile, the proportion of claimed dependents who are over 70 years old climbed to 27 percent in 2024 — a rise of 8.2 percentage points over the previous decade — while the share of dependents under age 18 fell to 37 percent, the ministry said.
In financial terms, this meant that the number of households claiming the special deduction for long-term care, and the total amount claimed, exceeded 400,000 households and NT$51.8 billion respectively, both record highs, it said.
That year, the total amount claimed under the special deduction for preschool children exceeded NT$100 billion, showing the government is committed to both long-term care needs and easing the burden on families with young children, the ministry said.

Egg freezing a hope for same-sex couples: doctor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:43:04 UTC
01:43:04 KST

Egg freezing offers hope to same-sex couples awaiting the legalization of assisted reproduction and an opportunity for comprehensive reproductive health screening, a doctor said.
Although same-sex marriage was legalized in 2019, same-sex couples still lack a legal path to having children of their own, Taipei Fertility Center attending physician Isabel Hsu (許嘉樺) said on Thursday last week.
Women waiting for the day assisted reproductive technology becomes legal for same-sex couples increasingly choose to freeze their eggs, she said, adding that one-third of her gay clients opted for the treatment.
Photo courtesy of the Taipei Fertility Center
LIFE-SAVING MOVE
A person identified by the pseudonym Hsiao Shan (小珊), 32, discovered that she had a 5cm ovarian tumor after a transvaginal ultrasound, a routine part of egg freezing treatment, Hsu said.
That type of ultrasound is effective in and necessary for determining ovaries’ egg reserves, and checking the reproductive system for tumors, cysts or other pathologies, she said.
Hsiao Shan was referred to a gynecologist and an oncologist who jointly weighed her medical options and successfully removed the tumor and froze her eggs, Hsu said.
The timely diagnosis likely saved Hsiao Shan’s life and preserved her healthy eggs, which would allow her to have children should Taiwan legalize in-vitro fertilization for same-sex couples, the doctor said.
Clinical data showed that more than 93 percent of frozen eggs survive the thawing process and their fertility rate is comparable to their natural counterparts, she said.
Lesbian couples who plan to have children should visit fertility experts to assess their ability to bear children and undergo reproductive health screenings, which would help create a tailored plan for them, Hsu said.
AWAITING LEGALIZATION
Creating legal pathways for people such as Hsiao Shan to have children should be a priority for a nation facing a precipitous population decline, she said.
The right of lesbian couples and single women to equal access to fertility care and chances to start a family should be protected, she added.

Blanket e-cigarette ban not enough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:43:02 UTC
01:43:02 KST

The Health Promotion Administration (HPA) on Sept. 8 set up e-cigarette collection spots across Taiwan, allowing people to voluntarily and anonymously dispose of their devices. In just more than one month, 633kg of e-cigarettes had been collected. Assuming each device weighs about 50g, that amounts to more than 12,000 e-cigarettes.
On Monday last week, civic groups called on the Legislative Yuan to expedite an amendment to the Tobacco Hazards Prevention Act (菸害防制法) that would penalize possessing e-cigarettes.
The law already prohibits the manufacture, importation, sale, supply, display, advertising and use of e-cigarettes. Users can be fined between NT$2,000 and NT$10,000, but a legal loophole remains when it comes to mere possession. Closing this loophole is necessary, but if efforts to curb youth e-cigarette use ultimately amount to little more than fining anyone caught with one, they would do little to address the more complex issues of online purchases, distribution on school campuses, disguised products and psychoactive substances being mixed into vape cartridges.
The largest challenge in regulating e-cigarette use is that the devices are small, come in a wide variety of designs and are sold largely through online channels. Some products resemble USB flash drives, pens or other electronic devices, making them difficult for parents and teachers to identify at a glance. Transactions can also take place through social media platforms, messaging apps or private groups.
The act prohibits the sale of e-cigarettes, but to effectively reduce young people’s access to these products, enforcement should prioritize supply chains and sellers. The government could establish a rapid, cross-platform reporting mechanism that allows health authorities, police and digital platforms to jointly investigate accounts selling illegal products, relevant keywords, payment methods and recurring sellers. Enforcement should be more stringent for those involved in large-scale imports, manufacturing or long-term sales than for people found in possession of e-cigarettes. As long as these products remain readily accessible, they would continue to find their way back into schools, even if on-campus inspections and penalties are increased.
The HPA’s latest survey on youth smoking behavior found that about 2.1 percent of junior-high school students and 5.1 percent of senior and vocational high school students use e-cigarettes, with an estimated total of at least 40,000 young users. For underage students caught in possession of an e-cigarette for the first time, the policy priority should be to stop them from using it, determine where it was obtained and prevent the child from developing a dependence.
If possession is formally criminalized or made punishable under future amendments, a tiered response system could be established. For the first offense, students could receive health education, smoking cessation counseling and consultations involving their parents. Administrative penalties could be increased for repeated offenses or cases involving the sale of e-cigarettes. Such a system would give schools more tools to intervene while reducing the risk of students hiding the problem for fear of being punished. Vape cartridges containing controlled substances should instead be handled under drug laws, with efforts to trace their source conducted simultaneously.
There are 432 e-cigarette collection spots across the nation, and more than 12,000 devices were collected in just more than one month. This suggests that there is a substantial number of e-cigarettes in circulation that need to be removed from the market. If possession is formally made punishable, the government could establish a clear grace period before the new penalties take effect, encouraging people to voluntarily surrender their devices and publishing details of collection methods and disposal procedures. This would help remove existing products from circulation while reducing controversy over people being penalized immediately because they are unaware of the new law.
Collection data could be used to identify product brands, sources, designs and areas where more devices are circulating. This would allow the government to track changes in the market without collecting anyone’s personal information. By linking the new e-cigarette collection system with enforcement intelligence, authorities could turn it from a transitional policy measure into an important source of data about the underground market.
E-cigarette governance must move beyond a blanket ban to a comprehensive system that prevents young people’s use of emerging tobacco products and other addictive substances. The government could publish annual data on youth usage rates, cases of illegal online sales, school reports, referrals for cessation treatment and sources of illegal products, while tracking whether legislative amendments have effectively reduced usage rates.
Administrative penalties can only address those who are caught. It is more important that the government makes it harder for these products to enter Taiwan and be sold online, while ensuring that students who try e-cigarettes for the first time can leave the environment in which they use them as early as possible.
The collection of more than 10,000 e-cigarette devices is a warning sign, but it is also an opportunity for the government to reassess its approach. Only when supply-side enforcement, school education, addiction treatment services, online regulation and legal accountability work in tandem can e-cigarette control move beyond simply catching offenders to becoming a public health policy aimed at reducing the risks of exposure and addiction for the next generation.
Roger Chen is a legal specialist for a technology corporation.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen
