India increases growth forecast for fiscal year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:30:00 UTC
01:30:00 KST

India increases growth forecast for fiscal year
October 29, 2026
India's Ministry of Finance expects India's economy to grow at a pace of 7.3% in the current fiscal year based on its latest assessment of current data, it said in its October economic review.
The estimate is a slight increase on the previous forecast of 7.1%.
India's current fiscal year, known as FY27, runs from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027.
The report contrasted these figures with global growth predictions of nearer 3%, saying "India's growth momentum, by comparison, has held firm."
The ministry said growth in various key indicators like energy consumption, port traffic, goods and services tax (GST) collections, and car sales had accelerated in the previous quarter.
Inflation, fueled by El Nino and geopolitics, poses a threat
However, the ministry also warned of continued inflationary pressure and pressure on the rupee currency, as well as downside risks from the El Nino weather phonemenon that could threaten soil moisture ahead of the winter sowing season.
It said that external factors like oil prices and "global uncertainties" — seemingly a reference at least in part to the instablity in the Middle East — continued to pressure the rupee's value and pose inflationary risks.
Consumer price inflation (CPI), the wholesale price index (WPI), food cost prices and fuel and power prices were all rising month for month, albeit at very different rates.
The CPI was up 5.54% year-on-year in September, but the WPI had risen more sharply at 11.39%. Food index inflation was up by 8% in rural areas, and a slightly more modest 7.18% in urban centers.
But, as in many other countries, fuel and power costs increases were in an entirely different league, at 25.85% inflation in September 2026 comapred to the same month a year earlier, prior to the outbreak of fighting in the Middle East.
Ministry says FX reserves ample, rupee's decline appears manageable
Although it has been a comparatively slow decline, the rupee has been consistently losing value against the US dollar over the past five years, threatening the country's relative purchasing power internationally. This slide has picked up pace in the last 15 months or so.
But the ministry pointed to foreign exchange reserves worth some $721 billion and said that India was "well-positioned" to weather such risks and sustain its expansionary trajectory..

50,000 Ethiopians flee clashes into Kenya, IOM says
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:29:17 CST
01:29:17 KST

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Some 50,000 Ethiopians have fled into neighboring Kenya, seeking safety following violent clashes in southern Ethiopia, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) has said.
The UN migration agency warned, in a statement issued Thursday, that further arrivals could place additional pressure on already stretched local services and resources.
IOM data showed that an estimated 50,000 people had arrived in Moyale, Marsabit County, as of Thursday. They are staying with local communities along the border or sheltering at five temporary sites.
As the situation continues to evolve, IOM said the Kenyan government and inter-agency partners are planning a response for up to 80,000 people, anticipating further arrivals and growing humanitarian needs.
"The situation remains fluid, and the number of arrivals could increase in the coming days," IOM Kenya Chief of Mission Nomagugu Ncube said in the statement.
Noting that most of the displaced are being sheltered by local communities, Ncube stressed that meeting their immediate needs, while also supporting the communities who are now hosting thousands, is "an urgent priority."
The UN agency stressed that newly arrived populations urgently need basic supplies, safe water, emergency shelter, healthcare services, critical protection and sanitation support.
The arrivals follow a week of deadly intercommunal clashes between Ethiopia's Somali and Oromo communities in and around Moyale, a border town. Media reports have linked the violence, which has reportedly killed scores of people on both sides, to tensions over a flag dispute. ■

15 injured in accident at copper mine in southern Mongolia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:29:10 CST
01:29:10 KST

ULAN BATOR, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Fifteen workers were injured in an accident at the large Oyu Tolgoi copper mine in southern Mongolia on Thursday, according to the mine operator.
"At around 6 p.m. today, a seismic event occurred along a rock fracture zone, causing tremors in the underground mine," said operator Oyu Tolgoi LLC in a statement.
The company said the tremors triggered a rockfall, injuring 15 workers. No fatalities were reported.
The injured workers are receiving medical attention and undergoing medical examinations, the company said, adding that an assessment of the situation was ongoing. The company said it would provide further information as it became available.
Located in the Umnugovi Province, the Oyu Tolgoi mine is one of the world's largest copper mines and the country's largest investment project to date.
At full capacity, the mine is expected to produce an average of around 500,000 tons of copper annually between 2028 and 2036 from its open-pit and underground operations. ■

China's Zhang wins 53kg total at weightlifting worlds
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:29:06 CST
01:29:06 KST

Total gold medalist Zhang Haiqin (C) of China, total silver medalist Miranda Eleanor Ulrey (L) of the United States and total bronze medalist Kim So Hyon of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) react during the awarding ceremony of women's 53kg at the 2026 IWF World Championships in Ningbo, east China's Zhejiang Province, Oct. 29, 2026. (Xinhua/Jiang Han)
NINGBO, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China's Zhang Haiqin won the women's 53kg title at the Weightlifting World Championships here on Thursday, holding off American Miranda Ulrey by one kilogram in the total standings.
Zhang lifted 98kg in the snatch and 123kg in the clean and jerk for a total of 221kg. Ulrey matched Zhang's 98kg in the snatch but managed 122kg in the clean and jerk for a 220kg total.
The two traded successful lifts throughout the snatch, both opening at 95kg before making 98kg. Both failed at 100kg on their third attempts, with Zhang taking snatch gold by virtue of her lighter body weight.
"I really wanted to make 100, that weight was over the record and I wanted it, but I rushed it a little," Zhang said. After the snatch, she initially thought she had finished second. "I didn't realize at the time, I thought I was second, and then my coach told me I was first."
Rosegie Ramos of the Philippines took snatch bronze with 97kg.
In the clean and jerk, Ulrey missed her first attempt at 119kg before making 120kg and 122kg. Zhang made 120kg and then 123kg on her second attempt, a lift she knew was crucial.
"The second lift is key. If you fall behind on the second lift it's very hard to come back," Zhang said.
Zhang then attempted 126kg on her final lift, which would have given her clean-and-jerk gold and broken the total world standard of 223kg, but she was unable to complete the lift.
"On the third lift I pulled too hard off the floor and my whole frame kind of collapsed, the weight just crushed me," Zhang told Xinhua. "I tried to stand up but I really gave it everything."
Clean-and-jerk gold instead went to Kim So Hyon of the DPR Korea, who lifted 123kg in the afternoon's Group B session before the Group A competition. Kim finished with a 214kg total, enough for bronze overall.
Because Kim reached 123kg first, she ranked ahead of Zhang in the clean and jerk. Zhang said she did not watch Kim's afternoon session.
"I was resting in the back, I didn't see it, it didn't affect my rhythm, I just focused on myself," Zhang said.
The world standards for the new 53kg category, which took effect Aug. 1 under the Los Angeles Olympic cycle, are 99kg in the snatch, 126kg in the clean and jerk and 223kg in total. Zhang lifted 101kg in the snatch and totaled 227kg at a national Grand Prix in August, but came up short of those marks on Thursday.
"Of course there's regret, the world record felt right there, but regret gives me even more motivation," Zhang said. "I just need to take it one competition at a time, make every lift, and go back and build a stronger, more solid base."
The men's 70kg Group A competition is scheduled for Friday. ■

Sweden's Center Party leader nominated for PM amid political deadlock
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:29:05 CST
01:29:05 KST

HELSINKI, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Swedish Parliament Speaker Andreas Norlen on Thursday nominated Center Party leader Elisabeth Thand Ringqvist as the country's next prime minister (PM), with a parliamentary vote scheduled for next Tuesday, marking the latest attempt to break the political deadlock following September's general election.
Norlen said the Nov. 3 vote would test parliamentary support for a proposed five-party coalition government comprising the Center Party, Social Democratic Party, Christian Democrats, Green Party and Liberal Party.
Thand Ringqvist confirmed to Swedish Television (SVT) that she had accepted the nomination, saying the Center Party would "continue to take responsibility and contribute constructively to ensuring that Sweden gets a government."
She said the speaker had decided to nominate her following their discussions, although she had also pointed out that other possible ways forward remained.
Norlen thanked Thand Ringqvist for her efforts to explore possible governing arrangements, saying they had helped deepen understanding of the political situation.
Drawing on lessons from Sweden's prolonged government formation process in 2018, Norlen said he wanted to link exploratory talks more closely with parliamentary votes to maintain momentum and gradually increase pressure on political parties to resolve the deadlock.
He also outlined the next step should Thand Ringqvist's nomination be rejected. Ulf Kristersson, leader of the Moderate Party and outgoing PM, would then be given one week, from Nov. 3 to Nov. 10, to explore the possibility of forming a government.
The latest development follows weeks of unsuccessful attempts to form a government after Sweden's Sept. 13 general election. On Oct. 15, parliament rejected Social Democratic leader Magdalena Andersson's bid to become the PM. Andersson had previously failed to secure sufficient support for a government after two rounds of exploratory talks.
On Oct. 19, Norlen tasked Thand Ringqvist with exploring the possibility of forming a government. However, after holding talks with other parliamentary parties, she reported back to the speaker on Monday that her efforts had failed to break the political deadlock.
The Social Democratic Party, Left Party, Green Party and Center Party together won 176 seats in the 349-member parliament in September's election, giving them a narrow majority but leaving them divided over the composition of a new government.
Under Sweden's constitution, a prime ministerial nominee is rejected if at least 175 members of parliament vote against the proposal. If four consecutive nominations are rejected, a new election must be held within three months. ■

China's Blue Bay Restoration Initiative named UN World Restoration Flagship
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:29:00 CST
01:29:00 KST

China's Blue Bay Restoration Initiative is named a World Restoration Flagship by the United Nations during the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia, Oct. 29, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Junfeng)
YEREVAN, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- China's Blue Bay Restoration Initiative was named a World Restoration Flagship by the United Nations on Thursday during the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia.
The initiative is jointly led by China's Ministry of Natural Resources and Ministry of Finance. This marks the second time a nationwide ecological restoration initiative from China has received the United Nations Decade on Ecosystem Restoration recognition, making China the first country to achieve the distinction twice.
Chosen from over 200 applications and more than 80 government-submitted nominations, the Blue Bay Restoration Initiative was recognized as one of the world's most promising, ambitious and inspiring examples of large-scale ecosystem restoration, said Inger Andersen, executive director of the UN Environment Programme.
The initiative aims to restore more than 150,000 hectares of coastal wetlands and over 2,000 km of coastline by 2030, bringing lasting benefits to local communities, she added. ■

Interview: More than an expo, Rwanda sees CIIE as a link to Chinese market, says official
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:28:59 CST
01:28:59 KST

KIGALI, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Rwanda's regular participation in the China International Import Expo (CIIE) reflects a strong desire to maintain a long-term close connection with the Chinese market, an official said.
In a recent interview with Xinhua ahead of the ninth CIIE from Nov. 5 to 10 in Shanghai, China, Rwanda Development Board (RDB) Deputy Chief Executive Officer Juliana Muganza said that rather than viewing the expo as merely an exhibition, the government recognized that the event offers a platform to promote Rwanda as an investment destination.
This view is backed by the growth in bilateral trade between Rwanda and China from approximately 300 million U.S. dollars in 2019 to 849 million in 2025, according to RDB data. Meanwhile, Rwanda's exports to China have also seen a significant surge from approximately 35 million dollars in 2019 to 227 million in 2025.
Calling China one of Rwanda's most important economic and trading partners, Muganza mentioned that for a country like Rwanda, the CIIE provides a vital opportunity for local companies, including small and medium-sized enterprises, to present their products directly to Chinese buyers, distributors, e-commerce platforms and consumers.
However, she added that Rwanda's participation goes beyond selling products during the six-day expo.
"We use the CIIE to build long-term commercial relationships, better understand developments in the Chinese market, promote Rwanda as an investment and tourism destination, and strengthen the broader economic partnership between Rwanda and China," she said.
Rwanda has participated in the CIIE since the first edition in 2018.
Muganza said the exhibition has also been instrumental in expanding investment cooperation.
Data from the RDB showed that registered investments by Chinese companies in Rwanda rose from 460 million dollars in 2024 to 548.5 million dollars in 2025. Chinese companies in Rwanda are increasingly active in sectors such as manufacturing, infrastructure, construction, energy and real estate.
Muganza said that while the achievements cannot be attributed to the exhibition alone, the CIIE contributed by providing Rwanda with a major platform every year to promote local products, investment opportunities and tourism.
During this year's CIIE, Rwandan exhibitors will showcase some of the country's most competitive and distinctive products, including specialty coffee, premium tea, chili and chili products, macadamia nuts, and other agricultural and value-added Made-in-Rwanda products.
Other products with considerable potential include honey, avocado, dried fruits and nuts, as market access for additional Rwandan products continues to expand.
Muganza emphasized that the CIIE, an exhibition dedicated specifically to imports, "sends an important message that China is not only interested in exporting to the world, but is also actively creating opportunities" for companies from around the world to access the Chinese market.
Pointing to win-win cooperation, Muganza said the exhibition helps foreign companies gain access to the scale and opportunities of the Chinese market, while Chinese companies and consumers benefit from a wider range of international products.
On China's zero-tariff treatment for 53 African countries, which came into force in May, Muganza said Rwanda considers the policy a very important development for Africa-China trade.
Muganza also noted that China's high-level opening up "sends an important and positive signal," creating opportunities not only for major multinational corporations, but also for producers and businesses from developing economies. ■

UN calls for faster ecosystem restoration
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
00:28:22 CST
01:28:22 KST

YEREVAN, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Around 252 million hectares of ecosystems worldwide are under restoration, but progress remains insufficient to reach the global target for 2030, according to a UN report published Thursday at the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in the Armenian capital Yerevan.
Titled "Restoration progress report: Nature's comeback -- Scaling ecosystem restoration for people and planet," the report was jointly published by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, the United Nations Environment Programme and the Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity.
The report takes stock of global ecosystem restoration halfway through the United Nations Decade on Ecosystem Restoration, providing a comprehensive assessment of restoration efforts across terrestrial, freshwater, marine and coastal ecosystems.
It warns that the world remains off track to achieve Target 2 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which calls for at least 30 percent of degraded ecosystems to be under effective restoration by 2030. Countries have pledged to restore around 1 billion hectares, but the pace of restoration needs to triple to meet the 2030 target.
Terrestrial ecosystems make up approximately 92 percent of the total documented restoration area covered by the report. Meanwhile, recorded restoration efforts in freshwater, marine and coastal ecosystems remain limited, highlighting the need to strengthen monitoring and reporting in these areas.
Drawing on China's 7th National Report to the Convention on Biological Diversity, the report also examines the country's ecosystem restoration efforts. According to country-level data compiled in the assessment, China has the world's largest documented area of ecosystems under restoration.
Yelena Finegold, one of the report's authors, said accelerating global ecosystem restoration would require increased financing, stronger cross-sectoral planning and coordination, as well as greater capacity to implement restoration activities and monitor progress. ■

Some of the world’s biggest bats are getting smaller
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:28:22 UTC
01:28:22 KST

These big bats aren’t quite the behemoths they used to be.
With a leathery wingspan of up to a meter and a half, fruit bats —some of which are called flying foxes — feel a bit like they’ve flapped out of a fantasy novel. Though flying foxes include the world’s largest bats, one species in Madagascar appears to be shrinking, researchers report October 29 in the Journal of Mammalogy. Hunting pressure by humans may be why.
The first hints that the bats might be shrinking came from scientific collections at the Field Museum in Chicago. Researchers at the museum — including flying vertebrate ecologist Emily Cornelius Ruhs and conservation biologist Steven Goodman — noticed something strange about the preserved specimens of Malagasy flying foxes (Pteropus rufus).
“It seemed like the [flying foxes] in the collections were a lot larger than the ones that [field scientists] had been catching in recent years in Madagascar,” says Ruhs.
To see if newer specimens were indeed smaller than older specimens, and to understand why, the researchers began taking detailed measurements of the bats. The team logged measurements of 12 different features of the skull and teeth over a total of 121 specimens stored within nine museums. The specimens were collected over more than 150 years, up to the present day.
Bats collected prior to the 1980s had skulls that were on average 3.6 millimeters longer, or about 6 percent longer, than those collected after the 1980s. Possible causes of the shrinkage included effects from climate change or habitat loss. But the timing of the shrinkage also lined up with the commercialization of flying fox hunting.
“Bats are eaten in Madagascar in certain villages and cultures,” Ruhs says. Up until the 1980s, the animals were mostly hunted on a very small scale to provide food for a family or small community. But around that time, people started selling more bats at markets and restaurants.
As hunting pressure increased, the biggest bats in the population may have been selectively targeted since they provide the “most bang for your buck” Ruhs says.
It’s possible that the smaller size could have long-term impacts on the population, says Emma Stone, a conservation biologist at the University of Bath in England. “Species are specifically adapted to their environments and adaptation takes place over thousands of years,” she says. Changes in the animals’ physical traits or adaptations caused by human pressures might make the bats less able to respond to environmental, climate or disease stresses.
The bats’ population has dwindled as well. There were an estimated 300,000 Malagasy flying foxes in Madagascar in the early 2000s. Researchers estimate the number has dropped two-thirds since then. The new findings raise concerns about how the bats’ shrinking bodies might be a bellwether for species-wide conservation risks. Future work on the bats’ genetics could tell researchers how modern populations are faring, Ruhs says. Other fruit bat species are also hunted and eaten in Madagascar, she notes, so seeing if similar shrinkage is happening in those species might be interesting.
“These are important food sources for people. But I think there is something to be said for understanding how to manage [their harvesting] a little bit more,” Ruhs says. “If this population isn’t doing so well, how do we overcome the needs of the people who live there while also protecting species?”

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. The West is working hard to sully the Russia-Africa partnership, TASS Director General Andrey Kondrashov said during a plenary discussion at the Russia-Africa media forum.
"Russia-Africa cooperation has become one of the main targets of information attacks by Western ill-wishers and their henchmen. Today, when Russia and African nations are working to build an equal partnership, any distortions are especially noticeable and come at a particularly high cost to both sides," he stressed.
Modern fake news is rarely based on crude fabrications, Kondrashov pointed out. Instead, it often relies on "seemingly harmless techniques," the distortion of motives and the use of reputable sources without providing evidence. As an example, he cited a deepfake video featuring Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova. Posted shortly before a Russian delegation’s visit to Kazakhstan, the fabricated video was intended to disrupt the visit but failed after the provocation was promptly exposed.
The TASS director general urged African journalists to pool their efforts to counter fake news. He noted that TASS and its partners had co-founded the Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN).
"We brought together 130 experts from 55 countries. This is an effective tool that will allow you to detect fake news almost automatically from the start," Kondrashov said, adding that media outlets could join the organization free of charge and that they did not have to pay membership fees.
Media forum
The Russia-Africa media forum is taking place in Moscow on October 26-29, bringing together leading Russian and African media outlets. Media leaders are discussing the role of the countries of the Global Majority in the international media landscape, exploring the prospects for the development of media resources as tools to combat disinformation, and assessing ways to "decolonize" media content.
TASS is an information partner of the forum.

How Trump's immigration crackdown could hurt him in the midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:25:18 UTC
01:25:18 KST

Breadcrumb
How Trump's immigration crackdown could hurt him in the midterms
When Donald Trump was running for president two years ago, Americans’ television screens were filled with images of migrant chaos. There were tent camps on both sides of the border, caravans of people trudging through Central America and concerns about newcomers overwhelming social services.
That turmoil faded as President Joe Biden tightened immigration enforcement after Trump clamped down even more. Now any chaos is on American streets, where violent and even deadly clashes have defined a deportation campaign that's designed to fulfill hardliners' goals of uprooting anyone in the country illegally.
The shift helps explain why Trump's effort to fulfill his promises has turned into a backlash, undermining one of the core issues that fueled his return to the White House. While Trump maintains some support for his handling of the border, polling shows voters disapprove of his approach to immigration, a striking turnaround that could undermine Republican attempts to maintain control of Congress in the midterms.
“The American people supported strong border security,” said Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat who has become a prominent critic of the administration’s policies. “What they got instead was shredding the Constitution, mass deportations and killing American citizens on the streets of Minneapolis.”
Trump's allies say the president is the victim of his own success.
“The disaster at the border and the impunity of people just walking over and being released into the country was hard to ignore,” said Mark Krikorian, executive director of the Center for Immigration Studies. Trump dramatically reduced illegal border crossings, Krikorian said, “and that’s often politically bad."
Krikorian praised Trump for adopting low profile but highly effective sweeps that have achieved month after month of record arrests. U.S Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers arrested almost 51,000 immigrants in the country illegally in August, according to the Department of Homeland Security, up from 49,000 in July and 43,000 in June. An estimated 660,000 people have been deported in the past fiscal year, according to the Migration Policy Institute, short of the administration’s goal of 1 million annually.
Biden's immigration policies remain a regular target for Republicans this year. Trump said at a recent Florida rally that Democrats let migrants “pour across our borders from all over the world.”
“If they win in the midterms, they'll do it again,” he warned.
Trump returned to White House with deportation pledge
In 2024, Trump warned repeatedly of an immigrant “invasion.” “They’re poisoning the blood of our country,” he said of people crossing the border illegally. He insisted, falsely, that immigrants were behind spikes in crime and eating household pets.
Even as Trump drew criticism for his rhetoric, his focus on the issue resonated with voters who had seen illegal immigration soar during the Biden administration, with border arrests from Mexico reaching a record 250,000 in December 2023.
Trump's victory seemed poised to reshape immigration politics. Forty-six Democrats in the House and a dozen in the Senate joined Republicans in voting for the Laken Riley Act, a bill named after a Georgia student killed by a man in the country illegally. The law requires detention without bond for noncitizens accused of murder and other violent crimes.
After Trump took office, he cranked deportations into higher gear. Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland resident, was one of the people caught up in that net. Despite a court order forbidding it, the administration sent him to his native El Salvador, where he was confined to that country's notorious central prison that was also used to house other Trump deportees.
The US Supreme Court directed the administration to “facilitate” Abrego Garcia's return, and Van Hollen flew to El Salvador to meet with him. Some Democrats questioned the wisdom of confronting Trump on an issue where the president was so popular, the senator recalled. Now his party is more emboldened on the issue.
“We’ve gone from some of that sniping on the sidelines to a clear vote among Democrats to defund ICE,” Van Hollen said.
Minneapolis crackdown leads to backlash
The early face of the Trump crackdown was top Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino, who swaggered through raids in tactical gear and deployed forces to Los Angeles and Chicago, where he led a helicopter raid on an apartment building.
But Minneapolis was the turning point. More than 2,000 federal officers were sent to the city, and scenes of masked agents spilling from convoys of unmarked vehicles became commonplace. Tens of thousands of protesters took to the streets.
Two US citizens - Renee Good and Alex Pretti, both 37 - were killed during confrontations with agents. In the weeks that followed, the White House pushed aside Bovino and Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.
Michael Pretti, Alex's father, said this week that the family is still troubled by the bystander videos of the shooting. He had a holstered gun that he was legally allowed to carry, and none of the footage shows him brandishing the weapon or attacking federal agents in the moments before he was killed.
“I think it haunts many Americans to see a US citizen who was peaceful and in his community shot multiple times on the back, in the back, while on the ground,” he told reporters.
Arrests dropped after the killings, although they eventually returned to record numbers. But the politics became more complicated, and Republicans’ immigration message has fractured.
There are hardliners like US Sen. Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee, who is vowing more deportations as she runs for governor. And there's Cuban-American Florida Rep. Maria-Elena Salazar, who criticized Trump’s migrant crackdown in a campaign advertisement filmed outside the White House.
Salazar has sponsored legislation that would allow immigrants who are in the country illegally to remain as long as they have otherwise followed the law. Among the sponsors is Republican Rep. Gabe Evans, the grandson of a Mexican immigrant, who is trying to distinguish himself from Trump while running in a Colorado swing district.
In New Hampshire, former Sen. John Sununu, running for an open Senate seat, has been critical of ICE tactics and the agency's use of masks to conceal agents' identities.
Republicans often try to connect immigration to voters' concerns about high prices. Ohio Sen. Jon Husted blasts Democratic opponent Sherrod Brown as someone who “voted to raise your taxes repeatedly and give those tax dollars to illegals.”
“Republicans are trying to turn voters against Democrats because of what Joe Biden did in failing to control the border effectively,” said Frank Sharry, a longtime immigrants' rights activist who consults with the centrist Democratic group Third Way. “So they’re trying to define Democrats as being for open borders and not serious about removing criminals.”
Democrats are changing their approach
But that comes as many Democratic candidates are shifting away from Biden-era messaging about immigration.
In Texas, Senate candidate James Talarico calls himself a “border security Democrat” who wants to hire more Border Patrol officers and increase the use of surveillance technology.
Talarico criticizes many of Trump’s immigration policies as wasteful, but doesn’t hold back when it comes to criticizing the last Democratic president.
“Joe Biden and his administration failed us on our southern border,” he said in a July press conference in a Texas county on the Mexico border.
Even some of the most liberal Democratic candidates, like Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, are careful to note that they want strong borders.
“I don’t know of a candidate who’s in a swing race who’s saying anything other than ‘We’ve got to secure the border’ and ‘We’ve got to remove criminals,’” Sharry said.
(The Associated Press)

How US sanctions are threatening political dissent in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:24:39 UTC
01:24:39 KST

Breadcrumb
How US sanctions are threatening political dissent in Europe
The United States is increasingly using its financial power to target political organisations beyond its borders, with consequences extending far into Europe. Under the banner of counterterrorism, US sanctions can effectively cut activists and organisations off from banking services, digital infrastructure, and the financial resources needed to operate, even when European authorities have not designated them as terrorist groups.
The case of Autistici/Inventati (A/I), an Italian digital network providing services to antifascist and anticapitalist organisations, illustrates how this works.
On 26 August 2026, the Trump administration sanctioned A/I alongside the British activist group Palestine Action and the transnational Palestinian organisation Masar Badil. Washington accused them of supporting terrorism, as part of a broader campaign against what it describes as violent far-left extremism.
A/I was designated a Specially Designated Global Terrorist by the US Treasury, which accused it of providing digital infrastructure and services to violent extremist organisations. The collective rejected the accusations, insisting that its work consisted of providing secure communications and digital services to political movements.
Yet the US decision's consequences were felt almost immediately in Italy.
A/I's bank, Banca Etica, suspended operations on its account because of the potential risks associated with US sanctions. The collective also reported disruptions to its website and payment services, eventually announcing that it would dissolve and wind down its activities.
The episode raises a troubling question: how can a decision taken in Washington effectively undermine the operations of organisations based in Europe, without any equivalent decision by European authorities?
Instruments of political pressure
For the European Legal Support Centre (ELSC), an organisation providing legal assistance to individuals and groups mobilising for Palestine, A/I's experience represents a dangerous precedent "that puts the very notion of Europe at risk.”
The case's significance extends beyond A/I itself. It exposes how international financial networks, banking compliance requirements and the threat of US penalties can become instruments of political pressure across national borders.
The US government argues that its sanctions target organisations providing support for terrorism, including violent attacks and damage to property. But the expanding use of counterterrorism measures against activist networks also raises questions about where political dissent ends, and terrorism begins, and who has the power to decide.
The very label of “terrorist” carries a long history of political use - which dates back to the British Empire - and appears to be applied selectively. The legal distinctions matter. A US sanctions designation is not a criminal conviction, nor does it automatically make an organisation illegal under European law. Nevertheless, the practical consequences can be devastating.
For banks and financial institutions that depend on access to USA financial networks, the risk of maintaining relations with a sanctioned organisation may simply be considered too great. This creates a system in which European organisations can face financial and social exclusion because of decisions made by a foreign government, even without direct legal orders from their own authorities.
The case of Mohammad Hannoun, a Palestinian activist based in Italy, demonstrates another dimension of this pressure. Hannoun faced restrictions on his banking activities before the US government sanctioned him in October 2024 over allegations relating to Hamas financing. Italian authorities subsequently detained him amid criminal proceedings alleging he funded the group.
Hannoun's case involves separate criminal allegations and judicial proceedings, which should not be confused with the sanctions themselves. Nevertheless, it illustrates how financial restrictions, political accusations and legal proceedings can intersect.
These developments reflect a wider system in which state authorities, banks, media organisations, universities, cultural venues, and lawfare groups can collectively contribute to isolating individuals, groups, and networks accused of supporting terrorism.
The impact on solidarity efforts
The implications are particularly concerning for activists and organisations supporting Palestine, whose activities have faced increasing scrutiny and restrictions in several European countries. In Britain, Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in July 2025 following its direct-action campaign against companies connected to Israel's defence industry. The group has challenged the ban in court, with the UK Supreme Court due to hear an appeal in November 2026.
The subsequent US designation of Palestine Action illustrates how one government's measures can be reinforced by another, potentially multiplying their impact on the organisations concerned.
But the A/I case points to something further: extending such measures to organisations that provide services and infrastructure used by political movements.
The question is whether European institutions have either the tools or the political willingness to challenge this expanding extraterritorial reach.
The European Union does possess a legal mechanism intended to protect European individuals and businesses against certain foreign sanctions: the Blocking Statute, introduced under Council Regulation (EC) No 2271/96. Originally adopted in 1996, the statute was designed to counter the effects of US sanctions on European economic operators. It was subsequently updated in 2018 in response to the reimposition of US sanctions against Iran.
The legislation can prohibit compliance with specified foreign sanctions and provide legal remedies to affected European operators. However, it applies only to the foreign legislation covered by its annex, which currently includes certain US measures concerning Cuba and Iran. It does not automatically protect organisations targeted under the US counterterrorism sanctions regime.
Extending or adapting such protections would require further action by European institutions, and would not necessarily eliminate the financial risks facing European banks.
Nevertheless, this legal mechanism shows that the EU has previously recognised the problem posed by the extraterritorial application of US sanctions.
As the ELSC pointed out: "We have this European law, but it has never been used on the scale required to counter the US sanctions."
The consequences of inaction are not merely financial. When an organisation loses access to its bank accounts, online services or funding channels, its ability to operate can rapidly disappear. The threat of sanctions can also discourage other organisations, financial institutions, and individuals from associating with it, even before any formal restrictions are imposed.
"The aim of the US sanctions is to isolate and fragment the European political movement for Palestine," the ELSC argued. "A sanctioned person will be concerned about how to recover funds instead of doing their work."
These chilling effects are difficult to measure, but they are central to understanding the wider implications of the sanctions regime. In the A/I case, the collective's decision to dissolve shows how legal uncertainty, financial pressure, and risk to associated individuals can make the situation unsustainable.
The European Union frequently presents itself as a defender of civil liberties, the rule of law and political freedoms. Yet these commitments face a practical test when European organisations are subjected to financial restrictions originating outside their own legal system.
The question is not whether organisations accused of terrorism should be exempt from scrutiny. Rather, the question is whether European institutions should allow foreign sanctions decisions, and the financial pressure they generate, to determine whether organisations operating within Europe can survive.
If the consequences of a US designation can effectively shut down a European organisation without an equivalent decision under European law, the boundary between US financial power and European political sovereignty becomes increasingly difficult to distinguish.
For European civil society, that boundary may be far more important than it first appears.

King faces calls for apology, slavery reparations in Caribbean
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:24:10 UTC
01:24:10 KST

King Charles faces renewed calls for slavery apology, reparations on Caribbean tour: "Pay us what you owe us"
Britain's King Charles III continued his nine-day tour of the Caribbean Thursday under mounting pressure to issue a formal apology for the U.K. royal family's historic role in the transatlantic slave trade and to support calls for reparations.
Charles was to visit Guyana on Thursday before traveling to Antigua and Barbuda for a meeting of heads of state of British Commonwealth nations, where leaders are expected to discuss the legacy of slavery.
His tour began Tuesday in the Bahamas, where the king addressed hundreds of young Bahamians and acknowledged Britain's colonial past.
"Some of what is best in Bahamian culture today, the most joyful, the most hopeful, the most bright, was born out of darkness," he said. "It is only right that we should acknowledge the great suffering and injustices of the past in these islands and beyond, even as we rejoice in the successes of the present and build new opportunities for the future."
On Wednesday, the king embraced the country's vibrant culture, joining a colorful Junkanoo street parade in Nassau surrounded by performers in elaborate costumes and feathered headdresses.
But around the celebrations, protesters held placards declaring: "Pay us what you owe us," demanding compensation for Britain's involvement in centuries of transatlantic slave trade.
Charles' remarks appeared to do little to satisfy campaigners who have long called for a formal apology and reparations.
Speaking to The Guardian newspaper on Wednesday, Dr. Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, chair of the Bahamas National Reparations Committee, dismissed the monarch's remarks as "hollow platitudes" and said, "we deserve so much more than what was offered."
Buckingham Palace has said Charles will not offer a formal apology for slavery, saying such decisions are for the British government, not the royal family, but that he will not shy away from broader discussions about the U.K.'s involvement.
Experts say the royals are concerned that issuing a formal apology could open the door to legal claims for reparations, potentially exposing the family, and/or the British government, to substantial financial demands.
"The reason why he doesn't go further is that he's aware [of] what it will mean to actually apologize, in terms of the legal obligation to make reparation," Esther Stanford-Xosei, a lawyer and reparations expert, told CBS News in 2023, as Charles' second son Prince Harry's book "Spare" acknowledged the family had profited from the slave trade.
Stanford-Xosei said the family feared a formal apology could end up costing the monarchy, "not only money, but status … He will be exposing the criminality of this institution."
Calls for reparations
Between the 15th and 19th centuries, approximately 5 million enslaved Africans were transported to the Caribbean, including more than 2 million to British colonies, where they endured brutal conditions working in sugar, coffee and cotton plantations.
Historians have documented the monarchy's direct involvement in the trade, including investments by King Charles II and his brother James in the Royal African Company, which trafficked enslaved Africans across the Atlantic.
When slavery was abolished across most of the British Empire in 1834, the government allocated £20 million ($23 billion in today's money according to one estimate) to compensate slave owners, but not the enslaved. The compensation was part of a political compromise that helped secure abolition's passage by British lawmakers.
Britain subsequently played a significant role in suppressing the international slave trade during the 19th century, deploying the Royal Navy and investing substantial resources in abolition efforts. Its West Africa Squadron seized more than 1,600 slave ships and freed approximately 150,000 Africans between 1808 and 1869. One study estimated that Britain's wider anti-slavery efforts cost the equivalent of 1.8% of its national income annually over that period.
The debate over reparations has intensified in recent years, particularly following the global Black Lives Matter protests in 2020, which prompted renewed scrutiny of Britain's colonial past and the royal family's historical connections to slavery.
Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley has been among the leading voices calling for reparations, including investment in education, healthcare and economic development.
Speaking to The Guardian, the head of the Caribbean Community Reparations Commission, Hilary Beckles, said people in the Caribbean wanted "proprietary justice, beginning with remorse" from British leaders.
She urged Charles to "dig deep within his consciousness" and to offer young people he meets on his visit "the empowerment that he would give to his own children."
Not everyone in the Caribbean supports the idea of direct reparations, however.
Rasheed Griffiths, a Barbadian economist, told CBS News that "Caribbean leaders have consistently refused to implement prudent fiscal policies over the last few decades, which has led to the decay of Caribbean economies. But instead of realizing they have all the power to turn these countries around they prefer to seek scapegoats."
"The calls for reparations from the U.K. are nothing more than Caribbean leaders attempting to externalize their own failures," Griffiths said. "It should not be taken seriously by anyone, least of all the U.K. public."
Charles previously described slavery as an "appalling atrocity" that "forever stains our history" during Barbados' transition to a republic in 2021.
During a Caribbean tour in 2022, heir to the British throne Prince William and his wife Kate also faced protests over slavery and demands for reparations. William expressed his "profound sorrow" and described slavery as "abhorrent," but stopped short of a formal apology.
Many of the Caribbean nations Charles is visiting are former British colonies and several, including the Bahamas and Antigua and Barbuda, remain constitutional monarchies, which, despite them having gained independence decades ago, makes Charles their official head of state.

Netanyahu uses fake image to exaggerate Arab voter turnout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:23:00 UTC
01:23:00 KST

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been accused of using an AI-generated fake image to exaggerate Arab voter turnout in the Oct. 27 parliamentary elections.
Netanyahu on Tuesday posted an image X showing people outside a polling station, claiming it depicted Arab voters in the southern city of Rahat.
"This is what is happening today in Rahat. You cannot stay home; go out immediately and vote Likud. We are fighting for our homeland," he wrote.
The British public broadcaster BBC, however, later analyzed the image and identified it as AI-generated or manipulated.
Netanyahu also shared a photograph of Tibi standing in front of a bus, which the Arab lawmaker had posted on his own X account several days earlier.
"Buses are heading toward polling stations, and reports indicate long queues in Arab towns," Netanyahu wrote.
He claimed that right-wing strongholds appeared slow to mobilize, warning his supporters that failing to vote could result in a government led by Arab parties.
The Joint List, an alliance of three Arab parties in Israel, also dismissed and challenged the claims.
In a statement condemning Netanyahu's conduct, the Joint List said the image purportedly showing voters in Rahat was "not real and generated by artificial intelligence."
The alliance accused Netanyahu of using fabricated images to incite against Arabs.
"Netanyahu is afraid of high turnout in our community because he knows it will bring down his government," it said.
The alliance warned that the image presented a misleading picture that could lull Arab voters into staying home by suggesting participation was already sufficiently high.
While turnout in Arab communities was encouraging, it said, a gap remained compared with the wider Israeli electorate, particularly in right-wing strongholds and settlements.
It urged Arab voters to continue heading to polling stations despite obstacles.
Arab lawmaker Ahmad Tibi, meanwhile, said that turnout in Jewish towns remained significantly higher than in Arab communities.
In a video statement Tuesday, he said that Arab participation was being misrepresented by the Israeli right.
"Since the morning, turnout in Arab towns has indeed been higher than in the past, but turnout in Jewish towns is higher, and there is a large gap between turnout in Jewish and Arab communities," he added.
Arab citizens account for 18% of eligible voters while Israeli citizens constitutes 77%, according to figures released by Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics two days earlier.

01:21:45 KST

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. The revenue of accredited IT companies for the first six months of 2026 amounted to 6 trillion rubles ($73.8 bln), Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said in a video address to the participants of the Kazan Digital Week - 2026 International Forum.
"At the end of last year, the revenue of accredited IT companies approached eight trillion rubles ($98.5 bln), which is almost 1.5 times more than the previous period, and it continues to increase. For the first six months of the current year, this figure has already reached 6 trillion rubles," the prime minister said.
Over the past 6 years, the share of the IT sector in the country's gross domestic product has more than doubled, Mishustin noted. In Russia, the registry of domestic software is expanding, with the number of registered solutions counting in the tens of thousands. Businesses and state corporations are increasingly using them in key sectors of the economy, which helps reduce dependence on foreign suppliers and optimize production processes, he stressed.
In the current situation with external restrictions, it is necessary to more dynamically expand the lineup of domestic software, cloud services, and industrial systems, while simultaneously accelerating the launch of competitive technologies, the prime minister noted. This will help improve people's quality of life, as well as address economic and social challenges both in the regions and across the country as a whole, Mishustin added.

Russia to Extend Diesel Export Ban, Use Quotas to Fulfill U.S. Deal, Sources Say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:21:05 UTC
01:21:05 KST

Russia will extend its diesel export ban until the end of the year while allowing some companies to ship fuel under a quota system to meet its new export commitment to the U.S., two people familiar with the discussions told Reuters.
Moscow and Washington agreed a diesel supply deal after Presidents Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump spoke by phone earlier this month. The energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine announced alongside the agreement has allowed Moscow to increase fuel production. At the same time, fuel shortages earlier this year have prompted the government to maintain tight controls on oil product exports.
Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Tuesday that three tankers carrying Russian diesel to export markets were already under way and that a fourth would sail on Oct. 28.
Novak also said Russian refineries were recovering quickly from repairs. The sources said refinery utilization had risen 25% at the end of October from the start of the month after drone attacks on facilities subsided.
Under the current diesel export ban, the government permits limited exports through a quota system. Those quotas will quadruple from October levels to 2 million metric tons, or about 0.5 million barrels per day, in November, the sources said. Shipments under existing intergovernmental agreements will also continue.
The Energy Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.
The current ban on diesel exports is due to expire on Oct. 31.
In October, the government exempted several refiners from the ban and granted them export quotas totaling 0.5 million tons, the sources said. A new government order expected in early November would expand the list of exempt refiners and set new export limits. If the quotas are used up quickly, the government could consider increasing them further, the sources added.
Nominal diesel production in Russia exceeds domestic consumption by about 40%. As refineries return to normal operating rates, they will need export outlets to prevent a domestic glut.

AI buildout hits snag as Google and Microsoft put off raising capex forecasts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:20:51 UTC
01:20:51 KST

The past few quarters of hyperscaler earnings have been marked by ever-increasing capital expenditure forecasts as tech giants race to build out artificial intelligence infrastructure to meet what they describe as insatiable demand.
At least for the moment, Microsoft and Alphabet are telling a slightly different story.
In their earnings reports Wednesday, both companies shared capex figures that came up shy of analysts' estimates. Microsoft reduced its capex forecast for the year to $170 billion from $175 billion, and Alphabet held its guidance at $195 billion to $205 billion.
The numbers suggest a slowdown is nowhere in sight, but they do represent another potential point of concern for the AI buildout. Shares of neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN all dropped after the reports, as did Oracle, which is one of the biggest spenders on AI infrastructure.
Microsoft CFO Amy Hood said on the software company's earnings call that third-party providers of graphics processing units had delays that will push out some available capacity until the first half of 2027. She didn't provide names, but Microsoft relies on CoreWeave, IREN and Nebius, among others.
Anat Ashkenazi, Alphabet's finance chief, told analysts that outside computing power "came online only at the very end of Q3." Alphabet shares tumbled about 10% in extended trading as the company missed on earnings and revenue and reported negative free cash flow of more than $9 billion.
Plenty of Alphabet shareholders remain faithful.
"We are pleased with what we see and what we heard, and trust management's approach to their AI spending," Chris Ballard, managing director of Check Capital Management, wrote in an email to CNBC.
Investors will get a final read on hyperscaler capex for the quarter when Amazon reports results after the close Thursday. In Meta's earnings report last week, the company said it expects full-year capex of $135 billion to $145 billion, raising the bottom of the range from $130 billion. Like with Alphabet, Meta shares sank as the company reported negative free cash flow.
Delays from emerging neocloud partners have occurred before at Microsoft, but they're more critical now as Anthropic gets set to go public. Anthropic counts on infrastructure from Amazon, Google and Microsoft for much of its computing needs, alongside capacity from SpaceX, Lambda and Nscale, which filed to go public in September but hasn't updated its prospectus in weeks.
At times this year, Anthropic's Claude assistant has been unavailable due to climbing demand. Rival OpenAI, which has said an initial public offering in 2027 is likely, is also in constant need of more capacity.
One big challenge for the market is that the neoclouds require billions of dollars in outside capital to fuel their buildouts but don't have investment-grade credit ratings. With interest rates rising and concerns about their debt loads mounting, lenders are pulling out of the market.
Last week, analysts at Gartner shared with CNBC the firm's prediction that, by 2030, 80% of neocloud companies will either be absorbed or completely cease operations. Nvidia-backed neocloud Firmus, based in Australia, withdrew plans to go public earlier this month, despite boasting large usage commitments from Meta and OpenAI.
None of that is to suggest the AI buildout is over, or even close to plateauing.
Microsoft's Hood said Wednesday that she sees capital spending accelerating in the first half of 2027 thanks to higher component costs and the delayed deliveries. As a group, hyperscaler capex is expected to top $1 trillion next year and, according to some estimates, continue rising from there.
Despite the third-quarter capex shortfall, investors cheered Microsoft's report on Wednesday as the company beat earnings and revenue estimates, driven by 48% sales growth in its Azure cloud business.
"We view the quarter as further validation of Microsoft's AI-led growth opportunity," Cantor analysts led by Thomas Blakey wrote in a Wednesday note to clients. They recommend buying Microsoft stock, and they pushed up their one-year price target to $630 from $608.

Israeli settlers target journalists, Palestinians in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:20:11 UTC
01:20:11 KST

Breadcrumb
Armed Israeli settlers threaten West Bank families, attack journalists
Palestinian families in the occupied West Bank faced renewed threats of forced displacement on Thursday, as armed Israeli settlers raided homes in the Jordan Valley and allegedly assaulted journalists and activists in Masafer Yatta, days after Israel's parliamentary election.
UK-based charity Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP) said masked, armed settlers entered the Palestinian community of Al-Shuneh, near Jiftlik, at around 2am, surrounding three homes and threatening to expel residents unless they left "voluntarily".
The settlers allegedly damaged a resident's car and stole a 1.5-cubic-metre water tank before returning to a nearby hill, where they appeared to have established an illegal outpost the previous day.
Aseel Baidoun, MAP's deputy director of advocacy and campaigns, told The New Arab that the outpost posed an immediate threat to the community's survival.
"For Palestinians in communities like Al-Shuneh, an outpost can spell the end of their community and displacement from their homes. What starts as a few caravans, tents or a settler farm can become a permanent settlement with full backing from the Israeli state," she said.
"Outposts can spread onto more land, link settlements and cut off Palestinian communities from basic services and healthcare. For families already facing attacks and threats, and unable to reach their grazing land for two years, every new development makes it harder to stay."
"That's why the speed of work on the hill overlooking Al-Shuneh is so alarming."
Around 80 families face uncertainty over whether they can remain in their homes, with residents already struggling to access basic services, according to MAP.
Settlers have reportedly spent several days clearing land and carrying out construction on the hill overlooking the community. More than three settler families have arrived at the site and begun installing what appear to be water pipes and electricity cables.
MAP also documented earlier threats against Al-Shuneh residents, including an August incident in which armed settlers allegedly assaulted a family and threatened to burn their homes and seize their livestock unless they left.
Baidoun warned that the outcome of Tuesday's Israeli election was unlikely to improve conditions for Palestinians.
"Whatever the outcome of Israel's election, there is little reason to expect a change in the policies driving settlement expansion and settler violence," she told The New Arab.
"All of Israel's major political parties support the settlement project, and Palestinian communities cannot rely on a new government to protect them from the violence and displacement it actively encourages and enables."
Journalists and activists assaulted in Masafer Yatta
In a separate incident, Russian activist Adele Shoko reported that Israeli settlers attacked her and two colleagues, US journalist Jasper Nathaniel and Israeli-Russian activist Andrey X, in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair, in Masafer Yatta.
Shoko said armed settlers beat the group, threatened them and stole equipment and personal belongings.
"Jasper and I were also beaten. Jasper was then pepper-sprayed and arrested," she wrote on social media, adding that Israeli forces had taken Nathaniel into custody.
"Andrey was severely beaten and lost consciousness several times in front of police. Despite this, he was denied hospital treatment. He was put in an ambulance – but instead of being taken to hospital, he was taken to a police station. He is still there, arrested and being denied medical care," she added.
Footage circulated online appeared to show several men, some armed, beating Nathaniel and Andrey X. Other footage showed Israeli authorities leading Nathaniel away as he shouted that he had been assaulted.
In later updates, Shoko said both men were "physically okay" and were "having their court hearing" following their detention.
Activists subsequently reported that Andrey X had been released after Thursday's court hearing. Nathaniel's status had not been publicly confirmed.
The attacks follow a warning on Monday from UN-mandated investigators, who accused Israel of committing "extermination" in the occupied West Bank.
Palestinians across the territory have faced escalating violence by Israeli settlers and soldiers, particularly since the start of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023.

German serial rapist sentenced to 12 years as police investigate 44 more cases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:19:58 UTC
01:19:58 KST

Frank S. was sentenced to 12 years in prison, followed by preventive detention. The 69-year-old from Berlin systematically drugged and raped 14 women and filmed the assaults. A further 44 cases are expected to be examined in a separate trial.
The court sentenced Frank S. to 12 years in prison, followed by preventive detention. The 69-year-old is unlikely ever to be released.
One of the worst serial rapists in German criminal history is believed by investigators to have drugged and raped 58 women, filmed his crimes and shared the footage online with other men. It was this that ultimately led to his capture.
After his chat partner was arrested, police tracked down Frank S., searched his flat and found the video recordings.
Frank S. had filmed a total of 58 women after drugging their drinks and sexually assaulting them. Some of the women were still conscious and begged him to stop. Afterwards, many were unable to remember what had happened because of the heavy sedation. As a result, Frank S. was not reported to police, while other women suppressed memories of what they had experienced.
It was only when police visited some of the women at home during the investigation that they first learned what Frank S. had done to them.
On Wednesday, Berlin Regional Court sentenced Frank S. to 12 years in prison, followed by preventive detention, for 22 rapes involving 14 women. In nine cases, he also violated their intimate privacy by recording them.
During the three-month trial, all 14 women testified as witnesses, with six also participating as joint plaintiffs. The perpetrator's videos were also used as evidence.
According to the court, the women were completely helpless and defenceless because they had been sedated with various medications. The judges found that Frank S. took advantage of this. The now 69-year-old filmed his acts and is said to have stored the video recordings digitally "like trophies in a cabinet". The court described his actions as particularly "contemptuous towards women".
Despite the confession delivered by S.'s defence lawyer at the start of the trial, the court ordered preventive detention after he serves his sentence. This measure is considered one of the harshest tools available to the judiciary. By the time he could be released from prison, he will already be over 80 years old.
The court did not consider his advanced age sufficient reason to conclude that S. would not reoffend. The presiding judge stated that the defendant had not fully understood what he had done to the women or the serious consequences his actions had had for them. The verdict is not yet legally binding, and S. can still appeal.
Frank S.'s devious methods
Over a seven-year period from 2016 to 2022, the now 69-year-old met the 14 women through dating platforms and deceived them. He gained their trust in a way that was, according to a court spokesperson, "particularly devious". He told one woman he was a police inspector and another that he was a helicopter pilot. Ultimately, the trained electrician invited the women to his flat and offered them drinks.
However, the alcoholic drinks were laced with substances that, combined with alcohol, left the women helpless and unable to resist. Some still tried to protest verbally, but S. ignored them. "What really mattered to him was to exercise power over these defenceless women," a court spokesperson explained. S. raped the sedated women, in some cases several times, in his bedroom, where a video camera was permanently installed.
The judge described S.'s methods as systematic and highly organised. His crimes followed a pattern. The court also stated that he acted like an archivist and, as became particularly clear from the videos examined, carried out his crimes in a calm and routine manner. He is said to have rewatched some of the footage while smoking a cigarette.
Four expert witnesses, including specialists in IT, toxicology and psychiatry, provided evidence during the trial. Six of the victims participated as joint plaintiffs during the three-month proceedings. Two of them attended the sentencing but declined to speak publicly.
Women avoid public attention as organisations show solidarity
"What is very important for me and also for my client is the preventive detention that has now been ordered, because the propensity to offend and the danger he poses, at least as things stand today, are very clear," said Silke Studzinski, lawyer for one of the joint plaintiffs.
Laura Leogrande, a lawyer for another joint plaintiff, also said "that there was indeed a reluctance to speak in public". She stressed that this was not a criticism, however. At the plaintiffs’ request, the closing statements were delivered behind closed doors. They decided to speak about the rapes they had suffered without members of the public present.
"I do find it remarkable that there was so much shame," Leogrande said, "about having been in this situation, about having become a victim of this crime, and having trusted this man enough to go home with him, and then something like this happens." The victims were not to blame.
Outside the courthouse, organisations such as Terre des Femmes and initiatives like "Die Scham muss die Seite wechseln" ("Shame must change sides") showed their solidarity. They called for protests and rallies.
"Terre des Femmes is here because we stand in solidarity with those affected and because we want to send a signal against sexualised violence," explained Sina Tonk, a department head at the organisation, in an interview with Euronews. "We know that only around three percent of rapes are ever reported to the police, and that happens out of fear or shame, or because many obstacles are placed in the way of those affected."
Another trial could follow. Police now believe there are 58 victims, and investigations into a further 44 cases are ongoing. Ten women believed to appear in the videos have not yet been identified.
Leogrande stressed that this is not a new phenomenon. Rather, rape after a victim has been drugged is "something that has only now come to the surface, that is only now being talked about and that is only now being investigated in real detail". The Pelicot case in France has drawn particular attention to the issue.
Berlin police became aware of Frank S. after officers in Lower Saxony passed on a tip based on a chat log. S. had exchanged information about his crimes with a suspected rapist in Verden, Lower Saxony. He was arrested in March 2026 and has remained in pre-trial detention since then.
The series of rapes is considered the largest case to date involving drug-facilitated sexual assault before the Berlin Regional Court. Germany has also recently tightened its laws on sexual violence, including provisions concerning the use of incapacitating drugs and the recording of crimes.

PM Radev Says Bulgaria Was Ready to Deploy Jets Against the Black Sea Drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:19:41 UTC
01:19:41 KST

Prime Minister Rumen Radev said Bulgaria was ready to deploy L-39 military aircraft against drones that attacked a commercial vessel in the Black Sea if the unmanned aerial vehicles had entered the country's territorial waters, adding that a French patrol aircraft had detected them at least 30 minutes before the strike.
The Bulgarian Air Force had L-39 aircraft stationed in Balchik on standby for a possible response, Radev said as he discussed the recent Black Sea incidents and Bulgaria's ability to counter such threats.
Radev said authorities had obtained video footage of the attack and were examining it in cooperation with allied intelligence services. Forensic analyses are also underway to establish where the drones originated.
“We have video footage, which we have shared with our allies. Every possible analysis is currently being conducted. I expect that we will finally have clear evidence as to where these drones came from,” Radev said.
The prime minister added that the footage would be released publicly as soon as possible, but stressed that he could not yet identify those responsible for the attack.
“We do not yet know where the drone originated. I have shared my logical assumptions with you, but I do not wish to jump to conclusions. I imagine you have seen discussions on social media, where all sorts of theories are circulating - suggesting, for instance, that the drone could belong to any of four or five different countries. However, such claims are not to be taken seriously. We intend to conduct a thorough and credible expert assessment in collaboration with our allies,” Radev said.
He described the coordination between the Bulgarian Armed Forces and allied aircraft conducting patrols over the Black Sea, saying a French reconnaissance plane had spotted the drones in time to warn the targeted ship's crew.
“We have been in constant communication with NATO, requesting assistance. As you know, there are already aircraft on patrol, including American ones. In fact, the French patrol aircraft spotted the drones at least half an hour before the strike; it detected them and even provided information on their trajectory. This gave the crew of the targeted ship the opportunity to take all necessary evacuation measures,” the prime minister said.
Radev said allied forces and the Bulgarian military were exchanging information in real time. He reiterated that Bulgaria had been prepared to respond militarily if the drones had entered its territorial waters.
“We were prepared to scramble L-39 aircraft based in Balchik and use their weaponry against these drones, had they entered our territorial waters. But it didn't come to that,” he said.
However, Radev warned that Bulgaria's response options were subject to legal and practical restrictions. International law prevents the country from taking military action outside its own territorial waters, while weather, available equipment, and surveillance capabilities also limit its ability to detect and respond to threats in the exclusive economic zone.
“Even if we possess the means to intervene, we cannot, from a strictly legal standpoint, take action outside our own territorial zones. We cannot do so, as it would constitute a violation of international law. Furthermore, there are various limitations regarding the capabilities at our disposal for surveillance, reconnaissance, and the detection of threats within the Exclusive Economic Zone,” Radev said.
He also pointed to Bulgaria's limited naval capacity, which prevents it from maintaining a permanent presence across the entire zone.
“Moreover, we are dependent on weather conditions. It is not always possible to fly, nor is it always possible to take action. Our fleet is limited in both number and capabilities. We are unable to maintain a continuous watch across the entire Exclusive Economic Zone,” the prime minister said.
Radev seeks additional NATO assistance
Radev confirmed that he had discussed the need for further allied support with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.
“We are waiting. I have also raised this issue with Mark Rutte. You can see that the quantities of weaponry available to NATO also have their limits. They are stretched from the Baltic Sea, across the land, to the Black Sea. So, everything that can be done is being done,” he said.
Bulgaria has also pursued diplomatic action at the highest international level, including through the United Nations, NATO, and European institutions, Radev said. He argued that military measures and allied assistance could reduce risks but would not ensure that attacks on ships stopped.
“From this point on, there is only one solution to ensure that these attacks finally come to an end: a ceasefire, sitting down at the negotiating table, and beginning talks. Until that happens, there is no guarantee regarding what can be done,” Radev said.
He said the European Union and NATO should support diplomatic initiatives aimed at ending hostilities, citing efforts to open talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, including those by Finnish President Alexander Stubb and the Norwegian prime minister.
“The only 100% guarantee is a ceasefire and the political will for dialogue. I believe the European Union and NATO should engage in these efforts,” Radev said.
The prime minister also pledged formal diplomatic action if expert assessments establish the drones' origin and responsibility for the attack.
“If the origin of these drones is proven, the Minister of Foreign Affairs will immediately summon the relevant ambassador to deliver a note of protest,” Radev said.
Three drones struck a vessel 16 nautical miles off Cape Kaliakra, and its crew was rescued. The incident involved the merchant ship CONTSHIP JET, which was hit on October 28 about 16 nautical miles from the cape. Although the crew survived, the vessel was reported to have sunk the following day.
The attack has renewed concerns about the safety of commercial shipping in the Black Sea and the risks to trade routes close to Bulgarian territorial waters.
The European Commission also reacted to the attacks on civilian vessels, calling them an “unacceptable escalation” that threatens EU interests, maritime transport, and supply chains. Brussels expressed solidarity with Bulgaria and Romania, warning that the consequences of the war in Ukraine continued to pose serious security risks in the Black Sea region.
Radev contrasts Bulgaria's response with Romania's
Radev defended Bulgaria's decision not to identify a country as responsible for the drone attacks before conclusive evidence was available. He cited Romania, which he said had blamed Russia but subsequently experienced another incident.
“Bulgaria did not make definitive accusations against any country because we lacked concrete evidence at the time. Romania stated that the aggressor and the source of these drones was Russia. Yet, this failed to protect them. The very next day, drones sank a ship—within their own territorial waters, no less. Do you see the difference?” Radev said.
He criticized Bulgarian politicians calling for the immediate naming of a suspected perpetrator, arguing that public accusations would not prevent further attacks.
“I want to address all our politicians who so convincingly propagate the notion that if we speak out and declare, 'You, Russia, are the source of the attack', if we shake our finger at them, that will protect us. It cannot protect us. Look at what happened in Romania: the very next day, a ship was struck and sunk. And I repeat - this did not happen in the exclusive economic zone, but in territorial waters,” the prime minister said.
Radev says government will follow court ruling on CEC complaint
Radev also commented on a Central Election Commission (CEC) decision concerning a complaint against him over his support for Iliyana Yotova's candidacy, which had been expressed through the government press office.
He said the Council of Ministers would comply with the commission's decision, while noting that the final course of action would depend on the court because the ruling had been appealed.
“The Council of Ministers will comply with the decision of the Central Election Commission. Whatever the Bulgarian court decides, that is what we will do,” Radev said.
