Flavio Bolsonaro’s great escape: Is this the beginning of the end for ‘Bolsonarism’?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:19:17 UTC
01:19:17 KST

Flavio Bolsonaro’s great escape: Is this the beginning of the end for ‘Bolsonarism’?
The Brazilian election results had barely been announced before the defeated presidential candidate, Flavio Bolsonaro, packed his bags and fled with his family to the United States. The move may have dealt a serious blow to the already tarnished family brand, but does it spell the end for “Bolsonarism”?
A few hours after touching down in Miami on Wednesday, Flavio Bolsonaro issued a statement declaring he was the “true president” of Brazil. He claimed he had been the victim of an electoral coup staged by Brazil’s Supreme Court and President-elect Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who won last weekend’s election by more than 4 million votes.
That, in Bolsonaro’s view, left him with no other choice but to flee.
Read moreFlavio Bolsonaro declares himself Brazil's 'true' leader after landing in Miami
According to several news outlets, the Bolsonaro family had already left Brazil on Tuesday. Their journey took them through both Argentina and Ecuador before they got on the private jet that would eventually fly them across the continent and keep the embattled far-right politician at arm’s length from Brazilian justice.
A family tradition
Although Bolsonaro’s whereabouts, and the destination for his escape, were initially shrouded in mystery, his ally US President Donald Trump appeared to almost have been waiting for him, greeting him with a US visa more or less the moment he arrived.
Bolsonaro currently faces a string of investigations in his homeland for suspected money laundering, corruption, and for having illegal accepted campaign funding from a donor network connected to US Vice President JD Vance.
By choosing the US exile route, however, Bolsonaro could deal a devastating blow to “Bolsonarism” – the macho ideology championed by his father, ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, and which glorifies the strong man who stops at nothing when the going gets tough.
But Bolsonaro junior is hardly the first in the family to have sought refuge in the US as soon as his political fortunes start to fade. His father did so in 2022 – just two days before Lula was inaugurated for a third presidential mandate – after facing a number of criminal probes. And last year, his brother Eduardo went into “voluntary” US exile after accusations he had sought to convince Washington to impose sanctions on Lula’s Brazil.
Fiona Macauley, a Brazil expert at the University of Bradford, labelled the escapes, and especially the latest one, as “very negative” for the Bolsonaro family brand.
“It’s an incredible admission of guilt,” she said, adding that many of the people who voted for him are likely to be disappointed.
“If you were one of the nearly 60 million people who voted for Bolsonaro, you would now be feeling very bitter about the lack of courage.”
In other words, the values defining Bolsonarism become hard to defend when the Bolsonaros’ systematically run to Trump for help every time they face any kind of legal woes.
Larissa Peixoto Gomes, a specialist in Brazilian politics at the University of Edinburgh, said it looks “really bad”, especially to undecided voters “who were key” in the elections.
Shadow government in the works?
Indeed the Bolsonaro family's multiple escapes make president-elect Lula, who has himself been subject to investigations and even served time in prison before finally being acquitted, look even stronger.
“It makes him look good,” Chris Lyon, a Brazil expert at the University of Birmingham, said. “Because when he faced corruption charges, he stayed, he didn't run away.”
With the elder Bolsonaro currently under house arrest (where he is serving a 27-year sentence), and two of his sons risking lengthy prison terms if they return to Brazil, it has become increasingly difficult for the family to exercise its political influence.
But experts say they could potentially set up a parallel or shadow government in the US, mimicking the Cuban or Venezuelan opposition in exile models.
However, Janaina Maldonado, a Brazilian politics expert with the German Institute for Global and Area Studies (GIGA), said that “the Brazilian scenario is completely different from what we had in Venezuela and what we have in Cuba”, making both her and her peers very sceptical that such plans would actually work. Not least because much of the international community – save Trump who suggested the election was “rigged” – has already recognised Lula as the legitimate winner.
Another potential hurdle is the Brazilian diaspora.
Macauley said that in contrast to the Cubans and Venezuelans in the US, most Brazilians living there are economic migrants and are not looking for a leader to rally behind.
The Bolsonaro reserves
This week's escape hardly spells the end for Bolsonaro politics being played out in Brazil. The Bolsonaro family is big and still very influential. “You've still got four Bolsonaros in the national elected office,” Lyon said.
The most prominent of them is Michelle Bolsonaro, Jair Bolsonaro’s wife who was recently handed a senator seat in Brasilia, as well as the couple’s second oldest son Carlos – also known as the family’s social media mastermind – who is a senator in Santa Catarina.
But there are more. The youngest son, Renan, is a federal deputy, and so is Bolsonaro senior's brother, Renato.
Corneel Weyers, a Brazil expert at Sciences Po’s Centre for International Studies (CERI) in Paris, said that while Carlos is expected to “carry on the Bolsonaro legacy”, Michelle has equally become a “major player”.
“She has a lot of influence and visibility with parts of the ‘Bolsonarista’ electoral coalition, especially among women and evangelicals.”
The day after the Brazilian election, the president of Bolsonaro’s party even had a meeting with her to discuss the party’s future.
Maldonado said the Bolsonaros who have just entered the political arena are likely to play the “political persecution” card going forward, hoping to galvanise the radicalised supporters who already subscribe to that idea even more.
“This part of the electorate is not minor,” she said. Flavio Bolsonaro “got 59 million votes, and these people have a lot to say still”.
This article was adapted from the original in French by Louise Nordstrom.

Aid mission set to enter Ukraine's Oleshky as localised ceasefire holds for third day
A humanitarian aid mission is set to enter the Ukrainian town of Oleshky, a Ukrainian official said on Thuirsday, as a localised truce between Kyiv and Moscow, brokered by US first lady Melania Trump, held for a third day. Some 2,000 residents in the Russian occupied city have been cut off from essential supplies amid reports that many are starving.
Humanitarian aid is poised to roll into the stricken city of Oleshky, a Ukrainian official said Thursday, as a localised ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine stretched into a third day and military units cleared away landmines.
Moscow and Kyiv have observed the truce in and around the devastated southern Ukrainian city since Tuesday, but remain otherwise locked in the war that began with Russia’s full-scale invasion more than 4 ½ years ago. Previous efforts to secure ceasefires either never worked out or the truces quickly fell apart.
Elsewhere, a jet-powered Russian drone hit two passenger trains stopped at a station in Dnipro in central Ukraine on Thursday, killing at least 14 people and injuring 14 more, including a 40-year-old man whose legs were amputated, officials said.
Read moreAt least 13 killed in 'horrific' Russian drone strike at Ukraine train station
Also, a Russian cruise missile killed two 15-year-old girls in the northern city of Chernihiv, and three more civilians died when a Russian drone hit an apartment block in the central Ukraine city of Kremenchuk, authorities said. In all, 56 people were injured in the strikes, including 10 children.
Russia’s Defence Ministry said air defences downed 1,214 Ukrainian drones overnight in one of the largest drone attacks launched by Kyiv. Around half of the drones were heading to the Russian capital, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said.
The planned six-day ceasefire around Russian-occupied Oleshky has brought a rare and welcome stillness for civilians in the nearby city of Kherson, which is held by Ukraine and has also been wracked by the war.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Both sides thanked US first lady Melania Trump for what the White House said was her role in helping broker the temporary ceasefire so food and medical supplies can be delivered to some 2,000 desperate people trapped in Oleshky. Pope Leo XIV also pressed for a truce.
“The parties are fully adhering to the agreements, and no violations of the ceasefire have been reported,” Ukrainian ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said Thursday, adding that aid deliveries were due to begin the following day.
His Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, confirmed the truce was holding and that Russian engineers are working on demining Oleshky's roads.
“Both sides are fully honoring their commitments, and no violations have been recorded,” she said. “This allows military personnel to continue clearing roads of mines and to prepare a safe passage for the humanitarian convoy.”
Local people will also be able to evacuate, either into Russia or Ukraine, officials say. The mechanics of how that might work are unclear.
Lantratova said she and her team were on their way to Oleshky for the aid delivery, adding that the operation was five months in the making.
Russian and Ukrainian representatives met in the Belarus city of Homel on Thursday to fly together to the Kherson region, Belarus state media reported.
A volunteer from Oleshky, Ksenia Arkhipova, told The Associated Press roughly 1,000 residents have told her they want to leave the city.
She said it was important that the Ukrainian delegation was present in Oleshky because many residents fear Russian authorities would identify individuals with pro-Ukrainian views or ties to Ukraine’s military.
In the nearby city of Kherson, growing numbers of people were out on the streets as the truce held.
Nataliia Myronenko, 42, had a steady stream of customers at her coffee kiosk since early Thursday.
“Now, during the quiet, we have people at lunchtime and in the evening, which we didn’t have under the attacks,” she said. “For a while, people would race down this street because they were afraid to stop.”
The pause has brought a sense of relief, she said. “It’s a breath of freedom, when you don’t look at the sky. You keep looking at your feet because of the mines, but you’re not afraid of dying. It’s so great,” she said.
“It’s such a privilege and a joy, but we understand it will end soon.”
Moscow and Kyiv are keen to curry favor with Washington ahead of possible three-way talks next month.
American military support is vital for Ukraine, but US President Donald Trump has waived sanctions on Russia and publicly chided Zelensky, indicating he is disengaging with Kyiv.
Tankers carrying Russian diesel are sailing to the United States, and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov is expected to attend a G20 ministerial meeting in Atlanta, Georgia, starting Friday, according to Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova.
European leaders, on the other hand, have been trying to diplomatically isolate Russian President Vladimir Putin over Moscow’s invasion and what they call a campaign of sabotage across the continent.
Ukraine earlier this month reported sudden and unexpected limits on Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service owned by Elon Musk’s SpaceX that is the backbone of Ukraine’s drone operations and communications.
Putin said Russia has been in contact with the American tech titan to coordinate their orbiting activities because it is building its own equivalent of Starlink.
“Elon Musk is a genius. Truly, a real genius,” Putin said late Wednesday.
“We and our American partners value this relationship, and despite all the political issues, we continue to work closely together,” he added.

Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland’s largest opposition party, has sparked controversy by appearing to suggest that Poland and some other allied European Union member states could launch the process of leaving the EU if they fail in efforts to reform it.
His remarks were condemned by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and other figures from the pro-EU ruling coalition, who have long accused Kaczyński and his national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party of seeking “Polexit” from the EU.
However, Kaczyński responded by accusing Tusk of misrepresenting his words, insisting that he wants Poland to reform the EU rather than leave it.
Kaczyński pomylił Krynicę z Kremlem. pic.twitter.com/tX0G04krze

The comments in question came in an hour-long speech by Kaczyński at the Krynica Forum, an annual conference bringing together leaders from politics, business and civil society, which he used to outline his vision for sweeping reforms of the EU.
Repeating his longstanding criticism of Brussels, Kaczyński warned that there had been a “consistent drive to transform the EU into a centralised state” with too much power over national governments. He also called the European Parliament in its current form a “parody”.
But soon, said Kaczyński, “a window of opportunity” for reform may appear because “completely different governments could emerge” in Poland, France and Spain, all of which will hold elections within the year.
PiS has previously enjoyed close relations with Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally (RN) party in France and the nationalist Vox party of Santiago Abascal in Spain.
The EU is preparing a "German plan" that would "annihilate the Polish state", said Kaczyński as Poland marks Independence Day.

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 11, 2023
Kaczyński suggested that Poland, if led by PiS, could work with other like-minded EU governments to push for reform of the bloc by influencing public opinion, identifying breaches of EU treaties, creating a blocking minority in the European Council, and trying to change the EU’s treaties.
However, the PiS leader then warned that, “if [those] approaches fail to yield results, the states that want change could conclude a new treaty with the elements we are seeking, but with a delayed entry into force”.
Kaczyński then noted that the EU treaties “include provisions specifying the terms under which a state may withdraw from the EU. This all begins with negotiations. And simply begin these negotiations”.
“It is a tough approach, a risky one, but the situation is so dire that it is worth employing such a method if all others fail to yield results,” he added.
The remarks immediately prompted condemnation from figures in Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. They accused Kaczyński of effectively calling for Polexit – something they have long claimed he wants, even though PiS has not explicitly called for it before.
“Jarosław Kaczyński has just announced that Poland should begin negotiations on the terms of its withdrawal from the EU,” wrote Tusk himself on X. “This is, among other things, what the current struggle in Poland is about – a tough struggle. I do not intend to lose it.”
“So they do want Polexit after all,” wrote foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. “Customs borders with Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Lithuania…An end to subsidies for farmers and investments…And they swore on their lives that they’d never do that.”
In a video published later on Thursday, Tusk declared that next year’s parliamentary elections would help decide “whether Poland remains in the European Union or leaves it”.

Poland has been the largest net recipient of EU funding since joining the bloc in 2004. A study published earlier this year found that the country’s economy is 42% larger than it would have been had Poland not been part of the EU.
Opinion polls consistently show a large majority of Poles in favour of remaining part of the EU. However, recent years have seen an uptick in support for Polexit, as well as for anti-EU far-right parties. PiS has increasingly found itself competing against such parties for votes.
Regular polling by state research agency CBOS shows that, while opposition to EU membership fell to a record low of 5% in 2022, it has subsequently risen and stood at 14% in the most recent survey.

Russian drone attacks community bus in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, killing 71-year-old woman – photos
Russian military personnel used a drone to attack a bus in the village of Bilenke, Zaporizhzhia Oblast, on 29 October. There were 20 people on the bus at the time, which was operated by the Proliska Humanitarian Mission to help vulnerable people. One passenger, a 71-year-old woman, was killed in the strike, and the driver is in hospital in a serious condition.
Source: Yevhen Kaplin, head of the Proliska Humanitarian Mission, on Facebook and in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda
Quote: "Russian terrorists have struck a social bus belonging to the Proliska Humanitarian Mission while passengers were on board using an FPV drone in Bilenke, Zaporizhzhia Oblast. There are casualties."
Details: Kaplin clarified in a comment to Ukrainska Pravda that the attack occurred at around 14:50. There were 20 passengers on the bus. The strike hit the roof of the bus between the driver's seat and the passenger area.
A woman aged around 71 was killed instantly. The bus driver is in hospital in a serious condition.
Another passenger, a 79-year-old man, sustained multiple shrapnel wounds and was taken to hospital. Other passengers suffered acoustic barotrauma and shrapnel wounds.
Kaplin also noted that the bus was attacked by a so-called "loitering drone".
"The 'loitering drone' was waiting under nets to carry out its 'mission'," he said. "And the bus was clearly marked. Social vehicles provide transport for people living in frontline settlements, particularly those who need transport connections with other hromadas A hromada is an administrative unit designating a village, several villages, or a town, and their adjacent territories ."
Kaplin added that the bus was "the only means of transport from the settlement that residents, who are mostly elderly people, could use to go to buy groceries, collect their pensions, or visit a hospital or pharmacy".
Background: A 49-year-old man was killed and three others injured as a result of a strike on Bilenke on the morning of 29 October. Russian forces also attacked public transport in the city of Zaporizhzhia three times in one day.

Netanyahu bids to discredit Israel vote with Arab fraud claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

Breadcrumb
Netanyahu tries to discredit Israel election with Arab vote fraud claims
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc on Thursday piled pressure on Arab-Israeli leaders over unproven accusations of foreign funding, in a push to neuter parties that could hold the key to forming a government after an inconclusive election.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog, who holds a largely ceremonial role, called for an investigation into allegations but cautioned against stigmatising the entire Arab-Israeli community, who voted at unprecedented rates.
Israel was nearing the completion of ballot counting from Tuesday's election, the first since Hamas's 7 October 2023 attacks, with neither Netanyahu nor the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot appearing able to secure a majority.
The Netanyahu camp's accusations, denied by both Arab-majority lists, could bring new uncertainty into the electoral process at a time when the threat of a new Israeli and US attack on Iran looms over the region.
The election saw soaring participation by Arab-Israelis, descendants of Palestinians who stayed after the country's creation in 1948, as outrage boiled at calls by officials such as National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir to treat their community much as Israel has dealt with Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Following Netanyahu's accusations, Ben-Gvir went so far as to encourage Israel to "immediately" order the arrests of Arab party leaders.
The Arab parties together have enough votes to take the opposition bloc over the finish line, but Eisenkot has baulked after relentless attacks by Netanyahu, who warned his right-wing Jewish base that voting for the opposition would put Arabs in power.
'Political earthquake'
Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, a conservative who heads the Central Elections Committee, requested an investigation by the Shin Bet security service into allegations that the Arab grouping Ra'am received money from Qatar, the energy-rich Gulf powerbroker that has channels to Hamas.
"The Ra'amgate scandal is a political earthquake. Israel's elections have been stolen!" Netanyahu's Likud party said.
Ra'am chief Mansour Abbas said his party had "no connection whatsoever to the affair", and welcomed an investigation.
The Joint List, which unites three Arab-majority parties, accused Netanyahu and his allies of a "campaign of incitement" that "exposes their fear" of Arab citizens' political strength.
Government officials did not offer evidence to back the allegations, and left-wing candidate Yair Golan accused Netanyahu of attempting to stir controversy after failing to get a majority.
"He is trying to challenge the election results," Golan said.
Netanyahu himself has long been under the cloud of allegations related to Qatar after the arrests last year of two of his aides for allegedly receiving payments from the Gulf state.
Qatari foreign ministry spokesman Majed Al Ansari called the latest accusations "ridiculous and dangerous".
Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, for years tacitly supported Qatar funding for Hamas-ruled Gaza, hoping to preserve stability.
That paradigm collapsed on 7 October 2023.
Kingmakers under pressure
With nearly 93% of the vote counted, Netanyahu's bloc was at 53 seats and the opposition forces led by Eisenkot on 48 - both under the 61 needed to form a government.
The two Arab formations were on track for an unprecedented 19 seats between them.
Yousef Jabareen, head of the Joint List, had told AFP that he was willing to cooperate with the opposition to bring down Netanyahu but without joining it in a government.
Eisenkot called allegations of Qatari interference "profoundly serious" and backed an investigation, but warned that Netanyahu may be trying to delay election results.
Netanyahu had tried during the voting to raise allegations of fraud, saying that Arab parties were caught with envelopes of cash, and his Likud party peddled the accusations throughout Thursday.
Police said they arrested three suspects but the election commission called it an isolated local case.
Dean Livne, acting director-general of the central elections committee, rejected a call from a right-wing lawmaker to convene a meeting on fraud, saying that any suggestion of widespread issues was "entirely groundless".
Another factor that could play into the formation of a government is an attack on Iran.
Netanyahu has repeatedly threatened to strike Iran, with President Donald Trump signalling he was ready to attack after next Tuesday's US midterm elections.
Eisenkot has warned the military that Netanyahu has no mandate and that officers must put Israel's security over the premier's "political needs".
An attack could raise pressure on Eisenkot to join an emergency unity government or keep the clock running until Israel can call new elections.
(AFP and TNA staff)

CCP leaders demand both more loyalty and more initiative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:16:00 UTC
01:16:00 KST

China leaders demand more loyalty and more initiative
October 29, 2026
The top echelon of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) held a four-day session behind closed doors in Beijing this week, with the talks focusing on strict leadership and discipline inside the ruling party.
Xi Jinping, who is both the CCP's general secretary and the head of state in China, signaled he would not only deepen the existing anti-corruption effort, but also ensure that party officials demonstrate more loyalty and more initiative at all levels.
According to the press release published on Thursday, the committee published a resolution praising the leadership and Xi Jinping for "enormous political courage and strong sense of responsibility" in tackling the issues of corruption and the weakening of the Party's governance.
The statement emphasized the need to "consistently advance comprehensive and strict Party leadership."
China's leadership fears instability
Kerry Brown, head of the Lau China Institute at King's College London, says Xi wants to minimize potential sources of instability.
Amid the current international tensions and the internal problems in China, including economic difficulties, Xi is pursuing his anti-corruption campaign and is demanding loyalty. "This is just going to intensify because if [the CCP] isn't disciplined and united, the party believes that it will go the same way as everywhere else in the world at the moment and become disunited and unstable," Brown told DW.
'Two-faced' party members targeted by Xi
Xi also recently spoke of the necessity to identify and remove "two-faced functionaries" from the political system.
In his speech, which was published in mid-October by the party's Qiushi Magazine, Xi referred to people professing loyalty to the central leadership while working against its instructions and following their own "individualistic" goals. The Chinese president described them as "political opportunists." He also criticized party officials pretending to be "nice guys," as in, those who use harmony as an excuse to stand aside when problems arise.
Brown points out that China's political system is now facing a crucial dilemma: If officials at all levels are now indeed expected to show innovation and courage in solving problems, the party's control could grow weak. This could, in turn, boost corruption.
However, if CCP leaders lean more on the "strict Party leadership" aspect and ramp up the pressure on the rank-and-file, there is also the danger of suppressing initiative. This could go beyond the party itself and could even affect the military.
The party is "very, very risk averse," Brown points out.
China 'kind of works' in a messy world
Chong Ja Ian, a political scientist at the National University of Singapore, notes that party functionaries under Xi only have a limited space to make their own decisions.
Taking this into account, the party's push for individuals to show initiative is not necessarily a major issue.
"I believe Xi would like for the officials to act proactively and decisively by conducting specific tasks; but he still doesn't want them thinking for themselves so much that they can question the agenda he prescribed. The 'proactivity' demanded by Xi is limited to the implementation, not decision-making," he told DW.
Brown adds that Xi seems to be ready to sacrifice a certain amount of operational flexibility to gain more control and stability.
"As long as you have unity, you live for another day, right? But if you have disunity, you probably die the same day," he told DW.
This approach "kind of works," at least at the moment, he added.
"It's not like the Chinese economy is disastrous. It's not great, but it's not disastrous. In any case, look at the outside world. It's a mess."
Who will succeed Xi Jinping?
Outside observers are also focusing on Xi's future and possible successors for the 73-year-old leader.
For now, Xi seems to be firmly in control. It is highly likely that he would be confirmed as the party's general secretary next fall, and could stay in that position until 2032.
This is due to the changes pushed by Xi in 2018, which removed term limits for state and party leaders.
Both analysts told DW that the issue of succession plays a major role in Xi's push towards internal stability.
"There's always a danger of differences in the party fragmenting it, especially when the question of succession comes up," says Brown. "And even though we don't expect to see a successor anytime soon, you know, there's going to be speculation about who might succeed Xi."
"He can't go on forever," he added.
Political scientist Chong Ja Ian says that Xi currently holds all the power. Therefore, the CCP leader could be afraid of his authority being undermined if he named a successor ahead of time.
"On the other hand, a failure to make preparations on time could create a power vacuum that can cause major instability," he told DW. "To solve this dilemma, the current leader needs to have both the necessary self-confidence and the readiness to take a step back — just like his predecessors did. But not everyone has that kind of confidence."
This text was originally published in Chinese.

historic perugia newsstand reconfigures into stepped red oak mini reading kiosk

historic perugia newsstand reconfigures into stepped red oak mini reading kiosk
along perugia’s sant’ercolano staircase, giuseppe arezzi transforms edicola 518 from a traditional newsstand into a micro-architecture featuring stepped oak seating, a drinking fountain, and street-step furniture.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
GIUSEPPE AREZZI RECONFIGURES PERUGIA NEWSSTAND INTO CULTURAL HUB
Located along the historic Sant’Ercolano staircase in Perugia, Edicola 518 is a renewed cultural kiosk and micro-architecture conceived by Italian designer Giuseppe Arezzi. Realized for the Laboratorio di Creatività Contemporanea open call, promoted by the Italian Ministry of Culture and won by Edicola 518 under the L’Edicola che Vorrei initiative, the project marks the site’s tenth anniversary. Reopening on June 1st, 2026, the intervention repurposes the historic newspaper kiosk typology, shifting it from a commercial sales stall into an open, community-oriented reading hub and public amenity.
STEPPED OAK MICRO-kiosk EXTENDS READING space ONTO URBAN STAIRS
The project by multidisciplinary designer Giuseppe Arezzi preserves the original exterior envelope while applying a monochromatic red finish that establishes a stark chromatic contrast against the stone staircase. Inside, Arezzi replaces the conventional vendor-counter barrier with a stepped, multifunctional furniture installation built from lacquered oak, concealing technical compartments while providing integrated bench seating. At the core of the timber structure, a stainless-steel fountain supplies free drinking water to pedestrians. The window frames are re-engineered to double as external display racks for independent magazines and art books, while an exterior platform extends outward onto the historic steps to ensure seating remains accessible outside business hours. Extending the program into the public realm, the installation incorporates Ambo, a 20-centimeter-high modular stool-bookstand designed in collaboration with the Seed Festival to negotiate the stairway’s grade shifts as both mobile seating and a display surface.
‘Observing the location of the Sant’Ercolano staircase, I wanted to preserve the daily ritual that historically belongs to the newsstand,’ explains the designer Giuseppe Arezzi. ‘While people once stopped to purchase information, today they pause to process it through rest and reading. I interpreted the kiosk not merely as micro-architecture, but as a versatile, spatial piece of furniture, where every technical element is conceived to foster interaction and the free enjoyment of public space.’

development collaborator: Matteo Pettorali | @matte_petto
technical partners: Seed 360 | @seed360official, Umbra Acque

‘Ra’am has no connection to the matter, and we will cooperate fully,’ Party’s chairman Abbas reacts to investigation into foreign interference in elections

Herzog: allegations “must be fully investigated”; warns against tarnishing “an entire community” that voted
President Isaac Herzog said he spoke with Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg and Shin Bet head David Zini and is “closely following developments in the investigation into the allegations published this morning.”
Speaking at an event at the President’s Residence honoring the Jewish Federations of North America’s Israel Small Business Loan Fund, he said: “The integrity of our elections is a supreme democratic value. The evidence and the allegations must be fully investigated, and those responsible must be arrested and held accountable according to the full extent of the law.”

Eisenkot says foreign involvement in Israel is “unacceptable and grave beyond measure”; Shin Bet must investigate election suspicions
Yashar Party Chairman Gadi Eisenkot said he welcomes Netanyahu “finally condemning Qatari involvement in the State of Israel,” calling foreign involvement “unacceptable and grave beyond measure,” especially when it concerns a state that funds and supports Hamas.
He said it is grave when it occurs within the Prime Minister’s Office and equally grave if it occurs within the electoral process, and that the Shin Bet must conduct “an impartial, thorough, and immediate investigation,” with an “iron fist” approach against anyone found to have compromised or attempted to compromise the integrity of the elections.
Balad chairman answers Likud election theft claims; says losing side “concocts a racist ‘blood libel’”
Balad Chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh, responding to claims made by Likud, said: “In any properly functioning society, those who lose an election take responsibility and go home. In Israel, the losing side concocts a racist ‘blood libel’ and calls upon the security establishment to use force to overturn the election results.”
The Arab party leader said what began with the unlawful disqualification of Arab electoral lists continued with incitement against Arab parties and the Arab public, and that on election day hundreds of armed far-right activists descended on polling stations in Arab localities in an attempt to suppress turnout.
Abu Shehadeh said Netanyahu and his associates are “dangerous individuals” building a narrative to reject the results of an election with “the most decisive outcome seen in Israel in decades.”
Golan says Netanyahu suffered “crushing democratic defeat”; accuses him of “ugly campaign of delegitimization”
In his own reaction to the news of investigations and the Likud Party accusing the Arab parties of fraud, Democrats Party leader Yair Golan said Netanyahu “has suffered a crushing democratic defeat” and “refuses to accept the voters’ verdict.”
Golan accused Netanyahu of trying to challenge the election results through “an ugly campaign of delegitimization,” directed against the will of the public and specifically against the Arab public.
He said any genuine suspicion regarding a compromise to the integrity of the elections “must be thoroughly investigated,” but that the “most grave instance of Qatari involvement” took place within Netanyahu’s own office, carried out by his closest aide.
Likud leads with 26 seats, Yashar 21, in unofficial count with 93.8% of votes tallied
The current coalition stands at 53 seats, while the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot stays at 48, and the Arab parties at 19.
The Joint List, currently at 11, was up one seat, competing over a single mandate with the other Arab party, Ra'am, which is back up to 8.
‘The "Ra'am-gate" affair is an earthquake. The elections have been stolen!’ Likud Party demands Shin Bet investigate Ra’am Party of fraud
Likud said the elections in Israel “have been stolen,” calling the “Ra’am-gate” affair “an earthquake” in a statement reacting to Justice Noam Sohlberg’s remarks about the involvement of foreign entities.
The party claimed that foreign entities intervened and bribed voters to benefit Arab parties, calling it an assault on democracy aimed at facilitating a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel and the ousting of the right-wing government.
Likud said that no Zionist party may cooperate with Ra’am or the Joint List, replace the Speaker of the Knesset using votes purchased with cash, or form a government that poses a danger to Israel.
Despite these claims, the election committee explicitly stated that its investigation is not related to claims made by the Likud Party.
In an unusual move, the Israeli election committee chief orders Shin Bet to investigate foreign funding and election bribery amid ‘serious suspicions’
Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg instructed Shin Bet head David Zini to investigate suspected foreign funding and election bribery involving foreign entities.
Reports said the letter followed a briefing in which Zini presented Sohlberg with information described as “exceptionally grave.”
The allegations concern improper influence over the elections through foreign funding from outside actors working against Israeli interests, though Sohlberg wrote that he “cannot attest to the nature of the above suspicions.”
Sohlberg asked Zini to bring findings, if any, within the coming week, citing the legally established timelines for filing an election appeal.
Ra’am receives another mandate at the expense of the Joint List
Reports indicate that Ra’am has won an additional seat at the expense of the Joint List, with 91% of the votes counted.
The two parties signed a surplus-vote agreement that decides who gets their shared 19th seat. Under the latest official figures, Ra’am is about 1,200 votes short of claiming it.
Under the new tally, Ra’am holds 8 seats, up from 7, while the Joint List drops to 11 from 12. The two parties’ combined total remains at 19, and no other bloc has changed.
Israel election by the numbers: who might form the next government?
Israel has voted, and neither Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition nor Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc is going to secure the 61 seats required to form government.
One of the two blocs will now need to begin the long and complicated task of negotiations between the smaller factional parties to form a government. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, will decide who gets the first chance to do so.
This could involve the Arab parties, who may hold the balance of power. Whether either bloc would welcome an Arab-aligned party into their coalition, however, remains to be seen.

Netenyahu's Likud party alleges interference and fraud in Israel's election

Qatar has denied interfering in the election or funding efforts to influence the result, calling the accusations “ridiculous and dangerous”.
Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party are alleging election interference and fraud after Israel’s election results left his bloc short of a parliamentary majority.
The final count, expected on Thursday evening, is set to confirm that Netanyahu's bloc has fallen short of the 61 seats needed for a majority. With around 90% of votes counted, Netanyahu’s bloc was projected to win 53 seats, the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot 48, and Arab-led parties 19.
The result represents major gains for the Arab-led parties, potentially giving them a decisive role in determining whether a government without Netanyahu can be formed.
The election saw record participation by Arab citizens of Israel, many of whom are descendants of Palestinians who remained after the country's creation in 1948. The campaign had seen Netanyahu and his far-right allies repeatedly portray Arab-led parties as a threat.
Netanyahu alleges interference
Netanyahu, who has served as Israel's prime minister on and off since 1996, has accused Arab parties of benefiting from foreign interference and funding. Neither he nor his allies have publicly provided evidence to substantiate those claims.
In a post on the social media platform X, Netanyahu quoted his Likud party, saying: "The elections in the State of Israel were stolen by Arab parties that support terrorism and the elimination of the Jewish state through serious criminal offences of bribery, threats, violence, forgeries, and the use of prohibited software to mobilise voters."
In another post on Thursday morning, he wrote: "Why did Ahmad Tibi visit Qatar 4 days before the elections?" Ahmad Tibi is a Palestinian-Israeli politician and a senior figure in the Ta'al party.
Israel's Central Election Commission has asked the Shin Bet security service to investigate alleged foreign interference. However, the request itself reportedly did not specifically accuse Arab-led parties of wrongdoing. AP also reported that the commission said there was no basis, to its knowledge, for claims of systematic violations of election integrity.
The Arab-led Joint List rejected the accusations, saying Netanyahu’s camp was trying to delegitimise the Arab vote because of its increased political influence. It accused Netanyahu of "working to steal the election".
Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas said he welcomed an investigation into allegations of wrongdoing but said his party had "no connection" with them.
Netanyahu himself has previously faced scrutiny over alleged links between aides and Qatar, after two of his aides were arrested last year on suspicion of receiving payments from the Gulf state.
Qatar has categorically denied interfering in the election. Its Foreign Ministry spokesman, Majed Al Ansari, said: "They accuse Qatar of buying off Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli political left and now, in this latest campaign, the Arab vote. These accusations are ridiculous and dangerous in equal measure."
Israel's President Isaac Herzog has also called for a full investigation, while warning against stigmatising the country’s entire Arab community.
What happens next?
The full count is expected on Thursday evening, although the official election results are due to be certified by 4 November.
President Herzog will then decide whom to ask to try to form a government.
The next Knesset is due to be sworn in on 10 November.
If no coalition can be formed after several attempts, Israel could face another election early next year.
The political uncertainty is unfolding alongside the possibility of renewed Israeli or US strikes on Iran, which could further complicate coalition negotiations.

But can the results of November's midterm elections really impact the cost-of-living crisis? "There isn't a ton that anyone can do about it, regardless of who wins the midterms," says Greg Ip, chief economics commentator at The Wall Street Journal.
"They can't stop the war in Iran, because that is the purview of the president (...) To the extent that tariffs are one of the sources of inflation that people are unhappy about, simply changing control of Congress doesn't affect that."
Ip says there is a disconnect between the messaging of the Trump administration, the economic data and voters' perception of the economy. "You know the old saying – you can't eat GDP. A lot of the growth in GDP that we're seeing is accruing to companies in the form of much higher profits, or to the more affluent households who own stocks in companies that are connected to the AI boom. So for the median household, their incomes are simply not keeping up with what the strong GDP figures are showing (...) So in some senses, it's two economies facing us in this midterm."
FRANCE 24's correspondents Pierrick Leurent and Valerie Defert report on the backlash against AI data centers in Republican strongholds like Texas. Ip says it's a rare unifying issue in a divided economy. "In my opinion, part of the opposition to data centres right now is reflecting this deep-seated anxiety about AI overall. Data centres aren't necessarily the immediate cause, but they're a good proxy or target for that anxiety."

Bolsonaro leadership claim fails to win support from allies in Brazil

- Key allies, including Liberal Party chief Valdemar Costa Neto and São Paulo Governor Tarcisio de Freitas, said Brazil’s election results must be respected and the country should move forward.
- Bolsonaro said he would lead the opposition from abroad, but party figures rejected fraud claims and backed Lula’s win, which was recognised by Brazil’s electoral authority and global leaders.
AI generated
SAO PAULO - Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro’s decision to declare himself the country’s rightful “leader” has failed to garner support from key figures in his political camp, leaving the right-wing lawmaker increasingly isolated in Brazilian politics.
Bolsonaro made the claim in a letter he posted on social media after arriving in the United States on Oct 28, having left Brazil following his defeat to leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva by more than four million votes in the Oct 25 runoff.
Bolsonaro has cited the fact that a Lula-appointed Supreme Court justice extended voting by two hours due to Lula campaign allegations of voter suppression in left-leaning northeastern states, though Bolsonaro’s campaign had also sought a voting extension due to rain in conservative southern states.
He alleged he was a victim of an electoral coup, but did not provide evidence for electoral fraud.
Lula’s victory has been recognised by Brazil’s electoral authority, global leaders, international observers, and Bolsonaro’s own party.
“I did not like it,” the head of the senator’s Liberal Party, Valdemar Costa Neto, told reporters on Oct 29 when asked about the letter. “Flavio went through a difficult situation - we understand that - but we do not approve of it. We want to move the country forward,” he said later.
Sao Paulo Governor Tarcisio de Freitas, a prominent Bolsonaro ally who campaigned vigorously for the lawmaker, told newspaper Estadao that Brazil’s election results must be respected and that it was time to move forward.
US President Donald Trump, who confirmed his administration had allowed Bolsonaro to enter the country, declined to comment on Oct 29 when asked who he thought was the legitimate winner.
“I watched the election. I didn’t take sides. I let it be. I was asked not to take sides by the president, the current president,” he said.
Parties recognise Lula’s win
Aecio Neves, head of the centre-right Brazilian Social Democracy Party and a vocal critic of Lula’s Workers’ Party, described Bolsonaro’s behaviour as “incomprehensible” in a statement, adding that opposition politics must be conducted from within the country.
Centre-right party Uniao Brasil, which backed Bolsonaro in the second round, said it was essential that institutions “remain greater than any individual.” The election was conducted with integrity and its results must be respected, it added.
The centrist Brazilian Democratic Movement (MDB) party, which also supported Bolsonaro in the runoff, struck a similar tone.
“The MDB reaffirms its total confidence in the Brazilian electoral system and, therefore, in the legitimacy of the result of the election last Sunday,” it said.
‘Flavio is venting’
In his letter, Bolsonaro pledged to lead the opposition from abroad and “assume the risks” that local politicians could not, adding he would support a potential bid by Senator Rogerio Marinho for Senate president in 2027.
Marinho, who served as Bolsonaro’s campaign manager, told reporters that Bolsonaro remains “a leader” and “the most prominent figure on the right” in Brazil, given the support he received from nearly 60 million voters.
But Marinho also rejected allegations of electoral fraud.
“The Liberal Party cannot make that claim, nor can I make that claim, because there is no evidence to support it,” he said.
“Flavio is venting in response to the second-round election results, which were unexpected for all of us.” REUTERS

The ‘breathing space budget’ – breathing space for the government, that is | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:11:11 UTC
01:11:11 KST

Maybe it had been one of the greatest acts of political genius after all. The day after the budget is usually the moment when things start to fall apart. When clued-up journalists and economists have had a chance to go through all the fine points the chancellor would rather everyone had missed. The forecasts that suggest everything is predicated on a wing and a prayer. The hidden unfunded tax cuts. The greater-than-expected spending commitments.
But on Thursday morning Andy Burnham and John Healey could afford themselves a sigh of relief. All had gone about as well as they could have hoped. It turns out that when you don’t make any massive tax or spending commitments, there isn’t a great deal to unravel. All there had been was a raft of small-scale interventions designed to help people with their personal finances. Call it the Martin Lewis budget. In fact, Healey and Lewis now seem unable to get through the day without spending some time with each other. They certainly can’t stop talking about one another. It’s becoming unhealthily co-dependent. The gods of small things.
It had been billed as the “breathing space” budget. A budget to help get everyone through the coming year more or less alive. No hiding under tables or breaking open the emergency supplies of baked beans. Apocalypse averted. But the breathing space might just as well have been for the government. Difficult decisions delayed. Hope that we all wake up in 52 weeks’ time and the world looks like a less frightening place. And even if it doesn’t, it will always have had a year’s grace. A chance for the Tories and Reform to implode. You can always hope.
Come the traditional morning-after interview with the chancellor on the Today programme, the presenter Nick Robinson seemed uncharacteristically subdued. Normally he’s a terrier on occasions like these. There’s never been a budget that Nick wouldn’t have been able to do far better himself. But this one? This one was something you might find on the consumer affairs programme, You and Yours. And the BBC was in the process of axing that.
So the 20 minutes passed with little fuss. More a softball back and forth. Healey started with his usual infectious brand of pessimism. He was born to be the bearer of bad news. The poster boy for assisted dying. Everything was absolutely terrible. He wasn’t quite sure why anyone was still bothering with anything. If it had been up to him he would have ended the interview before it had started. There was nothing to say. Other than that, given the chance, he wouldn’t have started from here. Brexit, the pandemic, Ukraine, Iran, energy prices. The world was screwed. Britain was screwed. Lie back and prepare for the worst 10 years of your already miserable life.
Nick tried to find a reason to believe. Couldn’t the chancellor have made just a little more effort? Having a plan to have a plan wasn’t the usual budget fare. Healey, AKA Dr Death, shrugged. It was one up on having a plan to not have a plan. By now Robbo was audibly struggling. How could he put it politely? In the third year of a government with a 160-seat majority, surely Healey could have been a little more ambitious. This wasn’t exactly the big transformation that had been promised.
Could he even say if he would bring down the benefits bill? Apparently he could. “There will be a reduction in the benefits bill,” said Dr Death. Cue panic stations in the Treasury. Within seconds of Healey opening his mouth, dozens of government spinners were on the phones to every journalist to tell them they hadn’t heard what they had just heard. There had been collective false consciousness. When Healey had said that he would be bringing down a benefits bill that everyone agreed was too high and that the country could not afford, what he had really meant to say was that he would not be bringing down the benefits bill that he had no idea how to pay for. Fag packets gratefully received. That was about as close to news as we got.
Maybe it was just that while Healey was having one of his better days, Robinson was having one of his worse ones. Because he had also sounded uninterested in his interview with Andrew Griffith an hour earlier. An exercise in box-ticking rather than revelation because the shadow chancellor never has anything useful to add on the day after. Sure enough, Griffith insisted that he would have done everything differently while never going into the details of how. At which point, Robbo opened half an eye and observed that if it was really that easy, how come the Tories hadn’t fixed it when in office?
Indeed, Nick continued, it could be argued that Labour had been left to clear up the mess the Tories created. “I’ve never shied away from saying that the Tories have a chequered record,” Griffith said defensively. Er, I’m not sure that’s entirely true, Andrew. Your usual line is that history started in 2024 and that everything is the Labour government’s fault.
That just left time for Robinson to remind the shadow chancellor that he had been part of the Treasury team that had defended the Liz Truss mini-budget even as it was being shredded. “I will never publish plans without saying where the money is coming from,” said Griffith, before announcing £30bn of planned tax cuts without specifying which benefits he would cut to pay for them. Fair to say, he’s not a man who seems to learn from experience. Once in the Truss image, always in the Truss image.
The final piece of the Thursday jigsaw was the verdict from the Institute for Fiscal Studies. In the past this has been enough to completely destroy the reputation of some chancellors. I could never look at George Osborne in quite the same way after the IFS had rubbished one of his budgets. It’s one thing to be thought of as an economic quarter-wit. What’s really devastating is to have it proved.
Helen Miller, the IFS director, looked a bit knackered. She and her team had been up most of the night, going through both the budget and the OBR figures line by line, searching for the fatal flaw. And she was gutted to announce that there actually wasn’t one. There was as little in the budget as had first appeared. She announced that she was grumpy about some measures. Disappointed in others. Another was cack-handed. The tax system had been made more complicated, not less. Yet, all in all, these were minor gripes.
“This chancellor is hoping that things get better without actually needing to do anything,” Miller said in conclusion. I don’t think that’s right. Healey never travels in hope. Like the rest of us, he’s pretty confident everything is going to be worse in a year’s time. But he had got himself some breathing space.

‘If this works, it will be the first real ceasefire across a large stretch of the front’: Russia and Ukraine maintain truce in occupied Oleshky for more than two days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:05:56 UTC
01:05:56 KST

‘If this works, it will be the first real ceasefire across a large stretch of the front’: Russia and Ukraine maintain truce in occupied Oleshky for more than two days
Russia and Ukraine have halted hostilities around the occupied city of Oleshky since October 27. The Verkhovna Rada’s human rights commissioner, Dmytro Lubinets, confirmed on the morning of October 29 that the ceasefire had held for more than two days. Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, said humanitarian aid — “food, fuel, medicine, and hygiene products” — had been sent to Oleshky.
Lubinets and Lantratova set out for Oleshky on the afternoon of October 29. Lubinets will be the first Ukrainian official of such rank to visit Russian-occupied territories. Both commissioners said their main task is to deliver humanitarian aid to residents and ensure the safe evacuation of those who want to leave.
Sources who spoke to the Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda and were involved in organizing the ceasefire said the ceasefire around Oleshky is meant to test whether Ukrainian and Russian military commanders can carry out political agreements to end hostilities.
Organizing a halt to the fighting turned out to be “an extremely difficult task,” according to the outlet’s sources. A political order to cease fire does not by itself guarantee automatic compliance on the front line, a source in Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s administration told Ukrainska Pravda. Even Ukrainian troops demanded guarantees several times that if they stopped, “nothing bad would happen afterward,” the source said. The source explained:
We want to get the military — both our General Staff and the Russian one — used to the idea that if the political leadership has decided that in a given sector of the front we stop, freeze in place, and no one opens fire, the military can make that happen. They can guarantee it. Not a situation where the political leadership has reached an agreement and the military says, “Sorry, we can’t stop, we’ve got something going on.”
It is easier for the Russian side than for the Ukrainian side to organize and maintain a ceasefire, according to Ukrainska Pravda’s sources. “They [the Russians] have a rigid military vertical. We have a decentralized army. And someone — some well-known military blogger — could stir up the mood on air so much that everything falls apart afterward,” a source said.
If the ceasefire in Oleshky can be maintained, as planned, until the evening of November 1, the Ukrainian side expects to repeat this kind of local ceasefire later along other parts of the front. “That’s precisely so the military can learn how to do this: stop, ensure safe passage, and so on. So that later, if there’s some major agreement, we could implement it right away,” a source who spoke to Ukrainska Pravda said.
If this works, this will be the first example of a real ceasefire across a fairly large stretch of the front. It’s come at such a cost — the military, Russia’s Federal Security Service, and everyone else are doing nothing but trying to sabotage it. But we believe it will work out and that this will set a precedent.
The war in photographs
Russia’s Defense Ministry announced that it had begun clearing mines from roads leading into Oleshky and published photos and video of sappers at work. Russian President Vladimir Putin, speaking at a plenary session of the Russia–Africa summit underway in Moscow, claimed it was Ukraine that had mined the approaches to Oleshky, creating “practically a humanitarian catastrophe.”

China’s Hainan boosts its international trade in services by 11.7% in nine months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:01:31 UTC
01:01:31 KST

HAIKOU /China/, October 29. /TASS/. China’s southern island province of Hainan increased its international trade in services by 11.7% year-on-year to 56.95 billion yuan ($8.48 billion) in January-September 2026, the region’s Department of Commerce said.
According to the department’s WeChat page, the province’s services exports increased by 14.9% to 40.41 billion yuan (around $6.02 billion) in the reporting period, while imports reached 16.54 billion yuan ($2.46 billion), up 4.7%.
The department said that the cross-border maintenance sector (for vessels and aircraft — TASS), inbound tourism and computer game exports demonstrated particularly impressive results over the nine months. Key transport and logistics companies such as COSCO Shipping played an important role in developing Hainan’s freight sector.
The Department of Commerce forecasted that Hainan’s international transport services sector would grow significantly by the end of 2026. The department highlighted the key role of the visa-free regime and air traffic growth, which have brought far more tourists from Russia, Kazakhstan and South Korea to the island.
In addition, the department noted that the quantitative growth in Hainan’s international services trade came with structural optimization, driven by both traditional and new factors. According to the published data, the Chinese special administrative region of Hong Kong, the United States, Russia, Ireland and Singapore are Hainan’s top five partners in this field. According to estimates, they accounted for more than 57% of total commercial activity in this segment of the island’s economy in the first three quarters of 2026.
The department also stated that the Hainan Free Trade Port would continue to use institutional and other advantages to strengthen the regional transport sector and inbound tourism and to introduce new types of services trade. At the same time, the province’s authorities plan to diversify the entry of local companies into foreign markets and ensure the high quality of their economic interaction with partners from other countries and regions.

Hidden ADHD common in women seeking treatment for depression and anxiety
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:00:01 UTC
01:00:01 KST

A recent study reveals that nearly one in five women seeking treatment for anxiety or depression also have attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, with nearly half of those cases having never been previously diagnosed. The research highlights how overlapping symptoms can obscure the underlying attention condition in adult women. These findings were published in The International Journal of Psychiatry in Medicine.
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, commonly known as ADHD, is a neurodevelopmental condition involving inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. During childhood development, hyperactive traits often fade, while inattentive traits tend to persist. Medical professionals historically diagnosed the condition much more frequently in males, and in clinical settings, the ratio of diagnosed males to females is roughly ten to one.
Population surveys show a much narrower gap, suggesting the condition often goes unrecognized in female populations. Women frequently display more subtle, internalizing symptoms like emotional sensitivity or internal restlessness. These internal struggles are easily mistaken for mood or anxiety disorders. Because conditions like major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder share traits with ADHD, such as difficulty concentrating, the underlying attention disorder is frequently missed.
An additional feature commonly reported by people with ADHD is hyperfocus. This phenomenon involves episodes of intense, prolonged concentration on specific tasks, often to the exclusion of everything else going on around the person. Though not an official diagnostic criterion, hyperfocus is well-documented and can substantially affect daily functioning.
Psychiatrists Hazal Yavuzlar Civan and Tonguc Demir Berkol from the Bakirkoy Prof. Dr. Mazhar Osman Training and Research Hospital for Psychiatry, Neurology and Neurosurgery in Istanbul, Turkey, conducted the research. They wanted to understand how ADHD manifests in women already seeking help for mood problems. They also examined hyperfocus to see if it could help clinicians distinguish these conditions.
The researchers recruited 170 female patients at outpatient psychiatric clinics. The participants first completed the Beck Depression Inventory and the Beck Anxiety Inventory, which are standard questionnaires that measure the severity of depressive and anxious symptoms. Women scoring above the threshold for clinical depression or anxiety then took additional surveys.
These follow-up surveys included the Wender Utah Rating Scale to measure childhood ADHD traits, a separate screening tool for adult ADHD symptoms, and the Hyperfocus Scale. Following the questionnaires, a trained psychiatrist conducted a structured clinical interview with each participant. The final diagnoses were based on standard psychiatric guidelines.
The clinical interviews revealed that 33 of the 170 women met the criteria for ADHD. Within this group, 15 patients had no prior ADHD diagnosis. ADHD was especially prevalent among women experiencing social anxiety disorder and a condition called double depression. Double depression occurs when a patient experiences a severe depressive episode on top of a chronic, long-term baseline of low mood.
The women with ADHD reported distinct life experiences compared to the participants who only had mood or anxiety disorders. They had more disciplinary issues in school, more frequent job changes, and a higher rate of family members with ADHD. The rates of past suicide attempts did not differ in a statistically significant way between the two groups, but the women with ADHD reported higher levels of current suicidal thoughts and feelings of failure.
When looking at specific depressive symptoms, the two groups diverged. The group without ADHD reported more concerns about physical health and changes in sleeping habits. The authors suggest this health-related worry reflects a somatic focus, which is a heightened awareness of bodily sensations commonly seen in anxiety and depression.
Conversely, individuals with ADHD often experience impaired interoception, meaning they have a harder time recognizing internal physical states. This altered awareness might reduce how often they notice or report physical symptoms like poor sleep.
ADHD was highly prevalent among women experiencing social anxiety disorder. The researchers suggest social anxiety in these patients may be driven by ADHD-related executive dysfunction, which impairs the brain’s ability to plan, organize, and interpret social cues. Difficulties in self-regulation often lead to repeated interpersonal failures, which can eventually create lasting feelings of shame and a fear of social evaluation.
The researchers also identified distinct patterns regarding symptom overlap. In the group without ADHD, higher attention deficit scores correlated with worse depression. Higher hyperactivity scores correlated with worse anxiety. Hyperfocus scores also rose alongside general ADHD-like symptoms in these women.
The women diagnosed with ADHD did not show these same statistical correlations. While their overall hyperfocus scores were substantially higher than the group without ADHD, the severity of their hyperfocus did not track directly with the severity of their mood or anxiety symptoms. The findings suggest hyperfocus may serve different roles depending on the diagnosis, acting as a coping mechanism in ADHD but manifesting as a maladaptive trait in mood disorders.
The study details how similar symptoms stem from different root causes. Both ADHD and anxiety can involve restlessness, distractibility, and tension. In anxiety, inattention usually stems from excessive worry, with mental energy consumed by ruminating or anticipating threats, and this type of distractibility often improves in relaxed environments.
In contrast, inattention related to ADHD is consistent across different settings and typically appears early in life. It is usually associated with poor task initiation, organizational difficulties, and mind-wandering that is completely unrelated to specific fears. The authors note that thorough developmental histories are required to distinguish primary ADHD from secondary attention problems caused by mood disorders.
The research relied on a cross-sectional design, meaning the assessments occurred at a single point in time. The methodology cannot determine the sequence of symptom onset. It remains unclear whether ADHD symptoms preceded the depressive and anxious symptoms, or vice versa.
The sample focused entirely on women seeking outpatient psychiatric care. The prevalence rates and symptom patterns might look different in men, people not seeking psychiatric help, or individuals treated in inpatient hospital settings. The group of women diagnosed with ADHD was also much smaller than the group without the condition, which limits the statistical power of certain comparisons.
Future research should follow patients over extended periods to track how these overlapping conditions develop over a lifespan. Incorporating biological markers or tracking symptoms in broader populations could further clarify how hyperfocus operates across different mental health diagnoses.
The study, “ADHD Comorbidity in Women With Depression and Anxiety: Prevalence, Clinical Features and Hyperfocus Dynamics,” was authored by Hazal Yavuzlar Civan and Tonguc Demir Berkol.

Bulgaria Failed to Prevent Starlink Arson Despite Advance Intelligence Warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

Two 19-year-old German citizens suspected of setting fire to Starlink equipment in Bulgaria and Lithuania are facing terrorism charges in Lithuania and opposing extradition to Bulgaria, while Bulgarian opposition lawmaker Ivaylo Mirchev has accused the country’s security services of failing to act on a foreign intelligence warning issued at least a week before the arson.
The two suspects, identified as Zeka I. and Tirpan B., were arrested in Duisburg on October 23 under European Arrest Warrants issued by Bulgaria. The Higher Regional Court in Düsseldorf ordered them to remain in custody, citing the seriousness of the allegations and the risk that they could flee. Both have refused to consent to immediate surrender to Bulgarian authorities.
Bulgarian investigators allege that the pair set fire to a Starlink ground station near Sofia on October 9, damaging or completely destroying eight of its 18 antennas. The arrest warrant states that they entered Bulgaria from Serbia on the day of the attack in a vehicle with German license plates and returned to Serbia shortly afterward. The satellite internet system is used in Ukraine’s defense operations.
German law allows German citizens to be extradited for prosecution abroad under certain conditions. The alleged crime must have been committed primarily in the country requesting extradition, which must also guarantee that convicted individuals can return to Germany to serve their sentences if they choose. Since the suspects have not consented to surrender, the Düsseldorf court must rule on whether extradition is admissible. Only after that decision can the German Federal Public Prosecutor’s Office authorize their transfer to Bulgaria.
Lithuanian authorities are also investigating the two men for involvement in an organized terrorist group linked to attacks on Starlink infrastructure in Bulgaria, Lithuania and Poland. Saulius Briginas, deputy chief of the Lithuanian Criminal Police, said one suspect holds dual German and Turkish citizenship, while the other holds dual German and Serbian citizenship. Both live in Germany, Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT reported.
Investigators have linked the pair to an attempted arson attack on Starlink equipment in Vilnius on October 18. The attackers used flammable liquids, but a security guard extinguished the fire before the equipment suffered serious damage. The company had received advance warnings and strengthened security, allowing the facility to continue operating without interruption.
Briginas said the suspects had no links to Lithuania and entered the country shortly before the attack, leaving immediately afterward. Lithuanian investigators believe the incident was planned in advance.
On October 27, the Vilnius Prosecutor’s Office charged the two men with forming and participating in an organized terrorist group, traveling for terrorist purposes, and committing a terrorist act that could have caused severe consequences. Lithuanian police have identified a direct connection between the attacks in Bulgaria, Lithuania and Poland. Briginas said the detained suspects are believed to have carried out the attacks in Bulgaria and Lithuania, while other individuals linked to the same group were responsible for the incident in Poland. At least four people have been detained in Poland.
Lithuanian investigators are also examining possible links between the suspects and Russia. The Vilnius Prosecutor’s Office said there were grounds for suspicion, although the investigation was still at an early stage. Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius has suggested that the attacks on Starlink could form part of Russia’s hybrid warfare.
Starlink infrastructure has been targeted in several attacks across Eastern Europe in recent weeks. A fire also broke out at a Starlink ground station in Poland, where authorities likewise suspect Russian sabotage. Lithuanian investigators have warned that such attacks could affect both national communications infrastructure and the wider operation of a system used by Ukraine.
The investigations are being coordinated closely by law enforcement agencies in Bulgaria, Lithuania, Poland and Germany. The two suspects remain in German custody while the Düsseldorf court considers Bulgaria’s extradition request.
In Bulgaria, Ivaylo Mirchev, a lawmaker from Democratic Bulgaria, said a foreign partner intelligence service had warned the country at least a week before the October 9 arson that Starlink equipment could be attacked. He accused the security services of failing to take preventive action and said two Interior Ministry patrol cars reached the site hours after the fire rather than guarding it.
Mirchev made the allegations after a parliamentary hearing on the incident was derailed by actions from Progressive Bulgaria. His remarks followed Prime Minister Rumen Radev’s decision to brief journalists rather than address lawmakers about the case.
Bulgarian authorities had not publicly disclosed the arson, which damaged antennas used to support communications for the Ukrainian army and provide internet access in a country under Russian attack. The incident took place on October 9, but information became public late on October 12, when Mirchev posted about it on Facebook. The Interior Ministry, security services and government declined to comment.
Media reports later identified the suspects as 19-year-olds Tirpan Beytulla and Zeka Islam. They entered Bulgaria through the Kalotina border crossing and left through the same checkpoint on the day of the arson without hindrance. Reports on October 19 said European Arrest Warrants had been issued, and on October 26, media outlets reported that the men had been arrested in Duisburg. Extradition proceedings are pending.
Radev spoke about the operation twice, first in the National Assembly and later to ministers at the Council of Ministers. His remarks indicated that the authorities had deliberately withheld information, saying the suspects had been identified the day after the arson but their names could not be disclosed because they were already abroad. He also described obtaining the European Arrest Warrant as a lengthy and cumbersome process that ultimately led to the arrests on Monday evening.
“Our security services alerted the partner nation about these individuals so they could be placed under surveillance. However, there was an extremely lengthy, cumbersome procedure that had to be followed to issue a European Arrest Warrant. We couldn't share all the information immediately; had our services or the Ministry of the Interior disclosed the perpetrators' names, they would likely have fled the country where they were staying. Sometimes, patience is required to successfully apprehend perpetrators,” Radev said.
The prime minister did not explain what might have motivated the two 19-year-olds to travel to Bulgaria, set fire to equipment supporting Ukraine and then leave the country. Democratic Bulgaria remained dissatisfied with his comments. Mirchev said the suspects had been driving a Volkswagen Touareg and suggested photographs could establish when the two Interior Ministry patrol cars arrived.
“Instead of a formal hearing, we saw the Prime Minister, accompanied by the Minister of Interior and the head of the State Agency for National Security (SANS), blithely declaring that the job was done. But since there was no actual session, they weren't in a position to answer certain questions. For example: were we warned by the intelligence services of a foreign nation at least a week in advance that such an arson attack was going to take place in Bulgaria? And if we were warned, did we take any precautions? How is it possible for two 19-year-olds to enter Bulgaria, set fire to the antennas, and leave, all without the Bulgarian services knowing a thing? There are many questions,” Mirchev said after Radev’s statement.
He also questioned whether any patrol had been stationed near the antennas despite the intelligence warning and what it had been doing during the arson.
“Is this work really something to be proud of?” Mirchev asked, suggesting that the security services’ handling of the case should be examined rather than simply praised.
Mirchev said the public had learned about the incident from outside sources 48 hours after it happened, and argued that authorities had avoided discussing who might have wanted to target Starlink equipment.
“In the end, it will probably turn out that two 19-year-olds got drunk in Germany, decided to cross the border in a Touareg, accidentally set fire to these antennas, and then just went back. 'The job is done, and we thank the security services' - that is what the Prime Minister said today,” Mirchev added.
He also indicated that he had photographs of the site showing when Interior Ministry personnel arrived, anticipating that someone might challenge his account.

Ambassador Trichilo concludes Italian Language Week and presents awards to the students
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:58:13 CET
00:58:13 KST

The Italian Ambassador to Croatia, Paolo Trichilo, concluded the events of Italian Language Week (Slim) in Croatia by participating in the awards ceremony for the winning students of the Slim Competition, organized by the Italian Cultural Institute in Zagreb—in collaboration with the Italian Studies departments in Rijeka, Split, Pula, Zagreb, and Zadar, and the Croatian Association of Italian Teachers (Acapi/Hupti). The aim of the contest was to celebrate Italian as the language of art, design, music, invention, and creativity.
                                    
The event featured the presentation of awards to winning elementary and secondary school students in various categories for their projects on the theme of the 26th edition of Slim: “A Brilliant Language: Conceiving, Designing, and Creating with Italian.” Awards were presented to students from the Vladimir Nazor Elementary School in Zagreb, the Malinska-Dubašnica Secondary School in Veli Lošinj, and the First High School in Split. Special awards for creativity were presented to students from the Catholic Elementary School in Šibenik and students from the Prva sušačka hrvatska Gymnasium in Rijeka. During his remarks, Ambassador Trichilo emphasized the importance of competitions of this kind in promoting and strengthening knowledge of Italian in schools across Croatia, noting that the winning schools come from all over the country.
                                    
The initiative is part of a packed program of activities organized in Croatia to celebrate the 26th edition of Italian Language Week in the World, which included numerous events in Zagreb, Rijeka, Split, Zadar, and Pula, thanks to the involvement of numerous organizers and partners, including the Italian Embassy in Zagreb; the Italian Consulate General in Rijeka; the Italian Cultural Institute in Zagreb; the Italian Union; the Italian community in Pula; the Swiss Embassy in Croatia; the Italian Studies departments at the universities of Rijeka, Pula, Split, Zadar, and Zagreb; the Faculty of Law at the University of Rijeka; the Dante Alighieri Society of Split; the Croatian Association of Italian Teachers – Acapi/Hupti; Edit; La Voce del Popolo; and various educational institutions.
