Netanyahu, at risk of losing power, steps up attacks on Israel’s Arab parties
JERUSALEM – Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu alleged on Oct 29, without providing evidence, that Arab parties’ record gains in an election this week were driven in part by voter fraud, a charge rejected by Arab leaders, who accused him of incitement.
The allegation represents an escalation of anti-Arab rhetoric by Netanyahu and his far-right partners after high Arab turnout in a national ballot on Oct 27 effectively blocked a smooth path to power for either him or his main Jewish rivals.
Israeli election officials said on Oct 29 that there was a probe into fraud allegations, though the election’s integrity was not “systematically compromised”.
Analysts and critics say that by stepping up attacks on Arab parties, Netanyahu may be trying to ensure his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, feels unable to even consider forming a minority government with Arab help that could oust him from power.
Netanyahu’s goal is “delegitimising any Arab-Jewish cooperation”, said Eytan Gilboa, professor of politics at Reichman University.
Election officials were expected to finish tallying votes later on Oct 29, in a tightly fought election that has produced no clear winner and is likely to be followed by weeks of protracted negotiations over a new government.
With nearly 93% of votes counted, Netanyahu’s nationalist-religious bloc held a modest lead in seats over a bloc of right-wing and centre-left parties led by Eisenkot, with both men’s coalitions short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in Parliament.
Parties representing Israel’s 21% Arab minority were projected to win an unprecedented 19 seats, leaving Eisenkot’s bloc, with 48 seats against Netanyahu’s camp of 53, with no realistic path to power without broad Arab backing, an option Eisenkot has so far ruled out.
However, Eisenkot’s camp could also try to form a minority government with Arab support from the outside, without including them in a governing coalition.
Netanyahu accuses Arab parties of fraud; Arab parties call it incitement
Ahmad Tibi, one of the leaders of the Arab Joint List party, said Netanyahu was on an orchestrated, toxic campaign meant to undermine the election results.
“This entire campaign is directed against Eisenkot, to prevent him, intimidate and scare him off forming a government that relies on external support from the Joint List or Ra’am,” Tibi told Reuters.
During and after the Oct 27 election, Netanyahu and his allies warned against rising Arab turnout, and his right-wing Likud party issued statements accusing the Arab parties of “stealing the vote”.
It demanded police and the Shin Bet domestic intelligence service investigate incidents of suspected election bribery and intimidation at ballot stations in Arab towns. It said it possessed evidence of such activity but has not presented it to the public.
The police say they have arrested at least seven people since Tuesday in Israel’s south, where many Arabs live, on suspicion of voter fraud. Israel’s public broadcaster Kan said they were suspected of attempting to bribe voters to cast ballots for the Arab-dominated party Ra’am, which has Islamist roots.
On Oct 29, the head of Israel’s Central Election Committee, Supreme Court jurist Noam Sohlberg, said he had asked the Shin Bet to investigate suspicions that unidentified foreign players had tried to intervene in the election.
Likud seized on Sohlberg’s request, alleging an attack on Israel’s democracy, “an Islamisation of Israel and the toppling of the right-wing in order to bring about IDF withdrawal and defeat on all fronts, foremost Iran”.
Likud said Qatar was behind the alleged election intervention, which Qatar later denied.
Ra’am head Mansour Abbas said on Oct 29 that his party was not involved in the reported suspicious conduct and urged a full investigation. He said that Netanyahu was on an incitement campaign against Israel’s Arab citizens.
“We have one message in response to the campaign of incitement and delegitimisation he is waging against Arab citizens: Nothing will come of it, because there is nothing there,” Abbas said in a statement.
In a letter sent to a parliamentarian and published by the Central Election Committee, the committee said that there was “no base for claims that there was systematic harm to the election’s integrity”.
Israeli President: ‘We must not tarnish an entire community’
After vote tallying is completed, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will consult with party chairs and choose a candidate who he thinks has the best chance to form a government.
The coalition that last toppled Netanyahu, in 2021, relied on Abbas’ Ra’am party. But Eisenkot’s underperformance means the opposition would now need backing from the Arab-dominated Joint List, which includes an explicitly anti-Zionist party. Most Jewish leaders have shunned formal alliances with Arab parties since Israel’s founding.
Eisenkot called for an investigation that would protect election integrity but said Netanyahu was exploiting the suspicions to “spread chaos”.
He said in a statement that Netanyahu’s aim was to “challenge the official election results, in which the Israeli public voted against the government”.
Herzog said the allegations must be investigated.
“But even at a moment like this, we must not tarnish an entire community that sought to exercise its right to vote and take an active part in democracy,” Herzog said in a statement. REUTERS

3 dead as ‘fairy chimney’ rock spires collapse at tourist site in Turkey’s Cappadocia

Turkey’s Cappadocia region, a magnet for tourists from around the world, is home to rock formations known as “fairy chimneys”, created by ancient volcanic activity.
“According to initial findings, two people were killed and five others injured in the incident,” Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said on X.
“Search-and-rescue teams are continuing intensive, coordinated operations to locate any other victims who may be trapped under the debris,” he said.
Rescue teams later pulled another body from the rubble, bringing the death toll to three, Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok said.
One of those killed was a foreign national while the other two were Turkish, he added.
The incident occurred at 3.15pm when a landslide triggered a rockfall in the town of Goreme near the open-air museum, Kok said.
The area was closed to the public following the collapse, according to reports.
Eyewitnesses described hearing a loud noise as the rock spire near a car park collapsed, sending up a huge cloud of dust.
The area was closed to the public after the collapse, according to local reports.
Rescue workers and excavators operated through the night under powerful floodlights before concluding the operation.
“As of now, all our operations have been completed. We have finished all checks and inspections,” governor Kok said in an updated statement.
“Our teams have been withdrawn after determining there is no further need to continue operations at this stage,” he said.
An investigation by the chief prosecutor’s office, together with expert assessments, will begin on Oct 30, he added.
Restoration
In 2024, another rockfall was reported in Cappadocia, although no injuries were recorded.
Turkey’s culture and tourism ministry has launched restoration work in the region to help preserve the fragile rock formations from climate-related damage, natural erosion and human activity.
A UNESCO heritage site since 1985, Goreme national park and the rock sites of Cappadocia are “a landscape of harmony combining human interaction and settlement with dramatic natural landforms,” according to the UN agency.
Some of the cones and pillars have experienced earthquake damage, but this is seen as a naturally occurring phenomenon.
“Overuse by tourists and some vandalism have been reported and some incompatible structures have been introduced,” it said on its website.
The Cappadocia region is also home to rock-carved underground cities and early Christian churches.
In 2025, some 4.5 million domestic and foreign tourists visited the region, according to tourism ministry figures.
Hot-air ballooning in Cappadocia is a thriving industry that sees dozens of balloons take to the skies on clear mornings. But concerns have been raised about safety following a series of fatal accidents.
In 2022, two Spaniards were killed and three others injured when their hot-air balloon crashed in high winds.
Winter Sleep, the acclaimed drama by Turkish director Nuri Bilge Ceylan that won Cannes’ Palme d’Or in 2014, was set in the Cappadocia region. AFP

Finland launches third Pohjanmaa-class corvette
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:14:38 UTC
23:14:38 KST

- Finland launched the third Pohjanmaa-class corvette at Rauma on Oct. 29, putting three of the four new warships in the water.
- All four corvettes are due to be completed by 2029 and will replace seven older Finnish Navy ships.
Finland launched the third of its four new Pohjanmaa-class corvettes at Rauma on Oct. 29, putting three of the Finnish Navy’s largest warships in decades in the water, the Finnish Navy said.
The ship was moved out of the construction hall at the Rauma Marine Constructions shipyard on Finland’s west coast, where fitting out will continue afloat. The Navy said all four corvettes are due to be completed by 2029 and will enter service in phases, and it has said it expects to take the ships into service between 2027 and 2029. The Navy did not say when the third ship will begin sea trials.
“The launch of the third vessel shows the progress of long-term and persistent work. This is an extensive undertaking that brings together the Navy’s future capability, domestic industrial expertise and close cooperation between different parties,” said Rear Adm. Tuomas Tiilikainen, commander of the Finnish Navy.
Construction has picked up pace across the four hulls. The first corvette, whose construction began in 2023, was launched in May 2025 and is now being fitted out. The second was launched on May 21 this year, less than a year after its keel was laid. Rauma Marine Constructions laid the keel of the third ship and started production of the fourth in January, putting all four under construction at the same time, and the fourth ship’s keel followed in July.
The corvettes are being built by RMC Defence, a subsidiary of Rauma Marine Constructions, for the Finnish Defence Forces Logistics Command under a program known as Squadron 2020. At 117 m (384 feet) long with a crew of about 70, the ships are the largest surface combatants the Finnish Navy has ordered since its coastal defense ships of the 1930s. Each is designed to stay at sea for 14 days and has a range of about 3,500 nautical miles.
The Pohjanmaa class combines several jobs that the Finnish Navy now spreads across older vessels. The four corvettes will replace seven ships: the four Rauma-class missile boats, the two Hämeenmaa-class minelayers and the minelayer Pohjanmaa, retired in 2015, whose name the new class carries. Each corvette carries anti-ship missiles, Evolved Sea Sparrow surface-to-air missiles in a vertical launcher, a 57 mm gun, torpedoes for anti-submarine warfare and rails for laying sea mines, an important task in the shallow, mine-friendly waters off Finland’s coast.
The ships also have ice-strengthened hulls so they can operate year-round in the northern Baltic, where the Gulf of Finland and the Gulf of Bothnia can freeze in winter, and they are fitted with composite ballistic armor to protect key areas. The Navy said the corvettes will give it new capability to defend Finnish waters and operate within NATO, which Finland joined in 2023.
The Navy plans to keep the Pohjanmaa class in service into the 2060s. The first ship is due to be handed over to the Navy in 2027, with all four in service by 2029.

A brewery with a 270-year history is closing in the Czech Republic due to falling demand for beer

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
16:13:50 EET

A brewery with a 270-year history is closing in the Czech Republic due to falling demand for beer
Kyiv • UNN
Velké Březno will cease production due to falling demand and rising costs. The Březňák brand will be moved to other Heineken breweries.
One of the Czech Republic’s oldest breweries, Velké Březno, will cease production after nearly 273 years of operation amid falling demand for beer and rising costs. At the same time, the Březňák brand will be preserved, while its production will be transferred to other Heineken group breweries. Bild reports, UNN writes.
Details
One of the Czech Republic’s oldest breweries, Velké Březno, located in the town of the same name in the north of the country, is ceasing production. Beer has been brewed at the company’s current site since 1753, while the history of brewing here dates back to 1606. As Robert Kičina, a representative of Heineken Czech Republic, told Ústecký deník, production was gradually reduced throughout 2026, and the remaining capacity will now be permanently shut down.
At the same time, the Březňák beer brand produced by the brewery will not disappear. Its production will be transferred to other Heineken group breweries, to which the Czech brewery has belonged since 2008. The logistics and sales divisions will remain at the former site. The reasons for the production shutdown include declining beer consumption in the Czech Republic, as well as rising energy and raw material prices.
Breweries in Germany are experiencing similar problems. In 2025, beer consumption in the country fell by almost 6%, and sales continued to decline in 2026. Amid falling demand and price competition, companies with decades-long histories are closing. For example, the Eichbaum brewery in Mannheim stopped production on September 30 after nearly 350 years of operation, while the 165-year-old Rupp brewery in Lower Saxony faced bankruptcy.

Israel elections: What the record tally by Arab parties means for Zionist politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:13:23 UTC
23:13:23 KST

Arab parties, which are mostly supported by the Palestinian citizens of Israel, received a resounding victory in the October 27 election, changing the balance of power in the Knesset.
With roughly 90 percent of ballots counted as of Thursday, the two main Arab-led parties – the Joint List and Ra’am – are on track for a combined count of 19 seats.
Their total is nearly double the previous count of 10 and well above the 2020 record of 15 seats.
According to the latest tally, Netanyahu’s right-wing and ultra-Orthodox bloc is expected to win 53 seats, while the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot is set to bag 48 seats.
Neither Zionist bloc is expected to reach the 61-seat threshold needed to form a government in the 120-member Knesset.
The projected 19 seats give the Arab-led parties significant leverage in coalition negotiations, but they do not guarantee a place in government.
It creates an opportunity for the two Arab parties to assert their democratic credentials in a country where Palestinian Israelis have long been treated as second-class citizens.
The community, which lives in separate towns, consists of the people whose ancestors stayed put during the Nakba, the mass expulsion of over 750,000 Palestinians following the creation of Israel in 1948.
The level of discrimination against Palestinian Israelis, who now make up roughly 20 percent of the country’s population, has risen dramatically since the October 7 attacks three years ago.
Towns dominated by the Palestinian Israeli community saw a significant shift in voting patterns. Their turnout hit 80 percent, the highest in decades.
They voted in large numbers because of deep frustration with the most right-wing government in Israel’s history and its far-right ministers, who have vowed to “Judaise” parts of Israel populated by Palestinian Israelis.
Experts say Arab parties made electoral gains despite Netanyahu’s campaign strategy, which centred on delegitimisation of Arab political participation in coalition-building.
Netanyahu’s Likud party has already claimed that the election was “stolen by Arab parties” that “support terror and the elimination of the Jewish state” through bribery, threats, violence, forgeries and the use of illegal software.
Main members from both Zionist blocs have said they wouldn’t include Palestinian Israelis in a coalition.
Ferit Belder, associate professor of international relations at Istanbul’s Marmara University, tells TRT World that opposition leaders largely deferred the question until after the vote to avoid the political costs of “normalising” Arab politics in the first election after October 7, 2023.
“Despite their electoral success, it is not guaranteed that the Arab parties will be able to translate this success into concrete gains and become part of the ‘legitimate circle of coalition-building’,” he says.
The Central Election Committee’s moves against Arab parties – left to the Supreme Court to resolve – further underscored the reluctance of Zionist parties to defend legitimate Arab participation, he adds.
Ozgur Dikmen, a scholar of Jewish politics, tells TRT World that Zionist politicians are more likely to frame the Palestinian Israeli gains as an element of insecurity and threat.
In a possible new cycle of elections, as seen between 2018 and 2022, such an “Arab threat” narrative would remain a useful tool for the right, he says.
A political force to reckon with
Numbers show the Zionist blocs’ dependence on Arab parties to reach a majority, raising the political costs of exclusion.
Gokhan Cinkara, director of Necmettin Erbakan University’s Global and Regional Studies Application and Research Centre, tells TRT World that the election results mark a significant turning point in Israeli politics.
He says the Arab parties have become a political force that can no longer be ignored.
“Anyone seeking to form a government will have to engage with the Arab parties in some way,” he says.
The two Arab parties approached the election with different strategies.
Ra’am, under Mansour Abbas, insisted on formal coalition membership to address the concerns of the Palestinian Israeli community.
Ra’am also joined the 2021 Bennett-Lapid government. Its integrationist approach and moves, such as placing former Yesh Atid lawmaker Yoav Segalovitz on the Knesset candidate list, already positioned the party as a potential coalition partner.
The Joint List, a union of communist Hadash, secularist Ta’al, and nationalist Balad groups, offered only external support for any anti-Netanyahu government in exchange for concrete improvements: stronger action against violence and crime, better housing, and the rollback of discriminatory policies of Netanyahu’s government.
Dikmen says that the chances of “formal inclusion” of Arab parties in the coalition remain limited.
It might be slightly more possible for the Eisenkot bloc to accept a coalition supported by the Arab parties, particularly with figures such as Abbas willing to serve as supporting partners, he says.
“I do not think it would be very realistic to expect seeing a Palestinian-Israeli minister,” Dikmen says.
Belder notes that the main task for the Arab parties is to convert their Knesset seats into material improvements in the daily lives of the Palestinian citizens of Israel.
Abbas of the Ra’am party has long argued that parliamentary presence without executive power confines the parties to the “world of slogans”, Belder says.
In the Knesset, a larger and more confident Palestinian Israeli caucus can at least be expected to reshape debates on equality and minority rights, even if fundamental arguments over the character of the state remain largely unchanged.
Dikmen points out that since December 2022, the Ministry of National Security under far-right Itamar Ben-Gvir has made serious reductions in the security budget of Palestinian Israeli-majority towns, contributing to skyrocketing crime rates – one of the drivers of the high turnout.
“I think such a reaction would reflect itself in the attitudes of Palestinian members in the Knesset,” he says.
Belder anticipates that far-right efforts to undermine judicial authority and policies that harm Palestinian Israelis’ daily lives – performative home demolitions and the humiliation of residents under Ben-Gvir – can be reversed or restricted.
Settler violence in the occupied West Bank might also come under closer government scrutiny, he adds.
Cinkara notes that the Arab parties will play an important role in advancing opposition priorities, including the election of the Knesset speaker and the allocation of committee seats.
“The key challenge for the Arab parties will also be to offer their voters practical policies,” he adds.

‘I fear for my family’: Berlin mayoral candidate’s leaked messages expose Hamas ties, spark uproar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:11:13 UTC
23:11:13 KST

Berlin has been engulfed in political turmoil since the Sept. 20 local elections. Although the radical left-wing Die Linke party won the election, all its attempts to form a left-wing coalition with the Greens and the Social Democrats have stalled amid revelations of antisemitism within the party and ties between many of its members and radical Islamist figures and leaders of Arab crime families in the city.
A new report published Thursday morning by the German newsmagazine Der Spiegel has exposed another dimension of the relationship between Germany's radical left and extremist Islam. According to the report, Elif Eralp, Die Linke's leading candidate for Berlin governing mayor, openly acknowledged that she and her family live in fear of Hamas supporters within her party. 
The controversy began with a mistake rooted in an outdated and questionable practice in German journalism, under which interviewees insist on reviewing and revising their quotations before publication.
Eralp, who had been interviewed by Der Spiegel, also asked to review her quotes before they appeared in print. After receiving them, she returned a revised version to the magazine.
But Eralp and her aides failed to notice that the document they sent back to Der Spiegel still contained their internal correspondence discussing the changes they wanted to make. On Thursday morning, that correspondence became the magazine's lead story and a major issue on Germany's political agenda.
In the exchanges, Eralp acknowledged that she and her family were personally afraid of becoming entangled with Hamas supporters associated with the party. She even tried to remove a reference to one of them, citing police advice not to publicly identify specific crime families in Berlin.
"My husband and I don't want to name specific people. We're both afraid of these people," she wrote.
Eralp's spokeswoman explained in the correspondence that they could not delete part of the interviewer's question, only portions of Eralp's answers.
Eralp responded in what could be interpreted as considerable alarm:
"But what am I supposed to do now? It was a mistake to agree to this interview in the first place. Until now, we were talking about people involved in organized crime. Now we're talking about people with connections to Hamas. I can't put myself and my family at risk for Der Spiegel. What do we do now? Cancel the entire interview?"
The Berlin Die Linke leader continued:
"Until now, when incidents came up, including the one involving Ibrahim Ibrahim (a member of an umbrella organization associated with Hamas and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine who appeared at the party's election victory celebration in Neukölln), I condemned them in general terms. But now we're talking about condemning an individual by name."
Even the center-left joins the criticism: 'Supporters of terrorism and antisemitism are deeply entrenched in the party'
Der Spiegel's revelations triggered an uproar across Germany's political establishment.
"Berlin needs a mayor who can stand up to extremists and doesn't give the impression that they are dictating what she can say before she has even been elected," said Christopher Förster, a conservative member of Berlin's state parliament. "If she can't do that, she cannot be elected to the position."
Another member of the Berlin parliament, Burkard Dregger, said: "Anyone who gets involved with Hamas criminals and their supporters in Berlin should not be surprised when they now demand payment for their support during the campaign."
Kristin Brinker, leader of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) parliamentary group in Berlin, also criticized Eralp.
"If even the most senior politician no longer feels safe, how are ordinary Berliners supposed to feel? Especially considering that they don't have personal security guards to protect them," she said.
Stefan Evers, the conservative candidate for governing mayor, added in a statement to the German newspaper Bild:
"Thursday's revelations deepen the serious concerns about a left-wing government in Berlin. How is Elif Eralp supposed to protect the safety of millions of residents as mayor if she herself is afraid of the Islamist connections within her own party? The warning signs can no longer be ignored, and it is not too late to act."
Michael Müller, a former governing mayor of Berlin, said Eralp's remarks "mean that Berlin's mayor would be vulnerable to blackmail. We need to acknowledge that clearly."
Criticism also came from the left side of the political spectrum.
Martin Hikel, the center-left Social Democratic district mayor of Berlin's Neukölln borough, said: "When someone allows themselves to be constrained in this way, it only shows how deeply these forces, which glorify terrorism and antisemitism, are entrenched in the Left Party."
At midday Thursday, during the inaugural session of the city legislature, Eralp responded to the revelations and sought to contain the damage.
"I won't let anyone intimidate me. I've made that clear. It's only natural to worry about your family," she said.
Daughter of Turkish immigrants draws support from pro-Gaza voters
Eralp, 45, is the daughter of Turkish immigrants who fled their country because of political persecution. She studied law and has worked extensively on immigration, discrimination, racism, asylum seekers and equal rights, including during her time at the United Nations.
Her success story as a member of a minority group and the progressive policies she advocates led some to dub her "Berlin's Mamdani" even before the September elections, when she emerged as Die Linke's candidate for governing mayor.
One of her campaign slogans played directly on that comparison: "From New York to Berlin, the left is back."
However, as in Mamdani's case in the United States, antisemitic and anti-Israel sentiment within Die Linke has intensified considerably under Eralp, particularly among the party's younger members.
Eralp has tried unsuccessfully to contain the major controversies sparked by the behavior of some party members. But in Berlin in 2026, displays of antisemitism do not appear to be driving voters away.
Eralp has to tread carefully on issues involving the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and the war in Gaza. Her party has taken a clear position on the issue, formally adopting in June the claim that Israel is committing genocide.
At the same time, Eralp has spoken out against extremist incidents, including a party gathering in Neukölln that ended with participants chanting "Death to the IDF." She has also pushed for an internal investigative committee to prevent the party from being tainted by antisemitism.
On the other hand, Eralp cannot afford to abandon the party's unequivocal support for Gaza, given the importance of Muslim voters and young supporters who helped propel Die Linke upward in the polls, largely because of its anti-Israel policies.
This summer, Eralp found herself posing for campaign photographs with activists who declared that "the Palestinian liberation movement will not end until Tel Aviv is in Palestinian hands."
Earlier this month, additional details emerged about Eralp, revealing that until just a year ago, she had been a member of Rote Hilfe (Red Aid), an organization whose motto is "The ends justify the means."
The organization provides legal and financial support to people convicted of crimes, provided their actions were motivated by left-wing ideology.
Many Germans had already raised concerns about the party's ties to Arab criminal clans and its desire to reduce police funding and presence.
Now, many voters are questioning whether Eralp's past involvement with an organization that supports violence or turning a blind eye to the law in pursuit of its goals could prevent her from becoming Berlin's democratic, law-abiding leader.

Polish army will soon receive first delivery of EU-funded vests and helmets
Poland's defence company Maskpol will deliver the first batch of bullet-proof vests and helmets ordered under the EU's defence funding programme SAFE, a deputy defence minister has said.
On Wednesday, at the Maskpol Protective Equipment Company's plant in Konieczki in southern Poland, which is part of the Polish Armaments Group, Cezary Tomczyk took part in a presentation of the first batch of equipment manufactured for the Polish Army under contracts funded by the SAFE instrument. Over the coming days, tens of thousands of new helmets and vests are due to be delivered to Polish military units, including those stationed in the east of the country.
“This is the first time that equipment from the SAFE mechanism has been supplied directly to Polish Army soldiers by Maskpol,” said Tomczyk during a press conference at the factory. In his view, this is a “turning point” in the process of army modernisation.
Tomczyk announced that by the end of 2026, 17,000 KKZ-01 type vests and 20,000 HBT-02 type helmets will be delivered. He added that the total value of the contract for the supply of individual equipment for soldiers from Maskpol under the SAFE programme is PLN 1.5 billion (EUR 340 mln).
Referring to the individual soldier equipment modernisation programme Szpej, conducted since 2024, Tomczyk said an audit carried out that year showed that only about one third of Polish soldiers had equipment that was up to the highest NATO standard.
He said that the number of composite helmets in the armed forces is set to rise from 84,000 at the start of 2024 to 350,000 by the end of 2026; while the number of bulletproof vests will increase from 60,000 to 180,000.
Under the SAFE programme, the MASKPOL company will deliver to the Polish Armed Forces 300,000 HBT-02 helmets and 50,000 KKZ-01 bullet-proof vests. (PAP)

"When human lives are at stake, saving people and achieving tangible results must come first, rather than political assessments. The temporarily occupied territories are part of Ukraine. A humanitarian mission must not become hostage to information manipulation," the statement said.
"The situation around Oleshky is unprecedented. We are doing something that has not previously been achieved in this format: seeking a way to save people who need help. We thank US First Lady Melania Trump for her assistance, coordination and concern for the fate of these people.
We therefore urge people not to create a sense of 'betrayal' where unity is needed. It is now very important to support the Ukrainian delegation and keep our fingers crossed for a successful outcome," Lubinets's office also stressed.

‘Genocide’ and ‘apartheid’: Harvard's hometown backs divestment from IDF suppliers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:07:48 UTC
23:07:48 KST

The city home to Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) moved Wednesday to promote divestment from companies supplying weapons and technology to the Israel Defense Forces.
The City Council of Cambridge, a university city of approximately 123,000 residents near Boston, narrowly approved a resolution calling on municipal employee pension funds to stop investing in companies involved in what the measure described as the "genocide, apartheid and occupation of Palestinians."
Among the companies identified were Israeli defense contractor Elbit Systems, U.S. technology company Palantir and aerospace giants Boeing, Lockheed Martin and GE Aerospace.
The vote followed a heated debate, after council members spent six hours at an earlier meeting hearing testimony from residents. When the vote was postponed at that meeting, audience members shouted, "You are all complicit in genocide" and "From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free."
The approved resolution calls on the city to develop its own list of companies that municipal pension funds could use when considering divestment. A separate proposal to extend the boycott to companies involved with the IDF through municipal procurement contracts, rather than investments alone, was also narrowly defeated.
A compromise over the BDS movement
The original proposal was introduced by City Council member Ayah Al-Zubi, a Harvard graduate. "This is the worst atrocity of our lifetimes, and we are invested in it," she said during the discussions. "I don't want blood on my hands, and none of us should."
Al-Zubi argued that while the United States imposes sanctions on countries such as China, Iran, Russia and Syria, it gives Israel a "blank check." Asked why she was singling out Israel, she replied, "I'm not making Israel look bad. I'm telling the truth."
Al-Zubi initially sought to adopt a list of approximately 100 companies compiled by the American Friends Service Committee (AFSC), a Quaker organization, which had gained support among activists affiliated with the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement against Israel.
Deputy Mayor Burhan Azeem, however, proposed a compromise: Cambridge would develop an independent list without formally adopting the BDS movement's platform. That version ultimately secured council approval.
According to Cambridge for Palestine, the activist group behind the initiative, the city's employee pension and benefits funds held approximately $24 million in investments in companies included on the original boycott list during fiscal year 2025. The group also claimed that Cambridge had spent about $4 million on contracts with companies supplying technology to the IDF and Israel Police.
The activists' list included three Israeli financial institutions, Bank Hapoalim, Bank Leumi and Israel Discount Bank, in which they estimated the municipal funds held approximately $660,000. The activists accused the banks of financing Israeli settlements.
One of the first companies on the list was Elbit Systems, which previously maintained offices in the area before leaving in 2024 following repeated pro-Palestinian demonstrations.
During one protest in 2023, nine demonstrators were arrested following clashes with police, even though the offices housed an Elbit subsidiary specializing in medical equipment development. Boycott activists portrayed the company's departure as a victory, while Elbit said the relocation was driven by business considerations.
The list also includes Palantir, the American software company that develops data analytics and artificial intelligence systems and works with security agencies, alongside major U.S. weapons manufacturers.
Broader boycott rejected over concerns for city services
The proposal to prohibit municipal procurement contracts with the targeted companies failed after Azeem, despite supporting investment divestment, voted against the broader measure.
He explained that such a restriction could undermine essential services and the city's ability to purchase equipment. During the debate, council members raised concerns that the proposed boycott could make it difficult for Cambridge to buy body cameras for its police officers.
Following the vote, pro-Palestinian activists shouted "Shame" at council members, while some left the chamber in anger.
The debate also divided the local Jewish community. Opponents warned that the resolution could fuel antisemitism and unfairly single out Israel. Jewish residents described fears about displaying their religious identity in public and incidents of harassment involving Jewish children at local schools.
Council members Denise Simmons and Patty Nolan also cited an incident in which an Israeli-owned business was vandalized with antisemitic graffiti while neighboring businesses were left untouched.
Simmons proposed applying a similar policy to companies implicated in war crimes around the world, rather than focusing on a single country.
Nolan warned that the measure was dividing the city and could attract unwanted attention from the Trump administration, which has already clashed with Harvard over allegations of discrimination and antisemitism.
Mayor Sumbul Siddiqui, however, defended the initiative, saying it was about "corporate accountability and how Cambridge invests public funds," rather than religion or identity.
Jeremy Burton, executive director of the Jewish Community Relations Council of Greater Boston, criticized the resolution's use of the term "genocide." He nevertheless welcomed the council's decision to reject the broader commercial boycott and avoid formally adopting the BDS platform.
Pro-Palestinian activists celebrated the passage of the divestment resolution but expressed disappointment over the failure of the separate procurement proposal.
Harvard and MIT not covered by the decision
The controversy also reached Harvard's student newspaper, The Harvard Crimson, where an editorial supported divestment. Three members of the editorial board dissented, arguing that the City Council should focus on residents' needs rather than risk pension funds to make a political statement.
Despite the debate's proximity to two of the world's most prominent universities, neither Harvard nor MIT is a party to the decision. Both are independent institutions, and the Cambridge resolution does not apply to their investments or their relationships with Israel.
Cambridge is not the first municipality in the Boston area to consider such a move. In neighboring Somerville, residents supported a nonbinding referendum calling for divestment from companies linked to Israel.
But the Cambridge resolution carries additional symbolic significance because of the city's global reputation as a center of academia, innovation and the technology industry.

Deadly train disaster deepens political crisis in Spain
A deadly high-speed train collision in Spain has deepened a political crisis engulfing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s government ahead of next month’s general election, as opposition parties demand accountability. The disaster, which killed at least 69 people, has sparked angry protests and calls for resignations.
The collision occurred near Urda in Toledo province when a high-speed train operated by Spain’s state railway company Renfe struck a stationary train. Audio recordings obtained by El Pais suggest controllers breached safety protocols despite repeated warnings from the stationary train’s driver. It was Spain’s second major railway disaster this year, following a collision near Adamuz in January that killed 46 people.
The tragedy has become a major issue in Spain’s election campaign, with the right-wing Vox party blaming Sanchez and the left-wing Frente Amplio coalition demanding political accountability.
“Beyond technical responsibilities, we demand the assumption of political responsibilities. Out of responsibility and humanity,” Frente Amplio said in a statement on Wednesday.
The coalition, which includes parties allied with Sanchez’s government, called for an independent audit of the railway network, describing two deadly high-speed train accidents in one year as “unacceptable.”
The leader of the main opposition People’s Party, Alberto Nunez Feijoo, also demanded an immediate investigation into the state of Spain’s railways, but stopped short of calling for resignations.
“Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure, what condition the tracks and safety systems are in,” Feijoo said.
Public anger spilled onto the streets of Madrid on Wednesday, where protesters clashed with police outside the Transport Ministry while demanding the resignations of Sanchez and Transport Minister Oscar Puente. Some demonstrators hurled flares and other objects at officers, who responded with tear gas.
Vox and its affiliated trade union Solidaridad staged a separate rally in central Madrid, where protesters carried a banner reading “Corruption kills.”
Sanchez has promised a thorough investigation, calling two such disasters in one year unacceptable. He has also pledged to strengthen railway safety while standing by Puente, according to El Pais.
The tragedy has added to the Socialist-led government’s troubles following parliamentary defeats and mass protests over soaring housing costs. Sanchez called early elections after parliament rejected key housing measures in September, with the vote scheduled for November 29.

Why some men don’t flex when their manhood is challenged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:00:50 UTC
23:00:50 KST

Men who blend emotional openness and progressive gender attitudes into their sense of manhood appear to be less reactive when their masculinity is called into question, according to new research published in Social Psychology Quarterly. While men often respond to gender-related insecurities by exaggerating tough, dominant attitudes, men in this experiment who more strongly endorsed a flexible masculine identity showed less of that overcompensation. The findings suggest that how men react to challenges to their gender status depends in part on how they define manhood for themselves.
In sociology and psychology, the dominant cultural ideal of manhood in a society is known as hegemonic masculinity. In the United States, this traditional standard expects men to be physically tough, emotionally guarded, self-reliant, heterosexual, dominant, and strictly avoidant of anything considered feminine. Because meeting all of these rigid standards at all times is nearly impossible, many men experience their gender status as fragile and easily challenged. When a man feels that his manhood has been doubted, he may engage in masculine overcompensation, which is the tendency to exaggerate aggressive, dominant, or traditionally macho behaviors in an effort to prove his status to himself and others.
Psychological research has repeatedly shown how easily this defensive reaction can be triggered. For example, a 2008 series of experiments demonstrated that people widely view manhood as an uncertain social status that must be earned and can be easily lost through a single unmanly act. Building on that idea, a 2013 experimental study found that men who were falsely told they scored in the feminine range on a survey about gender identity reacted by expressing greater support for war, more negative attitudes toward gay people, and stronger interest in purchasing sport utility vehicles.
When men face doubts about their manhood, the effects can be physical as well as attitudinal, and individual differences shape how strongly they react. In a study covered by PsyPost in 2017, men whose masculinity was challenged tried to display physical toughness by administering higher voltages of electric shock to their own arms, especially if they already saw themselves as highly masculine.
Most research on masculine overcompensation has assumed that all men measure themselves against a single, traditional standard of toughness and dominance. In recent years, however, sociologists have documented the rise of what they call hybrid masculinity, a gender style in which men selectively incorporate traits typically associated with women or marginalized groups into their identity.
A man practicing hybrid masculinity might openly discuss his emotions, follow a skincare routine, show physical affection to male friends, or voice support for feminism and LGBTQ+ rights. The authors of a 2014 sociological review argued that adopting these traits allows relatively privileged men to create symbolic distance between themselves and traditional macho norms while still retaining their broader social status.
If hybrid masculinity gives men a way to feel secure in their gender identity without relying on rigid toughness, it raises the question of whether these men still feel compelled to act dominant when their manhood is challenged. Justin Huft, a PhD candidate in sociology at the University of California, Riverside, designed an experiment to test whether endorsing hybrid masculinity shields men from the tendency to overcompensate. Huft also set out to create the first survey tool designed to measure hybrid masculinity in statistical research.
“While there has been interesting work done on masculine overcompensation, it has largely depicted masculinity as a monolithic identity,” Huft told PsyPost. “This is inconsistent with some other work in the masculinities literature, which depicts multiple forms of masculinity. My aim was to explore how masculine overcompensation looks when accounting for another form of masculine identity.”
To test this idea, Huft recruited 988 heterosexual adult men living in the United States through the online research platform Connect. The participants ranged in age from 18 to 83, with an average age of about 40 years, and reported an average household income between $50,000 and $59,999 per year. Roughly 65 percent of the men identified as white, 15 percent as Black, 10 percent as Asian, 8 percent as Latinx, and 2 percent as another racial background. Politically, about 46 percent described themselves as liberal, 31 percent as conservative, and 22 percent as moderate, while 54 percent reported having a religious affiliation.
Before receiving any feedback, participants rated their baseline level of traditional masculinity. They also completed Huft’s newly developed 20-item hybrid masculinity questionnaire on a 5-point scale. Statistical testing showed that the new scale captured two closely related aspects of hybrid masculinity: progressive gender attitudes, such as supporting women’s and LGBTQ+ rights or agreeing that men can wear makeup, and emotional expressiveness, such as telling others when feeling sad, showing empathy, and expressing affection toward male friends.
Participants also answered questions measuring three concepts from sociological identity theory: how important being masculine was to their overall sense of self (known as identity prominence), how frequently they thought about their masculinity in daily situations like work or social events (known as identity salience), and how much they felt close friends and family viewed their masculinity the same way they did (known as identity verification).
For the experimental manipulation, participants completed items that appeared to evaluate their masculinity and were then given false feedback on a 0 to 100 scale, where 0 represented feminine and 100 represented masculine. Men were randomly assigned to either a non-threatening group, where they were told that their answers placed them at the high end of the average male range, or a threatening group, where they were told that they scored at the high end of the average female range.
Following the feedback, participants completed a 21-item questionnaire measuring their agreement with traditional, dominant masculine norms on a scale from 1 to 7. This questionnaire assessed seven hallmarks of rigid manhood: emotional restriction, self-reliance, negative views of gay people, avoidance of femininity, placing a high priority on sex, desiring dominance as a leader, and valuing physical toughness.
Prior to receiving the false feedback, the two groups did not differ in their baseline traditional masculinity, measured with a separate questionnaire on which the sample averaged 5.08 out of 7. After the feedback was delivered, however, men who were told they scored in the average female range endorsed higher levels of rigid masculine norms, averaging 3.19 out of 7 compared to 2.97 out of 7 among men who were told they scored in the male range. That difference is small, about one-sixth of the typical spread in scores, but it indicates that the experimental threat triggered masculine overcompensation across the sample as a whole.
Huft then ran statistical regression models that controlled for baseline masculinity, identity importance, everyday awareness of masculinity, identity verification, religiosity, political conservatism, race, and household income. Even after accounting for all of those factors, receiving the masculinity-threatening feedback predicted a 0.17-point increase in dominant masculine norms in the baseline model, while scoring higher on hybrid masculinity was strongly linked to lower endorsement of those rigid norms overall.
When Huft tested how the two factors interacted, he found that hybrid masculinity moderated the impact of the threat, reducing the overcompensation effect by 0.23 points for each 1-point increase on the hybrid masculinity scale. In practical terms, men with low hybrid masculinity scores showed a larger increase in rigid, dominant attitudes after their manhood was questioned, whereas the gap between the threatened and non-threatened groups shrank toward zero among men who strongly endorsed hybrid masculinity.
Several background characteristics also predicted higher endorsement of rigid masculine norms regardless of which feedback participants received. Men who thought about their masculinity frequently in daily life, held more conservative political views, had lower household incomes, or identified as non-white tended to endorse traditional masculine norms more strongly.
The overall presence of a defensive reaction aligns with research covered by PsyPost in 2023, which found that threats to manhood heightened support for aggressive political and foreign-policy strategies, though that earlier work focused on political aggression rather than personal masculine norms and observed the effect among liberal men rather than conservative men. In Huft’s study, by contrast, men who scored high on hybrid masculinity tended to be more politically liberal and reacted less to the threat.
The new findings also stand in tension with a study covered by PsyPost earlier this year, which did not find an increase in conservative political views, support for war, or homophobia after a masculinity threat, though that study examined broader political and social attitudes rather than the comprehensive inventory of personal masculine norms used by Huft.
Huft offers two possible explanations for the buffering pattern found in his study. Men who embrace emotional openness and progressive views may have already loosened the tie between their sense of self-worth and traditional macho ideals, making feedback about feminine traits less upsetting, or they may draw on other aspects of their identity, such as emotional maturity or humor, to feel secure without needing to act tough.
While this flexibility appears to reduce aggressive overcompensation at the individual level, Huft cautions that hybrid masculinity does not automatically dismantle gender inequality in society. Instead, sociological theory suggests that blending softer traits into manhood can allow men to present themselves as modern and progressive while quietly preserving the social privileges associated with being a man.
“Masculinity isn’t just one thing,” Huft explained. “It contains different attitudes, behaviors, and characteristics. These different constellations of masculinity cause people to perceive and experience masculinity threats differently. This, in turn, creates different sorts of responses to masculinity threats.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. Because men who scored high on the new hybrid masculinity scale also tended to report that being masculine was less central to their overall identity, the questionnaire cannot completely untangle whether these men were strategically blending gender traits to maintain their status or whether they simply cared less about manhood altogether. In addition, the experiment could not capture why men adopted hybrid traits in the first place, such as whether they adopted those traits preemptively, in response to past challenges to their manhood, or for unrelated reasons.
Hybrid masculinity was also measured rather than assigned, so men who scored high on it differed from low scorers in other ways. Most notably, they tended to be much more politically liberal, and the study did not test whether political views shaped how men responded to the threat. The new scale has so far been tested in only this one sample, and the study did not report whether participants believed the false feedback.
The study also focused exclusively on heterosexual, cisgender men in the United States, meaning the findings cannot be generalized to gay, bisexual, or transgender men. According to hybrid masculinity theorists, the ability to adopt feminine or non-traditional traits without facing harsh social penalties is often easiest for white, middle-class, heterosexual men, so future studies will need to test whether hybrid masculinity works the same way across different racial and socioeconomic groups.
It is also possible that for men who pride themselves on being progressive and emotionally sensitive, being told they scored as highly masculine could actually feel like a threat to their progressive self-image, prompting them to distance themselves even further from traditional manhood. Finally, future research could explore whether men whose manhood is challenged try to restore their pride in areas outside of gender altogether, such as by emphasizing their career achievements or financial status.
The study, “Hybrid Masculinity as a Buffer against Threats to Masculinity,” was authored by Justin Huft.

Mistral Says Its AI Model ‘Le Chonk’ Has Leapfrogged China in the Open-Weight Race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

A few weeks ago, French company Mistral released an early version of its new artificial intelligence model, nicknamed Le Chonk. At the time, the company said it was the most advanced open-weight offering outside of China. After further refinement, Mistral now says Le Chonk is the “world’s best” open-weight model for automated coding and cybersecurity.
The advances, Mistral says, were made possible by feeding the model increasingly difficult cybersecurity and coding problems, which allowed the trillion-parameter Le Chonk to match or surpass models from leading Chinese labs like DeepSeek and Z.ai.
“It’s a pivotal moment in the global AI leadership race,” Pierre Stock, VP of science at Mistral, told reporters during a press briefing. “It offers frontier capabilities for enterprises and governments to defend against an increasing threat level in cyber.”
The finalized version of Le Chonk is now freely available for anybody to access. After a flurry of AI-related cybersecurity incidents, Mistral claims that it’s important for the West to have its own advanced open-weight models. “You have no guarantee that [Chinese models] won’t behave maliciously. They can be threat vectors,” Stock said.
The most high-profile episode occurred when one of OpenAI’s models broke loose from a testing sandbox and hacked into multiple companies over the summer. It sparked panic over the idea that AI could escape human oversight and be abused by threat actors to launch sophisticated cyberattacks. (One of the affected companies, Hugging Face, used an open-weight model from China to assess and defend against the attack.)
Since then, AI has unearthed security vulnerabilities in ubiquitous software, too. In October, a raft of websites were taken offline after an AI tool discovered serious flaws in a foundational piece of web technology.
Mistral pitches its open-weight models, like Le Chonk, as part of the solution. If AI is destined to become a central feature of both cyber offense and defense, the argument goes, businesses and governments will need to be equipped with models that are freely available and cannot be switched off remotely, unlike proprietary models from the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.
“AI is going to be like electricity. You don’t want to live in a world in which your neighbor can cut off electricity from one day to another,” Stock said. “Once you open source the weights, they’re all over the internet. It’s impossible to cut off access.”
The trade-off, however, is that freely available models can also be downloaded and customized by threat actors.
“It’s clearly a dual-use technology,” Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “Anything that’s available to download and circulate unfettered has the ability to be abused as well as used for productive purposes.”
According to Pilling, though it’s possible a Chinese model with internet access could siphon away data, all advanced models are capable of going rogue without careful supervision—no matter their country of origin.
“The technical realities and the narrative—which often has a nationalistic leaning—are two different things,” he says.“It’s about having the right monitoring and controls in place to be confident that, even if the model was trying to be deceptive or nefarious, you might have some way of detecting it.”

Russia’s Military Losses Hit All-Time Monthly High as Ukraine Reports Over 49,000 in October
Russian military personnel losses in October 2026 have reached 49,040 as of October 29, marking the highest monthly figure since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The General Staff reported that the previous monthly record was registered in December 2024, when Russian forces suffered 48,670 personnel losses.
With October still underway, Russia’s average daily personnel losses have reached approximately 1,750, according to Ukrainian military estimates.
The figures also indicate a substantial increase in Russian losses over recent months. In February 2026, Russian forces sustained an estimated 26,090 personnel losses, compared with 46,230 in September and 49,040 as of October 29.
“Why this matters: The rate of Russian personnel losses exceeds the military’s ability to replenish its units. Each month of the war is becoming increasingly costly for Russia’s armed forces,” the General Staff added.
Ukrainian drone strikes have killed or wounded more than 302,000 Russian military personnel since the beginning of 2026, averaging over 1,000 casualties per day in less than ten months, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense reported on October 27.
March recorded the highest number of Russian personnel casualties from Ukrainian drone strikes, with 33,989 soldiers killed or wounded. April followed with 33,961 casualties, while February saw the lowest monthly total at 26,204.
Throughout the year, Ukrainian drone units have consistently inflicted tens of thousands of casualties on Russian forces each month. Monthly totals exceeded 30,000 in January, March, April, May, July, and September.
In September alone, drone strikes killed or wounded 32,739 Russian troops. During the first 25 days of October, Ukrainian forces recorded an additional 27,829 Russian personnel casualties from drone operations.
Overall, as of October 29, 2026, Russia’s estimated personnel losses since the beginning of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine had reached approximately 1,584,910, according to Ukraine’s General Staff.

Russia has around 140 Su-34 aircraft of various modifications — DIU
Kyiv • UNN
Russia has around 140 Su-34s and continues to produce them. Since the beginning of the invasion, 43 aircraft have been destroyed and seven more damaged.
The Russian Aerospace Forces have approximately 140 Su-34 fighter-bombers of various modifications in service, which are the main carriers of glide bombs and precision-guided missiles used by the enemy to attack Ukraine’s frontline regions. This was reported by the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defence, reports UNN.
Details
Su-34 fighter-bombers are one of the key components of the aggressor state Russia’s strike aviation in the war against Ukraine. Their use as carriers of guided aerial bombs has enabled the occupation army to expand its ability to strike ground targets, particularly in areas of active hostilities and frontline settlements
The intelligence agency notes that, despite significant combat losses, Russia continues to produce and modernize Su-34s, attempting to maintain the size of its aircraft fleet and preserve the intensity of its missile and bomb strikes.
At the same time, the ability to further expand this capability depends on production capacity, the availability of technological components, and the ability of Russia’s defence industry to compensate for losses.
As of October 22, 2026, approximately 140 Su-34 fighter-bombers of various modifications, including modernized Su-34Ms (Su-34NVOs), are in service with the Russian Aerospace Forces
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, Russia has lost 43 aircraft of this type destroyed, while another seven have been damaged.
Such losses are quite substantial for the aggressor’s aircraft fleet, whose restoration requires a lengthy production cycle, significant financial resources, and specialized industrial cooperation. For comparison, the number of destroyed Su-34s is equivalent to approximately 2.5–3 years of their production at estimated capacities of 14–18 aircraft annually
During Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine, the role of the Su-34 in the aggressor’s strike aviation has undergone a significant transformation. At the initial stage of the invasion, these aircraft were primarily used to bomb ground targets with unguided aerial bombs, including FAB-250, FAB-500 M-62, and BetAB-500 concrete-piercing bombs.
The use of such weapons required approaching the targets, which increased the aircraft’s vulnerability to Ukrainian air defence systems.
At the same time, Su-34s began to be used as carriers of Kh-31 and Kh-59 guided air-launched missiles, as well as, in some cases, Kh-35U anti-ship missiles to strike ground targets.
We remind you
The Ukrainian Navy destroyed four Russian Su-34 bombers, while two more were damaged on the territory of Borysoglebsk airfield. This aircraft is a deeply modernized version of the basic frontline Su-34 bomber, which Russia began serial production of in 2020. Thanks to its new hardpoints, the aircraft is the main carrier of glide bombs and precision-guided missiles used by the enemy to attack Ukraine’s frontline regions.

Kazakhstan Tears Down Lenin Monument as De-Sovietization Efforts Expand Across Central Asia
Authorities in Kazakhstan have removed a monument to Vladimir Lenin from the village of Kushmurun in Kostanay region as part of wider efforts to reduce Soviet-era influence across Central Asia, Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service reported on October 29.
The monument was dismantled at the request of the regional administration after local residents collected nearly 400 signatures supporting its removal. Previous attempts to remove it in 2015 and 2022 had failed after opposition from supporters of the Soviet legacy.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The initiative group supporting the demolition linked Soviet rule directly to mass famine and political repression in Kazakhstan. Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service noted that estimates of deaths during the Asharshylyk famine of the early 1930s reach as high as 2.3 million people, nearly half of Kazakhstan’s population at the time.
Some researchers have described the catastrophe as the “Kazakh Holodomor,” drawing parallels with the Holodomor in Ukraine.
Ukraine’s intelligence service stated that the removal of the Lenin monument and growing public discussion of Soviet-era repression have unsettled Russian political strategists because they challenge Moscow’s narrative of a prosperous shared Soviet past.
Russia presents itself internationally as the legal successor to the Soviet Union. The intelligence service argued that renewed attention to the individual histories of former Soviet republics, including famine, repression, and forced political control, undermines the mythology surrounding the Soviet period.
Similar de-Sovietization processes have intensified elsewhere in Central Asia, although their form differs between countries.
In Kyrgyzstan, calls for broader decommunization and derussification have grown during 2026. Uzbekistan has been described as a regional leader in this process, while Tajikistan has emphasized national identity and historical memory.
Turkmenistan has pursued its own model centered on national sovereignty within an isolationist and neutral foreign policy.
Despite those differences, Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service assessed that de-Sovietization, decommunization, and derussification efforts across Central Asia share a common objective of reducing dependence on and influence from Russia.
The trend contrasts with Russian efforts to revive Soviet symbolism in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories. UNITED24 Media previously reported that Russian authorities in temporarily occupied eastern Ukrainian city of Luhansk promoted Stalin and Lenin imagery during a February 14 propaganda event, replacing traditional Valentine’s Day themes with Soviet symbols.

Most Americans Believe Putin Is Stalling Ukraine Peace Talks, Back More Weapons and Sanctions, Poll Finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:57:12 UTC
22:57:12 KST

- Category
- World
Most Americans Believe Putin Is Stalling Ukraine Peace Talks, Back More Weapons and Sanctions, Poll Finds
A majority of American voters believe Russian leader Vladimir Putin is deliberately delaying efforts to end the war in Ukraine, while nearly two-thirds support continued military assistance to Kyiv and stronger sanctions against Moscow if Russia refuses to negotiate and prolongs the war, according to the October Harvard CAPS/Harris Poll, conducted by HarrisX.
The survey, which polled 2,700 registered US voters between October 24 and 26, 2026, is part of one of the most consistent polling series tracking American public opinion on Russia’s war against Ukraine. Its regular measurements provide insight into how attitudes toward the war and potential peace negotiations evolve over time.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The latest findings show that 68% of respondents believe Putin is stalling negotiations with the United States and Western countries rather than genuinely seeking peace, up from 61% in September. Only 32% believe the Russian leader sincerely wants to end the war.
Skepticism toward Putin extends across political affiliations, with 74% of Democrats and independent or other-party voters saying he is delaying negotiations, compared with 58% of Republicans.
By contrast, 61% of Americans believe Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy genuinely wants to end the war, while 39% think he is stalling negotiations, a slight increase from 37% in September.
Support for Zelenskyy’s stated intentions is particularly strong among Democrats, with 69% believing he is genuinely seeking peace. The same view is shared by 61% of independent or other-party voters and 52% of Republicans.
Beyond perceptions of the two leaders, the poll also indicates substantial bipartisan support for maintaining pressure on Moscow if it refuses to engage in peace negotiations.
According to the findings, 64% of Americans support continuing weapons assistance to Ukraine and imposing additional sanctions on Russia if Moscow refuses to negotiate and prolongs the war.
Notably, support for these measures is nearly identical among Republicans and Democrats, with 67% of Republican voters and 66% of Democratic voters backing continued military assistance and additional economic pressure under those circumstances.
The findings highlight an area of bipartisan agreement on US policy toward Russia’s war against Ukraine despite broader political divisions in the United States.
The survey also found growing support for direct US security guarantees for Ukraine as part of a potential peace agreement involving Ukrainian territorial concessions. Some 64% of respondents supported such an arrangement, compared with 58% in September.
However, American attitudes toward economic measures targeting Russia become more complex when domestic energy costs are taken into account.
According to the poll, 61% of Americans oppose the United States purchasing Russian oil and diesel fuel while Moscow continues its war against Ukraine, while 39% support such purchases. Opposition is particularly strong among Democrats, with 73% against buying Russian oil and diesel, compared with 64% of independent or other-party voters.
Republicans were more divided, with 54% supporting purchases of Russian oil and diesel fuel and 46% opposing them.
At the same time, 63% of respondents said they prioritize lower fuel prices over restricting Russia’s ability to finance the war, revealing a contrast between opposition to Russian energy purchases and concerns about domestic energy costs.
The findings come as diplomatic efforts to arrange further negotiations between Ukraine, Russia, and the United States continue.
A proposed trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi remains dependent on confirmation from Washington, although both Kyiv and Moscow have expressed their readiness to participate, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists on October 28.
Zelenskyy explained that the timing of the talks, expected to take place in November, could be affected by Washington’s ongoing diplomatic engagement in the Middle East.

Macron accuses French far right of fomenting spread of racism
PARIS, Oct 29 - President Emmanuel Macron has accused far-right politicians including in Marine Le Pen's National Rally of fostering an "atmosphere of racism" across France, days after a racially motivated killing in a Paris suburb.
The attack last Friday, which left one dead and seven wounded, has unleashed a bitter debate over racism in French politics and the media as the country grapples with a broad set of social grievances, months ahead of a presidential election.
"There are political movements which have led to ... a kind of disinhibition of speech, an ambient racism," Macron told YouTube influencer Hugo Decrypte in a lengthy interview released late on Wednesday.
He cited the National Rally and "those close to it" as responsible — a statement quickly rejected by members of the anti-immigration party that is leading in polls.
RN lawmaker Jean-Philippe Tanguy told TF1: "It's Macron who has run France for the past nine years. It's on his watch that antisemitism, homophobia and hate has spread through France. He is to blame."
'WORDS CARRY WEIGHT'
French politicians on all sides have traded accusations of racism in the wake of the killing of 26-year-old Pengo Bossio Wangi in Trappes, a culturally diverse town 20 km (15 miles) southwest of Paris.
Anti-terrorist prosecutors said on Thursday the 39-year-old suspect, named Kevin T, acknowledged during questioning seeking victims of "African or Muslim type". His belongings included a copy of Hitler's book "Mein Kampf" and stickers mentioning the RN — though he said he did not support any particular party.
RN senator Edwige Diaz this week doubled down on comments by Jordan Bardella, now the party's leader, who in 2021 called Trappes a "mini-Islamic state". She said there was nothing wrong in that description.
"We can speak of a somewhat toxic climate in which certain people are constantly portrayed as suspicious or illegitimate," said Zineb Alami, lawyer for Bossio Wangi's father.
"Words carry weight," she said.
Numerous politicians on the right, including Bardella, and media commentators have blamed the rioting and looting that took place after street protests this month on immigration, without giving evidence. At a march in memory of Bossio Wangi on Sunday, people in attendance blamed the media coverage for inciting racial hatred.
Macron's minority centrist government also stands accused of not doing enough to tackle the spread of racist and far-right attitudes in society.
"The normalisation of the ideas of the far-right extends beyond the National Rally into the ranks of the government," sociologist Solene Brun told Reuters.
Aurore Berge, the minister for gender equality and anti-discrimination, was urged in parliament this week to take back her comment last month that it was legitimate to discuss the "Great Replacement", a far-right conspiracy theory that has been invoked by perpetrators of far-right attacks around the world in recent years.
In addition to the Trappes attack, far-right activists looking for confrontations with protesters were spotted across more than a dozen French cities last week, according to authorities. REUTERS

Meloni introduces personalised number plates, urges Italians to be 'creative'
ROME, Oct 29 - Italy's government will allow motorists to personalise the number plates of their vehicles, in a revenue-raising move that follows the example of the Unites States, Britain and other countries.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced the measure on Wednesday as she unveiled Italy's 2027 budget law, the last before a general election due next year, describing the number plate initiative as a "colourful note".
"One will be able to indulge oneself more or less as one sees fit, obviously at a cost. Something tells me that Italians' creativity could shine here," Meloni said.
Personalised plates will cost about €600 ($669) for cars and €360 for motor-bikes, according to a decree.
A Treasury official declined to estimate how much revenue the government expects the measure to generate.
Italian car number plates are currently made of a string of two letters, three numbers and two letters. The extent to which motorists will be allowed to stray from the standard formula is unclear.
The reform has triggered a wave of memes and jokes on social media, amid concerns that personalized license plates could open the flood-gates to insults and profanities.
One meme showed Meloni dressed up as Marie Antoniette, holding a platter of licence plates and saying, "Let them eat personalised plates" - a play on the famous phrase by the 18th century French queen "Let them eat cake".
Some welcomed the measure, including taxi drivers, who said distinctive personalised plates could make it easier to identify legitimate operators and combat illegal services.
Opposition parties on the centre-left were less enthusiastic, saying the licence-plate initiative was a distraction from more pressing issues that budget failed to address.
"Meloni should know that Italians have already chosen their personalised plate, and it reads: 'Meloni, go away'," said Francesco Silvestri, a lawmaker from the Five Star Movement. REUTERS

TRIPOLI, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- In a workshop humming with engines in Mayah, 40 km southwest of the Libyan capital Tripoli, 25-year-old Rawan Abu Aisha is building a career uncommon for Libyan women -- turning a childhood passion for cars into a business modifying engines.
Growing up, Abu Aisha often watched her father work as a mechanic. "The workshop environment was familiar to me from childhood because I grew up watching my father work with cars," Abu Aisha told Xinhua.
"Over time, that interest became something I wanted to turn into a profession," she explained, saying the opportunity came through an entrepreneurship competition in Libya that invited participants to present innovative business ideas.
Drawing on her family background, she proposed modifying car engines to meet owners' specific needs. The idea became real when a customer agreed to an engine replacement. The project subsequently grew into a company established in 2022, whose primary business is modifying engines using its own custom-built units.
"My father's support and practical experience helped me take my first steps in this field," she said. "His encouragement gave me the confidence to develop my skills and turn an idea into a real business."
Her studies in entrepreneurship also equipped her with knowledge of business management, marketing and accounting, helping the company move beyond its technical roots toward a more structured management approach. What began as a business relying largely on customer recommendations later expanded its reach through an online presence and social media platforms.
According to Abu Aisha, the company's social media page has attracted over 50,000 followers, and demand for its services has grown so rapidly that her current team can barely keep up.
"The growing number of followers and the rising demand for our services show that there is considerable interest in what we do," she said. "Our next step is to expand the business and improve our ability to meet customers' needs."
Abu Aisha also hopes to partner with companies abroad, stressing the importance of long-term planning and continuous development.
"Building a sustainable business requires more than providing a good technical service," she said. "It also requires organized management, continuous improvement and a clear vision for the future."
While she believes social acceptance of women in the workplace has grown in recent years, Abu Aisha's greatest lesson from entrepreneurship is that young women must take initiative and pursue their ambitions, rather than let stereotypes dictate their choices.
"Women should not allow stereotypes to decide what they can or cannot do," she said. "They should be willing to try, learn and discover their abilities through practical experience."
For young women considering careers in mechanics, engineering or other nontraditional fields, her journey shows how personal interests can be turned into professional opportunities through determination, learning and hands-on experience.
"I want to continue developing the business and provide services that customers can trust," she said. "I believe that competence and expertise, rather than gender, should determine whether someone can succeed in a particular profession." ■
