Across China: New study traces evolution of terrestrial animals on Qinghai-Xizang Plateau
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:53:45 CST
22:53:45 KST

CHENGDU, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- A new study has reconstructed the evolutionary history of terrestrial animals on the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau, offering a clearer picture of how the unique fauna of Earth's "Third Pole" took shape over millions of years.
The research, led by a team from the Chengdu Institute of Biology (CIB) under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, was recently published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS).
"Overall, the study deepens understanding of how mountain animal life evolves and provides a framework for studying how biodiversity forms in mountain regions worldwide," said Li Jiatang, a researcher at CIB.
Home to many species found nowhere else, the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau is one of the world's biodiversity hotspots, covering about 3.07 million square kilometers and ranging in elevation from 88 to 8,848 meters, according to the researchers.
The plateau platform, the Himalayas and the Hengduan Mountains are the plateau's three major subregions.
Scientists have long been interested in how the plateau's tectonic history and monsoon systems shaped the evolution of local biodiversity. However, earlier studies mostly looked at plants or single animal groups, leaving the overall development of the plateau's land animals poorly understood.
To fill this gap, the researchers combined time-calibrated evolutionary trees covering more than 20,000 species across invertebrates, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. They then reconstructed the evolutionary history of 527 endemic terrestrial animal species on the plateau.
The study found that most of the plateau's endemic land animals did not arrive from elsewhere and then become new species. Instead, many evolved locally, splitting into new species right where they were, something scientists call in situ diversification.
The plateau was also a major receiver of species. The study found that animals moved in nearly twice as often as they moved out. The Qinghai-Xizang Plateau therefore played two roles at once: it was a place where new species formed, and a biogeographic sink that took in more species than it sent out.
The three subregions played very different roles. The Hengduan Mountains were the main source of local species formation, producing many new species. The Himalayas were both a source and a sink, producing new species locally and receiving species from elsewhere. The plateau platform produced very few new species locally, with most of its animal life coming from immigration, making it an important sink and a major receiver of species.
The researchers also examined how geology and climate shaped this evolutionary history. They found that a major climate transition about 34 million years ago marked the onset of sustained species diversification and biological exchange. However, the timing of these processes varied across the three subregions, reflecting differences in their uplift histories and monsoon systems.
The study also found a consistent "plants first, animals later" pattern. By comparing animal evolution with plant studies, the researchers identified this pattern across the plateau and its subregions. Early-colonizing plant groups created suitable ecological niches, laying the foundation for later animal immigration and diversification. ■

A gala dinner where guests were served by people with disabilities who cooked the meal, handled table service, and enlivened the evening with live music. This event was hosted by Italy’s Ambassador to Japan, Mario Vattani, and the Minister for Disabilities, Alessandra Locatelli, at the ambassador’s residence in Tokyo, bringing together figures from the Italian and Japanese political, diplomatic, business, cultural, and artistic worlds. 
   This initiative, rather than merely discussing inclusion, offered a concrete demonstration of it, highlighting professional skills, creativity, and talent in an international setting. The message conveyed is clear: inclusion means creating opportunities so that everyone can participate, contribute, and demonstrate their abilities. The point of the initiative is that people with disabilities are not merely beneficiaries of inclusion policies, but active participants in professional, social, and cultural life. Organized to mark the 160th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Italy and Japan, the initiative strengthens the dialogue between the two countries on inclusion, employment, and social participation, involving institutions, businesses, the cultural sector, and people with disabilities.

   For Facchini, a chef and entrepreneur based in New York, in collaboration with the Ministry for People with Disabilities, “bringing these projects to the world means showing how cooking, hospitality, and the promotion of Italian products can create concrete opportunities, especially for workplace inclusion.” The best part is seeing the pride these young people feel while they work, the satisfaction of putting their skills to use, contributing, and feeling like they’re making a difference. Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:53:38 CST
22:53:38 KST

WINDHOEK, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Namibia has heightened disease surveillance and strengthened preparedness at points of entry following the spread of Ebola disease across several countries, although no suspected or confirmed cases have been reported in the country, the health ministry said.
In a public health update issued Wednesday evening, the Ministry of Health and Social Services said it was strengthening preparedness and improving healthcare workers' capacity to detect, report and respond to potential Ebola cases.
The measures follow the spread of an outbreak caused by Bundibugyo virus, with cases reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Kenya and Nigeria, raising concerns about cross-border transmission.
The absence of specific vaccines and treatments underscores the importance of early detection, effective surveillance and prompt medical care, the ministry noted.
It urged the public to practice good hand hygiene, avoid contact with suspected or confirmed cases and seek immediate medical attention if symptoms develop following possible exposure. People with relevant travel or contact histories were advised to inform healthcare personnel.
It also urged the public to remain calm and rely on official communications from the ministry, the World Health Organization and the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for accurate information.
The Bundibugyo virus outbreak was declared in the DRC on May 15, 2026, after cases were detected in Ituri and North Kivu provinces. As of Oct. 26, the DRC, Kenya and Nigeria had reported a combined 10,151 confirmed cases, including 4,930 deaths, according to data from the World Health Organization. ■

Antarctic sea ice loss disrupts ocean freshwater system: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
21:53:28 CST
22:53:28 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- The Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW) has rapidly become saltier and denser as Antarctic sea ice loss reduces freshwater input, potentially affecting deep-ocean warming and sea levels, according to new research.
The AAIW, a vast layer of fresh water spanning much of the Southern Hemisphere's ocean, helps store carbon, supply oxygen and drive global ocean currents. It plays a role in heat, freshwater and carbon redistribution around the planet, according to a statement released Wednesday by Australia's University of Melbourne.
The study, published in Nature Climate Change, found that Antarctic summer sea-ice melt helped maintain the AAIW from 1995 to 2015. From 2016, Antarctic sea ice declined to record lows. Between 2016 and 2024, reduced freshwater input led the water layer to become saltier, denser and deeper.
The team analyzed data from the global Argo program, a network of about 4,000 robotic floats that sample the upper oceans, along with satellite and atmospheric datasets.
Researchers said the last time the AAIW underwent a similar shift was at the end of the last interglacial period, around 130,000 years ago, when there was very little ice in Antarctica. However, that transition took thousands of years, rather than two decades.
The researchers said changes in the AAIW could affect the ocean's ability to store carbon and push more excess heat into deeper waters, meaning existing models may underestimate deep-ocean warming and miscalculate regional sea-level rise. ■

ZAGREB, Oct. 29 (Xinhua) -- Croatia has confirmed 25 cases of West Nile virus infection this year, including one death, the Croatian Institute of Public Health (HZJZ) said on Thursday.
Of those infected, 19 developed symptoms, including two having West Nile fever and 17 with the more severe neuroinvasive form of the disease.
Zagreb and the surrounding areas accounted for 15 cases, making the region the hardest hit. Most West Nile virus infections in Croatia are recorded between mid-July and the end of October. The HZJZ said the transmission season is expected to end as temperatures drop.
Since the beginning of this year, Croatia has reported more West Nile virus cases than last year, when it recorded six cases, but still less than the highest annual total of 63 confirmed cases, reported in 2018.
Speaking to local media, the HZJZ said that the European Union has experienced its most intense West Nile virus season to date, with the virus spreading to more northerly areas. ■

Will the new Flemish road tax be beneficial for you or are you better off sticking with the old scheme?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:50:35 UTC
22:50:35 KST

From today, everyone in Flanders can check for themselves whether the planned Flemish reform of road tax will work out more favourably or not. The Flemish Government is launching a website where you can work out the difference between the old and the new tax yourself. If the new scheme works out cheaper, you can indicate straight away that you wish to switch. Anyone who does not wish to switch need not do anything.
Will the new Flemish road tax be beneficial for you or are you better off sticking with the old scheme?
In 2027, the annual road tax (JVB) in Flanders will be reformed. For most vehicles, the Flemish government will use just two parameters: the car’s weight and its CO₂ emissions. “The lighter and cleaner your car, the less you pay,” is the message. For cars with a powerful engine (over 2400 cc), you’ll pay slightly more.
Anyone who wants to check for themselves whether the new road tax will be cheaper can do so from today via the website www.vlaanderen.be/vergelijker , but it will be handy to have somebody who reads Dutch on hand. The Comparison Tool makes the reform very clear.
How does it work?
To make a comparison, all you need is your number plate and your registration date. Simply enter these details into the new Comparison Tool and you’ll immediately see a comparison between your current road tax and the new rate.
If the new rate is cheaper, you can switch to the new system straight away. If the current rate is cheaper – which may be the case, for example, for cars with a powerful engine or older cars – then you don’t need to do anything, and you’ll remain on the current rate until you buy your next car.

European Defence: The E5 Aims to Build a Stronger Europe Within a Stronger NATO
France
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
14:46:27 CET
22:46:27 KST

European Defence: The E5 Aims to Build a Stronger Europe Within a Stronger NATO
Meeting in Paris on Monday, 26 October, representatives of Europe’s five leading military powers reaffirmed their determination to strengthen Europe’s role in NATO’s collective defence. In response to the Russian threat, France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom intend to step up their military and industrial cooperation while continuing their support for Ukraine.
Military and Industrial Cooperation to Strengthen NATO’s European Pillar
The E5 is a consultation framework bringing together the Defence Ministers of France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom. At their meeting in Paris on 26 October, hosted by French Minister for the Armed Forces Catherine Vautrin, the five countries reaffirmed the need for Europe to shoulder greater responsibility for its own defence while preserving its strategic partnership with the United States. “Produce more, produce faster,” Catherine Vautrin urged, calling for stronger European industrial capabilities and the development of equipment suited to both current conflicts and future threats. Achieving this ambition will require greater interoperability between armed forces, greater control over strategic technologies and closer coordination of defence investment. Also attending the meeting, EU High Representative Kaja Kallas stressed the importance of translating defence spending into tangible operational capabilities while maintaining pressure on Russia through sanctions. European Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius, meanwhile, emphasised the urgent need to accelerate industrial contracts and equipment deliveries, particularly through EU funding mechanisms designed to strengthen Ukraine’s capabilities.
In their joint statement, the E5 members reaffirmed their determination to build a stronger Europe within a stronger NATO, notably by increasing investment in Europe’s defence industrial capabilities.
A Stronger European Commitment to Ukraine
Support for Ukraine was also high on the agenda. “We are fully committed,” Catherine Vautrin affirmed, stressing the need to preserve European unity in the face of intimidation. In their joint statement, the five countries identified Russia as the most acute and long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security, citing its ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine and the growing use of hybrid attacks. German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius shared this assessment, stating that Vladimir Putin has shown no genuine willingness to agree to a ceasefire. As Russian strikes continue to target Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and civilian population, European countries continue to provide tangible support, particularly in air defence.
For Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto, this mobilisation directly serves Europe’s security interests: “Helping Ukraine is not simply about helping another country; it is about safeguarding our own future and security.” Polish Deputy Defence Minister Paweł Zalewski, meanwhile, emphasised the need to develop more affordable air defence systems and strengthen industrial cooperation with Kyiv. NATO Deputy Secretary General Radmila Shekerinska also stressed the importance of air defence, calling on Allies to step up their support to protect Ukrainian cities and infrastructure as winter approaches. British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting reiterated the UK’s determination to maintain economic pressure on Moscow and continue supporting Ukraine over the long term. The E5 members also reaffirmed the importance of countering Russia’s shadow fleet and their commitment to helping provide robust security guarantees for Ukraine once a ceasefire or peace agreement is in place.
A Common Response to Other Threats to European Security
Tensions in the Middle East were also discussed, particularly maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, two vital shipping routes for international trade and energy supplies.
Beyond these issues, the group plans to intensify dialogue between political and military leaders and strengthen cooperation between national defence industries. The next E5 meeting is scheduled to take place in Rome in March 2027, with the aim of continuing to translate this political alignment into tangible operational capabilities.

Ukraine prevented Russia from assuming the chairmanship of the Black Sea Commission
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

Ukraine prevented Russia from assuming the chairmanship of the Black Sea Commission
Kyiv • UNN
Ukraine prevented Russia from assuming the chairmanship of the Black Sea Commission due to its aggression and environmental damage. Kyiv called for the damage to be assessed and Russia’s participation to be limited.
The Ukrainian delegation prevented Russia from assuming the chairmanship during the 47th meeting of the Commission on the Protection of the Black Sea Against Pollution. This was reported by the Ministry of Economy and Environment of Ukraine, writes UNN.
A state waging an aggressive war and harming the marine environment should not head the body responsible for its protection
In her statement, she added that the Ukrainian side is drawing attention to the significant environmental consequences of Russia’s aggression for the entire Black Sea region. Attacks on infrastructure, damage to wastewater treatment facilities, pollution of water and soil, and the destruction of protected natural areas are creating threats that extend far beyond Ukraine.
Thus, the coasts of the Black and Azov Seas, the deltas of the Danube and Dnipro rivers, as well as wetlands of international importance, are suffering from the hostilities. Pollution is spreading through the sea, and the consequences for marine ecosystems may persist for many years.
The Ukrainian delegation emphasized that Russia’s actions run counter to international law and lead to marine pollution, undermining the joint efforts of coastal states aimed at fulfilling their obligations under the Convention on the Protection of the Black Sea Against Pollution (the Bucharest Convention).
It is noted that Ukraine called on the states parties to the Convention to provide a clear assessment of the actions of the Russian Federation and their environmental consequences, support the assessment of the condition of the marine environment and the damage caused by the war, and take joint measures to prevent further pollution.
Separately, the Ukrainian side raised the issue of the possibility of applying legal and procedural mechanisms to fully terminate Russia’s participation in the work of the Convention’s bodies. The relevant initiative is to be considered by the contracting parties.

Polish bishop convicted for failing to promptly report child sex abuse allegations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:45:01 UTC
22:45:01 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
In the first ruling of its kind in Poland, a Catholic bishop has been found guilty of failing to promptly inform the law enforcement authorities about allegations of child sex abuse committed by priests under his authority.
Andrzej Jeż, the bishop of Tarnów, was handed a non-custodial sentence that will require him to donate 25% of his earnings for two years to a charity that supports victims of child sexual abuse.
However, the verdict can still be appealed, and the diocese of Tarnów has already announced that it “disagrees with the court’s ruling” and that an appeal will be filed.

Ordynariusz tarnowski bp Andrzej Jeż jest pierwszym biskupem oskarżonym o zbyt późne powiadomienie prokuratury o pedofilii w Kościele. I pierwszym, który który został…
— Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 29, 2026
The case relates to alleged abuse by two priests who worked under Jeż’s authority. They can be identified only as Stanisław P. and Tomasz K. under Polish privacy law.
In 2022, prosecutors discontinued an investigation into allegations against Stanisław P. because the statute of limitations had expired, despite concluding that he had harmed at least 95 children and committed “sexual acts” against 77 of them over several decades in parishes in Poland and Ukraine.
In 2023, prosecutors decided to charge Tomasz K., who allegedly sexually abused children as early as 2018. However, they have been unable to formally present the charges to him because of his poor health, news website OKO.press reported earlier this year.
Though Jeż was not accused of complicity in the alleged abuse itself, he was charged under a 2017 law making it a criminal offence not to “immediately notify the authorities” of “credible information” about sexual abuse of minors. The offence is punishable by up to three years in prison.
Investigators say that, although an internal church probe into Stanisław P. was initiated in the 2000s and a decision to remove him from the clergy was made in 2013, Jeż only notified the prosecutor’s office in 2020. In the case of Tomasz K., the bishop notified prosecutors only in 2021.
In court, prosecutor Marcin Stępień said that Jeż’s failure to report the abuse promptly had allowed the statute of limitations to expire in the case of some of Stanisław P.’s victims.
Stępień also noted that the bishop had only come forward with the information when media coverage brought the allegations against Stanisław P. to light, reports broadcaster TVN.
A church commission set up to investigate child sex abuse in a Catholic diocese in Poland has identified at least 50 victims and 29 abusers.
It also found that bishops repeatedly failed to take action when credible reports of abuse were submitted to them https://t.co/MRNl5vWp4E
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 13, 2026
Prosecutors sought a 10-month prison sentence, suspended for three years, and a fine of 20,000 zloty (€4,550). Jeż, however, denied the allegations against him and sought an acquittal. He argued that he had reported the alleged abuse to the authorities as soon as there was credible information.
On Thursday, the court found the bishop guilty, giving him a sentence known as “restriction of liberty” (ograniczenie wolnośći), under which a convict is not imprisoned but required to do some kind of social good.
In Jeż’s case, the court ordered that 25% of his salary for two years be donated to the Empowering Children Foundation (Dajemy Dzieciom Siłę), which supports victims of child abuse. He was additionally ordered to pay 20,000 zloty to the Fund for Assistance to Victims and Post-Penitentiary Assistance.
In a statement after the verdict was issued, the diocese of Tarnów said that it “disagreed with the court’s ruling” and that, after a written justification from the court was reviewed, “an appeal will be filed”.
The Catholic church in Poland has in recent years been hit by a series of revelations regarding historical abuse of minors by members of the clergy and allegations that bishops covered cases up.
The Vatican has taken action against a number of Polish bishops over the issue. Most recently, in 2024, the Vatican announced the resignation of the bishop of Łowicz, Andrzej Dziuba, due to his “negligence in handling cases of sexual abuse against minors”.
In February, a commission created by the diocese of Sosnowiec following a series of scandals announced that it had identified at least 50 children who were harmed and 29 people suspected of abusing minors, most of them members of the clergy.

Bulgaria has the highest road traffic fatality rate in the EU, according to data published by the European Commission on 29 October. A Judicial Challenge to India’s Paternalistic Anti-trafficking Framework
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:44:00 UTC
22:44:00 KST

For decades, India’s anti-trafficking framework has rested on a flawed assumption: that trafficking and prostitution are essentially the same thing. As a result, women trafficked through force or deception, women who remained in prostitution after being trafficked, and adults who say they engage in sex work voluntarily have often been put through the same legal process. The law has frequently failed to distinguish exploitation from agency.
In Prajwala v Union of India (2026), decided on May 29, 2026, by a bench of justices – J. B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan – the Supreme Court has attempted to address this problem. The judgment, arising from a petition pending since 2004, lays down a detailed Victim Protection Plan, calls for a comprehensive anti-trafficking law, and, most importantly, recognizes that the existing framework inadequately separates trafficking from voluntary adult sex work. The distinction may seem obvious, but Indian law has struggled with it for decades.
The Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 (ITPA) emerged from a period when prostitution was viewed largely through a moral lens, and its machinery of rescue, detention, and rehabilitation reflects that origin. Over time, it treated very different women in the same manner. A woman trafficked against her will, a woman trafficked years earlier who remains in prostitution, and an adult voluntarily engaged in sex work may all find themselves before the same magistrate under the same statutory process. The court now recognizes that the one-size-fits-all model is a serious problem.
Its answer is a threshold inquiry. If an adult rescued during a raid states that she is engaged in sex work voluntarily and does not wish to be institutionalized, the magistrate must first determine whether that choice is genuine before ordering rehabilitation or long-term custody. This may seem procedural, but it is a significant shift. It challenges the assumption that every woman found in a brothel cannot make choices about her own life and introduces respect for agency into a framework long dominated by paternalism.
The Victim Protection Plan builds on this logic. It governs every stage of intervention, from rescue to prosecution and reintegration. It rests on principles such as non-criminalization, informed consent, privacy, and individualized care, and bars punitive practices inside protective homes. It also strengthens Anti-Human Trafficking Units and legal aid through District Legal Services Authorities.
The most compelling aspect of the judgement is its emphasis on dignity. Justice Pardiwala repeatedly stressed that trafficking violates human dignity because it reduces human beings to commodities. At the same time, the court recognized that the absence of dignity often precedes trafficking. Poverty, homelessness, lack of education, and economic vulnerability make exploitation possible.
Drawing upon Articles 21 and 23 of the constitution, the court held that rehabilitation is not merely a welfare measure but a right. This matters because governments have traditionally treated rehabilitation as policy rather than entitlement. By locating it within constitutional protections, the court elevated rehabilitation from charity to obligation, one a survivor can enforce in court. A survivor denied shelter, counselling, skills training, or support can now approach a court as a matter of right, rather than plead for a favor.
The judgement built on Budhadev Karmaskar v State of West Bengal (2022), where the court had already invoked Article 21 to uphold the dignity of sex workers. Prajwala insisted that the dignity of trafficking victims and of voluntary adult sex workers must both be protected.
Trafficking remains a serious concern in India. A government report revealed that India recorded 2,135 human trafficking cases in 2024, with roughly 5,800 victims identified. Yet a persistent criticism of India’s anti-trafficking regime is that success is measured by raids and rescues rather than long-term outcomes.
We know how many people enter the system, but far less about what happens afterward. How many survivors receive meaningful rehabilitation? How many gain access to education, employment, and stable housing? How many are retrafficked? The judgement acknowledged these shortcomings but offered limited answers on implementation.
Another unresolved issue is autonomy. The court observed that sex workers can hold rights even without a recognized right to sex work. While the judgment protects adult sex workers from arbitrary detention and police harassment, it avoids asking whether consensual adult sex work itself deserves legal recognition. If an adult engaged in sex work voluntarily is entitled to dignity, liberty, and constitutional protection, why does the law hesitate to recognize his or her agency fully? The court may have sidestepped the question because the case centered on trafficking, but the tension remains.
There is also a question of voice. Critics note that sex workers’ collectives, whose lives the judgment most directly affects, were not heard in open court. A framework that depends on distinguishing coercion from choice will work only if those who live that distinction help design and monitor it.
Implementation is the other test. The plan’s promises of privacy, individualized care, and legal assistance will be delivered by district officials, magistrates, and shelter managers who have long worked within a rescue-first culture. Guidelines on paper change little unless training and accountability follow.
The judgement also raises a broader constitutional question. Invoking Article 142, the Supreme Court has effectively created a nationwide anti-trafficking framework that will operate until Parliament legislates. The court may have felt compelled to act after more than two decades, but judicial directions cannot substitute for legislative reform indefinitely.
Courts can lay down guidelines; they cannot build the shelters, train the police, or fund the legal aid those guidelines demand. A statute could also do what a judgement cannot: align the ITPA, the trafficking provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, and child-protection laws into one coherent scheme.
Ultimately, Prajwala is as much a judgement about state failure as it is about trafficking. The court identified a flaw that has persisted in Indian law for decades, the inability to distinguish exploitation from agency, and laid the foundation for a more humane, rights-based framework. But without legislative action, institutional capacity, and sustained political commitment, even the most progressive judicial vision risks remaining on paper.
The Supreme Court has drawn an important line between trafficking and voluntary adult sex work. Parliament must now ensure that it becomes part of law and practice rather than another missed opportunity.

NAIROBI, October 29. /TASS/. Russia may launch Tanzania’s first Earth observation satellite into orbit in March 2027, according to the Ugandan news portal ChimpReports.
The spacecraft is scheduled to be launched using a Russian carrier rocket, the portal reported.
On October 28, Russia’s Roscosmos State Space Corporation and the Tanzanian Ministry of Communications and Information Technology signed a framework memorandum on strategic partnership and cooperation in the space sector on the sidelines of the third Russia-Africa Summit. The document provides for the joint development and launch of satellites, the creation of ground infrastructure for receiving space data, and the training of specialists. Russia also intends to assist Tanzania in establishing a national space agency.
Earlier, Roscosmos CEO Dmitry Bakanov reported that Tanzania is interested in building its own spacecraft and launching them into orbit using Russian carrier rockets. The Russian side also offered opportunities for Tanzanian students to study at specialized Russian universities, including programs involving the development and launch of student satellites.
According to the portal, Earth observation satellites are used to monitor agricultural production, forests, water resources, mineral deposits and environmental changes.

What a China-US AI Safety Channel Needs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:42:00 UTC
22:42:00 KST

The most concrete outcome from last month’s summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping was an apparent agreement to set up a China-U.S. AI incident reporting channel. But even if either government proves willing to use this direct line or start sending data across the Pacific, they must first address a more pressing issue: U.S. and Chinese frontier AI companies currently do not provide the information they would need.
In the U.S., no federal statute or regulation specifically requires AI companies to report safety incidents and dangerous capabilities to the government. Although some states have passed incident reporting laws, federal legislation – such as the AI Incident Reporting Act and the FRONTIER Act – has stalled in Congress. The industry is still largely regulating itself.
Moreover, while the White House Accord on Super Intelligence pledges to identify and remedy safety issues, it does not mandate notification to regulators or set reporting deadlines. The Trump administration’s separate Super Intelligence Force is developing government reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks, and other AI incidents. But it is not a regulator, and its recommendations would need to be implemented through enforceable measures.
There is also a severe lack of funding for federal government testing and oversight. According to Stanford’s 2026 AI Index Report, U.S. developers last year released 59 notable AI models, while British developers released just one. Yet the main U.S. federal AI-testing agency, the Commerce Department’s Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI), has an annual budget of only $15 million, whereas the United Kingdom’s AI Security Institute (AISI) has a budget of almost $90 million.
Given that the White House Accord seems to envision frontier labs doing the bulk of safety testing themselves, it remains to be seen what role the government would play in validating such testing, and whether any government body would have access to sufficient compute to conduct its own testing.
Unlike the United States, China’s government doesn’t face political bottlenecks, and it has already built a significant regulatory structure, with the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) recently calling for behavioral controls, model traceability, security testing, and safeguards against system vulnerabilities and loss of control. But there is still no Chinese equivalent to CAISSI – a specialized, centralized AI-safety body with a mandate. The government has plenty of authority over tech companies, but oversight is dispersed across the CAC, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, the National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC), the Ministry of Science and Technology, and other agencies.
Evaluating the risk of frontier AI models requires technical expertise and coordination among all the relevant Chinese government departments, including the security services. But some Chinese government agencies lack sufficient technical capacity, and many of the people with the deepest technical expertise sit in private research institutes with no authority to demand access to a company’s most advanced models, let alone inspect its internal logs or force it to make changes.
For now, the government has deployed officials from the CAC and NDRC to Chinese labs to discuss possibly gating the release of the most advanced models. But the authorities eventually will need to mandate internal safety-testing teams, access to sufficient compute, and pre-release testing of the most advanced models.
With the next Sino-American AI-safety dialogue scheduled for November, the United States and China should focus on what would make an incident reporting channel more likely to work. For its part, the U.S. government needs a transparent and mandatory policy for testing frontier models. Either the White House should disclose its current framework and make it binding, or it should work with Congress to pass legislation like the bipartisan FRONTIER Act. The federal government also needs to set rules for external audits of AI companies, giving auditors a clear mandate, reporting obligations, and meaningful independence (with auditors selected and paid by an industry body or government agency).
At the same time, the Trump administration needs to be more proactive in monitoring company compliance. It should use the Super Intelligence Force to review the current, flawed release process for the most advanced models, consider what to do about increasingly capable open-weight models, and begin moving toward an incident response mechanism that has teeth.
On the Chinese side, making the reporting channel operational would require closing the authority-expertise gap. The CAC could define safety expectations and reporting arrangements; technical bodies could develop and validate evaluations; the NDRC and other industrial agencies could weigh the effects on investment and diffusion; and the Ministry of Commerce would remain relevant to technology-transfer and export rules. With the United States empowering the Super Intelligence Force to conduct a thorough review of the U.S. government’s role, China should consider something similar.
China also needs to address its lack of evaluation capacity and access to sufficient compute across companies, evaluators, and government bodies. Rapid advances in Chinese open-weight models make this particularly important, because once model weights are released, developers have much less visibility into how their systems are being used or misused. The nascent Z.ai-Concordia framework is a potential template. It sorts models into three categories: green zone models that are safe to be fully released; yellow zone models that require a staged release, structured access for vetted researchers, or API-only hosting while weights are evaluated; and red zone releases that are suspended pending review.
AI safety is a global challenge. Addressing it depends on close and growing collaboration between the two leading AI powers, and a reporting channel for AI incidents is just a small step in the right direction. It will take the U.S. and Chinese governments a long time to reach binding, verifiable agreements. They cannot afford to be held up by failing to enact domestic reforms.

Qatar denies meddling in Israeli election: 'If it were true, Qatar would own all of Israel'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:38:48 UTC
22:38:48 KST

Qatar on Thursday rejected allegations that it had attempted to influence Israel's election results by transferring money, accusing Israeli politicians and media figures of spreading disinformation to drag Doha into Israel's post-election political disputes.
"We reject the allegations made by certain Israeli politicians and their media associates, who have launched yet another disinformation campaign aimed at dragging Qatar into Israel's political disputes following this week's elections," said Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari. "They accuse us of buying Netanyahu, buying the left, and now buying the Arab vote. If all these claims were to be believed, Qatar would probably own all of Israel."
In a post on X, al-Ansari described the allegations as both "ridiculous and dangerous," saying the repeated references to Qatar reflected an excessive obsession with his country among certain Israeli political and media figures.
"Do not use Qatar as a scapegoat for political failures," he wrote. "Instead of trying to divert attention toward Qatar, they would be better off focusing on voters, improving people's daily lives and repairing the damage they have caused in the region."
Qatar also emphasized that the matter concerned Israel's internal affairs.
"Any government emerging from these elections must uphold international law and relevant United Nations resolutions, engage seriously and sincerely with the Palestinian issue, and respect the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people, foremost among them the right to self-determination and an independent state along the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital," the statement said. "This requires responsibility and accountability."
Election chief orders Shin Bet investigation into suspected foreign interference
The controversy began with a letter sent by Central Elections Committee Chairman Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg to Shin Bet Director David Zini.
"The integrity of elections is at the heart of democracy," Sohlberg wrote. Although he stressed that he was unable to assess the credibility of the suspicions, he said the allegations required a thorough investigation because they involved possible foreign actors.
"Given that these suspicions concern foreign elements, there is an obligation to investigate them properly in order to safeguard the integrity of Knesset elections, prevent illegal activity intended to undermine democratic institutions and prevent subversion," he wrote.
Sohlberg instructed Zini to make every effort to provide investigative findings within a week. "I instruct you to do everything in your power to examine these suspicions thoroughly and use the Shin Bet's authority to identify evidence that substantiates or disproves them," the justice wrote. "Only in this way can we ensure public confidence in the election and the integrity of the democratic process."
Citing the legal deadlines for filing election appeals, Sohlberg asked Zini to present any available findings within the coming week.
Yesh Atid lawmaker Vladimir Beliak subsequently demanded that the Central Elections Committee's leadership convene to review the evidence underlying Sohlberg's decision to order an investigation.
Responding on Sohlberg's behalf, acting committee Director General Dean Livne emphasized that the election itself had been conducted lawfully. "The Knesset elections were conducted in accordance with the law. The integrity of voting at polling stations was carefully protected, and to the best of our knowledge, claims of systematic violations of election integrity are baseless," Livne said.
He added that statements made by the police commissioner and Shin Bet director on Election Day and afterward supported that assessment.
Livne explained that Sohlberg had written to Zini after receiving sensitive classified intelligence in his capacity as chairman of the Central Elections Committee. "The information raised suspicions that required further examination to determine whether there was substantiated evidence," he said. "Immediately upon receiving the information, the committee chairman instructed that the investigation be expanded."
Because the investigation is ongoing and the intelligence is highly classified, Livne said there was no justification for convening a meeting of the committee's leadership.
Why wasn't the suspected interference stopped before the election?
Questions have also emerged about why the Shin Bet did not act before Israelis went to the polls.
As an intelligence agency responsible for preventing threats to national security, the Shin Bet possessed information about the possibility of unlawful money transfers before the election, two official sources connected to the case confirmed to ynet.
However, Central Elections Committee officials said the Shin Bet participated in every security assessment held in the days preceding the vote and never informed the committee of any such suspicions or intelligence. Had the information been shared, officials said, the agency would immediately have been asked to act to prevent interference in real time and protect the integrity of the election.
"The obvious question is how the service could have possessed what was allegedly solid and deeply troubling intelligence before the election, yet failed to act or launch an investigation before voting took place," one official said.
Zini initiated a meeting Wednesday with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, briefing him on the case and presenting intelligence materials and suspicions that he described as "well-founded."
Yashar! chairman Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the largest political bloc opposing Netanyahu, received a briefing on the matter from Sohlberg on Wednesday and met Zini on Thursday. "During the meeting, Eisenkot was briefed on suspicions concerning foreign involvement in Israel's elections," his office said. "Eisenkot expressed his support for the Shin Bet and law enforcement authorities in conducting a swift and transparent investigation."
Likud links two separate investigations
Meanwhile, police had arrested seven suspects by Thursday morning in a separate election bribery investigation involving envelopes associated with the Arab party Ra'am that were discovered in the Negev. Tens of thousands of shekels in cash were found in the homes of some suspects.
That investigation is separate from the suspected Qatari funding case. It is being handled by the National Fraud Investigations Unit within Lahav 433, rather than by the Shin Bet. Three suspects were arrested on Election Day, while four others were arrested Thursday and taken for questioning.
Likud, which has been running a campaign challenging the legitimacy of Arab parties, sought to connect the two investigations. The party dubbed the controversy "Ra'amgate" and alleged that the election had been stolen. "This is an earthquake. They stole the election in Israel!" Likud said in a statement.
The party described Sohlberg's remarks about suspected foreign involvement and voter bribery benefiting Arab parties as an unprecedented political shock.
"This is an attack on democracy intended to bring about a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel and the overthrow of right-wing rule, leading to the IDF's withdrawal and defeat on every front, first and foremost Iran," the statement said.
However, the two investigations remain distinct, and no evidence has been publicly established connecting the alleged Qatari transfers to the separate election bribery case in the Negev.
Ra'am denies involvement: 'We have nothing to do with this'
Ra'am chairman Mansour Abbas denied that his party had any connection to either investigation.
"Ra'am welcomes the decision by Central Elections Committee Chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg to investigate suspicions of improper attempts to influence the election through foreign funding," Abbas said in a statement. "Safeguarding election integrity and the rule of law is a civic and democratic obligation that we have made a central principle of our party."
Abbas insisted that Ra'am had no connection to the allegations and pledged full cooperation with law enforcement authorities. "Ra'am has nothing to do with the affair in question or with any other affair, and we declare that we will cooperate fully with all law enforcement authorities to establish the truth," he said.
Abbas also directed a personal message at Netanyahu, using his nickname, "Abu Yair," and accusing him of employing Qatari agents in his office.
"And to Abu Yair, who employs Qatari agents in his office, we have one message in response to the campaign of incitement and delegitimization he is conducting against Arab citizens: 'There will be nothing because there is nothing.' But unlike you, in our case it is the truth, not another lie."
Over the past 24 hours, Likud has submitted materials to the Central Elections Committee that it says include firsthand recordings of individuals from Arab communities admitting to bribing voters with fuel vouchers and cash.
Police, however, rejected Likud's claims Thursday morning, saying there was "no evidence whatsoever" supporting the allegation that the election had been stolen.
The Central Elections Committee has likewise emphasized that voting was conducted lawfully and that it has no evidence of systematic manipulation of the results, even as the Shin Bet continues investigating suspicions of foreign interference.

Rock collapse causes casualties at Turkish tourist hotspot – media (VIDEOS)
At least two people have been killed and another injured after rocks broke off a natural formation at a popular tourist destination in Türkiye’s Cappadocia region, local media have reported, citing provincial authorities.
The incident occurred at around 3:15 PM local time on Thursday following heavy rainfall, Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok told reporters.
The collapse took place near the entrance to the Goreme Open-Air Museum, where rocks broke off one of the region’s distinctive fairy chimney formations.
Rescue teams recovered two bodies from beneath the debris, while another person was taken to hospital with injuries, according to the governor.
Police, gendarmerie, medical personnel, and disaster response teams were dispatched to the scene, he said.
Rescuers are continuing to search the debris for anyone who might still be trapped, while the authorities have yet to release the victims’ identities or nationalities.
According to media reports, rain and wind have affected the region intermittently this week, forcing the cancellation of Cappadocia’s popular hot-air balloon tours on Wednesday and Thursday.

Ieva Jāgere: Latvia must be among the first choices for international investment projects
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:36:02 UTC
22:36:02 KST

Internationally recognised site selection consultants whose recommendations influence global companies’ decisions on where to locate new manufacturing facilities, technology centres and other investment projects will gather in Riga this week. On 29 October, Latvia’s capital will host the Site Selectors Guild European Conference for the first time in the Baltic States. The Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA) sees the event as an important opportunity to strengthen Latvia’s position in the international competition for investment.
The Site Selectors Guild brings together internationally recognised site selection consultants who help multinational companies evaluate different countries and make investment location decisions. Eleven Guild members will visit Riga, including representatives of international consulting firms such as JLL, Newmark, BCI Global and IBM Plant Location International. Their recommendations can be decisive when companies are choosing between several countries competing for the same investment project.
“Investment does not begin with the construction of a factory. It begins with a decision about which country a company should choose for its development. And the people who have come to Riga this week play an important role in making those decisions. The fact that they have chosen to meet in Latvia is significant recognition of our country’s visibility, but making a good impression alone is not enough in the competition for investment. Companies need to know how quickly they can start operating, what support is available and who can help resolve specific issues. Latvia’s advantage lies in its ability to make decisions quickly and ensure direct cooperation with the people responsible. Our task is to make sure that the next time these consultants are looking for a location for a new factory or technology centre on behalf of their clients, Latvia is among their first choices. That is why, during the conference, LIAA will also present concrete opportunities and advantages that Latvia can offer international companies seeking to expand their operations and implement new investment projects here,” emphasises Ieva Jāgere, Director of LIAA.
Latvia’s competitiveness in attracting investment is also reflected in its results to date. In 2025, 31 investment projects with a total value of €1.01 billion were launched with LIAA’s involvement. Meanwhile, during the first nine months of 2026, the total planned value of investment projects attracted by LIAA reached €886.8 million, representing almost 90% of the agency’s €1 billion target for the year.
LIAA Director Ieva Jāgere will attend a meeting with conference participants on 28 October. During the conference, LIAA will use the opportunity to establish contacts with international consultants and present Latvia’s investment environment. Key elements of Latvia’s investment proposition include access to the European Union’s single market, a skilled workforce, the exemption of reinvested corporate profits from corporate income tax, and the opportunity for eligible investment projects to benefit from the Green Corridor initiative, which accelerates access to certain public administration services.
According to LIAA, maintaining cooperation after the conference will be particularly important to ensure that consultants have access to up-to-date information about investment opportunities in Latvia and direct contacts to facilitate future projects. This will help Latvia become involved at an early stage in the evaluation of new investment projects and compete for their implementation.
The second Site Selectors Guild European Conference will take place on 29 October at the Radisson Blu Latvija Conference & Spa Hotel in Riga. It will bring together site selection consultants and representatives of economic development organisations from Europe, North America and Asia. The conference programme will feature discussions on global investment trends, the impact of artificial intelligence on site selection, energy availability, clean technologies and the semiconductor industry.
The conference is organised by the Site Selectors Guild, with the Riga Investment and Tourism Agency (RITA) serving as the host partner.

BERLIN/BRUSSELS, October 29. /TASS/. Christine Lagarde has confirmed that she will leave her post early as President of the European Central Bank (ECB) on February 7 next year.
"I have just informed my colleagues that I will step down as ECB President on February 7, 2027," she wrote on X.
Lagarde has headed the bank since November 1, 2019, and her term was originally scheduled to end in late October 2027.
In a video posted by the ECB chief, adhesive bandages were visible on her face. To "avoid speculation on social media," Lagarde explained that she had undergone a minor medical procedure earlier in the week, and urged others to follow medical advice and get regular skin check-ups.
Meanwhile, European Council President Antonio Costa said he had received formal notification of her resignation. Costa thanked Lagarde for her service and announced that "the process to appoint her successor will be initiated today and will proceed without delay" to ensure the new ECB president is confirmed by the European Council before February 7.
In February, the Financial Times reported on the plans of Lagarde--a prominent French politician--to resign ahead of the April 2027 French presidential election. According to the newspaper, this is linked to concerns that Eurosceptics, led by Marine Le Pen, could win, which would complicate the selection of the next ECB chief in October.
Earlier, World Economic Forum (WEF) founder Klaus Schwab told the Financial Times that he had invited Lagarde to succeed him at the helm of the forum starting in early 2027. Lagarde has not yet publicly confirmed these plans.

When Philosophers Reinvent The Wheel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:33:17 UTC
22:33:17 KST

You may not believe this, but philosophers sometimes work in ignorance of research programs, bodies of literature, methodologies, and findings outside of philosophy that could be relevant to their work.
In a post at his blog, Ethan Landes (Eindhoven) shares how he recently discovered that the relatively young philosophical subfield of conceptual engineering, to which he contributes, appears to have reinvented a wheel produced 50 years ago by scholars in the field of sociolinguistics.
Neat find. But ouch.
He writes:
There is an entire literature that discusses things at a level that I (we?) all thought was unique to conceptual engineering. An entire literature the conceptual engineering literature could have drawn on for ideas and knowledge. But no one looked carefully, so we have a decade of literature of us forging our own paths.
It reminds me of the time I spent an hour fighting my way up an English hill through thick, knee-high heather, only to discover at the top that [there] had been an unmarked path 20 meters to my right the whole time.
Some degree of ignorance of other fields is a cost of disciplinary specialization for creatures who sometimes have to do things that cut into their research—like sleep, or die. Since specialization has its benefits, some ignorance is expected.
And its worth noting that philosophy is increasingly interdisciplinary, and on some measures, the most interdisciplinary field in the humanities.
Still, philosophy’s remit is about as broad as can be, so perhaps it has a greater risk of interdisciplinary ignorance leading to research which duplicates work done elsewhere, or research which would have been significantly advanced in light of awareness of very similar research already conducted outside of philosophy.
Dr. Landes gave us one example, but I’m sure there are others, both contemporary and historical. Let’s hear about them.

Western Europe is falling apart – we should prepare for what comes next
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:32:30 UTC
22:32:30 KST

Western Europe is falling apart – we should prepare for what comes next
For Russia, developments in the rest of Europe matter primarily insofar as they affect our national interests. Above all, this concerns security given that, for centuries, Russia has faced its greatest challenges from the West, and there’s little reason to assume that this historical pattern has disappeared.
Western Europe’s leading countries now stand at a crossroads, yet the choice confronting them isn’t simply between competing models of domestic development, it’s between war and peace with their neighbors, foremost among them Russia, whose size and historical role have repeatedly made it the principal obstacle to Western European expansion.
The unrest sweeping several European countries this autumn marks a new phase in the continent’s systemic crisis as it reflects the convergence of two long-term problems that much of Europe’s political establishment has proved incapable of resolving.
The first is the exhaustion of the socioeconomic model that sustained Western European prosperity throughout the Cold War and its aftermath. That model depended on Europe’s privileged position in the global economy and the absence of serious competitors beyond the Western world, but China’s rise, combined with increasingly limited resources, has undermined those advantages.
Closer economic integration with Russia, and access to its enormous natural wealth, might have offered Western Europe a final opportunity to preserve its exceptional position, but instead regional leaders allowed their own arrogance to prevent an accommodation with Moscow because they couldn’t accept that Russia wished to live peacefully with its neighbors, but on terms consistent with its own interests.
The second problem is Western Europe’s longstanding absence of genuine sovereignty.
Integration into the American-led NATO system has deprived even major powers such as Germany, France, and Britain of the freedom to pursue fundamental political change and one of the alliance’s practical functions has been to preserve the existing political order within its member states.
Any serious attempt to transform that order would require a reassessment of relations with Washington and such independence is something these European governments have long been unwilling, or unable, to contemplate.
Together, these structural weaknesses have left Western Europe’s political and economic establishments effectively paralyzed.
For nearly two decades, governments have substituted the appearance of activity for meaningful reform. Successive emergencies, involving migration, the pandemic, hostility towards Russia, and preparations for military confrontation, have allowed leaders to avoid addressing deeper problem and this helps explain the temptation to interpret today’s unrest as another exercise in political manipulation. Emmanuel Macron, for example, has repeatedly demonstrated an ability to survive the consequences of disastrous decisions through tactical maneuvering.
Yet it would be a mistake to dismiss the protests as artificial or orchestrated.
In France, the initial demonstrations were driven by schoolchildren and university students demanding more teachers and improvements to an education system suffering from declining standards, but these grievances are hardly unique to France and they reflect broader weaknesses in modern education, including funding arrangements that encourage institutions to compete for pupils rather than concentrate on teaching.
By early October, the French protests had expanded as other groups affected by Macron’s liberal economic policies joined the demonstrations. The authorities blamed the political left, while unrest escalated into rioting and looting.
Similar discontent emerged in Spain and Portugal, where soaring housing costs became the immediate trigger. Both countries have spent years occupying subordinate positions within the European Union, with little influence over its economic priorities, even as their former politicians find comfortable positions in Brussels.
Western Europe has consequently entered a period in which conventional political competition is increasingly accompanied by mass protest and the participation of young people is particularly significant.
In France, the EU’s most important military power and its only nuclear-armed member, it was students who provided the initial momentum. While much of the adult electorate has descended into political apathy under Macron, younger generations retain aspirations for a better future and their grievances are genuine. So, too, is the wider crisis that has brought people onto the streets.
There are therefore grounds to believe that public dissatisfaction may eventually bring new political forces to power, which from Russia’s perspective raises an obvious possibility in that perhaps Western Europe’s next generation of leaders will prove more reasonable on questions of security and relations with Moscow.
Such hopes, however, may be premature because they reflect less our actual experience of European politics than our desire to imagine a Western Europe capable of recovering its political judgement.
Indeed, the objective nature of the present crisis makes its possible consequences especially troubling and European history offers little reassurance that profound domestic upheaval produces peaceful relations with neighbouring countries. On the contrary, revolutionary transformations have repeatedly generated external aggression, and the French Revolution provides one example.
The upheavals of the late 18th century were followed by wars against neighboring states and, eventually, Napoleon’s attempt to dominate Europe.
The extraordinary energy released by revolution demanded an outlet, while new rulers also needed resources and opportunities for enrichment beyond their borders.
As Henry Kissinger observed in his early historical work, the internal foundations of Napoleon’s expansionism helped prevent a lasting accommodation with Russia after the disastrous campaign of 1812.
Germany offers an even more destructive precedent, where the political upheavals of the 20th century ultimately brought to power a regime whose ambitions extended far beyond Germany’s borders. The conquest of neighboring countries was followed by an attack on the Soviet Union and the most devastating war in human history.
Again, internal political transformation was accompanied by an effort to direct national energies towards external expansion and the consequences of that war fundamentally altered Europe’s position as many of its leading states lost much of their effective sovereignty and became dependent on the United States for their security.
Paradoxically, that dependence may now offer some protection against the most dangerous consequences of Europe’s internal crisis because governments that lack genuine strategic independence may also lack the freedom to embark upon adventures of their own choosing.
Nevertheless, Russia can’t base its security on the assumption that European political upheaval will produce more sensible leaders even if the temptation to hope for a peaceful transformation of Europe is understandable. Hope isn’t a strategy, and history provides ample grounds for caution.
Russia must therefore prepare not for the miracle of a Western Europe reconciled to peaceful coexistence, but for the possibility that its internal crisis will once again find expression in confrontation abroad.
Whatever political forces eventually emerge from the present turmoil, preparing for a military confrontation with our European neighbors must remain one of Russia’s central strategic priorities.
This article was first published by Vzglyad.ru, translated and edited by the RT team.

Higher energy prices trigger surge in inflation now at 5.26%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:31:51 UTC
22:31:51 KST

Inflation, the figure that reflects the general rise in the price level, has risen to 5.26 per cent this month. The cost of living in Belgium has risen mainly due to the sharp increase in the price of natural gas and electricity.
Inflation in Belgium continues to rise: whilst the cost of living rose by 4.69 per cent last month, inflation has increased to 5.26 per cent this month according to the statistics agency Statbel.
Anyone following the news on energy prices knows the cause all too well: the sharp rise in energy prices is caused by the ongoing tensions in the Middle East, which have been putting pressure on gas and oil supplies to Europe for months.
Following the US and Israeli attacks on Iran, inflation saw its first significant spike in April, rising to over 4 per cent. After a slight dip in June, inflation has been on a steady upward trend again since July.
Inflation has not been this high since April. Back then, too, sky-high energy prices were to blame.
Natural gas more expensive too
Compared with a year ago, energy inflation this month stands at 33.22 per cent, compared with 24.37 per cent in September.
Electricity is 23.7 per cent more expensive than in October last year, heating oil 30.8 per cent and natural gas as much as 52.5 per cent.
In addition to price rises for natural gas, electricity and heating oil, rising rents, higher tuition fees for higher education, more expensive clothing and airfares are also driving inflation.
The sharp rise in the price of external storage devices is also striking: +48.7 per cent. As a result of the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) computer applications, high global demand has led to a shortage of hard drives and memory cards.
Trigger index not exceeded
The health index, on which any indexation of wages and benefits is based, rose from 4 per cent in September to 4.53 per cent in October. The rise is not sufficient to trigger a 2% top-up.
The last time this happened was the case was in June. As a result, benefits and the salaries of civil servants got a 2% top up in September.
According to the Planning Office’s inflation forecasts from last month, the reference index was set to be exceeded again in November. The Planning Bureau will publish new inflation forecasts on Tuesday.

Foreign residents: get organised, starting with dual nationality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:30:59 UTC
22:30:59 KST

Foreign residents: get organised, starting with dual nationality
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Eelco Keij founded the Foundation for Dutch Nationals Abroad (SNBN), which lobbies for Dutch people living overseas. A bill due before parliament in December would allow dual nationality both for them and for foreign residents who naturalise here – but the coalition agreement only backs the first part. Keij says the international community needs to organise and lobby for itself, or risk being left behind.
Foreign residents in the Netherlands need lasting political influence, and could learn from another group that once had no voice in Dutch politics: Dutch citizens abroad.
In 2011, when I became a US citizen alongside my native Dutch citizenship, I realised that most Dutch people abroad could not have dual citizenship. As my case fell under one of the exceptions, I actually could be both. I felt lucky for myself, and pity for others. This is where my second realisation came in, possibly spurred by having worked for years in lobbying, advocacy and the Dutch parliament: no one in the Dutch political system would ever stand up for people like me, living abroad.
First, I set up a debate on dual nationality, from New York, and soon after, a petition among the Dutch abroad, reaching both astonishing numbers of citizens and articles in the Dutch national press. Aiming for a longer-term strategy, I studied how other European countries treated their citizens abroad. It turned out that in some countries the diaspora had organized itself in interest organisations, like the French, Danish and Swiss abroad.
Through this research, it became clear to me that the Dutch living abroad also needed a formal vehicle to be heard in Dutch politics. Together with other concerned Dutch citizens living abroad I founded the Foundation for the Dutch Abroad (SNBN), in 2019. The SNBN is a volunteer advocacy and lobby organization – strategic by design, focused on results.
Gaining recognition 
Aware that the Dutch political scene is fragmented, coalition-based, and unpredictable, our board is mostly formed of Dutch citizens abroad who are members of different political parties. That way, while remaining non-partisan as an organisation, board members have many formal and informal contacts with different political parties. As a consequence, Dutch politicians started hearing us, and seeing us.
Our efforts contributed to the 2022 constitutional change enabling Dutch citizens abroad to participate in elections for the Dutch Senate through an electoral college. Moreover, we saw how our outreach on various occasions led to mitigation of legislation and a willingness among Dutch politicians to engage with us, having discovered a new electorate.
Currently, we are fully focused on the advancement of a bill that was introduced almost ten years ago, which lies at the very heart of our foundation: allowing Dutch citizens abroad to have dual citizenship.
But the dual citizenship bill also covers foreigners in the Netherlands. If passed in full, it would also scrap the requirement forcing them to give up their original nationality.
Spoiler: that is not going to happen. The SNBN found there is currently no political majority to support foreigners in the Netherlands in their quest for dual citizenship. Their interests are beyond our mandate. But the political end result may be favoring the Dutch abroad, without equivalent progress for foreigners residing in the Netherlands – an aspect that could be dropped from the bill.
Time to start lobbying 
To our surprise, we have not seen a visible, coordinated lobby on behalf of foreign residents in the Netherlands in the debate on dual citizenship. The bill also covers them, yet they have been largely absent from the debate. So what to do now?
Unlike in countries such as Germany, Luxembourg and Ireland, where migrant-representing organizations already exist, we have not encountered a comparable, visible lobby in this debate on behalf of foreign residents in the Netherlands.
Perhaps with a suggested blueprint of the SNBN at hand, it may well be up to someone, a foreigner residing in the Netherlands, or a group of them, to step up and say: “Let’s start working on that.” Surely there are many issues this interest organisation could work on, including citizenship and naturalisation, family reunification, political participation and voting rights. Above all, it would give foreign residents visibility with Dutch politicians.
As SNBN we can attest to one thing: an important part of lasting political influence is to embed different political streams within the organization’s structure, whether it’s volunteer staff, board members or advisory board members. With that, and the right commitment, there is a real opportunity to build lasting political influence.
Readers: your turn.

Suicide deaths in Germany surge to 27-year high
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:30:31 UTC
22:30:31 KST

Suicide deaths in Germany surge to 27-year high
Germany has seen its highest annual suicide toll in nearly three decades, with 11,334 deaths recorded last year, according to the Federal Statistical Office. Experts suggest that the surge may be linked to a loosely regulated assisted-suicide system, which allows even healthy adults to seek help ending their lives.
The data set released earlier this month and analyzed in greater detail on Wednesday by Germany’s National Suicide Prevention Program (NaSPro) found a rise of 962 suicides, or 9.3%, in 2025, taking the annual toll to its highest level since 1998.
The total was greater than the approximately 7,677 people killed in traffic accidents, homicides, illegal-drug-related deaths and AIDS combined, the report said, adding that men accounted for 69.2% of suicides.
Since 2021, the annual total has climbed 23% though the number of suicides remains below its historical peak of 18,825 in 1981, NaSPro said.
While men accounted for most suicides, the increase was disproportionately concentrated among women, whose deaths rose 17.9%, compared with 5.8% among men. Most suicides (73.7%) also occur in the over-50 age group.
Although hanging remained the most common method of suicide (4,145), it was followed by medication (2,848 cases), which saw a striking surge compared to 2024, when it accounted for 2,002 deaths. This category alone accounted for nearly 88% of the entire annual increase.
The latest figures also point to an increase in suicide deaths among the German youth: among girls aged 15 to 19, deaths surged from 52 in 2024 to 84 in 2025, while the overall toll among teenagers rose from 188 to 208. Suicide accounted for approximately 18% of all deaths among people aged five to 24.
While the German government did not offer a definitive explanation for the dramatic increase, multiple experts linked it to the expansion of assisted suicides, which are not separately identified in official mortality statistics. Three major organizations providing such services reported 1,287 assisted deaths last year, up from 977 in 2024 and just 346 in 2021; medication is also the most common method used in assisted suicides.
Germany’s legal framework permits assisted suicide even for people who are not terminally ill or suffering from incurable conditions. Individuals willing to go this path are not required to provide any justification, and in principle, even a physically healthy young adult can legally seek assistance if the decision is voluntary, informed, and enduring. However, nobody is obliged to assist, and euthanasia performed directly by another person remains illegal.
Ulrich Hegerl, chairman of the German Depression Aid and Suicide Prevention Foundation, criticized what he described as the country’s “extreme position” on the matter, warning that “when assisted suicide becomes normalized as a service, this threshold is lowered, and the number of tragic, preventable suicides rises.”
Suicide researcher Ute Lewitzka of Goethe University Frankfurt, meanwhile, has offered another explanation, describing the surge as a crisis phenomenon. She suggested that financial hardship and uncertainty can intensify suicidal thoughts among vulnerable people, while social media could also contribute. Lewitzka also criticized what she described as Germany’s inadequate access to psychological care.
