Mission in Alyoshki and unacceptability of colonial practices: Putin’s statements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:28:13 UTC
22:28:13 KST

MOSCOW, October 29. /TASS/. The Russian business community rejects colonial methods and conducts business with African partners on respectful terms, investing in their countries, Russian President Vladimir Putin stated at the Russia-Africa summit.
It is hardly possible to speak of socio-economic development without guaranteeing security, he noted.
Putin added that a humanitarian operation is currently underway in Alyoshki in the Kherson Region to provide assistance to the civilian population.
TASS has compiled the key statements by the head of state.
Security
It is impossible to discuss socio-economic development without guaranteeing security: "Naturally, without resolving these problems, it is impossible to speak of any kind of economic or social development. It is self-evident. Of course, the UN Security Council must devote the necessary attention to this."
Ukrainian settlement and operation in Alyoshki
A humanitarian operation is currently underway in Alyoshki in the Kherson Region to provide assistance to the civilian population: "Regarding the zone of the Russian-Ukrainian conflict: an operation is scheduled right now, over these next few days, today or tomorrow, with the support of the First Lady of the United States [Melania Trump] by the way, to provide aid specifically to the civilian population."
Ukrainian forces have mined the approaches to Alyoshki in the Kherson Region, bringing the settlement closer to a humanitarian catastrophe: "The situation had been developing for a long time."
Russia is exploring options for a peaceful settlement of the conflict in Ukraine: "We are working on this as well, just as we are addressing issues related to a peaceful settlement of the Ukrainian crisis itself."
Alignment of positions between Russia and Africa on pressing issues
Russia and Africa are natural allies in building a multipolar world system free from dictates: "Russia and Africa are united by truly strong bonds of friendship and close partnership. We are natural allies in building a multipolar and truly democratic world order. A world order free of diktat and double standards, based on respect for the norms of international law and fundamental principles of the UN Charter and, what's more, in their entirety and interrelation."
The positions of Russia and African states on the most pressing issues of global politics are similar or coincide: "We advocate for an equitable dialogue and for taking into account the interests of all states."
Russia-Africa summits bring significant added value, as they give a powerful impetus to the development of mutually beneficial ties: "Such summits offer us a valuable opportunity to exchange views on the current state of Russian-African relations and give a powerful boost to our multifaceted and mutually beneficial ties."
Development of Africa
Moscow remains interested in seeing African countries develop, protect their sovereignty, and achieve sustainable economic growth: "Russia has been and remains interested in seeing African nations protect their sovereignty, achieve steady growth, and strengthen their economies and social sectors. To address these goals, we are ready to continue working together with you across all these areas."
Africa will be able not only to feed itself but also to become a major food exporter in the future: "We are convinced that through the application of modern agricultural technologies and the proper organization of agricultural production, as you have noted, dear friends, Africa will be able in the future not only to feed itself but also to become a major exporter of various types of food products."
Economic cooperation
Russia’s trade turnover with Africa has grown 1.5-fold since the previous summit, reaching $27 bln: "The momentum is good, but the true potential of our collaboration is significantly greater, of course," Putin added.
The Russian business community rejects colonial methods and conducts business with African partners on respectful terms, investing in their countries: "Our business community always approaches cooperation with African partners with honesty, respect, and good faith, conducting business on equal terms. Rather than siphoning off profits in the spirit of the colonial practices of former imperial powers, they invest what they earn in the development of your countries’ economies, eagerly share advanced technologies and expertise, and extensively engage local subcontractors, creating new production facilities and jobs."
Many Russian companies have long been successfully carrying out large-scale investment projects in Africa: "This refers to sectors including energy and the peaceful use of nuclear power, mining and mineral extraction, industrial cooperation, logistics, and tourism."
Russian businesses in Africa demonstrate social responsibility by caring for the well-being of local employees and the local environment: "What is important, Russian businesses operate in Africa in a socially responsible manner: they look after the well-being of their employees and their families, fund and participate in the implementation of significant humanitarian programs, pay close attention to ecological and environmental issues, and show respect for internal political processes."
Moscow has established an uninterrupted channel for mutual settlements with African countries, with the ruble accounting for 85% of those transactions: "All of this helps to shield our economic exchanges from external influence and makes them more resilient to fluctuations in the global economic and political landscape."
Russian companies are interested in relocating some of their production facilities to African countries, especially in the current sanctions environment: "I won’t say anything unexpected, but this is entirely in Russia’s interests, especially in today’s environment, with numerous sanctions being applied to the Russian economy and Russian enterprises. Our companies are interested in relocating certain production facilities to African countries."
African nations already enjoy certain advantages in trade with Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), including full exemptions from customs duties: "The EAEU’s unified system of tariff preferences offers African exporters significant benefits when importing goods into the Eurasian market. Forty-seven countries on the continent are eligible for these benefits, with 32 of them enjoying completely zeroed-out customs duties."
Initiatives to introduce advanced Russian services are underway in Africa with the participation of Russian businesses: "Promising initiatives to introduce advanced Russian digital services are being actively implemented on the continent with the participation of Russian businesses."
Ensuring stability and security
Russia is doing much to help African countries maintain internal stability and security, and to strengthen their defense capabilities: "As a permanent member of the UN Security Council, our country makes a significant contribution to resolving ongoing conflicts and preventing new ones on the African continent. That said, we consistently proceed from the fundamental principle that you yourselves have proclaimed: ‘African solutions to African problems.’ Russia is doing a great deal to assist African states in maintaining internal stability and security, and in strengthening their defense and security capabilities."
Diplomatic presence
Russia’s diplomatic presence on the African continent is being expanded systematically: "I must mention the systematic steps being taken by the Russian side to expand our diplomatic presence on the continent. Since the previous summit in 2023, eight new Russian embassies have begun operations in African states, bringing the total number to 48. At the same time, a network of trade missions is being developed; there are currently only six of them, but their activities cover 16 African countries."
Botswana, Seychelles and Togo are planning to open their embassies in Moscow soon, and Russia supports their intention: "We render all necessary assistance to African diplomatic missions operating in Russia. Their number is also growing. We also know about the intention of Botswana, the Seychelles Islands and Togo to open their embassies in Moscow soon and, naturally, we support them."
Middle East
One must not lose sight of the problems facing Palestine, which continues to suffer amid developments in the Persian Gulf: "Of course, amid the events in the Persian Gulf, we must not forget the problems of Palestine, which continues to suffer."
Russia believes a definitive resolution to the Palestinian question can only be achieved through the implementation of the principle of establishing two states: "Russia supports and believes that a final resolution to the Palestinian question can only be reached through the implementation of the well-established two-state principle, which includes the creation of a fully-fledged state on Palestinian territory, a Palestinian state."
Freedom of navigation
It is important to ensure freedom of navigation in all regions of the world, as well as compliance with international maritime law: "I would like to say that the most important thing here is to ensure adherence to the fundamental norms of international maritime law and to guarantee freedom of navigation. This should apply to all regions of the world."

Can EU and India work together to secure Indo-Pacific?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:26:00 UTC
22:26:00 KST

Can EU and India work together to secure Indo-Pacific?
October 29, 2026
The European Union is vying for a larger role in Indo-Pacific security as the US finds itself on the back foot in the Eastern Hemisphere.
India is among the regional powers looking for new allies. Its rising economy and increasingly global ambitions have pushed it into new forums and partnerships, including ever closer defense ties with the European bloc.
In January this year, India and the EU signed a Security and Defense Partnership, followed by their first formal Security and Defense Dialogue in March. More meetings followed throughout the year, including the fifth Maritime Security Dialogue in Brussels last month.
However, while both sides want to boost cooperation on maritime security, working together in the Indo-Pacific remains a challenge — India and European countries simply have different defense priorities.
France a player in the Indian Ocean theater
"Europe can be a credible defense partner of India, especially in the maritime theater in general and Indo-Pacific in particular," Mohan Kumar, a former Indian ambassador to France, told DW.
But Europe's capacity to expand its role is constrained by other security crises.
"European distractions such as the conflict in Ukraine, which is of existential importance for it, do detract from this objective and can be a limiting factor," he added.
France is a notable exception, given its established military presence in the Indian Ocean.
"France, with its presence in Reunion Island and Mayotte, is already cooperating with India in the Indian Ocean theater and this cooperation can be intensified," added Kumar.
Javed Ashraf, another Indian diplomat, said that France has been "a strong, trusted and consistent security partner across the full spectrum of defense cooperation."
"What makes the partnership easier is the acceptance that the two may not always agree or be in a position to cooperate," said Ashraf.
"France also stands out for India because [France] has currently no defense cooperation with Pakistan or with China."
EU disunited on security?
While France remains the EU's only nuclear power and maintains its strongest military force, a cooperation between Paris and New Delhi does not automatically translate into a coherent European security role across the Indo-Pacific.
"Europe as an entity has very little role in the Indo-Pacific security despite the announcement of a strategy in 2025," said Tara Kartha, a former member of India's National Security Council Secretariat.
She pointed to political differences among EU members as an obstacle to a coherent security outlook.
Those differences were on display during the EU's October 15–16 summit in Brussels, when leaders reaffirmed support for Ukraine, but also signaled disagreements over funding and national priorities.
What can EU offer to India?
This could also explain why, as India's defense ties with Europe keep expanding, much of that cooperation still takes place between New Delhi and individual European nations.
Germany, Spain, Italy and Poland have all emerged as important partners.
Ashraf said Brussels could signal broader support for its member states' partnerships with India and provide access to EU-funded programs, boosting cooperation in areas such as maritime security, space, critical minerals, chips and defense technologies.
"India is also becoming an important source of defense supplies for a re-arming Europe," the diplomat added.
There may also be opportunities to share experience in emerging areas of warfare.
"India could also access drone technology in light of valuable experience gained by Europeans in Ukraine," Kumar said.
Germany, the EU's largest economy, is another important part of this relationship. Alongside France, it has become a defense partner for India, including through major equipment purchases. India could push for its relationship with Berlin to include industrial partnerships and technology development.
But experts warn that closer defense ties should not be confused with a shared strategic outlook, as European countries have their own priorities.
Russia and China as major obstacles
The differences between Brussels and New Delhi are particularly clear when it comes to Russia and China.
India still relies heavily on Russian equipment and technology, even as it seeks to diversify its defense supplies. European governments, meanwhile, have been engaged in a tense standoff with Russia since its 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
That creates a problem for those seeking to deepen defense industry ties.
"Buying a few big-ticket defense items, such as Rafale fighter jets from France or submarines from Germany, is one thing," said Gulshan Sachdeva, a professor of European Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi.
"However, integrating India's defense industry into the expanding European defense value chain is more challenging as long as Russia remains Europe's principal security concern."
China presents a different but equally important challenge. For India, China is a rival and source of major security issues, including an ongoing border dispute. While the EU also sees China as a "systemic rival," its members differ in how they balance security concerns with their economic relationships with China.
These differences complicate attempts to develop a shared assessment of Indo-Pacific threats.
On a geopolitical level, India wants partnerships that strengthen its capabilities without requiring it to align fully with another power's strategic priorities. European governments are also weighing their regional ambitions against security demands closer to home.
Cooperation without a security umbrella
The new India-EU partnership creates a framework for closer engagement, but it does not amount to a joint security commitment.
Ashraf said the two sides could strengthen their mutual capabilities but were unlikely to exercise a visible influence on the global security order.
For now, maritime domain awareness, information-sharing, defense technology and selective industrial cooperation offer more realistic prospects than a common security role of the EU and India across the Indo-Pacific.

State-owned group to help set up Patriot missile maintenance hub in Poland
The Polish Armaments Group (PGZ) will be involved in establishing a maintenance centre for Patriot missiles in Poland, Finance and Economy Minister Andrzej Domanski announced on Wednesday.
Speaking at a press conference in Raciborz, Domanski described the project as a major investment.
"I hope this is the first step towards developing capabilities to service and manufacture missiles,” he said.
Domanski added that the details, including costs, deadlines and the final scope of the project, would be discussed with the US side.
PGZ has also confirmed that it is ready to contribute its expertise to the project. In a statement to PAP, PGZ said it had been actively involved in developing Poland's proposal to establish a European maintenance centre for PAC-3 missiles and would continue to support the initiative.
"The location of the centre and the precise roles of the participating companies will be agreed in close cooperation with the government and industrial partners. PGZ is ready to use its existing expertise and help further strengthen Europe's air and missile defence capabilities," the group said.
The US decision to establish a centre in Poland to service PAC-3 MSE missiles used in Patriot air defence systems was announced on Wednesday by Deputy Defence Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka. The location of the facility, the cost of construction and the expected launch date have yet to be decided.
She described the decision to locate the Patriot missile service centre in Poland as "historic".
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka told private broadcaster Polsat News on Wednesday that the investment was estimated to be worth around PLN 1 billion (EUR 226.7 million) and would take between 18 months and two years to complete. (PAP)

No Poles reported among Spain train crash victims, foreign ministry says
Poland's foreign ministry is checking reports of a fatal train crash in Spain, with no Polish casualties reported so far, ministry spokesman Maciej Wewior said on Wednesday.
Two passenger trains, including a high-speed one, collided on Wednesday morning near the Urda station in the Toledo province in central Spain, news agency EFE reported.
Spanish newspaper ABC, citing the country's Civil Defence Service, reported on Wednesday morning that at least 46 people had died in the collision on the Madrid-Andalusia route. The cause of the crash remains unknown.
In the early afternoon on Wednesday, Castilla-La Mancha regional government said the death toll increased to 64 people.
"We are checking media reports, and our consulate in Spain is active." Wewior told reporters. "As of now, there is no information about any Polish citizens being among the casualties."
Polish President Karol Nawrocki expressed his sadness about the tragic crash in a post on X on Wednesday.
"On behalf of the Polish people and on my own behalf, I offer my deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims. I wish all those injured a speedy recovery," Nawrocki wrote.
"In these painful moments, Poland mourns alongside the Spanish people. Our thoughts are with those who have lost their loved ones and with everyone affected by this tragedy," he added.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk reacted to the "devastating news from Spain" on X.
"I extend my deepest condolences to the families who have lost their loved ones and wish for a swift recovery of those injured. All Poles are with the Spanish people in this terrible time," he wrote.
Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski wrote on X on Wednesday that he was "deeply saddened by the tragic train accident in Spain".
"My heartfelt condolences go out to the families and loved ones of the victims. I wish all those injured a swift recovery. In these difficult moments, Poland stands in solidarity with Spain and its people. We stand with you," Sikorski wrote.
Polish Infrastructure Minister Dariusz Klimczak on Wednesday expressed his condolences to the families of those killed in the train crash. "My thoughts are also with the injured and everyone affected by this tragedy," he wrote on X.
Spain's Health Minister Monica Garcia told public radio station Cadena SER that the accident was "very serious".
Esther Padilla, a spokeswoman for the regional government of Castilla-La Mancha, which includes the Toledo province, confirmed that at least 10 people had died, the EFE reported.
Emergency services said two train carriages had fallen down an embankment. Numerous ambulances and helicopters were sent to the scene.
Nearby hospitals were getting ready to receive the injured on Wednesday morning, while authorities in Urda, near the crash site, were preparing a sports hall to accommodate casualties if necessary, at the request of the Civil Defence Service.
"I am deeply shocked by the serious train accident in Toledo province," Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez wrote on X. "My condolences, solidarity and support go out to all the victims and their families."
Political parties in Spain have cancelled events related to the ongoing election campaign. (PAP)

As North Korea’s Loudspeaker Broadcasts Loom, South Korea Has No Good Options
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:24:00 UTC
22:24:00 KST

On October 21, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, announced that loudspeakers for psychological warfare against South Korea would begin operations along the whole border before the end of the month, according to the North’s state-controlled Korean Central News Agency (KCNA). She made the announcement after inspecting fortification work at several border sites early that morning. The work followed a declaration by Kim Jong Un in late 2023 that the two Koreas were hostile states.
Pyongyang’s announcement about resuming the loudspeaker broadcasts came weeks after a land mine explosion in the southern border of the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) on September 21. Two blasts injured three South Korean soldiers in the DMZ, which divides the peninsula. On October 5, South Korean and United Nations Command investigators concluded that North Korea had planted the mines in violation of the Korean War armistice. However, Pyongyang has rejected the finding. In fact, Kim Yo Jong described the blasts in her statement of October 22 as a suspicious accident that South Korea created for itself.
A mine blast has led to loudspeaker use before. In 2015, land mines injured two South Korean soldiers, and Seoul turned its speakers back on for the first time in 11 years. The two Koreas agreed in 2018 to stop the broadcasts and took down their speakers. Under then-South Korean President Yoon Suk-yeol, Seoul resumed broadcasts in June 2024 in retaliation for trash balloons flown from North Korea.
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung chose the opposite course after taking office in 2025. He halted the broadcasts and began dismantling the speakers that August. North Korea stopped its own broadcasts around the same time. The blasts of September have put that policy under strain, as Pyongyang has pledged to resume broadcasts.
So far, Lee has answered the landmine explosion – and North Korea’s denial – with diplomacy. On October 22, his government sent a letter to the president of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC). The letter condemned North Korea for violating the armistice and called on Pyongyang to apologize. On October 25, North Korea replied with a letter of its own to the United Nations Security Council. The letter accused South Korean troops of firing warning shots at North Korean personnel and invoked the right of self-defense under the United Nations Charter.
In Seoul, the Defense Ministry ties its warning shots and broadcasts to a dispute over where the border line, formally known as the Military Demarcation Line (MDL), runs within the DMZ. On October 23, South Korea’s Defense Ministry proposed military talks to confirm where the MDL lies. The ministry had extended a similar offer in November 2025. Both times, North Korea ignored the proposal.
Instead, Pyongyang has decided to up the ante. Kim Yo Jong said North Korea’s resumption of loudspeaker broadcasts was retaliation for the South’s defense of the border.
While North Korea complains of “provocations” by the South, Lee is already under fire at home for not responding strongly enough. In an Armed Forces Day address on October 1, Lee expressed sorrow for the soldiers wounded in the landmine blast but did not blame North Korea. The leadership of the main opposition People Power Party (PPP) boycotted the ceremony in protest. On October 27, South Korean Unification Minister Chung Dong-young drew fire at a parliamentary audit for calling landmines defensive weapons.
Since then, the PPP has urged the government to restart loudspeaker broadcasts toward the North. Restarting the broadcasts would meet public demand for strong action against North Korea. Still, the move would undo the mutual halt that began in 2025. It would also let Pyongyang say that Seoul had started the loudspeaker war. As of this writing, the North Korean speakers are still silent, although locals reported hearing faint noises for four to five hours on the morning of October 29, in what Yonhap News Agency called “a test broadcast.”
Kim Yo Jong’s comments suggested that North Korea would resume broadcasts by October 31, the last day of the month. South Korea’s Defense Ministry has signaled that it would take a proportionate measure if the broadcasts begin. It has not specified what that measure would be.
Doing nothing has a cost of its own. Lee already faces accusations from the PPP that his government has deferred to North Korea. Talks would be the natural middle course, but Pyongyang has refused all requests for discussions. Nothing in the statements of Kim Yo Jong suggests that will change.
Instead, Pyongyang is seeking to impose its terms on the border unilaterally. Kim Yo Jong has cast the new North Korean fortification as a path to peace. According to her, a sealed border will lower the danger of military conflict. Her statement published on October 21 cited Kim Jong Un as wanting the border to be a lasting boundary. That leaves little hope that Pyongyang will agree to discuss the exact placement of the MDL with Seoul.
The loudspeakers are part of North Korea’s strategy. They are cheap for Pyongyang and force Seoul to respond. The older artillery that North Korea has placed in open view along its west coast serves the same purpose. On October 27, South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff described the guns as legacy systems rather than new weapons.
The timing may serve Pyongyang as well. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit opens in Shenzhen, China, on November 18. U.S. President Donald Trump has raised the prospect of meeting Kim Jong Un on the sidelines, although more recently he has voiced uncertainty about such a summit. If tension along the DMZ eases before then, it could look like a concession to Trump.
While the tensions between the two Koreas have risen, Kim Jong Un made an unexpected one-day trip to China. Accompanied by Kim Yo Jong, he visited the border city of Dandong on October 24 and returned home the same day. Neither side announced the trip in advance. Wang Huning, a member of the Standing Committee of the Politburo of the Chinese Communist Party, received him and conveyed greetings from Chinese leader Xi Jinping. No meeting with Xi was reported.
The trip came after several days of online rumors that Kim had died of a brain hemorrhage. In Seoul, the National Intelligence Service reportedly informed lawmakers on October 23 that the rumors were false.
Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said on October 27 that Kim and Chinese officials may have discussed talks with Washington. Cho also noted that Washington would prefer Seoul not to move too far ahead on potential North Korea-U.S. talks. North Korea official account of Kim’s trip mentioned neither talks with Washington nor the loudspeakers.
Whatever the motive, North Korea sets the tempo for engagement and tension alike, and Seoul can only react. Lee cannot ignore the loudspeakers, and every possible response – including no response at all – costs him something. Until Pyongyang agrees to talk, the Korean Peninsula is likely to drift toward more tension.
On a related note, Seoul’s JCS said on October 29 that North Korea fired a dozen of short-range ballistic missiles toward its east coast. According to the South’s military, the missiles were fired off from the Wonsan area around 12:30 p.m. KST, and flew about 250 km.

European Commission: Estonia among Europe's safest countries for road deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29

European Commission: Estonia among Europe's safest countries for road deaths
Estonia saw 43 road deaths last year, placing it sixth overall among Europe's safest countries, according to final European Commission figures for 2025.
This figure, at 31 deaths per million, puts it slightly ahead of Finland, Germany and the Netherlands and significantly better than Latvia and Lithuania.
Roads in built up areas of Estonia were, however, significantly safer than those in rural areas, and while the incidence of deaths on the roads continues to fall in Estonia, it is not falling at a rate fast enough to meet a state target of half of 2019's figure by or in 2030. Also, the first half of this year saw a rise in road deaths in Estonia.
Sweden and Norway recorded 19 road deaths per million in 2025, followed by Denmark and Switzerland at 24, and Iceland at 26.
These were the only countries to post figures better than Estonia's 31 per million. Estonia was followed by Malta and Ireland at 33, Finland, Germany and the Netherlands (all 34) and Spain at 36, according to figures published on Wednesday.
Lithuania posted 138 road deaths last year, or 48 per million, while Latvia's figure was 64 per million.
The other highest rates were seen in Serbia (75 per million), Bulgaria (71), Romania (68) and Croatia (67).
Across the EU, EFTA countries and Serbia, 19,350 people died on the roads last year, or 43 per million,
The Commission said road deaths across Europe fell 3 percent on year to 2025 (580 fewer), and by 15 percent compared with 2019 (3,400 fewer road traffic deaths).
The Commission noted that, however, compared with the EU average, Estonia had a higher share of fatal road accidents on roads outside urban areas.
Between 2019 and 2025 road deaths in Estonia fell 17 percent. This, the Commission says, suggests Estonia will likely not meet its 2030 target of halving road deaths compared with 2019, though the Commission noted that annual figures can fluctuate significantly given the country's small population and low number of deaths in absolute terms.
The same data shows that in the first months of 2026 road deaths in Estonia rose sharply again, by over 10 percent. ERR reported in August that 30 people had died on Estonian roads in the first seven months of this year, four more than in the same period a year earlier.
For Europe as a whole, preliminary 2026 data show that in the first half of the year more countries saw road deaths fall by more than 5 percent compared with the same period in 2025 than saw them rise. The overall trend is therefore positive, the Commission said.

The Regional Health Inspectorate in Vratsa has banned the use of tap water in Kozloduy for drinking and food preparation after tests found chromium concentrations above permitted levels, BNR reported.
Chavdar Manov, director of the Regional Health Inspectorate in Vratsa, issued the order following laboratory analyses that detected chromium levels between 81 and 97 micrograms per liter, above the maximum permissible limit of 50 micrograms per liter.
The local water utility must supply residents with water tankers. Water from the central supply network can be used only for household needs and hygiene, according to BNR.

Russia and India can help unlock Sierra Leone’s mineral wealth – minister (VIDEO)
The West African nation of Sierra Leone is looking to India and Russia for technology and expertise to process its mineral resources rather than remain a mere supplier to the world’s industrialized countries.
Sierra Leone wants to combine Russian mining expertise with Indian technology to develop its mineral wealth and expand domestic processing, the country’s Minister of Mines and Mineral Resources, Julius Daniel Mattai, told RT.
“Geology is not wealth,” the minister noted on the sidelines of the third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow on Wednesday. He argued that mineral resources must be combined with knowledge and effective governance to generate economic benefits. Sierra Leone is seeking investment and technology for this move.
More and more African leaders are emphasizing local processing as they push to move their economies up the industrial value chain. It was also raised at the summit by African Union chair Evariste Ndayishimiye, who called for partnerships that would help African countries manufacture finished products, RT reported on Wednesday.
'Sierra Leone is Looking to Combine Russian Know-How With Indian Tech Talent’ - Julius Daniel Mattai, 🇸🇱's Minister of Mines & Mineral Resources ‘If we combine Russian knowledge, resilience, technology, education, with the intellectual capacity and capabilities of India, that means we have good friends,’ Julius Daniel Mattai tells RT India, on the sidelines of the Russia-Africa summit.
— RT_India (@RT_India_news) October 28, 2026
“We cannot accept a future where Africa supplies the minerals … while value addition and manufacturing take place elsewhere,” South African President Cyril Ramaphosa told the BRICS summit in New Delhi last month.
Sierra Leone is preparing to sign a memorandum of understanding with the Russian State University for Geological Prospecting covering scholarships, staff exchanges, laboratory access, and technology transfer, Mattai said.
Russia’s expertise in geological data interpretation, mineral processing, smelting and refining could support Sierra Leone’s mining industry, Mattai said. He stressed that reliable energy would be essential to expanding domestic processing and manufacturing.
Sierra Leone also expressed interest in cooperation with Russia on rare earth minerals, with Mattai saying in June that deposits containing such minerals had been identified in the country.
India already has a presence in Sierra Leone’s mining and industrial sectors. An Indian company that initially used scrap metal to produce steel has secured a mining concession and plans to extract iron ore for domestic processing, Mattai told RT.
Indian companies are also active in information technology, digitalization, artificial intelligence, and solar energy, while educational institutions have been established with Indian involvement, he added.
Bilateral trade between India and Sierra Leone reached nearly $450 million in the financial year ended March 2026, according to India’s High Commission. Indian imports from Sierra Leone include minerals, ores, and metals.

A single brain signal may explain schizophrenia's most puzzling symptoms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:14:52 UTC
22:14:52 KST

A single brain signal may explain schizophrenia's most puzzling symptoms
- Date:
- October 29, 2026
- Source:
- McGill University
- Summary:
- Scientists have identified a weakened brain signal that may connect several seemingly unrelated symptoms of schizophrenia, including sensory processing difficulties, disorganized speech, and greater symptom severity. The surprising discovery could help explain the disorder's underlying mechanisms and potentially lead to earlier detection and new treatments.
- Share:
Scientists have identified a brain signal that may help explain why schizophrenia produces such a wide variety of symptoms, including difficulties with perception, movement, and speech. The discovery suggests that problems that appear unrelated could actually stem from a shared disruption in how the brain processes information.
Schizophrenia is a complex psychiatric disorder that can affect how people experience the world, interact with their surroundings, and communicate with others. These symptoms are typically studied as separate features of the condition, but new research suggests they may have more in common than previously recognized.
The study, published in Science Advances, was conducted by scientists from McGill University, the McConnell Brain Imaging Centre, the University of Montreal, the Research Centre of the University of Montreal Health Centre, and the Douglas Research Centre. Their findings point to a common brain mechanism that may help explain several distinct symptoms of schizophrenia.
A Weakened Brain Signal Links Multiple Schizophrenia Symptoms
To investigate this connection, researchers examined beta-band brain activity in 25 people diagnosed with schizophrenia and 25 healthy participants. Beta-band activity refers to rhythmic patterns of electrical activity in the brain that are involved in coordinating information processing, perception, and movement.
Participants completed tasks designed to test how accurately they could judge the timing of visual and auditory information. The researchers also analyzed their speech to look for signs of disorganized thinking and communication.
The results revealed a striking pattern. People with schizophrenia showed weaker and slower beta-band activity than those in the control group. More importantly, the participants with the most pronounced abnormalities in this brain signal also tended to have greater difficulty processing the timing of sights and sounds, more disorganized speech, and more severe clinical symptoms.
These three features of schizophrenia are usually investigated independently. Finding that they were all associated with changes in the same brain signal suggests that a shared underlying process may contribute to the disorder's diverse effects.
A New Window Into How the Brain Processes Reality
"This gives us early but compelling evidence that measuring the brain's operations, especially how it builds and revises its own model of the world, may help us appreciate that there is a common thread behind the confusing array of symptoms we see in disorders like schizophrenia," said Dr. Lena Palaniyappan, senior author of the study, Professor of Psychiatry at McGill and director of the Centre of Excellence in Youth Mental Health at the Douglas Hospital.
The brain constantly uses incoming sensory information to develop and update its understanding of the surrounding environment. This process helps people interpret what they see and hear, anticipate events, and coordinate their actions. The new findings suggest that disruptions in this process could help explain why schizophrenia affects several different aspects of behavior and perception.
The researchers used high-resolution magnetoencephalography, or MEG, to measure brain activity. This imaging technique detects the tiny magnetic fields generated by electrical activity in the brain, allowing scientists to track changes in neural signals with exceptional precision. The scans were performed at the McConnell Brain Imaging Centre at the Montreal Neurological Institute-Hospital (The Neuro).
"What struck us was that the same weakened brain signal kept showing up wherever we looked, whether patients were processing a sound, a sight or completing a movement," said Hsi (Tiana) Wei, lead author of the study and postdoctoral scholar in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and the Douglas Research Centre. "Seeing the same pattern across these different domains suggested there may be a common underlying process linking the symptoms."
Could the Discovery Help Detect Psychosis Earlier?
Beyond providing new insight into schizophrenia, the findings could eventually help researchers identify young people who are at greater risk of developing psychosis. Psychosis involves a disruption in how someone perceives or interprets reality and can include experiences such as hallucinations or delusions.
Early identification is particularly important because the first signs of schizophrenia often appear during adolescence but may go unrecognized for an extended period.
"The very first sign of schizophrenia begins in our adolescence, but this often gets missed for a long time. If this finding is confirmed in larger samples, we may have a potentially useful method to identify who, among youth seeking help for mental health, needs extra support to prevent psychosis," Palaniyappan said.
However, the researchers emphasized that the results are preliminary. The study included only 50 participants, and additional research involving larger, independent groups will be necessary to determine how reliably the brain signal is associated with speech disturbances and overall symptom severity.
"This is a first, modest-size study, and the associations with speech and clinical severity will need to be tested in larger independent samples before we can be confident in them," Wei said.
If future studies confirm the findings, measuring beta-band activity could potentially become a useful tool for identifying people who need earlier support. Wei also suggested that the brain signal may deserve investigation as a possible target for future schizophrenia treatments.
Story Source:
Materials provided by McGill University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Hsi T. Wei, Dominic Boutet, Rukun Dou, Jessica Ahrens, Nadia Zeramdini, Alban Voppel, Fernando Gonzales-Aste, Fatme Abboud, Sylvain Baillet, Lena Palaniyappan. Neurophysiological dynamics related to perception, action, and language in schizophrenia. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (43) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeh5819

Not just Batman and Superman: James Gunn reveals the plan for DCU
Kyiv • UNN
James Gunn explained the combination of standalone stories and a shared DC saga. The next Superman film will be released on July 9, 2027.
James Gunn once again defended his DC universe on Threads, and this time clarified his previously proposed eight-to-ten-year plan for developing the fictional world, more clearly outlining each character’s place in it. UNN reports this, citing Variety.
Details
"You can look at my quotes from January 2023, when we began working, and I said that we would do exactly what we are doing now," the head of DC Studios wrote in response to a since-deleted post.
"I said that some stories would stand alone, like the Guardians films (Clayface is exactly that), while some would be part of a larger narrative structure, which is the Superman saga. At the same time, every part of the larger story must work on its own, regardless of whether you need to watch everything else," Gunn noted.
In his second post, he continued: "There is also some conflation of different things happening here. The originally proposed ‘8-10 year roadmap’ included not only storylines (although that was part of it), but also a plan for DC’s development as a whole, including a focus on diamond characters (Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman), as well as lesser-known characters whom we could turn into diamonds (Krypto, John Stewart, Peacemaker), how we would foster filmmakers’ freedom and allow for different tones and ratings, the influence of ‘Star Wars’ and George R. R. Martin, and much more."
Gunn’s reference to the ‘8-10 year roadmap’ concerns a virtual Warner Bros. Discovery meeting in 2022 involving him and his co-chair, Peter Safran, where he said that they had developed an 8-10-year plan for DC’s development. In his third post, he added: "It’s exciting to see everything STARTING to come together, and all of this makes me even more interested in what we have in store for everyone in the film ‘Man of Tomorrow’."
On Saturday, Gunn took to social media to defend his decision to expand the DC universe through ‘standalone stories’ amid criticism of his films for not leading to a major crossover.
Responding to a commenter who noted that Gunn did not necessarily have to lay the foundation for one fully interconnected universe, he wrote: "I completely agree. The DC Universe is just an alternative universe; we can enter it at any place or time and tell that story. I don’t like the idea that individual stories have no meaning if they don’t lead to something else. I’m surprised people don’t understand this, because ‘Star Wars’ has essentially been doing this for 50 years in films, series, games, and books—albeit without a diversity of tone," he wrote.
Gunn’s next film, ‘Superman: Man of Tomorrow,’ will be released in theaters on July 9, 2027.

Shell rakes in $12B profit as Middle East war drives up prices
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Oil and gas giant Shell has recorded $10.8 billion in adjusted quarterly profits – double what it made in the same period last year – as war in the Middle East boosts energy prices.
Since the US and Israel began attacking Iran this year, Shell’s fuel products have risen in value, largely due to strikes on competing refineries in the region that produce petrol and diesel.
The corporation, which moved its headquarters out of The Hague to London in 2022, made record profits after Russia invaded Ukraine the same year, and has seen profits surge again since the outbreak of war with Iran.
MPs have called for a windfall tax to prevent Shell or other energy conglomerates from profiting from geopolitical conflict.
Shell’s move to London makes placing a levy on the profits harder, however, and the European Commission has also ruled out an EU-wide windfall tax, saying it’s a matter for individual nations.

Russian Help Would Make North Korea’s Missile-test Flurry Worse News
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:09:00 UTC
22:09:00 KST

North Korea has conducted a flurry of missile tests in the past few weeks. One of the biggest concerns is that Russia may have helped. Advances in North Korean missile technology are unwelcome in themselves, but any Russian technical backing behind the effort would indicate a tightening of the Moscow-Pyongyang partnership – and greater potential for more North Korean advances.
There have been at least four sets of North Korean missile launches in the past few weeks. On September 20, North Korea tested a new missile, thought to carry a hypersonic warhead. According to a South Korean report, North Korea’s Korea Central News Agency (KCNA) provided no details of the missile tested, but wording on the photo caption released by the agency referred to the “Hwasongpho-11Ma-1 flight trajectory.” So it is likely to be an “upgraded version of the Hwasong-11MA” hypersonic missile that North Korea first showcased in 2025. South Korean security analysts believe the Hwasongpho-11Ma-1 “combines a KN-23, or Hwasong-11Ga, missile body with a hypersonic glide vehicle-type terminal section.” They describe it as “a long-range precision-strike weapon designed to penetrate missile defenses through maneuverability while striking targets several hundred kilometers away.”
Two weeks later, on October 3, North Korea fired an intermediate-range missile into the waters off its east coast. According to the Asia-Pacific Security Magazine, the KCNA characterized it as another hypersonic missile test. The KCNA reportedly claimed that the missile had struck a target 1,000 km away, though both South Korea and Japan suggested a smaller range. The North Korean leader’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, also claimed that the missile could “maneuver at low altitude and incorporated unspecified artificial intelligence capabilities intended to complicate interception.” Maneuvering is a characteristic of a hypersonic missile. Kim also asserted the inability of Japan and South Korea to arrive at an accurate picture of the flight details, saying that “whenever we applied the wavelike trajectory mode to missiles, the enemy failed to track the targets from their first skip points.” More worryingly, she also described the missile as “strategic,” implying it was designed to deliver nuclear warheads.
About a week later, on October 12, North Korea reportedly launched multiple ballistic missiles of different types. The missiles were fired off its east coast, with at least one type flying more than 900 km, according to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff.
And on October 14 came news, credited to the KCNA, about North Korea test-firing two kinds of submarine-launched cruise missiles. These appear to have been fired from the Hero Kim Kun Ok, a submarine that was launched in 2023. There has been some skepticism about the capability of this submarine, but if this was the actual launch platform, this North Korean capability should be treated seriously. Previous underwater missile launches had been from a testbed rather than an operational submarine.
These launches raise concerns about how North Korea managed to make such rapid progress in missile technologies. Many security analysts have attributed North Korean progress to the closer relationship between North Korea and Russia. If they’re right, then we have more reason to expect rapid North Korean technical progress.
North Korea extended military assistance to Moscow following the invasion of Ukraine. In return, North Korea reaped economic benefits and access to military technologies. According to a South Korean think tank, Pyongyang’s arms sales and troop deployment generated more than $10 billion for North Korea, which is huge for a country whose GDP is around $27 billion. Most of this payment was in the form of sensitive military technology, weapon parts, or other materials. Studies also note that Russian companies Novator and Raduga could be assisting North Korea in further advancing the development of new cruise missiles of the Hwasal family.
Beyond missiles, North Korea appears to have gained access to other critical technologies from Russia. South Korea’s military has intelligence hinting at Russia supplying North Korea with submarine nuclear propulsion technology. South Korean Defense Minister Ahn Gyu-back revealed this in the parliament’s Defense Committee hearing in October 2025. Although the South Korean intelligence has not yet been verified, there is a reasonable suspicion that Moscow may have supplied two or three propulsion sets from its own decommissioned nuclear submarines. Some reports have also indicated the possibility of Russia providing North Korea with submarine noise-suppression technology.
In addition, Russia is known to have shared drone technology with North Korea. But the growing concern is that Pyongyang could gain access to more advanced and sophisticated drones that could be AI-enabled and jet-powered, such as the Geran-5. Further, North Korea’s Geumseong series tactical attack drones bear a close resemblance to Russian (and Israeli) types, which raises the strong possibility of Russian technology transfers to North Korea.
This article was originally published in ASPI’s The Strategist.

Details: According to DIU, Russia has lost 43 Su-34 aircraft destroyed since the start of the full-scale invasion, while another seven have been damaged.

"Despite significant combat losses, Russia continues to produce and modernise the Su-34, attempting to maintain the size of its aircraft fleet and sustain the intensity of its missile and bomb strikes," the intelligence agency emphasised.
Meanwhile, according to DIU, Russia's ability to further expand this capability depends on production capacity, the availability of technological components and the Russian military industry's ability to compensate for its losses.
Background: In October, Russian state corporation Rostec announced that a new batch of Su-34 aircraft had been delivered to the Russian Aerospace Forces. The number of aircraft delivered was not specified.

Turnover totaled NT$789.2 billion (US$24.4 billion). The total market capitalization of listed companies stood at NT$151.8 trillion, according to the Taiwan Stock Exchange.
All of the index's most heavily weighted stocks closed lower. TSMC fell 0.41% to NT$2,415, according to Yahoo Stocks.
MediaTek lost 4.49% to NT$4,045, while Foxconn declined 1.39% to NT$248. Delta Electronics fell 4.52% to NT$1,480, and ASEdropped 1.73% to NT$683.

UMC closed at its daily limit-down, while Vanguard International Semiconductor fell 6.57% and Mosel Vitelic declined 5.28%, according to Sinotrade.

This suggested that buying interest remained weak at higher price levels and that broader market momentum had yet to recover, according to CTEE.

Lower volume and easing selling pressure near that level could signal stabilization, while a break below it on higher volume could point to further losses and a prolonged correction.

Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:04:04 UTC
22:04:04 KST

Six popular sugar substitutes linked to faster brain aging
- Date:
- October 29, 2026
- Source:
- American Academy of Neurology
- Summary:
- A study of nearly 13,000 adults found that people consuming the most artificial sweeteners experienced a 62% faster decline in memory and thinking skills, equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of brain aging. Six popular sweeteners were linked to faster cognitive decline, raising concerns about the long-term brain health effects of common sugar substitutes, although causation was not established.
- Share:
Sugar substitutes are often promoted as a healthier way to enjoy sweet foods and drinks without consuming as much sugar. However, new research suggests that some of these widely used sweeteners may have an unexpected downside for long-term brain health.
A study published in Neurology, the medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology, found that people who consumed the most low- and no-calorie sweeteners experienced significantly faster declines in memory and thinking skills than those who consumed the least. The association was particularly pronounced among people with diabetes.
Researchers examined seven sweeteners commonly used in foods and beverages: aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, xylitol, sorbitol and tagatose. These ingredients frequently appear in ultra-processed products, including diet sodas, flavored waters, energy drinks, yogurt and low-calorie desserts. Some are also sold separately for sweetening foods and beverages.
"Low- and no-calorie sweeteners are often seen as a healthy alternative to sugar; however, our findings suggest certain sweeteners may have negative effects on brain health over time," said study author Claudia Kimie Suemoto, MD, PhD, of the University of São Paulo in Brazil.
Importantly, the findings show an association rather than a proven cause-and-effect relationship. Researchers cannot conclude from this study that consuming these sweeteners directly damages the brain or causes memory loss.
Study Tracks Nearly 13,000 Adults for Eight Years
To investigate whether sugar substitutes might be connected to cognitive health, researchers analyzed data from 12,772 adults across Brazil. Participants were 52 years old on average when the study began and were followed for approximately eight years.
At the beginning of the study, participants completed detailed dietary questionnaires describing the foods and drinks they had consumed during the previous year. Researchers used these responses to estimate each person's daily intake of the seven sweeteners.
Participants were then separated into three groups according to how much of the sweeteners they consumed. Those in the lowest consumption group averaged 20 milligrams per day (mg/day), while those in the highest group averaged 191 mg/day. For comparison, 191 milligrams of aspartame is roughly the amount found in one can of diet soda.
Of the seven sweeteners examined, sorbitol had the highest average intake, at 64 mg/day. Sorbitol belongs to a category of sweeteners called sugar alcohols, which provide sweetness and are commonly used as sugar substitutes.
Throughout the study, participants completed cognitive assessments at three points: the beginning, middle, and end. These tests measured several abilities essential for everyday mental functioning, including memory, language, and the speed at which the brain processes information.
Researchers evaluated verbal fluency, or the ability to quickly retrieve and produce words, along with working memory, which allows people to temporarily hold and use information. They also tested word recall and processing speed to determine how these abilities changed over time.
High Sweetener Consumption Linked to 62% Faster Cognitive Decline
The results revealed a striking difference between people who consumed the most sweeteners and those who consumed the least.
After accounting for factors that could influence cognitive health, including age, sex, high blood pressure, and cardiovascular disease, researchers found that participants in the highest consumption group experienced a 62% faster decline in overall thinking and memory abilities compared with those in the lowest group.
That difference was equivalent to approximately 1.6 additional years of cognitive aging over the study period.
Even moderate consumption was associated with measurable differences. Participants in the middle group experienced a 35% faster decline than those consuming the least, equivalent to roughly 1.3 additional years of cognitive aging.
These estimates describe changes in cognitive test performance rather than a direct measurement of biological brain aging. They also do not mean that everyone who consumes artificial sweeteners will experience memory problems.
Stronger Links Found in Adults Under 60 and People With Diabetes
When researchers examined different age groups, they discovered that the association was not consistent across all participants.
Among adults younger than 60, higher sweetener consumption was linked to faster declines in verbal fluency and overall cognitive performance. However, researchers did not find a similar association among participants older than 60.
The relationship was also stronger in people with diabetes than in those without the condition. This finding is especially relevant because people with diabetes frequently turn to sugar substitutes to help manage their sugar intake.
Examining the sweeteners individually revealed another important distinction. Six of the seven substances were associated with faster declines in overall cognitive performance, particularly memory.
Those six were aspartame, saccharin, acesulfame-K, erythritol, sorbitol and xylitol.
Tagatose was the exception. Researchers found no association between its consumption and cognitive decline in this study. However, that finding does not establish that tagatose protects the brain or is necessarily safer than other sweeteners.
Should People Rethink Artificial Sweeteners?
The findings raise important questions about whether replacing sugar with low-calorie alternatives always delivers the health benefits consumers expect, particularly when it comes to the brain.
"While we found links to cognitive decline for middle-aged people both with and without diabetes, people with diabetes are more likely to use artificial sweeteners as sugar substitutes," Suemoto said. "More research is needed to confirm our findings and to investigate if other refined sugar alternatives, such as applesauce, honey, maple syrup or coconut sugar, may be effective alternatives."
Researchers also acknowledged several limitations. The analysis did not cover every artificial sweetener available on the market, so the findings cannot necessarily be applied to all sugar substitutes.
In addition, dietary information came from participants' own recollections of what they had eaten and drunk. Because people may forget foods, underestimate portions, or inaccurately report their habits, these estimates may not perfectly reflect actual sweetener consumption.
The observational design also means that other factors could help explain the relationship between sweetener intake and cognitive decline, despite researchers' efforts to account for several important health differences.
Further studies will be needed to determine whether the sweeteners themselves contribute to changes in brain function, why certain groups appear more strongly affected, and whether different sugar alternatives produce different long-term outcomes.
The research was supported by the Brazilian Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Science, Technology, and Innovation, and the National Council for Scientific and Technological Development.
Story Source:
Materials provided by American Academy of Neurology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal References:
- Natalia Gomes Gonçalves, Euridice Martinez-Steele, Paulo A. Lotufo, Isabela Bensenor, Alessandra C. Goulart, Sandhi Maria Barreto, Luana Giatti, Carolina Perim de Faria, Maria del Carmen Bisi Molina, Paulo Caramelli, Dirce Maria Marchioni, Claudia Kimie Suemoto. Association Between Consumption of Low- and No-Calorie Artificial Sweeteners and Cognitive Decline. Neurology, 2025; 105 (7) DOI: 10.1212/WNL.0000000000214023
- Thomas Monroe Holland. The Dark Side of Sweet. Neurology, 2025; 105 (7) DOI: 10.1212/WNL.0000000000214129

Bulgaria Has EU’s Widest Rich-Poor Gap in Healthcare Costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:03:00 UTC
22:03:00 KST

Bulgaria has the European Union’s widest income-based gap in the share of people who consider medical care a heavy financial burden, with 42.5% of those in the lowest income group reporting this difficulty compared with 9.7% of the wealthiest according to Eurostat data for 2025.
The difference of 32.8 percentage points is the largest among EU member states, indicating a pronounced disparity in how households with different financial means experience healthcare costs.
Across the EU, 18.7% of people in the lowest income group said medical expenses placed a heavy burden on their finances, compared with 8.5% among those with the highest incomes. The resulting gap of 10.2 percentage points is more than three times smaller than Bulgaria’s.
Latvia recorded the next-largest difference between the two income groups, at 26.1 percentage points, followed by Italy at 22.5 points and Romania at 20.1 points. Spain had the smallest gap, at just 0.9 percentage points.
However, Italy’s figures show that financial pressure from healthcare expenses can also affect wealthier people. There, 25.1% of those in the highest income group reported a heavy financial burden, while the share in Poland reached 20.6%. In contrast, the figure was below 3% among the wealthiest residents of eight EU countries. The lowest proportions, at 1% or less, were recorded in the Netherlands, Finland, and Estonia.
The figures distinguish between the overall level of financial hardship and the difference between income groups. Bulgaria does not necessarily have the highest proportion of people struggling with medical expenses across every income category, but it has the widest divide between its poorest and wealthiest residents, giving the issue a particularly pronounced social dimension.
Poverty further widens the gap
Eurostat data for 2025 also show a difference in the financial burden of medical care between people at risk of poverty and those outside that category. Across the EU, 19.1% of people at risk of poverty reported that healthcare costs placed a heavy strain on their finances, compared with 12.5% of those not at risk, a gap of 6.6 percentage points.
In Bulgaria, the difference reached 23.1 percentage points, the largest in the EU. Latvia followed with 18 percentage points, Romania with 16.8 points, and Italy with 13.3 points. Spain and Slovenia recorded almost no difference between the two groups.
Italy had the highest proportion of people at risk of poverty who reported a heavy financial burden from medical care, at 47.6%. Slovenia recorded the lowest share, at 5.6%. Among people not at risk of poverty, the figures ranged from 34.3% in Italy to 2.8% in Estonia.
The Bulgarian figures point to a concentration of financial pressure among people with limited incomes. Although the statistics do not establish what causes the disparity, they show that healthcare expenses affect income groups unequally.
Health difficulties also reflect social differences
The study also assessed difficulties with basic daily activities. Across the EU, 24.9% of people at risk of poverty reported moderate or severe problems with walking, compared with 16.9% of those outside this group, a difference of 8 percentage points.
Problems with memory and concentration were reported by 20.6% of people at risk of poverty and 14.5% of those not in that category, a gap of 6.1 percentage points.
These figures add to the picture of social vulnerability, as people with lower incomes more frequently report both limitations in everyday activities and serious financial difficulties in paying for medical care. The data do not establish a direct causal relationship between these circumstances but show that they occur within the same social group.
The study draws on the European Union Statistics on Income and Living Conditions (EU-SILC) and covers 2025. Its target population consists of people living in private households, while those residing in institutions are generally excluded.
The comparison places Bulgaria first in the EU for the difference between the lowest and highest income groups in the share reporting that medical care represents a heavy financial burden. The 32.8-percentage-point gap highlights the role of income in access to affordable healthcare, as well as the challenges households face in protecting themselves financially against health-related expenses.

The grammar of political hate? How a single word choice predicts nastier Facebook comment sections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:00:50 UTC
22:00:50 KST

Subtle grammatical choices in political social media posts are linked to how much hostility users express in the comment sections below them. A large-scale analysis of Facebook discussions published in Social Psychological and Personality Science indicates that posts referring to political groups with nouns rather than adjectives, or making sweeping generalizations about a party, tend to attract a higher proportion of prejudiced replies. Although the effect of any single post is small, the findings suggest that everyday wording habits online could gradually contribute to political division.
Hostility between opposing party supporters, which social scientists call affective polarization, has risen in the United States and several other democracies. Affective polarization refers to the tendency for citizens to view members of an opposing political party with dislike and distrust while favoring their own political group. At high levels, this animosity can lead voters to treat political rivals as enemies rather than fellow citizens, a dynamic linked to eroding trust in democratic institutions.
Sorting people into “us” versus “them” naturally creates some group bias, yet the intensity of that bias depends heavily on a psychological concept known as entitativity. Entitativity describes the extent to which an observer perceives a collection of people as a unified, tightly knit whole rather than a loose assortment of individuals. Supporting this idea, a 2018 meta-analysis of 33 samples found that the more people view an outside group as a coherent entity, the more prejudice they tend to hold toward its members. In politics, research has indicated that believing partisans are fundamentally different kinds of people was linked to greater partisan hostility, through more blame and assumed malicious intent, whereas believing political views themselves are fixed was linked to less.
“In essence, perceiving a group as entitative makes group members appear more interchangeable,” study author Carsten W. Sander, a research associate at Humboldt University of Berlin who conducted the research at Universität Hamburg with co-author Juliane Degner, a professor of social psychology there, told PsyPost. “People then generalize one member’s behavior to the whole group, retaliate against one group member for offenses committed by another, and generally show more outgroup prejudice. We reasoned that this could also fuel political polarization, understood as growing prejudice toward the political outparty.”
Because national political parties contain millions of people, citizens cannot observe an entire party firsthand and instead rely on media and conversation to judge how unified the other side is. Beyond explicit statements about a group, grammatical structures can quietly signal uniformity. One such cue is whether a writer uses a noun label, such as “Senate Republicans,” or an adjective label, such as “Republican senators.” Using a noun defines a person primarily by a single group category, whereas an adjective treats party affiliation as just one trait among many.
Controlled experiments show that these grammatical distinctions shape how people judge unfamiliar or minority groups. For instance, a 2020 study of print news readers found that articles describing an ethnic minority member with a noun rather than an adjective led readers to express slightly greater prejudice toward that entire minority group, whether the story was positive or negative.
A second cue involves generic statements, which are broad claims attributing an enduring trait to a group as an abstract whole, such as “Democrats want climate action,” rather than non-generic phrasing like “some Democrats want climate action.” In a 2010 experimental study of children and adults, participants who learned about a fictional animal category through generic statements were more likely to treat its members as sharing the same underlying nature, though the effect was weaker in children.
Most evidence on noun labels and generic phrasing comes from laboratory studies involving fictional or unfamiliar categories. Sander and Degner wanted to test whether these subtle wording differences also influence hostility toward established political groups like U.S. Democrats and Republicans in real-world online conversations. The authors noted that the relative frequency of partisan noun labels in U.S. online news has risen substantially in recent years, raising the question of how such language plays out on social media.
To examine this in a natural setting, the researchers gathered public Facebook posts and comments through the Meta Content Library. They selected Facebook because it has a diverse American user base and frequently hosts text-based political discussions. After excluding posts in which party labels referred to institutions or events rather than people (such as “the Democratic Party” or “the Republican primary”), the final sample included 45,780 posts and 769,684 direct replies written by 391,386 unique users across 3,878 pages and profiles. News media outlets contributed the largest share of posts, alongside public figures, politicians, and government officials.
To analyze hundreds of thousands of messages, the authors fine-tuned five artificial intelligence models built on transformer architectures, which are machine-learning programs that process language by evaluating how words relate in context. They trained and tested these models on thousands of human-coded examples, supplemented for two of the models with 600 synthetic posts written in matched pairs that differed in only one feature. One model classified whether a post used a party label as a noun (such as “voting Democrats”) or an adjective (such as “Democratic voters”). A second model identified whether the post made a broad generic claim about a group as a whole or a non-generic statement limited by qualifiers or referring to a single past action.
To account for other factors that might provoke angry replies, the models also tracked whether each post referred to a single individual, a subgroup (such as “House Republicans”), or the broader party, and whether the original post itself expressed hostility toward a political party. A separate model evaluated all 769,684 comments to detect partisan prejudice, defined as dislike or negativity aimed at a political group or collective target (such as “Dems are the worst” or “Idiots!”), while excluding remarks aimed only at a single person (such as “I hate Biden”). The researchers publicly registered their hypotheses and analysis plan in advance.
The researchers then used multilevel statistical models to test whether the wording of a specific post predicted the proportion of prejudiced comments below it. Comparing different posts published on the exact same Facebook page allowed the analysis to account for unmeasured differences between pages and their audiences. Across all 45,780 posts, posts using noun labels received a higher proportion of prejudiced comments than posts on the same page using adjective labels. Before controls, the odds that any given comment expressed partisan prejudice were 1.39 times higher beneath noun-label posts than beneath adjective-label posts, an odds ratio that fell to 1.15 after controlling for post prejudice and whether the target was an individual, subgroup, or whole party.
In practical terms, on a typical Facebook page where 59 percent of posts used noun labels, the model predicted that 16.7 percent of comments under a noun-label post would express partisan prejudice, compared with 14.8 percent under an adjective-label post. That is an absolute difference of 1.9 percentage points, or a relative difference of about 13 percent. By contrast, a page’s overall average use of noun labels across all its posts was not a statistically significant predictor of comment prejudice after controls were added, which the authors interpret as a sign that commenters were responding to the wording of the specific post, though they caution that comparisons between pages are vulnerable to hidden differences.
For their second main analysis, the authors tested generic language across the 26,026 posts and 437,744 comments that referred to political groups or subgroups rather than specific individuals. Posts using party labels generically drew a higher share of prejudiced replies than non-generic posts, with an odds ratio of 1.22 before adjustments and 1.20 after controlling for noun usage, post prejudice, and whether the post targeted a subgroup or the broader party.
On a typical page where 29 percent of posts were generic, the predicted probability of a prejudiced comment was 22.2 percent under generic posts versus 19.2 percent under non-generic posts, an absolute difference of 3.0 percentage points or a relative difference of roughly 16 percent. At the page level, pages that posted generic statements more often actually drew somewhat fewer prejudiced comments once other factors were accounted for, a pattern the authors attribute to other differences between pages rather than to the wording itself.
In that second analysis, noun labels continued to independently predict higher rates of prejudiced comments alongside generic phrasing, indicating that each feature was linked to online hostility on its own. Supplementary analyses also showed that these patterns held true whether posts mentioned Democrats or Republicans. Even when comparing different comments written by the exact same user across multiple posts, noun and generic labels still predicted more prejudiced replies, which the authors interpret as a sign that the language affected how users commented rather than merely attracting already hostile users.
These findings align with a study covered by PsyPost in early 2024, which found that broad generic statements about political parties led people to perceive a wider ideological gap between Democrats and Republicans than statements containing qualifiers like “some.” That earlier research measured perceived ideological divides in survey experiments, whereas the new study indicates that generic phrasing is also linked to hostile expressions in real-world social media discussions.
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. Because the study observed existing social media activity rather than randomly assigning different wordings to readers, it cannot establish with certainty that grammatical labels directly caused the increase in prejudiced replies. In addition, the study only captured whether someone wrote a hostile comment in the moment, leaving open whether noun or generic labels create lasting attitude shifts or briefly trigger existing frustrations.
“The key caveat is that the findings are observational,” Sander explained. “Features of the post content that we didn’t control for could be driving both the labeling and the prejudiced comments, so the results shouldn’t be read as showing that labels cause prejudice.” Still, he added, “our results and earlier experimental research are consistent with that possibility.”
The automated classifiers were also imperfect. In test data, the model that detected prejudiced comments caught about 73 percent of them, and about 68 percent of the comments it flagged were truly prejudiced, so some misclassification is likely.
Another caveat is that the statistical effects of a single post’s wording are small, and subtle cues from nouns or generic statements might be overshadowed by explicit news about party infighting or unanimous votes. At the same time, the authors propose that labeling habits could spread through social networks, as one person’s phrasing influences another’s, a possibility they say still needs testing. They also argue that even if a post only briefly nudges a few users to leave hostile replies, those comments remain visible on the page, where they could give other readers an exaggerated impression of how much the opposing party dislikes them.
“The effects were small: about 15% prejudiced comments under adjective labels versus 17% under noun labels,” Sander said. “If they turn out to be causal, though, they could nevertheless matter in practice: Labeling choices by high-reach news outlets could affect very large audiences, and small effects may accumulate as people read many posts over time.”
To test whether changing how parties are labeled actually reduces online hostility, the researchers hope to evaluate these wording variations in real-world trials over extended periods. “The next step would be an experimental replication, for example in collaboration with an online news outlet that would let us randomly vary the labeling in its social media posts, as this would allow us to establish causality,” Sander noted.
Future studies could also examine whether shifting toward adjective labels, qualifiers like “some,” or person-first phrasing such as “people who voted Republican” helps cool down political comment sections. Researchers might additionally test whether describing discrete past actions, such as “Republicans voted,” rather than permanent group traits, such as “Republicans are,” tempers partisan animosity.
The study, “Constructing the Enemy: Noun and Generic Party Labels Predict Partisan Prejudice in Social Media Comments,” was authored by Carsten W. Sander and Juliane Degner.

China’s fourth aircraft carrier, widely believed to be the country’s first with a nuclear-powered system, could launch as early as next year, according to US researchers, as Beijing pursues a fleet capable of projecting naval and air power far beyond its shores.
A launch in 2027 would coincide with the centenary of the People’s Liberation Army, with the anniversary falling on August 1. Beijing has previously used major military anniversaries to showcase developments in its armed forces.
