AI is changing the way we think. The question is whether we’ll notice in time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

AI is changing the way we think. The question is whether we’ll notice in time
Artificial intelligence promises to make life easier. With a few keystrokes, it can write emails, summarize reports, generate ideas and answer complex questions in seconds. For many people, it feels like a technological leap on par with the arrival of the internet itself.
But according to neuroscientist David Rock, the bigger question is not what AI is doing for us. It is what it might be doing to us.
“In some ways, technology isn't changing us at all,” Mr. Rock told us.
Human brains still make decisions, solve problems and respond to challenges much as they have for thousands of years. Yet history shows that major events and long-term pressures can leave lasting marks on the brain, shaping behaviour for years or even generations.
The great paradox of AI
Today’s technological revolution may be one of those moments.
The difference, Mr. Rock argues, is that technology increasingly gives us a sense of control over almost everything. Need a ride? Press a button. Want dinner delivered? Press another. Looking for information? It is available instantly.
That growing sense of autonomy can be liberating. But it also creates a subtle trap, especially as AI systems become capable of performing tasks that once required significant mental effort.
‘Keep your brain in the game’
The real concern is not that AI is becoming more powerful. It is that people are becoming too willing to hand over their thinking.
Mr. Rock recently described the current moment as a transition from “AI FOMO” to an “AI hangover”. Organizations rushed to adopt generative AI tools, often before fully understanding their long-term effects. Now the consequences are becoming clearer.
What he sees worries him.
A small minority of workers, perhaps five to 10 per cent, are using AI as intended: offloading routine tasks and freeing up mental capacity for more demanding work. Most, however, are doing the opposite.
Change has never been this fast, but it will never be this slow again – Dr. David Rock
“The brain loves conserving energy,” he said. “It’s very tantalizing to save your brain from thinking at all.”
The result, he warns, is a gradual erosion of judgment. When people outsource not only routine work but also analysis, evaluation and decision-making, they risk losing the ability to distinguish good ideas from bad ones.
AI may provide answers quickly, but speed is not the same as wisdom.
“Keep your brain in the game,” he said. “When your brain’s not in the game, you very quickly lose those skills.”
A crisis of attention
The rise of AI comes at a time when many people are already struggling to focus.
According to Mr. Rock, the greatest challenge facing workers today is not a lack of information but an overwhelming excess of it.
He compares the current moment to the arrival of email, which dramatically increased the amount of information people had to process. Today, however, the scale is far greater. Workers are bombarded by messages, updates, notifications and AI-generated summaries, often far beyond what the human brain can realistically manage.
“Our brains actually have real limits,” he said.
Computers can process thousands of decisions in moments. Humans cannot. Yet many organizations continue to operate as though people have unlimited capacity for attention and decision-making.
Mr. Rock believes society is still in a “settling-in period” with AI, much like the early days of automobiles before traffic laws and speed limits existed. The technology has arrived faster than the social norms and guardrails needed to use it responsibly.
The technology that wants to be your friend
Unlike previous technological breakthroughs, AI may be transforming something even more fundamental than work.
“It hacks attachment,” Mr. Rock said.
While televisions, books and smartphones competed for our attention, AI increasingly competes for our relationships. More and more people are turning to chatbots not merely for information but for conversation, companionship and advice.
That trend concerns him.
Research, he noted, suggests that people who spend significant time interacting with AI companions may feel more lonely rather than less. Other studies point to links between heavy reliance on chatbots and increased disconnection from real-world social interactions.
The human brain evolved around relationships with other people. Replacing too much of that interaction with machines may come at a psychological cost that society is only beginning to understand.
As AI becomes more sophisticated, and as robotics, faster computing and next-generation internet technologies converge, those questions are likely to become even more pressing.
Why human connection may become more valuable
Paradoxically, the more capable machines become, the more valuable human relationships could become.
Mr. Rock believes the future will place a premium on trust, authenticity and genuine human connection. In a world where machines can generate content, analyse data and imitate conversation, what remains uniquely human may become more precious.
“The human experience is going to be that much more high value,” he said.
Rather than replacing people, AI may ultimately increase the importance of human networks, deeper relationships and meaningful collaboration.
That future is not guaranteed. But it is one possible response to a world of accelerating technological change.
And acceleration is exactly what Mr. Rock expects.
“Change has never been this fast,” he said, “but it will never be this slow again.”
The skill that may matter most
So how can people adapt?
Mr. Rock's answer comes down to a single concept: metacognition, or thinking about thinking.
Instead of allowing AI to take over, he argues that people should remain firmly in control, using these systems to challenge and expand their perspectives rather than replace them.
AI can help people consider viewpoints they might otherwise overlook, test assumptions and explore alternative interpretations. But the responsibility for judgment must remain human.
He calls this approach “human in the lead”.
The technology, he says, works best when it deepens thinking rather than substitutes for it.
As AI becomes woven into everyday life, that distinction could prove critical. The machines may become smarter and faster, but the challenge for humanity will be ensuring that our own minds remain engaged.
Because the future may depend not on how intelligent AI becomes, but on whether we continue exercising the intelligence we already have.
Dr. David Rock, who coined the term “neuroleadership”, is the co-founder and CEO of the NeuroLeadership Institute, a global consultancy that applies neuroscience to leadership and organizational performance. Author of several books, including the bestseller Your Brain at Work and his latest, Your Story Has a Villain, he is one of the keynote speakers at UN Skills Fest 2026, themed People at the Centre.

Lithuania to introduce universal military conscription in 2032, president says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:55:00 UTC
20:55:00 KST

Lithuania plans to introduce universal military conscription in 2032, requiring a larger number of young people to serve in the armed forces amid security concerns, President Gitanas Nausėda said Thursday.
The State Defence Council, which comprises the country’s political and military leadership, agreed on the timeline at a meeting, Nausėda told reporters afterward.
Women would continue to be able to perform military service on a voluntary basis, he said.
Lithuania currently drafts more than 5,000 young people into the armed forces each year. Under universal conscription, the annual number would rise to about 7,500, accounting for demographic trends and the fact that some young people are deemed medically unfit for service, the president said.
Nausėda said the 2032 target would give the country time to invest in adequate accommodation for the larger number of conscripts and train enough instructors.
The authorities also need to balance conscript training with refresher training for reserve personnel to ensure both are carried out effectively, he said.
“I think implementing conscription from 2032 is optimal,” Nausėda said.
According to Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius, the government wanted a quicker transition to universal conscription, but were convinced by the military to push back the date to 2032.
“You could say there is political will, but at the same time, there is the question of the military’s readiness. The military has clearly stated that they would be ready by 2032,” Sinkevičius told reporters after Thursday’s State Defence Council meeting.
The date for introducing universal conscription was discussed “at length and in detail, with lively debates” at the council, the PM said.
“Everyone agreed that this isn’t a race, nor is it a matter of setting a specific date in stone – that we must move toward universal conscription and that it is inevitable, but needs to be done when you’re prepared,” he said.
The preparations would include training some 300 instructors and building suitable facilities to house the young draftees, he added.
The council also agreed to expand the range of service options available to conscripts. These could include training as drone operators or assisting the State Border Guard Service and firefighting and rescue services, the president said.
After trying to switch to fully professional armed forces, Lithuania restored partial conscription in 2015, citing increased security threats following Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014.

'Feels like being hit by a bus': Rib remodelling beauty surgery on the rise

PRESS REVIEW – Thursday, October 29: Spanish papers discuss Wednesday's deadly train collision. The New York Times investigates whether a "safest seat" in the event of a train crash exists. Next, we look at a report about "the shocking rise of rib remodelling". We end with some photos from the Arctic and Antarctica.
Spanish papers are reacting to the devastating train crash that killed dozens of people on Wednesday. Both El Mundo and El País emphasise that it's not the first time this has happened – the last train accident in Spain was only nine months ago. El País also has a first-person story: "I travelled on this train", writes a journalist who works for the paper. He happened to be there during the crash. He already covered the Adamuz disaster in January and now he writes: "I had that feeling again of living through a nightmare". He also describes the strange calm and how he and other passengers managed to free themselves from the last carriage.
The New York Times asks the question "Is there a safest seat in a train crash?" The answer is not so simple. There's a rough consensus that it's best to sit in the middle of the train, in case of a hit from the front or the back. Some experts are even more precise, saying the best bet is sitting in the middle, in an aisle seat facing backward – that's because if the train suddenly stops, the whiplash would be less brutal and there's a smaller chance of being hit by flying objects. But experts told the paper that there are too many variables in train crashes to say for certain. This time in Spain, for example, the hit was from the back, so the safest place to sit would have been in the front of the train. But of course passengers couldn't have known in advance of the nature of the crash.
The tragedy is still very recent, but it could already have political repercussions. According to Democrata, it could harm Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's reputation before snap elections that are happening in only a month's time. The weak link among his ministers is Oscar Puente, the transport minister, who was already in post in January during the first train crash. According to the paper, he has three options: "continuity, resignation or dismissal". Puente is under fire, and not only because of the actual crashes. Some time after the previous rail disaster, he appeared in a comedy video in which he imitated a derailing train.
Next, The Guardian reports that rib remodelling surgery is on the rise. First, the patient's ribs are fractured, and then the person has to stay in a corset for three months, almost 24/7. The idea is to give the person a wasp-like waist. The Guardian spoke to people who went through it, who say it's extremely painful and feels like "being hit by a bus". One lady who did it couldn't sleep comfortably for more than a week because she was in constant pain. Although the procedure remains rare, more and more people are deciding to do it. Between 2018 and 2024, there were more than 2,300 patients, with an overall complication rate of 3.7 percent, which remains quite high for beauty procedures.
Finally, a new photography book by polar specialists Sue Flood and Ian Dawson captures the Arctic and Antarctica. The Times shows its favourite photographs that "document life at the frozen edges of the world".
You can catch our press review every morning on France 24 at 7:20am and 9:20am (Paris time), from Monday to Friday.

Hackers expose US immigration surveillance network
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:53:26 UTC
20:53:26 KST

Hackers expose US immigration surveillance network
Personal and operational details of more than 41,000 US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) employees and contractors, including undercover immigration agents, have been leaked online, reportedly exposing the department’s internal structure and surveillance operations.
The disclosure comes amid growing public anger over President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign, with the department’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facing growing criticism over aggressive raids, detention conditions, and the use of force against migrants and protesters.
Released on Wednesday by transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets), the files contain names, contact details, job titles, and internal system access groups across ICE, Customs and Border Protection (CBP), and other DHS agencies.
DHS confirmed to the media that it is “aware of a potential breach” and is working to address it, adding that it will protect employees and update the public “when more information is available.”
What’s in the files?
Dubbed ‘Icepick’, the archive was supplied to DDoSecrets by a hacktivist group called ‘Department of Peace’. It contains around 21,300 CBP records, 6,600 linked to ICE, and 3,400 to Homeland Security Investigations, along with records from immigration services, cybersecurity, and other DHS divisions. Some records match employees’ social media profiles, but others exposed internal organizational charts and previously undisclosed programs and operations.
According to Wired, the files reference undercover investigations, wiretapping, and immigration databases, with internal access groups linked to surveillance tools including Palantir’s Falcon software and Mobile Fortify, a facial recognition system used by immigration agents. Other groups reference AI services including OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Google’s Gemini, and Elon Musk’s xAI chatbot Grok. Access groups are lists of employees authorized to use particular systems, which means the records could help identify which employees have access to surveillance tools and how DHS operations are organized.
“This dataset is massive in terms of both size and impact,” investigative journalist and hacktivist maia arson crimew, who developed a searchable version of the archive, said in a statement accompanying the release. She called it “a complete game changer for anyone investigating DHS,” arguing that it could help identify agents and their chains of command.
DDoSecrets co-founder Emma Best said the files go beyond an ordinary employee directory.
“Rather than an indiscriminate directory of every DHS employee, Icepick identifies many of the architects and drivers of DHS policy and operations,” she said, pointing to officials overseeing covert investigations, efforts to identify government leakers, and deportation programs.
The hackers claim to have obtained the records through DHS’s Okta employee login system, though Okta denied that its systems were compromised.
Why now?
The hackers linked the leak to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s pledge to intensify immigration enforcement. Speaking after two fatal ICE shootings in Texas and Maine, Mullin said federal agents are “turning up the heat on the streets,” despite growing criticism of their tactics. “On July 17th, Markwayne Mullin said he was ‘turning up the heat.’ This is what happens to ICE when you do that,” a Department of Peace spokesperson said in a statement published by DDoSecrets.
The disclosure comes amid growing backlash over Trump’s immigration crackdown, a central priority since his return to the White House in January 2025. His push for mass deportations, expanded detention, and tighter border controls has sparked protests over aggressive raids, masked agents, and alleged racial profiling.
Anger intensified after federal agents fatally shot US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota in January, followed by other violent incidents involving ICE officers. Just this month, federal agents shot and wounded a Dominican migrant during an arrest in New York, prompting further demonstrations.
ICE has also faced scrutiny over detention conditions, with at least 52 deaths in its custody during Trump’s first 500 days back in office, according to Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights.
The administration maintains that its operations are necessary to enforce immigration law and remove dangerous criminals. The Icepick publishers say the records can help journalists, lawmakers, and civil liberties groups investigate DHS activities. Emma Best argued that the disclosure can enable investigations, congressional inquiries, and legal challenges by replacing the administration’s “anonymity with accountability.”
Yet another breach
The disclosure adds to a series of US government data security incidents.
In September, hacking group ShinyHunters claimed that it stole personal data on nearly all FBI agents and their spouses, including sensitive job details and medical information. The group said the attack was “not financially motivated” and demanded that the FBI withdraw a cybersecurity advisory published in May that it claimed contained false allegations about it.
Separately, a Pentagon personnel system breach reportedly exposed Social Security numbers, personal details, and military job records belonging to more than 3 million people, including service members and their families. The incident prompted a class-action lawsuit last week.

Ukraine has a national typeface called Zakon — what makes it distinctive
Kyiv • UNN
The Zakon typeface was created based on Ukraine’s artistic tradition for documents and the visual identity of government institutions. It will be introduced gradually.
Ukraine has unveiled the national typeface Zakon. It was created based on the Ukrainian artistic tradition. The Ministry of Culture of Ukraine reported this on October 29, UNN writes.
Details
"The new national typeface Zakon was presented publicly for the first time in Kyiv. It was developed by Ukrainian designers based on the historical heritage of the country's lettering tradition. The new typeface is intended to establish Ukrainian identity in the state's visual space and gradually replace typefaces of Russian origin in official documents," the Ministry of Culture noted.
The development of a national typeface is provided for by Resolution No. 4764-IX of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine dated January 2026, "On Strengthening the Role of the Ukrainian Language in Establishing the Ukrainian State."
"We continue to establish Ukrainian identity in the visual space. The creation of a national typeface is an important step toward ensuring that state institutions represent Ukraine through our artistic tradition and contemporary Ukrainian design. A typeface is part of a state's recognizable image. Through the form of its letters, it conveys the character of our culture and makes it present in everyday life. We seek to ensure that Ukrainian design shapes the image of our state and that cultural heritage becomes a source of new solutions," said Deputy Prime Minister for Humanitarian Policy — Minister of Culture of Ukraine Tetiana Berezhna.
What the typeface is for
The initiative, the Ministry of Culture noted, is aimed at creating the state institutions' own visual language. After all, certificates, letters of appreciation, diplomas, awards, and plaques are still designed using typefaces of Russian origin, including Izhitsa and Petersburg, as well as typefaces Cyrillicized by the Russian studio ParaType.
The Ukrainian typeface tradition in contemporary design
Zakon is a classic Ukrainian antiqua that combines national graphic traditions with modern requirements for document design.
The development was based on the legacy of six outstanding masters of Ukrainian lettering. Heorhii Narbut was the author of the first Ukrainian banknotes and the coat of arms of the Ukrainian State under Hetman Skoropadskyi, and one of the founders of the Ukrainian Academy of Arts. Many of his typographic solutions remain part of Ukrainian identity to this day.
Vasyl Krychevskyi was the author of the coat of arms of the Ukrainian People's Republic and left a significant typographic legacy.
Yakiv Hnizdovskyi lived in emigration but sought to bring the Ukrainian alphabet closer to the Western typographic tradition. His work also helped contemporary masters.
Robert Lisovskyi was a graphic artist, a master of Ukrainian book type, and a follower of Mykhailo Boichuk and Heorhii Narbut.
During the Soviet era, Vasyl Khomenko created a Ukrainian typeface that was used virtually until the end of the Soviet Union.
Vasyl Chebanyk is a luminary of contemporary calligraphy who designed the ceremonial copy of the Constitution of Ukraine and left a rich typographic legacy.
The typeface incorporates characteristic features of Ukrainian graphics: asymmetrical serifs, diamond-shaped dots above the letters "і" and "ї," and the distinctive mark above "й" in the tradition of Heorhii Narbut. Its proportions also draw on the European tradition of classical antiqua typefaces.
Four Ukrainian type designers worked on the creation of Zakon:
-  Oleksii Chekal is a calligrapher, a research fellow at the Museum of Books and Printing of Ukraine, and the author of typefaces for the Orthodox Church of Ukraine; 
-  Hennadii Zarechniuk is a researcher of Ukraine's typographic heritage and a co-author of the Kobzar KS, Zahar, and Dnipro typefaces; 
-  Dmytro Rastvortsev is the author of the e-Ukraine typeface and a co-author of UAF Sans for the Armed Forces of Ukraine; 
-  Andrii Shevchenko is the author of the Arsenal typeface, which won a competition for a contemporary Ukrainian typeface for official business use. 
The project manager is Taras Ishchyk, a serviceman and the author of the graphic style of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
Three typefaces for the state's different needs
The Zakon typeface family consists of three typefaces:
-  Zakon Text is intended for office work, official documents, and everyday text work. It is freely available for use; 
-  Zakon Decor was created for designing ceremonial documents, awards, and inscriptions; 
-  Zakon Letterpress is intended for printing original copies of regulatory and legal acts of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine. 
The two latest typefaces are available under a closed license to a limited number of users. The font includes four styles: Regular, Italic, Bold, and Bold Italic.
How the national font will be implemented
The transition to Zakon will take place gradually, without additional costs for the mass replacement of existing signs, forms, and other materials.
After the presentation, the Ministry of Culture of Ukraine will provide government institutions with the font and instructions for installing it. At the first stage, Zakon Text will be tested during the preparation of letters, orders, forms, and other documents. The feedback received will help the developers improve the font.
At the same time, the Ministry of Culture of Ukraine is working to make Zakon the font used for the official publication of regulatory legal acts.
You can learn more about the national font, download it, and leave feedback on the website of the Ministry of Culture of Ukraine.

these glowing amber sculptures begin with a natural polymer produced by tiny insects

these glowing amber sculptures begin with a natural polymer produced by tiny insects
ori orisun merhav explores a future of multispecies design, where biological processes inform how we manufacture and inhabit the world.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
insects make the material for ori orisun merhav’s sculptures
Brussels-based designer Ori Orisun Merhav is experimenting with a natural polymer produced by tiny lac insects, transforming their resinous secretions into glowing sculptures and sculptural furniture. Through her research practice Made by Insects, she heats and blows the amber-colored material into clusters of translucent bubbles, some perched on branching steel structures, others suspended as elaborate chandeliers.
The material is known commercially as shellac, a substance typically used as a protective coating. Here in Merhav’s hands, it takes on a completely different spirit.
Her latest works extend the research into 3D printing and large-scale installations, imagining how an insect-produced material might become part of our built environment. After years of research into the insects themselves, the designer has received a 2026 Dutch Design Award for her experimental approach to material production.
the tiny insects behind an unlikely design material
The insects that produce this shellac are known scientifically as Kerria lacca, and are roughly the size of a grain of sand. They attach themselves to the branches of host trees and feed on their sap, converting sugars into a natural resin that hardens around their bodies. This protective enclosure allows the insects to develop and reproduce. The hardened resin can then be collected from the branches, washed and processed into shellac, a material humans have used for centuries in furniture finishing and other applications.
Designer Ori Orisun Merhav first encountered the insects while researching ecological relationships during her studies at Design Academy Eindhoven. She was fascinated by their ability to manufacture a polymer through their own biological processes, and she traveled to Thailand to study lac cultivation and meet the communities who harvest it. There, she learned about the insects’ life cycles and the agricultural practices surrounding their production.
The research became her 2022 graduation project, The Lac Lab Open Source, an evolving archive of material experiments that eventually grew into Made by Insects. It also introduced her to the economic realities of shellac production, as synthetic alternatives have steadily reduced demand for the natural resin.
learning to build from the insects themselves
Back in her studio, Merhav began testing what the material could do beyond its traditional applications. Shellac softens when heated and hardens again as it cools, allowing her to stretch it into thin membranes and blow it into hollow forms using techniques borrowed from glassmaking.
Her earliest experiments produced large, individual bubbles, but their delicate walls made them brittle and difficult to transport. Looking more closely at the insects’ protective structures, she discovered that their enclosures comprised many smaller, interconnected cells.
The observation changed her approach. Merhav began blowing smaller volumes and joining them into larger structures, developing a new language of clustered forms that draws directly from the insects’ construction methods. In works such as Branching Insects Chandelier and Meet Me Under the Insects Tree, the amber bubbles grow along slender metal supports, casting warm light through their uneven surfaces.
The finished pieces have an almost botanical appearance, although their structural logic comes from the resinous shelters of insects.
3D printing a polymer made by another species
Merhav’s experiments have since expanded into digital fabrication. Working with Ginger Additive, Reflexlab and Aeditto, she produced her first 3D-printed shellac objects in 2023, later continuing the research with material engineer Tom Samson and the Bio-Polymer Lab at Avans University of Applied Sciences in the Netherlands.
The process explores how a naturally occurring polymer can move through a printer without chemical modification. Temperature and the material’s behavior during extrusion influence the forms as they take shape, leaving behind uneven surfaces and visible layers of hardened resin.
Her Morphopoiesis vessels offer a closer look at this emerging technique. The objects rise in irregular, cellular walls, with ridges of deposited material forming dense networks around their hollow interiors.
a woven insect canopy takes shape in london
At Sarah Myerscough Gallery, Merhav’s ongoing research has grown into an environment visitors can move through. Portal Into The Multi-Species, on view from October 14th to November 7th, 2026, occupies the gallery’s entrance corridor with delicate shellac bubbles attached to steel branches. Further inside, the forms become larger and more textured.
In The Woven Insect Canopy, palm sheaths coated in insect-produced resin are held within sculptural steel supports, their fibrous surfaces illuminated from within by LEDs.
The series includes Awakening, Regeneration and Bifurcation, the latter reaching 140 centimeters in height. Light passes through the shellac-coated fibers to reveal their interwoven structure beneath the amber surface. The works point to an interior shaped by biological processes. A material originally created as a protective shelter has become part of an imagined architecture.
who makes the materials we live with?
Merhav’s interest in mutualism runs through the project, beginning with the relationship between lac insects and the trees that sustain them. The insects depend on their hosts for nourishment, while cultivation involves managing the trees’ health and the insects’ reproductive cycles.
Human participation adds another layer, through the farmers who maintain these environments and the makers who work with the harvested resin. The ecological relationship itself is complex, yet the research draws attention to the many participants involved in producing a single material.
These sculptures, for Merhav, are part of a much longer exploration of how these relationships might inform design. The work remains experimental, with the material’s fragility and the demands of fabrication continuing to shape its possibilities. Still, her lamps and vessels offer a tangible glimpse of an unusual manufacturing future. An insect produces a polymer to protect itself on a tree branch. Generations later, a designer studies that structure and finds a way to build with it.
project info:
designer: Ori Orisun Merhav | @ori_orisun
research practice: Made by Insects

How two high-speed trains collided in central Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:50:00 UTC
20:50:00 KST

Two high-speed trains collided just before 9 am on Oct 28 in Spain, killing at least 68 people and leaving more than 50 injured. Rail services between Madrid and the southern Andalusia region have been suspended. It is Spain’s deadliest train crash since 2013.
An Iryo express train had stopped at a red signal when it was struck by a Renfe high-speed train between the towns of Los Yebenes and Urda, near Toledo, about 118km south of Madrid by rail. The trains were both heading south from Madrid to Seville.
The crash is the second collision between high-speed trains on the same line in nine months. An accident between trains operated by the same two companies killed 46 people in January. Iryo is a private high-speed rail operator, while Renfe is owned by the Spanish government.
Addressing reporters in Madrid, Spain’s Transport Minister Oscar Puente said a computer malfunction had automatically stopped all traffic on part of the line. Puente said the fatal train crash occurred after the central command centre erroneously told the Renfe train to restart, without any speed restrictions.
Authorities said there were 147 passengers on the Iryo train, and 397 were on the Renfe train.
Prior to the crashes in 2026, Spain’s last major rail disaster occurred in 2013, when 80 people were killed and 145 injured after a high-speed train veered off the track on a sharp bend as it approached the north-western city of Santiago de Compostela.

mcdonald’s recycles happy meal toys into wireless mouse shaped like french fries
developed with lenovo, this french fry-shaped wireless mouse brings a familiar red carton to the desktop, giving recycled toy plastic a new day job.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
MCDONALD’S AND LENOVO PUT FRENCH FRIES ON THE DESKTOP
McDonald’s China is giving its fries a place beside the keyboard. Developed with Lenovo, the brand’s French fry-shaped wireless mouse translates its familiar red carton and yellow contents into a computer accessory, incorporating plastic recovered from old Happy Meal toys. The collaboration brings together two recognizable features of the fast-food experience: the packaging that holds lunch and the small plastic object that tends to outlast it. This time, the latter gets something useful to do.
The design keeps the visual shorthand intact. A red lower shell carries the Golden Arches, while molded yellow fries rise across the top, giving the mouse an uneven silhouette that departs from the anonymous curves of conventional office hardware. The food reference determines the object’s shape as well as its colors, turning a piece of takeaway packaging into something intended to stay on the desk.
RECYCLED HAPPY MEAL TOYS FORM THE MOUSE’S PLASTIC SHELL
According to the product information, more than 60% of the exterior casing is made from recycled plastic sourced from collected Happy Meal toys. Lenovo describes a process involving sorting, shredding, purification, and material modification to produce recycled ABS suitable for manufacturing. The toys lose their original forms along the way: their material returns to production, eventually taking on another distinctly McDonald’s identity.
The collaboration sits within McDonald’s China’s Reimagine Good Things initiative, launched in 2021 to explore new uses for recovered materials. Previous products have included trays and flowerpots, extending the program into everyday objects. Here, the shift from toy to computer accessory also changes the intended user and setting. Something once handed out with a children’s meal reappears among the equipment of adult working life, retaining a little of its former playfulness.
WIRELESS CONNECTIVITY HIDES BENEATH THE FRENCH FRY SHAPE
Behind the sculpted fries, the mouse offers Bluetooth and 2.4GHz wireless connectivity, quiet-click buttons, and three adjustable sensitivity settings. A 380mAh rechargeable battery powers the device. Its accompanying carrying pouch unfolds into a mouse pad, allowing the accessory’s protective cover to become part of the desktop setup. The specifications give the novelty object a practical role, although its distinctive outline alone says little about comfort over a full working day.
This limited release places the mouse between functional equipment and branded collectible, with its appeal resting on an immediately legible transformation. A carton normally associated with a brief stop for food becomes an object designed for repeated use. Whether that makes answering emails more appetizing is another matter.
project info:
name: French fry-shaped wireless mouse
brands: McDonald’s and Lenovo | @mcdonalds and @lenovo
location: China

India’s refining boom finds an opportunity in the global diesel crunch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:46:54 UTC
20:46:54 KST

India’s refining boom finds an opportunity in the global diesel crunch
India’s long-planned refinery expansions could make it an even bigger diesel supplier in 2027, just as disruptions to Russian and Middle Eastern shipments have created an unexpected export opportunity for Indian refiners.
State-owned refiners plan to add 16.5 million tons of annual diesel production capacity next year, executives said at an industry conference in Goa on Tuesday. The projects were originally intended to meet India’s growing domestic fuel requirements, not the current global diesel shortage.
“The expansion is driven by a portfolio, but the opportunity is in diesel,” XAnalysts founder and chief oil analyst Mukesh Sahdev told RT.
Why are global diesel supplies tight even as oil demand is falling?
The US-Iran war has disrupted Middle Eastern fuel shipments, while attacks on Russian refineries and export restrictions have reduced supplies from another major producer. Diesel powers transportation, factories, and farms, and the shortages are largely driving the current price inflation and affordability crisis.
Global diesel and gas oil availability fell by 1.7 million barrels per day – equivalent to roughly two-and-a-half times Japan’s daily diesel consumption last year – in the third quarter, compared with a year earlier, according to figures from the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the Energy Institute.
Wholesale diesel prices surpassed $200 per barrel in September, nearly double their prewar levels, and reached around $220 in Europe and the US, the IEA said.
The shortage persists despite weakening overall oil demand, as diesel consumption has remained comparatively resilient and inventories have fallen, the agency said. On October 15, IEA members agreed to accelerate emergency stock releases, including over 20 million barrels of diesel.
How are Indian refiners positioned to benefit?
Indian Oil Corporation, the country’s largest refiner, expects expansions to add around 8 million tons of diesel a year. Hindustan Petroleum Corporation’s new Rajasthan refinery is expected to produce 3 million tons next year, while the expanded Numaligarh refinery in Assam state will add another 3 million tons, Reuters reported.
Bharat Petroleum Corporation plans another 1.5 million tons of annual output. In all, India’s plans will expand overall refining capacity from 267 million tons annually to 300 million by 2030.
The country already produces more diesel than it consumes.
Refiners produced around 59 million tons from April to September, against domestic consumption of around 46 million, according to Oil Ministry data cited by Bloomberg.
The additional volumes are coming onstream amid a global shortage, creating a commercial opportunity for projects originally designed around Indian fuel demand, ICRA senior vice president Prashant Vasisht told RT.
Russian crude ‘a natural fit’
New refining capacity alone does not guarantee more diesel. Refineries need suitable crude oil, while equipment limits how much of it they can turn into diesel, Vasisht explained.
“Indian refineries are also getting the right quality of crude oil,” Sahdev said, noting Russian, Iraqi, and heavier Venezuelan grades as suitable feedstocks for diesel production.
Russian crude is “a natural fit for the Indian system,” he added. The new Rajasthan refinery can process Russian Urals and Iraqi Basrah grades, S&P Global reported in July.
Sahdev said India’s reliance on Russian barrels has also grown as production from traditional suppliers in Malaysia and West Africa declined.
Can India fill the global supply gap?
India is already the world’s second-largest seaborne diesel exporter after the US, according to data analysis firm Kpler. Exports reached 596,000 barrels per day in September, compared with the year-to-date average of 482,000 barrels per day, the data shows.
Additional Indian production could make a meaningful difference to global supplies, but it cannot replace all the diesel lost because of disruptions affecting Russia and the Middle East, the analysts cautioned.
“We are providing very large quantities to Europe and some of the other regions, but these are still not enough,” Vasisht said.
Not all the additional diesel will be available for export. India’s growing domestic demand, refinery operations, and freight costs will determine how much reaches overseas buyers.
The IEA expects global refinery output to recover in 2027, but warns that depleted inventories could keep diesel markets tight well into next year.
But expanding production alone is not enough, Sahdev cautioned. India also needs stronger commodity-trading networks and financial mechanisms to capture the full value of its growing refining capacity.
“If India does not do this, then somebody else will make money on Indian capacity,” he said.

Spain’s deadly train crash adds new complication to Sanchez’s re-election campaign
- Spain’s deadly train crash in Toledo killed 68 people and hit Pedro Sanchez’s snap election campaign, forcing him to face anger over rail safety and possible underinvestment.
- Sanchez promised an investigation and said any failures would be fixed, while opponents demanded accountability and a full review of the network.
- Public trust in high-speed rail is weak, with polls showing most Spaniards doubt safety, and the crash may turn Sanchez’s transport record from an asset into a liability.
AI generated
MADRID – Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez had hoped to ride a wave of public anger over the eviction of an octogenarian, who later died, to win re-election in a snap election, but the deadly train crash on Oct 28 has dealt a serious blow to his campaign.
The accident in Toledo province killed 68 people and came just nine months after another deadly crash on the same line, leading to accusations from experts and the public of underinvestment in railway infrastructure under Sanchez’s government after years of rapid network expansion.
Oscar, a 24-year-old who declined to give his last name, said at Madrid’s Atocha station on Oct 28: “If we were scared of taking trains before, now we’re even more so... Just when you think nothing else could possibly go wrong, something new happens. There needs to be major change.”
At the accident site on Oct 28, Sanchez said the “terrible tragedy” would be investigated and pledged to address any failures that came to light.
“If we need to further strengthen safety in order to rebuild confidence in our high-speed rail system, we will do so, because it is unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year,” he said.
Sanchez, who had been trailing in most opinion polls, had appeared to be gaining some traction, with an October survey by state-run pollster CIS showing his party ahead with just weeks to go to the Nov 29 election.
The death of Maricarmen Abascal, who was evicted from her home of more than 70 years, sparked widespread protests across Spain, focusing political attention on a housing crisis that is cited in polls as the top priority for most Spaniards.
The outcry over Abascal, which led Sanchez to call for a snap election on Oct 5, was an opportunity to divert media attention from his government’s handling of a migrant crisis in Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta this summer.
Right-wing parties and security forces had accused the Socialists of underinvestment in border infrastructure despite repeated warnings from staff.
No room for ‘triumphalist rhetoric’
Sanchez, 54, has pitched himself as the candidate representing progress instead of a return by the far right to government for the first time since the death of dictator Francisco Franco.
He has so far run a positive, upbeat campaign, giving interviews on pop culture talk shows and podcasts as his party attempts to mobilise millions of undecided left-leaning voters to the polls.
“I don’t think that triumphalist rhetoric... has any place right now, and I suspect it will be a long time before we see that kind of attitude return,” said Paco Camas, public affairs director at pollster Ipsos.
This week’s crash will force a shift towards a more sombre tone, Camas said.
Sanchez’s opponents immediately called for accountability and said they would not be silenced by mourning.
“Pain does not oblige us to keep quiet. Serenity is not silence... Spaniards will ask urgent questions which deserve answers,” said Alberto Nunez Feijoo, president of the conservative People’s Party, promising a full review of the network if he came into power.
Protesters gather in Madrid
On the evening of Oct 28, hundreds of mostly far-right demonstrators gathered in front of Spain’s Transport Ministry to call for Sanchez’s resignation, with one carrying a banner emblazoned with the words, “Spain can’t take it anymore”.
“This government has destroyed absolutely everything, including infrastructure,” said Santiago Abascal, the leader of far-right Vox at a rally that day. “We will not let them use the mourning we share, the anger, pain and indignation, to silence even for a second the condemnation of what is happening in Spain.”
Transport Minister Oscar Puente rejected allegations in a press conference on Oct 28 that Spain’s railway system was dangerous, stating it was “reliable and safe... with the limits of the material itself and of human action, as is the case with any form of transport”.
No trust in rail services
Sanchez once touted the country’s 4,000km high-speed rail system – the world’s second-largest after China’s – as a political asset, though it may now become a liability.
Polls in Spanish media conducted in January after the last fatal crash showed 57% perceived a worsening of rail services since Sanchez came into office and nearly 60% stated they had little or no trust in Spain’s railway system.
An investigation into the cause of that accident is still under way, according to Spain’s Transport Ministry, with a preliminary report identifying a fracture in the rail which appeared to have occurred prior to the derailment.
High-speed rail use, which had broken records in 2024 and 2025, fell 15% in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, data from Spain’s competition authority showed.
Puente declined to say on Oct 28 whether he would step down, stating it was “not the time” to talk about himself. REUTERS

Possible dwarf planet discovered beyond Pluto
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:40:07 UTC
20:40:07 KST

Possible dwarf planet discovered beyond Pluto
Astronomers have discovered a large icy object beyond Pluto that could qualify as a dwarf planet, potentially adding a new member to the solar system’s officially recognized group.
The discovery was announced on Thursday by the US-funded Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile, which houses the world’s largest 3.2-gigapixel digital camera, built specifically for astronomy.
Researchers estimate that the object, provisionally named 2026 ED138, is between 600 and 1,500 km in diameter and may be one of the largest dwarf planet candidates ever found. It currently sits roughly 46 times farther from the Sun than Earth. Pluto’s average distance, for comparison, is about 40 times Earth’s.
The object likely escaped detection until now because it appeared against a crowded backdrop of millions of stars near the plane of the Milky Way. However, Rubin’s repeated images and tracking software has now allowed scientists to pick out its movement.
#ICYMI: our Solar System has a newly-discovered dwarf planet candidate! Meet 2026 ED138, recently revealed by NSF–DOE Rubin Observatory ☄ Let's get to know this new world a little bit, shall we? https://t.co/wTOg898zBu https://t.co/RC0HP5rZiL
— NSF-DOE Rubin Observatory (@VRubinObs) October 28, 2026
If confirmed, ED138 would join five dwarf planets recognized by the International Astronomical Union, which include Eris, Haumea, Makemake, Ceres, and Pluto, which was considered the solar system’s ninth planet until it was reclassified in 2006. Dwarf planets orbit the Sun and have enough gravity to become roughly round, but share their orbital neighborhoods with other bodies.
ED138 may be large enough to meet the roundness requirement, but astronomers still need more research and better measurements before determining its status.
“The main thing we need to do is to establish the physical size of 2026 ED138,” discoverer Matt Holman, an astrophysicist at the Center for Astrophysics, Harvard and Smithsonian, told Reuters. He explained that ED138’s size is currently estimated from the sunlight it reflects. However, a small shiny object can appear just as bright as a large, dark one, Holman said.
To narrow down the true size of the object, researchers could use Chile’s ALMA telescope which can detect radiation emitted by ED138 itself, helping get a more accurate measurement.
The last dwarf planet officially recognized by the International Astronomical Union was Haumea in 2008. Other candidates have since emerged, including 2017 OF201, whose discovery was announced in May 2025, but none have yet been formally added to the list.

New restrictions for anglers starting November 1: where fishing will be banned and what fines will be imposed
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
13:39:50 EET
20:39:50 KST

New restrictions for anglers starting November 1: where fishing will be banned and what fines will be imposed
Kyiv • UNN
The ban will be in effect from November 1, 2026, until the beginning of the 2027 spawning season. Violations will incur fines, confiscation, and compensation for damages.
From November 1, 2026, a seasonal ban on catching fish and other aquatic biological resources in wintering pits will come into effect in Ukraine. It will remain in force until the beginning of the spring-summer spawning period of 2027. UNN reports this, citing the State Environmental Inspectorate and the State Fisheries Agency.
Why a ban on catching fish is being introduced
Wintering pits are deep sections of rivers, lakes, and reservoirs where fish gather as the weather turns colder. In cold water, their activity decreases, metabolic processes slow down, and their need for food diminishes. Mass fishing in wintering areas can cause significant damage to populations, so these areas are protected until the beginning of spawning.
This is an annual seasonal restriction provided for by the Recreational Fishing Rules, approved by Order No. 700 of the Ministry of Agrarian Policy dated September 19, 2022. The exact date when the ban ends will be determined depending on the start of the spawning period in the respective water bodies.
Where fishing will be prohibited
The ban does not apply to all water bodies or every deep-water area, but only to officially designated wintering pits. Their lists and boundaries are approved by the territorial bodies of the State Fisheries Agency in separate orders.
In particular, 78 wintering pits have been designated in Rivne region. They are located in separate sections of the Horyn, Sluch, Styr, Ikva, Liiva, Pripyat, and Putilivka rivers, as well as in the Basivkut Reservoir and Lakes Nobel and Ostrivske.
In Zhytomyr region, the restrictions will apply to designated sections of the Sluch, Teteriv, Irsha, Irpin, Uzh, Ubort, Khomora, Hnylopiat, Zdvyzh, and other rivers. Environmental protection authorities in Volyn also announced the start of the ban.
It is important to understand that fishing within a wintering pit is prohibited even from the shore. Before traveling to a body of water, anglers are advised to check the map or description of the boundaries of prohibited areas in the orders of the relevant territorial office of the State Fisheries Agency.
What fishing gear is permitted outside wintering pits
Outside designated wintering pits, recreational fishing is permitted by law unless other local or seasonal restrictions apply to the water body.
If a body of water is covered with ice, ice-fishing rods and tip-ups may be used. If there is no ice cover, fishing is permitted with float and bottom rods, spinning rods, and fly-fishing gear using natural or artificial bait. The total number of hooks on all of one angler’s gear must not exceed seven.
From freeze-up until the ice breaks up, fishing gear with hooks in which the distance from the shank to the tip of the point exceeds 10 millimeters is also prohibited. The use of poaching gear and other prohibited fishing methods is not allowed regardless of the time of year.
How much fish may be caught
On waters of general use, the daily limit for most fish species is three kilograms and one additional fish of any weight that meets the minimum permitted size. For certain species, including bleak, Amur sleeper, and pumpkinseed, no weight limit has been established. However, these limits apply only where fishing is permitted. They do not grant the right to fish in wintering pits. Restrictions on catching certain species and rules introduced for the period of martial law in specific regions must also be observed. Current restrictions should be checked before every trip.
What fines are предусмотрed for violations
For violating fishing rules, citizens face a warning or a fine of between 34 and 170 hryvnias. A serious violation, including the use of prohibited gear, carries a fine of between 340 and 680 hryvnias, with possible confiscation of the gear and catch. If illegal fishing causes substantial damage, criminal liability may arise under Article 249 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. The sanction provides, in particular, for a fine of between 17,000 and 51,000 hryvnias or other types of punishment stipulated by law.
In addition to fines, violators must compensate for damages for each fish caught illegally. For example, the charge is 5,117 hryvnias for one catfish, 3,706 for a common carp, 3,587 for a pike-perch, 3,468 for a pike, 3,162 for a perch, and 1,649 hryvnias for a bream.
The amount of compensation is determined according to government rates, regardless of the weight of the individual caught. That is precisely why fishing in a prohibited area can cost significantly more than an administrative fine. To avoid trouble, environmental inspectors urge people to check the official lists of wintering pits in advance and comply with seasonal restrictions.
We would like to remind you
Earlier, we reported that in the Kharkiv region, an illegal fish catch worth more than UAH 2.6 million was uncovered.

Four women on trial after séance at Dutch cemetery
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Four women went on trial in a Utrecht court earlier this week for desecrating children’s graves during a séance they held at Amersfoort’s Rusthof Cemetery five years ago.
Prosecutors have demanded community service sentences of up to 200 hours for the women, who were trying to contact the dead after hours during a paranormal gathering. Two others with them, who are said only to have observed the ritual, are not being charged.
The cemetery’s director at the time was fired for giving the women permission to conduct research into the “so-called energies of the deceased” after closing time. The parents of children buried there had not been notified of the gathering.
Desecration?
The case has been before courts before, but the legal question now is whether the women’s activities constitute desecration.
The participants, who were found out after the father of a buried child discovered a camera at the grave site, allegedly used cat toys with lights to help them communicate with the dead children.
“It is terrible to be confronted with this kind of fact after the loss of a loved one,” prosecutors said. “The way the suspects have dealt with the graves goes against any sense of respect.”
At least 10 relatives have reburied their loved ones in other graves as a result.
Distraught parents
“When people ask me how it feels, I say it feels like rape,” Radia Drost-Laabidi told RTV Utrecht. She and her husband buried two of their daughters at Rusthof. She’s suffered from insomnia ever since and barely visits her daughters’ graves. Now she’s looking for answers. “Why?” she says. “That is my question.”
Only one defendant turned up in court this week, 81-year-old Irene B. Lawyers for the defendants argued that since nothing was damaged or destroyed, there is no desecration.
The court is expected to deliver its verdict next month.

Ukraine: 14 killed in Russian drone strike on train station

"Despite an increased threat warning, people were on the platform," the company said.

In images circulating on social media, bodies could be seen strewn across a train station platform, with police officers kneeling beside them.

Less than 42 minutes of bright daylight linked to higher dementia risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:30:32 UTC
20:30:32 KST

Less than 42 minutes of bright daylight linked to higher dementia risk
- Date:
- October 29, 2026
- Source:
- Wiley
- Summary:
- Getting more daylight could be linked to a surprisingly powerful benefit for brain health. In a study of more than 87,000 adults, researchers found that higher daytime light exposure was associated with a 16% lower risk of dementia, with longer exposure to bright light linked to even greater reductions. Remarkably, getting less than 42 minutes of bright daylight daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than six established risk factors.
- Share:
Could the amount of daylight you get each day offer clues about your risk of developing dementia? A large new study suggests that exposure to brighter daytime light is associated with a lower likelihood of developing the condition.
The findings, published in General Psychiatry, point to daytime light exposure as a potentially overlooked factor in brain health.
Brighter Daylight Linked to Lower Dementia Risk
To investigate the connection, researchers analyzed data from 87,577 adults who wore wrist devices equipped with accelerometers. The devices allowed scientists to measure participants' exposure to light during both the day and night. Over a median follow-up period of 8.1 years, 741 participants developed dementia.
The results revealed a notable pattern. People exposed to average daytime light levels exceeding 1,000 lux (a moderately bright light level equivalent to an overcast day outdoors) had a 16% lower risk of developing dementia. Spending longer periods in even brighter daytime light (at least 5,000 lux) was associated with further reductions in risk.
Too Little Daylight Emerges as a Surprising Dementia Risk Indicator
One of the most striking findings involved people who received very little bright light during the day. Getting less than 0.7 hours, or 42 minutes, of bright daytime light daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than 6 established dementia risk factors.
Interestingly, researchers found no statistically significant connection between nighttime light exposure and dementia risk. This suggests that daytime brightness, rather than light exposure at night, may be particularly relevant to the relationship identified in the study.
"Daytime light exposure may serve as a novel indicator of dementia risk," said corresponding author Hongliang Feng, PhD, of Guangzhou Medical University, in China.
Although the findings reveal an association, they do not establish that getting more daylight directly prevents dementia. Instead, the research highlights daytime light exposure as a potentially valuable indicator of dementia risk that deserves further investigation.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Wiley. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Nana Zheng, Wei Wang, Biao Li, Xionge Mei, Yue Liu, Jing Du, Ngan Yin Chan, Joey W. Y. Chan, Xiaoman Xing, Xiao Tan, Christian Benedict, Yun Kwok Wing, Jihui Zhang, Hongliang Feng. Associations between wearable‐device‐measured daytime and nighttime light exposures and dementia risk: A prospective cohort study. General Psychiatry, 2026; 39 (3) DOI: 10.1002/gps3.70039

Poland to Send Ukraine 2 More Soviet-Designed MiG-29s—Only One Is Airworthy
Unknown

- Category
- World
Poland to Send Ukraine 2 More Soviet-Designed MiG-29s—Only One Is Airworthy
Poland will transfer two Soviet-designed MiG-29 fighter jets to Ukraine in the near future, along with ammunition and other military equipment as part of a new aid package worth roughly $55.7 million, according to Rzeczpospolita on October 29.
Dariusz Łukowski, director of the Strategy and Defense Planning Department at Poland’s Ministry of National Defense, confirmed that.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“In the near future. The decision has been made, and these two MiG-29s will be transferred,” Łukowski said when asked when Ukraine would receive the fighters.
According to information obtained by the Polish outlet, one of the two aircraft has already reached the end of its service life, while the second remains airworthy.
The fighters will form part of a broader Polish military assistance package valued at about $55.7 million.
The package is also expected to include 155mm and 152mm artillery ammunition, ammunition for the six-barrel cannons used by F-16 fighters, and missiles for Poland’s Piorun man-portable air-defense systems.
Poland’s Defense Ministry has officially confirmed that Warsaw is preparing another military aid package for Ukraine, although it has declined to disclose the complete list of weapons and equipment for security reasons.
The ministry said the final scale of the package will depend on Poland’s own national security requirements and the capabilities of the Polish Armed Forces, as determined by the chief of the General Staff.
Some of the equipment being transferred is expected to come from systems Poland is withdrawing from active service as they reach the end of their planned operational life.
Warsaw stressed, however, that equipment no longer required by the Polish military may still provide significant value to Ukraine, which continues to operate Soviet-designed aircraft and weapons alongside its growing fleet of Western systems.
The additional MiG-29s would add to Poland’s previous transfers of the fighter type to Ukraine and could provide Kyiv with another airworthy aircraft as well as a valuable source of spare parts and components for keeping the remaining fleet operational.
Previously, reports emerged that Ukraine is restructuring its combat aviation around Western-style fighter wings, has already established the 107th F-16 Aviation Wing, and is preparing airbases capable of supporting multiple aircraft types—including Sweden’s Gripen—as part of a long-term Air Force transformation through 2035.

Minimalist House in Japan by FORM/Kouichi Kimura is "reduced to the essentials"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Minimalist House in Japan by FORM/Kouichi Kimura is “reduced to the essentials”
A monochrome palette and pared-back, open interiors define the aptly named Minimalist House, a home in Japan designed by local studio FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects.
Located in Shiga prefecture, the 73-square-metre home is formed of cubic volumes clad in corrugated metal and black render, perched on a hill overlooking the nearby Lake Biwa.
Minimalist House was designed for a single occupant, but FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects wanted to challenge the assumption that this would mean small-feeling interiors.
This led the studio to create a series of voids and long sightlines that it said help to “liberate space”.
“When hearing ‘a home for a single occupant’, people typically imagine a compact house,” founder Kouichi Kimura told Dezeen.
“Here, living alone is regarded not as a spatial constraint, but as a condition that liberates space,” he added.
“Starting from the individual as the base unit, the house explores a new way of single-person living through the minimal composition reduced to the essentials, with the space that invites in the surrounding view, light, wind, and sound.”
The plan of Minimalist House revolves around a tall void cut through its centre, which extends upwards into a skinny, double-height volume projecting from its roof with a large window.
Finished with grey-plastered walls and dark stone floors, a kitchen, dining space and study occupy the ground floor, with metal and concrete steps leading up to a living space and bedroom above.
Facing the road, the front of the home has been left almost entirely blank. Instead, the interiors open up on the opposite side towards views of the lake in the distance, with the dining table, study and bed pushed up against large, deep-set windows.
“Each floor is designed as a single open layout,” explained Kimura. “The double-height space vertically connects the upper and lower levels. Manipulating floor and ceiling levels gently articulates each space without clearly dividing them.”
“The living space on the upper level is designed not only for daily life, but also for enjoying music. Within the double-height volume, sound resonates off the walls and ceiling, filling the entire space,” he added.
A glass corridor with sliding doors separates the main home from a single-storey washroom, which the studio introduced to ensure that this everyday passage would capture views out over the lake.
“Placing these wet areas away from the main structure creates a natural flow of movement in daily life,” Kimura explained.
“Walking through the glazed corridor in between allows one to touch the landscape, light, and breeze, offering a gentle transition in the everyday time,” he added.
Minimalist forms and interiors often feature in the work of FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects, with the studio’s previous projects in Shiga including a blocky hair salon and home and a skinny home with carefully-placed windows to avoid overlooking.

Estonia's volunteer rescuers send 146th aid shipment to Ukraine
The Estonian Rescue Association (Päästeliit) has sent aid to Ukrainian rescuers, funded by donations and the Foreign Ministry, providing shelter, power and heating for over 30,000 people this winter.
The Kyiv consignment has included a minibus, two high-pressure tents with trailers, diesel heaters, power stations, lighting towers and heated blankets, enough to set up two emergency centers, Estonia's Embassy to Ukraine announced.
"This was our 146th shipment to Ukraine. Every time we hand over new equipment, we hope the situation will improve. Unfortunately, the head of Kyiv's rescue service confirmed that the situation is already worse than ever, and that the coming winter will put civilians — especially children — in an even more difficult position than last year," said Piia Kallas, head of the Estonian Rescue Association, a volunteer organization which complements the Rescue Board (Päästeamet).
Estonian Rescue Association delivered emergency tents and equipment to Ukraine's rescue services @SESU_UA. The aid will provide temporary shelter, electricity and heating for more than 30,000 people during the winter. The package was funded by @MFAestonia and donations. https://t.co/fOGAZI2tOy
— Estonia in Ukraine (@EE_Ukraine) October 28, 2026
The shipment delivered to Kyiv included a minibus, two high-pressure tents with trailers, diesel heaters, battery power stations, battery-powered lamps, lighting towers, heated blankets, folding tables and chairs, fast chargers, thermos flasks, changing mats, children's toys and play mats. With this equipment, rescuers can set up two emergency centers where residents can find temporary shelter and warmth, charge their devices and receive psychological first aid.
A second delivery reached rescuers in Rivne oblast in southeastern Ukraine, including an off-road vehicle, a generator, battery power stations, lighting towers and heaters. The generator was donated by a private donor who decided to give their equipment to those who need it most.

Firehawk raises $150M at $1.4B valuation to build more rocket motors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-29
11:26:16 UTC
20:26:16 KST

- Firehawk raised more than $150 million in a Series D led by Advent and Rochefort Asset Management, valuing the company above $1.4 billion.
- The funds will expand its Oklahoma propellant plant and Mississippi missile integration site to scale rocket and artillery motor production.
Dallas-based rocket propulsion firm Firehawk has raised more than $150 million in a Series D round that values the company at more than $1.4 billion, money it will use to scale up U.S. production of rocket propellant, solid rocket motors and artillery motors, the company said on social media on Oct. 28.
Private equity firm Advent and Rochefort Asset Management, co-founded by Dallas investor Kyle Bass, led the round, with new and existing investors and strategic partners also taking part. Firehawk said the round was upsized and oversubscribed, and the Dallas Morning News reported its original target was $100 million. The company did not disclose how much each investor put in.
The money will fund the build-out of Firehawk’s propellant and rocket motor plant in Lawton, Oklahoma, and its missile integration facility in Crawford, Mississippi, along with new research and development sites and more hiring, the company said in its funding announcement. Firehawk plans to produce more than 100,000 artillery motors in 2027 under a commercial agreement with General Dynamics, and its Oklahoma plant is expected to start low-rate production by mid-2027.
Firehawk was founded in 2019 by CEO Will Edwards to make hybrid rocket engines powered by 3D-printed fuel, and it now describes itself as covering the whole chain from propellant to motors to complete rounds. Its pitch is volume: the U.S. military’s appetite for rockets and missiles has outrun the small number of established solid rocket motor suppliers, and Firehawk says its patented manufacturing process can produce propellant faster and at larger scale for smaller tactical weapons.
The company broke ground on its Great Plains Arsenal rocket motor and propellant plant in Lawton in April. Its Crawford site can integrate 40,000 tactical rockets a year, and Firehawk says it plans to raise that to about 120,000 at full-rate production.
Much of that work centers on the Hydra-70, the 70 mm unguided rocket fired from U.S. Army attack helicopters and other aircraft. This summer the U.S. Army picked Firehawk as one of four new companies to build Hydra-70 rockets, alongside iRocket, Nammo Perry and Albers, with each required to deliver 24 prototype M151 rockets within 18 months. In August, Firehawk fired six Hydra-70 rockets at Yuma Proving Ground in Arizona, all of which worked as intended.
The Series D follows a $60 million Series C that closed in September 2025 and a strategic investment in November 2025 aimed at speeding up solid rocket motor production and integration.
Firehawk has not said how many Hydra-70 rockets or rocket motors it has delivered to the U.S. military so far, or when its Oklahoma plant will reach full-rate production.

The pharmaceutical giant now expects adjusted earnings to be between $2.77 and $2.82 per share. That adjusted profit outlook is up from a previous range of $2.66 to $2.76 per share. The guidance now includes a one-time charge of $400 million, or 12 cents per share, related to its licensing agreement with the Chinese cancer drugmaker SciBrunch.
Merck also narrowed the low end of its 2026 revenue guidance, now expecting sales between $66.8 billion and $67.3 billion. That compares to a previous outlook of $66.3 billion to $67.3 billion.
The company has been on a deal spree as it races to offset generic competition for Keytruda after key patents begin expiring in 2028.
Merck is also positioning the new form of the drug, Keytruda Qlex, as a cornerstone of its growth strategy. The goal is to transition patients from the original intravenous version to Qlex, considered a more convenient under-the-skin injection. This strategy allows the company to defend its market share and sustain Keytruda's blockbuster sales beyond the original version's loss of exclusivity.
Keytruda raked in $8.60 billion in sales for the quarter, beating the $7.73 billion that analysts were expecting, according to StreetAccount. That includes $830 million in sales for Qlex – the highest seen in a quarter since it launched in 2025.
Analysts were expecting $649 million in sales, StreetAccount estimates said. The blowout quarter for the shot suggests it could soon eventually be a multibillion-dollar product annually.
Here's what Merck reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
- Earnings per share: $2.49 adjusted vs. $2.08 expected
- Revenue: $18.09 billion vs. $17.31 billion expected
The company posted a net income of $5.07 billion, or $2.04 per share, for the quarter. That compares with net income of $5.79 billion, or $2.32 per share, for the year-earlier period.
Excluding acquisition and restructuring costs, Merck posted earnings of $2.49 per share for the third quarter.
Merck raked in $18.09 billion in revenue for the quarter, up 5% from the same period a year earlier.
Beyond Keytruda, Merck's newer products also showed strong growth.
Winrevair, which is used to treat a rare, deadly lung condition, generated $694 million in sales for the quarter, up 93% from the same period a year earlier. Analysts were expecting sales of $645 million.
Meanwhile, the Gardasil vaccine, which prevents cancers from HPV, a very common sexually transmitted infection, drew about $2 billion in sales due to higher demand in the U.S. That tops the $1.76 billion in sales that analysts were expecting.
That strong revenue comes after Merck last year grappled with elevated Gardasil inventory and weak demand for the vaccine in China.
Meanwhile, Merck's animal health business posted $1.68 billion in sales for the third quarter, which came in slightly below analysts' estimates.
