Taipei Fine Arts Museum scores with Sakamoto exhibition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:40:33 UTC
19:40:33 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Piano keys and the hum of a bassline introduce Taipei Fine Arts Museum’s latest exhibition, a retrospective on the life and work of Ryuichi Sakamoto — providing a counterpoint to the usual focus on visual arts.
The Japanese musician, who passed away three years ago at 71, was an Oscar-, Grammy-, and Golden Globe-award-winning pop star, film composer, and the voice of a generation.
A classically trained pianist, he co-founded the influential early electronic music band Yellow Magic Orchestra in the late 1970s. He then struck out on his own, or in collaborations with leading lights such as David Bowie, David Sylvian, David Byrne, Alva Noto (Carsten Nicolai), DJ Spooky, and many others.
His works ranged from the earwormy theme tune for the movie “Merry Christmas, Mr. Lawrence,” the score for “The Last Emperor,” and well-known solo piano pieces such as “Energy Flow.”
Starting around the beginning of the new millennium, Sakamoto focused more on large-scale installations at museums and festivals that incorporated visual elements. At the same time, he continued to experiment with sound, presenting field recordings, working with unconventional instruments, and using technology to expand the horizons of electronic music.
In doing so, he profoundly influenced contemporary music and interdisciplinary art, according to TFAM. Appropriately, it is this part of his oeuvre that the art museum focuses on in its latest exhibition, which opens Saturday and continues until March 14 next year.
TFAM Director Loh Li-chen (駱麗真) commented: “While presenting Ryuichi Sakamoto’s explorations of the forms that art can take, this exhibition also leads visitors to ponder the relationships among sound, time, space, technology, and bodily sensation.
“We hope that when visitors enter our museum, they will listen and see in new ways, and so experience how art changes our understanding of the world around us.”
“Ryuichi Sakamoto, Seeing Sound, Hearing Time, New Ways to Sense the World through Sound, Space, and Image” is curated by Sachiko Namba and comprises seven large-scale installations, in addition to providing archival materials about the works and his collaborations. They sum up Sakamoto’s vision of music being “an ‘art of time’ and existing only in time.”
The first exhibit of note is not technically a Sakamoto piece. However, as TFAM points out, it does echo his belief that all sounds are equal and is an extension of the artist’s “prepared piano” works.
Two “sound boxes” have been installed in the entryway to the exhibition, which allow visitors to generate their own soundscapes using field drums, percussive elements, levers, and dials. Ambient noise from outside the art museum is also incorporated, and afterward the result can be downloaded to a phone via a QR code. It’s a neat start.
Afterwards, visitors are encouraged to stroll around and examine the rest of the installations, or take a seat and immerse themselves in rooms that offer mindful visions and stimulating soundscapes.
“Async-immersion” by Sakamoto and Shiro Takatani presents a long LED video wall and a multichannel sound system. It is based on Sakamoto’s 2017 album “Async,” and was first shown at “Ambient Kyoto” in 2023.
The setup means visitors stand inside the music rather than simply listen to it. Scenes such as reeds on a riverbank, a grove of trees, or a coastal view are gradually erased by horizontal bands of light that move from one side to the other.
At the same time, ambient music rises and falls with the appearance and reappearance of either natural scenes or visual representations of electronic interference. The loop continues, bringing forth a feeling of endless repetition and rhythm that is both hypnotic and reflective.
“Async-volume” from 2017 is a collaboration with Zakkubalan, a Tokyo- and New York–based artist and filmmaking collective. The video and sound installation is eerie in that it feels like breaking into the artist’s house after it has just been vacated.
A film continues to play in the empty sitting room, while a gong in the studio moves slightly as if it was hit and is now coming to rest. Outside the house, there is a broken window, and branches on a tree move in the wind. It is as though we are peeking surreptitiously into Sakamoto’s private life.
Elsewhere, there is a container of water, which is disturbed by water dripping from above, creating plops and plinks, and bubbles. Alternatively, the container is shaken or stirred, creating ripples across the water’s surface.
Another exhibit sees a penguin drift by on the screen and bleached bones in a natural history museum, all elegantly accompanied by Sakamoto on the piano. Time slows while the sound and visuals create a contemplative atmosphere.
TFAM Media Associate Daisy Tian-Rong Shiou (修天容) said the art museum team saw the original Sakamoto exhibition that was presented in Tokyo in 2023 and wanted to reproduce that here. She described the original show as “marvelous” and added that the team felt that TFAM’s high ceilings and acoustics would suit it perfectly.
It does.
“Another reason for the exhibition is that our museum is expanding and will be completed in 2029,” Shiou said. “For that museum we are thinking of having experimental art or new media arts, so in the years before then we will also try not only visual arts, but cross-media arts.”
The NT$5.2 billion (US$160 million) extension is being framed as “art within a forest,” since it is being built within Taipei Art Park. It will have one above-ground level and two underground levels, making it Taiwan’s first earth-sheltered museum.
There is a dedicated third-floor observatory of sorts at the back of TFAM that presides over the ongoing construction of the museum extension. After sampling Sakamoto, it is a cool space to rest and decompress for a while.

Protests take place all over Italy amid big police presence, fears of violence
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:31:28 CET
19:31:28 KST

Big demonstrations were under way in
cities all over Italy on Friday in relation to a general strike
called the USB grass-roots trade union over the cost-of-living
crisis, war, rearmament and the policies of Premier Giorgia
Meloni's government, among other issues.
                                    
The marches were taking place amid a big police presence with
fears of more of the violence that overshadowed protests here in
recent weeks.
                                    
Shocking scenes of rioting and looting of by youths in Milan on
the weekend of October 17-18 were followed by protests that
turned violent in Turin, Rome and Bologna last Saturday.
                                    
On Friday thousands of workers, university and high-school
students and, in some cases, their parents were marching in
dozens of cities including Rome, Milan, Naples, Turin, Venice
and Palermo.
                                    
"We are taking to the streets alongside workers who are
mobilizing against the high cost of living and policies of war
and rearmament," said the 'La Rete della Conoscenza, Link -
Coordinamento Universitario' and 'Unione degli Studenti' student
groups.
                                    
"This day of action coincides with an international mobilization
of dockworkers across more than 40 ports in the Mediterranean
and Europe, who are downing tools to protest against the arms
trade, the militarization of infrastructure, and the involvement
of ports in war operations.
                                    
"We are taking to the streets because we can no longer accept
that the cost of crises is systematically offloaded onto our
lives.
                                    
"Rising prices—for rent, utility bills, and basic
necessities—make it increasingly difficult to cover daily
expenses, while wages and salaries continue to lose their
purchasing power.
                                    
"These are not merely individual hardships; they are the
consequences of an economic model that subordinates social needs
to rent-seeking and profit.
                                    
"It is the same model that breeds job insecurity, inadequate
wages, and the progressive erosion of public services, forcing
new generations to adapt to ever more precarious living
conditions.
                                    
"We reject the notion that our future must be defined by
'poverty-wage' jobs, intermittent contracts, vulnerability to
exploitation, and the inability to build a life of genuine
autonomy".
                                    
Images of the faces of Meloni and Higher Education Minister Anna
Maria Bernini were burned in Naples, while a photo of Education
Minister Giuseppe Valditara got the same treatment in Padua.
                                    
Two bins of manure were dumped outside Turin city hall as part
of the protest there.

Italian inflation hit 5.4% in October says Istat
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
11:29:14 CET
19:29:14 KST

Italy's annual inflation rate climbed
even further this month, driven by soaring energy prices linked
to the Iran war, hitting 5.4%, the highest level since August
2023, according to a preliminary estimate for October released
by Istat on Friday.
                                    
The annual inflation rate was 4.2% in September.
                                    
The national statistics agency said energy prices had
accelerated, going from +22.6% to +31.4%.
                                    
"The acceleration of inflation was mainly due to the dynamics of
prices of non-regulated energy products (from +22.5% to +29.4%)
and of regulated energy products (from +25.8% to +59.5%), of
unprocessed food (from +5.5% to +7.5%), of services related to
transport (from +1.6% to +3.1%) and of processed food including
alcohol (from -0.6% to -0.2%)," Istat said.
                                    
The agency said its consumer price index was up 0.9% in
month-on-month terms.

On Monday, South Africa’s ambassador to the US, Roelf Meyer, said the government “is no longer troubled” by its exclusion from the Miami summit.
South Africa had “moved on and was already talking” to next year’s G20 host, the UK, Meyer said, according to the Daily Maverick.

When knowing how to save life is not enough: Doctors recall Gaza's preventable deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:17:40 UTC
19:17:40 KST

Two-year-old Alia was thrown from the second floor of a building by the force of an explosion near her home.
Although conscious, Alia appeared confused as she was rushed to hospital. At a makeshift emergency department, the doctors treating her suspected she had a brain bleed.
Nour Sharaf, an American emergency physician used to working in hospitals where urgent diagnostic scans are readily available, requested an immediate CT scan to assess her injuries and determine whether surgery could save her life.
But in Gaza, even that wasn’t simple.
It took four hours to obtain the scan. By the time the results confirmed the bleeding, the opportunity to save the little girl had passed.
“Even if we were able to get her [to] the operating room on time, they actually didn’t have the resources in the operating room to be able to save her life,” Sharaf recalled, citing a conversation with a paediatric neurosurgeon.
The toddler’s death exposed the grim reality of Gaza’s devastated healthcare system: patients were dying not only from their injuries but also because the means to treat them had disappeared.
Years of Israeli bombardment, repeated attacks on medical facilities and severe restrictions on the entry of essential supplies have left Gaza's healthcare system struggling to function.
Hospitals that once provided specialised care have been damaged or forced to close, leaving overwhelmed medical teams to treat critically injured patients with dwindling resources.
In September 2026, the World Health Organization reported that only 19 of Gaza’s 36 hospitals were functioning even partially, with none fully operational. Essential medicines, diagnostic equipment and fuel remained critically scarce.
The deteriorating health conditions in Gaza come against the backdrop of findings from a United Nations commission of inquiry, which concluded in September 2025 that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
Israel rejected the findings, maintaining that its military operations targeted Hamas following the group’s October 7, 2023, attacks.
Hospitals without the means to heal
Sharaf visited Gaza three times between July 2025 and June 2026, working at Shuhada al Aqsa Hospital, Nasser Hospital, and al Shifa Hospital.
At al-Shifa Hospital, she recalled a makeshift emergency department, converted from outpatient clinics, where as many as 300 casualties could arrive simultaneously.
Patients lay on the floor; some arrived without relatives, while others needed procedures doctors could no longer perform with standard equipment.
“We actually ran out of chest tubes,” she said, describing how medical teams improvised devices to drain blood from patients’ chests.
Even routine cardiac care had become precarious. Sharaf said doctors lacked essential diagnostic tests and stents used to open blocked coronary arteries.
Mohammed Adeel Khaleel, a US-based spine surgeon who visited Gaza three times between April 2024 and August 2025, said the devastation was visible in operating theatres.
He recalled treating a man in his twenties whose spinal cord had been damaged by gunfire.
With no complete set of modern spinal fixation equipment available, Khaleel said staff recovered surgical instruments from another hospital that had ceased operating, piecing together mismatched screws to stabilise the patient’s spine.
The young man was unlikely to walk again, yet Khaleel remembered him smiling and joking with the anaesthesiologist before surgery.
“This is Gaza, everybody has an injury or a disability,” a hospital staff member told him.
Not every story ended in despair, though.
Khaleel also recalled operating on an 18-year-old girl paralysed after an injury. With only CT imaging available, he identified blood compressing her spinal structures and operated.
Before he left Gaza, she could move her toes, and months later, he learned she could walk again.
When treatment becomes impossible
Both physicians described restrictions on bringing medical supplies into Gaza. Khaleel said Israeli authorities confiscated equipment from his medical team and denied them entry during an attempted return mission.
Their accounts echo findings by Physicians for Human Rights, which documented restrictions on essential supplies ranging from anaesthetics and chest tubes to surgical instruments and orthopaedic screws.
In a March 2026 WIRED investigation, Israel’s Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) acknowledged that customs officials confiscated microsurgical instruments carried by another American surgeon because they had not received prior approval.
COGAT rejected allegations that it was deliberately undermining medical services, saying restrictions were necessary for security and to prevent equipment from being diverted for non-humanitarian purposes.
For doctors inside Gaza, the consequences of shortages were immediate.
Khaleel recalled hospitals removing metal pins used to stabilise fractures from deceased patients, sterilising them and reusing them because replacements were unavailable.
Sharaf said many patients who might have survived in American hospitals died in Gaza.
When hunger became another emergency
By Khaleel’s third visit in August 2025, starvation had compounded the injuries arriving at hospitals. He recalled a badly burned child with a partially amputated hand gesturing towards his mouth to indicate hunger.
Other patients arrived with gunshot wounds after attempting to collect food at distribution points operated by the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation.
The UN Human Rights Office documented at least 2,319 people killed while seeking assistance between late May and September 17, 2025, including 1,202 near militarised distribution sites. Most deaths were reportedly caused by live fire.
Khaleel said he treated children and teenagers with gunshot wounds to the chest and other parts of the body. He believed some injuries suggested deliberate targeting.
An October 2025 ceasefire reduced the scale of bombings but did not end the killings. Israeli strikes and gunfire continued to cause casualties, while hospitals struggled with patients suffering from untreated chronic illnesses.
Neither Khaleel nor Sharaf encountered Hamas fighters, weapons or tunnels in the hospitals where they worked.
The lasting memory for Khaleel was not only of destruction, but of Palestinian medical workers who continued treating patients despite the danger.
Among those who stayed with Khaleel was a young Palestinian general surgeon hoping to pursue specialist training. Despite the strain of working in Gaza’s overwhelmed hospitals, they discussed medical exams and qualifications.
Those ambitions have become increasingly difficult to realise amid the destruction of Gaza’s healthcare system.
“These are normal people with hopes and dreams,” Khaleel said.
Sharaf says seeing families who, despite having little food themselves, insisted on feeding visiting medical workers left a lasting impact on her.
Both doctors, returning to their lives in the United States, carry memories of patients they could not save.
“I absolutely would go to Gaza,” she said.
“If it’s easy [to] turn off the channel or scroll past it, just remember that people in Gaza or anywhere in the world where they’re suffering, they don’t have that choice.”

Episode 5: Kleptocracy: Exposing It is Not Enough
Why civil society, financial institutions and governments must connect their evidence and capabilities to dismantle kleptocratic networks.
Kleptocracy is not simply corruption on a grand scale. It is a system in which stolen wealth is used to capture institutions, preserve political power and extend influence across borders. Exposing these networks is essential, but exposure alone rarely brings them down.
In this episode of the Suspicious Transaction Report, Kinga Redłowska is joined by Zoë Reiter, Director of Combating Kleptocracy at the National Endowment for Democracy (NED), and Tom Keatinge, Director of the Centre for Finance & Security at RUSI.
Together, they explore what it takes to detect, deter and dismantle kleptocratic systems, and why the work of investigative journalists and grassroots civil society must be connected to financial institutions, law enforcement, policymakers and international standard-setters.
The conversation also examines cryptocurrency's dual role: providing kleptocrats with alternative ways to move wealth while creating opportunities for tracing illicit flows and supporting civil society operating under authoritarian regimes.
From professional enablers and sanctions to blockchain analytics and the challenges of funding local investigators, the episode makes the case for a coordinated response that turns evidence into meaningful disruption.
Further reading
Podcast Series
- The Suspicious Transaction Report This podcast explores the financial dimensions of today’s leading transnational security challenges. Host Tom Keatinge and the team from the Centre for Finance and Security at RUSI bring you unique insights on the challenges posed by illicit finance and practical analysis of the policy responses. They interview top thinkers and influential voices who unpack the complex world of money laundering, corruption, sanctions evasion and illicit flows, and explain how this shapes the evolving global security landscape, and what democracies and international institutions must do to stay ahead when it comes to the financial dimensions of the global threat outlook. Lithuanian university finds plagiarism in premier’s doctoral thesis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:39:36 UTC
19:39:36 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
A Lithuanian university has found plagiarism and other academic integrity violations in Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius’ doctoral thesis, giving him six months to address the shortcomings, broadcaster LRT reported Friday.
The Ethics Commission of ISM University of Management and Economics found violations involving academic writing, citations and source attribution in the dissertation, which Sinkevicius defended in 2015.
The commission also identified instances of plagiarism and said the thesis did not meet the requirement for independent doctoral research, according to the university's findings.
The university has given Sinkevicius six months to address the violations.
It did not recommend revoking his doctoral degree.
The dissertation examined factors influencing alcohol consumption.
Sinkevicius has previously denied plagiarism, saying he wrote the thesis himself and adhered to academic standards.

Azerbaijan calls for stronger trade, transport ties among Turkic states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-30
10:35:06 UTC
19:35:06 KST

Burc Eruygur
30 October 2026•Update: 30 October 2026
Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov on Friday called for stronger economic and transport links among Turkic states, saying their geographical position and energy resources offered significant opportunities to expand their role in global trade and energy security.
Addressing the 13th summit of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) in the Turkish capital Ankara, Bayramov highlighted the development of the Middle Corridor and expanded transport connections between member countries as ways to boost their collective economic potential.
"Our primary objective is to leverage these opportunities not merely for transit transport, but also to foster mutual trade, industrial cooperation, and investment," he said.
Bayramov said cooperation in energy, digital connectivity and emerging technologies had reached a new stage among OTS member states, with Azerbaijan playing a key role in establishing green energy and digital links between Central Asia and Europe.
He also highlighted the OTS+ format as a means of expanding ties with third countries and international organizations, while urging continued efforts to secure observer status for the OTS at the UN General Assembly.
Recalling that Azerbaijan assumed the organization's chairmanship at its 12th summit in Gabala last year, Bayramov said regional peace and security had been central priorities.
He noted that global developments over the past year had reinforced their importance amid growing tensions in international relations.
"In such an environment, Azerbaijan continues to serve as a zone of stability and security. Our country not only ensures its own security but also plays a stabilizing role in strengthening peace and stability across a broader region," he said.
Armenia urged to take steps toward peace treaty
Bayramov said Azerbaijan's restoration of its territorial integrity and sovereignty had resolved the long-standing conflict in the South Caucasus, with normalization efforts now underway with neighboring Armenia.
"A de facto state of peace exists in the region. Nevertheless, we expect Armenia to take the necessary political and legal steps toward the signing of a peace treaty," he said.
He stressed Baku's commitment to establishing a "long-term, reliable" peace and replacing the "era of conflict" in the South Caucasus with an "era of cooperation."
Bayramov also thanked Türkiye for hosting the summit and congratulated the Turkish people on the country's 103rd Republic Day, celebrated Oct. 29.
He wished Türkiye success as it assumed the OTS chairmanship from Azerbaijan and congratulated Mirvokhid Azimov on his appointment as the organization's new secretary general.

Iran names 16-man squad for 2026 AFC Beach Soccer Asian Cup
TEHRAN – Iran national beach soccer team head coach Ali Naderi has named a 16-man squad for the upcoming 2026 AFC Beach Soccer Asian Cup, scheduled to take place in Thailand from Nov. 18 to 28.
Naderi announced the squad following the conclusion of the final stage of Iran’s Premier Beach Soccer League, selecting 16 players to begin preparations for the continental tournament.
According to the Iranian Football Federation, the national team’s training camp will get underway on Oct. 30 at the National Football Center in Tehran, where the players will begin their preparations ahead of the competition.
Iran have been drawn alongside Afghanistan, Vietnam and Lebanon in the group stage of the tournament.
The Iranian side will be looking to deliver a strong performance in Thailand and maintain their reputation as one of Asia’s leading beach soccer nations.
Iran have enjoyed considerable success in international beach soccer in recent years, establishing themselves as a formidable force on the continental stage.
The upcoming tournament will provide another opportunity for Naderi’s men to demonstrate their quality and compete for Asian honors.
The 16 players called up to the national team are:
Mohammad Dastan, Reza Dayeri, Reza Amiri, Saeed Piramoon, Ali Nazem, Davoud Shokri, Ali Mirshekari, Movahed Mohammadpour, Mohammadali Mokhtari, Mohammadali Nazarzadeh, Mohammad Masoumizadeh, Abolfazl Sharifpour, Aydin Teshnehkam, Sobhan Faleh, Mehdi Shirmohammadi, Mehdi Mirjalili
The coaching staff will assess the players during the training camp as Iran step up preparations for their opening group-stage matches.
With a blend of experienced internationals and talented players, Iran will aim to make a strong start against Afghanistan, Vietnam and Lebanon and advance to the knockout stages of the competition.
